WEDNESDAY, MARCH 14, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to call, in room 1301, New House Office Building, at 10:40 a.m., Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding.

The committee meets this morning in open session to begin hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act for 1962. The witness this morning is the Honorable Fowler Hamilton, Administrator for the Agency for 

International Development. 

Mr. Hamilton, you have a statement, and you may proceed as you wish.

STATEMENT OF HON. FOWLER HAMILTON, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. HAMILTON. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

If I may, I will summarize part of the statement and then read part of the statement.

Chairman MORGAN. We will incorporate your whole statement in the record, including the appendix. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Thank you, sir. I shan't read the appendixes.

First, I should like to express Secretary Rusk's regret that he could not initiate these hearings. As you know, he is in Geneva and couldn't appear.

The statement that I have to make to you, ladies and gentlemen, covers four points:

A brief résumé of the background of our foreign aid program insofar as that background is relevant to a consideration of the authorization being recommended;

A brief description of the present program from the standpoint of the measures that have been taken to carry out the development aspects;

A brief description of the military assistance aspects of the present program; and then 

A statement of the program that is proposed for your consideration for fiscal year 1963.

Addressing myself to the first point-that is to say the background: 

As you ladies and gentlemen know much better than I, since we first started foreign aid programs back with lend-lease in 1940, upon the recommendation of 4 Presidents, 11 Congresses have appropriated very large sums of money for what may be divided into approximately 1

9 different programs, 9 different foreign aid programs. Commencing with lend-lease, there followed the very substantial sums that one can group together under the general phrase "relief and rehabilitation," that were expended for the relief and rehabilitation of the stricken territories of our allies and former foes. 

Then we come to the Marshall plan, which had as its responsibility and objective the reconstitution of the developed countries of Europe. 

Thereafter followed military security, which was a very substantial part of all the funds appropriated, when one takes account of both the military hardware and supplies, and also of the funds that were made available to governments in those areas which we regarded as strategic in our own interest, to enable them to maintain military effort on a scale they could not otherwise afford. 

Then there was the point 4 program, the Public Law 480 program, the development loan program, and now there is the alliance for progress.

One of the things that struck me as a newcomer when I undertook the responsibility for the administration of this agency late in September was the fact that such a small part of the fund had been devoted or appropriated for purposes of development. That is to say, of all the funds that had been appropriated, beginning with the Marshall plan down through the end of the last fiscal year, those that were appropriated expressly for development were $1.2 billion that had been appropriated for technical assistance and the $2 billion that had been appropriated for development loans. 

That sum of $3 billion-plus was considerably less than 10 percentabout 5 percent in fact of the total sums that have been appropriated. 

Of course, it is necessary quickly to add that many of the other funds had a developmental effect. The interesting thing about the new program is the emphasis upon the development aspects of it. 

With that by way of background, I should like, if I may, to turn to page 3 of the statement that has to do with the reorganization of the assistance programs.

Our aid program has achieved the important objective of revitalizing Western Europe and curbing the broad expansion of communism, and significant steps have been taken to improve human resources in less-developed lands. 

But because the program had built up through a series of legislative measures and administrative procedures conceived at different times and for different purposes, it became clear in 1961 that the legislative framework of foreign aid needed substantial revision to deal effectively with the challenges of today. 

One year ago, President Kennedy sent to the Congress proposals to reorganize foreign aid. As enacted last year the principal features of the new program are consolidation of foreign aid in the Agency for International Development, greater emphasis on overall long-term development of recipient countries, and establishment of standards of self-help and comprehensive long-term planning. 

In the few months since the 1961 act became effective, however, there has not been time enough to put these new principles into full effect. 

This is and must be a year of transition. 75

NEW AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

In that regard, I may refresh your recollections that the authorization act was enacted on September 4 and the appropriation act was enacted on September 30. The new Agency itself was established on 

November 4.

When I assumed my duties in October, it was clear that the first task was to organize the new Agency and provide it with the best available top management. Almost all of the top executive team has now been assembled, including two Deputy Administrators and the four Regional Assistant Administrators who have full responsibility and authority for operations within their geographic areas. 

I am appending a list of these principal executives with a brief biographical note covering each. 

The new Agency has assumed responsibility not only for the technical and supporting assistance programs of the former ICA, but also has become one of the largest lending institutions in the world. In addition, we administer aspects of food for peace and coordinate military assistance with economic assistance. 

The personnel immediately available to the new Agency were almost exclusively from the former ICA, which was staffed primarily along functional lines for a wide range of technical assistance programs. 

The new Agency, as presented to the Congress, was to be staffed essentially along geographical lines, requiring substantial reassignment and recruitment of personnel. 

A partial evaluation of Agency personnel had to be made to meet the November deadline set under section 621 (d) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, and about 287 ICA employees were determined not to be necessary for the operations of AID. 

When we faced in October the task of merging into this single Agency the former ICA agency, the Development Loan Bank, and certain additional functions of a banking or quasi-banking character that were put upon us, we found ourselves rather in this position: 

The ICA had 17,000 employees, more or less: 8,500 of those were non-U.S. citizens located abroad and approximately 8,500 are U.S. citizens.

Most of those people, as well as most of the directors and deputy. directors of the 70 missions that the agency had, were people whose background and training had stemmed largely from the point 4 and technical assistance type of activity.

I think it would be a reasonably accurate statement to say that approximately 95 percent of the personnel involved in the 8,500 U.S. citizens were people who had backgrounds in such fields as agriculture, public health, and public administration. 

On top of that organization there was responsibility for the development loan activity, for which $1,112.5 million was appropriated last year and authorization was further given and responsibility imposed, for the programing forward of maximum amounts of a billion and a half for 4 years, for a total of $7.2 billion. 

It was rather as though-and this is a somewhat exaggerated analogy—one had taken a large international organization such as the Red Cross or a merchandising organization and imposed upon it a financial institution larger than any other government financial insti-

tution, and far larger than any private financial institution such as a large bank like the Bank of America or a large insurance company. 

With the inception of the alliance for progress, responsibility for coordination of the expenditure of funds with the Export-Import Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank involves a further quasi-financial kind of operation. So that it has become necessary, not only to carry on technical assistance and related programs on a scale that is larger than the previous year, but also to shape this merged organization in such a way that it could discharge these additional responsibilities and focus them on the development aspects of things. 

That has been one of the principal themes with which all of us have been concerned in the 4 months we have had available to work toward the effectuation of the organization to carry out those responsibilities. 

We are also still in the process of organizing the administrative structure in Washington and in the field. Line operations are being concentrated in the four regional bureaus. 

We have created a new Director of Engineering to keep check on engineering plans and are setting up a new Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise to encourage private enterprise to play a larger development role, as well as to insure adherence to sound standards for development lending. 

Given the magnitude of the task and the time available, the establishment of the new Agency and the recruitment of needed personnel is making good progress. We are bending every effort to complete this formidable task as soon and as effectively as possible. 

PROGRAM IS DIRECTED AT OVERALL COUNTRY DEVELOPMENT 

To the extent that there was an ICA development program, it consisted largely of a wide variety of individually valuable but not necessarily correlated technical assistance projects in such fields as education, public health, public administration, agriculture, industry and transportation, and labor. 

The Development Loan Fund and the Export-Import Bank made loans for worthwhile development projects, but almost exclusively on a project-by-project basis. 

With all the U.S. development assistance authority, except Export- 

Import Bank, vested in AID, it is now possible to assess the overall development needs of a country on a priority basis and to extend grants, loans, or technical assistance to those projects that will best further the overall development of the recipient country. 

This new program approach is well launched. By October, an extensive program guide had been prepared and circulated among field missions for use in giving direction to fiscal year 1963 program proposals and to the extent practicable in shifting the fiscal year 1962 country programs to the coordinated development objectives. 

EMPHASIS UPON SELF-HELP 

Perhaps the most important new emphasis of the AID program derives from our recognition that the country's own efforts will be the main determinant of successful growth and development and our decision that U.S. aid will be used to encourage self-help efforts.

Prudent fiscal management, progressive tax and land laws, honesty and efficiency in Government, and a large measure of social justice can only be attained by the country's own efforts. As Secretary Rusk observed to you last year, "Self-help must be our principal 'string'-and an insistent one. 99 

There has been a growing awareness by recipient countries of the importance of effective self-help action. But sweeping self-help efforts sometimes simply cannot be achieved in the short run or require skilled and experienced administrators and technicians not available without additional training.

By comparison, several decades elapsed in the United States between proposal and enactment of the progressive income tax. In our attempts to encourage self-help, we must be insistent but also flexible and realistic.

LONG-TERM PLANNING AND COMMITMENTS 

During this transitional year, countries receiving our assistance are being encouraged to improve their planning capabilities. Countries with meager per capita physical resources must budget their limited capital and personnel resources even more carefully than do highly developed countries if they are to achieve any significant economic growth.

The purpose of planning is to provide a framework for rational government action and private initiative. It corresponds to sound budgeting procedures followed by government and successful private enterprises in advanced countries. 

Here, again, there has been progress made during the past year. In 

Latin America, nearly all countries have intensified their efforts to improve their planning processes.

The African countries are latecomers to planning, but several have made good progress. Nigeria has a promising 6-year plan which avoids wasteful prestige projects and includes a major role for private investment.

Pakistan's third 5-year plan, developed with the assistance of a U.S. private foundation, was reviewed by the IBRD and an international consortium of assisting countries and, after revision, provides the basis for substantial long-range commitments from the United States and other consortium members.

Despite the increase in planning activity, less-developed countries still face serious obstacles to adequate planning. In most cases completed planning is some years away because planning organizations and techniques must be perfected and information assembled. 

If a country's leaders apppreciate and apply a rational approach to resource allocation and are actively working toward a national plan, this justifies our assisting a program conditioned on progressive implementation of planning standards.

A principal stimulus to better long-term planning by the developing countries is the capacity of the Agency to enter into long-term commitments with countries having sound and feasible plans. 

Long-range commitments under new AID legislation have been made thus far to Pakistan and Tanganyika.

Programs now being developed in several other Asian and African nations may well warrant additional commitments by the end of fiscal year 1963. However, on the basis of the criteria proposed to and approved by Congress last year, use of this technique will continue to be limited in the immediate future. 

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

President Kennedy proposed the alliance for progress last March as a means of mounting a vast cooperative effort to satisfy the basic needs of the people of Latin America for work, land, health, schools, and homes. Two months later, Congress appropriated $500 million to help implement the principles of the Act of Bogotá. 

The alliance for progress was enunciated formally last August when the United States joined with the other free Republics of Latin America "in a common effort to bring their people accelerated, economic progress and broader social justice within the framework of personal dignity and political liberty." 

The alliance is a long-term program contemplating a decade of development. It has only been in effect half a year. In this short period of time, much has been accomplished. 

A number of Latin American nations have moved ahead on tax reform, land reform, labor legislation, economic stabilization, and national planning. Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Panama, and Venezuela have completed country development plans or major sections of such plans.

The Organization of American States, the Economic Commission for Latin America, and the Inter-American Development Bank are providing technical assistance in development planning to a number of countries which have requested it. 

In the social development field, the IADB has approved loans for projects in rural living and land use, public housing, and water supply and sewage.

During the first year of the alliance members have received more than $1 billion of U.S. assistance from the Export-Import Bank, food for peace, AID loans and grants, and the social progress trust fund administered by the Inter-American Development Bank. Much of this aid has, of necessity, been used to meet immediate short-term needs.

Several Latin American countries have required prompt financial support to make development possible or to complete projects already underway. The major portion of this assistance, however, has been directed toward the long-term development goals set forth in the Charter of Punta del Este. 

As we approach the second year of the alliance, we recognize that the road ahead is still difficult. We must expect some disappointments and frustrations. Any enterprise so large necessarily must start slowly and generate momentum as it moves forward. 

We, therefore, consider critically important the long-term authorization of funds for support of the alliance and the congressional endorsement of the purposes of the alliance in title VI proposed in the new act, which demonstrate to our Latin American neighbors the importance which we attach to the alliance and its objectives and

assure them that our support is not limited to short-run objectives but can be relied upon over the long pull. 

Such reassurance will do much to bolster progressive forces in Latin America and to provide a sounder basis for the kind of longrange planning so urgently required if the objectives of the alliance are to be realized.

MULTILATERAL COOPERATION 

The past year has seen notable progress in efforts to coordinate and increase the flow of assistance from our allies to the less developed countries.

Economic aid to the underdeveloped areas from public free world sources other than the United States is now in the neighborhood of $2.3 billion per year, as compared with such assistance from the 

United States of about $3 billion. These other free world countries are actually contributing a larger proportion of their gross national products to foreign assistance than is the United States. Several nations have substantially liberalized their loan terms in the past. 

Perhaps yet more significant, Germany, France, Belgium, and Canada have established new aid agencies and the United Kingdom and Japan have also made organizational changes evidencing their assumption of responsibility in this area. 

To encourage closer cooperation and coordination of effort among the nations supplying capital and technical assistance to the developing areas, several types of multilateral organizations and groups have been formed.

The World Bank has taken the lead in organizing consortia to support the development plans of countries such as India and Pakistan, The Development Assistance Committee of OECD is undertaking a similar coordinating role with regard to technical and capital assistance to countries where its members have substantial interests. 

The International Development Organizations Staff of the AID 

has just been organized to give new force and leadership to our efforts to coordinate our assistance activities with those of all other free world countries.

MILITARY AND SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

Economic and social progress requires a reasonable degree of internal security and the capacity to meet direct threats of external aggression.

This requirement is especially important in those countries which face the Sino-Soviet bloc. Korea, China, Vietnam, Laos, Pakistan, Iran, Turkey, and Greece all must maintain larger military forces than they can afford to support out of their own resources. Without our military aid, these nations could not train and equip the troops which are literally manning the frontline against Communist aggression.

The military assistance program will be discussed in detail later by 

Secretary McNamara, General Lemnitzer, and other witnesses from the Department of Defense. 

I wish to stress at this time, however, the importance of this aspect of the foreign assistance program, which not only gives our allies some defense capacity against Communist invasion but also provides forces to counter Communist agitators, infiltrators, and guerrillas who sow discord and death within the countries which they seek to dominate.

со We must adhere firmly to a policy of collective security and bolster the military capabilities of our partners in this struggle. But military assistance in the form of military weapons and supplies will not alone suffice.

These nations need financial supporting assistance. Without it, they would be faced with internal economic and political disintegration which would seriously weaken and might defeat their ability and will to withstand external aggression. In these cases, supporting assistance is just as vital to security and freedom as is military assistance. 

Defense of the free world, however, does not end at the periphery of the Sino-Soviet bloc. The attempts of the Communists to create or exploit economic and political instability are worldwide. Our program to thwart them must be as comprehensive as their attempts at subversion. 

Because of the major purpose of the foreign assistance program is to promote economic and social development, we are making concerted efforts to reduce the number of countries receiving supporting assistance and the amounts provided to these countries. 

During the past year, it has been decided that several countries will not in the future require this form of assistance. But the need for supporting aid cannot be entirely eliminated. The kinds of situations with which it deals-military budget support, access to base rights, prevention of short-run political and economic crises, alternative to sole reliance on Soviet bloc aid with the jeopardy to freedom that entails-are, unfortunately, likely to continue to occur in the future. 

REQUIREMENTS FOR FISCAL YEAR 1963 

For fiscal year 1963, the President has requested Congress to appropriate a total of $4.878 billion in new funds, of which $3.378 billion would be for economic purposes and $1.5 billion for military assistance. 

Within this worldwide total, we are requesting a special appropriation for the alliance for progress of $600 million in loan and grant funds for next year, as part of a $3 billion long-term authorization through fiscal year 1966.

The remaining $2.778 billion of economic assistance funds consists of $1.250 billion for development loans, $335 million for development grants, $481.5 million for supporting assistance, $148.9 million for contributions to international organizations, a $400 million contingency fund, $5 million for investment surveys, $10 million to expand our reserves for investment guarantees, and the balance for administration.

In addition, we seek enlargement of our authority to guarantee private investment in less developed areas. 

I am submitting an appendix to this statement in which the proposed expenditures in each category of assistance for next year are set forth in detail.

In conclusion, we who are responsible for the administration of this Agency are keenly aware of three duties: to administer the Agency honestly and efficiently, to adhere to the program criteria laid down by Congress, and to report to Congress the measures we have taken under the authority established by it. (The prepared statement of Mr. Hamilton and appendixes are as follows:)

STATEMENT OF HON. FOWLER HAMILTON, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, Secretary Rusk has asked me to convey to the committee his regret that the disarmament negotiations in Geneva have made it impossible for him to make this opening statement as he had planned. During the past 15 years this committee has played a vital and constructive role in shaping the foreign assistance program to deal with the differing international economic, political, and military problems successively and so far successfully faced by our country during that period. 

In my remarks this morning, I will first comment on the background of foreign aid as it relates to this year's program. Secondly, I will report on this year's reorganization of the Agency and of our development program to carry out the mandate of last year's legislation including the alliance for progress and on our efforts to increase and coordinate contributions from other developed nations. 

Thirdly, I will report on this year's military and supporting assistance. Finally 

I will outline our requirements for the fiscal year 1963 program. 

BACKGROUND 

Despite the miracles of science and technology which are daily opening new vistas in the United States and other developed nations of the world, the peoples in less developed areas are still living in conditions which have changed very little since Galileo launched the experiments from which much of modern science developed. Disease, poverty, and ignorance shackle these hundreds of millions of people. Two out of three are unable to read and write. About 12 billion people have an average annual income of less than $100. 

Whatever the past or present cause for the conditions that prevail in these countries, there is no doubt about the desire of the people for improvement. 

The poor and the uneducated have been filled with hope that these conditions can be changed, and this surge of hope is rapidly leading them to action. With proper leadership within these countries and proper aid from without, this surge of hope can power a most constructive era of development. 

But the Communists seek to exploit the impatience of these people and sow the seeds of anarchy and violence. Our foreign aid program has been and remains our most effective resource in discouraging and defeating communism by helping others to move toward fulfillment of their development aspirations and at the same time achieve and extend their own freedom. 

The basic objective of our foreign assistance program has always been to advance the national interest by promoting the development of a community of free nations in which economic growth and political democracy can flourish, but the specific focus and content of the program has changed from time to time as the nature of the challenge facing us has changed. 

The Marshall plan provided the margin for quick recovery by our European allies whose economies and institutions were highly developed but whose stability and capacity for growth were imperiled. With point 4 in 1950 we began to extend modest technical assistance to less developed countries; and shortly thereafter we began to extend military assistance and defense support to maintain the independence of nations directly threatened by Communist aggression or subversion. Since the mid-fifties, though the bulk of our assistance has been military, we have increased economic assistance to less developed areas largely through development loans with easy terms of repayment. During this period, also, more of our surplus food and fibers were used for humanitarian and development purposes. 

REORGANIZATION OF U.S. ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS 

Our aid program has achieved the important objective of revitalizing Western Europe and curbing the broad expansion of communism, and significant steps have been taken to improve human resources in less developed lands. But because the program had built up through a series of legislative measures and administrative procedures conceived at different times and for different purposes, it became clear in 1961 that the legislative framework of foreign aid needed substantial revision to deal effectively with the challenges of today. 

One year ago, President Kennedy sent to the Congress proposals to reorganize foreign aid. As enacted last year the principal features of the new program are consolidation of foreign aid in the Agency for International Development,

greater; emphasis on overall long-term development of recipient countries, and establishment of standards of self-help and comprehensive long-term planning. 

In the few months since the 1961 act became effective, however, there has not been time enough to put these new principles into full effect. This is and must be a year of transition.

REQUIREMENTS FOR FISCAL YEAR 1963 

For fiscal year 1963, the President has requested Congress to appropriate a total of $4,878 million in new funds, of which $3,378 million would be for economic purposes and $1,500 million for military assistance. Within this worldwide total, we are requesting a special appropriation for the alliance for progress of $600 million in loan and grant funds for next year, as part of a $3 billion long-term authorization through fiscal year 1966. 

The remaining $2,778 million of economic assistance funds consists of $1,250 million for development loans, $335 million for development grants, $481.5 million for supporting assistance, $148.9 million for contributions to multilateral agencies, a $400 million contingency fund, $100 million to expand our reserves for investment guarantees, $5 million for investment surveys and the balance for administration. In addition we seek enlargement of our authority to guarantee private investment in less developed areas. 

I am submitting an appendix to this statement in which the proposed expenditures in each category of assistance for next year are set forth in more detail. 

CONCLUSION 

In conclusion, we who are responsible for the administration of this Agency are keenly aware of three duties: to administer the Agency honestly and efficiently to adhere to the program criteria laid down by Congress, and to report to Congress the measures we have taken under the authority established by it.

APPENDIX 2 FISCAL YEAR 1963 AID REQUIREMENTS 

Development lending.-Dollar repayable development loans now constitute the major instrument of U.S. economic assistance. In fiscal year 1963, about 

52 percent of the new funds requested will be utilized for this purpose. Congress has already authorized the appropriation for fiscal year 1963 alone of $1,500 million for development loans. We are requesting that $1,250 million (not including alliance for progress funds) be appropriated in fiscal year 1963 under this authorization. These loan funds will be concentrated in countries capable of utilizing development loans most effectively-countries which either have sound and well administered long-term development programs or have the capability to devise sound projects which can be individually financed. 

Experience has indicated that there are certain sequences of need through which countries are likely to go as they progress from the earlier to the later stages of development. When the human and institutional base of the society has developed to the point where the planning and management of available resources is relatively efficient, lack of investment capital becomes a critical bottleneck to further growth. Since the rate of domestic capital formation is usually too low to support required rates of investment, this capital must come from external sources. 

Many of the developing nations have reached this stage of growth. 

Some of these, such as India and Pakistan, require massive amounts of external assistance if their national product is to rise faster than the rate of population growth. In other countries, the need is considerably smaller in magnitude but nevertheless essential to their growth because of their inability to finance vital imports from available foreign exchange resources. 

There is a detailed discussion of development loans in the unclassified presentation book, and we have detailed estimates and justification in the classified regional and country statements. Although this committee is not required to act on the appropriation requested this year, I would emphasize that the amount requested for this purpose is vitally needed and will be utilized soundly in accordance with the criteria which Congress has provided. 

Development grants.-We are requesting a total of $435 million for development grant activities in fiscal year 1963, of which $100 million is included in the separate request for Latin America. Although the funds requested for development grants represent less than 10 percent of the total proposed in this legislation, they are vitally important. Material resources and capital, necessary as they are, cannot be utilized effectively unless there are adequate numbers of people with skills and capabilities to plan, allocate, and manage these resources. 

Yet, most of the less developed nations-especially those at the lower end of the scale of development—are seriously deficient in this respect. Our development grant programs can provide the margin necessary to overcome these deficiencies in time to permit orderly development. 

During the past year, we have made an intensive review of development grant programs, asking each U.S. AID mission to evaluate each project in terms of its priority in the country's development plan or program, the degree to which it accelerates the development process of the country as a whole, and its effect on encouragement of self-help. 

As a result of this review, the fiscal year 1963 development grant program is much more highly concentrated than it has been in the past. Most U.S. AID missions identified education and training, public administration and agriculture as among the top priority goals. It is expected that with greater emphasis on projects in these sectors, our grant program will have greater long-term impact on social and economic development. 

Supporting assistance. The need for assistance outside development cannot be ignored. Supporting assistance is designed to meet such predictable requirements in selected countries. In my statement I described the kinds of situations which require our supporting assistance. In fiscal year 1963, we are requesting $481.5 million in new funds for activities of this kind. Most of these funds

are provided to three Far Eastern countries on the periphery of the Sino-Soviet bloc which are subjected to direct and massive Communist pressures. 

It is significant to note that we propose granting supporting assistance to 18 fewer countries than those receiving this form of assistance in fiscal year 1962. 

This reduction reflects our concerted efforts during the past year to replace supporting assistance, whenever appropriate, with development loans. Last year we made a similar reduction in the number of countries for which supporting assistance was programed. Unexpected natural disasters, economic crises and accelerated insurgent activity made it appropriate to extend supporting assistance to some but not by any means all of the countries dropped. Last year we predicted that supporting assistance would be programed for 15 countries and 2 regions in fiscal year 1963. Actually we now plan such assistance for this number of countries but for only one regional organization. 

Military assistance.-The request for military assistance funds for fiscal year 

1963 is $1,500 million-$385 million less than that requested last year. The largest portion of these funds is required to support the valiant efforts of our allies in southeast Asia and the Far East to maintain their independence in the face of direct and indirect aggression by Communist China and other forces of international communism. We intend also to continue our support of the armed forces of the CENTO and NATO countries in the Middle East who are sharing the burden of common defense against the pressures of the Soviet bloc in that area.

In addition to assisting these nations on the periphery of the Sino-Soviet bloc, the efforts of the Communist bloc to subvert the developing nations of Africa and Latin America require that they strengthen their internal security forces. 

Approximately 7 percent of the military assistance funds requested are required for these areas. 

Contingency fund.-The need for an unprogramed reserve for contingencies is crucial in a large and complex operation such as AID. It is impossible to predict accurately 1 year in advance where critical situations that threaten our national interest will arise. Yet, when these crises do arise, they must be met with speed and effectiveness. Threatened breakdown of law and order in a newly independent nation of Africa, an economic crisis in the Middle East which threatens to overturn a pro-Western government, the stepping up of Communist guerrilla actions in the forests of southeast Asia-these are the kinds of unanticipated events for which the contingency fund is required. 

Experience has shown that the most likely use of these funds is to provide additional aid to countries receiving supporting assistance. The programed level of supporting assistance has been held to an absolute minimum, because we want to persuade the countries receiving such assistance that they must utilize their own resources most effectively and qualify themselves as soon as possible for development loans. As a result, these countries have been left with little margin to meet unexpected conditions which might arise during the fiscal year, whether of a natural, political, or economic character. If, for example, military budgets have to be expanded to meet threats of internal subversion or external aggression, or exports fall because of crop failures and a foreign exchange crisis results, it would probably be in our interest to increase our support beyond the amount programed. 

The contingency fund constitutes a reserve against the unexpected. In fiscal year 1963 we are requesting that the Congress make available for this purpose $400 million, small in proportion to our overall budget and certainly a conservative amount in view of the complexity and importance of the problems we face. 

Contributions to international organizations. In addition to providing economic and military assistance to the developing countries on a bilateral basis, it is in our long-range interest to strengthen and support those multilateral institutions which participate with us in helping to stabilize and expand the economic strenth of the free world. As in the past years we are requesting funds under the proposed act to support such U.N. organizations as the United Nations Special 

Fund, the expanded technical assistance program, UNICEF, World Health Organization, the U.N. Congo economic program, and the U.N. Relief and Works 

Administration. We have included in this category also the U.S. contribution to the Indus Basin Trust Fund administered by the World Bank. The total amount for these purposes in fiscal year 1963 is $148.9 million. 

Investment guarantees and surveys.—One of the most important objectives of the foreign aid program is encouragement of private investment in less developed areas. We believe that economies will develop most soundly if private investment controls much of the means of production. Furthermore, public funds

cannot possibly finance more than a fraction of the capital investment essential to the economic growth that must take place in these areas. But an investor in a less developed country faces special risks against which conventional insurance is unavailable. Our investment guarantee program bridges this insurance gap and thus substantially stimulates the necessary flow of private capital. 

Response of American business to our investment guarantee program has been such that we will probably exceed authorization limits next year unless they are expanded. We therefore request authority for an additional $300 million of special risk guarantees and $90 million of all risk guarantees and appropriation authorization for an additional $100 million for reserve purposes. We also request authority for an additional $50 million of guarantees for investment in the important pilot housing project program in Latin America. 

We further request $5 million to finance surveys for investment opportunities in less developed lands which are frequently necessary preliminaries to investment.

Mr. HAMILTON. I would say, sir, that these programs, as I understand the facts, have evolved out of the past. There have been shifts in emphasis to meet shifting conditions in the world and shifting moves that the Communists have made. Let me say it this way: 

In the current fiscal year the program that was enacted by the Congress carried out and increased the emphasis upon various developments that had been underway, one, a shift in emphasis from military assistance to development assistance, another, a shift from grants to loans. At the present time, the program contemplates making more of these loans than grants.

This year no changes of as extensive a character as proposed last year are suggested.

LTON 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right, sir.

Mr. BURLESON. Do you think, Mr. Hamilton, you will be able to change methods and operations to an extent which you feel will produce more satisfactory results than experienced in the past? Do you think we are going to demand a greater quid pro quo in some of these efforts we are making, which I don't think we have done in the past? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Maybe I can respond if I may, Mr. Burleson, in this way: We are engaged in an exercise in persuasion. We are trying to persuade people in many countries to make substantial changes in the way they have been doing things. 

We have two arguments, really. One is an argument of self-interest, which means we are willing to cooperate with them if they make the changes.

The other is based on humanitarian considerations and idealism. 

These are the two kinds of arguments that you have available in any kind of exercise.

It seems perfectly clear that we must be reasonably resolute in saying, in cases where we are negotiating with people: We are willing to work with you, we are working in our interest, we think it is in yours, if it isn't in both of our interests we can't work together. 

No partnership can exist unless it is of advantage to each partner. 

Unless we are resolute in insisting on what we think is in their interest and our interest, I suppose the forces of inertia would keep people from making changes.

In response to the question of Chairman Morgan, I said we had only obligated $111.7 million of the total of $1.112 billion. This is not because we are endeavoring to make people do what we want, but because we want to work together with them in a program that we think is jointly constructive. 

And we are trying to say, I hope and believe with considerable success, that we are trustees of this money, we are administrators, we can't make it available except on the terms of the indenture and as we achieve some results. 

Mr. BURLESON. It is a matter of judgment as to the degree of persuasion which we practice. At one end would be a blackjack and a gun, and at the other would be turning the cheek, which we have been doing all these years with less success than I think we have been entitled to have with all the money we have spent. 

I hope that you, Mr. Hamilton, and your people, can, in subsequent discussions, tell us (1) the willingness of your administration to be more realistic, and (2) how and by what methods you expect to accomplish more than has been accomplished in the past. 

Mr. HAMILTON. We certainly intend to do that, sir.

Mr. MERROW. To return to a question that has already been touched upon this morning, on page 7 of your prepared statement, you stated that- prudent fiscal management, progressive tax and land laws, honesty and efficiency in government and a large measure of social justice can only be attained by the country's own efforts.

Then again on page 10, it is stated that- A number of Latin American nations have moved ahead on tax reform, land reform, labor legislation, economic stabilization, and national planning. 

And in reference to the money that is unobligated at the present time you state, in words to this effect, that it would not be obligated unless the country accepts the conditions which you are pressing them to accept. 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right.

Mr. MERROW. Specifically, in working out programs with an individual country, is a study being made of what the agency feels ought to be done in that particular country, and then after you have decided on what ought to be done in the country, is it written into any kind of a contract before the aid is extended? 

In other words, I would like to get a little more of the actual specifics of the situation as to how you are pressing these reforms in connection with the money that is being loaned. 

Mr. HAMILTON. May I do that by an anonymous illustration which 

I will be glad to identify in the executive session, Mr. Merrow? 

Before we sit down with country A to negotiate, we have analyzed the country's situation. Let's assume they have a bad balance-of-pay-

ments situation, that their foreign reserves are contracting, that they have an ambitious development program, which calls for, let's say, just to pick a figure for illustrative purposes, a $5 billion investment. 

Let's assume further that the country is in Latin America where 80 percent of the money is to be generated locally. 

We review the program before we start negotiating over assistance to see whether or not it looks as if in their present situation they are going to be able to generate 80 percent of the money. 

We give them the benefit of our views and they give us the benefit of their views. Then we endeavor to work out, before the obligation is made, a program that seems to us and seems to them to be designed to carry out their $5 billion program over a period of some years ahead-in which they will be generating 80 percent of the funds, we will be putting in 10 percent and we will help them find the other 

10 percent.

We embody that in an informal document, which is not an agreement but which will, for example, indicate that our money will go in by a certain date if certain measures have been taken. Not all of our money will go in at once, but a part of it. 

Further amounts of our money will go in as they demonstrate their capacity over the future period to generate their share of the funds and as they put into effect the measures that we have agreed upon as necessary to produce that consequence. 

But no written, nor formal agreement and no legal obligation on either side is made until those terms are spelled out. 

The first arrangement is simply an expression of conditional intent to go forward with them if they will carry out what they say they will do. 

That is a reason why we have only $111.7 million obligated out of $1,112.5 million.

Mr. MERROW. What is your position on the desire of the countries to be helped to cooperate along the lines you have outlined? 

Mr. HAMILTON. I speak with diffidence, of course, in view of my brief experience, on the basis of what I am told by people who have had more experience, plus some of my own. 

A country is not one individual, of course, or one single entity. I think one finds different groups in a country, some of which are not at all interested in moving forward because they are perfectly satisfied with where they are personally, so to speak. There are other groups in a country that are interested in moving forward. 

Then we always have our Communist friends who want to mess everything up.

The Of course, what we are endeavoring to do is to work with and strengthen the position of those who want to work with us. number and influence of those people, of course, varies from country to country.

Note on data. Data are taken from the OECD document "The Flow of Financial Resources to Countries in Course of Economic Development in 1960." 

Data are all on a gross disbursements basis and do not reflect loan repayments. 

Column 1 includes bilateral grants and grants and capital subscriptions to international organizations. Note on loan terms. According to the latest informal reports from the governments concerned, repayment periods and interest rates are currently as follows: Canada instituted in 1961 a new program of loans for financing exports, with repayment periods of 10 to 15 years and interest 1 percent above market rates. French loans for commercial-type projects are at 5 to 15 years and 5½ percent interest and for public infrastructure projects are at 12 to 20 years and 2 to 3 percent interest. In exceptional cases longer repayment periods are some-

times allowed. In the German program, commercial-type project loans are for 

10 to 15 years at 54 to 54 percent interest and infrastructure projects are at 

12 to 20 years and 22 to 42 percent interest. Grace periods run 3 to years.

Under Italy's new Martinelli law enacted in 1961, the Government can guarantee private financial credits of up to 10 years repayment, and provision is made for approving longer periods as exceptions. Interest rates under a proposed interest subsidy program would be below market rates. Japan's Export- 

Import Bank normally lends at 5 to 7 years and 4 percent interest. Its loans to India and Pakistan as part of the consortia were for 15 years at 6 percent. 

In 1961 Japan established a new Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund which normally can lend at terms of up to 20 years and 32 percent with a grace period of 5 years.

There is no legislative limitation on providing even more liberal terms. The Netherlands has made loans up to 12 years and usually 3 percent interest. Portugal has made loans to her oversea areas at 15 to 24 years and 

3 to 42 percent interest, with grace periods of 2 to 7 years. British loans range up to 30 years at 5% to 6% percent interest, with grace periods running up to 7 years. U.S. development loans under AID run normally up to 40 years repayment, with a credit fee as low as 4 percent, and with grace periods up to 10 years. U.S. loans under the Export-Import Bank run from 7 to 20 years repayment, 5 to 7 percent interest, and 1 to 3 years' grace.

Mr. COFFIN. We will get into this, I hope, at one complete session on what other nations are doing. I would say in general that the terms of these other credits are from 10 years to, in some instances, 20 years. The interest rate ranges from 3 to 5 percent and in some cases 6 percent.

When I was in Europe in January they were debating whether to expand their authority to make local currency repayable loans.

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. (The list of self-help measures taken in Latin America is as follows:) 

SELF-HELP IN LATIN AMERICA 

The following list cites examples of self-help already to be observed in Latin 

America: 

AGRARIAN REFORM 

Brazil. An agrarian reform law was passed in the State of Sao Paulo in 

December 1960. It includes a graduated land tax and provisions that will help small farmers acquire both land and tools. 

Colombia.-Agrarian reform legislation, enacted by Congress in November 

1961, provides for colonization of public domain, resettlement or parcelization of purchased land, and consolidation of small plot farmers. Purchase and appropriation in the public interest is authorized. The Agrarian Reform Institute established under the law can carry out extension and development work of almost any description. 

El Salvador.-In a series of decree laws enacted in 1961 the Government established à "law for the protection of farm laborers" regulating working conditions for both permanent and migratory agricultural workers. Additional laws established a minimum diet and a mandatory weekly day of rest with pay for rural laborers. (These laws were strongly opposed by agricultural producers' associations and as a result the Directorate made temporary modifications in them. However, the basic content and purpose of the laws remained the same.)

Venezuela.-The March 1960 agrarian reform law has resulted in the distribution of about 1,600,000 hectares to approximately 44,000 families. Most of this has been taking place since the Bogotá Conference. During 1961, the 

Government provided $18.6 million in credits to settlers under the reform law and to other small farmers. Distribution and settlement of large haciendas became more important during 1961 as the supply of Government-owned land dwindled. 

TAX REFORM 

Bolivia.-In June 1961 Bolivia enacted a revised customs code. An official first draft of a tax code was completed July 1, 1961. Better tax enforcement generally, under the guidance of five U.S.-trained men, has resulted in revenues in 1961 being 30 percent above their level in 1960. 

El Salvador.-A highly significant step was taken in 1961 when the income tax law was amended to provide increased exemptions for children and increased tax rates in the higher personal brackets and for corporations. The personal bracket rate at $75,000 is now 76.5 percent. 

Panama.-In December 1960 the National Assembly increased income tax rates by 20 percent. The revision was designed to raise an additional $2 mil-

lion. Other forms of taxes, including the tax on urban real estate and on agricultural land, have also been strengthened. Additional changes were made in 

December 1961, including the institution of a pay-as-you-go system. 

Uruguay.-Uruguay enacted in November 1960 a tax law that included the first income tax in the country. The law also contained provisions designed to benefit productive use of land and penalize nonproductive use. Other modifications were made in the tax laws for the purpose of simplification and better administration.

Venezuela.-Two major changes were made in 1961 in what already constituted an updated tax system. One provided for withholding on interest and royalties paid to nonresidents. The other gave power to the President to raise income tax rates, a power which he has exercised. 

EDUCATION Colombia.—In December 1960 the Ministry of Education announced a 4-year plan to provide a minimum of 5 years of schooling to every child. The plan envisages the building of 22,000 schoolrooms and the training of 16,000 teachers in this 4-year period. (AID is assisting in this program with a grant of $3,770,000 out of the Public Law 86-735 funds for social development.) 

Costa Rica. The GOCR has prepared a 10-year plan for the overall improvement of its education system. It includes a high degree of budgetary support for school construction, vocational education, and university expansion. (AID is assisting at the elementary school and teacher training levels with a grant of $550,000 of social development funds.) 

Guatemala.-A self-help school construction program, begun in 1960, calls for construction of 2,200 classrooms. This has been done thus far under a tripartite arrangement with contributions from the local communities, the national government, and the United States. The program is running ahead of schedule with more than 100 new schools having been opened by July 1961. (The United States contributed $2.4 million of a total of $5.7 million for the initial stage of the program. U.S. grants for this project are not being continued and apparently the 

Guatemalan Government will seek loans from the United States to help continue the program.)

PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION 

Argentina.-The Government is taking steps to improve public administration, including the selling of a number of Government facilities to private enterprise and is attempting to eliminate 70,000 employees from the National railroad; a reduction of 20,000 has been made to date. 

Guatemala.-A public administration development center, started in January 

1960, offers many courses, has a library and a workshop program; 2,000 have already participated in this program. Decrees, dated August 1960 and July 1961, were issued toward the implementation of other administrative reforms. A civil service (merit) law is under consideration by Congress and expected to pass this year. The Institute of Administrative Sciences giving 2-year courses will start in November 1962.

Paraguay. In 1961 the Government instituted administrative reforms in the customs service, designed to control appraisers, warehouses, and underevaluation. In November collections were up 25 percent apparently as a result of this program.

NATIONAL PLANNING 

Six countries have established national planning boards since September 1960. 

They are Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Panama, Peru, and Uruguay. One nation,

Ecuador, has given additional status and authority to its already existing planning board. Four countries-Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, and Panama-have completed long-range plans or important sections thereof. Bolivia and Colombia have submitted their plans to the OAS Panel of Experts for review, as provided at the August 1961 conference at Punta del Este. Chile has submitted its plan to the IBRD for review. Haiti has requested the OAS, ECLA, and the 

IDB for assistance, in improving its national planning and a 12-man mission has arrived in Haiti in response to this request.

REMOVAL OF PERSONNEL 

In accordance with the request, a statement follows concerning those removed from service pursuant to section 621(d) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

A total of 345 ICA employees were not considered necessary for transfer to the Agency for International Development. Of these individuals, 233 accepted an opportunity to seek consideration for reemployment. Of these review cases, 71 were adjudicated in favor of the employee. As of March 14, 1961, a total of 274 employees had been separated, retired, placed in other agencies (some by virtue of reemployment rights), or were in process of clearance for separation, including continuing outplacement assistance. 

Mrs. CHURCH. This refers to the subject of poor administration. 

Last year when your predecessor was here, we asked him if he could eliminate some of the deadwood under the new legislation. 

His answer was that he could at least move some of it. That was not too hopeful an answer.

I am now wondering about the 287 ICA employees referred to as "dispensable." Were they eliminated, or were they moved? And this leads to the question I am going to ask:

Do you think that you yourself have sufficient control of the program and of your own work, to permit you to stay on top of it? May I include in that a question as to the making of policy: How far does your authority extend?

Mr. HAMILTON. Let me answer those questions, if I may, in reverse order, beginning at the top. 

As regards the making of policy, my answer is, "Yes" for the reason that I report to the Secretary of State and to the President. I do not report to any other official in the Department of State. It has been clearly established, beginning about a month after I took office, that as to AID matters I have the primary responsibility for advising the 

Secretary of State.

If there are political considerations in respect to AID questions, as there almost always are, it is the duty of the AID official with whom the question starts to get in touch with the appropriate political officer. In the case where it starts on the political side, it is the duty of the political officer to get in touch with his opposite number in AID. 

The matter proceeds up to the Assistant Secretary of State on the one hand, who is kept informed of it, but it flows for action through the Agency for International Development and ultimately comes to one of the regional assistant administrators. 

There may be a difference of view-and there have been honest differences of view-between the Assistant Secretary of State and the Assistant Administrator. The usual case is that the Assistant Secretary of State feels quite generally that sufficient consideration is not being given to short-term political considerations, whereas the AID Administrator generally feels those should be subordinated to longer term development considerations. If there is a difference of view, it comes to me. I decide what I think about it, and then make a recommendation to the Secretary of State.

Then there is no litigation; that is to say, I then do not sit down with him and discuss the matter with any of those on the political side.

If he wants to, of course, he can get advice from anyone. 

I may say, for example, in the case of the proposed question, "This is a close question. The Assistant Secretary of State feels very strongly this should be modified, and I think you might want to get his opinion."

So far, I can say from my own standpoint and that of the discharge of my responsibilities under the statute and its criteria: this situation has worked well. 

Mrs. CHURCH. It may be a trifle unfair, and I do not mean to be unfair, to ask you to answer the next question with only 30 seconds remaining for your answer.

The second question is, what is that effect upon the gold position of the United States- Mr. ADAIR. I said "balance of payments," the gold position, yes. 

Mr. HAMILTON. It is a complicated and difficult question to answer. 

I will do the best I can, according to my understanding of it. 

The way AID now operates, if goods are not bought in the United States, they may be bought anyplace else in the world except in 19 countries if they are under limited procurement regulations. Those 

19 countries are the highly industrialized ones. 

At the present time, through this fiscal year, of the 100 percentage points of money that AID obligates, we hope that 73 to 74 percent will be obligated in the United States, perhaps higher. It will be about 73 percent, and if one includes the military, and all other aid items covered in the budget, we will have obligated over 85 percent in the United States.

Of the 27 percent of AID money spent outside the United States, all but about 4 percent will have been spent in less-developed countries. Almost all of those countries have an adverse payments position vis-a-vis us as to balance of trade. Presumably the aid dollars would flow back to us from them. 

Of the remaining 4 percent that is the 4 percent spent in the highly industrialized countries-half of that is spent in countries like England and Japan, who buy more from us than they sell to us. Presumably they would use those dollars to buy goods from us. 

Only 2 percent-this is getting pretty fine and you will realize I am oversimplifying-on this statistical analysis only 2 percent of the funds would be spent in countries that have a favorable balance of trade with us.

Those are the underlying facts. What effect it would have on the gold drain is an awfully complicated thing, since money is so fluid. 

I think the most impressive thing is what is spent in the United States, because once it goes abroad it is difficult to tell where it goes.

(The information is as follows:)

LONG-TERM AND SHORT-TERM PROJECTS 

The distinction between long-term and short-term projects must be somewhat arbitrary, because a loan or grant for short-run or immediate needs usually has longer range effects. Without a reasonably stable political scene or economy, economic and social growth is difficult, if not impossible. For example, a loan to meet an immediate balance-of-payments problem in a particular country may be urgently required to restore business confidence and create the stability necessary to attract and retain private investment, one of the most important components of economic development. Thus, assistance calculated to bring short-term benefits may be extremely useful to long-term programs. It would be more precise, perhaps, to refer to (1) projects which are based primarily on long-range development considerations and (2) projects in which important short-run or emergency considerations are of major consideration. On this basis, the slightly more than $1 billion which was provided from the announcement of the alliance for progress through February 1962 in assistance may be roughly divided into 54 percent which fit under (1) and 46 percent which fall into class (2).

Alliance-for-progress developmental projects financed through AID, the Inter- American Development Bank, the Eximbank, food for peace, and so forth, have followed criteria for long-term assistance. Loans or grants for nonproject purposes, such as budget support or import financing (other than those specifically for the financing of capital goods related to development), are based partly on short-run considerations. Recent examples of this type of assistance have been an AID supporting assistance loan to the Dominican Republic when it was in a precarious situation resulting from the overthrow of the Trujillo dictatorship, an AID balance-of-payments loan to Colombia, an AID budget support loan to Ecuador, and a $90 million Eximbank credit to Mexico to underwrite imports from the United States.

I also know that the political decisions are not yours to make. Nevertheless, it seems to me that in your position there should be a good deal of influence that you can carry in the determination of those political positions.

I don't want to belabor the alliance-for-progress question. However, it has been rumored, and I don't have any means of pinning it down, that some of our people have been told that if you don't assist the particular country, despite the fact that it has said that it cannot meet the requirements that have been laid down, you are going to aid them, and that the reason is that they said if you don't aid them the government is going to fall.

Now, I say this: That if the Government is going to fall for lack of our assistance, that it is not going to remain standing with our assistance.

I would hope very much that your organization wouldn't permit any such talk, because if they are unworthy they are unworthy on aÏl points.

Furthermore, if one country gets away with it by giving you that line, others are going to find out very quickly, and they are going to try to get away with it.

It would appear to me further that it might not be a bad idea to have an example set with one country and let that government fall. 

That is some gratuitous advice. You can pay attention to it or you don't have to.

I want to go from that part of the world to the Near East. There is a country in the Near East that is carrying some of our burden in Africa. I am talking about Israel. Yet we find that our country

directs its representative in the United Nations to vote against the resolution which requests that the Arab countries sit down at a peace table with Israel. That is something I can't understand. 

Furthermore, we assist countries that we know are not peace loving, who have threatened to exterminate Israel and drive it into the sea. 

If you can explain that, I can't.

We assist countries who refuse to permit Americans of Jewish descent to put foot into their country. They treat us as second-class citizens. We haven't succeeded as yet in doing anything about that. 

I wasn't here when Mr. Pilcher completed his statement. But I understand when his airplane was approaching one of the Near East countries they inquired whether there was a Jewish Member of Congress on that plane. Until they were assured there wasn't, they wouldn't allow that plane to land. 

Your money and my money and the money of every Jew in this country goes to support these Near East countries. I say these are political questions and not for you to determine. 

Nevertheless, it would seem to me that it is something that you might well take up with the State Department and exert whatever influence you think is proper under the circumstances. 

Thank you.

This is true especially when one considers some of these new shaky countries and the fact that the Communists, with all their resources and power, were working just to create violence and anarchy. Britain to their colonies.

Mr. COFFIN. These other countries have increased particularly since 1956, they have increased percentagewise more than we have. 

I think they have increased their assistance over those years some 60 percent, to the point where in calendar 1960 their total public and private investment in developing countries was more than ours. 

This was not all aid, because a lot of it was private investment, and our private investment has not gone to these developing countries as much as theirs has. 

There are changes. My judgment after touring virtually all of the large donor capitals is while they are not doing as much as we would like them to do-as Mr. Nix eloquently said, to carry out their own obligations, not ours-they are doing more than most Americans think.

As Mr. Hamilton said, even in France the percentage per capita is greater than ours.

I think very significant in this picture is the establishment within the past year of aid organizations geared to do an aid job, not an intercabinet ad hoc grouping, but an aid organization in most of these countries. That is a development that will be increasingly significant.

Mr. HAMILTON. I will supply it for the record. (The information is as follows:)

EFFECT OF AID ACTIVITIES ON EXPORT-IMPORT BANK VOLUME 

AID activities do not result in any decrease of the volume of Export-Import Bank loans. Each loan application which is presented to AID is cleared with a joint committee of Export-Import and AID staff to ascertain whether the Bank has an interest in considering whether it will finance the project. If the 

Bank feels that the proposal would be eligible for Bank financing, AID does not consider the project and refers the applicant to the Export-Import Bank.

There is no evidence that AID activities result in an increase in Export- Import Bank lending in the short run except insofar as the procedure mentioned above brings applications into contact with the Bank who would not have otherwise considered a loan from that source. Over the longer run, however, the AID program helps less developed countries through the initial phases of economic development and increases their capacity to service loans on Eximbank terms. 

Among the largest recent borrowers at the bank are countries which decreasingly require development assistance on a grant or extremely long term loan basis but which still require substantial development financing to assist their further industrialization. Japan, Spain, Yugoslavia, Israel, and the Philippines are examples of varying stages of this progress. 

In sum, AID and the Eximbank complement each other, and it is extremely difficult to cite a specific net effect that either has on the volume of activity of the other. (The following information has been supplied for inclusion in the record in response to a request by Mrs. Bolton. See p. 21.)
