THURSDAY, MARCH 15, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to call, in room 1301, New House 

Office Building, at 10:10 a.m., the Honorable Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding. 

The committee meets this morning in open session to consider the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. Our witness this morning is the 

Honorable Robert S. McNamara, Secretary of Defense, and General 

Lyman L. Lemnitzer, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. 

Mr. Secretary, and General, you both have prepared statements. 

You have testified before the committee on previous occasions. I think the best procedure would be to let the Secretary deliver his statement first, and you follow with your statement, General, after which we will question you as a team. 

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. MCNAMARA, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Today we are presenting the first military assistance program prepared wholly by President Kennedy's administration, and also the first to be developed under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

As you know, no new authorization for military assistance is required this year. The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 authorized $1.7 billion in fiscal year 1963, which will permit appropriation of the $1.5 billion actually requested.

During the past year, the administration has made numerous changes in Department of Defense programs and in their method of formulation and review. These changes have been designed to increase the strength of our strategic deterrent forces-both missiles and bombers; to increase the active forces available for ground warfare and tactical air warfare; and to increase the capabilities of our 

Defense Establishment to move men and materiel quickly to the scene of any crisis. For these improvements and for the continued maintenance of our Defense Establishment the administration has asked for $50 billion in new obligational authority for Department of Defense programs, excluding military assistance. The administration's new obligational authority request of $1.5 billion for military assistance is about 3 percent of the DOD budget. This ratio tends to obscure 65

the vital significance of military assistance to the security of the 

United States.

The whole of our defense program, of which military assistance is a vital part, is geared to our global requirements over the long term. 

We are well aware that the Berlin crisis is but another chapter in the continuing struggle between the nations of the Communist bloc and those of the free world. Even while we meet here today, a war of covert Communist-directed aggression is being carried on in South Vietnam. The sovereignty of Laos still hangs in the balance. The 

Communists are seeking to gain a foothold in the Congo and already they have secured a grip on Cuba, only 90 miles off our own coast. 

Serious instability in other parts of the world may provide the Communists other opportunities to enlarge the area of struggle. As we have seen in the past, they are quick to take advantage of a breakdown of law and order in any part of the world. They are quick to identify themselves with any change in the status quo, and with any emerging threat to existing authority. One has only to contemplate the ferment which exists in many countries around the globe, including the Western Hemisphere, to appreciate the potential for new crises. Clearly, one of the major problems confronting this Nation, its allies, and other free world nations is how to help safeguard freedom during a period of rapid and often drastic change in many parts of the world.

The problem is particularly acute in the emerging nations of Africa, the relatively new sovereignties in southeast Asia and in those nations in South and Central America which are now and will be going through a period of great social reform. 

Obviously, military power alone cannot solve all of these problems. 

Diplomacy, economic assistance, and ideological conviction all have their roles to play in the struggle to safeguard freedom. The principal purpose of our military programs, including military assistance, is to deter the Communists from resorting to the use of armed force in seeking to achieve their objectives. Even here, the line of demarcation is far from clear. As we have seen in recent months, the Communists have stepped up what Mr. Khrushchev calls wars of national liberation but which, in reality, are wars of covert aggression, guerrilla warfare, and subversion. To meet this form of the Communist threat, new means must be devised. 

Our military policy continues to be firmly based upon the principle of collective defense of the free world. Not only are we stronger united than alone; but any loss in the free world position is a loss to our national security. For the sake of our own safety we must be prepared to defend the outposts of freedom around the world. We must be ready to meet the Communist challenge with whatever means-military, economic, political, and ideological-best serves the purpose.

We cannot and need not do this job alone. U.S. defense planning takes into account the great and growing economic and military strength of our allies. The defense of Western Europe is a NATO, not a unilateral, responsibility. Greece and Turkey, which remain free countries in part due to our military assistance in the late 1940's, provide significant land and air forces on the periphery of the Soviet Union.

The ready incountry capability to defend Korea against renewed Communist attack depends in large part upon strong, reliable South Korean forces. The protection of Japanese land and sea areas is bolstered by Japanese self-defense forces. A significant portion of the 

Chinese Communist military strength is tied down to the mainland area near Formosa by the presence of strong Republic of China forces. 

These capabilities of our allies, so essential to our own security are, in large part, the results of previous U.S. military assistance, they must be maintained by continuing programs. 

FISCAL YEAR 1963 PROGRAM 

We have taken advantage of 1 year in office to review both the management of military assistance and the level necessary to support U.S. military and foreign policy objectives. 

The result is a significant reduction in new funds requested for fiscal year 1963 despite the increasing military assistance in southeast Asia. 

This year we are asking new obligational authority of $1.5 billion; last year the request was for $1.885 billion; and the preceding year's was for $2 billion. This reduction has been made possible by careful country-by-country study of the requirements for military assistance, by tighter controls, and by a further reduction in the programs for 

European countries.

During fiscal year 1962 we have made a special effort to make recoupments from the "undelivered and unexpended" balance of prioryear programs, and will continue this special effort into fiscal year 1963. We are estimating recoupments in fiscal year 1963 at $205 million. This may be too optimistic, but we think it is wise to use it in our program at this time. 

Thus, with a request for only $1.5 billion in new obligational authority (plus the reappropriation of $25 million it is estimated will remain unobligated on June 30, 1962), we are able to propose a program of $1,730 million.

The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Europe is $314 million, about $100 million less than in fiscal year 1962. In fiscal year 1960 the program for Europe was 38 percent of the total, in fiscal year 1961 it was 28 percent, and in fiscal year 1962 it was 21 percent, and it is only 18 percent of the proposed fiscal year 1963 program. This is as we believe it should be. Most of the nations of continental Europe have developed economically to the point where they can carry their own defense burdens. By reducing grant aid programs to Western 

Europe, the United States in no way indicates any loss of interest in the continued freedom of the Continent. The recent strengthening of 

U.S. forces in Europe indicates our determination that Communist force shall not be the arbiter of European developments. 

In the major NATO countries of Western Europe, our fiscal year 1963 programs will go toward certain earlier commitments, and otherwise only to training courses intended to keep these countries abreast of U.S. military thinking, thereby promoting standardization of operational doctrine and compatibility of national forces. At the same time, we enrich our own military schools by an influx of new ideas brought by these students. We also will continue to pay our share of NATO infrastructure and overhead costs and similar multilateral programs.

For north Africa the program is primarily associated with the maintenance of U.S. bases, and with it moderate needs of the new nations of this area. For the remainder of Africa the United States provides small programs of arms and light equipment to help selected countries maintain the internal stability which we believe essential for economic and political growth.

The military assistance level for Greece and Turkey is designed to maintain existing forces and permit gradual selective improvement of their NATO forces. In Iran and Pakistan military assistance continues to be required to assist those nations in meeting the Communist threat. 

The military assistance program level for the Far East is responsive to the progressively increasing threat of Communist expansion in this area. The proposed Far East program is 48 percent of the total proposed fiscal year 1963 program. Of the fiscal year 1962 program, 46 percent went to Far East countries, in fiscal year 1961 it was 41 percent, and in fiscal year 1960 it was 38 percent. 

We believe we must continue major programs in military assistance to the Republic of China and Korea. Japan's economic progress makes possible a progressive reduction in MAP, now largely confined to a minor portion of the total cost of various important items. 

The members of this committee are well aware of the present critical situation in southeast Asia. In this public hearing, I can best summarize by saying that both the U.S. military advisory effort and our military assistance have been greatly accelerated and augmented. We mean to insure that the free people of Vietnam will not want for equipment and training to cope with Communist aggression. 

The United States will also continue in fiscal year 1963 to assist the member states of SEATO which do not have the economic capability to carry alone the burden of their defense requirements (Thailand, Pakistan, and the Philippines); emphasis will be on the continued maintenance of existing forces, with some force improvement. 

The Latin American program for fiscal year 1963 totals $77 million for all purposes including training. The materiel program will not exceed the legislative ceiling of $57.5 million now imposed by the 

Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

U.S. aid for Latin America emphasizes the economic development and social welfare envisaged by the alliance for progress. The military assistance program is designed to promote internal security, and to develop antisubmarine warfare capabilities in selected cases. where they can be made really effective as a complement to our own efforts.

CIVIC ACTION 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 in section 505b states that tothe extent feasible and consistent with the other purposes of this part, the use of military forces in less developed countries in the construction of public works and other activities helpful to economic development shall be encouraged. 

In the military assistance program "civic action" is a term for the use of military forces on projects useful to the populace at all levels in such fields as training, public works, agriculture, transportation, communications, health and sanitation. In countries fighting active campaigns against internal subversion or covert aggression, civic

action is an indispensable means of establishing a link between army and the people; it is an integral part of the work of the forces we help to support. In countries where subversion or attack is less imminent, the technical know-how developed within selected military forces can add substantially to economic development. The proposed program continues the support of civic action in Latin America by such troops as engineer battalions and air transport units, and in addition $10 million is included in the nonregional portion of the program to encourage civic action projects by the development of new units or supply of special equipment. 

SALES 

To the greatest extent possible, military sales are being utilized to replace grant aid. Eligible foreign countries may purchase on a government-to-government basis military materiel which is not normally or readily available on the commercial market. 

Most military sales are made on cash terms. We expect direct sales to total $722 million in fiscal year 1962, more than twice the fiscal year 1961 amount. Such sales, of course, create a balance of payments advantage to the United States. This amount is more than double the amount of procurement offshore which will result from the fiscal year 1962 military assistance program. TRAINING Probably the greatest return on our military assistance investment comes from the training of selected officers and key specialists at our military schools and training centers in the United States and overseas. 

These students are hand-picked by their own countries to become instructors when they return home. They are the coming leaders of their countries, the men that will have the know-how and impart it to their own forces. I need not dwell upon the value of having in positions of leadership men who have firsthand knowledge of how Americans do things and how they think. It is beyond price to us to make friends of such men. LEGISLATION

I am requesting, that the authority of section 510 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 to "draw down" up to $300 million in defense stocks be renewed for fiscal year 1963. I told the Congress last year when we discussed this section that this authority would only be used in cases "vital" to the security of the United States. Despite the problems of Berlin and southeast Asia, it has not been necessary to invoke this authority. I also stated last year that I did not intend to use this section as a deliberate supplement to the military assistance request. We will continue to adhere to this policy. 

DEFENSE INTEREST IN ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE 

In addition to the military assistance program itself, I would like to stress the importance of certain programs not directly under my jurisdiction. As you are aware, in many countries where we have major military assistance programs, the country is not capable of providing adequate financial support to its military forces unless it continues to receive U.S. economic assistance. This assistance can be pro-

vided through supporting assistance or food-for-peace programs; it is vital to the total defense program, for without it the foreign country could not maintain a defense budget sufficient to support its forces, nor could it maintain the hardware which we consider essential to our collective security. 

The justification of specific dollar appropriation requests for defense support will be made by Mr. Fowler Hamilton, Administrator of AID. 

The amounts to be allocated to the local defense budgets have been arrived at after careful consideration, both in the countries concerned and at the Washington level, of the validity of the defense budget needs of the key countries affected-notably Vietnam, Korea, and Turkey.

In past years, the Congress has expressed its disapproval of the size of the supporting assistance account, and has imposed sharp cuts in that account. As a result, we in the executive branch have made the most stringent efforts over the past year to reduce supporting assistance wherever possible, and to insure that the amounts requested are in fact absolutely essential either for military budget support, or for some valid political or economic purpose. I wish simply to state that of the total $481 million being requested for this year roughly 50 percent represents essential military budget support needs in key countries. In addition, where the local currency is allocated to economic programs, the effect can be to free additional local resources for military purposes, so that there is a major indirect contributing effect also.

In sum, we believe the supporting assistance request has been cut to the bone this year and I most strongly urge that the Congress not impose further cuts, which would have a serious effect on the necessary defense effort of the countries concerned. 

SUMMARY 

In closing, let me emphasize that the threat to the security of the United States has by no means lessened during the past year. There is no prospect that Communist pressures will relax during the coming year. They are more likely to increase. 

The reduction in the military assistance program request results from the downward trend of aid to prosperous European nations and from better programing. In no way does it suggest that the threat to U.S. interests throughout the world has been reduced. The United 

States cannot let its defensive posture be weakened. The military assistance program is essential to the maintenance of that posture. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, for the opportunity to present this statement.

General Lemnitzer.

STATEMENT OF GEN. LYMAN L. LEMNITZER, U.S. ARMY, CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF General LEMNITZER. Mr. Chairman and members of the commit tee, I am pleased to have the opportunity to appear before you in support of the military assistance program for fiscal year 1963. This program of military assistance to our allies, in my opinion, is absolutely essential to our own U.S. national security interests. In my statement this morning I shall give you the reasons which I believe support this opinion. 

The threat our country and our allies face today is a very real one. 

There can be no question but that the military strength of the Communist powers is steadily increasing; no question but that the Communists remain committed to their goal of world domination; no question but that they are using every resource and every tactic, on a global scale, to subjugate and control peoples now free and extend the influence of communism. 

This is a long-term struggle for survival in which we are engaged. 

The stakes could not be higher. This assessment of the threat is accepted by every military leader I know.

It is a simple truth, in the light of the magnitude of this threat, that we need to apply our resources with wisdom in facing the long haul ahead. The military assistance program as it will be described for you in detail during the course of this hearing, is a wise application of our resources. 

I want to stress the fact that the nature of the threat is such that we cannot successfully meet it by ourselves, or with only our own resources. But, the strengths of the free world, bound together through a system of alliances, with each member of the alliances contributing to the common defense, provide a basis for facing the future with confidence.

The collective security arrangements are in the interests of all who have joined in them--and specifically they are in the interests of the 

United States.

As President Kennedy stated in his message to the Congress on this subject, refering to the nations to be aided by our programs- *** all of our armies and atoms combined will be of little avail if these nations fall, unable to meet the needs of their own people, and unable to stave off within their borders the rise of forces that threaten our security. This program-and the passage of this bill-are vital to the interests of the United States.

I recently reviewed again the report submitted by the President's 

Committee To Study the U.S. Military Assistance Program in 

1959. This report made certain observations which were important then, and which remain pertinent today. 

Addressing the question as to whether these programs are more useful implements of national security policy than equivalent efforts and resources devoted to other areas, the Committee had this to say: 

The only alternative we can see to the interdependent allied free world, strengthened by our aid where needed, would be the Fortress America concept-taking our first stand in the last ditch.

We are all convinced that the mutual security program both in its military and in its economic aspects is a sound concept. What is needed is the determination to continue it and the ability to administer it well. 

In my opinion, the Committee chose its words well. The security of the United States, which depends upon the security of the free world alliance as a whole, requires the continuance of our military and economic assistance programs. 

The threat we face is a global threat. The security problems arising from this threat are therefore global problems, problems which can only be solved by mutual effort. 

I would like to mention some of the ways our security interests are served by our military assistance programs. 

The recent increase in Communist guerrilla activities represent a grave danger to many of our allies, and for an understanding of this danger we need only read Chairman Khrushchev's speech of January 6, 1961, entitled "For New Victories of the World Communist January 6, 1903 in which he reported on the results of the November 

1960 Conference of World Communist Parties. 

Khrushchev stated that- Liberation wars and popular uprisings will continue to exist as long as imperialism exists. he asserted- Such warsare not only admissible but inevitable. *** We recognize such wars. and will help the people striving for their independence. 

We help

We are clearly warned by these statements, which reinforced the conclusions to be drawn from the pattern of Communist activities that we have observed all over the world, that the Soviet's have every intention of sponsoring subversion wherever they see the opportunity to do so.

Our mutual security programs provide us with a means of meeting this threat to our allies the threat of Communist-sponsored guerrilla warfare, the object of which is to subvert existing governments and substitute Communist rule-not "liberation," as Mr. Khrushchev would have the world believe. 

The real source of the guerrillas' ability to fight is provided by the people of the countryside whose support is extorted by the ruthless use of terrorism. The support of the local population is absolutely essential if the Communist guerrilla forces are to be defeated.

This fact emphasizes a point which I believe to be of fundamental importance in assessing the contribution which our programs, both economic and military, can make. 

To counter the pressures used by the guerrillas to extort support from local populations, a key requirement is for local government programs which make it clear to their people that their interests lie with those of the government, and not with the interests of the Communist guerrillas. But such programs, on the scale required, are beyond the capabilities of certain governments which now face a guerrilla threat.

Only with our assistance can the threatened friendly governments pursue the local programs needed to successfully meet and overcome the guerrilla threat. Our programs for southeast Asia, for example-

and again I speak of both the economic and military programs—are vital to the accomplishment of our objectives in that area. 

I believe that through our military assistance programs we have made substantial progress in providing a firmer foundation for the alliances on which the collective security of the free world is based. 

Quite clearly, they need to be further strengthened, and such strengthening is important to the future posture of the free world. 

Devoting approximately 3 percent of our total defense expenditures to such an end seems to me to be a wise use of our resources. 

As I stated in my appearance before this committee last year, our military assistance programs are a realistic, hardheaded, commonsense approach to our very difficult security problems-problems we mutually share with other nations of the free world. 

It is in this sense that I urge your support of programs designed to contribute to the vitality, cohesiveness, and military strengths of the alliances upon which the free world is dependent for its security. 

It is necessary that we fully appreciate the extent to which the friendly and noncommitted nations are looking to us for leadership in the struggle of the free world against the threat of communism. 

The manner in which we exercise our leadership through our mutual security programs is being watched closely in all areas of the world. 

Continued acceptance of our responsibilities-evidenced by our willingness to assist where assistance is required-will stimulate the determination of our friends to remain firm with us in opposing communism. Such determination is one of the keys to the future. 

Mr. Chairman, before concluding there is a collateral benefit of our military assistance programs which is not generally appreciated. 

As Secretary McNamara mentioned, our military assistance programs do not result in a flow of gold from the United States. The contrary is true. The net result of all military assistance programs for fiscal year 1962 will be an inflow of gold. 

Out of the total military assistance program for fiscal year 1962, $335 million will be spent outside the United States, which is more than offset by the $800 million to be received from the sale of U.S. military equipment under the military assistance program. 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, in making this statement I am speaking not only for myself, but also on behalf of all the members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. They join me in endorsing the essentiality of the military assistance program. The Joint Chiefs of Staff regard the program as an extremely important part of our total defense effort. 

That concludes my statement, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General Lemnitzer.

Mr. Secretary, on page 5 of your statement you say that the European nations are now able to carry their own defense burdens. 

Many people in the United States cannot understand why it is necessary for the United States to provide military aid to Europe. 

Europe apparently is more prosperous than ever. I understand we no longer give military aid to Germany and France, but according to annex A in your statement, the United States is planning to pay $82 million for infrastructure in 1963. 

Why shouldn't the larger and more prosperous nations of Europe finance the infrastructure program?

Secretary MCNAMARA. The larger countries of NATO other than the United States are increasing their share of the infrastructure payments. This we believe is as it should be. 

Our share is now approximately 30 percent down within the past 18 months from about 37 percent. Our share is related to the structure of logistical support required by our troops and by our forces deployed at present. It seems to be a reasonable share. 

We have taken steps, as you can see from the program, to substantially reduce both the dollars in absolute terms and the percentage of the military assistance program being applied to Western Europe. 

I have personally spoken to the Defense Ministers of most of these nations, particularly those of France, Italy, Belgium, and Holland, pointing out that the economic growth in those nations makes it possible for them now to finance their own defense. We propose to follow that policy in the future. 

There are some commitments from past periods which we believe we are obligated to fulfill, which account for a major part of the $14 million. These commitments will be gradually falling as the years advance. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, you say you have had consultations with the Defense Ministers of Germany, France, Belgium, and some of the more prosperous nations in Europe. Was the result of the consultations any indication that these countries would provide assistance for some of the less prosperous countries of Europe? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I was pleased with the results. I think it is recognized by the Western European nations that they must bear to an increasing measure their own defense. That is particularly true of the nations I mentioned, West Germany, France, Belgium, Netherlands, to some less degree Italy. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, on page 9 of your statement, when you refer to section 510 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, which provides authority to draw down $300 million in defense stocks, and you ask that this section be renewed for fiscal year 1963. 

As one of the conferees last year, we were interested in limiting this authority to 1 year, because we wanted to be very cautious with respect to this particular section in the 1961 act. 

I am glad to see you come out with a strong statement that it has not been necessary to use this authority, and state it will not be used unless there is an absolute emergency.

You stand on that statement that it will not be used unless there is an emergency? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. This committee queried me on it, as did the other congressional committees concerned. I stated then, and I state now, we will use it only as a last resort. We have not used it this year, and I hope it will not be necessary to use it in fiscal 1962.

Chairman MORGAN. Mrs. Kelly. 

Mrs. KELLY. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Secretary and General Lemnitzer. I note quite a pessimistic attitude throughout both statements. It refers to the long-term struggle, President Kennedy's address "Nations must not fall and Communist strength is increasing." With this in mind, do you believe the Communist military threat has increased over the past year and, if so, do you believe that the U.S.S.R. peace offensive is a policy of the past and the U.S.S.R. is now returning to the phase of a military offensive? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. May I answer, and then ask General Lemnitzer to comment also on this. 

First, if the statement carries an implication of pessimism it wasn't intended. I am quite optimistic about the long-term outcome of the struggle in which we are presently engaged. It is a struggle. It does require intense effort. It requires effort greater than the free world has applied to it in the past. 

Second, I think that the Soviet Union's policy was very well reflected in the speech which Premier Khrushchev made on January 6 of last year. At that time, you recall, he outlined his views on war. 

He categorized war as falling in three classes. He spoke of thermonuclear war, limited wars, and what he called wars of liberation, wars of covert aggression. He spoke of the great risk and danger of thermonuclear war.

It was quite interesting to me to observe that he was, in effect, saying that no longer did the Communists think of thermonuclear war to spread Communist revolution. It was too dangerous. It was quite clear, I might add, that he would still continue to use the threat of thermonuclear war to prevent the free world from resisting Communist encroachment. He stated he didn't consider it necessary to

engage in thermonuclear war to advance the Communists' aims. He pointed out local wars or limited wars were more probable, but also to be avoided because they might well escalate into thermonuclear wars. But he emphasized the third category, the so-called wars of liberation.

These are the types of operations which the Communist world, both the Red Chinese and the Soviet Union, appear to be sponsoring and engaging in with increasing intensity. 

The program for military assistance in fiscal 1963 is particularly directed toward preparation for those types of operations. 

Mrs. KELLY. Do you have a statement, General Lemnitzer?

General LEMNITZER. I was not intending to be pessimistic either, Mrs. Kelly.

Mrs. KELLY. I have used the wrong term. I know the military never receives enough authorization and appropriations for modernization of our armies, but I do note a great emphasis on the U.S.S.R. threat.

General LEMNITZER. I could in executive session give you detailed information on the threat.

As I did point out, if we and our allies continue our system of alliances and the programs on which we are embarked, and do not let ourselves become divided as a result of Communist divisive efforts, and continue particularly with our military assistance program, Í feel we can face the future with confidence. That is what I said in my statement.

In certain areas of the world it is obvious that there has been a step-up in the activities the Communists are pursuing toward their objective of world domination. 

I refer particularly, as I did in my statement, to Communist guerrilla warfare in southeast Asia. There has been a great increase in the intensity of effort on the part of the Communist guerrillas. There isn't any question about it.

Mr. Khrushchev has referred to these as wars of liberation. I prefer to refer to them as wars of Communist-sponsored subversion. 

That is one of the reasons why we are stepping up our materiel support, our training, and our advisory support and our materiel in 

South Vietnam.

1963 proposed program. It looks to me as if there is a phasing out of a good deal of the military support which is so necessary in Europe, and a request that these nations pick up their own share. 

In view of the greater increase of economic aid to the underedeveloped areas, I would like to know if you feel the modernization of the forces in Europe are meeting the goal to the degree hoped for? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I would answer that in two steps: First, no, they are not meeting the goal.

However, second, there is an increasingly rapid rate of modernization taking place.

I am very encouraged by the progress that the Western European nations have made since mid-1961, both to increase their forces in terms of numbers, and also to modernize their forces in terms of equipment and logistical support.

Mrs. KELLY. I assume we will have a discussion of missiles in executive session?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes. 

Mrs. KELLY. Let me refer to southeast Asia and the importance of Vietnam. We must at all cost maintain that section of the world. The survival of freedom and independence of the nations in that area is paramount; specifically, the most anti-Communist nation on the mainland of Asia: Vietnam.

Secretary MCNAMARA. I believe we must make every effort possible to save Vietnam. I wouldn't like to try to rank south Asia in order of priority as opposed to other areas of the world. 

I would also like to emphasize the importance of assisting the nations of Africa and Latin America to provide the internal security which must be a foundation for their political and economic growth and development.

Mrs. KELLY. A few year ago one in the executive branch of Government claimed that the fall of Vietnam would be the beginning of the dominoes falling and the beginning of the fall of free nations in that area. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think dominoes could fall from anywhere.

I wouldn't wish to say that southeast Asia is the only priority. 

Mrs. KELLY. I emphasize that the cost to save Vietnam is so great that we can consider it the cost of our own survival. 

Chairman MORGAN. Dr. Judd. 

Mr. JUDD. 

Gentlemen, it is nice to have you here. I have appreciated the frank and forthright and competent statements that General Lemnitzer has been making to us for many years, and you, Mr. Secretary, have performed by the highest standards since you have been in your present position.

I am happy to see from your testimony that it has been possible to tighten up and have greater efficiency and economy in the pipeline, so that commitments that have been sterilizing money for long periods of time are reduced.

We have often urged that this could be done, but you report it has been done. I compliment you. You have discovered some other things also. One and I won't be political either-that I am glad you have discovered down there is that the missile gap is in reverse from what it was reported to be a couple of years ago. It was the 

Soviet Union that was behind in missiles, and the size of the gap by which it is behind us is larger, not smaller than was understood at the time. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Mr. Judd, may I comment on that by saying that I have personally reviewed the national intelligence estimates relating to missiles in great detail. 

I think that the controversy over the missile gap reflected a very important limitation or weakness in our military affairs. We are dealing with a closed society. It is extremely difficult to estimate properly the force levels and combat potential of that society.

The national intelligence estimates were the foundation for the statements made by those discussing the subject of the missile gap, and I think they discussed it in all good conscience. 

I am delighted we have what we believe to be more accurate estimates today.

Mr. JUDD. I wasn't suggesting anybody was trying to misrepresent. I was trying to let our people know officially that there is and was no gap on our part. The only gap was that which the Soviet 

Union had with respect to us. 

It is a fatal mistake to underestimate the enemy. But we should not underestimate ourselves either. I think some were more likely a year or so ago to do the latter than the former. 

May I ask if the funds for what you describe as the greatly accelerated and augmented advisory effort and our military assistance in southeast Asia are to come out of this $1.5 billion? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, sir, they are. Plus the recoupments that I mentioned earlier, recoveries, if you will, of prior-year funds. 

Mr. JUDD. The costs of increased operations in Vietnam don't come largely out of your own Department of Defense budget? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. There are two types, of course. There are certain service-supported functions associated with military assistance, particularly that which relates to the payroll of the military personnel. And to the extent that military personnel are functioning in the capacity of advisers, those payroll charges are not borne by the military assistance program. 

There are certain pieces of equipment also that our own troops are utilizing for their own purposes, which are not charged to the military assistance program. To the extent that equipment is provided to the South Vietnamese for their use, to their civil guard, their self-defense corps, their regular army, their air force or navy, those charges, of course, are made to the military assistance program and are provided for in this appropriation request.

I interpret that as something comparable to the feeling in an earlier period in our own country, when we didn't want to have any part of the wars and quarrels of the Old World. 

Last year I did this largely for the record-I made it clear in the public hearings that what we were doing in the way of military aid for Africa was merely for internal security and on a small scale. 

I notice that for fiscal 1963 we are following the pattern of last year, with only 2 percent of our authorization for military aid going to Africa.

Is that being done because it is your intent that Africa shall not be in the zone of the cold war? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. May I respond by saying no. It is being done because we believe that the fundamental requirement in Africa is the economic and political development of the emerging nations that have come into being in many cases within the past few months. The military effort required should be an effort directed at maintaining the internal security-the internal stability from which will flower the economic and political developments that those nations require. 

We believe these funds, $38 million of assistance from us will provide that military assistance that will lead to internal security and stability.

Mr. O'HARA. The purpose is to make more efficient the economic aid we are giving to Africa?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It is.

We hope the European nations will further accelerate their efforts to strengthen their defenses. They have already done so since last summer. Many of the nations have increased their budgets and added to their military personnel.

I think in appraising the efforts of the Europeans in relation to defense, it is important to recognize the general level of gross national product that exists in those countries, and the percent of that gross national product that they are devoting to their defense effort.

about $1,350 per year. That is less than half of ours. That, of course, affects the amount that they can properly devote to defense purposes.

Some of these nations are devoting about 7 percent of their gross national product to defense. It is difficult for them to quickly increase that.

We think in many cases they should. We have engaged in discussions to that effect already with most of those nations. Both Secretary Rusk and I at the December meeting of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization emphasized in our prepared statements and in our informal comments the necessity for each of the NATO nations to further strengthen their defense establishments. We don't like the pressures the Communists put on us. We don't like the hit-and-run tactics in Vietnam, and you say they are difficult to combat, and I agree with you. 

I just pass this on to you for whatever it is worth. If there are a few holes blown in that wall some night, they won't blame you.

Chairman MORGAN. Dr. Judd. 

Mr. JUDD. I came in again, General, just when you were talking about the armed forces in Korea. I want to concur in what you said about the chairman of the junta that is running Korea. He is one of the most impressive men I have seen. 

Apparently he isn't much of a backslapper and doesn't speak English, so he had not attracted too much attention from our folks. He is more of an ascetic. 

I felt the Korean Army-and this is true in some other countries today-is in some respects the stablest element in the country. 

General LEMNITZER. I agree. 

Mr. JUDD. These armies are no longer personal armies or private armies of individual dictators or warlords, as was the case in much of the world for centuries. Under our guidance and counsel, they have been raised by conscription so they come from the rank and file of the villages and farms. They represent the people. They have a feeling of pride that they are helping to defend their newly won independence, not just followers of a particular adventurer. 

There is less graft, there is less chicanery and devious maneuvering. 

They more nearly represent the true interests of the people and the country. 

---

I said to one of the keymen in the junta, a military man, “Military dictatorships don't easily lead to democracy." 

He said:

Yes; that is right, but neither does chaos or communism. 

He said:

If we don't succeed within 2 years in getting good government and the corruption and rottenness cleaned out and a government established which the people of Korea can keep sound and clean by elections, then the army itself will become corrupted and there won't be anything left on which we will be able to build.

When military leaders perceive that deeply, when they see the necessity to do their job in a way that will let them end their own control in 2 years or else they will have failed in their mission and destroyed their own organization, that is the kind and caliber of leadership that gives more confidence than we have had during the long 10-year period of laying the foundations and getting things started. 

I agree so wholly with what you have said here, that probably the best money we spend is the bringing of foreign military leaders from colonels on up, to our country where they spend 6 months at Fort Benning or Fort Sill, or at one of the air schools. They learn modern techniques, yes, but they see how things are done and how an army should be the servant of the people, and the country. That probably has done more good than a lot of our other cultural relations. It has imbued sound democratic ideals in the minds of people who have great influence when they go back to their country. 

What Secretary McNamara said earlier is so true. Our problems are tough, but there is less confusion about the Communists, and the issues are clearer.

There is also almost total disenchantment in free Asia with respect to communism as furnishing the answer to their problems. They are afraid of it. But they are not attracted to it now as a few years ago. 

They have seen what happened to people in Tibet and North Korea and now in Red China, and in Hungary and Cuba. 

Therefore, the feeling that they ought to go Communist in order to carry out the economic and other development that they badly need and which it seemed the Soviet Union and China could do very quickly, that is almost all gone.

This is a most encouraging thing. The Communist propaganda has flopped because it has not been followed by performance. 

The time is here for us to take the initiative in this period of great weakness, ideologically, which the Communists are facing. 

Some fear that for us to take initiative may provoke them into war. Well, there is risk in whatever we do or don't do. But there is greater risk if we don't take that action, through our discouraging and weakening the allegiance and confidence in us of the people who want to be on our side. 

I am convinced that the best way to influence the enemy is to show him that we stand resolutely by our friends. We have sought peace all these years by trying to woo or persuade the enemy. The idea seemed to be that if we treated our friends as if they were our enemies, our enemies would rush to become our friends, so that we could do the same to them.

That day should be over. The way to defeat the enemy is not to help him win, but to make him lose. 

You didn't ask for a speech. But I am encouraged rather than discouraged. A lot of our people think because of the blustering and so on, that the Communists have superior power. They don't have. 

They only have the initiative because we let them have it. Let us take it.

Mr. HAYS. I hope everything you say about South Korea comes true. I expressed some doubts before you came in, I think.

Without any reflection on anything you have said, a good many of the things that you said about South Korea was also said by Mr. 

Castro, or very nearly that, in his triumphal tour through the United States.

That is one of our difficulties, the public's memory is short. He was going to clean up corruption, elections, and all that. 

Maybe General Park is going to clean it up. Maybe there will be a new day for Korea. On the other hand, maybe General Park is going to channel all the graft into his own pocket. I don't know. guess the test of him will be to wait and see what happens.

I hope you are right and he doesn't turn out to be another one like so many of the dictators who start out with a lot of high-flown promises and they turn out to be camouflage for their real intentions. 

I want to say, and I want it in the record, that I don't want to put up with doing business with all these petty dictators as they come along, because we have had our fingers burned a lot of times. 

Mr. JUDD. I checked very carefully when I was there last fall into these stories that he himself, because of a brother, had been connected with the Korean Communists. He isn't a fellow that makes big promises. He is not in any sense like

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Barry. 

Mr. BARRY. You said we were in Vietnam at the invitation of the 

Vietnamese Government. We have been having difficulties in Laos. 

Certainly Boun Oum, Souvanna Phouma and Souphanouvong haven't

been able to get together in a meeting to bring any real stability toward unifying Laos. 

Have we been invited by the Central Government in Laos to help stabilize their military and internal security?

Secretary MCNAMARA. We were asked, and I think probably the word "asked" or "requested" is a more accurate description than "invited," both with respect to South Vietnam and Laos. We were asked by the governments to assist them in training their troops and providing logistical support. 

Mr. BARRY. In Laos as well? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, as well as in South Vietnam.

Mr. BARRY. The extent of your assistance to Laos is limited by what?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Limited to the military assistance program which we have presented to this committee, training and logistical support. 

Mr. BARRY. Is it intended to increase that during the coming year, to strengthen the hands of the Central Government? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. At the present time, as you know, it is the policy of the U.S. Government to try to obtain a neutral independent 

Laos, and all of our efforts, political and otherwise, are being directed to that end.

Mr. BARRY. In attempting to get this compromise, do you think we would have a better chance if the Boun Oum government were strengthened so that Souphanouvong and Souvanna Phouma might be more willing to come to terms if they felt the Central Government was stronger?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think the State Department should discuss that issue. It falls within their responsibilities. 

Mr. BARRY. There is no slackening up on the part of the military assistance program in Laos as far as strengthening the Boun Oum government, is there?

Secretary MCNAMARA. We are maintaining the training assistance which we have been requested to provide to them. 

Mr. BARRY. You mentioned earlier that our SEATO partners are willing to make military plans for their mutual defense in the event of an undescribed happening which you didn't elaborate upon but which we could anticipate. 

Do you feel that with England and France being members of SEATO, where one abstention nullifies the entire SEATO decision as to what the rest might want to do-do you feel their membership is a deterrent in getting a stronger procedure or policy statement from SEATO at a time when the area might be threatened by this undisclosed military aggression that you have referred to?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think that Secretary Rusk in his joint communique with Minister Thanat addressed himself to this issue last week when he said we recognized our obligations under the SEATO Treaty and would act without depending upon the action of others. 

Mr. BARRY. As far as SEATO is concerned, if the pact could not be tightened to exclude this power of nullifying the weight of the majority by one abstention, would you be in favor of another form of military alliance in southeast Asia that might bind our partners to carry some of this load with us?

Secretary MCNAMARA. We have participated with the other SEATO powers in a series of military planning operations over the past year. I believe it is an effective alliance and would like to see it continued in its present form. 

Mr. BARRY. You don't feel that we might be heading for a future embarrassment when we and our southeast Asian friends might be ready for strong measures against the Communists of the north only to have France nullify and embarrass us? Secretary MCNAMARA. I do not. 

Mr. BARRY. Mr. Secretary, the command in Vietnam was under 

General McGarr, I believe.

Secretary MCNAMARA. Under General Harkins. 

Mr. BARRY. What was the purpose of putting a military commander over General McGarr?

Secretary MCNAMARA. The effort was to be increased. General 

McGarr's health had been poor. As a matter of fact, upon doctor's orders he has been returned to this country within the past 10 days because of ill health.

For both reasons therefore it seemed desirable to ask General 

Harkins to journey to South Vietnam.

Mr. BARRY. Do you look to a time when we might have a military commander in southeast Asia as distinct from Vietnam where we could be looking more specifically toward what support we could have from our SEATO partners by having a commander in the area, rather than based at Pearl Harbor?

Secretary MCNAMARA. No; at the present time it is the view of the 

Chiefs and mine as well, that the present unified command organization with headquarters in Honolulu and with a commander of the Military Advisory Command in South Vietnam, is quite satisfactory. 

To insure that it is satisfactory, General Lemnitzer and I have held these conferences in Honolulu during the past 3 months. 

Mr. BARRY. Insofar as the threat of the Communists in the north is concerned, do you feel that a mobile military force somewhere in southeast Asia made up of a combination of troops, shall we say, from Okinawa, from the Philippines, from Pakistan, from Thailand, and any other country which wishes to join in guaranteeing the security against the Communists-do you think such a military force backed up with transportation systems from our own Department of Defense would operate as a deterrent to any aggression that the Communists from the north might initiate in the future? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. No, I don't. I think the type of aggression that is being carried on-covert aggression, subversion-would not be deterred by that type of force.

Mr. BARRY. Even though that kind of force might have helicopters as a method of transportation which could possibly drop troops at any point in the line, shall we say, all the way from India to Korea-the soft underbelly of Asia?

Secretary MCNAMARA. No, I don't believe it would be a deterrent. 

Mr. BARRY. Do you think the Communists are concerned particularly about our military might when we sent the 7th Fleet down to southeast Asia as a sign of our strength? Do you think that is a deterrent to guerrilla tactics that are inland hundreds of miles away?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think it is effective as a deterrent to possible future action. I think the Communists are well aware of the power of this Nation. I think they are well aware of the actions that we have taken since last July. I think this is the primary deterrent to Communist aggression. 

Mr. BARRY. We have made the rest of the world realize we are dead serious in regard to our intent. 

I do believe that SEATO suffered a pretty black name in the eyes of world opinion because it did not come to the defense of Vietnam, and has not been formidable in thwarting the Communists. Certainly something should be done in southeast Asia to beef it up or strengthen it. We should give it strong leadership and have a policy there that others can hold to. 

I may say my view has been shared by many people in southeast Asia, our own ambassadors as well as heads of state, and some of the latter are willing to contribute forces, and I am sure you are aware of this, to strengthen just the image, if nothing more. 

We have NATO on the one hand with military forces backing it up, and a NATO commander. In SEATO there is a noticeable absence of a SEATO commander, and there is a lack of military force. 

Do you care to comment on that?

Secretary MCNAMARA. The SEATO operations are different from 

NATO in many respects. Among them are the commitments of the members of SEATO, particularly the Western members, to other areas of the world. 

Britain and France are contributing significantly to West European security at the present time. In that sense, SEATO differs very substantially from NATO. 

Further, at the present time, the requirement is not for active combat forces of a NATO character in southeast Asia, but for the assistance in terms of training and logistical support that we are providing both in Laos and South Vietnam. 

Mr. BARRY. I am concerned about the public image. They look upon NATO as a bastion of strength and SEATO has recently demonstrated that it is weak and that the members don't hang together. 

There is nothing worse than deluding ourselves into a position, and deluding the rest of the free world into a position where they think SEATO wil be a bastion of support, when one of the partners of SEATO could nullify the acts of the rest by abstaining or voting against what the majority decided.

Secretary MCNAMARA. The question of SEATO and its powers is a question that no doubt you will wish to discuss further in executive session. We will be happy to do so. 

We consider it to be an effective alliance, one which is providing a deterrent contribution in southeast Asia today, and one which is not standing in the way of the type of assistance that these countries need today-training assistance, logistical support. 

Mr. BARRY. I think perhaps the public may not be aware of the 

Communist intent in southeast Asia, certainly with Vietnam and Thailand being countries that can produce more grain than they need, and the colossus of the north being unable to produce as much as they need, Indonesia, the fifth largest nation in the world, with

close to 100 million population, and with a vast expanse of the continent of Australia below it-this area of the world is ripe for Communist aggression and needs the vital attention which your Department is giving it. 

I certainly join in anything possible to strengthen our position and to strengthen the free world in the area. 

I can say again that those in southeast Asia with whom I have been visiting recently are hopeful of a determined, positive policy on behalf of the United States, one that they can follow. They are not at all opposed to promoting military force if the United States will take the lead.

Mr. Nix. Then I must again come back to where I was in the beginning. We have not succeeded in reaching the objective we seek. Mr. Nix. Mr. Secretary, I am still where I was before, nevertheless. I will ask the second question they will ask me. Whatever I say to them they are going to conclude that we are on the defensive in these places. Then they are going to say to me, "What about Latin 

America where it is possible in their view for us to take the offensive?" 

They are going to ask me what has been done along that line, to take the offensive in those countries. Do we have the offensive in those countries in Latin America?

Secretary MCNAMARA. These are certainly questions that again more properly should be directed to the State Department. I think it is perfectly clear that the President's alliance for progress is a program directed toward strengthening the economic and political institutions of South and Central America. It is far from a defensive program. I would say it has a strong positive objective. It is associated with assisting those nations to achieve both political and economic reform.

It provides for the expenditure of huge sums of money to accomplish that objective. I am very optimistic about the results that will accrue from it.

Mr. Nix. They are going to take me to task further. They are going to say it is understood that the support of local population is absolutely essential if the Communist guerrilla forces are to be defeated. They are going to say to me that the Communists were able to impress the local population, either your terroristic activities or otherwise; nevertheless, the fact remains that they were impressed into the Communist service. They are going to say to me: What kind of a countermeasure have you; have we got to do the same thing?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think the answer is very clear and I would use South Vietnam again. The fact is that the rate of economic growth in South Vietnam is so great that it provided the same kind of danger to North Vietnam that West Berlin did to East Germany. 

North Vietnam in effect was forced to take action to try to dim that window into the West. They have applied terror tactics. They have literally chopped off the heads of the village elders, mounted them on poles, and used these actions as pressure upon the villagers to support the Viet Cong.

Under these circumstances, I think it is quite apparent we must take military action. We must assist South Vietnamese to take that action to counter the terror tactics. There must follow the economic and political development which the same government is applying as the Viet Cong are moved out of the villages where they have achieved control by the terror tactics.

Mr. Nix. Last year I was told the lack of interest of the Vietnamese was that they did not have the will to fight. These students are going to ask me: Is our economic program directly related to the will to fight which they apparently have now?

Defense Department.

Mr. Nix. I am afraid it was.

Mr. Nix. I think I made a mistake. I think the reference was made that their income-I have forgotten the amount, the yearly income was set at some particular figure. There wasn't any particular reason why they should fight.

Secretary MCNAMARA. I don't believe the will to fight is a function of economic well-being. 

Mr. Nix. I don't think so.

Secretary MCNAMARA. I think it is a function in a belief in one nation, the objectives of that society. 

I think it is those beliefs that are underlying the will to fight today. 

I don't believe the will to fight of the Vietnamese today is any different than it was a year ago. The will to fight exists today. 

Mr. Nix. I am afraid these students will say that the will to fight is inextricably combined with the economic well-being of the country, what the country does for the citizen, which is based in the economy of the country. I think they are going to tell me that. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I would say that you can plot the gross national product per individual throughout the world and there will be no direct correlation between that and the will to fight. 

I think an important contributor to the will to fight is the moral and political beliefs and objectives of the people. 

Mr. Nix. I believe the will to fight arises out of personal considerations. Certainly love of country has something to do with it. It arises out of personal considerations, both for the present and for the future.

It arises out of the desire to stabilize some place that belongs to you, that is going to serve your family, your heirs, in the future. I think it is basically economic.

The committee reconvened at 2:30 p.m., the Honorable Thomas E. 

Morgan (chairman) presiding.

The committee meets this afternoon to continue hearings on the 

Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

Our witnesses this afternoon are General Lemnitzer, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; General W. B. Palmer, Director of Military 

Assistance, and Mr. William P. Bundy, Deputy Assistant Secretary of

Defense. 

There are no prepared statements this afternoon, are there? 

General LEMNITZER. I do not have a prepared statement. 

Chairman MORGAN. We can proceed directly with the question and answer period.

General, we will direct our questions to all three of you as a team. 

I have some questions that the staff have prepared. The staff survey team last year looked into the NATO NIKE program and found that some missiles were delivered 2 years or more before they were installed at the permanent sites. There appears to have been an undue delay in getting the sites ready. Do you know anything about this NIKË problem?

STATEMENT OF GEN. W. B. PALMER, DIRECTOR OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

General PALMER. In all the places where we have given the NIKE, I think without exception, there have been real estate difficulties and legal difficulties about sites [security deletion]. 

I am not absolutely letter perfect on it. 

[Security deletion.] 

Chairman MORGAN. General, in Turkey, then, you have an installation of the JUPITER, the intermediate ballistic missile, which is financed out of military assistance. Are all the IRBM's financed with military assistance funds, or are some of them financed with the 

Department of Defense funds?

STATEMENT OF GEN. L. L. LEMNITZER, CHAIRMAN, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF 

General LEMNITZER. There are the THOR missiles in England and the JUPITER missiles in Italy and Turkey. The THORS in England are supported out of military assistance funds. The JUPITERS in Italy and Turkey are completely supported by military assistance funds.

General PALMER. Our contribution in the United Kingdom is very small.

General LEMNITZER. About [security deletion] millions for fiscal year 1963.

General PALMER. Entirely for maintenance of THOR's. 

Chairman MORGAN. The cost of the JUPITER intermediate IRBM 

to us would be quite a large part of the military assistance funds that actually go to Turkey? The JUPITER is quite expensive, isn't it?

STATEMENT OF WILLIAM P. BUNDY, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRE- TARY OF DEFENSE, INTERNATIONAL SECURITY AFFAIRS Mr. BUNDY. It is [security deletion] million in [security deletion] 

round numbers, Mr. Chairman, in the program we are presenting to you.

Chairman MORGAN. Secretary McNamara this morning mentioned the recoupment in fiscal year 1963 of $205 million in the military assistance funds; on page 7 of the Black Book there is a reference to recoupments. What does this mean?

Mr. BUNDY. I can explain it in general, and then perhaps General 

Palmer can give you the precise explanation. Every year we have a certain amount of funds that we commit for items which change in price prior to delivery and for items which become excess in the interval between funding and delivery, in which case we only have to pay repair and rehabilitation costs. There are also programs that may be canceled for certain various reasons [security deletion]. 

There are recoupments of that sort. In addition, we conducted a very thorough review of the actual experience in consumption of spare parts and certain consumable items. We checked what the field was expecting to get and found they weren't expecting to get as much as we were expecting to send. We could therefore go back into those accounts and, in effect, get that money back. It wasn't going to be needed.

I think I better turn it over at that point to General Palmer, who knows this subject a good deal better than I do. 

Mrs. KELLY. Are you discussing at this moment the "recoupment"? 

Chairman MORGAN. Yes. It was mentioned on page 7.

General Palmer. 

General PALMER. The sources of recoupments are (a) price reductions, (b) changes of source, and (c) cancellation of programs. 

Programs are canceled for many reasons: (1) Funds are recaptured because of slippage of the program, failure to receive delivery; (2) the recipient country may not be able to take delivery, to receive, store, and maintain and utilize the equipment so that it may be de-

ferred; (3) unrequisitioned, and here is where we begin to get into the pay dirt. Consumable items and spare parts are not programed in specifics; in other words, we don't say we will deliver Turkey so many spark plugs, and so many cotter pins, and so on, but there is a bulk setup. 

What we have found, as Mr. Bundy has said, there is always a certain amount of this failure to requisition after the bulk credit is given. 

We believe about $100 million a year would cover the slippages, price changes, and the other factors aside from this failure to use the bulk credits for the consumables.

What happened last year, or in this past year, was this. Everybody had felt and the GAO had criticized military assistance for a long time as a badly managed business because the countries were exaggerating their spare parts requirements, and then in addition duplicating their requisitions that is to say, sending in a requisition for something they had requisitioned already but hadn't received yet. 

There had been an accumulation of badly computed requirements. 

As Mr. McNamara said last year, I believe to this committee, he could take you into the best run businesses in the United States—as I recall he cited Ford, General Electric, American Telephone & Telegraph-and find these same difficulties in handling spare parts, in controlling the inventory, figuring out what you had and where it was. 

We decided we would examine this, or actually that we would go back through the considerable unexpended balance we had and see if there were dormant funds in it, if there was money there that appeared to be committed for something but wasn't being used. 

The place where we appeared to be most likely to find a reward was in the area of spare parts and consumables where there had been bulk authorizations against which the people could requisition for their requirements. They had stated large requirements, but when the time came to submit the requisitions they were actually managing their business better; in other words, time was going on, and they were performing better, themselves, and they found they didn't need as much as they had said they were going to need a year or a year and a half earlier when they began to make the program up to come to Congress. 

So the money had been set up for them, on which to draw for spare parts and consumables, and it was lying there unused. 

This is the main story of this recoupment question. The other factor that entered into it was brought out by the Appropriations Committee. Last year in our examination by them, they said that we were using money every year that we never told them about. It was pointed out that in the programing figures, and so on, that these recoupments were occurring, and we weren't counting them as part of the program. It does give you an awfully nice flexibility to deal with emergencies, of course, when you have money coming to your hand because it isn't used due to price changes and these other things that we have mentioned, the failure to call for deliveries, the slippages because people aren't ready to take delivery, the slippages because it doesn't come off the production line to be delivered. Because of all these things you have money in hand, but we weren't programing the use of that money in the regular way. 

The new thing that Secretary McNamara told you about this morning was, we are honestly putting the estimate of recoupments in this

program. This program counts upon $1.5 billion in new obligational authority, $200 million that we think we can get back by recoupment, and $25 million which is the tag end that won't get obligated by the end of the fiscal year. 

Does this answer the question?

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General. 

Mr. Chiperfield. 

Gentlemen, each year I have asked for three charts which I think have been helpful to the committee and helpful on the floor. The first of these show the amount we have spent on NATO since its beginning. 

Then the second item on that chart shows the amount that our allies in NATO have spent. And then the same chart, it shows the men under arms, the number of airplanes and the number of ships. The purpose is this: Many people think we pay out all the NATO expenses, and that chart will show that our NATO allies perhaps paid out five times as much during that period as ourselves. 

Then you have a chart that shows what it costs a year to maintain a Chinese soldier, a Siamese soldier, a soldier in Turkey, France, or England, however you wish to do it, and then what it costs to maintain a fully equipped U.S. soldier. 

In other words, we couldn't afford to do it by ourselves. Maybe it costs $3,000 to maintain a U.S. soldier in this country, and $500 in 

Japan for a Japanese soldier, or a Korean soldier in Korea for $300 or $400, whatever it is.

The third chart I would like to have show the same thing as far as those three categories are concerned with reference to the cost for our own services. I don't care how you go about it.
