The 2 sales agreements that have recently been publicized were the sale of 70 TV-2 aircraft-that is a 2-place single engine jet trainer which was obsolete for Navy use-and 130 F-86D's, the first models going back to 1948. It is an old plane and has been phased out of the National Guard, and there is considered to be a few in the program but otherwise obsolete. 

These transactions arise from a military assistance sales agreement with Yugoslavia that was entered into in 1957. This was a basic agreement that the Yugoslavs could come to us and ask for sales of this sort. Both these transactions, one in 1960 and one in 1961, were reviewed by the State and Defense Departments, and were finally cleared in late 1960 for the TV-2's and in January 1961, for the F- 86D's by the Eisenhower administration. The deliveries on those sales were carried through principally last fall, last September and October. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Do we know where these planes are located, and what they are actually doing in Yugoslavia? 

Mr. BUNDY. We have had the assurances of the Yugoslav Government that they actually arrived [security deletion]. We do not have any MAAG relationship with Yugoslavia at the present time. [Security deletion.] The total number of aircraft that we have supplied to 

Yugoslavia under the 1957 grant arrangements, plus these aircraft, is something in the order of 700. Those are all in Yugoslavia except those phased out.

Mr. BROOMFIELD. You mentioned the F-86 planes were obsolete. Is it not true in some of our NATO bases that we have a plane, the F-84, which is even older and still in use by NATO?

Mr. BUNDY. The F-84F is much more effective. [Security deletion.] 

General LEMNITZER. The F-86 is a single plane tactical fighter, whereas the F-84F is a fighter-bomber and is a very important part of our overall tactical fighter-bomber capability. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. I would like your opinion, General Lemnitzer, whether it is a good policy to continue giving these planes to Yugoslavia. I know you are not negotiating any deal. I wanted your own personal opinion about selling military aircraft to Yugoslavia. 

General LEMNITZER. Weighing the pros and cons, at the time the sales were made it was the opinion of the U.S. Government that it was in the national interest to make the sale. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Do you go along with this policy that we shouldn't know what these planes are doing, what they are using them for? 

General LEMNITZER. I would prefer to know what they are doing, what they are using them for, and we do know. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. It is true under your new program that they will still be able to purchase spare parts for these planes? 

Mr. BUNDY. Spare parts directly related to previous purchases are still being sold to the Yugoslavs. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Is there anything beyond that as far as parts that might be part of the military buildup or posture? 

Mr. BUNDY. Nothing that is not related directly to a previous purchase.

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you. 

Chairman MORGAN. Judge Saund. 

Mr. SAUND. General, in your statement you said this morning that the military assistance program will result in the inflow of gold. 

General LEMNITZER. I did not understand the question. 

Mr. SAUND. How would the military assistance program result in the inflow of gold to the United States? 

General LEMNITZER. Of the total military assistance program for 

1962, as an example, all except about $335 million, which is the only flow out of the country, it is estimated that approximately $800 million of U.S. military equipment, spare parts, and so on, will be purchased in the United States for dollars under the mutual security program. The largest purchaser is West Germany. They are buying a large number of tanks and personnel carriers, and they are paying cash for their purchases. The outflow of gold, represented by 

MAP dollars spent overseas, is much smaller than the dollars which enter the United States as the result of purchases made of U.S. military equipment manufactured in the United States. 

Mr. SAUND. How does that come under the category of military assistance? When Germany, India, or any other country buys caterpillars or bomber planes, they buy it for different reasons. When we give military assistance to any country we just give it to them. from our own funds.

General LEMNITZER. Grant aid is part of the program, but only a part. When the program was first established in 1950 we called this part of the military assistance program reimbursable aid. It is the military sales part of the program which enables friendly countries, through the mechanism of the military aid program, to buy U.S. equipment in the United States and pay for that equipment in U.S. dollars. 

Mr. BUNDY. May I add one thing, Congressman? In addition to the $722 million of direct sales, including heavy German purchases, we have the purchases that are made in the United States directly

from U.S. companies, as a result of the various cost-sharing agreements that were entered into in the past. Those are agreements where military assistance has put in part of the total kitty. For example, on the F-104 consortium deal in Europe where we put in $145 million against a contribution by the European participants of $1,188 million, our share was on the order of 1 to 9. The amount being spent in the United States, to U.S. contributors, which doesn't flow through 

Government hands, and isn't in the $722 million is $275 million. The total in fiscal 1963 from this kind of transaction is $418 million. 

That alone more than outweighs the $335 million in offshore procurement, and in infrastructure, and so forth-the expenditures overseas. Then you add to that-and I think it is justified to add to thatthe $722 million in direct sales, which is in large part negotiated by the military assistance advisory groups, and arises out of the whole relationship of which military assistance is a part, and you have a plus contribution to the balance-of-payments situation. 

Mr. SAUND. I won't argue with that. Maybe I can't understand it. 

You give $20 million to Korea in military assistance. What effect does that have on Germany buying bombers in the United States?

I was not satisfied with an answer of the Secretary this morning to the question: Why are not some of the forces of other SEATO countries, as volunteers or technicians, being used in Vietnam? I have in mind the reasons why the United States or the Russians or the British forces are not used by the U.N. in the Congo. There is a reason for that. I can understand what it means. For propaganda purposes, it may not be good policy to use white soldiers in Vietnam. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. BUNDY. I don't know if we approached them specifically to this end. [Security deletion.] The South Vietnamese were looking to us. 

I would like to ask General Lemnitzer to expand on that as point 1. 

[Security deletion.] 

General LEMNITZER. As a result of the Geneva accord of 1954, South 

Vietnam was established as a separate government. It was the policy of the United States to assist that Government with a Military Advisory Group, to raise forces and to assist in the very difficult economic situation in which they found themselves. 

I can recall, and I think members of this committee can recall, that in 1954 and 1955 there were many people in this country who wouldn't have given a plugged nickel for chances of keeping South Vietnam from being dragged behind the Iron Curtain. We had a MAAG there as part of our commitment. We also had a U.S. mission there which handled our economic aid program. It is largely the results of these two efforts in assisting Vietnam that kept South Vietnam on this side of the Iron Curtain. The recently increased Viet Cong guerrilla action and subversion efforts, however, have required a higher level of activity on the part of both the Governments of Vietnam and the 

United States.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. General Lemnitzer, can you tell us about the extent of our paramilitary efforts? Is the budget for paramilitary activities included in the military aid program? 

General LEMNITZER. Our teams with the South Vietnamese forces assist in their training-paramilitary operation. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. We were told last year that paramilitary forces and operations would provide the best deterrent against guerrilla activities

and Communist activities in southeast Asia. We were told that type of activity would be stepped up. I wondered if it has been stepped up under our military assistance program- 

General LEMNITZER. The U.S. Army has [security deletion] special forces which are particularly trained, organized, and equipped for counterguerrilla or guerrilla operations. These teams in both Laos and South Vietnam only assist in training the Lao and South Vietnamese. That is the only use presently being made of them. We have not and do not use these forces in combat either in Laos or in Vietnam. They are there to assist the Vietnamese and the Lao forces in training.

Mr. CHIPERFIELD. Judge Saund, you were raising the same question 

I asked this morning. [Security deletion.] Why didn't we consider that if we were going in there we would have to have SEATO's help? 

General LEMNITZER. [Security deletion.] The cease-fire in Laos is still a cease-fire. The operations in South Vietnam today are covert guerrilla insurgency-type operations. I would say that if there is open aggression or a resumption of hostilities in Laos with the Pathet Lao reinforced with the Vietminh it will be up to SEATO to consider [security deletion] whether or not SEATO forces are to be put in to stem the tide of communism in southeast Asia.

[Security deletion.] We can look again to see if something should be substituted, but I think the initial feeling will be to keep the bird in the hand.

General LEMNITZER. [Security deletion.]

But however late it is, it is going to be later tomorrow.

Colonel EATON. The strategic importance of Europe to the United 

States, and the part that NATO plays in the defense of freedom may be summarized by the following two statements made by President Kennedy:

The defense of Europe and the assurances that can be given to the people of Europe, and the defense of North America, are in divisible.

and Our NATO alliance is still as it was when it was founded, the world's greatest bulwark of freedom.

The extent of our military assistance programs for individual European countries has been reduced appreciably in recent years, and this reduction is even more pronounced in the programs proposed for fiscal year 1963.

Both the country and regional materiel programs take into full account the increased financial capabilities of individual countries to meet their own requirements, and the measures they are taking to this end. 

In the application of this increasingly selective approach: 

As in recent years, new grant materiel programs continued to be excluded for Germany, Luxembourg, France, and the United Kingdom. This policy has been extended this year to include Belgium, Italy, and the Netherlands, in view of the improved economic situations in these countries.

Colonel EATON. Sir, this concludes my statement. I would like to, if I may, summarize what I think are the highlights, the significance of this presentation. There are five points which occur to me to be significant.

First, the Department of Defense is paying continued attention to the reduction of our Military Assistance Programs in Europe. This is represented by a reduction this year in approximately $100 million to those programs, and by the policy decision to delete three additional coountries this year from new materiel undertakings: Belgium, Italy, and the Netherlands.

Second, even among the European countries which might be termed "well off," we must recognize our existing commitments from the past. 

Third, there are two programs which tend to be listed as straight aid but which I feel are of benefit to us individually or multilaterally. 

First, there are the continued training programs which bring foreign students to the United States to see our way of life, our materiel, our equipment, our training objectives, [security deletion] and we hope they not only will buy equipment, but that this will tie them more closely to the United States. [Security deletion] Germany, which is of course able to pay for all of its own, [security deletion] as a matter of fact is spending in cash some $10 million to train in the United States in fiscal year 1962. 

There are also the multilateral obligations [security deletion]. 

Fourth, there [security deletion] are continuing programs for Norway, Denmark, and Portugal. [Security deletion.]

Fifth, there is the special case of [security deletion] Spain. 

[Security deletion.]

STATEMENT OF WILLIAM R. TYLER, ACTING ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EUROPEAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. TYLER. I would be very happy to, Mr. Chairman.

I have no prepared statement, but if I may I would like to make a few comments on the political developments affecting the European area since Assistant Secretary Kohler appeared before this committee last June, and then address myself to one or two points which I believe are of interest to this committee, including matters relating to Italy. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If you will proceed, sir. 

Mr. TYLER. Mr. Chairman, since June of last year, when Mr.

Kohler appeared before this committee, the situation in Europe and in particular in the area of our relations with the Soviet Union has not in the slightest evolved in a favorable or less dangerous direction. 

The Berlin crisis has continued to preoccupy us very greatly, and the presentation of the aide memoire by Khrushchev in June of last year was followed by preparations on our part to ward off the threat and danger, to make adequate preparations for strengthening our defenses in the light of the declared aggressive intentions of the Soviet Union.

We have engaged in considerable consultation with our NATO allies, and we have urged them to increase their defense efforts, to increase their contribution to the whole Western defense program. 

I would like at this point, if I may, to give some detailed indications of the fact that our efforts have been successful, though not to the extent that we would really ideally hope, but we have made some progress in influencing our NATO allies to contribute a larger share to our collective defense efforts. 

The total of defense expenditures for the European NATO countries last year was, as I believe Colonel Eaton has already referred to, $15.3 billion, which is an increase of about 25 percent over the amount which was spent in 1958. 

The trend toward increased defense expenditures is expected to continue. Every NATO country has increased its defense expenditures this year over the previous year. 

The Netherlands is planning a significant increase in its defense spending in 1962. 

Norway has announced a 7.6-percent increase.

And in 1960 the Italian Government put into effect a 4-percent progressive annual increase, and more recently the Italian Government has obtained parliamentary consent to accelerate this increase. 

The Belgian defense budget for 1962, which was recently approved by the Parliament, represents a 4.6-percent increase over 1961. 

And the French military. budget for 1962 is 3 percent over last year's.

German defense expenditures have nearly doubled between 1958 and 1961.

Whereas in 1953 the United States was paying about one-quarter of the total defense expenditures of our European NATO allies, in 1961 we paid less than 4 percent, and this includes Greece and Turkey. 

We will continue to make all efforts to urge our NATO allies to increase their defense expenditures. We believe that there has been some response to our efforts, though I repeat, Mr. Chairman, we do not consider that the efforts that have been made hitherto are adequate and we will continue to press them. 

I would now like to address myself, if I may, for a few minutes to the situation in Italy. 

As you may know, Mr. Chairman, there has recently been a political development in Italy which has been widely commented on in the press and which is referred to as the "opening to the left." 

The background of this development really consists of the chronic inability of Italian governments since the war to find a broad base of parliamentary support.

They have been unstable because they have had tiny parliamentary majorities. The Christian Democratic Party, which formed the last government before this new one which has just come into power, only had 46 percent of Parliament behind it, and it could therefore not govern without support from the left or right. 

There have been differences within the Christian Democratic Party as to whether the alinement should be toward the right or toward the left, and each wing within the Christian Democratic Party has pulled in its own direction. The result has been, as previously, that there have been unstable governments in Italy, and they have not been capable

because of this instability to carry out vigorous and sustained programs. 

During these years prosperity has increased in Italy, in spite of the instability of the governments. The economic progress has been spectacular. The gross national product has risen 7 percent a year in real terms for the last 7 years.

With this increasing prosperity there has been developing a new trend in Italian domestic political thinking. The Socialist Party, the so-called PSI, has, since events in Hungary, been moving in a direction toward relative independence of the Communist Party. 

Previous to that, the Socialist Party of Italy and the Communist Party had been linked by a common action program which really made them more or less indistinguishable from each other in their influence and effect in internal affairs and their behavior in Parliament.

Since Hungary, there has been this trend, as I say, toward a divergence between the Italian Socialist Party and the Italian Communist Party.

There has, of course, been opposition to cooperation with the Italian Socialist Party from those people in Italy who feared that such cooperation would have adverse effects on Italy's foreign policy. 

But increasingly there have been signs that the Socialist Party was trying to find a way to disassociate itself from the allegiance which it had previously rendered to the Communist Party. And the Italian who has been at the head of this, what is called the autonomous trend in Italian politics and the Italian Socialist Party, is Nenni. 

Pietro Nenni, who has long been a leader of the Italian Socialist Party, has taken positions which have increased the belief that it might be possible for a cooperative arrangement to be arrived at in Italy, whereby a government would be brought into power which would have the support of the Italian Socialist Party in Parliament, the Italian Socialist Party in return agreeing to abstain on votes of confidence and agreeing more or less to accept passively and not to go into declared opposition against Italian foreign policy. 

So this government, which has just come to power, came into being. 

It is made up of the Christian Democratic Party which is the largest party in Italy. It is the party that has been most active in support of NATO and in support of European integration policies. 

The government also has within it the Democratic Socialists who are moderate or rightwing Socialists who some time ago broke from the Socialist Party. 

The ministers of the new government include the foreign minister of the previous Italian Government, Foreign Minister Segni, who is well known to us and who has long been an advocate of NATO and 

Western defense and of European integration.

It also includes the previous Defense Minister Andreotti, who is also well known to us and is a stanch advocate of all our major 

Western policies and goals.

The program of the new government is not yet announced but is expected to be based on the following: No change in foreign policy. 

Some new internal measures, such as school construction and better taxation and modernization of Government operation and nationalization of atomic energy.

At this point, Mr. Chairman, if I may, I would like to go off the record and express some political considerations with regard to the prospects. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Off the record. 

(Discussion off the record.) 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Tyler.

I am sure your reply will be helpful. My only regret is that the latter part of your discussion, in which you did not refer directly to what could be a very sensitive matter for the Italian Government, was not included in the record. 

Can that be made available for the members who are interested? 

Mr. TYLER. I would defer to Colonel Eaton on this. 

Colonel EATON. I am not sure of what you are speaking.

STATEMENT OF A. W. ROBINSON, JR., ASSISTANT DIRECTOR OF DEFENSE RESEARCH AND ENGINEERING (INTERNATIONAL PROGRAMS), DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE 

Mr. ROBINSON. Could I take 2 minutes to place my answer in the proper framework?

The mutual weapons development program is now going through somewhat of a transition. When it started 8 years ago it was primarily an aid program to individual countries who could benefit from it, such as France, United Kingdom, and so on. 

We are now going through a transition, first, because the countries who received most of the aid then do not require it now. [Security deletion.]

These now have the necessary potential capability for research and development. This is a shift in countries eligible for our support. 

Second, the bulk of our programs soon will be going toward doing our share of the support of NATO rather than of individual countries. 

In this case we are contributing in cooperation with other countries, in trying to make cooperative research and development in support of NATO work as well as possible. 

This is slower than we would like to have it, because when you are trying to get 15 nations together on something as intangible as R. & D., it is rather unwieldy. 

There are a number of NATO working groups trying to get certain R. & D. projects started. We are working with about every single one of those working groups, wherever we see good possibilities and a general interest.

As we see the mutual weapons development program, it will place its emphasis more and more on the projects of overall NATO interest; in other words, doing our share of the NATO work. And I would say that, with this cooperative effort getting started, we will get better standardization of equipment, better utilization of technical manpower. The more of these projects that get going, the more they will require mutual weapons development financing. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. ROBINSON. There are a number of cooperative NATO projects underway, such as the maritime patrol aircraft, which is a five-nation cooperative development. The second prototype of this airplane flew a few days ago.

There are other projects where possible cooperative developments are being studied by the NATO group which includes a good proportion of U.S. experts. 

Mr. ADAIR. Thank you, sir. 

Mr. ROBINSON. This is a little general background. 

Mr. ADAIR. That is very helpful.

I observe now on page 93 of the book the list of items which are involved here.

Mr. ROBINSON. Right.

Mr. ROBINSON. You are talking about the Hawker 

Mr. ADAIR. It was not a vertical takeoff.

Mr. ROBINSON. We are definitely avoiding putting any funds in a program in a country like the United Kingdom or France, which would be strictly to help that country. In other words, a program for us to contribute would have to be of a general NATO usefulness, rather than this particular country. 

Mr. ADAIR. That is my question.

Mr. ROBINSON. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. ROBINSON. These projects are scrutinized to be sure that the concept being evaluated is of broad NATO battlefield interest, not just of interest to one country. In particular, we want to avoid supporting a country for a development which merely allows it to compete in the foreign market. 

Mr. ADAIR. This is the question, the last few words you have said have answered my question. 

Mr. Chairman-excuse me.

Mr. ROBINSON. I was going to say you will notice there is now a trend down in the funds earmarked for the mutual weapons development program. The more rapidly we can get these NATO countries, the key countries that have developed those capabilities, to participate in cooperative effort, the more opportunity we will have to contribute to worthwhile overall NATO efforts.

Mr. BARRY.  

Gentlemen, I think the significant thing that caught my eye in what has been presented thus far was the fact that basically Europe is providing around 96.7 percent of Europe's total military requirements, and it is only 3.7 percent, as you brought out in your statement, that we are supplying.

It doesn't leave a lot of room for us to cut down. Since we are ahead of Europe in development as indicated in testimony brought out by Mr. Frelinghuysen, training programs along technical lines where we have that know-how, such as in missile development are essential. 

What I didn't quite understand when Mr. Tyler was addressing himself to us, was that one of the Italian political parties is proposing a unified Germany, which was referred to as in accordance with our policy.

Some of us here on the committee have been urging the Executive to toughen our position in Berlin and elsewhere in Eastern Europe, and to hammer away at a unified Germany, so that when we go to the bargaining table we will have something to give up that we don't really believe we are going to get, rather than just negotiating the demands of the opposition.

I am very enthusiastic about hearing that there is support among our NATO partners for making a similar demand. I think it would be helpful if the President is willing to embarrass himself to ask for something he knows he isn't going to get, which a dictator can do

Khrushchev has no qualms about talking on one tack and then changing it. He doesn't have to get reelected. It takes a courageous man to ask for something that he knows he isn't going to get in the kind of society we have where a political leader has to go to the voters and say "Vote for our party anyway, even though we know we failed to get what we claimed we would get." 

Mr. TYLER. The key word which I should have mentioned, if I did not mention it when I made my statement, is the word "neutralized," a reunified neutralized Germany. That is what would be very dangerous for us.

We have in the last 12 years been pressing for the reunification of Germany and freedom based on free elections so the German people can determine what kind of government they want to have. 

The Soviet Union has persistently refused to agree to free elections in that part of Germany which it controls. 

We, of course, cannot be a party to conditions of reunification which would make it easier for the Soviet Union to move westward into Europe, into the Rhine and beyond. 

We have constantly resisted reunification except on terms where the German people could say what they want. 

We have every confidence if the Soviet Union would agree to that, that Ulbricht and his regime would be swept out of power.. 

The Soviet Union knows that and won't accept it. 

When people talk about the reunification of Germany on the basis of the neutrality of Germany, we see in this merely a device which would benefit the Soviet Union and would make the people of West Germany feel they had been abandoned, because they don't feel neutral and they feel a part of the West. 

The Italian Socialist position with regard to the reunification of Germany is consistent with ours insofar as the idea of reunification goes, but not so far as the neutralization of Germany goes. 

Mr. BARRY. My castle has been destroyed as quickly as it was built. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Is there any part at all on our side of it, the West, that the reunification of Germany might possibly mean in some years to come another desire for a German empire?

Mr. TYLER. I think that a great deal of thought has been given to that. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Surely the Russians are thinking that..

Mr. TYLER. Yes. That is why our policy and that of Chancellor 

Adenauer have had other things in common. The whole task of the 

West is to integrate Germany thoroughly into the Western framework, so that never again would it be possible for the German people to be- 

Mrs. BOLTON. Far-reaching words "never again."

Mr. BARRY. Is the MWDP program administered by NATO in Paris?

Mr. ROBINSON. The mutual weapons development program is a 

U.S. program which works primarily with NATO, but also with individual countries. It is a U.S. program administered by the Department of Defense.

Mr. BARRY. Here in this country?

Mr. ROBINSON. It is administered here in this country, with a group of U.S. people in Paris, one block away from the NATO headquarters. 

This is the U.S. name 

Mr. BARRY. It doesn't pyramid to General Norstad, it pyramids to our Chief of Staff and the Secretary of Defense? 

Mr. ROBINSON. Yes.

Mr. BARRY. It has been in existence for 8 years? 

Mr. ROBINSON. Yes.

Mr. BARRY. In your opinion, has it been satisfactory? I noticed you were reluctant to give it great praise in your answer to previous questions.

Mr. ROBINSON. I think my reason for this is that there were certain initial objectives which were met. We are now in a period of transition in the objectives. 

The original objective of the program was to help individual countries, such as the United Kingdom, France, and so on, to develop their own research and development capabilities so they would be in this position of developing their own equipment and equipping themselves rather than depending on the United States. This was mentioned before in the discussion of France. 

These countries, thanks to their increase in both economic strength and in research and development capabilities, do not now require this kind of help. However, some other countries are in a position where they now have the potential to start absorbing this type of help. But more important NATO, as a body, the alliance, is getting more and more in a position of being able to sponsor cooperative research and development programs for the NATO battlefield as a whole. 

So the emphasis is going from the help to the individual countrieswhich was the original objective and was quite well met—to the help of NATO, which is now starting up. 

Mr. BARRY. When NATO is developed to the extent that all member countries having military problems in the development field can find solutions at NATO instead of MWDP, this is a program that could be cut out, isn't it? This is a program that will no longer be required when once it launches every country up to a point where it is possible to key their development, or to transfer it to ÑNATO development. 

Mr. ROBINSON. I think what you are talking about is a bookkeeping change. If we are going to be contributing our share to NATO, there is a certain element of contribution to NATO research and development which now is being made through the mutual weapons development program. 

Mr. BARRY. This then is our liaison to NATO? 

Mr. ROBINSON. So we may say that if we no longer have a mutual weapons development program, we should support NATO through some other instrumentality. It amounts to a change in name. 

Mr. BARRY. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If there are no further questions, the meeting stands adjourned. (Whereupon, at 12:40 p.m., the committee adjourned, to reconvene at the call of the Chair.)

STATEMENT OF BRIG. GEN. STEPHEN 0. FUQUA, JR., U.S. ARMY, DIRECTOR, NEAR EAST, SOUTH ASIA, AND AFRICA REGION, OFFICE OF THE ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF DEFENSE FOR IN- TERNATIONAL SECURITY AFFAIRS 

General FUQUA. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a privilege to appear before you for the purpose of discussing the military assistance program in the Near East and south Asia region. 

In the Near East and south Asia region, the cumulative program to June 30, 1962, will total $4.6 billion, of which it is expected $4 billion will have been expended by that date and $652 million will still be in the pipeline.

The proposed fiscal year 1963 military assistance program for the Near East and south Asia region is $422.9 million, which is one-half million more than the fiscal year 1962 program of $422.4 million. We propose fiscal year 1963 grant aid programs for nine countries in this region, the same number as in fiscal year 1962. Of the nine countries, Greece, Turkey, Iran, and Pakistan account for 98 percent of the total requirement.

STRATEGIC SIGNIFICANCE TO THE UNITED STATES 

This region is important strategically to the United States because of its focal position on major sea, air, and land routes of the world, because control of the region as a base of operations is critically important either to ourselves or to the Communist bloc; and because it contains 65 percent of all petroleum resources which are not behind the Iron Curtain.

Greece and Turkey are members of NATO; Turkey, Iran, and 

Pakistan are members of CENTO; and Pakistan is also a member of SEATO. 

The loss of any part of this region to the Communist bloc would have far reaching and very dangerous effects. No country in the. area is industrially able to support effective armed forces and in gen-

eral the low economic standard cannot be improved without outside aid.

I will now discuss the individual country programs. 

Afghanistan: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Afghanistan [security deletion] provides for the continuation of a training program [security deletion]. 

Greece: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Greece is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than in fiscal year 1962. 

Force improvement in fiscal year 1962 amounted to [security deletion], while [security deletion] is proposed in this category for fiscal year 1963.

The essentially fixed charges and force maintenance requirements in Greece remain practically the same for fiscal year 1963 as in fiscal year 1962. Greece is strategically important to the United States basically because of its geographic relation to the Turkish Straits. 

Both the United States and NATO enjoy important base rights in Greece.

Iran: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Iran is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than in fiscal year 1962. Force improvements in fiscal year 1962 amounted to [security deletion] whereas in fiscal year 1963 we propose [security deletion]. 

The essentially fixed charges and force maintenance requirements in fiscal year 1963 are [security deletion] less than in fiscal year 1962. 

As an active member of CENTO, Iran makes an important contribution to the defense of a key section of the Middle East from both a strategic and resources-particularly oil-viewpoint. 

Iraq: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Iraq is [security deletion]. The program consists only of training [security deletion]. 

Jordan: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Jordan is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than it was in fiscal year 1962. [Security deletion.] Our program in Jordan is designed to help maintain the existing friendly government. 

Lebanon: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Lebanon is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than it was in fiscal year 1962. The program consists only of training. 

[Security deletion.] 

Pakistan: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Pakistan is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than in fiscal year 1962. Pakistan is strongly pro-United States and is important strategically to the United States because of its membership in both CENTO and SEATO, and because geographically Pakistan lies athwart the historic land approaches to the Indian subcontinent from central Asia.

Saudi Arabia: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Saudi 

Arabia is security deletion] which is [security deletion] than in fiscal year 1962. Saudi Arabia is strategically important to the 

United States because of its oil resources. The fiscal year 1963 program will furnish training and training aids only. 

Turkey: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Turkey is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than in fiscal year 1962. 

[Security deletion.]

Force improvement in fiscal year 1962 amounted to [security deletion] while [security deletion] is proposed in this category for fiscal year 1963. The essentially fixed charges and force maintenance requirements in Turkey remain practically the same for fiscal year 1963 as in fiscal year 1962. 

[Security deletion.] AREA PROGRAMS 

The Near East and south Asia area program proposed for fiscal year 1963 is [security deletion] which is [security deletion] than in fiscal year 1962. The program includes [security deletion] for operation and maintenance of a military assistance program stockpile in [security deletion] and [security deletion] for the U.S. share of the estimated fiscal year 1963 operating costs of CENTO headquarters in Ankara, Turkey. The cost of these two operations is the same as in fiscal year 1962. 

The remaining amount of [security deletion] in the proposed fiscal year 1963 area program is for training [security deletion]. 

In summary our major programs are concentrated in Greece, Turkey, Iran, and Pakistan and are designed to assist those countries as necessary to achieve or maintain conditions which will enhance their ability to maintain internal security and bolster their will to resist Communist subversion and aggression. 

The other country programs in the area are principally confined to training with the objective of maintaining a pro-Western influence. 

Sir, this completes my statement.

General PALMER. We know, or at least have reason to believe from reports we have from the MAAG countries that of all the materiel programed, the money which has been spent for military materiel rather than services, 64.2 percent is still in the inventory and still serviceable.

Of course, the 36 percent which is no longer in inventory includes all the ammunition that has been fired up, all the petroleum, oil, and lubricants that has been used up, all the trucks and stuff that have worn out.

Of the total amount that has been given for military assistance for the purchase of things, 64.2 percent remains in the inventory and serviceable as of the 30th of last June 1961. That represents a much lower rate of depreciation, actually, than the inventories of the U.S. services. Of course, this equipment isn't used as hard probably as it is used in our services. It is a reasonable depreciation or writeoff for the equipment over a period of time. 

It would be perfect folly, Mr. Whalley, for me to tell you that the military assistance program is 100 percent effective, when you are giving this equipment to many people who hadn't seen anything more mechanical than a camel 10 or 12 years ago.

We are trying to lift these people up to approximately our level of sophistication in no time at all. There has inevitably been slowness to learn. But this is the equipment, the only equipment that would do them any good to fight a war if they get into it and they are just having to learn. We are having to teach them as best we can while they are using the stuff at the same time. 

It has been, I want to tell you, a heartbreaking process for our people who have been out in the field working on this. It has been really a backbreaking job. It has gotten a great deal better, but still if the time ever comes when you can say it is of high class-we haven't gotten there yet.

Mr. WHALLEY. How is the schedule for military assistance set up in the first place? Does the country getting the assistance make the request? Do they tell you what they would like to have?

General PALMER. We have these Military Assistance Advisory 

Groups, or MAAG's, in each country. The country forces and MAAĞ are working together. Of course they are in close consultation all the time because that is what we have the advisory group there for.

The country is consulted as to what they feel they could use, whether they feel they could use it, in fact. They would like to get a lot of stuff. [Security deletion.] 

It is worked out in the field. The MAAG, country team, the Ambassador, and the economic assistance people have all consulted on this thing and made it up. It then goes to the U.S. unified commander. Admiral Felt, who will be here this afternoon, represents the whole Asian area, Far East. General Norstad, who I believe is to be with you on Friday of this week-this area we are talking about today comes under his jurisdiction. In the unified command headquarters where they have a broader view and a more complete understanding of the whole thing, they give it a good going over, and trim it down, of course, to come within the fiscal limits. There is a tremendous weighting of priorities in this whole thing-what comes first; what is most important because we never have the money to support everything we would like to. 

Finally, it comes in here to Washington. 

Mr. WHALLEY. Wouldn't it be better to send in about two-thirds as much equipment and send in more people to show them how to set the thing up, their inventories and their spare parts? It appears a lot of equipment is sent that they don't need or don't want. Mr. Mc- 

Namara has had tremendous experience in industry and you would think that would be the first thing he would set up, the type organization that would be able to handle this equipment and put the project in first-class shape.

Are we allowed to send in a lot of people to train these people and keep them there?

General PALMER. A number. We can give you the figures on it country by country. 

Mr. WHALLEY. How do we do as compared to Russia? Is their system more effective?

General PALMER. I don't think it is any more effective, Mr. Whalley. 

Of course, the Russian military assistance embraces all they give to their satellites who are practically in their own front yard, you might say, and it also embraces what they give to Cuba and to Egypt and to places of that sort, where I suspect it is very badly cared for indeed. 

Mr. WHALLEY. It would appear in a case of an emergency from what Mr. Pilcher and Dr. Judd and others say that these countries wouldn't be ready to do the job. 

General PALMER. No country has ever gone into a war really ready to do the job that they were called upon to do. There are always defects. I assure you that our inspector general and the General 

Accounting Office go around finding fault with our own services right here in the United States on almost as liberal a scale of fancy adjectives as they use to describe the [security deletion]. 

Mr. WHALLEY. The best thing to do would be to effect a plan that is more capable. I am in the automobile business. Of course Mr. 

McNamara was in the same company and the same business. I know what it is even with a parts room over 2 or 3 years of time if you don't have an expert parts man. I suppose the same thing would be for a spare parts program on other countries. You can't have equipment on the road unless you have the parts for it.

General PALMER. I wish Mr. McNamara was here to talk to you about this. Last year he said, I think to this committee, that he could take you into the best run companies of the United States—and he named Ford, General Electric, American Telephone-and find the same deficiencies that we are finding in these recipient countries, and that this problem was not going to be solved in a year or 2 years. He made that statement.

Mr. WHALLEY. He is aware of the situation and will do his best to make it succeed. 

General PALMER. Very much so.

Mr. JUDD. McNamara's and Whalley's Fords are on the road going, and these [security deletion] are not firing. If an emergency came, they are not in condition to fire. 

Chairman MORGAN. Any further questions? 

Mr. JUDD. One thing more, Mr. Chairman. I believe they ought not to use this per capita business as an argument. We have heard that through the years. It may impress somebody, but it doesn't impress this committee. There are countries where our aid has been $1,000 per capita, and it ought to be in terms of the security of the United States. There are other places where it ought to be $2 per capita. Saying that we have given $15 per capita to the Pakistanis as compared to $8 per capita to the Indians doesn't mean we have treated them better than we ought. Take a country like Laos. Per capita, we have given it enormous amounts. If you consider the length of its borders with Red China and North Vietnam, that is a great deal different-it may be far too little aid. Maybe the aid ought to be based to some extent on the strategic location, geography, resources, and so forth, rather than the number of people. Sometimes the attitude of the government and people of the country is also a great deal more important than their number. 

Chairman MORGAN. Any further questions? 

Thank you, General Palmer. The committee stands adjourned until 2:30 this afternoon. (Whereupon, at 12:40 p.m. the committee adjourned, to reconvene at 2:30 p.m.)

AFTERNOON SESSION 

(The committee reconvened at 2:30 p.m., the Honorable Thomas E. 

Morgan, chairman, presiding.) 

This after- noon we continue hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

Our witness this afternoon is Adm. H. D. Felt, U.S. commander in chief, Pacific.

Admiral Felt has been before the committee several times and we are glad to welcome him this afternoon. 

Admiral, without further ado, you may start your testimony.

STATEMENT OF ADM. H. D. FELT, U.S. NAVY, COMMANDER IN 

CHIEF, PACIFIC 

Admiral FELT. I have a written statement, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman MORGAN. You may proceed. 

Admiral FELT. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I 

appreciate the opportunity to appear before you and make a state-

ment in regard to the military assistance program which is essential to the forward strategy carried out by the United States in the Pacific area. Diplomacy has woven the fabric of our strategy. It could not have been done, however, without the muscles of not only our own armed power but also the military strengths which our aid has helped to build up in the free countries of Asia. 

Aggressions against our friends and allies in Asia continue. Currently, we are dealing with subversion and insurgency. 

In Korea, Okinawa, Thailand, Burma, and Indonesia, Communist organizers are attempting to subvert the people, with their ultimate goal the overthrow of recognized authority. 

In Laos and South Vietnam, Communists have taken up more violent means to attain their ends by using armed force against the people, their officials and their protective security units. All of these aggressions are controlled and supported from outside the countries under attack.

The aggressors maintain strong bases and military forces in Red China, North Korea, eastern U.S.S.R., and in North Vietnam. Supplies and replacements come across the Bamboo Curtain and into the territory of men who are living free of bondage. Routes for supplies, propaganda agents and guerrilla units can become invasion routes if the Communists should decide that there is acceptable risk in the venture.

I have just been to southeast Asia. In South Vietnam a vicious war is being waged. The Communist armed forces, called the Viet 

Cong, are conducting a campaign of terror, ambush, assassination, armed raids, and sabotage. Hanoi announced last September that insurgent activities would be stepped up in South Vietnam. Thus we find a Soviet-Sino satellite openly announcing direct support of insurgent terrorism in another country. 

The guerrilla Viet Congs are getting support and sanctuary from across the border. The guerrilla irregulars and the regulars of the 

Viet Cong operate against governmental authority and levy requisitions on the population in hamlets and villages. Their aim is the piecemeal destruction of Government forces and leaders. They raid and burn. They murder civilian officials. They kidnap boys of military age. They tolerate no neutrals. They plunder and kill those who do not join them. When the rural populace cannot depend on 

Government protection, the people become victims of Communist intimidation and violence. It can and will be stopped-with the help of the American military assistance programs. It will take time and material. It will take fighters. Time is neutral. As to fighting qualities, the South Vietnamese are now on the offensive and they do not regard the Viet Cong as 10 feet tall. I can assure you that the people in our military assistance groups are superb. They are assisting with concepts, techniques, communications, and transport. With the combination of skills and strengths and by living up to our commitments, there is no question as to who will win this war. 

In Laos, there has been a cease-fire during which a negotiated settlement has been sought to achieve a free, independent and truly neutral nation. Security and safety of the people is basic to achieving such a settlement.

In Thailand, Communist subversive elements are at work in the north and northeast territories into which agitators have infiltrated.

The Government is taking civic and military actions with our assistance to control the situation and not let it grow into more dangerous terroristic insurgency. 

Cambodia is threatened.

Korea and the Republic of China live under the threat of overt invasion. 

Such is the situation. 

Since I have the military responsibility for defending the United States from attack through the Pacific and to help carry out foreign policy in the area, the image of free world strength in the minds of Communist strategists is terribly important to me. The ability of our combined strength to deny Communist domination of our peoples lies in the credibility given to those strengths by the Communists. 

A basic factor is their assessment of our armed force in terms of types and mix—our abilities to use it at critical points of decision-and our will not to avoid conflict if fight we must to preserve the interests of free men.

We on our side must maintain a military force responsive to the threats and fully capable of causing the Communists to fear results of rash actions on their part. The basic guarantee in the Pacific area is in the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force striking power which is assigned to my command. U.S. ships, planes, weapon systems, techniques, and fighting men are fundamental to preserving the freedom of all men in my area.

The mutual arrangements we have made with allies makes it possible not only to project our power overseas into the continent of Âsia but also to sustain our forward position along the periphery of the Communist-controlled mainland. Equally essential to the building of strength on our side are the security forces of the nations in the Western Pacific and southeast Asia. It is mainly the U.S. efforts which guarantee preservation of integrity and independence of all free men. We must pay a price, therefore, to help Asian nations insure the safety of their peoples.

How can we demonstrate the U.S. national will to preserve the freedom of men who wish to remain free? We must first continue with the premise that superiority of American strength in the Pacific must be maintained. This is fundamental-without U.S. fighting superiority, there is no hope for freedom. But, closely associated with this basic premise are the needs of free people in Asia to have the means for maintaining law and order in their own countries. From lessons learned in the past, we know that insurgency must be countered by the intended victims. Our military assistance programs in the 

Pacific are designed to provide the people of Asia the means and the will to carry their own responsibilities. They will continue to have the will if they have the conviction that there is genuine safety in their association in the combined effort. 

The fiscal year 1963 military assistance program before you represents a carefully considered combined effort. It is designed to preserve security and freedoms for millions of our fellow men. 

I thank you for hearing me and I recommend your support of the program now being considered by your committee. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Admiral.

Admiral, I understand you are also prepared to brief us about the current situation in South Vietnam and Laos. Would you wish to speak to some of the current situation now? 

Admiral FELT. Yes, Mr. Chairman. Would you like to see a chart?

Chairman MORGAN. Yes. 

Admiral FELT. This is going to be a little difficult. Maybe we will all have to get around here. It is not very big. 

I present this a little bit differently. Some of you have seen it in my shop out in Hawaii. I present it differently than in the normal case. Can you see it back there? 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral FELT. The terrain is different in each of the [security deletion] areas. In the north it is very rugged, and with very few communications, roads, and so forth. In the second [security deletion] area, the central area, it is what they call the plateau area, although it is quite rugged. I flew over it the other day. The third [security deletion] area is the delta area. Populationwise, the greatest concentration of population is in the delta area. 

For orientation, there is Saigon, the capital city. In this area there are tribesmen, just as there are in Laos, who traditionally have known loyalty only to their tribal chieftains. 

In this area there are still some of the religious sects which although defeated by Diem in 1954-55, still have loyal followers.

The little men you see on the chart, the blue men are the armed forces of the Government of Vietnam. You can see how they are spread throughout the country. The red men are the Viet Cong. The men of this size are of battalion or battalion equivalent, and the smaller are of company and company equivalents. 

Here are the figures on the numbers in each of the corps areas. 

ARVN means the Regular Army of Vietnam. You see this [security deletion]. This reflects the population concentration. 

This is Civil Guard, and it is in companies. A company goes from anywhere from 100 to 190-some people. You can see there are [security deletion] a lot of Civil Guard here. 

In addition, and not shown on the chart, is an organization called the Self-Defense Corps. The regular forces are up around [security deletion] total today. The majority of it Army, but a little Air 

Force and a little Navy, both getting better. Then we have the Civil 

Guard, which in a province is like our National Guard. A province chief will have charge of the Civil Guard. And then Self-Defense 

Corps, which are village defense organizations. 

One of the encouraging things about the situation in South Vietnam today is that some few months ago President Diem agreed that the training of the Civil Guard and Self-Defense Corps would go to the Department of Defense in Vietnam. They, in turn, came to us and we with our military assistance program are now training the Civil Guard and the Self-Defense Corps. This is good. It is very good.

That gives you a picture of the "measles" that is in South Vietnam and has been there for some long time. 

Perhaps I better let it go at that, Mr. Chairman. 

Would you like to ask me more questions about this? I can tell you about some recent actions if you would like to hear that.

Mr. ADAIR. How about the American measles on that? 

Admiral FELT. We have, for example [security deletion], U.S. 

Army helicopters [security deletion] in the country now. The Vietnamese have some of their own. [Security deletion.] 

Mrs. CHURCH. What is the composition of a helicopter company? 

Admiral FELT. About 20 helicopters and a couple of small ones to get around in. The type of helicopter is the H-21, the Banana twin rotor thing. [Security deletion.] 

I think I have said this before, when I have had the privilege of appearing before this committee, that as one studies this problem and looks at this problem he is convinced immediately that the No. 1 and 

2 priority items are transportation and communications. 

Mr. BARRY. Where is the buildup of supplies coming from the opposite direction, from those that the Soviet Union is dropping? 

Admiral FELT. Here is the 17th parallel. Here is Laos. This is the Ho Chi Minh trail. Over these trails with coolies have come supplies and infiltrators in about five different places through here. 

[Security deletion]. 

Mr. JUDD. How many are coming by sea and how far down the coast?

Admiral FELT. I am going back further to answer your questionto help these people with patrol at sea. The head of the Navy-maybe this is something we should do in our country-the Chief of Naval Operations is a Commander. He organized a junk force. He started it up here, off the coast here. He recruited fishermen, fishermen who can't read or write, but who can be told how to use a simple radio and sail a junk, and use a light weapon. The words "I hate Communists" are tattooed across his stomach so that fellow won't be taken prisoner. 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral FELT. The Vietnamese do all the work. We are there to advise and help. They have been arresting junks, but so far, to answer your question, out of hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of junks you find very few that are real agents. 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, why the larger concentration in the south?

Admiral FELT. They stayed there after the fighting was stopped by the Geneva Accord in 1954. The Vietminh left a lot of their people. down there, left a lot of their cadres down there. 

Mr. JUDD. In violation of the accord? 

Admiral FELT. That is right. You remember President Diem brought down over a million refugees from up north. Most of them settled in here. The Communist cadres have been working on these people, terrorizing these people ever since. It is only, however, in the past I would say 12 months where it has grown to the point where you see organized units [security deletion] in action. 

Chairman MORGAN. Where is their source of supply?

Admiral FELT. From many sources. They make their own weapons, for example. I wish I had some pictures here with me. Maybe some of you saw them at my headquarters, some of their weapons. Homemade, crude-looking things. Have you heard about the spike in a board in a swamp where people stepped? This spike with a fish hook

thing goes in a man's foot. That puts him out of commission. So the people wear steel plates in their shoes now. 

Mrs. CHURCH. Were the newly established settlements abandoned, up on the high plateau?

Admiral FELT. No. There is a program now, President Diem told me the other day, to consolidate a little, though. He has had going for a long time a land reform and a resettlement program. He settled, made new towns, new villages, all up and down the country. He was particularly interested in getting up into this country, as you know.

This is a place where the Vietminh will establish a government, if they can, in South Vietnam. [Security deletion.] 

Mrs. CHURCH. Is there much counteractivity up there?

Admiral FELT. Yes. You can see by the numbers of people. There are not as many people in opposition. Within the past week there were about eight significant actions in this country. By "significant" 

I am talking about numbers of people killed. Seven are here and one up here, [security deletion]. Two or three weeks ago before that the 

Communists seemed to be concentrating on the coast line to try to cut the railroad. There is one railroad and road that comes up the coast here. It looks as if they are trying to cut the country off. 

[Security deletion]. 

Mr. JUDD. Admiral, the terrain is such that they can't bring much stuff in across the 17th parallel, isn't that right? They have to go around through Laos?

Admiral FELT. Dr. Judd, a lot of people at one time believed this was like the demilitarized zone in Korea, where we had people all along both sides and a neutral zone in between, a sanitized zone in between. 

That is not so. [Security deletion.] But this rugged mountainous country, insofar as protection, is wide open. They can come through there on foot, but they find it easier to come through some of these passes this way [indicating]. 

Mr. JUDD. You told us several years ago that the key to Vietnam was Laos.

Admiral FELT. I still believe that is so. 

Mrs. CHURCH. Is it appropriate to ask a relevant question at this time or should it be delayed?

Chairman MORGAN. I think perhaps we should delay until we start in regular order. 

Admiral FELT. Let me mention one thing: 

I am asked is there any improvement, and I say yes. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. Is there anything we in the Congress can do or this committee can do to speed up that improvement even more, or are you improving about as fast as the shock troops will absorb it? 

Admiral FELT. It is nice to know that the Congress would like to do this, but I think, Mr. Seely-Brown, we are pushing this about as hard as we can now. 

The other thing that they have is some air support. We put an AD squadron in there a year and a half ago. They have air support. 

They are learning how to use it. This is the important thing. [Security deletion.] When a village is struck now and a Self-Defense 

Corps unit or something is struck, first they have the communications,

which they didn't have before. They holler for help and the help comes. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. ADAIR. Mr. Chairman; on that point I am not sure, Admiral, whether you had an opportunity to exhaust the question that I had first asked. 

[Security deletion.] 

Chairman MORGAN. With reference to the two air force pilots that defected and bombed the executive palace 3 or 4 weeks ago, was this actual Communist defection or was it just people who were against the ruling government?

ADMIRAL FELT. I can only give you my impression and what people told me when I was there about a week ago. The impression I got was that one lad's father had been arrested about 2 years ago for I don't know what, and it had been preying on his mind for a long while. So he and another boy decided, I suppose, to take vengeance that is the word I am looking for. 

An interesting thing, the boy who was shot down by the little navy there and crashed in the river was dressed in pajamas, so he intended to get out of his airplane and disappear in the crowd, I guess. But that isn't the answer to your question, of course. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. JUDD. Do our people who work with the air force every day think there is a substantial sentiment to this effect? 

Admiral FELT. No, they don't.

Mr. JUDD. They think this is or was an individual person's operation?

Admiral FELT. I was out in Bien Hoa where these people were stationed before I left Saigon the other day. Bien Hoa is a military field 15 or 20 minutes by helicopter from Saigon, and we met the chief of the air force out there and some of his people and our own people. They just wanted to get back fighting again. 

Chairman MORGAN. This mission from which these planes broke away on the morning of the bombing, was it on a regular mission against the Viet Cong? 

Admiral FELT. Yes, as I understand.

Chairman MORGAN. They were equipped to carry out a bombing mission?

Admiral FELT. They aborted a regular mission and turned around and went after the palace. There were a lot of confusing reports. 

There were four planes in the air. A lot of people thought that the four were bombing the palace. That wasn't true. 

The second two had been scrambled out of Bien Hoa to see if they could shoo the first two away from the palace and make them stop the bombing. 

Chairman MORGAN. I understand the second plane got to Cambodia. 

Was that pilot taken by the Cambodians?

Admiral FELT. He was taken into custody by the Cambodians. I haven't heard anything more about him. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mrs. Bolton. 

That is somewhat similar to Mrs. BOLTON. On page 2 you have described the Viet Cong are conducting a campaign of terror and so on. what the OAS is doing?

Admiral FELT. Yes. 

Mrs. BOLTON. We haven't gone very far.

Admiral FELT. There is an interesting little development recently. 

This hasn't been going on long enough to really assess it, but the kidnapings have fallen way down. As long as I can remember, one of the objectives when they came in and terrorized a village would be to take boys and make soldiers out of them. This has gone way down. 

I am not sure I know the answer. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mrs. BOLTON. I would like to say again what your briefing in 

Hawaii did for me. It made this whole thing very real. I think that is one of the problems that we have. We are so far away from everything. The people of the United States just think it is a kind of play, but thanks to you, Admiral, I have long since ceased to feel that way. 

No more questions, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Hays. 

Mr. HAYS. Admiral, do you really believe that the bulk of the people support the Diem regime there or not? When I say "support" it, I mean wholeheartedly, not just passively. 

Admiral FELT. I don't think you can say that about the bulk of the people in any country out there, Mr. Hays. The bulk of the people in 

Thailand, the bulk of the people in Laos, the bulk of the people in South Vietnam don't even know the name of the King or the Prime Minister Their loyalties are to their own chieftain, to their own village province chief, and so forth.

I think we pose this question unfairly. Now, the people need security. In order to work their rice paddies they must have some kind of security. They are illiterate, most of them peasants. When some gang comes in-some bunch of gangsters-into a village and says, "Give me your rice, give me your money, give me your young sons,' and murder the village chieftain, and then say, "Now, you continue to do this or else we are going to give you this kind of treatment," then the Communists have access to those people. 

They have gotten access by this terroristic method. But, if, on the other hand, the Government can give them protection, then I think they will be against the Communists. They don't like the Communists. 

Basically the Buddhists, the Catholics, whoever they might be, don't like the Communists.

What have they done? They have organized these villages and hamlets. They are building protective devices around these villages. 

They have given them communications, weapons. We have taught them how to sleep out in the jungle at night rather than their huts. 

Recently when the Communists have come in to attack, they have found these villages ready and the Communists have lost. 

We found one village coming to the assistance of another. This was unheard of a few months ago. I don't think it is a question one should pose that way. I don't think we should say, Are the people for or against them?

The people are for a free life, to work and to do as they wish to do as freemen. The Government is for that. This is why we support the Government.

Mr. HAYS. What about all these stories you read in the press about the graft and the corruption and the high living and the wealth in Saigon? I have never been there, and the fact that this doesn't get beyond Saigon. Is this true or not?

Admiral FELT. I think some of it is true, just as it is true in any 

[security deletion] country. [Security deletion.] 

I do think Diem is honest. [Security deletion.] Look at the things that Diem has done. A million refugees came down in 1954 when nobody believed the country would exist for another 6 months. 

[Security deletion.] 

I can't give you the dates, the exact sequence of this, but there was a constitution adopted by the country and a general election. 

A land reform program was put in. This has worked. There have been troubles and gripes, but it has worked. He has given the people a lot more security than they would have had without this land reform and resettlement. He is building roads so people can have access to each other, little airfields all over the place. 

In 1955 to 1956 there were a total of 2,900 college students in the. whole country. In 1960 to 1961 this figure had increased to 11,500. 

Mr. HAYS. I am very interested in your answers. I must say they are rather encouraging to me, but on another phase of it-maybe you don't want to go into this, but this is executive session and I think a lot of us would have more enthusiasm if we could explore this and find out some satisfactory answers. 

I don't know much about military tactics, but I remember when I was in OCS one of the things they taught us is that you can't win a war unless you go out and dry up the enemy's source of supply one way or another. Either you cut his supply lines or you attack the source at its source or you do something of the kind. 

Do you really think that you can win this unless you do move into these other areas and you do try to cut off these supply lines [security deletion].

Admiral FELT. I repeat what I have said consistently. Laos is the key to this whole thing.

Mr. HAYS. You don't think that you can close the border by taking the Communists into the Government and giving them the office of whatever they call it, which amounts to the chief of the police? 

Admiral FELT. You are talking about Laos now? 

Mr. HAYS. Yes. 

Admiral FELT. All I can say about that, Congressman Hays, is that, as I read it to you here, and I emphasize the words "truly neutral, and for it to be a truly neutral country the people must be protected, and some decisions have to be made, and I can't make them. 

Mr. HAYS. I am not trying to put you into an untenable position with unfriendly questions, but I think your answers, while they have been carefully phrased, show you think somewhat like I do, and I am under no compulsion not to say the wrong thing because of my superiors, because, unfortunately, a lot of people think, I don't happen to have one. I don't think you can win the thing in Laos if you take the Communists into the Government because I think they will be in a position to see that you don't. You don't need to say anything. I will put that much in the record. 

Chairman MORGAN. Dr. Judd.

Mr. JUDD. 

Admiral, it always gives us a lot of reassurance to know that you are in charge out there, because you have been a good, loyal admiral, and you are a good American, too. 

Mr. HAYS. Is there a difference between the two?

Mr. PILCHER. There might be. 

Mr. JUDD. Yes, sometimes.

You told us from the beginning that you thought the key to Vietnam was Laos. That has not been official policy under either administration. It doesn't do you any good to be vindicated, but it gives us even greater confidence in you and your judgment now. Since the key to the whole area basically is Red China, what are you finding out with respect to present conditions in Red China? No. 2, how about Korea?

There is disagreement as to whether things are better or worse in 

Korea since the military takeover in May. And, third, the recent military coup in Burma. Would you comment on those three?

Admiral FELT. First, as to Red China, Dr. Judd, I try to pick up as much information as I can. When I was in Taiwan the other day 

I tried to add to my appreciation of what is going on there. I don't think there is any doubt that agriculture is the key to the problem there. People are hungry and the crops have failed. The following benefits are available to the family of servicemen who die on active duty. The benefits are the same whether the death occurs during peacetime or wartime. (a) Gratuity pay.-The death gratuity is a lump sum payment by the military departments to the survivors of a serviceman who dies while on active duty. 

This payment equals six times the monthly basic pay (plus special and incentive pays but not allowances) at the rate to which the deceased member was entitled on the date of his death, but may not be less than $800 or more

than $3,000. The death gratuity is paid as quickly as possible to the survivors first listed in the order shown below: (1) Spouse. (2) If no spouse, the children (without regard to their age or marital status) in equal shares. (3) If no spouse or child, the parent(s) or brother(s) or sister(s) including those of half-blood and those through adoption, upon designation by the deceased. (4) If no spouse or child and no designation by the deceased, the parents in equal shares. (5) If no spouse, child, or parent and no designation by the deceased, the brothers and sisters including those of the half-blood and those through adoption in equal shares. (b) Dependency and indemnity compensation. This compensation is payable monthly by the Veterans' Administration. (1) A widow is entitled to payment at a monthly rate equal to $112 plus 12 percent of the basic pay of the serviceman. Depending upon various factors set forth in 38 U.S.C. 411, this rate might be increased. (2) If there is no widow, children would be paid at the following rates: one child, $70; two children, $100; three children, $130; more than three children, $130 plus $25 for each child in excess of three. (3) Payments to parents are based on graduated scales, depending upon the parents' income. (c) Social security.-If the deceased was not a fully and currently insured individual under the social security laws, payments are nevertheless authorized to be made to the widow under 38 U.S.C. 412. (d) Educational assistance.-Eligible children are authorized educational assistance under the War Orphans Educational Assistance Act. As amended by Public Law 86-785, this act applies to death occurring during the existence of the Universal Military Training and Service Act. (e) Burial benefits.-The military departments provide for the care of the remains and delivery to the place designated by the adult next of kin and will pay an interment allowance to assist the next of kin in paying the cost of interment. The standard of services obtained by military authorities provides every proper consideration. These services include preparation at the place of death (pickup, embalming, and other preservation, casket and outside case, and hearse service to a local cemetary or shipping terminal), funeral directors services, transportation of remains accompanied by an escort and a flag to drape the casket. The maximum allowance is $200 when burial is made in a civilian or private cemetery; $125 when remains are consigned to a funeral director designated by the next of kin and subsequently interred in a national or post cemetery; $75 when military authorities consign remains direct to the superintendent of a national cemetery for interment therein. In addition, the survivors are entitled to a headstone or grave marker.

STATEMENT OF BRIG. GEN. STEPHEN 0. FUQUA, JR., U.S. ARMY, DIRECTOR, NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA AND AFRICA REGION, OFFICE OF THE ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF DEFENSE FOR INTER- NATIONAL SECURITY AFFAIRS 

General FUQUA. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a privilege to appear before you for the purpose of discussing the military assistance program in the Africa region. 

In the Africa region, the cumulative program to June 30, 1962, will total $107.3 million, of which it is expected $71.7 million will have been expended by that date and $35.5 million will still be in the pipeline.

The proposed fiscal year 1963 military assistance program for the Africa region is $37.6 million, which is $7.2 million more than the fiscal year 1962 program of $30.4 million. 

We propose fiscal year 1963 grant aid programs for the same eight countries as in fiscal year 1962 plus a special Africa program to cover anticipated requirements in some other countries.

General FUQUA. The force improvement includes naval patrol craft, vehicles, weapons, ammunition, communications equipment, and liaison, trainer, and transport aircraft.

Strategic significance to the United States: Over 60 percent of 

U.S. imports of asbestos, chromite, cobalt, columbium, tantalum, palm oil, and thorium come from Africa. African countries bordering on the Mediterranean have special strategic significance. 

Our air bases [security deletion] and our communications facilities [security deletion] are vital links in our worldwide strategic position. 

It is most important that the United States prevent significant gains

by international communism in Africa. Bloc offers of military assistance to Ghana, Guinea, Morocco, Mali, and Sudan are evidence that the Soviet bloc is seeking opportunities to exert its influence in thisarea.

The United States has agreed to, and has completed a refitting of this ship for use as a training ship for the Ethiopian Navy. It has put in certain facilities, such as air conditioning and quarters, so that it could be used as a flagship for the Emperor of Ethiopia. Certain moneys have been expended for that purpose.

Chairman MORGAN. General, I had my staff do a little study on this because it interested me. We have had some previous experience with

General FUQUA. I am not informed on that particular question, sir.

STATEMENT OF HENRY J. TASCA, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR AFRICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. TASCA. May I add something to this?

It is quite normal in tropical Africa for the various countries there-both newly independent and those that have been independent for a longer period of time for them to bring in expert personnel. 

They usually call them expatriates. You will find them in all of the newly independent countries. They have British or they have French or they have Belgians. Even in the Congo you still have a lot of 

Belgians, people who are very important in terms of the transition to the time when the governments can train their own people to do the job.

As long as they are getting Norwegians, French, and British, they are a lot better off than if they brought in somebody else, from the 

Soviet bloc, for example.

I think there is a great desire on their part to try to replace these people as quickly as they can. They do want to Africanize their services. On the other hand, they feel there are certain things they want to have done now. 

In the case of Ethiopia, I think you have stated very clearly that the Emperor feels this ship is something very important to him.

Kagnew is of very great importance to us. This is one of the things that we felt in terms of the overall interest of the United States would be a useful thing to provide.

COUNTRIES OTHER THAN AFRICA WHICH COULD SUPPLY THE UNITED STATES WITH ASBESTOS, CHROMITE, COBALT, COLUMBIUM/TANTALUM, PALM OIL, AND THORIUM 

The United States could not fulfill its needs of these materials wholly from non-African countries because of the grades desired and for reasons of international trade. Countries, other than Africa, from which the United States imports these materials and which provide approximately 40 percent of our needs are as follows:

We feel that it is most important for Africa not to get into an arms race. So as far as arms supply policy is concerned, we are very reluctant to give anything but the very minimum.

And when I say "minimum," I am thinking in terms of something that can be used for internal security or can be used-which we think could be an important case—in this special category for roadbuilding and engineering- Mrs. CHURCH. I would applaud that criterion, giving less rather than too much, in caution against starting an arms race.
