Mr. TASCA. I would say the political motivation is in the recognition that these countries are newly sovereign. They do want to have some armed forces. We think it ought to be at a minimum because they ought to give the stress to economic development and not the military side.

We also realize that as sovereign countries they want to have a sense of security. We have encouraged them as much as we can. We will certainly do this in the future encourage other arrangements for security, rather than build up their own armed forces.

Considering the nationalism, and, I would say, the understandable nationalistic spirit prevalent in Africa today, are we so building up their military strength that we might be contributing to the danger of their developing a sudden decision to engage in joint action against South Africa or Angola? 

Mr. TASCA. I wouldn't think so. I would say the amount of aid that we have given so far in tropical Africa and that we have in prospect would be most unlikely to come anything near being able to do that kind of job.

I would like to add, if I may, one further note on our arms policy because I think it is important for the committee to know, to see that we are trying to do everything we can to keep down any possibility of these countries wasting their resources or our resources in building up their arms.

We feel very strongly that wherever the former Metropole has had a role to play, such as France, we [security deletion] must be very careful not to try to substitute-for example, the French are giving quite a bit of military aid to West Africa. 

[Security deletion.]

Mr. TASCA. At the recent meeting in Lagos, Nigeria, about 20 African countries got together and they talked about their problems of security. They talked about agreeing with each other not to interfere in the internal affairs of each of the countries present. 

That is the kind of thing that we think will help to save these countries. That is the kind of approach, "Don't try to build up your armies. That doesn't make any sense. This is the way to get security." 

Second, if that doesn't work there is a United Nations, and in some cases these countries have agreements with the former Metropole to help them in the event of any difficulties in the field of security. 

So taking all of this together, we put our stress on economic development, on trying to find some other answer to security rather than building up armed forces which are not going to be a real answer. 

Mrs. CHURCH. I can see only danger in pursuing any other course, because in no place in the world where we have tried to win friendship by bribes has such effort ever proved successful. 

Chairman MORGAN. I want to announce to the committee that Dr.

Erich Mende, chairman of the Free Democratic Party in Germany, which is part of the coalition with the Christian Democrats, will be here for an informal visit at 2:30 p.m. He would like to talk to as many members of the committee as possible. 

If you have a little spare time, the chairman would appreciate it if you would come up and say hello to Dr. Mende. 

Mr. Fountain.

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I have only one question. You concluded your statement by saying, "We believe that the amount requested is the minimum amount needed to assist in achieving U.S. [security deletion] objectives in the African region."

It may be like playing an old record to some extent, but I wonder if you would tell us just what our [security deletion] objectives in 

Africa are [security deletion]. 

Mr. TASCA. I might say that our general objective in Africa is to keep Africa friendly to us, so that we do have countries in Africa, in the world conflict with the Soviets, more on our side than the Soviet bloc side, on matters of critical importance. 

A second point is that, if the Africans are able to maintain their independence and freedom as they see it, as Africans, the chances are rather good that they are going to want to remain free-which is, after all, the thing that is going to give us the most security in terms of keeping the Soviet bloc out of the area. 

A further point is that this is an area that is important for its raw materials. Some of them are very important, and the largest part of the world's supply does come from Africa. We would want to be sure that the free world or we ourselves specifically had access to these raw materials.

Finally, we also feel that it would be very serious for our whole posture in both Europe and other parts of the world if the Soviet bloc were to get a real foothold anywhere in Africa and build up from that. We know from what they have said, what their leadership has said, that they are going to try to expand and grow. A Red Africa

would pose a real threat to us in Europe, NATO, and to our general position in the world. 

We feel that the kinds of policies that we want to follow are the policies that are going to give us an independent Africa, an Africa that is meeting the aspirations of the people through development, an Africa that is going to be very wary of Soviet efforts to obtain a foothold.

The committee meets this morning in executive session for the continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962.

East region, the cumulative program from 1950 to June 30, 1962, will total $7,803,621,000, of which it is expected $6,602,450,000 will have been delivered by that date and $1,201,171,000 will still be in the pipeline.

Admiral HEINZ. The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for the 

Far East region will provide $139.7 million for essentially fixed charges such as training, supply operations, and international agency support; $345.4 million for force maintenance to provide spare parts equipment; attrition replacement, ammunition, repair and rehabilitation of equipment and other consumables for forces currently in being; and $345.6 million for force improvement.

The force improvement would include selected items of more modern equipment to improve the military capabilities of the recipient nations' forces. Modern aircraft, missiles, ships, and electronic equipment fall in this category.

Admiral HEINZ. Strategic significance to the United States: The 

Far East area is of increasing strategic importance to the United States. Through our military alliances there, our forward defense area is placed 5,000 miles from the west coast of the United States. 

The Far East contains the world's fourth largest industrial complex, Japan; it is rich in natural resources, rubber, tin, and oil; it has a large food production potential; it lies across lines of communication to the Indian Ocean area; and it contains 300 million people allied with or friendly to the West. 

Since 1950, the Republics of Korea and China, with substantial U.S. assistance, have been successful in repelling the Communist attacks of open aggression. Also, Communist attempts to subvert the 

Far Eastern governments of Malaya and the Philippines have been repulsed.

Today, Vietnam and Laos are being subjected actively to what Mr. 

Khrushchev calls "war of national liberation." We know this as a war of infiltration, terrorism, subversion, and insurgency. It stems from Communist-inspired, led, and supported guerrilla operations. 

It is war of covert military aggression. 

The Communist objective is to extend their colonial empire and to gain for their own use the economic and human resources of this rich and important area. The loss of any of these countries to the free world community would have substantial and far-reaching effects on the security of the United States. 

The main burden of local defense against covert aggression, subversion, and guerrilla warfare must rest upon local populations and

forces. But given the seriousness of this threat, we must be prepared to make a substantial contribution toward this defense. 

The active and growing threat in several countries in the Far East will not permit us to reduce our vital assistance to these countries now and probably not in the near future. 

More and more in the Far East, our military assistance program is being tailored to meet the forces of active Communist-inspired and led insurgency and subversion rather than the latent threat of open Communist aggression.

I will now give a brief discussion of the individual country programs. 

Japan: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Japan is [security deletion] less than the actual fiscal year 1962. Of this amount [security deletion] million for force improvement is programed on a cost-sharing basis with Japan. 

This program responds to a situation unique in the Far East. Although Japan is an economically prosperous nation with a modern economy, Japan has a constitution renouncing the use of force and the maintenance of war potential [security deletion]. 

As the Japanese forces have grown, they have assumed the former duties of U.S. forces in Japan. They have become less dependent on the United States for materiel. [Security deletion.] 

We are convinced that we are helping to produce a greater local defense effort by continuing to provide military assistance of a highly selective kind. Our program now consists almost exclusively of offers to pay a part of the cost of new force improvement projects. 

By expending 25 to 35 percent of the initial cost of such a project [security deletion] the Japanese not only pay the bulk of the initial cost but also assume the entire burden of continued maintenance. 

Not only are all our expenditures made in the United States for equipment which the Japanese cannot yet produce, but the Japanese also spend part of their share in the United States. 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral HEINZ. In fiscal year 1963 we propose to concentrate on assistance to Japan's [security deletion] program. Japan is willing to undertake the construction of new naval vessels. We are planning to place aboard ordnance, fire control and electronics gear that is not available in Japan. This incentive arrangement has stimulated the steady modernization of the Japanese maritime forces. 

The military assistance program contributes to Japan's readiness [security deletion]. 

Finally, it encourages Japan to budget for an increasing share of the cost of modernizing and improving its forces. [Security deletion.] 

Korea: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Korea is [security deletion] million, approximately the same as fiscal year 1962. 

Force improvement items total [security deletion] million, about the same as fiscal year 1962, devoted to air defense, [security deletion] replacement and additional [security deletion]. 

Almost 9 years have passed since the Korean Armistice was signed. 

Today, the prospects for a peaceful resolution of the Korean problem still appear to be a long way off. We, along with the Republic of 

Korea, must still maintain sizable military forces to face a determined, well-armed enemy along a 155-mile front.

The military assistance program continues to be the sole source of armament and equipment for the ROK forces. The ROK provides a well-trained and combat-tested army of [security deletion] active infantry divisions, an excellent marine corps division, a small but efficient navy of [security deletion] combat ships, and an air force of [security deletion] squadrons of jet fighters.

The ROK military government has made great strides in reducing the diversion and pilferage of military supplies and equipment. IIlegal diversion is now about 4 percent of what it was a year ago. Loss of supplies during transportation is about 10 percent of its previous rate.

Improved management control, greater economies, and stricter discipline are being instituted in the ROK military forces. This is not to say that all the deficiencies in logistics are being corrected. 

There is still much to be done and more time will be needed. However, vigorous action has been started and we expect it to continue. 

The North Korean Air Force with its [security deletion] modern jets presents a serious threat to the U.N. Command defense posture in 

South Korea. Steps to improve the air defense capability of the ROK forces were initiated in the fiscal year 1961 military assistance program and are being continued in the fiscal year 1963 program [security deletion].

Military assistance has enabled Korea to maintain strong deterrent forces. We are examining closely the levels of assistance needed in the future. However, there is no question but that military assistance must be continued if the Republic of Korea is to maintain its freedom. 

Republic of China: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for 

China is [security deletion] less than fiscal year 1962. Force im provement items total [security deletion]. 

The security of the GRC is vital to U.S. security. Their territory astride the Chinese Communist sealanes is strategically important. 

[Security deletion.] 

In Taiwan this year we are supporting with military assistance funds a military establishment of [security deletion] men. This is a considerable reduction from the high of [security deletion]. 

Some of this reduction has been made possible by the release of about 40,000 ineffectives and also by a reorganization of the force structure. However, the effectiveness of the GRC forces has not been impaired by this reduction [security deletion]. 

Without the military assistance program the GRC would not have been able to withstand two major assaults against the offshore islands which were described by the Communist Chinese as part of an attack against Taiwan. Great courage was manifested by the Chinese in the defense of their country against these Communist assaults. Any weakening in the resolve of the GRC to defend itself would be reflected throughout the Far East. This we cannot afford to let happen. 

Philippines: The program proposed for the Philippines totals 

[security deletion]. Force improvement will total [security deletion]. 

The Philippines with its key U.S. naval and air bases is extremely vital to the strategic posture of the United States. Clark Air Force 

Base and Subic Bay are cornerstones of any U.S. staging of military operations to the west or southwest. The geographical position of the 

Philippines places them across many key air and sea lanes.

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral HEINZ. Our military assistance program is designed to encourage improvements in the Philippine Armed Forces and to provide those resources which are required to supplement the Philippines' own defense effort.

Our primary objectives in this field are to create a Philippine security establishment which is capable of safeguarding the people of that country against insurgent and bandit elements and of contributing to both the defense of the Philippines and the collective defense of the western Pacific area.

Vietnam: Compared to the fiscal year 1962 military assistance program for Vietnam of [security deletion]. We realize, however, that the internal security situation in Vietnam is fluid. To combat and defeat the Communist controlled and supported war of covert aggression will undoubtedly require additional military assistance resources. 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral HEINZ. Vietnam is a cornerstone of a free and independent southeast Asia. It is in Vietnam that the free world is being put to the test. Here the Communists intend to show that free world assistance to an anti-Communist government in an underdeveloped, recently colonial country cannot prevail against their tested blueprint. 

Beginning in 1959, the Viet Cong intensified their subversive attack to such an extent that the bulk of available armed forces were required to augment the newly organized and partially trained police-type organizations. As a result, training of both the regular forces and the police-type organizations was slow and disjointed. 

During 1961, with the GVN in the midst of its most critical phase thus far, the Communist threat gained further momentum. While maintaining the initiative against government forces, the Communists increased their armed guerrilla forces [security deletion]. Casualties on both sides averaged 2,750 per month during 1961 and incidents of violence rose to between 300 and 500 per week. 

In the present phase of increasing Communist attack, there is obvious danger of Communist success before the Vietnamese have sufficiently strengthened their security forces through the additional materiel and training that the United States is now providing. 

Short of sending U.S. combat troops, we have taken steps to assist the Vietnamese with U.S. personnel and materiel to perform tasks that they will not be able to perform themselves during the present critical period.

For example, we have sent U.S. helicopters [security deletion] to improve the mobility of their armed forces and thereby realize greater combat potential from these forces. 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral HEINZ. The struggle in Vietnam will be hard and long. 

Of this we have no misconception. [Security deletion.] 

We are doing all within our power to assist the Government to win its war. However, sufficient time has not passed since the start of our increased effort for me to give you an exact evaluation of how this effort is affecting the military situation. We hope and expect that we will succeed in our effort.

Cambodia: The proposed program for Cambodia is [security deletion]. Of this, force improvement totals [security deletion]. 

Cambodia, flanking Vietnam, Thailand, and Laos, occupies an important position close to Communist-held territory. 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral HEINZ.

Cambodia, so far, has refused all offers of bloc military aid. [Security deletion.] 

So far, Communist subversion has remained latent in Cambodia. 

It is our objective to keep it so. With the Government enjoying a degree of popular support and an absence of domestic opposition which is unparalled in southeast Asia, prospects of success in this endeavor are good.

Thailand: Military assistance to Thailand is proposed in the amount of [security deletion]. However, Communist pressures may make it necessary to increase this amount before the end of the program year. 

[Security deletion.] 

Admiral HEINZ. Force improvement items in fiscal year 1963 [security deletion].

Allied with the United States through SEATO, Thailand occupies important land areas vital to the defense of southeast Asia. Were war to occur there [security deletion] Thailand would be a major key to success.

It was stated last year that with Communist advances in Laos and increased activity by the Communist insurgents in Vietnam, the threat to Thailand had become increasingly more serious. These words are as true now as they were then, but the threat is even more intense.

Through military assistance, the United States has supplied equipment which Thailand itself cannot produce or afford to purchase. 

Thailand, with U.S. assistance, has standardized, improved, and reorganized its forces and increased personnel strength of its units. 

A training program has been conducted to teach the latest tactics and techniques of warfare. Currently, the greatest stress is being laid on learning and developing the techniques of antiguerrilla warfare. 

There has emerged a military force of high morale and vastly increased combat capability.

The job, however, is not completed. With the immediacy of the 

Communist threat, the continuation of United States support to Thailand is necessary if the Thais are to cope with the threat. 

Laos: The proposed fiscal year 1963 program for Laos is [security deletion]. 

The U.S. policy is to reach a settlement in Laos through political negotiations. If our present objective of securing a peaceful, neutral, and independent Laos is successful, our military assistance program in Laos will probably be drastically reduced, if not totally discontinued. 

[Security deletion]. 

Admiral HEINZ. Our military assistance efforts to date have produced a base from which further improvement can be made by continuing our programs for training, increased mobility of ground forces and improved logistic and combat support systems. 

The uncertainties of the international situation surrounding Laos make it difficult to propose a firm program for fiscal year 1963. Our

tentative program is designed to produce further improvement in the capability of the Lao forces [security deletion]. 

Conclusion: In concluding, I desire to stress to you that in the Far 

East we find ourselves in close confrontation with Communist power. 

Here our allies are engaged in a war of subversion. We cannot afford to lose this area to Communist control. U.S. interests are at stake, as well as the interests of the countries themselves. We believe our military assistance program serves these interests.

Admiral, on page 6 of your statement dealing with Korea, reference was made to reduction and diversion and loss of supplies. 

In the past the committee has been told that it was impossible to estimate the amount of theft and diversion. How can such precise percentages be given this year?

Admiral HEINZ. We have reports from General Meloy on this diversion. This has been worked out jointly with the ROK Government and with our own people in Korea. 

I have tables here showing a comparison of U.S. aid as army property, lost, stolen, and recovered. I cannot state precisely how 

General Meloy determined these figures. But I do have these from 

General Meloy. He shows in the first 6 months of 1961 we had a net loss of $94,000. In the last 6 months, the monthly average was a loss of $19,000.

I have a copy here of loss breakdown by post exchange items, POL, and communication material. We do have detailed figures on that. 

In addition, I have some tables which were prepared by the Korean Army showing this diversion factor. This shows how this diversion has been drastically reduced in the past year. 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, you know the Subcommittee on Mutual Security Review held long hearings in the fall of 1958. We were very interested in this subject. I think some of the hearings that we held at that time stimulated our own military forces to get busy. 

You think now since the new military regime in Korea took over there has been a further cleanup of some of the thefts and diversion? 

Admiral HEINZ. I think there is no question of it, Mr. Chairman. 

Shortly after the new Government came into power it took drastic steps to eliminate corruption in Korea. 

In regard to the diversion or theft of military supplies, they instituted the death penalty, and shortly after they came into power they caught two people in the Korean Army and they executed them. 

This word got around very quickly, and in addition to these people who were executed there were severe sentences handed out to people for relatively small thefts. There was then a sudden drop in diversion. 

The Government has made this one of their particular points of reducing corruption, not only in regard to military items but corruption throughout the Government.

South Korea forces have not been built up to try to match the North

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, on page 161 of the book, column (b), including [security deletion] Cambodia. Last September the civilian airlines were not able to travel across Cambodia because Cambodia had broken off relations with its neighbors and would not permit overflight.

When the relations are so strained, is it not dangerous to provide Cambodia with that which could be used against Thailand and Vietnam, which are both friendly to the United States? 

Admiral HEINZ. The fact that we are giving military assistance to Cambodia is well known to both Vietnam and Thailand and has never been questioned by either of those governments. 

We are providing [security deletion] equipment to Cambodia. I would feel certain that neither country, that is, Thailand or Vietnam, considers Cambodia a threat. Actually what we are providing to them is equipment which we feel would be used in internal security. 

The Cambodian armed forces have a very, I would say, relatively small capability, and particularly would have a very limited capability outside of their own country. 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, I have just one more question. The report of the staff survey team on conditions in the Philippines in 1960 indicated that our military assistance program was not operating too well.

They found a military hospital built with U.S. funds which was not being used because no water was available. 

They found at one airbase five fire trucks-crash tenders-had been deadlined for several months-there were only two or three in service. 

The trouble was that the Philippines wanted the five trucks shipped to Japan for repair while the United States insisted that they be fixed in the Philippine military shops.

At a reserve division depot on the island of Mindanao where only a training operation was being carried on, there were 30 34-ton rear axle assemblies in stock. 

At the depot of the only active division in the Philippine Army, there were no 34-ton axle assemblies in stock. 

The whole situation indicated that the Philippine military was not able or willing to manage its affairs properly. 

Has the situation really improved since then?

Admiral HEINZ. The situation has improved. It has not improved anywhere nearly to the extent that we would like it to improve. 

For instance, we spent the year trying to get a new supply center established. This order was signed, I believe, 3 days ago establishing it. This I hope will be a big step forward. 

We have increased our logistic MAAG people; that is, storekeepers and people who can get in and help them with their maintenance and logistic effort. That has some effect.

I have been through Cavite. I have seen the navy is improving its maintenance. I wish I could say as much for the army. I think the air force is improving. The new administration says it will improve the armed forces, reduce corruption, and reduce nepotism and this sort of thing. We have yet to have proof of that. Time has not allowed them to prove their statements. 

This has been the biggest problem in the Philippines. I would end by saying there has been some improvement. The improvement has not been as great as we would like. 

Chairman MORGAN. Do you think now since they have a new government, a new political party taking over, there will be any incentive from the new President to help improve the military situation? 

STATEMENT OF AVERY F. PETERSON, DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRE- TARY OF STATE FOR FAR EASTERN ECONOMIC AFFAIRS Mr. PETERSON. Mr. Chairman, I personally, and I think the State 

Department generally, feel greatly encouraged by the new administration. I had the honor of meeting President Macapagal 10 days ago; also, his Vice President. I had to do with their group that came over, Mr. Sison, their Acting Secretary of Finance. And I believe, and Í feel that Governor Harriman believes from personal contact there and the assessment of our Embassy, that there is every prospect of a turn of the road in the Philippines. 

Our way of life has been associated with the Philippines for about 300 years. We as a nation have been associated there for 60 years. 

And if we have a chance to show how our economic organization can produce results that meet the people's needs, I am confident we should take advantage of it.

In short, I am greatly encouraged by the vigor and personality and dedication of the new leaders in the Philippines. They, too, have made vigorous steps with respect to corruption. People have been incarcerated recently who there seems to be some evidence were acting in a corrupt manner in the political field.

They have established provincial councils. They are planning on holding national assembly elections. They have strengthened [security deletion] their intelligence system. They have an anticorruption campaign going on.

I feel, and I would like Mr. Peterson to comment more on this aspect of it, but I do not have fears of that at the present time.

The people, however, went through a very difficult, a very bad war from their viewpoint; they lost, they lost miserably in the end, and it had a great psychological effect on the people. Therefore, although they are improving economically, although their armed forces are being built up, there is still this complex of "We don't want to get into another war if we can help it" thought. 

Therefore, the people who take a more practical view [security deletion] who see that Japan will need defensive forces in the future, if it is to continue its present political existence, have this psychological imprint in people's minds as to what they are up against. 

I feel Japan is very strongly an ally of the United States, and that if the chips were down we would find them a great help to us.

I would like to ask one question of Mr. Peterson, if he would elaborate a little more on his discussion with President Macapagal and some of his cabinet members on this tobacco situation in the Philippines.

Mr. PETERSON. Mr. Chairman, the discussion-I did not participate-Governor Harriman undertook that discussion with President 

Macapagal. I can only give it secondhand.

At the present time, the supreme court is going to rule on the validity of an order by the previous administration that the tobacco be released to the importers. If the court of first instance ruling that it

should be so released is upheld, President Macapagal has indicated he would abide by the decision of the court. 

The agreement is that in equity the tobacco should not be imported because it was to be used for political purposes to assist in the campaign of a third party, which campaign was thought would be sufficient to split the vote to permit President Garcia to be reelected. 

It is quite understandable, I am sure you will understand, that that sort of maneuver was not very palatable to the President-elect. He has also taken a position that graft and corruption are to be extinguished in the new Philippine government, and he believes the allowance of the import of this tobacco into the country would represent acquiescence to the forces of graft and corruption. 

However, if the supreme court decision reverses that of the lower court, I am confident of several things: First, that the tobacco will not be burned, as once was alleged. I would be confident in my own mind that the tobacco would be allowed to be reexported. 

I think because the tobacco has intrinsic value for blending purposes in the Philippines, and because there is need for well-blended cigarettes in that market to prevent the importation and black marketing of so-called blue seal American cigarettes, that some arrangements should be made within reason to retain that tobacco in the Philippines and feed it out on a gradual basis so that it is effectively and efficiently consumed.

Following an investigation of how the Philippines might improve its economy, the growth of Virginia-type tobacco, which is the Fluecured tobacco used for blending purposes, has been stimulated. They have a surplus because it is under a price-support proposition. they have some of the problems that we are familiar with in our own country. So

Mr. Nix. 

I might digress to say, Mr. Chairman, that I have been classed as a big spender since I have been here, and I am glad to know that that group is being augmented.

It says that the Communists' objective is to extend their colonial empire and to gain for their own use the economic and human resources of this rich and important area. I understand it, Admiral, the encroachment of hostile powers. It is to preserve the economic integrity of the United States. It is to maintain our strategic battle positions all around the hostile territory.

Those are problems that you must confront and overcome, if you are to maintain the advantage that you already have.

Almost 9 years have passed since the Korean armistice was signed. Today, the prospects for a peaceful solution of the Korean problem still appear to be a long way off.

We had to readjust our thinking to face such a problem; is that true? 

Admiral HEINZ. I believe it is, Mr. Nix. I believe that this realization is coming to more and more people in this country. 

It certainly has come to the military in their thinking, that we are going to have this trouble with us for a long time, that we can see at the present no clean-cut solution, that we can see no battle that will decide it—a decisive battle as we have had in the past. 

Our thinking in the military is increasingly oriented to how we can combat this new type of warfare. And I feel confident, increasingly certain that this is a long, difficult problem. 

Mr. Nix.

I think the preferred position of the United States is everywhere apparent in the Filipinos' general outlook.

Chairman MORGAN. Very well. 

(The remainder of General Enemark's prepared statement is as follows:)

The strategic importance of Latin America to this country cannot be overestimated. Latin America is a major source of essential raw materials and a major market for U.S. products. Its nations have been our traditional allies in peace and war and their friendship is necessary to effective U.S. use of the 

Atlantic and Pacific sealanes in the event of any major hostilities. 

The existence of hostile governments in Latin America would be a grave menace to the United States should we become engaged in warfare on any considerable scale anywhere in the world. 

The denial to this country of the resources of the area for any extended period would have grave consequences to the United States, both in the prosecution of war and in recuperation from war damages.

Today, Latin American political, economic, and social instability is a serious danger. Cuba has shown us what can happen. 

The President's alliance for progress was conceived to meet these circumstances. Extremists both left and right can be counted upon to use every means including subversion, terrorism, and civil war to defeat the effort to bring the alliance for progress to fruition. 

The role of the security forces in Latin America, both police and military, therefore, assumes paramount importance. If the alliance for progress is to have its chance, governments must have the effective force required to cope with subversion, prevent terrorism, and deal with outbreaks of violence before they reach unmanageable proportions. They must be able to sustain themselves against attacks by the international Communist organization and its indigenous members. 

[Security deletion.] 

In addition to the internal security threat there is a threat to the sealanes. 

We seek to meet this threat by working closely with the Latin American navies in the field of antisubmarine warfare. [Security deletion.] They will also contribute to internal security by patrolling their coastal waters in order to detect subversive infiltration by surface or submarine craft.

We have already loaned a total of 20 destroyers and submarines to South American countries. Of these, 16 have been delivered and 4 are being readied for delivery. Two of the latter are being rehabilitated in shipyards and should be ready for delivery in calendar year 1962. Funds to rehabilitate the other two are included in the fiscal year 1962 program and work on them should begin this year.

The military assistance program for fiscal year 1963 contains funds to activate and modernize [security deletion] additional destroyers [security deletion]. 

For these, ship loan legislation will be required; a bill is being submitted to the 

Armed Services Committees in this session. 

Twice in the last 3 years CINCLANT Fleet has sent a task group composed of U.S. destroyers, submarines, and patrol aircraft around South America to conduct combined antisubmarine warfare exercises with South American navies. 

The quality of the forces has been improved greatly and the Latin American navies have developed mutual respect and a willingness to cooperate. 

The program outlined above will maintain and strengthen the close friendly relationship between the United States and Latin American military which has become a tradition; it will contribute a significant element of support to the 

U.S. position and prestige in the area [security deletion]. 

We foresee an intensification of the revolutionary danger to the hemisphere during the next several years. Last year's crisis in Brazil precipitated by the resignation of President Quadros showed that there is a grave potential for Communist-supported violence in the largest nation of the hemisphere [security deletion].

In fiscal year 1962 we completed the commitment to Brazil under the Fernando de Noronha agreement wherein we obtained authority to establish missile tracking facilities. [Security deletion.] 

As part of the Castro regime's effort to subvert its neighbors it has publicly called for the overthrow of the democratic constitutional Government of Venezuela. Political terrorism [security deletion] but has been held in check [security deletion]. Our program for Venezuela includes training [security deletion]. 

[Security deletion.] 

The Dominican Republic has only begun the difficult transition from tyranny to representative government and will be vulnerable for some time to propaganda and subversive assaults sponsored or supported from Cuba and the deposed Trujillos.

After having abrogated the military assistance agreement with the Dominican Republic in 1960, we are now preparing a new program designed to strengthen this new and friendly Government and to assist in reorganizing, training, and reorienting the armed forces. 

At the request of the Dominican Government, a Department of Defense survey team visited the Dominican Republic in late January to discuss the development of a military assistance program, the signing of a new military assistance program agreement, and the establishment of a MAAG. 

As a result of the survey, programs were developed for fiscal year 1962 and fiscal year 1963. [Security deletion.]

A mutual defense assistance agreement with the Dominican Republic was signed on March 8, 1962. A Presidential determination was made on March 14, 1962, to cover the fiscal year 1962 materiel program. 

[Security deletion.] 

In Colombia, long-existing violence and bloodshed in the rural areas are a constant menace and do not fail to attract Cuban attention. 

[Security deletion.] 

In recent years, the character of Latin American military establishments has been undergoing a significant change. The day of the caudillo or militarypolitical tyrant is passing and the Latin American armed forces are becoming increasingly dedicated to the preservation of constitutional government and reflective of public opinion. 

It is this change in outlook which makes them receptive to civic action activities which are an integral part of internal security. They are seeking a better relationship and closer identification with the civilian population. 

Other examples of the change in outlook are found in Argentina and El Salvador. 

[Security deletion.] 

For Latin America as a whole, the alliance for progress holds great promise both to the other American nations and to ourselves. Nevertheless, during its formative stages, the immediate prospect is for increasing tension, growing subversion, and further revolutionary outbreaks. 

We therefore consider that the training and equipping of the necessary internal security forces of the Latin American nations should be pressed forward with all possible decision and speed while maintaining a minimum antisubmarine warfare effort. They must be able to protect themselves against the Communist threat of violence and subversion, including guerrilla warfare, and the movement of armaments and men clandestinely across land, sea, and air borders for subversive purposes.

A good start has been made and we are continuing to build upon this foundation in fiscal year 1963. The chief emphasis throughout is on training, communications, transportation, and civic action for the ground forces; training and air transport capacity for the air forces; and antisubmarine and coastal patrol effectiveness for the naval forces.

STATEMENT OF LT. GEN. ANDREW P. O'MEARA, COMMANDER IN CHIEF, CARIBBEAN General O'MEARA. The maintenance of internal order in Latin 

America is essential if the social and economic reforms stimulated by the alliance for progress are to gather impetus and accomplish their objectives.

Extremists of both the right and the left will seek to block reform and to exploit change by violence ranging from street demonstrations to armed insurrections.

Governments endeavoring to carry out their commitments under the alliance for progress must have internal security forces adequate to forestall or counter such violence. Lack of active, effective internal security forces weakens the will to move ahead with reforms and opens the door to extremist action leading to totalitarianism as in Cuba.

The fundamental element in a good internal security system is the presence of an effective, properly oriented military force. Good police supported by adequate intelligence are the first line of defense, but behind them must be a military force adequate to sustain the constitutional government. 

During the past 2 months we have had examples in Venezuela and Guatemala of the Government calling on the military to take over the internal security role from the police.

What are needed today are good infantry battalions and companies, whether they be conventional infantry, paratroopers, or marines. 

Their necessary characteristics are good communications, good mobility, and the training and effectiveness to permit small units to act rapidly and independently.

Prior to the fiscal year 1962 military assistance program, our efforts in Latin America were directed toward developing and supporting forces designed for hemispheric defense. In fiscal year 1962, the legislation authorizing military assistance for Latin America retained the philosophy of hemispheric defense in that it permitted support of units for internal security only on the basis of Presidential determination of the requirement therefor. 

Utilizing such determinations, it was possible to shift emphasis to internal security in the fiscal year 1962 program. 

We doubled the number of small infantry units to which military assistance was given and increased more than 50 percent the number of air transport squadrons to which we give support. These are very important to move infantry units fast when the time comes. Specialized training related to internal security, such as counterguerrilla tactics, was doubled. The fiscal year 1963 program carries on the essential work of building internal security capabilities. 

Much remains to be done. While there are infantry units in Latin 

America which any general in the U.S. Army would be proud to have under his command, there are many units which suffer grave deficiencies.

Lack of adequate communications and adequate transportation, whether it be air transportation or surface transportation, is the rule rather than the exception. In some cases, there are weapon shortages. 

In several countries, the quality of troops is impaired by internal problems varying from a high percentage of short-term conscripts to budgetary shortages which result in the troops being poorly housed, clothed, and fed.

In the past the military forces have generally been able to control subversive actions in or near the capital cities. A flight of fighter aircraft has sometimes been sufficient to quell a budding insurrection in the provinces. Today, greatly improved forces are required to forestall attempts, organized and directed by national and international Communists, to gain domination over these countries. 

The personnel resources for such forces are at hand. The fiscal year 

1963 program will continue the support of the infantry and marine battalions which we are supporting this year and will furnish support to five additional battalions. The number of air transport units supported will be increased by one. 

The fiscal year 1963 military assistance program can play an important part in securing the internal order necessary for the success of the alliance for progress. 

In addition to furnishing the force necessary to defend duly constituted governments against the attacks of subversive elements, the armed forces of Latin American countries can make an important contribution to democratic objectives through civic action programs. 

These fall into two categories. The first category, which can be carried on by any military unit, comprises such things as conducting literacy training, assisting in school construction or improvement, assisting in inoculations, organizing baseball or other athletic teams.

In general, such activities identify military units with the improvement of the community and identify the military service and the central government with the individual welfare of the citizen. This type of activity can be carried on without decreasing the military effectiveness of the unit and at insignificant cost. 

The second category consists of such things as organizing and equipping engineer battalions for road construction, developing of air force transport squadrons to give access to remote regions where scheduled airlines are not commercially feasible, and establishing military communications systems which can accept civil as well as military traffic. 

The military equipment required for such projects is obviously more specialized and expensive. The projects themselves need financing from some source.

We have examples of highly successful projects of this sort which were initiated some years ago in Peru and Bolivia. Brazil and Chile have fine programs which they have financed without help from us and which can be expanded to advantage if funding is available. 

We must not expand the type of civic action project which I am now discussing at the expense of the military efficiency of the vital internal security units. 

One other aspect of military assistance in Latin America is of great importance to the United States. As a result of efforts on the part of the U.S. Navy extending over more than 30 years, we have, in 

South America, navies with high standards of seamanship and professional competence, both in officers and enlisted men. 

For the past 10 years, the U.S. Navy's effort has been concentrated on developing antisubmarine warfare capabilities in these navies. 

When it is appreciated that a greater tonnage of shipping clears Venezuelan ports each year than sails from the port of New York, that the economic life of South America and our access to the resources of South America are dependent upon shipping, it becomes self-evident that an antisubmarine warfare capability in the maritime nations of South America in any major war, atomic or nonatomic, is of great importance to the whole Western World. 

Today, we have brought the maritime powers of South America to a point where their antisubmarine warfare potential can be of high value. This potential will only be realized if more effective electronic equipment and replacements for outworn ships are placed in the hands of the fine sailors of South America.

We must retain the competence which we have already developed by giving support to the best of the existing antisubmarine warfare vessels and by a limited ship-loan program. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General.

General O'MEARA. Of course, I could see ways where we could spend more than $57.5 million. On the other hand, it is not my business to evaluate the relative importance of the programs that we have here against the very great needs of other parts of the world.

A more complete answer to your question, I think, is to say that Latin America is now a very explosive area of the world. How much it is going to change in the next year, I don't know.

We can carry on our antisubmarine warfare program to a constructive extent this year. 

We are transferring several ships which have been planned for transfer for some time, but the transfer will be completed in 1962. 

If the situation deteriorates, if things 6 months or 3 months from now look worse than they look today, it may well be that I will feel called upon to recommend more military assistance effort than can be funded in this $57.5 million, and then it would be a matter of departmental policy and governmental policy to decide whether my recommendations warrant support or not.

Washington, D.C.

 10:50 a.m., Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding. 

The committee meets this morning in executive session for continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

Our witness this morning is General Norstad, Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.

General, we want to apologize because we do not have a full attendence. When we scheduled this hearing today, we expected that the House would be in session and we would have all of our members in town. 

I am glad we have enough members here to go ahead. Will you proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF GEN. LAURIS NORSTAD, SUPREME ALLIED COMMANDER, EUROPE 

General NORSTAD. Mr. Chairman, I have submitted a statement, which is really an opening statement. If it is agreeable to you, I will not burden you by reading it. It is in the record. I prefer to follow the practice of the past, if I may, of just speaking very directly and more or less extemporaneously. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, then, General, we will put your statement in the record. 

(The prepared statement of General Norstad is as follows:) STATEMENT OF GEN. LAURIS NORSTAD, SUPREME ALLIED COMMANDER, EUROPE 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, this is the sixth time I have appeared before this committee to support that part of the mutual assistance program which is designed to create strength and to maintain confidence in the area for which I have military responsibility-particularly in that vital region whose security is guaranteed by the North Altantic Treaty Organization. 

My presentations to you have been given their pattern by the problems of the day, and I need not remind you that there have always been problems, serious problems. The context formed by the events of this year emphasizes, it seems to me, the challenge of opportunity as well as the challenge of threat. 

You will recall that almost 14 years ago, in 1948, the very life of Berlin was threatened by a blockade imposed by the Soviets. That threat provided the major inspiration for 12 nations to join together to form NATO for the common defense of common principles. 81496-62-pt. 2- -6 281

Then, as now, Berlin was a symbol of a larger issue, a greater problem. But it served well to remind us of our duty. Our response, the creation of and support for the alliance, was an effective one. More than that, it has provided an example of collective-defense-in-being of great current authority and historical significance.

Today Berlin, a city that since the war has been separated by the influence, the pressure and the force of the authoritarian Communist regime, is physically divided by barbed wire and concrete walls. The Communist leaders have built these barricades not to keep people out, but to hold them in; not to defend, but to enslave. 

In the London Times of March 19, a Berlin manufacturer is reported to have commented that the wall was "a flagrant defeat for the Russians and their East German satellite. It is, after all, rare to see with one's own eye a Communist paradise which has to be contained with barbed wire to prevent the elect from running away."

You will have noted that since the 8th of February there have been almost continuous efforts to harass the allies as they use the established air corridors between Berlin and the West.

You may gage the success of this exercise by the fact that the passenger traffic over these corridors in the month of February 1962 was very substantially greater than during the same period of 1961-18 percent in fact-and that each succeeding week up to the present date has seen an actual increase in allied air traffic. 

For instance, the weekly average in February 1962 was 24,200 passengers; during the first week of this month the number was 25,900; and in the second week of 

March, 27,100 were carried.

The serious problem of which the wall and the harassment in the air corridors are symbols has shaped and conditioned many of the actions of the West. The crisis which has developed over Berlin has not changed our basic tasks, but it has compelled us to review the status of our forces, our equipment and our organization, and to take urgent and important steps to improve our readiness. 

On behalf of my command I presented to the NATO Council in the course of last summer a plan of action for the member nations of NATO-a plan for rapidly improving the military strength of Allied Command Europe. 

The undertakings which were proposed were considered in two phases; the first emphasized those actions capable of producing results before January 1, 1962, and the second phase concerned actions which, under emergency condition, could produce further and greater results during the course of the year 1962. 

In the study we identified for NATO nations specific actions which could achieve the necessary improvements within the two time frames. 

The forces which we sought, which we are developing for this particular purpose and at this particular time, follow the existing plans and are consistent with already approved programs, except in one important respect-they greatly speed up the achievement of our program objectives. 

So, in general, our requirements are within agreed goals which have been carefully developed, as well as within country force programs that have been refined during recent months under normal procedures. 

In expediting our programs we proposed that specific actions be taken according to the following general priorities: first, strengthen the personnel and equipment level of existing and deployed combat units; second, add necessary combat units not presently available to Allied Command Europe to bring us closer to the established goals; third, add combat and service support units and supplies at a minimum level; and, fourth, improve the status of reserves and reinforcements, both combat and support. 

Of all of these actions, the fastest, most economical and most effective is the first; that is, raising the personnel and equipment level of existing units. 

Time does not permit me to give you details of the actions that have been taken by the NATO countries, but they have had a considerable effect. 

We are stronger in conventional forces, our nuclear capability has been improved. 

An estimate of the improvement in the overall strength and effectiveness of Allied Command Europe cannot be precise, but I can safely say that the effectiveness of our deployed forces in central Europe had by the first of January of this year been increased by more than 25 percent. 

This action gives encouragement to us. It must certainly impress the Soviets with the seriousness of our intentions. However, it clearly does not yet give us the strength we need to meet the requirements of the times. More must be done and done promptly-and whatever is done I know involves a considerable cost in money, in effort, and in sacrifice.

Progress has also been made in fields which, though primarily military in nature, serve to strengthen the political and economic posture of the alliance. 

Europe will soon witness volume production of the F-104G all-weather fighter and tactical support aircraft. The production capabilities of Germany, the 

Netherlands, Belgium, and Italy have been integrated to produce a modern and highly sophisticated piece of military equipment. 

This common production effort will provide these four nations with a common ability to support a commonly produced aircraft for a common purpose. Added to this effort is the production of this same aircraft type in Canada and in the United States, the source of the design for this model. 

The F-104G consortium is not an isolated instance. There are other joint efforts producing the HAWK antiaircraft missile, the SIDEWINDER missile, and the Mark 44 homing torpedo. All of these systems were originally American developments which are now being produced on a coordinated basis in Europe.

European nations are also developing source material for common production. 

For example, the G-91 aircraft, the French AMX series of tracked vehicles for use as self-propelled artillery, light tanks, personnel carriers, and the SS- 10/SS-11 ENTAC series of antitank missiles. 

Development is also continuing on a European design of a maritime patrol aircraft and a vertical-takeoff support aircraft. 

The projects to which I refer are to some extent a symbol of the increasing strength of the central European NATO partners-a strength that has been recognized by the decreasing amount of U.S. military assistance being requested for them.

In the program under consideration, the only military aid being requested for central European nations is that required to provide a modest amount of training and materiel to meet previous U.S. commitments. As these commitments are met, grant-aid requirements will continue to decrease. 

The improving situation is reflected by the fact that the military assistance for NATO countries under the fiscal year 1962 program is about $110 million less than we provided in fiscal year 1961; and the amount requested for fiscal year 1963 is, in turn, $120 million less than that of 1962. 

What I have just said concerning the limited requirement for outside assistance to support the military strength of the central European countries does not, unfortunately, apply to the countries on NATO's flanks, some of which are not industrially advanced at this time. Norway and Denmark require assistance. 

This, I think, is obvious when one realizes that more than one-fourth of NATO's 4,000 miles of frontline a distance roughly equivalent to that from Washington to Houston, Tex.-falls in a country of 3½ million people. 

In the southeast, the requirement is even clearer. The people of Greece and 

Turkey will, within limits, make available such forces as are needed under NATO plans, but what can be supported effectively must be measured in large part by the amount of external assistance. 

It has been said that the military assistance dollar buys more defense than any other we spend. Nowhere is this truer than in these allied countries which lie in exposed flank positions, where the aid dollar contributes directly to the political and moral, as well as the military, strength. 

These countries, though lacking in population and the products of great industry, are loyal friends and stanch supporters of the United States. They are indispensable members of the alliance. They require assistance. They deserve our full support. 

Within the last year there were two developments which relate particularly to NATO's flank positions which will be of interest to the committee. 

Last July a dynamic new element in the form of a mobile force was activated. 

The object was to provide a small but highly mobile unit, multinational in composition, capable of quickly reinforcing any threatened point within the NATO area.

If directed to do so by proper political authorities, this force could demonstrate NATO solidarity and unity of purpose in a threatened area. It could make clear to an aggressor that the NATO commitment to recognize an attack against one as an attack against all is an accepted and vital fact in the life of the alliance, and not merely words written into a treaty. 

The mobile force is drawn from military units already committed to NATO and consists of land, sea, and air elements which may operate separately or in any desired combination. At this time its components are drawn from the

forces of seven nations: the United States, United Kingdom, Belgium, Holland, Italy, Canada, and the Federal Republic of Germany. 

Last October some elements of this force carried out a small-scale deployment exercise in Sardinia for the purpose of testing command and communications. 

One point which was confirmed by this experience was that our soldiers can and do operate effectively together in spite of different languages, different ways of life, and a variety of equipment. On the other hand, many problems of organization, movement, communications, and logistics were emphasized. 

We propose by early fall to test a truly integrated mobile force on a considerably larger basis. We hope to have, for instance, in terms of the ground forces involved, as many as 3,000 men organized into 4 to 6 reinforced battalions. We expect also to have corresponding air force units in the maneuver. This time, in order to test the force in an area where it might be used, we propose to exercise it in the southern flank. 

Another interesting development is the recent formation of the Baltic Ap proaches Command. Last year I believe I reported to this committee on the progress we were making in unifying the forces which are charged with the responsibility of defending the vital area of Denmark and the Baltic exits. Now, after many months of negotiations, a command has been established, effective the 8th of December 1961. It will be activated as a fully operating command sometime early this summer. 

Comprised of Danish and German forces from the three services, the Baltic Approaches Command will be directly subordinate to CINCNORTH and will be responsible for the defense of NATO land, sea, and air areas in the vicinity of the Baltic exits, the Danish Straits, and the approaches thereto. Staffing of the various headquarters will be composed primarily of Danish and German officers, but the representation from other nationalities as well will emphasize the true allied character of this command and its subordinate units, just as the establishment of the command represents another outstanding example of NATO nations joining their efforts for a common purpose. 

It is certainly not necessary to explain to this committee in detail the relationship of the military assistance program to the activities and the developments to which I have made reference. It is sufficient to say that everything I have mentioned has been made possible by or depends to some extent on the military assistance programs-past, present, or future. 

This applies equally to the buildup of strength to meet the Berlin crisis, common production efforts, the mobile force, and, perhaps most directly, to the strength of some of NATO's members.

I urge you to support the military assistance program as an essential contribution to the achievement of our national as well as our NATO purpose, to provide "for collective defense and for the preservation of peace and security." 

General NORSTAD. As I recall, this is the sixth year in which I have appeared before this committee. General NORSTAD. When we get down to the actual military aid program, you will see the most important single problem is that of the flank countries, particularly Greece and Turkey. They are in an exposed and extremely important position. [Security deletion.] 

In addition to that, they are so remote that they may need at any time some tangible evidence that we propose to carry out article V of the treaty-that we will come to their defense if they are attacked. 

We have organized a mobile force, a task force, with a number of force combinations. You can change these combinations to fit any situation. At the present time, we have [security deletion] Belgian, German, Italian, British, Canadian, Dutch, and American ground and air forces that are readily available. [Security deletion.] 

The thought is, while this force is small, that we could move it very rapidly by air to a threatened area. So a small force, supported with good firepower, could have a substantial influence from the military standpoint.
