STATEMENT OF HON. FRANK M. COFFIN, DEPUTY ADMINISTRATOR FOR PROGRAM, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. COFFIN. 

This morning I would hope to cover two areas of importance to the committee, (1) free world assistance other than that furnished by the United States. 

Chairman MORGAN. Pardon me; what statements do you want included in the record now? 

Mr. COFFIN. At this point, Mr. Chairman, the statement on free world assistance. (The statement on free world assistance is as follows:) 

STATEMENT OF HON. FRANK M. COFFIN, DEPUTY ADMINISTRATOR FOR PROGRAM, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT I. INTRODUCTION 

Mr. Chairman, our subject today is one of the principal elements of our program for spurring the growth of the less developed areas. The subject is the mobilizing of greater contributions from our friends in other industrialized countries and the coordination of their programs and our own into a more effective free world common aid effort. A major aid effort is a priority political and moral responsibility of all industrialized countries—not just a U.S. responsibility. 

A successful effort in the less developed areas requires substantially more foreign aid than the United States alone can provide. 305

Today I can report to you with some satisfaction that significant progress has been made in the last year toward a greater and more concerted free world effort. The prospects for further progress are bright. I hasten to add that the other industrialized countries have by no means fulfilled our expectation, Much more needs to be done in amount and quality. However, a great sense of motion is now fully evident among the other industrialized nations toward meeting their responsibilities to the less developed areas. My confidence and sense of encouragement is compounded of both the increased effort that has been achieved and the basis that has been laid for a much more intensive cooperative effort in the future. In particular, the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) of the 

Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) has now begun to assume a major responsibility for aid coordination. 

In January and February of this year I made a 32-week trip to seven major donor capitals to gather information firsthand on the activities and attitudes of the other donors, as well as to convey to them the sense of urgency that we attach to increases and improvements in their efforts as we increase and improve our own. I visited Bonn, Paris, London, Brussels, Rome, Tokyo, and 

Ottawa, and met with officials of the OECD, DAC, and the European Economic Community (EEC) as well as the governments in those capitals. I had joint meetings and private sessions with a total of 280 officials from foreign governments and international organizations. I would like to report to you in some detail on my findings and conclusions from that intensive donor survey trip. 

Before lauching into the subject, however, I would like to summarize for you the broad overall points I want to stress and illustrate. 

First, the other donors are doing more than is generally known and their efforts are improving both in quantity and quality. This applies to the magnitude and terms of their aid, to the types of aid tools they employ, to the spread of countries they assist, and to their organizations, programing, and coordination. 

Second, I have to conclude at the same time that the other industrialized countries are still not doing enough. The overall magnitude must be increased, there are qualitative gaps in their efforts, and coordination needs to be greatly improved. In saying that greater effort is needed, I also will want to point out to you the nature of some of the problems that must be overcome to achieve enlarged and improved aid programs. 

Third, I want to describe some of the things we have done already to elicit improved efforts and greater coordination. Under this heading I will go into the work of the DAC, the consortia of the World Bank (IBRD), stabilization packages under the leadership of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and coordination efforts we are contemplating at donor capitals, in Washington, and in the field.

Fourth, I want to describe the new work program for foreign aid coordination that the industrialized nations have agreed to undertake with DAC. 

Finally, I have attached two annexes to my written statement. One shows the aid efforts of the United States and the other donors in absolute amounts and as a percentage of GNP. The second annex is a list of coordinated aid programs and projects undertaken in the past several years involving the United States, other donor countries, and international organizations. 

II. OTHER DONORS ARE DOING MORE THAN IS GENERALLY KNOWN 

The other industrialized countries are doing more than is generally known. 

I found that there was an almost universally accepted moral obligation to give aid and a general belief that an adequate level of aid is in the political and economic interest of the free world. The sense of moral obligation was expressed both in general, and specifically, in relation to certain countries toward which donors felt a special responsibility. The importance of aid in the cold war was underlined by several donors. Aid from the other donors was also motivated by a recognition of their interest in expanding international markets. (a) Aid disbursements are rising Knowing these attitudes, one is then perhaps less surprised to find that disbursements of aid by the other industrialized countries are rising. Gross official aid disbursements of the other OECD countries and Japan--for grants, loans of greater than 5 years and contributions to international organizations-rose 90 percent from $1 billion in 1956 to $1.9 billion in 1960.¹ If reparations, consolida- 

1 References, unless otherwise noted, are to calendar rather than fiscal years, to conform to the reporting of aid statistics by the OECD.

tions of older credits, and purchases of IBRD securities are included, the total disbursements of the other OECD countries and Japan rose from $1.3 billion in 

1956 to $2.3 billion in 1960. U.S. disbursements in those years were almost entirely in the first category of grants, loans over 5 years and contributions. 

Although larger than the total for the other donors combined, U.S. aid disburse ments increased at a slower pace of less than 50 percent from $2.1 billion in 1956 to $3.0 billion in 1960.

Although even preliminary disbursement figures are not yet available for 1961, I received clear indications from some governments that they would be higher than in 1960. For example, officials of the British Treasury stated that in spite of Britain's economic difficulties they expected that aid disbursements, which totaled £150 million in their financial year 1960-61, were likely to rise 20 percent to £180 million in 1961-62 and, based on existing commitments, would continue to rise in the following financial year. In Germany, too, existing commitments will result in sharply rising disbursements in 1961, 1962, and beyond. (b) Aid commitments are rising

Although OECD data on commitments cover only 1960 and are incomplete, it is clear that new public aid commitments are rising and thus will lead to higher disbursements in future years.

To illustrate, I was told in Bonn that in 1961 Germany committed or earmarked $1.375 billion under a new long-term bilateral loan program, not to mention lesser amounts for technical cooperation and contributions to international organizations such as the U.N. Special Fund. This contrasts dramatically with 

1960 when Germany committed only $322 million under all programs. It should be said, however, that Germany reached an exceptionally high level of commitments in 1961 (about 2 percent of GNP and in excess of original authorizations) which the Government is not intending to match in 1962. In 1961 the ministries responsible for aid were desirous in the first year of the new loan program to reach a sufficient amount of activity to insure forward motion and an early attainment of significant disbursement levels. In addition, nonrecurring funds such as the proceeds from the sale of the Volkswagen works were available and could be tapped in 1961 to cover the commitments. Nevertheless, 1962 commitments will still remain well above the 1960 figures and should rise in subsequent years.

Canada provides another example of increased aid commitments. In 1960 

Canadian commitments totaled $72 million for all programs. In June 1961 Canada initiated a new $200 million long-term loan program. By the beginning of February of this year, after only 7 months of operation, commitments under this authorization alone had reached $100 million. In addition, of course, Canada's grant programs are also continuing. 

The Overseas Development Fund of the Common Market (adminstered by the 

Commission of the European Economic Community in Brussels) provides additional evidence of the rising trend in aid commitments. The Fund was originally established with $581 million in resources to be committed in the 5 years from 1958 through 1962 or an average of about $116 million per year. Last December the six member nations of the Common Market agreed that, at a minimum, they would renew the Fund at least for another 5 years and at the same level of activity. Indications in Brussels now are that in connection with the renewal of the Fund the member governments are likely to make available resources considerably in excess of $150 million a year over the next 5 to 7 years. (c) Aid as a percent of GNP is rising

Total gross official disbursements of the other OECD countries and Japan for grants, loans over 5 years, and contributions to international organizations increased as a percentage of GNP from 0.36 percent in 1956 to 0.53 percent in 1960. 

Comparable U.S. disbursements increased as a percent of GNP from 0.51 percent in 1956 to 0.59 percent in 1960. In comparing these figures, we should note that although U.S. disbursements as a percent of GNP remained in the lead, the other industrialized countries had narrowed the gap considerably from 0.15 percentage points difference in 1956 to 0.06 percentage points difference in 1960. 

If reparations, consolidation credits, and purchases of IBRD securities are included, the disbursements of the other OECD countries and Japan show an increase from 0.46 percent of GNP in 1956 to 0.64 percent of GNP in 1960. This 

1960 figure is actually higher than the comparable U.S. figure of 0.59 percent. 

Of course we justifiably attach considerably greater importance to the hard-core aid consisting of grants, loans, and multilateral contributions, because many of

the IBRD security purchases are short term and bear favorable interest rates; because the consolidation credits do not always extend repayment much beyond 5 years; and because reparations are an obligation quite independent of aid considerations. However, in spite of these qualifications, reparations, consolidations, and IBRD security purchases do represent important resource transfers benefiting the developing countries and therefore cannot be overlooked in measuring the aid efforts of the other industrialized countries. In any case, including reparations, and so forth, the efforts of the other OECD countries and Japan have been rising faster as a percent of GNP than our own and in 1960 approximated our effort. (d) Aid terms are being liberalized Other donors have also significantly liberalized their loan terms. For ex- ample, German loans prior to 1960 did not exceed 5 years and were at commercial interest rates. Now commercial-type project loans are for 10 to 15 years and 

52 percent while infrastructure project loans are for 12 to 20 years and 2½ to 42 percent. Grace periods run 3 to 5 years. The new Canadian loans are authorized up to 15 years. Italy has now provided for interest rate subsidies on guaranteed private financial credits which run to 10 years and longer. 

A new Japanese Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund established in March 

1961 can make loans for periods of 20 years at 3½ percent interest with up to 5 years' grace to complement their existing Export-Import Bank loans. These loans normally are for 5 to 7 years at commercial interest rates, but the terms have recently been stretched to 15 years with interest at 6 percent for the India and Pakistan consortia. Britain and France continue to give a major share of their aid as grants. (e) Aid tools are being diversified A variety of aid tools is needed if the diverse aid needs of less developed countries are to be met. Therefore, it was encouraging to me to learn on my trip of a number of initiatives to institute additional tools in existing aid programs. I have already mentioned the new loan program in Canada. 

This is a radical departure from past Canadian thinking that all aid should be grants. The loan program should introduce an important element of flexibility into Canadian efforts. 

The Overseas Development Fund of the Common Market is likewise planning to broaden into loans from a purely grant program. The Commission is also seeking authority from the six member governments to start an investment in less developed countries in partnership with private enterprise and then later sell out its share when a new enterprise is on its feet. It will be interesting to watch this important experiment which employs in a bilateral program the mechanism the Interational Finance Corporation has successfully been using multilaterally for several years. The Japanese are also trying this technique in their new Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund I mentioned earlier. 

In addition, research is being turned to as a necessary means for solving many development problems, both technical and social, and for adapting new scientific knowledge to the special situations of the developing countries. For example, the French aid budget for 1962 includes $11 million for development research of all types. The British technical cooperation program is also significantly engaged in research.

It might be noted that in many of these new steps, as with guarantees, the other donors are undertaking efforts we have been successfully employing in our programs. In the case of research the French and British have a headstart on 

And turnover equity investments are a tool we have not yet tried. us. (f) Coverage of aid recipients is beginning to be broadened Diversification of aid recipients was universally accepted as a desirable goal by the officials I talked with. A broader spread of donors provides greater assurance of independence to a recipient. A broader spread of recipients of, say, German, Canadian, and Japanese aid helps former colonial powers with some of their special burdens and offers to the donors wider market development potential. More than that, broader recipient coverage is a direct indicator of greater involvement in and commitment to the worldwide aid task. 

Actual widening of aid ties has begun and will continue. For example, Germany has expanded her program to cover 40 countries in all four regions of the world. Italian technical assistance goes to 30 countries. France has at least taken a significant token step beyond her heavy traditional ties by con-

tributing to the India and Pakistan consortia. Britain, facing the rising costs of aid to African areas, is planning to start a small technical assistance effort in Latin America. Canada has recently broadened significantly beyond her former Commonwealth aid ties through a number of sizable loan commitments to Latin American countries. Japan, although primarily concerned with the 

Far East, has gone beyond her regional priority with participation in the India and Pakistan consortia and the Brazil multilateral aid package. Japan is also active in Africa. (g) Aid organization in donor governments is improving As you all know from our experiences with a variety of organizational structures for U.S. aid programs, the effectiveness of the aid effort is greatly influenced by the nature of the organization. Perhaps our main conclusion from 

15 years of aid programs is that a single unified organization with overall responsibility for aid is the critical organizational factor. 

Most other OECD countries plus Japan are now gearing up organizationally for a sustained aid effort. Germany, France, Belgium, and Canada have recently established new aid ministries or departments, the United Kingdom a new Technical Cooperation Department. Japan is creating an Economic Cooperation Bureau to focus on aid policy in its Foreign Office. On the operations side, Germany is planning the development corporation for turnover equity investments I mentioned, and Japan has its new Overseas Economic Cooperation 

Fund. 

Although the establishment of new aid ministries, departments, and operating organizations cannot be directly translated into increased aid efforts in dollar values, these new structures are indications of the seriousness of intent of governments in the aid field. They should insure better advocacy of aid considerations in governmental discussions on policy and funding. (h) Aid programing is beginning to improve Increases in the amounts of aid provided to developing countries are plainly not the answer to development in themselves. That aid has to be well planned, effectively administered, and closely related to self-help efforts of the recipients. 

This is, of course, one of the most fundamental elements of the U.S. philosophy of the decade of development. 

On this count, too, I found significant signs of progress. For example, to provide for improved project analysis Germany has charged its Reconstruction Loan Corporation, which has had a central role in the rebuilding of postwar Germany, with that responsibility. Although the extent of the role of the new 

Ministry for Economic Cooperation has not been finally determined, it is clear that it, the Economics Ministry, and the Foreign Office see the need for greater study on the relation of aid projects to the overall economy and self-help efforts of developing countries. In Japan, the Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund is planning a 50-percent staff increase from 40 to 60 to improve project analysis capability, and the Japanese Export-Import Bank supplements its staff with loan project analysts from city banks. 

Progress on broader country and sector planning was evident in Japan. The 

Japanese Planning Agency, whose primary focus is Japan's domestic economy and carrying out the 10-year plan to double national income by 1970, was also very interested in the planning problems of the developing countries. For example, the agency held a 6-weeks' seminar on planning last summer which was attended by 30 persons from southeast Asian and Latin American countries under Colombo plan funding. The agency's long-range planning bureau, which includes 30 economists, is currently collecting information on and assessing the country plans of six Far East and south Asia countries. The new 

British Technical Cooperation Department emphasized the need to increase programing and introduce the concept of concentration of aid in British technical cooperation efforts. (i) Untied procurement with a balance of payments is gaining acceptance The OECD countries have reached agreement that as a matter of principle, aid procurement should be untied unless the donor has a balance-of-payments problem. In practice, the exception has been followed more than the rule. 

However, in two cases, Germany and Italy, it is possible to report progress. 

Both countries have enjoyed major balance-of-payments surpluses for several years running and both have built up unusually large reserves as a result. In keeping with this situation, the German Government has established a policy

of untied procurement for its new long-term loan program. Recent Italian legislation authorizes the guarantee of private credits with up to 10-year maturities. The absence of a mandatory requirement for procurement in Italy is a noteworthy feature of a significant portion of this authorization. (j) Aid coordination through the DAC is moving into a more intensive stage My visit to Paris in January coincided with a meeting of the OECD Development Assistance Committee at which the member governments reached two important agreements. One was to conduct an annual confrontation review of each member's aid program. The other was to establish informal, voluntary, ad hoc coordinating teams of small groups of DAC members to focus on the aid needs of particular priority recipient countries. These agreements reflect the growing active support for coordination of aid that I discovered in all capitals. They also represent the coming of age of the DAC as a multilateral instrument for aid coordination.

In my talks at capitals, it was clear that aid coordination in all forms was a major concern and desire. There was general enthusiastic response to my proposal to reinforce the DAC mechanism by annual bilateral meetings of senior programing officials at capitals for the purpose of relating aid programs at an early stage of the planning and programing process. There was equal support for frequent ad hoc visits by programers and technical personnel to iron out specific problems that might arise any time during the year. Virtually everyone I talked to saw the need for closer working relations in the field both in preparing programs and in carrying them out. 

In reporting to you on these most recent developments in the DAC and at capitals, I also want to underline the value of the World Bank consortia organized in the past several years for aid to India, Pakistan, and the Indus River Basin development scheme. (k) Recapitulation of the accomplishments of the other donors I have now run down a lengthy list of criteria for measuring the aid performance of the other industrialized countries. I think you will agree that the record is encouraging. On the scale of the aid efforts of other donors, disbursements and commitments have been rising sharply, aid has become an appreciably increasing percent of GNP, and there are numerous examples of important liberalizations of terms of repayment and interest. On the breadth and effectiveness of their aid efforts, I have pointed to the introduction of new kinds of aid tools, to the broadening of the coverage of recipients, to the setting up of new aid organizations, and to certain improvements in programing. 

Finally, I have illustrated the growing support for aid coordination among other donors. It is a good record, and the other donors deserve due recognition.

III. OTHER DONORS ARE NEVERTHELESS NOT DOING ENOUGH 

But it is not good enough. While this performance is praiseworthy for the period now ending, it is not a performance that can be permitted to level off and stabilize for the future. The acceleration of effort from generally small beginnings a few years ago is noteworthy. But this momentum has to be kept up to insure continuing increases in aid levels and program effectiveness. (a) Inadequate levels and terms The overall magnitude of the combined aid effort of the other OECD countries and Japan must continue to rise. Total resources now being made available to developing countries do not, when combined with their own efforts, permit a growth rate that will show significant worldwide development gains beyond matching the increase in population. This is not to speak of narrowing the gap in per capita GNP between the developing and the developed countries. 

If I may, I would like to repeat one of the points I made to the assembled delegates in the Development Assistance Committee on January 16 on this subject. I said: "We must have a sense of history. It has been our fortune to live at one of the high tension points in the history of people. "Two of the large facts of life are the tension between the have and the have not countries and the frustrated aspiration of all less developed nations to grow rapidly. Two Newtonian laws could be stated for our time: "I. Great disparity in wealth plus knowledge of the injustice of this disparity equal tension.

"II. Aspiration to develop rapidly plus inadequate capacity to satisfy this aspiration equal frustration. "These are the laws of the dynamics of disparity. We cannot hope to eliminate poverty, disease, or ignorance. We cannot, in our lifetime, erase the gap between the developed and developing nations. But we can, if we will, provide a framework for orderly and reliable progress. We can supply the basis for hope."

Unfortunately, as with most other things, there is inflation in the field of hope too. There is a rising price trend attached to the "basis for hope" in the world market of men's political and economic aspirations. In this market of aspirations the other industrialized nations are still not doing enough on behalf of the free world.

In relation of their own capacity they are also not doing enough. Both they and we have thus far fallen short of contributing 1 percent of GNP as official aid to developing countries—a rough target which the United States has supported as a reasonable objective for the industrialized countries as a group. 

But when the other great common effort of the free world is taken into account the common defense effort, the aggregate record of the other industrialized countries falls well behind our own. 

Some aid donors could be called on to increase faster than others. Countries that have not had colonial ties or only limited ones with developing countries have tended to be late starters in the aid field. For example, Italy, Germany, Japan, Sweden, and Switzerland are still developing an aid effort. They are all considerably behind France, Britain, Belgium, and the Netherlands as well as the United States. On the other hand, Canada undertook major programs of assistance to European recovery in the years immediately after World War II which subsequently slackened off. She too is now far behind the leaders in aid to the developing countries. 

Terms of aid have improved but have a long way to go to match our own or those of the International Development Association. For example, U.S. repayment periods on AID development loans are ranging between 30 and 40 years, while Italy and Canada are only in the 10to 15-year range. Germany and Japan have a current ceiling of 20 years. When warranted, AID loans are made at subcommercial interest rates and even at no interest other than a three-fourths-of-1-percent service charge. Britain and Canada, on the other hand, offer interest rates only comparable to those of our Export-Import Bankthe Treasury borrowing cost plus a service charge. (b) Narrowness and weakness in performance and structure In spite of the accomplishments cited in creating new tools of aid, broadening recipient coverage, and improving organization and programing, there are major gaps and weaknesses. For example, neither Italy nor Switzerland has a Government fund for capital assistance. Both rely on private investment and the money market for capital flows to developing countries. Neither Germany nor Japan operates a grant aid program to share in the burden of budget support, now largely borne by the United States, France, Britain, and Belgium. There are only the beginning of aid diversification by former colonial powers beyond their areas of traditional interest or of general aid to Latin America from the other donors.

Aid organization has a long way to go. Responsibility for aid remains highly dispersed in certain governments. In one major donor country, technical assistance has been centralized, but the administration of capital assistance is still widely dispersed. None of the other donors has a field organization of noteworthy proportions. (c) Inadequacies in coordination

While the will to coordinate aid was great, concrete action has been undertaken only in a relatively few instances. Policy differences on general aid objectives and differences in attitude or priority on specific recipient countries have not been adequately discussed or reconciled. Programing concepts and techniques have not been interrelated among donors. Partly for lack of policy directives and partly for lack of field staffs, coordination in the field has been poor. In fact, in a few instances free world aid programs have been somewhat competitive. This situation must be remedied. Coordination of aid packages and of such aid operations as recruitment of technicians, placement of trainees, and procurement of equipment need considerable further development. Only the surface has been scratched in the coordination of bilateral programs with those of the United Nations and its specialized agencies.

(d) Problems to overcome in improving aid efforts Having enumerated many of the current deficiencies as I see them in the aid efforts of other donors, I think it would be useful to mention a few of the problems and obstacles standing in the way of improvement before I pass on to discuss U.S. actions in this field. Many of these problems are well known or self-evident, but bear repeating. 

Perhaps the most general problem is the development of a domestic political climate favorable to an increase in aid. In the case of France, aid levels are already much higher in relation to GNP (1.59 percent in 1960) than for any other donor including the United States and the Algerian problem has been absorbing much of the national energy. A proper focus on aid policy has been impeded in Belgium as a result of the Congo experience and in Italy because of the major realinement of political parties. In both of these countries the situation appeared temporary. Domestic opposition also appeared to be a problem in Canada where the provincial governments offer competing demands for 

Federal assistance.

In Italy and Japan, two donor countries quite far down the scale of per capita GNP themselves, economic development at home is a major national policy requirement limiting their foreign aid capability both in economic and in political terms. In the case of Britain, the need for a measure of domestic economic revitalization is a deterrent to major aid increases. 

In Germany, there is a double fiscal problem. The income tax structure of the country is such that the state governments collect almost two-thirds of the total and nearly all run heavy annual surpluses, while the Federal Government in Bonn now faces deficits as it attempts to raise its defense effort and other competing programs. The Finance Ministry holds a heavy hand on aid increases. The constitutional change required to revise the distribution of the income tax receipts would be very difficult to get approved. Current balance-ofpayment difficulties prevent serious consideration of offshore procurement in Japan and Britain. 

IV. WHAT WE HAVE DONE AND PLAN TO DO TO ELICIT IMPROVED EFFORTS AND GREATER COORDINATION 

Some of the actions the United States has taken or participated in to elicit improved aid efforts and greater coordination have already been mentioned implicity in my discussion thus far. Now, I would like to describe them and our plans for future action a little more systematically. (a) World Bank coordinating efforts The IBRD has, until now, been the primary organization involved in organizing and administering consortia to provide financing for economic development. The 

Bank has sponsored consortia to support the development plans of Pakistan and India, and is the administrator of the Indus Basin Development Fund, which is also financed by a consortium of donor countries. 

1. Indian consortium.-The Indian consortium was organized to provide financing for India's third 5-year plan, which calls for total expenditures of $20 billion, including some $6 billion in foreign exchange, in the period April 1961 to March 1966. In May-June 1961, the consortium (Canada, France, Germany, Japan, United Kingdom, United States, IBRD-IDA) considered India's needs for the first 2 years of the plan and made commitments amounting to about $2,225 million for the period April 1961 to March 1963. Another meeting is now scheduled for May 1962, to consider additional aid for the second year of the plan (April 1962 to March 1963). While commitments made so far have enabled India to launch the 5-year plan with confidence in being able to maintain a steady rate of progress, the Bank and other consortium members believe that the $2,225 million committed for the first 2 years of the plan should be increased to about $2,500 million in order to cover all required expenditures in this period.

The United States has committed $1,045 million, or roughly 47 percent of total Indian consortium commitments. However, the U.S. commitment is contingent upon adequate performance by other consortium members; the United 

States has indicated to the consortium and to India that it may not be able to make this full commitment unless other member contributors bring total commitments to about $2,500 million for the first 2 years of the plan.

2. Pakistan consortium.-The IBRD also organized a consortium (same membership as the Indian consortium) in support of Pakistan's second 5-year plan, which calls for total expenditures of $4,830 million between July 1960 and June 1965, with a foreign exchange requirement of $2,300 million. Consortium meetings in June 1961 and January 1962 succeeded in raising $945 million in commitments for fiscal years 1962 and 1963. With approximately $230 million in commitments previously applied to fiscal year 1961, foreign exchange in sight for the first 3 years of the plan came to $1,175 million. The United States committed $629.6 million, or about 54 percent of the total amount. Consortium commitments were sufficient to enable Pakistan to pay for essential imports required to maintain the economy during the coming year and to sustain the momentum of development. The consortium will meet again in February 1963, to consider financing for the last 2 years of the plan. 

3. Indus waters project.—The Bank was instrumental in reaching a settlement of the Indus waters dispute between India and Pakistan. The settlement includes a plan of water replacement and water resources development works to be financed through the Indus Waters Development Fund, to which a consortium of six donor countries (Australia, Canada, Germany, New Zealand, United Kingdom, and United States) plus the IBRD, Pakistan, and India have contributed.

Commitments to the fund, in foreign exchange and local currency, amount to $894.6 million of which the United States has contributed $482 million, or about 

53 percent. The U.S. contribution is in dollar grants ($177 million), dollar loans ($70 million), and local currency grants and loans ($235 million). (b) Aid for balance of payments and monetary stabilization purposes In addition to the important and expanding role of international lending agencies and industrialized countries other than the United States in providing aid for economic and social development, such agencies and countries continued in 1961 the efforts noted in last year's presentation in organizing and providing financial assistance to less developed countries for balance of payments and monetary stabilization purposes.

In the aggregate, more assistance of this nature is still provided by the International Monetary Fund and the United States than by other agencies or countries, but increased international cooperation in assisting less developed countries with financial problems was clearly evident last year and a continuation of increasingly close international cooperation in solving these problems is confidently expected.

The expanding role played by countries other than the United States in pro-viding financial assistance is illustrated by the decreased dependence on the U.S. dollars in drawing from the International Monetary Fund. In 1961 drawings from the IMF were higher than in any previous year of the Fund's history. 

Even if the $1.5 billion drawing by the United Kingdom is excluded, the remaining drawings, which were made mostly by less developed countries, still exceeded the level of total drawings in any previous year. Despite such heavy use of 

IMF resources in 1961, drawings in U.S. dollars amounted to only 33 percent of total drawings. In 1960 dollar drawings amounted to 53 percent of all drawings. 

This increased use of currencies other than the U.S. dollar in IMF transactions has materially eased pressures on the U.S. balance of payments and represents a real and significant degree of international cooperation in providing financial assistance for stabilization purposes. The significance of this development can easily be obscured owing to the fact that the IMF, rather than individual countries acting separately, is the vehicle for providing this type of assistance. 

A partial list of coordinated international efforts in providing assistance for stabilization programs was contained in last year's summary presentation on pages 152-153. 

The largest single coordinated package last year, was one for Brazil, which was under negotiation at the time of last year's presentation. 

In this program a total of $608 million was made available to Brazil-$338 million from U.S. Government sources, $160 million from the IMF, and $110 million from European countries. In addition, all these creditors plus Japan stretched out or otherwise liberalized the repayment terms on existing debts amounting to several hundred million dollars. 

Recent new instances of such closely coordinated international programs for providing stabilization assistance are to be found in the programs for Syria and Turkey. A "package" for Syria is just approaching completion at the present time. The United States is making available $14 million, new IMF assistance will be $6.8 million, and expected assistance from Germany and Italy would bring 81496-62-pt. 2-

the total to $41.8 million. Turkey has its 1961 stabilization agreement under renegotiation with a view toward the probable provision of an additional $45 million by the European Fund of the OECD and $31 million by the IMF. In addition, financial assistance agreed to by Germany and partially utilized in 1961 will continue to be available. The United States continues to provide large-scale aid to Turkey, but such aid is not clearly classifiable as balance-ofpayments aid.

U.S. balance-of-payments aid to Chile in 1961 totaled $30 million, while funds made available to Chile by the IMF amounted to $91 million. In early 1962 

Germany independently provided $25 million in balance-of-payments aid to Chile. 

(c) The work of the Development Assistance Committee 

The DAC's predecessor, the Development Assistance Group (DAG), was created, as you know, on U.S. initiative in early 1960. Simultaneously, a transformation of the old Organization for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC) which sparkplugged the Marshall plan and European reconstruction after World War II was gotten underway. These two initiatives were designed to focus the attention of the industrialized countries on the developmental problems, not only of southern Europe, Greece, and Turkey, but more generally, of the less developed countries throughout the free world. Some of you may recall when I sat on the opposite side of this table I participated in a congressional study mission of the European subcommittee which recommended the establishment of a forum of industrialized countries. Now, with the incorporation of DAG as 

DAC into the reconstituted OECD, this has been accomplished. 

The past 2 years were a formative period. Results primarily of an indirect nature were achieved through the impact of group consultation on individual governments. I think it is fair to say that the DAC deserves a large share of the credit for the impressive changes in other donors' aid programs I have described above.

The common aid effort resolution agreed on in March 1961 at London marked the beginning of the first major formal intergovernmental effort to coordinate foreign aid programs. The ministerial level representatives agreed to recommend to their governments the common objective of an aggregate expansion of the volume of resources being made available to the developing countries. With the establishment of the OECD last fall, involving the establishment of the Development Assistance Committee as one of its principal instruments, the coordination effort received a new impetus. 

This past January an implementing or policing mechanism, the DAC annual review, was constituted. The annual review will provide for a careful scrutiny of each donor's program as to amount, terms, and effectiveness. It will also afford the opportunity to gain further agreement on important fundamental aid policy concepts such as self-help. The first review meetings will take place this May.

As I mentioned earlier, the DAC also decided in January on the establishment of voluntary, informal, ad hoc coordinating teams of DAC members and nonmembers to focus on the aid needs of particular priority recipients. In these teams donors will exchange information, work toward a division of labor in providing aid, and consider the feasibility of agreements with the recipient on organizing a formal consortium. 

To complement the DAC's own primary focus on financial and capital assistance, the members created a Technical Cooperation Working Group a year ago. 

This subcommittee is assuming responsibility for the technical assistance aspects of the annual review. It has already laid the statistical groundwork for TC program coordination.

Another initiative taken by the DAC was the approval of a development center to be established as an autonomous body under the Secretary General of the OECD. When actually set up, it will provide a strong intellectual focus on development problems and will facilitate training, planning, and research in critical development fields. It will also be an institution where experts from industrialized and less developed countries can meet and fruitfully discuss development problems.

The importance of the organized exchange and publication of statistical and descriptive information on donor aid programs and policies is an accomplishment of the DAC and OECD that should not be underestimated. Half of this very presentation would have been impossible to make in the absence of the OECD statistical information flow.

Bearing indirectly on the aid field is the agreement reached last fall in the OECD Council on a combined growth goal of 50 percent for all OECD countries over the next 10 years. This is significant, for it institutionalizes the concept of the expanding economy in an international framework that is also committed to the requirement of providing an expanding flow of resources to the less developed countries.

To help support these efforts of the OECD and DAC we are continuing to strengthen our mission to the OECD with experienced officers highly qualified to perform the aid coordination function. In addition, we are lending men of the highest competence to work in the Development Department of the OECD. 

The chairman of the DAC is Ambassador Riddleberger, whose last previous assignment was as Director of the International Cooperation Administration. 

In the period ahead, we look forward in May and June to the first DAC annual review when our program will be assessed by three other examiners— France, Japan, and EEC; we in turn will join in examining the programs of 

Germany, Belgium, Italy, and the United Kingdom. In July there will be a ministerial meeting of the DAC to focus top level attention on the results of the first review. Subsequently, we expect to hold subministerial level DAC meetings in various donor capitals to stimulate public understanding of and support for increased aid efforts. 

We are already in the midst of negotiations on the establishment of DAC coordinating teams and hope to establish the first ones in the coming weeks. The 

U.S. Ambassador to the OECD has just completed a trip to the capitals of several major DAC countries where he was able to expedite consideration of the launching of a series of coordinating teams. (d) Coordination at donor capitals, in the field, and in Washington Parallel to action going forward in DAC, we plan to increase coordination contracts at donor capitals. We shall strengthen the arrangements for permanent liaison on a day-to-day basis between our embassies and the aid officials of other donors to reinforce the work of the DAC. And I have already spoken of our intentions with respect to annual bilateral program coordination meetings, supplemented as necessary by ad hoc program and technical trips as problems arise.

To improve field coordination, we are urging other donors to improve their field representation. We will also take steps through DAC and bilaterally at donor capitals to reach agreement on instructions to field missions on coordination.

Here in Washington we have built a fourth leg under the coordination table along with the DAC, other donor capitals, and the field. A new International 

Development Organizations Staff (IDOS) has been established in AID under the leadership of a senior career official. This Staff joins in one office the multilateral aid mobilization and coordination functions that formerly were dispersed in various parts of AID and the diplomatic side of the State Department. IDOS will furnish staff services to the regional bureaus of AID in order to facilitate the formation of coordinated aid programs.

V. CONCLUSION 

This completes the first major presentation we have ever made of the aid efforts of other free nations. It should be recalled that we are speaking of a substantial effort which is in being and on the rise only a dozen years after the first Marshall plan deliveries began to arrive in a devastated Europe. Our partnership with the countries we have helped in the past faces new horizons of responsibility and opportunity. There is a long way to go to meet the responsibility and seize the opportunity. But a good beginning has been made.

Mr. COFFIN. Later on and still this morning I will address myself to Sino-Soviet bloc assistance. 

Both are areas that do not fall within any particular region, but they are a part of the foreign aid picture and they both are important to you in grappling with this problem or in answering questions on the floor. 

With regard to free world assistance, I will not attempt to read the statement at this time. I will summarize what I think are the most important points and follow that summary with a brief exposé of several charts that will give a clear picture as to disbursements and commitments. 

With me this morning, also to respond to questions on free world assistance, is Ambassador Tuthill, who is our representative to the 

OECD, the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development, in Paris. This is an organization which, incidentally, he helped bring about in late 1959 and 1960. This is the successor of the OEEC, which was the group of European nations which administered the Marshall plan.

As it is reorganized, this group consists not only of 18 European nations but also of Canada and the United States. 

It is now oriented not only in the direction of general economic policy, and matters involving trade, but also, through its Development Assistance Committee (DAC), to the objective of supplying aid to less developed countries in a large and growing measure and in a more coordinated fashion. 

You have never had presented to you a detailed story on what other nations are doing. I therefore think this year that the material in the statement is well worth your detailed scrutiny. 

I don't wish to oversell the statement. In general, I make two major points: First, other nations in the free world are doing far more than most of us have thought they were doing; second, they are not doing as much as they should do. 

Part of the new Agency for International Development is specifically oriented to this task of making contact with other nations, of trying to help them increase the resources made available for aid, and to coordinate their efforts better with ours and with those of the leading international financial institutions. 

To approach this task we in AID have equipped ourselves with a new unit, a staff called the International Development Organization staff, under Mr. Jacob Kaplan.

This staff has within it some people who formerly were within the diplomatic side of the State Department in the economic area. Mr. 

Kaplan has two principal functions under him, one is to deal with the U.N. and various U.N. agencies; the other side of his operation is to backstop our DAC operation in Paris, which is under Ambassador Tuthill.

To be able to give you a feeling for what other nations have been doing, I personally took a trip in January which carried me to Bonn, Paris, London, Brussels, Rome, Japan, and Ottawa. These were the capitals of the major donor-lender countries in the aid picture. 

This was a fascinating and productive trip. Much of the information we present to you was derived from talks with the aid officials, the foreign ministries, and the financial ministries of these countries.

I also came back with the conviction that we had a great deal to accomplish that would be to our mutual benefit if we maintain such relationships, both at the very top levels of our governments, and also at the program and technical levels. 

Let me summarize the conclusions from this trip and from our studies of the data that have been made available to us. 

The first part is that addressed to the proposition that these other countries are doing more than we think they have been doing. 

The first observation is that their aid disbursements have been rising. From 1956, when their disbursements were in the order of $1 billion for grants, for loans over 5 years, and for contributions to international organizations, they rose in 1960 to almost $2 billion, or $1.9 billion.

In the same period, from 1956 to 1960, our disbursements rose from $2.1 to $3 billion. In other words, in 1956 the percentage of aid given by other donor countries was 38 percent of the total, if we count in not only grants, loans over 5 years, and contributions to international organizations, but also reparations, consolidation credits, and purchases of IBRD notes.

In 1956 they were 38 percent of the total. In 1960 they were 44 percent of the total. We can conclude that disbursements have risen and we can predict they will continue to rise. 

Germany, for example, last year made a tremendous commitment for itself, a commitment that involved over a billion dollars for loan money. And they did it deliberately to reach a high plateau of disbursements. They did it using some credits which will not be recurring, such as sales of Volkswagen stock. Nevertheless, because they have taken this extraordinary measure to get up on this plateau, their disbursements will rise during the years ahead. 

But commitments are also rising. In Germany last year they made commitments and earmarkings of $1.3 billion for loans, plus technical cooperation and contributions to international organizations. 

Canada supplemented its Colombo plan contributions with a $200 million credit act and appropriation.

The Common Market itself over the 5 years through 1962 has averaged $116 million a year in grant commitments and for the next 5 to 7 years the Common Market anticipates an average of $150 million a year, and possibly more.

So disbursements and commitments have risen. The percentage of gross national product devoted to aid has also increased. The disbursements of these other free, industrialized countries in 1956 were 0.36 percent of GNP, and by 1960 they had risen to 0.53 percent. 

At the same time the United States had increased from 0.51 to 0.59 percent. They have narrowed the gap from 0.15-0.15 percentage points in 1956 to 0.06 percentage points in 1960.

Aid terms also are being liberalized. In Germany before 1960 the ordinary term for loans was 5 years at commercial rates. Now for private projects they go on the average from 10 to 15 years at 512 percent, and for public works projects, infrastructure they go from 12 to 20 years at 21/2to 412-percent interest with grace periods of 3 to 5 years. Canada has brought its loan period up to 15 years. Italy now has authority to guarantee private loans for periods of 10 years, and with the expectation of going over this limit. Japan can now loan

for 20 years at 31½ percent with a 5-year grace period. Its own export-import bank can loan up to 15 years. 

Britain and France give a great deal with the majority of their aid in grants. But in loans the United Kingdom has now gone up to 30' years, 512 to 65% percent with 7-year grace periods.

I should point out that the International Development Association (IDA) is a vehicle for these other countries to make extremely long term, low interest rate loans through their contributions to IDA. 

Every time that IDA makes a 50-year loan at three-fourths of 1 percent interest with a 10-year grace period, you know there is some European money in that package. 

The aid tools are diversified. In the past a country would do just project lending or perhaps just budgetary support or perhaps just a little technical assistance. But Canada, which has been a charter member of the Colombo plan, has recently expanded its tools to engage in lending. I told you about the $200 million appropriation for loans. 

[Security deletion.] 

The Common Market through its oversea development fund has been making grants, and now will add a long term, low interest loan capacity to this fund. At least, this was very much in the forefront of debate when I was over there in January. They also are prepared to make investment guarantees and are getting for themselves broader authority for technical cooperation. 

In Germany they not only have made this very large loan commitment and earmarking last year but they are planning to establish a corporation, a gesellschaft, which will be prepared to purchase equities in new ventures and then turn these equities over to private investors when the venture proves it can survive. 

Japan has just set up an oversea economic cooperation fund. 

When I looked at the charter in Tokyo in late January it looked familiar. They told me this was modeled in large part on our own 

Development Loan Fund Charter. This fund not only can loan money but can also make turnover equity investments. 

France has been in the aid business a long time and has, as you know,. a higher per capita burden by far than we do. It also, this was interesting to me, has a substantial research program committing some $11 million to research in connection with its development work. 

Another item that was of interest was the extent to which they are covering additional countries. We are accustomed to think of the 

European countries as directing a great deal of their aid to their former dependent territories or colonies. This is still true to a large extent, but Germany, for example, which does not have the colony problem, has aid programs going in some 40 countries. Italy has programs in 30 countries. France, although giving most of its aid to its former dependent territories in Africa, which account for a goodly parcel of the newly emerging countries, has also contributed to the Pakistan and India consortia. The United Kingdom is preparing to do technical assistance in Latin America. Canada has been making loans under its new authority in Latin America. 

And Japan, although its primary area of interest is in the Far East, has joined the Pakistan and India consortia and also participated in the Brazil package a year ago.

Another area of interest to you, I think, is the extent to which these countries have formalized their operations though aid organizations. 

In the past this was done through interministerial committees. But virtually all these countries have now established aid ministries or departments. This has been true in Germany, France, Belgium, and 

Canada. In the United Kingdom they have just established a new technical cooperation department. In Japan they have an economic cooperation bureau, which is new, as well as the oversea economic cooperation fund. I have told you about the new development corporation planned in Germany.

Still another area of interest to me on my trip was the extent to which they are programing their aid more professionally. In Germany there is increased interest in the analysis of projects, and they have delegated to the reconstruction loan corporation additional duties in this kind of analysis. 

In Japan they have increased the staff by 50 percent of their oversea economic cooperation fund. Their export-import bank draws on city bank experts to help them analyze projects. Their very sophisticated Japanese planning agency, which has the main job of trying to make Japan accomplish its 10-year goal of doubling its income, is also working on the problems of underdeveloped countries. 

They currently are studying the plans of six Far East and south Asian countries. 

The United Kingdom, as I have said, has through its new technical cooperation department shown a new interest in the programing of aid.

As far as untied procurement is concerned, Germany has given its most recent loans on an untied basis, and Italy under its new law is equipped to guarantee a portion of its private loans without any legal restriction as to tied procurement. 

Mrs. BOLTON. What do you mean by "tied"?

Mr. COFFIN. Purchases only from its own country. We have tied procurement because of our balance-of-payments problem. 

Now, I would like to concentrate for a moment on what I think is the most important development that has taken place within the past year, and that is within OECD and particularly in the Development Assistance Committee (DAC). Everything I say has been the result of the labor of Ambassador Tuthill and the people working with him. 

In the first place, there was a resolution establishing a common aid effort, in which all the countries stated that it was part of their objective to mount a common aid effort. And a substantial part of their resources would go into this. 

The second thing that happened this happened when I was in Paris at the DAC headquarters-a resolution was passed adopting the annual review procedures, whereby each aid giving country is examined by other donor countries and in turn has the right to examine other countries. Our examination will take place in May and June. 

We will also be examining the programs of other countries. 

A third thing happened, also while I was there, after months of negotiation, and it is a development I cannot underestimate: that is, the adoption of the principle that DAC members will join in ad hoc coordinating teams to study the problems of particular countries or regions or even projects.

These are informal teams. The studies might result just in aid to a particular project. They might result in a coordinated aid package for the whole country's plan. 

It is through this mechanism that we expect to involve donor countries, not only insofar as increasing their amounts of aid are concerned, but also to sitting down with them and gradually getting a feel for a given recipient country. We hope to be able to talk to them about the terms of their aid to that particular country so that we will have a better balance than we have had in the past. 

This is a vehicle which is of great significance to our common aid effort. We would hope to be able to report next year that several teams have not only been formed in all the areas of the world, but that they have produced rather remarkable results. 

The OECD is also on the point of serious consideration and adoption of a development center, which will be a facility to help them in their techniques of giving aid. It will be of help to the recipient countries and, also, I am hopeful, will have an influence in mobilizing private capital, both from Europe and America. 

The statistical service is improving. Most of the figures that I have put into my report have been taken from the statistics already developed by the OECD and its predecessor agency, the OEEC. 

The OECD also adopted this last spring a growth goal of 50 percent in 10 years for OECD members. Or is it 50 percent in 9 years? 

Mr. TUTHILL. In the sixties.

Mr. COFFIN. This is significant because the ability of countries like 

Japan and Italy to contribute to aid will depend upon their meeting this kind of growth goal. It is also significant for Great Britain if 

Great Britain is to take on renewed responsibilities. 

The chairman of DAC is our own Ambassador Riddleberger. He is an international civil servant and presides over this committee. 

Ambassador Tuthill is our advocate, our strategic leader and tactician, as we try to make up these coordinating teams. 

During May and June we will be examined by France, Japan, and the Common Market. We will be on panels to examine Germany, Belgium, Italy, and the United Kingdom.

There are problems. We are not blinking the fact that both as far as levels are concerned and terms, we are not doing enough on liberal enough terms to satisfy what we think are the needs in the developing countries or what we think is a fair balance among all the donor countries.

There is still a weakness in the aid structures of these other countries. There is not enough centralization of responsibility in some of them. In some countries, such as Italy and Switzerland, there is no government fund for capital assistance. In Germany and Japan there is no grant aid for budgetary support, whereas Britain and France find a great deal of their aid in that kind of funding. 

We would like to look forward to a broadening out of the recipients. of these various countries. We would like to look forward to increased coordination in policies and programing in the capitals, in Paris and in the field. 

Let me just now bring this discussion to a conclusion by reviewing the problems that these other countries face.

France, with 1.59 percent of GNP put into aid of various kinds, finds that this burden is extremely high. If and when Algeria is settled, this will ease part of France's problems. Nobody can say that France is shirking its load. 

In Belgium, the Congo has been a great preoccupation. We will not be able to expect great increases from Belgium or great broadening of recipients until that situation has become more stable. 

In Italy, the Government has just gone through a realinement of parties. Their big problem is to get aid into the budget. Most of their loan aid is done through subsidizing the interest rates which the Government guarantees; that is, the Italian aid has not been put into the budget on an annual basis, as it has here. But to crash through the budget barrier in Italy is a job that will take great political stamina.

In Canada, the Government there faces [security deletion] the problem of the relation between the Federal Government and the 

Provinces. [Security deletion]. 

Italy and Japan, although growing very fast, are still underdeveloped in many parts of their own nation and realize that they have domestic problems to satisfy, particularly in Italy where the south is a great underdeveloped area in itself. 

The United Kingdom is currently confronted by a very serious balance-of-payments problem. 

And Germany, although prospering and growing, is saddled with a difficult tax structure where most of the revenues come from taxes raised by the states, and are not available to the federal government unless on a loan basis, or some other extraordinary basis. It is as if the Federal Government of the United States could not count on the income tax to finance all of its expenditures but on a much more restricted tax with the States having the prior revenue source. This is a structural difficulty that confronts Germany.

In my statement I have summarized the commitments and the progress on several consortia sponsored by the IBRD. I have also included a rundown of the various group efforts to meet balance of payments and stabilization needs where we and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other countries have participated. 

I think I have said enough to give you an idea of the current status of free world contributions. Before we turn this part of the session to questions, I want to show you two or three charts which will summarize what I have said in terms of figures. (The following charts were then shown:)

This first chart I told you about. This is official Government assistance from the United States and from the other developed 19 members of the OECD and Japan, where we in the United States went from $2.1 billion to almost $3 billion in the 5 years from 1956 through 1960, and the other OECD countries went from $1.3 to $2.3 billion.

This includes what we call pure aid, which is grants and loans over 5 years and contributions to international organizations. It also includes reparations, refinancing of older credits, and purchases of World Bank securities. There is more of the latter in the totals of other countries than in ours. 

Mr. O'HARA. What does LDC mean?

Mr. COFFIN. Less developed countries. It is bureaucratic jargon. 

Mr. O'HARA. I would like to get away from these initials. 

It would be easier for us if you would get away from the alphabet. 

Mr. COFFIN. We will bear that in mind, Mr. O'Hara. It is a shortcut I will admit. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Every time you come up you have more new ones.

Chairman MORGAN. Automation, Mrs. Bolton. 

Mr. COFFIN. Public and private resources are greater in the OECD countries than they are from the United States. Our total investment in 1960 was $4 billion. The other countries are $4.4 billion because they have so much more private investment in South Asia, in Africa, and the Far East.

Our investment in Latin America was very high. As you know, after the Cuban problem there was a fall off in private investment. 

So the total resources shows gain, not that we are not doing more as a Government than all others, but that others are doing more than I think most Americans think they are doing. 

One more chart that shows the percentage of GNP spent on aid. 

This official assistance includes grants and loans over 5 years. It also includes contributions to international organizations, the reparations and the other type of aid we have talked about. And it includes our long-term Export-Import Bank loans and Public Law 480. 

You see, percentagewise, France is still very much at the top of the list, even if we took out Algeria which is in here. If it were out they would still be about 0.9 percent.

Mr. O'HARA. What is in there pertaining to Algeria, the military expenses?

Mr. COFFIN. No. This is economic. This is not military. 

Belgium, 0.8. United Kingdom, 0.6. We are about 0.6. Germany, 0.56 and so on. Canada is quite low, 0.21.

Chairman MORGAN. What is the reason for the decrease on the part of Canada since the Marshall plan?

Mr. COFFIN. I don't know. They were a leader in the Marshall plan days. They have fallen off. Mr. Diefenbaker is proud of the fact that under his administration they increased their Colombo plan from $35 million to $50 million a year. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. COFFIN. They have just started an aid organization in Canada. 

I went up to Ottawa several weeks ago. They have now a separate organization for aid. Herbert Moran is head of it, and Peter Towe, whom Ambassador Tuthill knew in Paris at DAC, has gone back to

be deputy. They are both able people. I think we can look toward deepening our relationship with their organization and seeing their resources pulled in. 

Perhaps we could turn this over to questions. I do have, I think, an interesting set of facts on Sino-Soviet aid. If you want me to cover it now I can, and we can let the questions address both Sino- Soviet aid and free world aid. 

Mr. HAYS. Could I ask a question right here that might help my understanding. What is DAC?

Mr. COFFIN. DAC is a committee of the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development.

Mr. COFFIN. I think Mr. Hays may be skeptical but I would think about 7 minutes.

Mr. HAYS. I will take a little bet on that, since you brought my name up.

Mr. COFFIN. The Sino-Soviet bloc has been in aid operations for 7 years since 1955. My prime message to you this morning is to examine two opposite conclusions that we find ourselves making, both of which are wrong.

The foregoing points, I feel, give us a fairly clear picture of what sort of competition we have to deal with in the foreign aid field. 

The Russians are by no means 9 feet tall, but neither are they midgets. 

They have their problems, as we do. They make mistakes, they run into implementation difficulties, they struggle with language barriers, they are not 100 percent successful, or anywhere close to that perfect figure. The governments of the newly developing countries on the whole would probably rather have all their needs filled from Western sources. They would rather have Western goods and Western aid. 

Most of them know that bloc aid is based on the strictly political motives of the moment. Most of them are aware although apparently some still have much to learn, of the serious risks of political subversion when they deal with the bloc, of dangerous dependence on bloc sources and markets which can be cut off at will, of critical spare parts difficulties, of pricing, cost, and repayment problems. But at present, when the overall need for aid is so great, the bloc is a force and an influence which we cannot ignore and with which we must reckon in our dealings and discussions with the countries of the less developed areas. 

One is that it deserves nothing but gold stars for its effort, that all of its technicians are multilingual, that they all establish good relations with the recipient country, that they do this job a good deal better than we do. 

The opposite conclusion is that they don't know this business at all, that their aid commitments are hollow promises which are never

followed up, that they supply shoddy goods and unskilled services, that the few items they do are really showpiece projects in critical countries.

So I have tried to devise my testimony to take what I call the 10 myths of Soviet aid and give you a little bit of the facts exploding each myth.

The first myth is they start with a splash but there is no followthrough. Actually, their commitments have risen steadily to the point where they have now extended economic aid of about $412 billion, running about a billion dollars a year. This fluctuates, but over the past 3 years the average has been a billion. Seventy percent is from Russia, 20 percent from Europe, and about 10 percent from 

Red China.

The second myth is they do it in only a handful of countries. It is true that 80 percent of bloc aid goes to seven countries, but this is also true of us. I think 65 percent of our aid goes to 10 countries and 80 percent goes to about 20. The Soviet bloc is aiding 28 countries. Last year they added four more: Cyprus, Mali, the Somali

Republic and Sudan. I think they will add others in Africa and 

Latin America.

The third myth is that their aid is overvalued because we convert their commitments into dollars at unrealistic levels. Actually, most bloc aid is fixed in its gold content whether we phrase it in terms of rubles or whatever currency. Many commitments are framed in dollars. The pricing of commodities and services usually reflects free world prices.

Sometimes the recipient country will use a Sears Roebuck catalog to determine what the price ought to be. There are some examples of complaints, as in Afghanistan, Indonesia, and Iraq. Ghana has been the most recent country to complain of the Soviets trying to put an unrealistic price on aid under a commitment. On the whole, we can't say that this $4.5 billion of economic aid and $2 billion of military aid is an unrealistic estimate. 

The fourth myth is they do it with easy credit and terms. It is true their interest rates are lower than most of our aid. But U.S. aid is for a longer period. Also the Soviets sometimes can compensate for its low interest rate when it negotiates the actual deal. 

The fifth myth and the most dangerous myth is that their aid goes into showpiece places that are not very sound but may be glamorous. 

The facts are these: over 50 percent of the projects we have identified, which is about $3 billion worth of projects, are in industry. They are in steel, cement, textiles, sugar, assembly plants, machine tool, farm tool plants, bicycle and tire factories, fruit canneries, pharmaceutical, and even some nuclear reactors. Over 15 percent of these are in transportation and communications; 12 percent is in multipurpose hydroelectric projects, 11 percent is in mineral exploitation, and under 3 percent are what we would call showpiece projects. 

The sixth myth is that they are very fast in giving their aid. Sometimes they are. But after 7 years they have expended less than 25 percent of the amounts that they have committed. Even in 1961 their actual rate of expenditure had reached only $300 million. 

Sometimes they give priority to a country and speed up there and drop everything else. But they have problems as we do in transportation, material shortages, lack of skills or lack of local currency. They

have been fast in Afghanistan, Yemen, and India. They have been very slow in Ethiopia, Indonesia, and Iraq. 

The seventh myth is that they only use obsolete equipment. In general their equipment, whether military or civilian, is not as good as ours, but it is adequate to the task. 

They have had persistent trouble with drills for construction work. 

These have broken down and caused all manner of difficulties. There was a cement plant in Afghanistan which didn't work out. In Egypt there were diesel locomotives that couldn't work in that climate. În 

Indonesia a sugar mill that didn't work out, and 4,000 jeeps that weren't usable in that climate. 

Their aircraft that they have supplied in civilian programs have been costly, with excessive speed on the landing and inadequate speed on the takeoff. 

But in their military aid they have given some advanced tanks, bombers, Mig-19, and Mig-21 jet fighters. 

They have had some poor naval vessels in tropical countries. You can't say that everything has been a flop. On the whole, these recipient countries want this aid and it is useful to them. 

The eighth myth is that there is no such thing as an "Ugly Russian." 

There are probably more Russian technicians in the 28 countries it is operating in than there are U.S. Government technicians even worldwide. When you count private contractors, then we would have to add a component of people. But they have increased their technicians 30 percent over the past year. 

Sometimes these technicians get into very difficult kinds of problems. In one country some ambitious technicians were arrested for accosting a lady. In Guinea, a couple of Soviet technicians were accused and I think convicted of putting diamonds in coffee bags. 

This therefore should be taken into account as we look at our own efforts. They are not 10 feet tall. They do have difficulties. 

The ninth myth concerns local language: Their diplomatic people speak local languages quite frequently. Their aid people more often do not speak local languages. They need an interpreter. The United 

States is often at an advantage since English is understood in many of these countries. 

Finally, the myth that the U.S.S.R. cannot afford this. Well, the 

U.S.S.R. is contributing about 1 percent of its GNP on all foreign aid. At the moment, it hasn't realized the drain on resources because, except for its aid and other bloc countries, most of it has been in the form of commitments rather than expenditures. There are some internal strains as they try to get equipment for aid. 

I will close this with an observation that I think is well to bear in mind. I am told that Izvestia carried a story from one of its reporters who had gone to Egypt. He had asked a local Egyptian about the great Aswan Dam that was being built. The local Egyptian with whom this reporter talked said, when he was asked who was building it, that the Egyptian Government was. In other words, they don't get credit for what they do sometimes, just as we don't sometimes.

I think I have lost my bet. But pehaps I can just show a couple of charts before we go into the questions on bloc aid. (The following charts were then shown:)
