 (The prepared statement on Sino-Soviet bloc aid is as follows:) 

SINO-SOVIET BLOC AID: MYTHS AND FACTS 

The Sino-Soviet bloc aid program is now in its seventh year. It was in 1955 that the Soviet Union, its satellites and Communist China followed the example of the United States by extending long-term credits and grants to the newly developing countries of the free world. The past 7 years have seen a sizable growth in the size and scope of the bloc aid program. They have also seen a sizable growth in the number of myths, misconceptions, and misimpressions that surround the program's operations. Much has been spoken and written on the subject, but for some reason most of what has been said has tended to center around two opposite poles of comment. On the one hand, the bloc gets virtually nothing but gold stars for aid efficiency, performance, and impact. This line of comment has no room for the "Ugly Russian." Bloc technicians are portrayed as multilingual; they know the country they work in and mix in perfect harmony with the local population. On the other hand, the bloc aid program gets nothing but brickbats. This line holds that bloc aid is long on promises but short on followthrough. Commitment values are inflated, bloc goods are shoddy, the aid goes mostly for showpiece projects of little intrinsic economic worth. 

The program is limited to a handful of countries; it made a big initial splash but is petering out, and so forth.

After 7 years, I think we now have a better awareness of what the bloc is doing. We have gained enough knowledge of bloc operations to put their aid program in correct perspective. I should like to devote the discussion today to dispelling some of the myths, both good and bad, that have arisen around the bloc program so that we can all have a more realistic picture of what we have to deal with.

Myth. The bloc program started off with a big splash of publicity and many promises of large-scale aid, but the initial impact has worn away and the program has fallen off in the last few years. 

Fact.-Bloc aid commitments have risen steadily since 1955. Communist bloc aid to nonbloc countries in the less developed areas reached an estimated total of some $6.5 billion by the end of 1961-about $4.5 billion in economic credits and grants and about $2 billion in military aid. Economic aid commitments alone have averaged about $1 billion annually for the past 3 years. The Soviet 

Union is the largest supplier, providing over 70 percent of the total. The 

European satellites account for about 20 percent and Communist China for less than 10 percent.

Myth.-Bloc aid goes to only a handful of countries and is really overplayed in terms of its worldwide effect. 

Fact. It is true that some seven countries account for about 80 percent of total bloc economic and military aid. Those seven are Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Indonesia, India, Iraq, and Syria. However, substantial amounts of aid are going to many other countries. Some 28 nations are now listed as bloc aid recipients, and the list is constantly growing. Last year four new countries were added: Cyprus, Mali, the Somali Republic, and Sudan. The bloc is expanding its program in Africa and in recent months has been pushing harder in the Latin American Republics. In all probability, we shall see the bloc aid list continue to lengthen.

Myth. The whole bloc aid program is overvalued. Commitments are converted into dollars at unrealistic official rates. The true worth of the program is only a fraction of the $6.5 billion figure. 

Fact.-Most bloc agreements spell out the fixed gold content of the currency in which the aid is valued, whether it be rubles, pounds, rupees, dinars, or rupiah, so that there is no question of inflated official rates. In many cases, the value of the aid agreement is denominated directly in dollars. The figures of $4.5 billion in economic aid and $2 billion in military aid are fairly realistic valuations of the bloc commitments to date, but it should be noted that there is room for overpricing in the bilateral negotiations on particular projects and technical services. In general, it appears that the prices for machinery and construction conform to those prevailing in the free world, although there have been notable instances in Afghanistan, Indonesia, and Iraq for example-where countries have complained about overpricing and price hiking after terms had been agreed upon. Recently, Ghana complained strongly that the Soviets were charging far too much in maintenance and salary costs for their aid technicians. 

Myth. The bloc gives easy credits on terms much more favorable than the 

United States.

Fact. It is true that bloc interest rates tend to be generally lower than those of the United States. However, there are a number of significant offsetting factors that should be taken into account. U.S. loans usually carry longer amortization periods than bloc loans. Thus, annual payments on U.S. loans tend to be lower and can be met with less strain than payments on bloc credits Moreover, the longer repayment schedules for U.S. loans mean that the recipient country will have more time to expand its productive capacity and to improve its ability to pay before fully discharging its debt. Finally, low bloc interest rates must be considered in the context of the negotiated price arrangements that apply to the assistance agreements. There is sufficient flexibility in the terms of those agreements to make it possible for the bloc to compensate for its low interest rate.

Myth.-Most bloc aid goes for showpieces which make a big visual impact but are of little real economic worth to the recipient country. Projects are papier mache, nice to look at but without substance. 

Fact.-More than half the value of the $3 billion worth of bloc projects thus far identified is for expansion of the industrial sector of the recipient countries' economies. Projects in this sector include not only such heavy construction as the Bhilai steel mill in India, but a whole variety of industrial installations, large and small: cement plants, textile mills, sugar refineries, assembly plants, machine-tool factories of all types, farm-tool factories, bicycle and tire plants, fruit canneries, electric bulb and pharmaceutical factories and even small nuclear reactors.

About 15 percent of the $3 billion of agreed-on projects goes for transportation and communications: highways, ports, airfields, bridges, and railroad projects. 

Twelve percent goes for multipurpose hydroelectric power projects such as the Aswan Dam in Egypt and smaller powerplants; 11 percent for mineral exploitation, especially petroleum development in Afghanistan, India, and Pakistan. 

Less than 3 percent of bloc economic aid goes for the type of "showpiece" projects represented by the hotel in Burma, or the Asian games stadium in Indonesia, or the various gift hospitals that are a part of so many bloc offers. 

Myth.-The Soviets execute their programs with jetlike speed, making the 

U.S. programs seem snaillike by comparison. 

Fact.-Perhaps the best way to put this claim in correct perspective is to note that out of the $4.5 billion in economic aid commitments to date, only about $1 billion or less than 25 percent has so far been expended. Bloc expenditures were at a peak in 1961, totaling some $300 million, but at the rate of $300

million a year it would take another 10 years to exhaust the present unexpended balance, even if no new commitments were made. However, I think we can expect the rate of expenditure to speed up considerably as surveys are completed and more and more projects move into the implementation stage. 

It is true that in several cases, especially where the political stakes were high, the Soviets have moved ahead rapidly to carry out their program. We saw this in Afghanistan in the road-paving, bakery, and silo projects. But in the overall picture, it seems that the Soviets have run into the same difficulties in performance that we have: transportation problems, material shortages, lack of expertise and skills in the recipient countries, shortages of local currency, and similar impediments. In some countries, bloc implementation has moved at a creditable rate-in Afghanistan and Yemen for example, where roads, airfields, ports, and several factories have been completed. In India, the U.S.S.R.-built 

Bhilai mill at Madhya Pradesh is now producing at the rate of 1 million tons of steel annually; the plan is to expand output to 2.5 million tons a year. Czechoslovakia has completed a number of cement and sugar plants at Assam and Madras. In other countries, however, the programs have barely gotten off the ground despite the age of the commitment. This is true in Ethiopia, in Indonesia and in Iraq. There are many countries where longstanding umbrella credits have not yet been obligated because of the inability of the bloc and the recipient country negotiators to reach agreement on specific projects. 

Myth. The bloc gets rid of its obsolescent equipment through its aid program. Military aid equipment in particular is outmoded and of no further use to the Soviet Union. 

Fact.-In general, bloc equipment and construction materials, while in most cases below Western standards of quality, tolerances, and finish, appear adequate to do the job for which they are intended. There have been many instances, however, where bloc equipment has caused considerable difficulty and significantly delayed progress on individual projects. 

Russian drills have been a particular object of complaint. In India, the petroleum exploration program has suffered a number of setbacks because of the poor quality of the bits on Soviet turbodrills. The bits wear out after only a few feet of drilling. Drilling rigs are antiquated, heavy, and hard to handle. 

Argentina has also found Soviet oil-drilling bits unsatisfactory. Drilling equipment used at the Aswan Dam in Egypt is reported to be of inferior make, accomplishing only a fraction of the work that similar Western-type equipment could do.

A Czech-built cement plant in Afghanistan reportedly did not turn out too well. The cement apparently was of such poor quality that it could not be used for Soviet airfield construction at Bagram so that the Afghans were forced to import cement from the Soviet Union. 

Egypt received a large number of diesel locomotives from Hungary which turned out to be inoperable because of faulty assembly, inadequate inspection, and damage in transit.

The stories in Indonesia of the continually failing East German sugar mill and the 4,000 jeeps with defective windshields and steering gears are already familiar.

Soviet aircraft have proven more expensive to operate and maintain than comparable Western planes. Nor are they as satisfactory from safety and performance standpoints. Cabin pressurization is faulty, takeoff speeds too slow, and landing speeds too fast. Soviet IL-18's have frequently crashed and eventually had to be grounded. 

The story on bloc military aid is similar-generally satisfactory but with several exceptions. While it is true that many of the items delivered may be obsolescent by advanced Soviet standards, it is nonetheless a fact that those items are a desired and welcome addition to the military establishments of the recipients. Even so, not all of the equipment is outmoded, by any standards. 

Russian aid includes late model T-54 tanks, TU-16 jet bombers, Mig-19 and even Mig-21 jet fighters. Some short-range tactical missiles are also reportedly being delivered.

Here, too, there have been quite a few instances of defective equipment being received. Bloc naval vessels sent to Indonesia were not designed to operate in hot climates and have broken down frequently. Compressors have gone bad because of overheating. Spare parts have been unavailable, so that many ships have been rendered inoperable for long periods.

All in all, however, it appears that such deficiencies have not been major obstacles to the bloc aid program as a whole. Recipient countries complain, argue, bargain, and adjust, but desirous, and in some cases desperate, for more aid, they continue to move ahead with the bloc on project agreements and new aid commitments.

Myth.-Countries are not overrun by large numbers of bloc aid personnel. 

There are no "Ugly Russians" among bloc technicians working abroad. Bloc technicians mix well, cause little friction, and stay out of trouble. 

Fact. Actually there are probably more bloc aid technicians in their 28 aidrecipient countries than there are U.S. Government technicians in the 80-odd countries to which we give aid. A major reason is that the bloc aid program is more heavily project-oriented than is our own program at present, so that more people are needed to survey, plan, supervise, and construct. Of course, this comparison does not take into account the technicians of private U.S. companies abroad or those of other Western nations. 

It is estimated that about 8,500 bloc economic technicians were working in the less developed countries during the last half of 1961. This was a 30-percent rise over the number in 1960. There were nearly 2,000 technicians in Afghanistan, over 700 in Egypt, over 500 in India, and large numbers in Guinea, Yemen, Iraq, Syria, and Indonesia. While in general Soviet personnel appear businesslike and competent, although too narrowly specialized, there have been a number of instances where the Russians have gotten out of line-too much drinking, gross rudeness, dissatisfaction with local living conditions, and racial friction. 

Recently in one country, two Russians, evidently the worse for vodka, accosted a lady in the street and tried to follow her into her house despite the loud protests of her husband. They were saved from a beating by an indignant crowd of local citizens only by the timely arrival of the police. 

There has been a recent report that several Russian technicians were caught smuggling diamonds in coffee bags while supposedly working on mining projects in Guinea.

From all evidence, Soviet technicians do not mix well. They keep pretty much to themselves, living in self-contained enclaves, keeping their own schools, and shying away from social invitations. They do like to shop in the bazaars and marketplaces, however, and they are known, not too kindly, as very hard bargainers and very frugal tippers. 

Myth.-Russian technicians speak the local languages fluently and are thus able to get along better with the people of the country they are working in. 

Fact.-Bloc aid personnel usually have not had language training, but propaganda has exploited exceptional instances in order to create an impression that bloc countries have available large numbers of language-trained technicians. 

There are some reports of bloc technicians speaking fluently such languages as Hindi, Persian, Pushtu, and Farsi, but proficiency in foreign languages is the exception rather than the rule as far as bloc aid personnel are concerned. By contrast, it appears that bloc diplomatic personnel are generally well trained in the language and culture of the country to which they are assigned. Diplomatic officers reportedly receive a bonus of 10 percent of their base salaries for competence in European languages and 20 percent for exotic languages. 

Reports indicate that bloc technicians occasionally attempt to learn the language of the area of their assignment, but that usually they are content to depend upon their own and foreign translators. Interpreters are an integral part of the Soviet technician team. A few bloc technicians may be competent in the second language of an area, such as English in India, but in general it appears, on the basis of available evidence, that bloc aid personnel probably encounter greater difficulty than American personnel in overcoming language barriers. In Burma, for example, it has been reported that American personnel are at an advantage because of the prevalence of the English language, whereas most bloc personnel have to be accompanied by interpreters. In Iraq, the Russians have encountered great difficulty with Arabic, and they are short of interpreters.

Myth. The U.S.S.R. cannot afford to continue an aid program of over a billion dollars a year to the free world, especially since it is also giving substantial amounts of aid within the bloc to the satellites and to North Korea and North Vietnam.

Fact.-Despite heavy demands at home for military spending, the space effort and domestic investment, the Soviet leadership apparently feels strongly that it is in its national self-interest to carry the added buden of foreign-aid com-

mitments, both within and outside the bloc. Soviet aid to other bloc countries is estimated at some $6 billion since 1955. Aid commitments to the newly developing nonbloc countries have recently been about a billion dollars a year. 

Together, Soviet aid to the bloc and nonbloc countries represents on the order of 1 percent of Soviet gross national product, about the same proportion as our own but from a smaller base. It should be noted, however, that although commitments are substantial, actual deliveries are spread over a period of years so that the real drain on Soviet resources is somewhat reduced at present. 

Undoubtedly requirements of the Soviet-aid programs have caused short-run strains in certain sectors of Russian industry, especially in the case of capital equipment. Shipments of complete plants, such as sugar and oil refineries or cement mills, appear to have caused some difficulties but not major ones. 

Similarly, requirements for such major projects as the Bhilai steel mill, the Aswan Dam, and the oil refinery in Iraq have sometimes conflicted with bloc internal needs, but these conflicts are not judged to be of a serious nature.

Chairman MORGAN. STATEMENT OF HON. JOHN W. TUTHILL, U.S. AMBASSADOR TO OECD 

Mr. TUTHILL. I must confess I have not seen the article in the Washington Post, Mr. Congressman, so I can't address myself specifically to that.

To go back to the theory as to why we started this, and it was at American initiative: we started with the suggestion in January of

1960 that the Development Assistance Group be formed, consisting of the major donor countries in the Atlantic area, plus Japan, plus the European Economic Commission, in an effort to increase and improve development assistance, especially in terms of better coordination, so that we all would know what the other people were doing. 

We took this initiative, of course, at a time when we were very much concerned about the disproportionate burden that the United States was carrying in the world, in terms of foreign aid and in terms of military expenditure.

All of our allies knew that we felt that some of them were really quite well behind in the game, especially in foreign aid. So we wished to find a way to get them to do more, at the same time to coordinate that aid so we would know what each of us was doing, each of the individual countries and the world institutions. 

The first effort of the Development Assistance Group was really to put sort of a general pressure on those countries that hadn't really done very much. 

Frankly, Germany hadn't done a great deal through 1960, through the period in which these figures were given. But in 1961, as Mr. 

Coffin said, I think in part because of the activities of the Development Assistance Group, Germany came forward with a very considerable commitment and a move forward. 

Now, we think other countries might also move forward. 

However, in the field of general approach, we agreed on this annual review confrontation that Mr. Coffin has mentioned. This is patterned very much after the NATO confrontation; that is, a review of what a country is doing. We think this will help to reveal the adequacies or the inadequacies in country programs. 

Mr. BURLESON. If I may interrupt you, Mr. Ambassador. Do we feel it is likely to lessen our burden? 

Mr. TUTHILL. I don't think we expect it will reduce the American program, but we think it would increase other people's programs, and also make both theirs and ours more effective. 

Mr. BURLESON. Then on the other end, for example in country X, they could only absorb so much help in a given period of time. Who decides that? Does this committee also decide that? This is an old question around here of appropriating so much money to a country, then we send somebody over there and we don't know whether they are too well qualified to do it, but they decide we better get up a project since money is earmarked for it. To find a program and spend the money is to accomplish the purpose. 

Mr. TUTHILL. That question, Mr. Congressman, leads into our next phase in the committee. The reason that I am back now is to see whether we can't agree with our major donor allies to go into three or four countries, say one in Latin America, Africa, one in southeast Asia and perhaps one in the Near East, on a pilot basis. We would like to see whether we or the major donor countries and the World Bank, or in Latin America the Inter-American Development Bank, can't go into a country, exchange information about what each of us is doing and what we are intending to do, and then, of course, with the approval of the recipient country, sit down and find out logically what it is that should be done in an overall basis. We want to examine the development plan of the country through a multilateral pro-

cedure, which perhaps could be a little more effective than a straight bilateral procedure, and try to answer those questions; that is, how much money can one really put into country X, and what kind of money should it be.

In my own view, I think in the first place this will help us considerably with the question that you ask: How much can this country absorb over a period of years, and what will be its capacity to pay after a series of years.

Second, I think it can help us in being more specific in terms of the donor countries making their development assistance available on terms that are more appropriate for the recipient country. 

As Mr. Coffin said, many of the other donor countries are making aid available in many cases on terms that we think are too short and with interest rates which are too high, particularly in comparison with our own.

We feel that if we can get these coordinating teams going, we will have the benefit of a general appraisal in the annual aid review, and we will then have a general idea of which countries are a little behind. 

Then we can talk in specific terms with the Germans and Italians and Japanese and others as to whether they are extending their aid in a manner consistent with the needs of the countries and whether they are giving it in a manner that allows them to carry a fair share of the burden.

AID PROCUREMENT POLICY AND RELATION TO THE U.S. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Procurement in the earlier years of the mutual security program was on a worldwide competitive basis. This resulted in substantial budget savings to the program. During the period of worldwide dollar shortage this policy did not result in any harm to the United States, since dollars paid to foreigners for goods and services purchased abroad were generally used quite quickly by the recipients for purchases in the United States. With the increasing economic recovery in Western Europe and Japan this became less and less the case and assistance dollars spent abroad tended to increase the accumulation of foreign reserves. With the increasing competitiveness of foreign producers, the redirection of the AID program from Europe to the underdeveloped countries, and the progressive shift in the financing of agricultural exports from AID to the Public Law 480 program, the share of mutual security dollars spent in the United States dropped to a low level. In 1959 only 47 percent of ICA commodity expenditures were in the United States and four-fifths of those abroad were for purchases in countries whose dollar reserves were rising. 

This situation was met by policy changes in October 1959 and December 1960. 

At first it was decided that the Development Loan Fund (DLF) would place primary emphasis on financing goods and services of U.S. origin in financing the foreign exchange costs of development projects. This policy was not only designed to reduce adverse impact upon the U.S. balance of payments directly, but also to provide an inducement to the other industrialized countries to establish or increase their assistance programs. Since that time there has been a substantial increase in the amount of financing available to the less developed

countries by the other industrialized countries and an improvement in the terms on which it is made available. 

In December 1960, a modification of procurement policy was adopted by ICA. 

Exports from 19 financially strong industrialized countries are no longer eligible for assistance financing, except under very exceptional circumstances. Ocean freight payments are now financed by AID only for shipments made on U.S.-flag vessels, unless a waiver of policy is authorized by the Administrator. In a determination pertaining to foreign assistance procurement, dated October 18, 1961, the President emphasized that most of the foreign aid procurement would take place in the United States. Limited amounts of goods would continue to be procured outside of the United States, but only in underdeveloped countries which have a general need for foreign exchange. 

The impact of these changes on the AID program has been substantial. 

Current estimates for fiscal year 1962 obligations are that 73 percent of those AID-administered funds (i.e., excluding military assistance program and all 

Food for Peace funds) will be spent directly and immediately for U.S. goods and services. This compares with 57 percent for fiscal year 1961 obligations. 

If the military assistance program and the movement of surplus agriculture -commodities abroad under Food for Peace are included (and AID has a role to play in the programing of these funds), the figure is over 85 percent for fiscal year 1962.

We hope and expect to increase these percentages in fiscal year 1963. 

Estimated percentages of AID procurement (i.e., excluding the military assistance program and all Food for Peace) and sources follow:

United 19 prohibited States countries Other offshore Percent Percent Percent 5223 57 73 76 17 222 26 23 21 The greatest part of Government foreign assistance programs benefits the economy by directly financing exports. In 1960, 12 percent of all U.S. exports were financed by economic assistance programs. These exports provide thousands of jobs throughout the country in agriculture, industry, mining, transportation, and other services. All forms of Government grants and credits abroad have in the past been estimated to finance over 700,000 jobs for Americans. 

There are many reasons why it does not appear feasible or in the national interest to limit AID exclusively to financing American goods. A number of countries need financial support to meet local costs for which the financing - cannot be quickly provided through transferring U.S. goods. This is particularly true of such urgent and sensitive situations as have been met in Laos, Vietnam, and Jordan. Also the trade patterns of many African territories will have to be substantially revised before dollars provided to support the local costs of development projects can effectively be used for imports from the United States. Every effort is being made to accomplish the change. Many countries which need U.S. aid need it to pay for imports of which the United States itself is also a net importer. In some cases, the needed materials may not be obtained from the United States. Finally, there are a number of commodities where the -cost disadvantage of importing from the United States rather than from a nearby country is extremely great, and the adverse impact of the added cost is greater than that of the non-U.S. procurement.

Mr. Khrushchev is alleged to have made the statement-I believe 

I read the quotation someplace that Russia gives aid more for political purposes than for economic development. 

In your analysis of the aid provided by the Sino-Soviet bloc, have you been able to reach any conclusion as to whether or not that statement is true, and to what extent?

Mr. COFFIN. My judgment is that their overall objective is political. 

This means in some instances that they would do a spectacular project-the Asian Games Stadium in Indonesia, for example. But in most other cases they feel they can accomplish their political purpose by building sound economic projects. 

Sometimes their purpose is to provide an alternative to a country just as we seek in some countries to provide an alternative to complete reliance upon the Soviets. 

In Cuba, for example, it is obvious that they deem it an opportunity to have massive domination there. 

In India, where our aid is far greater than the Soviets, they may feel that at least to the extent which they help will mean that India has an alternative, even though it is unlikely that India will use it. 

In Indonesia, their aid has been far greater than ours. Even though 

Indonesia is troublesome as far as we are concerned, it is still not a bloc satellite.

I would say in many cases their efforts have been to provide the alternative. This is particularly true in Africa. But this does not mean that their projects are flimsy or unsound. In some cases if they were interrogated by their own congress they couldn't say, for example, that the Aswan Dam, which in 1956 seemed to be a great stroke for them, really has made things any easier for them in Egypt. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Does any of the material that we have give information indicating the extent to which each country is helping itself as a result of our aid incentives?

Mr. COFFIN. We have in the books, in the Latin America region particularly-I think that is the only place where we have done it systematically-we have a page for each country showing what measures it has taken or what it is doing by way of self-help or planning.

Mr. FOUNTAIN. With respect to loans primarily, I realize that you can't treat these countries as I would be treated if I go to a bank for a loan. Mr. COFFIN. Increasingly. I think it started by doing that in a country like India, where we and the World Bank and other nations were involved increasingly. This is part of the capacity we hope to put into our missions in the field, an ability to look at the financial

statement of a country-at or what lies ahead and what seems sen-sible and to gear our aid to that situation, and also other countries' aid through DAC.

We take the same factors into account. This was not done as we started our program. We went into point 4 with technicians doing good things. There were usually a wide variety of projects that were excellent but they did not involve the repayment capacity of that country.

Now we are having to make that kind of economic analysis much much more broadly and much more deeply than we ever used to.. 

It will take some time before we have in all of our missions the type of person who can make a very informed judgment as to what is ahead.. 

This is our direction.

FURTHER STATEMENT OF HON. FRANK M. COFFIN 

Mr. COFFIN. Private enterprise.

Chairman MORGAN. You may proceed. 

(The statement is as follows:) STATEMENT OF THE HONORABLE FRANK M. COFFIN, DEPUTY ADMINISTRATOR FOR PROGRAMS, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 1. INTRODUCTION 

Last June, when I appeared before this committee, I spoke (among other things) of the necessity of mobilizing into the AID effort the substantial resources and skills of American private enterprise. I spoke also of the contribution which can be made by the private sector to the economic growth and development of an underdeveloped country. 

In the foreign assistance presentation book submitted to the Congress at that time, we said that "to approach a truly national effort in assisting the economic and social modernization of the less developed nations, we must find and utilize more effective means of enlisting these private resources." 

There was established as "a basic policy of administration of the development assistance program that actions aimed at providing incentives or protection to U.S. private enterprise shall be for the objective of enlisting private American business in the public purpose of assisting economic growth in less developed countries. To the degree that special governmental incentives or financing devices are employed to this end, the businesses that use them are engaging in a public service, not merely a private one." 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 amply demonstrated that the Congress shared the view that it should be the policy of the United States "to encourage the contribution of the U.S. enterprise toward economic strength of less de veloped friendly countries, through private trade and investment abroad * * *.”

As we know, that act provided augmented authority to encourage and facilitate private participation in our efforts to achieve the aims of the AID program. 

II. METHOD OF OPERATION 

The Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise has been established as a focal point within AID for contact with private business interests. It is intended that this Office will be the driving force to encourage private enterprise to play a larger development role, as well as to insure adherence to sound standards for development lending. 

In my testimony last year I pointed out that, in general, responsibility for administering the authorities relating to the participation in the AID program of private business will be placed in the same line of authority as other authorities of the new program. Accordingly, these responsibilities have been vested in the Regional Assistant Administrators. However, as I pointed out at that time, the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise will be staffed with highly qualified professional personnel whose job it will be to assist the Regional Assistant Administrators in the utilization of the authorities offered to private enterprise under our act and to develop improved methods and proce dures to bring private American business into a productive relationship in every manner possible.

Moreover, in certain instances (notably in the case of the specific risk investment guarantee program) where the orientation of an activity is predominantly in the private sector, we have centralized this authority within the Office of 

Development, Finance, and Private Enterprise to insure maximum utilization of this authority and maximum convenience to U.S. business interests. Thus, while we contemplate private sector activities and responsibilities in each of the four regional bureaus, we also propose to avoid excessive fragmentation and consequent weakening of AID private enterprise activity by maintaining a strong and centralized private enterprises group in this Office to complement the regional efforts.

Finally, the Assistant Administrator, who will head up the Office of Development, Finance, and Private Enterprise, also will be responsible for advising the Administrator on policies, standards, and practices governing the provision of capital assistance through loans and guarantees. Thus, this Office not only

will have the opportunity but the responsibility, as well, to review on a day-to-day basis the activities of these AID programs and therefore will be in a position to insure that the interests of private enterprise are properly considered. 

III. CURRENT ACTIVITY 

The AID Administrator, Mr. Hamilton, has explained that during the several months since the AID agency has been established, of necessity, emphasis has been placed upon the organization and staffing of the line operations. Thus, when we speak of the Office of Development, Finance, and Private Enterprise we must speak in terms of our plans for the immediate future rather than of past accomplishments. Nevertheless, I am able to report significant current activity within AID of particular importance to the private sector. I would like, therefore, briefly to review the principal private enterprise activities of the new AID agency. (a) Liaison with the business community First, I would like to speak of our liaison activities, both with business groups and with individual businessmen. The U.S. business community has expressed a lively interest in the AID program. 

Obviously it is concerned with the fact that a very high portion of the AID dollar cost goes for the purchase of U.S. goods and services. But the interest of the business community transcends these important commercial considerations.

U.S. business is actively concerned with the public purposes of AID. Thus, one of the important functions of the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise has been and will continue to be to meet with business groups and individual businessmen to explain the AID program generally and to assist in locating specific business opportunities arising out of the AID program. (b) Dollar loans to U.S. and foreign private enterprise 

Chief among the several tools which AID has, to work with U.S. and foreign enterprise, is the authority to make dollar loans to qualified ventures, be they new projects or expansions of existing facilities. 

Development loans may be made to U.S. or foreign private business enterprises. In order to avoid an accelerated dollar drain on a developing country a two-step lending procedure has been worked out which contemplates loans to private enterprise on relatively short terms but ultimate repayment to the United States in dollars through the host government over a substantially longer period of time.

During the past years the authority to make dollar loans has been used extensively to finance private enterprise activities. Within the last few months, AID has extended financial assistance to a variety of private projects, including a truck manufacturing facility in India, a tire cord manufacturer, also in India, a cement plant in Korea, and a development bank in Pakistan. (c) Cooley program (Public Law 480, sec. 104(e)) 

January 3 saw the transfer to AID of the Cooley loan program. Prior to that time the Export-Import Bank had this responsibility. AID has established its procedures for processing applications. In effect, they are a somewhat streamlined version of the Export-Import Bank's procedures, utilizing substantially the same criteria.

As this committee knows, Cooley loans are made from the foreign currency proceeds of sales of surplus agricultural commodities. These loans may be made to U.S. business firms or their affiliates, for business development and trade expansion. They also may be made to domestic or foreign firms for the establishment of facilities abroad to assist in the use, distribution or increased consumption of U.S. agricultural products. The basic purpose of these loans is to promote balanced economic development and trade among nations. 

At this time there are more than 60 applications in various stages of processing in the Agency. Typical of the Cooley loans authorized are one for a corporation in India which will process synthetic rubber, and one for a company in Pakistan which will manufacture automobile tires. (d) AID participation in investment surveys The 1961 act authorized AID to encourage the undertaking by private enterprise of surveys of investment opportunities in less developed friendly countries by agreeing to share up to 50 percent of the cost of these surveys.

Previous experience indicated that many a potential investment was not being made because managements were unwilling to spend the necessary funds to identify specific investment opportunities. Under guidelines published earlier this month, AID proposes to reimburse any enterprise undertaking a qualified survey up to 50 percent of the survey costs should the enterprise decide not to invest in the project surveyed. In such a case the enterprise must turn over to AID a professionally acceptable report on the project. The guidelines also provide for sharing 50 percent of the cost of such surveys regardless of the outcome of the survey in cases where making the survey primarily is in the interest of promoting the AID program. 

Over 100 inquiries about the investment survey program have been received by the Agency. While the planning behind some of these applications is clearly more advanced than others, it appears that this year AID may be instrumental in assisting private investors in surveying investment opportunities in a number of countries including Colombia, Ecuador, Nigeria, and Vietnam. (e) Feasibility surveys One of the more important AID responsibilities is to make efforts to improve the climate for private enterprise and investment, local or foreign in less developed countries. This is accomplished in part by assisting a host government to identify existing obstacles to private investment and by suggesting remedies. 

Such studies have been made under AID sponsorship in many parts of the world, particularly Latin America.

In this connection AID also sponsors surveys to establish what industries are feasible in particular areas, and conversely, what areas lend themselves to particular industries.

Over 30 feasibility surveys are now in process within the regional bureaus, the largest project being an "industrial growth" contract which the Agency has concluded with the Government of Nigeria involving a 2-year agreement to help that Government expand its economy, create new industries, and stimulate private investments. (f) Specific risk investment guarantees

The specific risk guarantee programs, which have been available to and utilized by private investors since 1948, was continued by the 1961 act with clarifications and enlargements in its coverage. 

Perhaps the most significant clarification is the definition of expropriation to include any abrogation, repudiation, or impairment of contract by a foreign government, which, not being the fault of the investor, adversely affects continued operation of the project. 

Another significant provision is the expansion of eligibility for guarantees to include foreign chartered subsidiaries wholly owned by a U.S. corporation. 

The scope of war loss coverage has been significantly broadened to permit coverage against losses from revolution or insurrection. 

Finally, the ability of a guaranteed investor to obtain speedy and final settlement of a disputed claim for coverage is increased by the new statutory authority to refer such disputes to arbitration. 

With the liberalization of the legislation covering the specific risk guarantee authority, there has been a noticeable increase in investor interest in the program. In the 6 months ending September 1961, when the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 was signed, 163 applications were received covering $416,275,000 of guarantees. In the 5 months from September 1961 to March 1962, 232 applications for a total of $350,205,000 were received. The backlog on hand as of early 

March 1962 was 570 applications for a total of $2,089 million. 

In the same 5 months' period, 20 guarantees were issued totaling $77,200,000. 

Investments covered were made in such projects as a fertilizer manufacturing facility in Taiwan, the petrochemical industry in Argentina, the manufacture of refrigeration equipment in India and in Malaya, and an investment in a private development bank in Morocco. 

Investment guarantees are now available in 54 underdeveloped countries and in the dependent oversea territories of France, Denmark, Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. Negotiations are continuing to add a number of the newly independent African countries to the program as well as to complete our agreements programs in Latin America. 

Since 1948, when it was first established, the investment guarantee program has been funded by the issuance of notes to the U.S. Treasury, the so-called borrowing authority. Congress last year expressed a preference for the appropria-

tion procedure, when the borrowing authority issue was explored at some length in connection with funds for development lending. For this reason we are requesting in the form of an appropriation an additional $100 million for support to the investment guarantee program. As a corollary we are requesting increases in the guarantee ceilings: for the specific risk guarantees from $1 to $1.3 billion, for the extended risk guarantee program from $90 to $180 million, and for the housing guarantee program from $10 to $60 million. (g) Extended risk guarantees

This program, which is new to the Agency for International Development this year, and therefore, new to the American businessman, holds great promise. 

Much hope is held that many projects which might otherwise have to be financed by loans from AID to American business or to a foreign government rather may be financed privately with the assistance of this authority. 

There is every indication that the American commercial, investment, and institutional investment community is prepared to make loans and take equity participation in projects which have extended risk coverage where they would not otherwise be legally able or willing to take a risk. 

Since November four applications have been received: Two in Venezuela; one in Nigeria; and one in Pakistan. (h) Housing investment guarantees in Latin America The housing guarantee program, as a new and experimental program, required AID to work out with potential investors the methods by which long-term investments could be made by the investors in Latin American pilot housing projects. 

AID prepared information sheets to assist the encouragingly large number of interested investors in preparing applications. Of the many inquiries, several very promising proposals have been received and the basic groundwork laid for going ahead on these projects. 

Investors and AID have been attempting to work out arrangements whereby the investors would be able to invest their money within the limits of the 75-percent ceiling for an AID guarantee. It is expected that arrangements will be made so that the first guarantee agreements can be concluded in the near future. (i) AID loans to development banks for relending to private borrowers Because it is administratively impossible for this Agency to process loan applications from each deserving small businessman operating in less developed countries, we have devised the technique of providing dollar assistance to development banks in such countries for their relending to small private businessmen. 

As of January 31, AID, through its predecessor agency, the Development Loan Fund, has made loans totaling $156 million to 23 different institutions in developing countries. These institutions in turn had made 565 subloans, aggregating $54 million to a great variety of subborrowers. 

There are in various stages of review within the regions applications from more than a dozen development banks. We are greatly encouraged by the sublending accomplished by these institutions and plan to expand this program to its fullest. (j) The Office of Small Business The Office of Small Business, established under the direction of the Assistant Administrator for Material Resources, is established in accordance with section 602 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. It is responsible for assisting American business particularly small independent enterprises to participate equitably in the furnishing of commodities and services financed by the Agency for 

International Development.

The Office publishes small business circulars giving information to the business community on AID-financed purchases. It also publishes small business memorandums, award notices, and procurement information bulletins. 

An experienced staff of former businessmen are available to discuss various opportunities with small businessmen. 

Arrangements have been made for oversea libraries to be stocked with current catalogs giving procurement information. 

The Office has assisted in educational efforts by appearing on panels discussing export opportunities which AID offers. 

An effort is being made to assist small business manufacturers to organize their own export trade groups. These groups will consist of trade associations dealing with a particular industry. This promises to help solve a difficult problem of long standing by making it possible for the small manufacturer to organize all over the world at a minimum cost.

IV. CONCLUSION 

We in AID are keenly aware that a great deal has been said in the past about the importance of private enterprise in our foreign aid programs. We are also aware, however, that the measurable results of our private enterprise activities have fallen short of our good intentions. Moreover, we do not pretend to hold the key to the manifold problems of bringing the resources of the private sector to bear on the economic development of the underdeveloped countries. It is our opinion, however, that the first step to meet this challenge is to establish a strong office of private enterprise, staffed with skilled personnel and given the necessary authority and support to carry out its vital mission. 

Mr. COFFIN. Mr. Chairman, I would like to summarize our activities in the field of private enterprise to tell you how we have organized ourselves to deal with the programs in this field, and some of the activities that have been carried on and are in the process of being carried on.

Under the regional organization of the AID agency, in each of the regions there will be responsibility for seeing to it that the interests of private firms here are taken into account in planning of the programs for these regions, and also that proper activity takes place to stimulate the development of private sectors of our program abroad. 

This year, Mr. Chairman, you will note that we have added as an additional name to the Office of Development Finance the words "Private Enterprise."

This is not merely an additional name. This signifies our intent to upgrade in this Office's activities the functions related to dealing with the private business and financial community in this country, to provide a center of information about how our program operates, so that a businessman who may not understand exactly where to go in our Agency can get proper advice.

The second activity affecting private enterprise is our lending operation itself. Since we last appeared before you we have developed a method of making loans to private enterprise in oversea countries within the framework of our long-term dollar repayable loans. 

We lend to a private company in a two-step operation. Let's take a tire manufacturing company in India. We would make a loan to that company and it would be repayable on what would be normal terms for a private company in India, 12 or 15 years. 

Repayment would be in local currency to the Government of India. 

The Government of India, however, would be obligated to pay us in dollars over a longer period of time.

Were it not handled in this way, we would find that foreign countries would not encourage private loans because they would be a drain on foreign exchange. If we were to make a loan for 40 years to a particular private company, it would be in a sense a windfall. This has worked out well, with loans to a truck company and a tire company in India, a cement plant in Korea, a development bank in Pakistan.
