(The statement is as follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. FRANK M. COFFIN, DEPUTY ADMINISTRATOR FOR PROGRAM, AID 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, the Foreign Assistance Act of 

1961, although noteworthy in a number of respects, included one new elementauthorization to initiate a program of development research—which, by the end of this decade, may well prove to have been as important a factor in accelerating the economic and social growth of the less developed countries of the free world as in moving the United States into the space age. 

Despite the substantial help to emerging countries afforded by our assistance in the past, there still remain built-in barriers to economic, social, political, and cultural changes necessary to stimulate the process of development. 

The fundamental purpose of research is to discover, through scientific investigation, new and practical means of removing these barriers and creating the kind of environment needed for the effective use of development assistance from the United States and other free world sources. 

While much of the research already undertaken by U.S. Government agencies and private organizations is relevant to development assistance generally, only a small fraction has been specifically directed to problems encountered or anticipated in AID programs in some 80 countries spread all over the globe. 

Some problems, however, are common to numerous emerging countries in comparable stages of development and the solutions uncovered through scientific research can be applied, with minor adaptations, wherever the problem exists regardless of the geographic region in which the country falls. 

Responsibility for direction of this research effort and closely related functions, therefore, has been assigned to a newly created AID Staff Office of Research, Evaluation, and Planning Assistance.

This organizational arrangement is believed to provide the most effective means of maintaining a worldwide perspective of the dimensions of the problems relating to development assistance that need to be resolved and for keeping the outlays for AID-financed research activities within reasonable bounds. 

A. RESEARCH 

In the research area, the challenging task still looms of identifying and establishing priorities among research needs, determining the relevance of those needs to existing research activities, stimulating new research to fill major gaps, correlating isolated research activities and relating them to development assistance problems.

Greater knowledge also must be accumulated with respect to the following: 

1. The processes of political, economic, and social growth; the cultural and institutional changes needed for such growth; and factors controlling the speed of these changes. 

2. The conditions under which U.S. and other free world technical and capital assistance can most effectively contribute to change and growth in the less developed areas. 

3. The people best qualified to implement foreign aid programs (particularly technical assistance); how to identify them; and how and in what specialties to train them. 

4. The political, ideological, psychological, and cultural impact of various forms of foreign aid, and of the methods of administering such assistance, in different areas. 

5. The methods by which Western scientific and technological knowledge can be best adapted to the individual needs and differing characteristics of some 80 countries receiving U.S. assistance. 

6. The means by which progress achieved through foreign aid programs can be continuously and accurately measured. 

Research in these areas and on individual problems, and its application to development activities, will gradually improve both the direction and content of development assistance programs and thus become a decisive factor in the attainment of development goals. 81496-62-pt. 211

The nature of the AID research program The AID-financed research program will emphasize imaginative adaptation of basic knowledge to local conditions, the testing of new techniques in the environment in which they are to be used, the systematic evaluation of new ideas as they are put into practice, and encouragement of a flexible approach by the less developed countries toward resolving their problems. 

Research financed by AID will supplement but not duplicate activities already completed or underway. Nor will it result in a diminution of future research activity by universities, foundations, private enterprise, or other U.S. Government agencies.

Research needs generally are so great that the independent and cooperative efforts of all private and public organizations will be required to make the decade of development a success. 

Beyond this, the AID-sponsored research program will perform an important function in stimulating wider awareness in the U.S. research community of the problems of the less developed countries, and in nurturing a growing pool of talent with the training required for effective participation in development programs.

Research activities planned for fiscal year 1962 Research projects planned for fiscal year 1962 and already funded, or in a sufficiently advanced stage to warrant financing before the close of this fiscal year, will require a total of about $6 million. All are addressed to significant problems which are known to exist; some are expected to produce innovations or a scientific advance speeding progress in areas where problems are particularly acute.

Some of the more important projects deal with: 

1. Research on the problem of shortage of power at the local level.—AID experience with community development programs strongly suggests that lack of power may be a major barrier to effective self-help efforts at the local level. 

A simple power unit would supply the light to enable illiterate laboring populations to learn to read at night; make their labor more productive by day; and provide a stimulus for group action to raise living standards in their villages. 

The exploratory phase of the project, to be financed in fiscal year 1962 and expected to be completed early in fiscal year 1963, is designed to examine the economics of small-scale powerplants already in use to determine what practical improvements can be made. 

These initial studies might reveal opportunities for lowering costs, simplifying maintenance, and encouraging the widespread use of power through experimentation with cheaper alternative fuels, modification of design, and the establishment of rural facilities providing credit on liberal terms. Field tests of these innovations in a few representative locations would be financed in fiscal year 1963. 

2. The development of planning and planning assistance criteria.-If the new emphasis on development planning is to produce worthwhile results, most of the emerging nations will have to increase their planning capability and improve their planning techniques during the next few years. 

The proposed project will help to meet both of these needs. Its specific objective is to devise new and improved planning criteria and techniques for specific use in dealing with the economic and social development problems of countries in the less developed areas. The project will focus primarily upon- (a) the importance of setting realistic and adequate development goals, (b) the selection of planning techniques appropriate for the country's stage of development, (c) methods of improving such techniques, (d) procedures required for effective administration, coordination, and monitoring of development plans, and (e) methods of strengthening governmental and popular participation in the planning process. 

3. Research to improve land reform activities.-The agrarian structures under which most of the people in the less developed countries earn their living constitute major obstacles to progress toward individual freedom, political equality, and economic growth. The need for reform has long been evident and has now become a key policy issue, particularly in Latin America. 

Under the proposed research project, an extensive analysis is to be made of the manifold problems involved in land reform programs in selected countries in this region, and of the different ways in which the various governments have dealt with these problems.

The results of this project, to be conducted under contract by a U.S. university having particular competence in this field and extensive experience in the region, are expected to have wide application to other developing countries and areas. 

Research activities proposed for fiscal year 1963 Research activities proposed for funding in fiscal year 1963 will require at least $20 million for inaugurating an estimated 50 projects in 10 major areas of research. This sum is considerably larger than obligations for fiscal year 1962, which will fund less than 6 months activity by an office only recently activated. 

Some of the projects planned for fiscal year 1963 will be extensions of research activities begun in fiscal year 1962, which were limited to meeting immediate needs. Most of the projects to be financed in fiscal year 1963 will be new and concentrated in areas where research could uncover practical solutions to problems blocking progress toward development goals. 

Among the projects proposed for fiscal year 1963, the following are addressed to particularly significant problems: 

1. Development of novel teaching techniques to offset the shortage of teachers.— 

Economic and social development efforts in the less developed countries are hampered by the shortage of teachers at all levels. Several methods, used in varying combinations, could help overcome this shortage: (a) Course content might be improved and condensed, reducing the time each student would have to spend in school and enabling the teacher to train more students; (b) Improved techniques might be incorporated in existing teaching manuals, enabling students to become teachers without lengthy training courses; and (c) Mass communications methods, such as radio and movies, might be used as a temporary substitute for individual teachers, or to release more teachers for discussion, laboratory supervision, and testing. 

This project would involve the establishment of an educational research services center in one or more regions to demonstrate and test these methods. 

Each center would have a small professional research staff for this purpose and would undertake the training of local staff to develop the indigenous capability for educational research. 

2. Agricultural development planning.-The adaptation and application of modern agricultural methods and new technology are essential to realization of the agricultural potential of most of the less developed countries. This project will involve comparative studies of farming experience in various typical countries in order- (a) to identify the extension training methods best adapted to the differing economic and cultural environment in a particular region; (b) to analyze the advantages, if any, of mechanizing small farms; and (c) to determine the types of training and purchasing arrangements required to enable the farmers to make effective use of mechanical equipment. 

3. The role of cooperatives in development assistance.-Although the cooperative form of organizing private activities has proved attractive to the populations of the emerging nations, U.S.-financed activities to date have failed to take maximum advantage of our own experience or assets in this field. This project proposes to discover the particular situations in which cooperative enterprise may be uniquely appropriate to aiding in developmental progress. 

4. Encouragement of small industry through industrial research institutes.— 

A number of industrial research institutes already exist in several of the less developed countries. Generally, however, they have had relatively little if any impact on the growth of small private industrial enterprises in the country or region in which they are located. This project involves— (a) survey and analysis of selected, existing industrial research institutes to determine the degree to which present facilities are being used, and the ways in which their research findings can be made more widely available throughout the region; and (b) establishment of one or more demonstration and training research institutes in areas where none exist and where conditions are such that their services could help small industry flourish. 

5. Improvement of indigenous materials and structural design for low-cost construction.-The purpose of this project is to identify locally available materials which can be effectively combined with other products, such as plastics, to produce inexpensive construction materials to meet the exceptional demand for housing, community facilities, and classrooms.

It will also include the development of structural designs best suited to the climatic and social environment of the given country or region. 

This project will capitalize on earlier, scattered experiments in this field, with a view toward achieving a faster solution to the acute building shortage which exists in most of the less developed countries. 

B. EVALUATION 

The evaluation function of the research, evaluation, and planning assistance staff aims to bring relevant experience of this Agency and of others working in development assistance to bear on the activities of the Agency. 

This purpose differs from those of the evaluations carried on by the Inspector General and the auditors in that it is to improve the effectiveness of Agency operations in achieving Agency purposes, rather than to assess performance in relation to particular regulations or procedural codes. 

In short, the research, evaluation, and planning assistance staff evaluation is the mechanism analogous to operations analysis as used by the Air Force and other large and complex organizations to distill the lessons implicit in current and past experience and feed them back into ongoing and future operations. 

There are two operational aspects to this work: (1) The development of standards or criteria that will enable the decision makers at all levels to consider the problems they face in the full context of Agency objectives, and to achieve a reasonable consistency across the wide span of Agency activities in different fields and different countries; and (2) The provision of the means for subsequent evaluation in ongoing and new activities so that the experience being gained therein will become readily and usefully available to insure that Agency purposes are being served as fully as possible by these activities. 

The standards or criteria being sought are simply the means of measuring performance attained against that which was intended. To find them demands a three-part analysis of past performance in terms of the purposes, stated or unstated, for which the varied activities were undertaken. 

1. One part of the analysis would deal with the effectiveness with which resources external and indigenous-were used to accomplish the immediate purposes of the particular activity under study. Beyond these direct and intended results, what other results were achieved, and were these other results helpful or counterproductive, in terms of Agency and country objectives? 

2. Another part of this analysis aims to discover whether the activity was worthwhile, again in terms of Agency objectives. Assuming that the activity achieved its own limited purposes, did these also serve the broader purposes of the sector program under which the activity was undertaken? And did the sector program contribute as intended to the development plan? 

3. The third part of the analysis has to do with the means used in the activity being studied. Administratively speaking, does hindsight indicate that a different combination of capital and technical assistance would have better served Agency purposes in that country? Would external assistance have been more appropriately administered through multilateral than through bilateral channels? Were the people involved-indigenous and United States—properly selected and adequately qualified? Did the terms of the contract further or inhibit the effectiveness of the activity?

For example, a number of farm-to-market road construction projects have been undertaken in the past. In evaluating their effectivness, reasonable standards must be established-and they will probably be quite different for the various countries-for judging whether the roads were appropriately designed to serve the areas and markets selected, whether the construction met the specified requirements and schedule, and whether the intended use was actually realized. 

Beyond these evidently intended results, criteria also must be defined by which unstated and unintended results of the projects may be assessed: Was the local highway department capability increased? Was it necessary to resort to forced labor because money or other incentives were inadequate? Was the right-of-way laid out to serve the needs of the community or to serve the convenience of the local large landholder? 

To judge the effectiveness of an activity, all the results that affect Agency purposes must be considered-not just those in the particular technical field.

The assessment of how worthwhile it was to undertake these road construction projects demands criteria against which to measure the answers to such questions as these:

Did the farm-to-market road strengthen agriculture and transportation in ways that furthered the desired development in these sectors, or did it simply add to existing surpluses and traffic jams? 

Were adequate marketing and distribution facilities available or being provided through the existing bazaar, its expansion, or the establishment of a producer cooperative?

It is also necessary to ask whether the impact on the sectors affected was serving the broad development plan purposes in employment, institution building, or balance of payments. 

Finally, it is necessary for the Agency to know if the form and administration of assistance were effective in getting the roads built. Could better results have been achieved if greater emphasis had been placed on training indigenous personnel in maintenance as well as construction of roads? 

Were Agency employees suitably selected and trained to accomplish this training?

Would the use of personnel from a third country have been more effective? 

Is there indication that United Nations or other multilateral channels would have been more effectively used for this purpose? 

It is evident that these three categories of questions need to be asked, not only of project activities, but of programing and planning ones, and of activities internal to the Agency, such as personnel. 

It is also evident that the provision of criteria for evaluation in most cases also provides criteria for the design and implementation of the next work to be undertaken. And it will also be clear that the analysis of experience across the broad range of Agency concerns demands that facilities external to the Agency be used.

It is in this way that the evaluation function of the Research, Evaluation, and Planning Assistance Staff provides an input to the research function. 

The second operational aspect of evaluation-providing means for subsequent evaluation in ongoing and new activities-should contribute directly to the increased effectiveness of Agency operations through their concurrent evaluation and, in addition, make current experience gathered in one program available immediately elsewhere.

The measures comprise two sorts of reporting: one concerned with defining the situation before the introduction of the assistance being provided, and the other with periodic reporting on the various changes from this baseline in relation to Agency program goals. 

To the extent necessary, research funds will be used to finance the additional cost of these kinds of reporting by the contractor, or, in some cases, by indigenous research facilities. The use of Peace Corps volunteers is also a possibility. 

As an illustration of this aspect of evaluation activity, plans are now being drawn up by the Brazilian Government for the installation of a large number of electric power generating units in remote locations of northern Brazil. 

The problems arising out of this phase of the program will be technical as regards operation and maintenance of the generators and the power-consuming equipment, social with reference to the changes in the way old jobs will be performed and new ones introduced, economic in the impact on standards of living and the market relationships of adjoining areas, and even political in view of the probable changes in the ways in which the courses of the communities are determined.

Partly to insure that such problems are detected or anticipated before they become serious, and partly to increase our understanding of the impact of power technology on rural communities, measures are being taken to build the kinds of reporting activities mentioned into this operation. The resulting continual and close contact with the project's progress will enhance Agency effectiveness in the attainment of Agency goals in each of the several hundred locations involved. 

C. PLANNING ASSISTANCE 

One of the chief tasks of AID is to assist the underdeveloped nations of the world in planning the intelligent use of available and potential resources toward the attainment of a better life.

Neither the United States, nor its allies, nor the underdeveloped countries have sufficient resources to achieve this end if these resources are scattered abroad on ad hoc schemes, without regard to priorities and without relation to a coordinated comprehensive development effort of any one country. 

Planning one's own future, or the future of a business enterprise, a public utility, a nonprofit institution, or a combination of all these simply makes good sense. Such planning is an investment of intelligence and information in the process of growth. It means knowing what you are doing, where you are going, and, to the extent humanly possible, how you are going to get there. 

We are all familiar with the "command" plans undertaken in countries within the Sino-Soviet bloc. What we are interested in sponsoring are "consensus" plans where those involved participate in the process, help determine the goals, and agree upon the methods of implementation. This is planning in and for freedom.

In the past year several young nations, with our encouragement, have begun this process.

In Tunisia, as one example, the people's hopes and aspirations for development over the next 10 years have been embodied in a plan which was discussed at all levels of government, private business, trade unions, and in every provincial unit in the entire country. 

The final product will truly reflect the wishes of the vast majority of Tunisians. 

Planning in and for freedom then, is what we in AID are proposing to assist, and this assistance will include plans which clearly provide for the expansion and encouragement of a private sector. 

Planning assistance is closely related to "self-help." We can only assist, we would never think of constructing entire plans for these countries even if requested. The people who must ultimately do the work and make the sacrifices must participate in the planning process. Their conviction and enthusiasm is an absolute necessity for the success of any plan, and without this evidence of self-help on their part we can do very little. 

As a matter of fact, a genuine planning process is the best available instrument for insuring a rational use of the countries' own resources and for a more efficient use of U.S. and other external assistance. It serves to make the mutuality of commitments to the development goals a living reality. 

Development planning will steadily improve in quality. We are prepared to assist in this gradual but steady improvement. Our successes in this field will be unspectacular since we will be concerned with plans and the ability to implement rather than the actual construction of a dam or powerplant, the particular community development project, credit institute, or child feeding program. 

The coordination of all these activities, however, is part of planning assistance. 

Before I describe the tools we have in AID to promote this process, let me briefly outline the basic components of the process. An underdeveloped country wishing to improve its lot and deciding that an overall plan for the use of total resources is needed usually begins by sorting out certain overall goals associated with maximum increases in personal incomes compatible with higher levels of savings, equitable distribution of incomes, fuller employment, a more effective and in some cases diversified economy, upgrading of human resources, and an adequate level of social services. 

To attain these aims men, money, and natural resources are needed in a variety of combinations. If these goals are then quantified, it becomes possible with modern techniques to ascertain approximately the amount of all types of resources that will be needed. 

Next, surveys are required to discover if the resources are available and if not immediately available, over what time period might they become so. 

The outcome of such a census of resources will then determine the chance of reaching the original goals and how they should be tailored to fit the cloth. 

Once desires and resources have been generally equated, it is necessary to plan more precisely at the various sector levels, i.e., industry, agriculture, health, education, transportation, et cetera; then individual project plans and analysis must be undertaken. 

Finally, the necessary coordinated action must take place to carry out the plans successfully. 

This entire process calls for a formal organization, generally located in the central government and staffed with highly specialized experts. Once the plan has been developed, various governmental, semigovernmental, and private organizations must be available to refine and implement the plan.

The most sophisticated, scientific plan in the world will be of little use if adequately staffed organizations are not available to carry out the plan in orderly fashion and with broad popular participation. 

What can we in AID do to assist this process? President Kennedy led the way by announcing to the world our intention to encourage this type of planning. 

Mr. Hamilton has since followed up with guidance to all our field missions as to the importance of this function and the need to assure ourselves that each host government is aware of this emphasis. 

In Washington we have established development planning staffs in each of the four regional bureaus and a specific planning assistance staff to service the Agency as a whole. 

Since planning mainly involves human skills, planning assistance is deeply concerned with helping to provide such skills in the form of expert advisers and of facilities, where host country officials can be trained in the several disciplines associated with development planning. 

It is our policy, wherever possible, to alert the foreign government of the availability of suitable experts and then allow that government to contract with the experts directly. Sometimes the country pays the full salary of the experts, while on other occasions we make up the difference between what the host government can afford to pay for such services and the requirement. 

Other tools utilized by planning assistance concern the development and col lection of research and publications on the process of economic growth and the planning process, and the encouragement of seminars where top officials can exchange experiences while participating with some of the leading authorities in the field.

Also, we have discussed these problems with the Peace Corps. Mr. Shriver believes it possible to find Americans with competence in economics and statistics to help at the lower echelons of the pitifully undermanned staffs in the planning departments of underdeveloped countries. 

What is the magnitude of this operation? It has not been extensive, to date, but it is decidedly on the increase. In over 80 countries where AID operates, less than one-third are carrying out formal long-range development plans. 

In Latin America only three such plans have as yet been submitted to the "nine wise men," established under the charter of Punta del Este. But nearly all the other countries are working on such plans. 

As for U.S. experts, between 75 and 100 short- and long-term specialists in economics, statistics, and so forth, have been sent abroad in fiscal year 1962, and 65 participants in activities related to development planning have come to the United States. These are not large figures, either in terms of man-hours or funds expended.

In fiscal year 1963, if even one-half of present requests are filled we will come close to doubling the number we send abroad in this field while increasing the number of participants by as much as 50 percent. 

The funds involved are a tiny fraction of the total requested in any one category, but upon the success of the job done may well rest the outcome of the decade of development. 

It is gratifying to know that our own efforts in this matter are related to a large and growing volume of similar efforts by private organizations, by other governments, and by international organizations. 

D. UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON THE APPLICATION OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE LESS DEVELOPED AREAS 

In addition to its normal functions, the research, evaluation, and planning assistance staff has been assigned primary responsibility for directing and coordinating the substantive aspects of U.S. participation in this Conference. 

Purpose of the Conference

This U.N. Conference which is scheduled to take place in Geneva in February 1963 is intended to provide an opportunity for a comprehensive view and critical assessment of the impact, actual or potential, of science (physical, biological, and social) and technology on the process of development of the less developed countries. More specifically, it is intended that the Conference provide 1. A general stimulus for the organization of scientific and technological institutions in newly independent states; 

2. Cooperation in scientific and technological fields between the developed and less developed countries; and 

3. Assistance in identifying areas where research applications are needed.

Reasons for U.S. participation in this Conference 

As a leading nation in the fields of science and technology, the United States can make significant contributions toward advancing the welfare, health, and general benefits of mankind in the less developed areas of the world. 

The United States was the major proponent for the adoption of the resolution to convene the Conference, since it is contemplated that this Conference will be a centerpiece in the "United Nations Decade of Development”—a concept which the present administration has initiated and is now propagating. 

Preparation for the Conference

Approximately 2,000 eminent scientific and political leaders from some 100 countries will attend the Conference. Some 500 papers will be presented and discussed. For the United States the challenge of the Conference is immense. 

This is an exceptional opportunity to help make the United Nations Decade of Development a significant success. The capacity and prestige of American science and technology will be under examination, as will the effectiveness of American economic and technical aid programs in some 80 foreign countries. 

The challenge will occur in the face of an all-out Soviet bloc effort to demonstrate that they have far more to offer the less developed countries than we do. 

In view of the critical need for a successful U.S. performance at the Conference, it is necessary to tap the wealth of experience accumulated by AID and its predecessor agencies, as well as all other governmental and private agencies and institutions. 

The Department of State has overall responsibility for the U.S. participation, for selecting and accrediting representatives, advisers, and delegates, and for on-the-site arrangements in Geneva. 

In keeping with the President's desire for a unified foreign assistance program administered within the policy direction of the Department of State and in view of the nature of the Conference, AID has accepted responsibility for directing and coordinating the substance of U.S. participation. This includes the following functions: 

1. Abstracts and papers; 

2. Exhibits and allied presentation material; 

3. Public information activities; 

4. Preconference logistical and supporting services; and 

5. Technical and professional participation in Conference sessions. 

The research, evaluation, and planning assistance staff has been assigned the primary responsibility within AID for performing these functions. This as- signment reflects the emphasis of the Conference on scientific research and its impact on economic development in the less developed areas. To carry out this responsibility the science conference staff has been established within the research, evaluation, and planning assistance staff under the direction of Dr. 

Edward C. Fei.

A U.S. Public Advisory Board has been appointed to help formulate policies that will govern U.S. participation and to assist the science conference staff in its preparatory work. Dr. Walsh McDermott of Cornell University is Chairman of the Advisory Board. 

The President's science adviser has taken an active interest in planning activities and, as Chairman of the Federal Council for Science and Technology, has solicited the assistance and advice of other Government agencies. 

Private contractors will be employed to prepare a presentation book and exhibits illustrating the role of American science and technology in the development process. The presentation book and the exhibits will elaborate on the papers presented, in terms of the general theme of the Conference. Current thinking is that these will take the form of case histories of successful projects. 

Last year the committee approved the initiation of research as a function of the reorganized Agency. At that time we were instructed to seek funds for this function from our general program. 

Here, again, we have had less than 4 months in which to start operations in this important field. I personally feel that years from now we will look back and feel that the work we are doing in this area is perhaps the most significant of any of the work that we are doing in the Agency.

I have here today with me Dr. Edward Fei, who is the head of our Research, Evaluation, and Planning Assistance unit. 

Dr. Fei is an economist who has studied and taught in a number of U.S. institutions. But, more than that, he has had field experience in Pakistan and countries in the Middle East and Far East. 

Actually, it was with difficulty that we were able to persuade Dr. 

Mason to release him from a project in Pakistan to come back and head this up.

He has proceeded, I think, in the way that the committee last year wanted him to proceed, in the sense that his first task was to begin to assess what the needs were for research information, the priority of these needs, find out what is being done, and then to try to stimulate new research, not in government, but in institutions with a research capacity, and to coordinate these activities for the maximum effectiveness of the program. 

The areas for research are the following: 

The processes of growth; how economic assistance can best help these processes; what kind of people are needed and under what circumstances are they most effective in helping other countries in their social and economic growth; the impact of the various forms of aid, and then how these forms can be appropriately administered, how to adapt the forms of aid to different kinds of countries, and how to measure what we are doing.

In fiscal 1962-or rather in the past half year-Dr. Fei and his associates have started research projects which probably in all of fiscal 1962 will have committed some $6 million to research. 

One project has to do with power-how we discover ways of generating power in very underdeveloped areas, what kind of small-scale power units make sense. If a big hydroelectric dam is not necessary, how can we, nevertheless, generate power for schools and for industry with small-scale power units?

This is one project which is very interesting because it involves some academic institutions and industrial firms in a consortium arrangement.

Another involves planning criteria. How to help these countries plan. What does planning mean? What kinds of planning assistance make sense in a given country, at a give time, with a limited number of skilled people? Another is, how can we labor for land reform? We talk about it, but how can we really implement it? What are the practical things to do? This is another research project that will be of profound significance for Latin America, in the first instance, but for other parts of the world, too. 

For fiscal 1963 we contemplate research in the order of magnitude of $20 million. This was the sum that we asked for last year. This will be about six-tenths of 1 percent of the economic funds we shall be administering if Congress grants our request. 

These projects will range from improved methods of teaching, how to make shortcuts, how, for example in Africa, to teach English in as short a time as possible, how to make a breakthrough in the teaching of science, how we can utilize the intellectual and cultural background to bring about an educated class capable of going out and working productively as soon as possible.

Another field that he is interested in is agriculture development, training and extension work. How to induce local primitive farmers to use mechanized equipment, how to take care of this equipment, how to devise the best kind of purchasing arrangements so that farmers can purchase some simple but nevertheless much more efficient equipment than the have had. 

The role of cooperatives offers a great deal to the economic progress in some of these countries. 

The role of small industries leads Dr. Fei to endorse a project involving the setting up of and cooperation with several industrial research institutes abroad. 

Then there is a vast field of investigating the use of local materials. 

We talk about housing and yet even low-cost housing is very expensive. 

But we feel that if we knew more about the usability of low-cost indigenous materials and designs we would multiply the housing we could see take place, the classrooms we could see built, the community facilities we could see erected. 

So, I hope that you have questions of Dr. Fei, because we are very proud of what he has done and of the work that can be done as we go forward.

As I said this morning, we are not alone in this field. The French have a research capability of some $11 million for their program. 

Research is not the only department under Dr. Fei. There is a very important unit called Evaluation. I like to think that we are using our experience of the past 15 years and are now profiting by some of the lessons, one of which is that we should learn by this experience, that we should be better evaluators of what we have done. 

This is similar to the Air Force capability to feed back information that it gathers from its own experiments and activites. 

This evaluation has two great objectives: One, to set certain standards of performance; the second is to measure-have our mission directors, program officers be able to measure-what they have done and to evaluate what they have done so that our program can constantly improve.

For example, I think the best illustration of what we mean by this is on pages 10 and 11 of the statement, where we talk about building a farm-to-market road.

I am reading from the bottom of page 10: 

Reasonable standards must be established-and they will probably be quite different for the various countries for judging whether the roads were appropriately designed to serve the areas and markets selected, whether the construction met the specified requirements and schedule, and whether the intended use was actually realized. 

Beyond these evidently intended results, criteria also must be defined by which unstated and unintended results of the projects may be assessed: Was the local highway department capability increased?

Was it necessary to resort to forced labor because money or other incentives were inadequate? Was the right-of-way laid out to serve the needs of the community or to serve the convenience of the local large landholder? 

To judge the effectiveness of an activity, all the results that affect Agency purposes must be considered-not just those in the particular technical field. 

The assessment of how worthwhile it was to undertake these road construction projects demands criteria against which to measure the answers to such questions as these: Did the farm-to-market road strengthen agriculture and transportation in ways that furthered the desired development in these sectors, or did it simply add to existing surpluses and traffic jams?

Were adequate marketing and distribution facilities available or being provided through the existing bazaar, its expansion, or the establishment of a producer cooperative?

It is also necessary to ask whether the impact on the sectors affected was serving the broad development plan purposes in employment, institution building, or balance of payments. 

And so on.

This is evaluation. To have a few people devoting themselves to this, sending out guidelines to the field and insisting that people in the field give a feedback of information and opinion, this it seems to us is an important part of our function. 

As we go into northeast Brazil with a power program, we are deliberately putting into our program some money to enable us to answer questions as to the effectiveness of this project. 

Finally, under Dr. Fei there is an essential unit devoting itself to planning assistance. In the 80 countries in which the AID agency operates or has a program, probably under one-third of the people are working on long-range plans, but many are working on some kind of plans, and nearly all in Latin America are working on long-range plans.

Three countries have submitted plans to the panel of experts. We estimate that in this past and this present year, fiscal 1962, we have sent 75 to 100 specialists abroad. We have brought 65 planning technicians to the United States for training. 

We anticipate that in fiscal 1963 we will double the number sent abroad, and will increase the people brought here by about 50 percent. 

We must approach the selection of these people with great care. 

We must see to it that we do not approach the University of Indiana for too many competing projects in Colombia, Iran, or Vietnam. 

We must see to it if the specialist we need is a sector specialist, or a technical expert in a particular function, that we do not waste a person who is expert or competent at judging and working with an overall plan.

Planning assistance, therefore, helps our regions get the right man for the right country at the right time. 

Then, in its concluding section, the statement is not discussing a permanent element of our research activities but a function that has been thrust upon it this year. I refer to the forthcoming U.N. Conference on Science and Technology, which is to be held at Geneva in February of 1963. This is a challenge and a great opportunity. 

There will be 2,000 scientific and political leaders there from about 100 countries. There will be 500 different papers submitted and commented upon.

This is an arena where we must put our best foot forward, particularly as it affects the use of science and technology for peaceful development objectives. 

The backstopping of this operation is one of Dr. Fei's major responsibilities in the forthcoming months.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I have concluded my major presentation. I would like to say a word just about the books. 

You have before you the brown book and the tan book, which are classified. They are not secret this year but they are confidential

In the books you will find regional statements that are classified. 

They complement the regional statements in the green book, which are unclassified.

We classify them in the book before you because we can make more candid assessments, and we have to say some things about governments-corruption and absence of self-help or nepotism-occasionally. 

So we do have a complete assessment in the brown and tan books. 

Also, these books look toward the future. We classify them because we cannot give away our bargaining position. We cannot tell others outside the Congress what we contemplate might be the range of lending for a given country for this forthcoming year. 

Within those limitations we have tried to declassify as much as possible.

GUARANTEE CEILINGS AND FUND REQUEST 

In the past there has been no direct relationship between the ceilings and the funds requested to finance investment guarantees. We believe that the establishment of "liberal" ceilings serves two useful purposes. First, it represents an attitude of AID and congressional support for the private enterprise oriented investment guarantee program. Second, it avoids the necessity for premature amendment of the Act for International Development if the demand for investment guarantees exceeds our current expectations. 

The funds supplied by the Congress to finance this program are the basic controlling element. As the reserves established vary depending upon whether the risk involved is specific or all risk, it is not possible to estimate precisely the amount of reserves needed for our funding guarantees in the future. Reserves for all risk guarantees are presently established at 50 percent; specific risk at 

25 percent of face amount. However, the AID estimate of $100 million needed for added reserves is probably conservative. It is estimated that there will be available for obligation in fiscal year 1963 from present reserves, fees, and other sources some $50 million. Although we have not yet had sufficient experience to make an accurate estimate of the fund requirements for the all-risk program it is believed that this $50 million together with the $100 million of new funds requested will enable us to issue guarantees up to about 70 percent of the requested ceilings and will be sufficient to meet our needs for fiscal year 1963. attached tabulation shows how this estimate of 70 percent was reached.

ROAD CONSTRUCTION IN TANGANYIKA 

The Government of Tanganyika has adopted a 3-year development plan, based on an IBRD survey, at a cost of $67 million. The second largest sector of the plan is improving communications and access to markets by trunk and feeder road development and improvement, which comprises 17.5 percent of the plan's expenditures.

In 1961 the Development Loan Fund (now incorporated in AID) made a loan of $1.9 million to the Government of Tanganyika for the rebuilding of a 142mile all-weather road between Mwanza and Musoma in Lake Province. The road will serve one of Tanganyika's major agricultural areas, including about one-half million people engaged in cotton, coffee, and other agricultural production. Work is presently underway. 

The Government of Tanganyika has applied for an IDA loan for their trunk road program. IDA is awaiting further information on the proposed program. 

In the meantime AID has been holding discussions with IDA-IBRD with a view to coordinating an approach to Tanganyika's road development program.

CRITERIA FOR GUARANTEES 

In the past it has not been possible to forecast with any great accuracy what dollar value of guarantees will materialize from a given dollar value of applications, but a rough estimate would be about 20 percent. 

This low ratio usually results from changes in the applicant's plans and is seldom because we turn down the application. It is rare that an application which has been determined to meet statutory criteria is turned down once it has been accepted for processing. Requests covering projects that contribute little to economic development and therefore do not meet statutory criteria are ordinarily turned down as promptly as possible and are not shown as applications. 

On the other hand, among the reasons why applicants withdraw or abandon their applications are: (1) In many cases, applicants abandon their applications for guarantees on proposed projects because further examination of the project indicates that it is not economically feasible to go ahead.

(2) In many cases, applications are abandoned because the applicant cannot find the financing necessary to go ahead with the project. (3) In some cases, applicants are unable to reach satisfactory agreements with their foreign partners and abandon the project. (4) In some cases, applications are abandoned because the applicant is unsuccessful in obtaining a concession from the foreign government, or is an unsuccessful bidder on a project, or because a competitor establishes the proposed type of plant before the applicant can make satisfactory arrangements and a second plant is not economically feasible. (5) In some few cases, foreign governments have failed to grant the necessary approval for guarantee. 

In light of the above, despite the indicated magnitude of applications we believe that the funds requested will be sufficient to meet our needs.

Mr. MONAGAN. I have had some question raised about our policy in another connection. You have mentioned the Alliance for Progress. 

People have asked with reference to some of the Latin American countries, as to our willingness to distinguish between private enterprise and state enterprise in fields like power development and so forth in connection with our decision to give assistance. 

Just what is the policy of AID, and if you can speak about the Inter-American Bank, what is its policy in that regard? 

Mr. COFFIN. I can answer best by citing the general AID policy which is to instruct our mission directors, the people in the field, to try to be as ingenious and as persistent as possible in impressing upon other countries the need for important private sector enterprises. 

We don't try to sell it on an ideological ground solely, but on a practical ground, that this is the way to develop resources that are both human and material.

We have been in this business long enough to realize that some countries, when they first start out on a plan, are apt to be "stateized" in their planning. But like India, they will see some of the disadvantages and they will relax and they will add one sector to another as areas where private enterprise should not only be tolerated, but encouraged.

Two of the loans that I have mentioned that were made by the new Agency in the private sector have been in India, which is quite remarkable when we look back 10 years. 

It is not a matter of preaching to anyone and saying, "We won't do this. This is in the state sector. It has to be in the private sector or else." We try to do it as diplomatically as possible and show by experience that a substantial private effort is a prerequisite of every serious development plan. In Pakistan, under the Finance Minister, there is increasing emphasis on the private sector. This we expect will take place in Latin America, too, although, as you say, at the moment, it is difficult to see in any given area what the real policy is. 

Mr. MONAGAN. There is a power company-I think it is in Monterrey, Mexico which had been privately operated and the state took it over and the rates were increased up to 140 percent. That might be an extreme example, but they had been operating privately at a profit before that and it seems to me there is a danger in that situation, one that we should be aware of, and that there is an economic justification on an efficiency basis for supporting the proposition that we should encourage the private sector. 

Mr. COFFIN. I think one of our assets is the panel of experts that will review the development plans. I think that these gentlemen are sophisticated economists and fully appreciate the importance of private sector activity. And the whole approach to the Alliance, when we talk in the rough terms that were talked about a year ago, where $20 billion was projected over 10 years, a great part of this

was private industry, both from the United States and Europe. The 

Europeans today are interested in Latin America. But largely because this is a way that their companies and groups of companies can make long-term investments.

I agree it is something we should watch and it is something we should work toward. There will be different ways of exerting pressures, and we are mindful of this as a necessity if the alliance is to work. 

Mr. MONAGAN. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Barry. 

Mr. BARRY. No questions.

Mr. MURPHY. No questions.

Mr. COFFIN. May I, Mr. Chairman, just respond to Mr. Monagan on his previous question by stating that as a result of the Hardy committee investigation, the AID Administrator, Mr. Hamilton, last stated that he would review the AID procedures in an effort to prevent even the appearance that we are providing aid for Communist bloc assistance projects. This review is going on. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Coffin, in your statement you say that we are all familiar with the command plans undertaken in countries by the Sino-Soviet bloc. What do you mean by the command plans? 

Mr. COFFIN. Well, I mean by that a plan that would best be illustrated by one of the satellites behind the Iron Curtain: They have a 5-year plan which is given out from above, very much like the early plans within the Soviet Union, itself, with a production goal of so much, and an agricultural goal of so much. This is the type of thing that Red China had, that has given it so much difficulty. Our emphasis is not on that kind of plan, but on a plan that results from talking with government officials and outside experts and our own mission, so that we come up with what we call a consensus plan, saying what goals we think are feasible; goals that should be reached and which have the backing of the people and the key ministers. Dr. Fei, do you have something you can add to that? 

Mr. FEI. I would like to add what I think would be a successful instance of what we would call planning for freedom or a consensus plan. That is where we can get private enterprise involved-get the citizens of a country involved in trying to reach these goals, because they consider it part of their own plans, and not through forced labor, where people are forced to work at the command of the ruling group. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Coffin. The committee stands adjourned until 10:30 tomorrow morning. (Whereupon, at 4:13 p.m., the committee adjourned to reconvene at 10:30 a.m., Tuesday, March 27, 1962.)
