TUESDAY, MARCH 27, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

10:50 a.m., Hon. Clement J. Zablocki presiding. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The committee will please come to order.

The chairman is appearing before the Rules Committee and has asked that I chair the meeting in his absence. 

We are fortunate to have Hon. Fowler Hamilton, the Administrator. of the Agency for International Development, as a witness this morning. With him is Hon. Walter Lingle, Deputy Administrator. 

Mr. Hamilton.

STATEMENT OF HON. FOWLER HAMILTON, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. HAMILTON.  It is a pleasure for 

Mr. Lingle and me to be here. I believe each of you ladies and gentlemen have met him. He is the senior man in the Agency. We are trying to work in an interchangeable way. Mr. Coffin is in charge of programing. Mr. Lingle has general supervision of the functioning of the Agency. 

At the outset I would like to say, I realize we have presented the committee a great deal of material in the form of these books, two of which are confidential. If it will facilitate the use of the books by the committee, we will be glad to see to it that AID staff is available to take the books at any time that the committee members wish, to their offices, and comment about the material. 

Second, I would like to say in reading the testimony that I gave to the committee last time, I pointed out to the committee that we had obligated approximately $111.7 million of the $1,112.5 million of development loan funds. And I emphasized that one reason for that was that while we had made commitments in the sense of programing, these commitments were in many cases contingent commitments. 

I want to say that in part, the reason that the obligations have not gone forward as fast as they otherwise might is because we are in the course of changing the organization and have had a staffing problem. So in part the reason that those funds have not been obligated to date is because we have not yet got an efficient organization functioning—that is, the organization is not functioning as efficiently as we want it to. 389

The reason why the funds have not been obligated is also because we have made some conditional commitments, conditional upon other countries undertaking certain measures. We don't intend to disburse the funds until those countries meet the conditions. 

I have a statement which I have prepared. If it is agreeable, I will submit that for the record. I believe copies have been furnished to the members of the committee beforehand. (The prepared statement of Mr. Hamilton is as follows:) 

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, I am pleased to be back before this committee and I am particularly pleased to introduce Walter Lingle, our new Deputy Administrator, who is here with me. 

This morning I will first comment on the administrative reorganization of the AID and summarize our requests for additional legislation in this area and second, I will discuss our 1963 program proposals. To some extent will be reviewing matters referred to briefly during the open session, but I can go into them in more detail now. Background 

ADMINISTRATIVE REORGANIZATION 

First I would like to emphasize the size and complexity of the reorganization, both in administration and program. The framework of the congressional mandate for this decade of development was handed down on September 4 of last year and the money for the first year's operation was appropriated on 

September 30. After

The Agency did not formally come into existence until November 4. these few months we think we are off to a good start, but we do not realistically expect either the administrative or programing reorganization to be completed in a short period of time.

The reorganization is such a big job because of the necessary but far-reaching overhaul of foreign assistance last year. The 1961 Foreign Assistance Act brought together in the Agency for International Development a series of loosely connected programs: Technical assistance stemming from point 4 and administered by ICA; defense support and special assistance derived from Mutual 

Security and also administered by ICA; coordination of economic and military assistance from the Department of State; development lending administered by the Development Loan Fund; the Cooley loan operation administered by the 

Export-Import Bank; and the programing of projects overseas financed by proceeds from sales of Public Law 480 surplus food and fibers. 

Merely to digest these diverse functions would be a normal year's job, but the new assistance criteria also direct that foreign economic assistance be focused on overall long-term economic development on a country-by-country basis.

And, finally, Congress codified as part of its mandate the principle that development depends in the long run more on the self-help efforts of the recipient countries than on the extent of our assistance. 

The tools available to this Agency when it came into existence in November had not been designed for the task to be performed. Our various foreign assistance programs had been developed over a number of years to meet pressing world challenges as they arose. 

By last year the time had come to reappraise the entire aid fabric and to develop new concepts and build a new structure to deal with the world situation facing us in the sixties. The various programs turned over to the Agency were only tenuously coordinated with each other; indeed, the various kinds of technical assistance had not even been fully coordinated within the predecessor agency.

The principal emphasis of our foreign aid over the years has been to meet short-term crises-not long-term development. Technical assistance and Export- 

Import Bank loans were not designed to make a large-scale attack toward economic progress.

The Public Law 480 programs were designed more for disposal of surplus commodities than for development needs. 

Only the Development Loan Fund had rapid development as its primary aim and even that did not focus on overall development needs of assisted countries. 

Total Development Loan Fund approvals of $2 billion through June 1961 are less than 4 percent of the $60.6 billion of U.S.

foreign assistance (military,

economic, and food and fiber) since the end of the Marshall plan, and the Development Loan Fund accounted for only 156 of the 17,000 people made available to AID.

No agency had ever systematically examined the overall development goals or priority needs of assisted countries; and little attention had been paid to persuading the governments of some 80 countries to make rational allocation of their available resources or adopt the self-help and reform measures so urgently needed.

Finally, the great majority of the personnel available to the Agency in Washington and overseas had been engaged in technical assistance programs and were largely unprepared to cope with the complicated problems of economic analysis of long-term development, negotiation and administration of substantial development grant and loan programs, and persuasion of and assistance to foreign government officials in planning and self-help measures. 

Progress to date

Under these circumstances, I, as the new Administrator of AID, had to assign priorities to the steps necessary to turn around the structure, personnel, and program of foreign aid to conform as promptly as possible to the congressional directive, without unduly disrupting the many worthwhile foreign assistance programs already underway. 

The first priority duty was to fill the top administrative positions in Washington and in the country missions with people competent to carry out the new program. Simultaneously, however, we had to create a new organizational structure, reevaluate existing programs and devise new programs which are responsive to the new aid criteria. 

I should like to point out that this is something of a "chicken and the egg" proposition: it is extremely difficult to revamp the organization at the same time as the new programs are being devised which will affect the organizational structure, and furthermore while new people with fresh ideas are being hired. 

Also of prime importance but impossible to fulfill immediately was the need to formulate, distribute, and put into practice literally scores of new procedures and practices without which no program as vast as this can long function smoothly.

And, finally, each of the positions supporting the top administrators must be filled with a person with the best skills and experience obtainable, involving reassignment and on-the-job evaluation of present employees and, in a substantial number of cases, recruitment of new people from other Government agencies, private enterprise, and other outside organizations. 

I can report most progress in fulfilling the first responsibility of attracting men of the highest quality to the top management posts in Washington. I submitted biographic sketches of the Deputy Administrator of AID, Mr. Walter L. 

Lingle, Jr., and the Deputy for Programing, Mr. Frank M. Coffin, 2 weeks ago.

I also submitted the biographies of the Assistant Administrators for the four geographical areas. 

I am now happy to submit brief biographies of men filling other top positions. 

Highly recommended candidates are being sought for the remaining key jobs, and we hope to announce the filling of these posts in the near future. 

We are in the midst of a nationwide recruitment program to make sure that all oversea mission directors and deputy directors are fully qualified to carry out the expanded aid obligations. 

We have succeeded in interesting leading business executives and professional people; and we have also been gratified at the response from the labor and cooperative movements and the academic field. Close to 25 men of the highest caliber should shortly be starting special executive training courses, including language, where necessary. 

The search for the best people for these key mission posts will be never ending, but the initial compelling demand is well on its way toward satisfaction. 

Simultaneously with executive recruitment came the restructuring of the foreign assistance organization to concentrate programing and operating authority in the four regional bureaus. 

This transition from the former ICA functional approach to the regional approach has proceeded in accordance with the plans outlined to you last year, and the basic structure of the regional bureaus is now established. 

The chain of communication from Washington through the ambassador to the AID mission is firmly established so that all U.S. economic and political representatives in foreign countries are now working together as a team, coordinated through the ambassador.

The AID functional offices provide staff support and program review and evaluation for all four regional programs and operations. The structure of these offices also follows the proposals presented to you last year, except for the new Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise and the Office of Engineering, to which I made reference at the open session. 

Because of the priority attached to establishing strong regional bureaus and because of the necessity of assigning many key persons from former functional offices of ICA and from the DLF to the regions, not all of the supporting staffs can yet perform the tasks assigned to them at fully satisfactory levels. However, we are now in a position to give these functional staffs the attention they deserve.

Work is already started in preparation of manuals, instructions, forms, and other procedural mechanism reflecting the structural and program reorganization, but these cannot be completed until we have more experience under the reorganization. 

The personnel initially made available to the Agency consisted of former employees of ICA and DLF. We are making every attempt to make sure that each of these persons is assigned to a job commensurate with his skills and experience. But with the changes in emphasis, there are many key jobs for which these persons are not qualified. 

We have, therefore, been recruiting a number of persons from other Government agencies and private enterprise specifically qualified for the new AID responsibilities. This process of reassignment and recruitment is well underway but much remains to be done. 

It was necessary during my first weeks in office to determine which former ICA and DLF employees were necessary for employment in AID. This was a crash operation required under section 621(d) of the 1961 act and was not an effective procedure for building up the sort of supporting staff which the complexity of the AID program requires. 

However, we were able to achieve some benefit from this procedure, despite the fact that we had to act rapidly. We took all feasible steps to assure each employee equitable treatment, but such a personnel evaluation working against a deadline cannot help but result in injury to employee morale. 

To sum up on administration: The reorganization job is as difficult as it was sorely needed. We are well underway, but we have much more to accomplish. 

This year should be viewed as a period of transition. When I assumed office, I pledged to myself that AID would, in due course, become the best run agency in Washington. I am happy to report that my confidence that we will fulfill that pledge received a tremendous boost the first of this month when Walter Lingle joined us as Deputy Administrator. He has already given us ample evidence of his unusual organizational talents. 

Request for new legislation We have several requests to make of Congress to help us complete the job of organizing and staffing so that AID can administer the important foreign aid program efficiently and effectively. 

In order to assure recruitment of a satisfactory supporting staff for the complex administrative, financial, economic, and legal jobs in Washington and overseas, we urgently need authority to employ 150 persons exempt from civil service qualification and tenure rules. That will give us needed flexibility with respect to policymaking positions. We have carefully analyzed the jobs involved and believe we can justify at least 125 supergrade positions under any criteria for such jobs.

Most persons, who are qualified for the top supporting AID jobs and are serving in other Government posts, already occupy supergrade positions or are at the stage in their careers where they would normally expect now to step into such positions.

The businessmen, bankers, lawyers, economists, and other professionals whom we are actively recruiting almost invariably earn salaries higher even than those provided for supergrade positions. If we are to obtain the high-quality people necessary to run this aid effort we must be able to have enough supergrades to attract talent. 

The proposed 1962 act as submitted to you contains no supergrade compensation provisions because AID should be able to obtain sufficient supergrade authorization under the Executive Pay Raise Act now before Congress if it is enacted. Should such legislation not be enacted in substantially its present

form, however, we would expect to request appropriate supergrade authorization from the Congress.

New AID employees hired primarily for executive service overseas should in many cases serve first in Washington to gain necessary experience. Therefore, we request that section 625(d) (2) be amended to give AID authority similar to that which other agencies now have to assign persons hired under the Foreign Service Act for an initial tour of duty in Washington. This tour will not exceed 2 years, and the authority is to be exercised only after a finding of necessity by the President or his delegate. 

It is my intent that this power will be used sparingly and only when it is clear that the person involved is destined for overseas. 

Finally, we are requesting an increase in our administrative budget to $55 million. In order to deal imaginatively and efficiently with the complex and novel problems that constantly confront an agency of this magnitude in the difficult fiield of international relations, we must have enough staff and a staff of the highest caliber. We must offer realistic and thorough staff orientation and executive training programs so that our people will be as well prepared as possible, and our Washington experts must be able to make frequent trips to the field, since we clearly cannot have experts of all kinds in every mission. 

Staffing, training, and travel budgets will increase next year, and other important needs are becoming more and more apparent as the reorganization progresses.

The $55 million we are requesting for administration is actually less than 2 percent of the approximately $3.3 billion requested for economic aid, without even considering our Cooley loans, military, and Public Law 480 responsibilities. 

Indeed, as the actual administrative requirements of the new aid program have come into sharper focus since our fiscal year 1963 budget was prepared last December, it has become evident that our request of $55 million may not be adequate to do the total job. Nevertheless, I have frozen our request for $55 million in the light of the authority contained in section 610 which permits us to transfer program funds to meet administrative requirements. This authority, which we are forced to use in fiscal year 1962, will continue to be used sparingly and only when it is determined by the President and the AID Administrator to be essential to carry out the functions and programs of the Agency. 1963 PROGRAM I believe that the 1963 AID program, stressing the new assistance criteria, represents a promising start toward fulfillment of the congressional mandate. 

But I wish to emphasize that a complete turnaround cannot take place in 1 year. 

The peoples of less developed countries are not yet sufficiently aware of the need for some of the self-help measures we seek to encourage. Even under the best political circumstances, many self-help measures take substantial time. 

But progress has been and is being made. 

Our programs and the reactions of the 80-odd less developed countries must be viewed not as a 1or 2-year undertaking but as the beginning of a decade of difficult development effort that is slowly gathering momentum. 

I should like to discuss briefly our plans for the 1963 program in the light of our experience and current political and economic conditions. 

Far East

In this area, where today the cold war is at its hottest, we propose a program of $200-$280 million in development loans, $75 million in development grants, and $349 million in supporting assistance. 

It is unnecessary to belabor the Communist threat in this area, and Department of Defense representatives have already filled you in on our critical military programs. But we all recognize that the outcome of the battle for allegiance of these peoples depends ultimately on whether they can see their hopes for a better life materialize under our free principles. I shall therefore comment on the real opportunities we now have to significantly accelerate development in this region. 

In free China, great strides have already been made. Despite an onerous military burden, the standard of living has risen markedly and we can now begin honestly to visualize the prospect of self-sustaining economic growth. The progress which has been made is reflected both in the reduction of development grants from [security deletion] and in the increase in the country's capacity to service loans.

We project development lending next year in a substantial range. [Security deletion.]

The Philippines is a country rich in natural resources, and its literate people have long been ready for development but generally have lacked leadership. 

Now there is a new and promising administration which we believe is determined to take the self-help measures necessary for development progress, in which event we are now prepared to help provide the necessary external financial assistance with development loans. [Security deletion.] 

Thailand has substantial natural resources, a strong and stable currency, and a growing cadre of able middle rank administrators, but its top leadership has failed to push necessary economic and social changes. Communist pressure from the north and population pressures from within have contributed to the need for increased growth and more equitable distribution of wealth. country's leadership is now beginning to recognize the necessity of development and is taking steps in that direction.

The Last year American experts made a special study which pointed out promising Thai development prospects. [Security deletion.] 

Thailand is also an apt example of our determination to deal with the crucial problems of rural poverty, isolation, and discontent before the Communists move in to exploit prevailing misery and obstruct belated development programing. 

Our Thai program is designed for the development of heretofore neglected rural regions, particularly in the northwest territory which borders on Laos. Both loans and grants are proposed for a broad community development self-help effort which should also give the people a sense of identity with the nation as a whole.

The increase in supporting assistance in the Far East results from special and nonrecurring situations in Korea and Burma-a recession in Korean business following the May 1961 military coup and fulfillment of a highway commitment in Burma made in 1959. 

[Security deletion.] 

Near East and south Asia

This strategic region contains the world's largest non-Communist population. 

In addition, it accounts for much of the free world's oil supply and within it lie vital trade routes and lines of communication. 

We propose, for fiscal year 1963, $850 to $950 million in development loans, $78 million in development grants, and $100 million in supporting assistance. 

Our proposals emphasize economic growth with a 50-percent increase in development lending, while supporting assistance would be cut in half. 

The chief recipients of development loan assistance are India, Pakistan, Iran, and Turkey. Despite low per capita income and rapid population growth, these countries have the raw potential for development and governments which seek increasing realization of that potential. Moreover, these countries have taken concrete steps to create the conditions which merit substantial external assistance.

All four countries have raised the level of tax revenue. Turkey has adopted stringent fiscal reforms. Both India and Pakistan have proportionately decreased military expenditures and increased development expenditures. Iran now has a government, with support of the Shah, that is attempting to carry out basic reforms despite attacks from the far right and the far left. 

We have reason to expect that our assistance to these countries will significantly contribute to long-term social and economic development because all of them possess or are in the process of drafting-comprehensive development plans.

Existence of carefully conceived plans in India and Pakistan has enabled us to make commitments to each of them for more than 1 year and these commitments in turn provide a basis for further and more effective planning. It is presently believed that Turkey and Iran will complete plans next year, and it may similarly be in our interest to give them longer term commitments. 

Supporting assistance has been reduced to the bare minimum in the Near East and south Asia region. [Security deletion.] 

This heavily populated area has been the principal target for Sino-Soviet bloc economic aid-more than $2 billion through 1961. Large amounts have gone to India, but proportionately still larger sums have gone to Nepal, Ceylon, United Arab Republic, and Afghanistan. 

The failure of the Soviets to achieve domination of any of these countries results in substantial part, we feel, from the availability of our foreign assistance

program which provides an alternative to exclusive reliance on bloc assistance. 

It is gratifying that our Western allies appreciate the importance of this region and participate with us in consortia to underwrite the external assistance requirements of India's and Pakistan's development efforts. 

Africa-Europe region

Although the problems confronting development in Africa are numerous and weighty, the situation there does have several favorable aspects. A number of our European allies, particularly France and England, are providing substantial assistance. In most countries the forces of reform and economic progress are in the ascendancy, and popular will for improvement is strong and pervasive. 

We propose a program consisting of $200-$270 million in development loans, $117.5 million in development grants, and $32.5 million in supporting assistance. 

The development grant figure is particularly large because we are emphasizing education and training programs for these countries in early stages of development and because there could be no reasonable prospect of repayment of loans from most of these countries. 

In Africa, north of the Sahara, programs are proposed for Morocco, Tunisia, and Libya. Assistance to Libya helps support the American airbases in that country, but we are trying to encourage economic development by increasing the proportion of development grants. 

The Tunisian program is being greatly enlarged because it has a [security deletion] stable government bent on development and sufficient administrative capacity to utilize significant amounts of development capital. 

[Security deletion.] 

South of the Sahara most of our development assistance is concentrated in Nigeria, Sudan, and Liberia, countries that have real development potential and give promise of 'promoting moderation and responsibility in African politics. 

We have also made an advance commitment under section 202(b) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 to Tanganyika, another most promising country. 

In addition, there are small grant programs scheduled in most other African countries, including former colonies primarily supported by France. We feel it is important to have programs in these countries so that [security deletion] our assistance will be available in fields where we have particular technical competence.

Nigeria, with 36 million people one-seventh of the population of Africaabundant natural resources, responsible and competent leadership and an industrious people vigorously pressing for economic and social progress, has the highest development and political potential in tropical Africa. 

The [security deletion] of development loans programed for Nigeria will not only move that country toward rapid development but also will help demonstrate to the rest of Africa that their economic and political aspirations can be fulfilled under freedom. 

[Security deletion.] 

Liberia has strong ties with this country, and mineral resources being developed by Western capital give Liberia a good basis for economic growth. 

Substantial assistance in developing Liberia's human resources and integrating rural regions into the monetary economy will help this friendly nation become a relatively healthy and influential factor in Africa. 

Latin American region

In Latin America the alliance for progress is beginning to move ahead despite tenacious obstructionism from the extreme left and extreme right. But the first year of a program designed to overcome a century and a half of stagnation is inevitably a year of great difficulty. Traditionalist elements continue intransigent; the leftist elements continue to attack the alliance and indulge in obstructionist tactics.

In view of the normal administrative and legislative obstacles to rapid reform action as well as the extreme political pressure mentioned, I am gratified that significant self-help measures have been taken during the alliance's first year and that the momentum of such actions continues. 

The confidential regional paper for Latin America contains an extensive list which is merely illustrative of the measures initiated. Almost all of them require further action, and there is no question that every country must do yet more. But these first steps are encouraging.

We have also demanded that countries realistically assess their capacity to use capital. [Security deletion.]

The attention Latin American governments are paying to development planning reflects their recognition that we mean business. Chile, Colombia, and 

Bolivia have completed comprehensive development plans and submitted them to the panel of experts of the Organization of American States for review and evaluation, and it is expected that Venezuela will submit its plan soon. Other countries are in the process of developing such plans or organizing machinery to do so.

For fiscal year 1963 we are requesting appropriation of at least $500 million for development loans and up to $100 million in grants as the first installment of the proposed $3 billion authorization for the next 4 years of the alliance. 

[Security deletion.] 

The proposed recipients of development loans are principally Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Colombia. Argentina is in many ways the most advanced Latin 

American country. Its large population includes persons with substantial managerial and technical skills. We cannot yet assess what effects recent political events will have on our Argentine program next year. 

Brazil is the colossus of Latin America and could become a great and powerful ally. We cannot afford to ignore it. While its national government has not been able [security deletion] to carry out the overall reforms which are needed, the development plans for the poverty stricken, heavily populated northeast section of the country were sensibly conceived and merit our substantial assistance. Real development progress is possible in that region where extreme leftist agitators are omnipresent. We are still holding back some of the funds committed last year until the criteria for those funds are met. 

Chile has been one of the first countries to prepare development plans [security deletion]. In Colombia the Government has already made significant reforms and laid the foundation for effective utilization of external aid. you know, the Government coalition prevailed in last week's elections. As

The road ahead in Latin America will be hard and not without disappointments and setbacks. We can only promise that if American determination, initiative, and toughness can make this alliance work, it will work. 

We strongly urge that Congress indicate its willingness to support the responsible and progressive forces in Latin America during this first half of the decade of development. The stakes are too great for us to exert less than our full effort.

APPENDIX 

John L. Salter, 49, Assistant Administrator for Congressional Liaison.-Born at Everett, Wash. Attended St. Joseph's College, Mountain View, Calif. Received an M.A. degree from St. Patrick's College, Menlo Park, Calif., 1935.

Worked for Washington State Department of Social Security and in 1938 was appointed director of employment for the State of Washington. Served with the National Youth Administration during 1939-40 and became administrative assistant to Representative Henry M. Jackson, of Washington. Named regional director, Office of Price Stabilization, for Northwest in 1951. Served as administrative assistant to Senator Henry M. Jackson, of Washington, from 1953 until his appointment as deputy director for Congressional Liaison, International

Cooperation Administration, early in 1961. Designated for present post with 

AID by President Kennedy in January. 

Herbert J. Waters, 49, Assistant Administrator for Material Resources.-Born at Santa Rosa, Calif. Educated in Santa Rosa public schools and for 18 years was associated with Santa Rosa daily newspaper as a reporter, farm editor, managing editor, and editor. 

Joined staff of U.S. Department of Agriculture in 1949 at the request of Secretary Charles A. Brannan. During his work with USDA was actively interested in work of United Nations' Food and Agricultural organization, and took a leading role in interagency development of U.S. policy on encouragement of land reform policies abroad. 

In 1953 he joined staff of Senator Hubert H. Humphrey of Minnesota as agricultural specialist. Later became legislative aide and administrative assistant from 1955 until his appointment as a special assistant to the Director of the International Cooperation Administration in February 1961. Designated by President Kennedy for his present post in January. 

Edwin R. Bayley, 48, Director of Public Affairs.-Born at Chicago, Ill. Educated in Wisconsin public schools and graduated from Lawrence College, Appleton, Wis. Attended Yale University Graduate School.

Reporter for Green Bay, Wis., Press-Gazette, 1941-42. Served as gunnery officer in U.S. Navy during World War II. Political reporter for the Milwaukee 

Journal, 1946-49, when he became executive secretary to Gov. Gaylord A. Nelson of Wisconsin. Appointed Director of Public Information for the Peace Corps in February 1961. Joined White House Staff September 1961. Appointed Di rector of Public Affairs for AID in December. 

Hollis B. Chenery, 43, Director of Program Review and Coordination Staff. 

Born at Richmond, Va. B.S. degree in mathematics, University of Arizona, 1939; 

B.S. in engineering, University of Oklahoma, 1941; Ph. D. in economics from 

Harvard University, 1949. While studying for his doctorate he was a member of the economics faculty at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. 

Came to AID from Stanford University where he had been teaching economic development and international economics for the past 9 years. At Stanford he also served as codirector of the Research Center in Economic Growth. Has served as chairman of a group of programing experts for the U.N. Economic 

Commission for Asia and the Far East; as economic consultant to the U.N. 

Economic Commission for Latin America and U.S. Foreign Operations Administration in Turkey; as an economic adviser to the Bank of Sicily, the Bank of Israel, and the Government Planning Boards of Japan and Pakistan; as chief of program division of Mutual Security Agency's Mission to Italy (1951 to 1952) and as economist with Economic Cooperation Administration analyzing economic development programs in Portugal, Greece, and Turkey. 

Thomas A. Kennedy, 45, Director, Management Inspection Staff.-Born at

Chicago, Ill. Educated at Wilson College, Chicago; DePaul University, L.L.B., 1939. Attended Harvard University, Communications and Intelligence School while in U.S. Navy. Loyola University, B. Sc., 1949.

With Government Services Administration since 1953, Assistant General Counsel, 1953-56, and Assistant Commissioner for Transportation and Utilities since 1956. General counsel, House Committee on Government Operations, 1949-53. 

Private law practice, Chicago, 1946-49. U.S. Navy 1942-46. Illinois Department of Labor, part time, and National Youth Administration, Chicago, 1936–39. 

Industrial Bank, Chicago, 1940-41. 

Donald L. Roberts, 50, Director of Office of Engineering.-Born in South

Dakota and graduate of South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, B.S. 

1933, C.E. 1939. Graduate studies, University of Tennessee, 1941. 

Has had extensive engineering experience in foreign countries. While with 

Bechtel engineering companies for nearly 20 years, he supervised projects in Venezuela, the Philippines, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, England, and Canada. As vice president of Bechtel International Corp. in San Francisco, he headed public works projects in Saudi Arabia and oil terminal installations in Kuwait. Most recently, he has served as a special Bechtel consultant, analyzing the economic and engineering feasibility of major projects. 

Prior to his association with Bechtel, Mr. Roberts had Government engineering experience with the Tennessee Valley Authority, and as project engineer in building dams, highway bridges, and land utilization projects. (Discussion off the record.)

Mr. HAMILTON. The necessity for classification arises from two matters that are in the book. One, they show what we are tentatively programing forward for these countries. We would not like those countries to know about next year's proposals because we would lose our trading position with them. They could say "Give us the money 

AID has programed," and we might not want to go forward with programs because they failed to go along with us in some things we want.

Second, we want to speak in considerable candor about people who administer the governments in these matters, mentioning things such as corruption, political views, and things like that, in an endeavor to report to you adequately.

Instead of reading this document that we had submitted, if it is agreeable to the committee I would like to summarize it and focus my summary on three points: The present program in light of its background, the program that has been proposed to the committee for

approval in 1963, and certain considerations that may be relevant to the committee's consideration as to whether it wishes to adopt the proposed program. 

I will turn to the first point which the present background gains from the past foreign aid programs. The phrase "foreign aid" has been used to apply to a variety of programs that have changed and evolved over the years, beginning as long ago as 1940 with the lendlease under President Roosevelt. That was followed by relief and rehabilitation under his administration. 

The first 11 pages is the first point-that takes us up to the 1963 program. The second point takes up the remainder of the statement, and then I thought I might mention certain considerations which might be of interest to the committee which are not covered in the statement.

As the committee will recall, we have had these nine programs from 1940 down to date. They have involved an expenditure of very large sums of money. Four Presidents and 11 different Congresses have appropriated these sums.

The first programs I mentioned were those of President Roosevelt and the Congresses of his day which authorized lend-lease and relief and rehabilitation.

Then under President Truman, the 80th Congress authorized the Marshall plan. President Truman also started under his administration, the military security program-stemming historically from the Greek program-and then on through programs after the Korean war. Further under his administration, the point 4 program was initiated.

Coming to President Eisenhower's administration: he initiated the 

Public Law 480 program-surplus food and fiber. It was also during his administration that the activities of the Export-Import Bank, which had started in 1934, were increasingly correlated into the foreign aid program. And finally, he initiated the development loan programs in 1957 with the establishment of the Development Loan Fund. 

President Kennedy's administration so far has been most closely associated with the alliance for progress. 

Even this brief review clarifies two important aspects of this foreign aid program. One is that they are bipartisan. As I mentioned, it was the 80th Congress, which was controlled by one party that at the suggestion of Mr. Truman, a member of the other party, enacted the Marshall plan.

The administration of the programs has also been bipartisan. That doesn't mean they are not involved in politics. Because, of course, when any Government agency is spending these enormous sums of money, it is obviously necessary and essential that it be given the closest scrutiny and that the people consider the merits of the programs carefully--both their substantive merits and the manner in which they are being administered.

Mr. Lingle and I, who happen to illustrate the bipartisan character of it, welcome this scrutiny. We will do what we can to facilitate it. 

The second important aspect of the program has been that it has been evolutionary; that it has changed and accommodated different threats to American interests. 

If you exclude the Marshall plan and putting aside Public Law 480 money, the sum of approximately $46 billion has been appropriated

by the Congress for these various programs since the Marshall plan. 

Of that sum, all but $3 billion has been appropriated for immediate national security goals. That is to say, as I read the history, it has been appropriated either for immediate military security or to help the immediate political interests of this country. It has been military and immediate political security as opposed to development programs. 

The funds that have been expressly appropriated for development, as I read the record, are $3 billion-plus out of this $47 billion. That is to say, the total amount of funds that the Congress has appropriated for point 4 has been $1.2 billion. The total amount of funds that have been appropriated for the Development Loan Fund have been $2 billion, of which so far, because of the long-term nature of the projects, steel mills, fertilizer plants, only $600 million has been expended. 

So that up until the present phase, the overwhelming predominant characteristics of these programs as I read the background was for immediate and military security. 

The Congress last year, carrying out this evolution of the programs toward development-changed the past history and placed increasing emphasis on development. In terms of the funds of money, for example, that change is illustrated by this: 

The amount of money that Congress appropriated last year—almost $300 million for technical assistance was more money than had been appropriated for technical assistance by the Congress during the first 6 years; that is to say, from 1949 through 1954. This apparently evidenced the desire of Congress to give increasing emphasis to the development, training, and education of people. 

The funds that were appropriated for development loans-of $1,112.5 million-were more than half as much as had been theretofore appropriated for the whole Development Loan Fund, and twice as much as had been actually expended in development loans. 

The point is further emphasized by the fact that the Congress authorized an additional billion and a half a year for 4 more years. The result was that the present program differed primarily from previous programs in that instead of being heavily balanced toward the military, the development aspects were almost balanced with the military. 

I come now to the description of the present program and what we have done about it. When those of us who were given the responsibility for the administration undertook the assignment, we found that the principal problems with which we had to deal arose out of a singular set of circumstances: that while about 17,000 people were transferred to this Agency-of whom 8,500 were non-U.S. citizens abroad and 8,500 U.S. citizens-only 256, I believe it was, came from the Development Loan Fund. 

Of the 8,500 U.S. citizens, practically all of them had point 4 types of background. They had been engaged in education and agriculture; over half of them had an agricultural background because of the emphasis of point 4 on agriculture. 

We had this organization of 8,500 Americans that might be likened to the International Red Cross in the sense that they were people trained in helping people. In this organization, they were trained to develop skills in agriculture, plant breeding, animal breeding, hybrid seed corn, public health, and literacy. 

Superimposed upon that was the Development Loan Fund, which is the largest lender in the world, although it is not lending, in the

commercial sense, nor grants. Then the alliance for progress, with the responsibility for watching over certain additional funds, notably the funds that have been administered by the International Development Bank, and with a coordinating function with the Export-Import Bank, was put on top of that. 

So that the one problem was not necessarily to fire a lot of people but to get people who were competent to discharge, in addition to this technical assistance responsibility that Congress had put upon the Agency, this long-term development program, and keep administering the military funds. 

Second, the Congress had indicated to us quite clearly that it wanted a change in the form of the structure of the old ICA organization. 

I would like to hand out some charts of the organization prior to AID which I think might illuminate the problem somewhat. 

ICA had been organized with 4 regional offices, and 11 or 12 technical offices: agriculture, public health, community development, education. They were all spread out on an equal basis and they reported to one man, who was Dr. Fitzgerald. 

The plan that had been put before the Congress for the Agency of International Development contemplated a much simpler structure. It contemplated that of these 11 or 12 separate offices and other units, the 4 regional offices would be retained as the primary organizational units. The seven other technical offices would be reduced to staff offices. The 7 technical offices had approximately 70 people in them apiece, so that there were 840 people in these technical offices.

The program that the Congress approved indicated, as we read it, that we should take these technical people and disperse them into the regional offices, keeping the senior people in the technical offices with one or two assistants to provide a staff and advisory function. 

Under the old organization, under ICA, you had a situation like this: A program would come up from a regional office. Then if it related to public health or water, it would go to the technical office where there would be some engineering. Then if it were worked out, the actual contracting would be done by someone in the management office where they had contracting supervision. 

Mr. BARRY. Was this beforehand?

Mr. HAMILTON. Beforehand under ICA. It was very difficult to find out in the case of a project who really had the responsibility, where the "buck stopped." So we understood Congress direction to mean we were to take these contracting functions and take these technical functions and disperse them geographically, so that in the case of the Far East, Mr. Janow-who happens to be head of that—would be responsible for all the operations in the Far East.

Mr. HAMILTON. We understood that the Congress direction in connection with the Agency for International Development was to concentrate the operations in the four regional bureaus, which are in the AID chart before you. There are also the various staff offices which assist those bureaus. 

The Agency was established on November 4. It is a little less than 

5 months old at the present time. That was a painful process. I can illustrate it by what happened when I first discussed it with the 

General Counsel, a very able man. And I said, "We are going to make these regions completely integrated operations and all of us will work with them."

He said "That is all right for these other fellows, the legal fellows and others. But you and I are lawyers, and you know we have to have a cross-fertilization of ideas."

I said, "We will make them integrated units and they will have their own staffs, including legal advice. You will be the senior officer. 

If we have problems with the Department of Justice, the Bureau of the Budget, that is your responsibility." 

We want as much of the work done in these bureaus as we possibly can, so that the bureaus are responsible for everything in their area of operations, all the functions, including the development loan functions, except, of course, when they take a measure that has a political effect or affects something outside general policy that comes up and is coordinated. It comes to Mr. Lingle and me. 

The various groups that have been interested in these various functions, like Public Health and Education, and the experts, have a feel-

ing at the present time, at least in some quarters, that their interests are not being represented because they don't have these separate offices with these large staffs. 

It is going to take us some time to convince them, as I am sure we will be able to do, that the organization along regional lines is going to give adequate representation to their interests.

Mr. BARRY. Referring to the chart in the green book, bottom line, the words "country level," I can envision a country team, a USOM team, where we have an economic officer and a program officer. Would there be someone in each country team, if it is a large one, representative of each one of the others one from management planning, one from personnel, one from program support, one from engineering, one from materiel resources, and so on? 

Mr. HAMILTON. It would depend, as you say, on the size of the 

USOM team. There are about 70 different missions in the world. 

Ten of them account for the expenditure in toto of almost two-thirds of the money. Twenty of them account-20 of the countries, the areas that they represent-account for 80 percent. 

On the one hand, you have a situation like some of the small countries in Africa where we don't plan to have a mission. We will have one AID man, but he will be part of the Embassy staff. 

Mr. BARRY. Do they report in an integrated way right on up to the administrator of the bureau, and then do they also report functionally to the administrators over here?

Mr. HAMILTON. No, they do not. They report only geographically. 

Mr. BARRY. There is not a General Motors type of planning. 

Mr. HAMILTON. I am not familiar with General Motors. If there is an engineer, as there would be in a country like Pakistan- 

Mr. BARRY. Do you have functional reporting as well?

Mr. HAMILTON. No, sir. The engineer in Pakistan would report to the mission director in Pakistan on a fertilizer plant. That report would then go to the Ambassador who would see it, it would then come to Washington and be sent to the Pakistan desk in the Near East-south Asia region. That region would have an engineer there. The desk man would talk to him about it. Say "This is a problem. right?" 

Is this

If it was a real tough problem it would go to our senior officer. We have an office of engineering, as you will note. He might say "This is

so important"-as, for example, if you were talking about a $40 million fertilizer plant in some country, that he would say "I think we ought to go out and get a firm of engineers to have a hard look at this thing and see if it will work and do a feasibility study." 

The top engineer's responsibility is staff. Nobody can go out to the engineering community without going through him. 

Mr. BARRY. You are doing functional management but you are doing it by going outside.

Mr. HAMILTON. Channeling it geographically. It gets functional when you get a functional problem.

Mrs. CHURCH. I am interested in the fact that you list your ambassador and mission director in a relationship one above the other. 

Does that indicate a change in the present relationship of the two? 

Mr. HAMILTON. It indicates the relationship established by the President in early 1961 in which the mission director reports through the ambassador, but the ambassador can't stop it. If the mission director differs from the ambassador in his appraisal of the situation, the mission director has the right-as far as I am concerned and my colleague, the Secretary of State is concerned-and the duty to give us the benefit of his judgment.

Mrs. CHURCH. Would the ambassador also give you the benefit of his judgment, and would he report his variation of opinion to the 

Secretary of State?

Mr. HAMILTON. The form of his communication would be addressed to the Secretary of State, but the minute it came in the building, a copy would go to the region concerned in the AID. I have the responsibility to advise the Secretary and the President on all matters that are primarily aid, including taking account of the political aspects. 

If, for example, an Assistant Secretary of State should have a different view on an aid matter from the political perspective than the assistant administrator for the area, if they can't work it out, they come to me or Mr. Lingle. We try to adjust the views. Then we make our recommendation to the Secretary of State. Then we don't litigate. 

In other words, that is our recommendation. 

Mrs. CHURCH. He makes the decision?

Mr. HAMILTON. The Secretary of State or the President. They are the clients. We make our recommendation.

There have been a few cases in which there have been differences of view. In every instance so far, the Secretary of State has happened to take in substance our position.

Mr. CURTIS. The Eximbank seems to be getting more and more into the aid picture.

Mr. HAMILTON. Particularly with the alliance for progress. 

Mr. CURTIS. How far would that come to you through these organizational channels, and how far would it be outside? 

Mr. HAMILTON. That comes in, in two ways. If there is a loan in question, for example. the staff working on that reports to the Eximbank just to let them know that it is in the works, because our money is the last money out.

In other words, if anybody can get any money from the Eximbank, from the World Bank, from anybody from private industry, first, then they shouldn't get this development loan. As we understand it, this is your direction to us.

Mr. BARRY. The same people in Pakistan would be developing the 

Eximbank loan as they would be developing other loans; is that not so? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Actually, at the present time, Mr. Barry, the way it works is if anybody wanted a loan in Pakistan, for example, a private business group, they would come to the Eximbank here. They wouldn't go to our mission out there. 

If the Eximbank gets a request for a loan from Brazil, for instance, they let our people know about it. Before we approve a loan, it goes before a committee called the Development Loan Committee of which I am chairman, on which are representatives of the Eximbank, the Treasury, and the various other financial institutions of the Government on it.

They then make their recommendation to me. If it is an Eximbank loan it goes before the National Advisory Council, which we are represented on. 

Mr. BARRY. When do you send it out to the field? 

Mr. HAMILTON. You mean an Eximbank loan?

Mr. HAMILTON. We don't pass on it, but they let us know about it.

Mr. LINGLE. I thought I might say one thing. I am very new at this, and this may not be entirely accurate; if not, I will ask the Administrator to correct me. But certainly our ultimate objective, as

We have just been going through that process in Pakistan, where Pakistan has put forward a long-term development plan and needed sources of money from various places in order to accomplish that plan. Our mission director in Pakistan served as the local coordinator, working with the Ambassador, and then funneled it back up to Washington where additional coordination is necessary in order to bring together all of the agencies who were necessary to contribute to that consortium in Pakistan. 

Some of the money had to flow from our own funds, some had to flow from the Export-Import Bank, as I understand it. And in that case some had to come from foreign countries. I believe England, Germany, and perhaps some other countries participated in that. 

I believe our concept is that our mission director at the country level and our Agency in Washington are responsible for helping coordinate the sources of these various funds, not having any authority to do so, not having authority to tell these different agencies what they are to do, just as we have no authority over the Export-Import Bank. But we are the organization which is expected to know where the money should be coming from, to try to give some coordination to it.

Mr. HAMILTON. I will move to the present program. The present program has three aspects: the military aspect, which has evolved way back as early as the Greek situation down through President Eisenhower's administration; then it has the development aspects, which started with point 4 back in 1949; and the Development Loan Fund under President Eisenhower in 1958.

In discussing the development program, I think it may be useful for purposes of analysis to keep two different situations in mind. One has to do with the development of less developed countries. 

These new countries-this exploitation of sovereignties which has followed the withdrawal of the powers since 1945-there is a situation where the circumstances are such that it may be in the interest of the United States to assist in the development of those countries. 

Then, there is a second set of circumstances that relate particularly to countries that have been independent countries for almost as long as we have. And I have in mind the countries of Latin America, the so-called Alliance for Progress countries. 

Turning for a moment to the new countries, the situation in many of those countries, of course, as we all know, is that the first and most significant, crying need is for education, to train their people. 

I don't mean, of course, by that just training lawyers. I mean, training people who are technically competent to increase the productivity in the first place, and just to administer the government in many of these countries because they don't have enough people who have had governmental experience. 

Second, to help the lesser developed country increase its productivity-agricultural products primarily. There is no point, for example, in having a development loan to build a road unless you have people in a country that can maintain the road and operate the equipment that is needed to maintain the road and furthermore maintain the equipment that is needed to maintain the road, so to speak. 

In those countries the development is, in the first instance, an education and training, with a small "e" and "t." 

In the second instance, it is helping them through development loans to build the kind of things that we used to develop the West in this country, which were primarily transportation, some small industries, things of that kind. ess.

There the process, I think we all realize, is going to be a long proc- It varies considerably from country to country. It is perfectly apparent, I submit, that a country like Nigeria, which is going to be running 40,000 or 50,000 barrels of oil a dav, which will be sold in the world market, which has good reserves of iron ore and coal, has, relatively speaking, a cadre at least of trained, competent people who have been British trained and educated. which has a common language in 

English, which is almost a sixth of the total population of Africa, is the kind of country where one may expect long-term progressive development.

Turning to Latin America. There the circumstances that give rise to a set of facts from which one can argue that it is in our national interest to help these countries develop, as I understand them, are these:

From 1946 until 1954 the prices of the raw materials that the Latin American countries were selling were rising faster than the price of the manufactured goods they were buying. 

Furthermore, they had accumulated very substantial reserves of foreign exchange during the war when they were selling raw materials at good prices, but all of our output and European output was going into weapons of war so they weren't able to import manufactured goods they wanted. 

That situation commenced to turn over in 1954 with the result that by 1960 it, in effect, cost the Latin American countries $1.350 billion more to buy imports from the United States in 1960 than it would have cost in 1954 because of the change in the terms of trade. 

Another reflection of it was the fact that their foreign reserves, all the Latin American countries, decreased from 1956 to 1960 from $4 billion to $3 billion. That balances the other figures. They were having to draw down their reserves. 

Another aspect of the similar problem is that the decline in raw material prices in 1958 deprived the less developed countries of foreign exchange earnings, which were somewhat greater than the total amount of foreign aid which had gone into those areas before. 

You are all familiar with that.

In Latin America, then, we have had a balance-of-payments crisis. 

This economic situation, in turn, has had its political repercussions, and the interplay between these two has contributed to a set of problems which, of course, we are now endeavoring to deal with in the alliance for progress, stemming historically from the Act of Bogotá of 1960.

In that area, in light of those sets of circumstances, we are endeavoring to work with those countries in the alliance for progress to help them help themselves. 

In some of those countries, of course, because they are much older societies, there are more technical skills, there are more government administrative resources available then, for example, in Africa. But at the same time there are encrusted in the Latin American societies attitudes and customs, with which you are all familiar, which don't exist in the case of a new society and may be a brake upon development. 

It is for that purpose, as we understand the legislation, that the self-help measures, the so-called reforms are designed to break through those habits, customs, and circumstances to facilitate the development in light of the fact that we are only programing about one-tenth of the total amount of investment that is contemplated by the Charter of Punta del Este. 

The charter contemplates from external sources, United States and other countries' sources, $20 billion over 10 years will be required. 

But it contemplates four times that much will be available from the countries themselves; from investment, local savings, or measures they will take to generate capital by increasing tax collections or selling their local securities.

That is the substance of the present Latin American program. 

There are a few aspects of the total program that may be of interest to you, just to recall them to you.

As you know, beginning in 1960 the limited procurement policy was initiated earlier for the Development Loan Fund. The statute

requires that we purchase in the United States under certain circumstances except to the extent that the President waives it. 

The President has said that there are 19 countries which would be excluded from procurement except in unusual circumstances. They are the highly industrialized countries. 

At the present time, if one includes the military purchases out of the total amount being obligated, over 80 percent is being obligated in the United States.

Of the amount that is not being currently obligated for U.S. purchases, 4 percent approximately these are somewhat theoretical considerations-goes to these 19 countries, the industrialized countries of Europe and Japan. 

Of the 4 percent, only about half of it, or 2 percent, goes to countries that have a favorable balance of trade with us. As you know, Japan and England, for example, where some of this money goes, have unfavorable balances of trade with us in the sense that they buy more from us than we buy from them. 

Another aspect of the present foreign aid program that may be encouraging is the fact that the Marshall plan countries are themselves doing a very substantial amount. 

The figures, as you recall, were in 1960, the Marshall plan countries, with a little assist from Japan and Canada, put in the form of foreign aid in the sense of noncommercial investment, approximately $2.3 billion into these underdeveloped countries. We put in $3 billion. 

Of course, because they have a smaller gross national product than we do, in terms of percent of gross national product they did about as much as we did. 

What is even more astonishing is the fact that the total amount of investment that flowed into these underdeveloped countries in 1960 was more than that which flowed from the United States. Taking both public and private from Europe and other countries outside the United States, $4 billion went into the underdeveloped countries from those countries. We did about $4 billion. 

The amount going in is very, very substantial from other sources, roughly equivalent to ours.

When one compares that with what the Russians and Chinese have available, even including their military aid, which is excluded from the free world $8 billion I gave you, the Russians and Chinese are making commitments at the rate of about $14 billion. 

The total resources available from the free world and actually moving into these less developed areas is very, very much larger than the Communists.

Turning to the third item, that is, the present request for the present program- (Discussion off the record.)

There are the principal new items-one has to do with the Alliance for Progress. That is a request for authorization for $3 billion for 

4 years forward.

The background of that request, just to refresh your recollection on it, is this: That last year the Congress appropriated for development loans the sum of $1,112.5 million. That was the appropriation. 

The authorization was about $1.2 billion, as I recall it. 

Mr. JUDD. $1,250 million, wasn't it?

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right, $1.2 billion. Then the Congress authorized $12 billion for 4 years forward. 

In addition, the Congress had previously appropriated $600 million that were to be used in Latin America: $100 million for Chilean disaster relief and $500 million to the Inter-American Social Progress Fund, of which $100 million is to be administered by the Agency for International Development for grant aid in the fields of education and health, and of which about $400 million was to be administered by the Inter-American Development Bank for soft currency loans in the fields of agriculture and housing, and others as I recall. 

So that, in effect, there was $600 million available on a 2-year basis for Latin America from those $600 million of funds. 

With respect to long-term authorization, there is already authorized $12 billion for this year in development lending. 

We are seeking an appropriation of $14 billion to implement that general loan fund authorization. In a separate title for the Alliance for Progress we are requesting that the Congress authorize a total of $3 billion for 4 years.

We are requesting that $600 million, an amount roughly equivalent to the $600 million that I described before, be appropriated-$90 million for grants and $510 million for development loans, repayable in hard currencies.

The question may well arise- 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Did you say hard currency?

Mr. HAMILTON. Yes, sir; dollars. Long-term loans but hard currency loans.

The question may well arise as to why, in view of the fact that, as I will come to in a moment, we haven't obligated more for the Alliance for Progress-why we are asking you for this longer term very large authorization.

The answer, at least the recommendation that we are making to you, is that that is appropriate and will be helpful for this reason: 

We are running into in Latin America in some areas, of course, resistance on the part of some of the governments to comply with these conditions.

We are endeavoring to take the position with them that we are very serious about these terms and conditions that we believe are necessary to make this alliance work, if it is going to work at all. 

As in any other great enterprise, one has to take account of the possibility of failure in certain areas. We feel that really the advance the alliance has made so far, and this is based on reports-I am not an expert on Latin America; I haven't been to South America since 

I have had this position-they report to us that there is a widespread interest in these countries for the Alliance for Progress, that there are groups in these countries that are enthusiastic and want to work with it.

That is not only from our people but the nine wise men. They are very good, and sort of take the heat off us because they can be tougher with these countries without creating offense in a way than we might. 

We have to stall, but they can come out and tell them. They tell us there is widespread promise and expectation that if we can be resolute and adhere to our programs, not put these moneys out unless there is a compliance with these terms, that at least in some of these countries there will be political support upon the government that

will be strong and persuade them to go along, not in all the countries but some.

What we are really asking for is a bigger size of bait. That is the reason why we make this recommendation.

It is twofold. (1) We think it will dramatize the interest of the 

United States in really working with these Latin American countries if they will work with us; and (2) we think as a result of that they will be more forthcoming in working with us. 

Those are the considerations.

Then we have asked, in addition, for an investment guarantee reserve appropriation of $100 million. We have now authorization for two types of guarantees. 

One is a limited-risk guarantee, to which we have a ceiling of $1 billion we can guarantee, and another is one that was given last year, all risk, which has a $100 million ceiling that we can guarantee, of which $10 million is for pilot housing projects in Latin America. 

But in the second case the person who gets the guarantee has to take 25 percent of the risk.

We have the power to guarantee as to 75 percent of the investment all of the risk. On the limited-risk guarantee, which means convertibility, expropriation and war risks, we can guarantee 100 percent of the investment against those kinds of risks.

For the specific risk guarantees, the amount that has to be appropriated and made available for reserves is placed at a figure of at least 25 percent of the total risk.

Unhappily, so as to speak, what we would like to do is create a climate where nobody would want a guarantee. On personnel we have a problem. It relates to a point that Mr.

together here that can do this complicated problem of investment and trading job.

I don't know. What we are asking for is permission to do two things. The Congress gave the Agency 51 so-called supergrades who can be hired and fired without regard to civil service, and 12 Presidential appointments. We are asking for two things. We are asking that that be increased in number to 150 people who can be hired and fired without civil service.

We are not asking that they all be supergrades, because that supergrade, as I understand it, has to do with the amount of money that you pay the person, if they get more than grade 15, about $15,300. We are asking authority to increase the number of people we can have in this Agency in Washington that can be hired or fired without the civil service, to 150 from 51. Some of those may very well be below the $15,000.

We are also asking for permission to take on Foreign Service Reserve people and keep them here initially for 2 years in Washington. 

This is before they go to the field. 

The Department of State has this and the Peace Corps has it. 

Apparently there is some doubt about whether we have it legally. 

The reason we would like that is because it would give us more administrative flexibility and would enable us to select people to go to the field and give them some training here and get them, particularly younger people, give them a couple of years here before they go out. 

If the committee feels it desirable to put some limit on the number of high ranking Foreign Service Reserves, if you don't want to give us a blank check, we feel we could live all right with a limitation on FSR-1's and FSR-2's of 30 of those.

I have been reminded by my colleague, I should add, if the pay bill doesn't go through, out of the 150 people we are requesting to hire and fire without civil service limitations, we would like to have 125 of those in the supergrade category, which would be an additional request for 75.

tanto, the amount appropriated from other sources under your authorization.

Any organization in the United States, whether it is a labor organization or the University of California or a business, always plans 5 or 10 years ahead, for example, if the university wants to know what the school population is going to be. We do that sort of planning instinctively here. 

Mr. LINGLE. We send special teams to the country for that purpose. 

We have six teams right now to help countries make such plans and so that we can orient ourselves to its plans. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The bill before the committee does not contain a request for supergrades?

Mr. HAMILTON. No; it doesn't, because of the fact that if the proposed Federal Salary Reform Act is passed, that will take care of our requirement for the supergrades. In other words, under the authority the executive branch would have under the President's proposed Salary Act we could obtain these people. The present bill does request that we be able to employ people without regard to civil service. It doesn't set the compensation.

The statute authorized the bringing over of all of those people and all of the assets of ICA into the new agency. But with respect to people, it provided that only those of the 6,300 people could be brought over who were found to be necessary.

Mrs. BOLTON. Why has there been this questioning of your right to do away with 340-odd?

Mr. HAMILTON. I don't think once it has been explained that there was any question as to the power to do it. The organization of Government employees objected very strongly because the statute provided that it should be done without regard to veterans' rights and civil service.

We set up a couple of boards and tried to have as extensive reviews as we could, but the power had to be exercised. Whatever was done had to be done between September 30 and November 4.

Mr. HAMILTON. In the first place, we have had only 10 new mission directors appointed since I came in. Each of the 10 were people with 

Government experience. None were from outside the Government. 

Mr. JUDD. Is that so? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Yes; that is true.

Mr. JUDD. I heard a report the other day to the contrary.

Mr. HAMILTON. As to the 10 that have been appointed, they are people who have all been in the Government. We don't intend to send any new people abroad who have not been in this Agency until they have had a thorough training course and until we have had a chance to look at them and see how they are operating. 

When it comes to the four regional bureaus, the impression that you are reporting is a widespread impression. It is a wrong impression to a substantial extent. Each of the men who is in charge of a region is a man from outside. That is true. But there is no man in charge of a region who has not had very considerable Government experience. Gaud, whom I believe you may have met, had experience out in India and China during World War I. Janow has had extensive experience. He is an independent businessman. Gaud is a lawyer. 

Furthermore I should say Gaud has as his deputy a man who has been in this enterprise for 10 years. Janow has a man as his deputy, a man named Fowler, who has been concerned with ICA for 10 years. 

Moscoso is getting a man from the Foreign Service who has had experience in Latin America and will complement Moscoso in that he knows the Government.

Hutchinson was in business for 22 years. But the rest of his experience has been in Government. 

In respect to the mission appointments, just as with respect to Washington, there have been no wholesale replacements at the top. 

Mr. LINGLE. I was responsible for the Procter & Gamble oversea business for about 15 years, so I have had a good deal of experience of sending people overseas.

I fully appreciate the question that people may have in their minds about businessmen as such coming to the program. I have had experience with businessmen who have no national sensitivity, and I have seen it work the other way as well. 

We are faced with a primary personnel problem here, with people who must have almost a superhuman competence. For example, they have to have a business competence, an economic competence. We are going to have to draw those people, I think, from all sources. 

We need right now about 50 men to fill those positions which are either vacant or have to be replaced within the next 6 months. We are trying to draw those people from all types of business, Government, education, and so forth.

At the present time, of the mission directors, we have only 26 percent who have had any business experience at all. That means working for a company 2 or 3 years.

Mr. LINGLE. That is right.
