Mr. CURTIS. Mr. Administrator, we read that the French have spent a great deal of money on their French-speaking African colonies. Are we also doing much in those same colonies? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Not nearly as much as we are elsewhere. The 

French are spending funds down there largely to help maintain the public services. In many cases, the people they pay, like the people we pay, are their own nationals, people who have been advising governments, maintaining schools, and things of that kind.

Mr. CURTIS. The reason I ask that question is that some of us feel that we are getting a little overextended on this program, reaching 80 countries all over the world. If part of it could be regarded as the duty of others that would certainly help that situation. Mr. HAMILTON. In the French countries, in general, we have small programs which are primarily just to express an interest. 

Mr. CURTIS. I would like to bring up the same question as to former 

British colonies. They have done a lot in Nigeria. Couldn't we properly expect them to carry on development work in their former colonies, and ease up on our own activities there? 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is an interesting and difficult question. I think the British plan to make £200 million available this year. They are putting funds into Nigeria. I don't recall how much. 

Mr. Hutchinson will go into this in more detail. Nigeria is really one of the countries over there that is the strongest and the most promising. We can advance the interest of the United States in political and economic stability in Africa more by contributing to a strong Nigeria than by chopping up the funds and putting them around in smaller amounts in other countries. 

The capacity for Nigeria according to our economic analysis to absorb prudent investment from the standpoint of productive development is sufficiently great so that at least the advice we get is that the expenditure of funds in Nigeria is a prudent investment, despite the fact the British are also putting in substantial amounts. 

Mr. CURTIS. Do you think there is any attitude on the part of other countries that we are trying to take over too much and get into situations which they have been handling in the past? 

Mr. HAMILTON. I think if we pushed into the former French colonies we would promptly meet that reaction. 

The French are very jealous of their cultural influence, of which, of course, you know they are very proud.

In those countries we don't do anything in the way of education, except maybe help them build some buildings. I think the British, on the other hand, feel that their responsibilities are so great in terms of their former colonies that they cannot shoulder them without help. 

They want to maintain a position in India for obvious reasons. They are putting money into Ghana. They are putting money into Tanganyika and the Sudan.

I think they will welcome our participating rather than the reverse. 

We are running into one problem. We afford soft terms on our loan money. As Dr. Judd knows, in the case of the Japanese, they feel one result of our buy American policy, plus this cheap money, is to re-replace them in markets which they regard as traditionally theirs. 

Mr. CURTIS. We pick up the tab for what you call cheap money, which is harder to get back later, and some other countries go in with harder headed propositions. 

Mr. HAMILTON. One of the interesting effects of our having the least expensive money is to force other lending countries down. The 

Germans started with 7 or 8 percent. Now they lend for terms of 1212 years at 212 or 3 percent interest. Recently they made loans that were untied because of the competitive effect of our soft-term loans.

Mr. BARRY. You say you may request a total of 150 supergrades.

Mr. HAMILTON. Supergrades-

Mr. HAMILTON. To some extent, people in the Agency that we would want to promote might be promoted to supergrades, but by far the preponderant part would be new people. With the new developmental emphasis, if you have a really first-rate fellow-in a technical assistance field, for example-on the Nigerian desk, the very qualities of experience that make him good at technical assistance means he probably hasn't had time to develop competence at analysis and administration.

Mr. BARRY. You need a banker-trained individual at the top? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Analyst training. The increased supergrade authority is primarily to get people from outside.

Mr. BARRY. This would be a method of bringing them into your present structure? 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right.

Mr. BARRY. You cannot do it by promotion within-I thought when you first mentioned additional supergrades that is what you needed. I didn't see how a pay raise would do it. 

Mr. HAMILTON. We are asking in this legislation for the authority to engage 150 people without reference to civil service requirements. 

They are not supergrades in the technical sense, as I understand, because a supergrade is one who may or may not be in an exempt position, but who has a salary in excess of $15,300. 

In the first instance we are simply asking for authority to have these jobs that are exempted. We aren't asking for any supergrade authority for those because, if the President's pay increase bill goes through, we will be able to pay 125 of those at the equivalent of supergrade salaries. If the pay bill doesn't go through in substantially its present form, we would ask authority to compensate 125 of the 150 at the supergrade level. 

Mr. BARRY. Those 125 are not presently employed? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Fifty-one are. 

Mr. BARRY. The supergrade? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Yes; 51 of the 125.

Mr. BARRY. You said if the pay raise goes through there would be 

125 that would be at that pay level, but don't they have to be employed to get the raise in pay-or are these job openings? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Job openings that could be filled from below or horizontally. 

Mr. BARRY. How many of the 8,500 are on civil service now? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Of the 8,500, there are 1,700 that you take out because they are on contract.

Mr. BARRY. Is that on a per diem basis or annual basis? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Usually on a term basis. 

Mr. BARRY. That is where you could cut down?

Mr. HAMILTON. We have complete administrative flexibility over them.

Mr. BARRY. How many do you envision that the banker function will require, which is what you are moving into? The whole AID agency is moving toward a great Development Bank. How many do you envision of the 8,500 that you will end up with when you really streamline this thing?

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Lingle suggests, and I am sure he is right, that we don't know. I think some order of magnitude may be gotten on this. I mentioned that 80 percent of the money goes into 24 countries. In each of these countries you would want one very senior person, maybe the mission director, who would have this kind of competence. You would want several programing people in a mission like that. And you would certainly want one or two men who are competent from the engineering standpoint, because we have, as I mentioned earlier, responsibility not only to see that the money comes back but also more importantly to see that the supported project works.

One of the things that you run into with the less developed countries is that they have acute national pride and they want to own things. 

It is not a question of whether a nation owns the project or private enterprise does; they are short of know-how in both the public and private sectors.

I would say that we are talking about at least several hundred persons with such general administrative competence, as an order of magnitude.

Mr. BARRY. What you are really going to set up, which I think is good, is four regional competing banks under your overall administration from the top which will act more or less as a loan committee? 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right. They are fighting for the budget. 

Mr. BARRY. You are going to quickly see one of these take off and do an excellent job, and some of the rest of them may be weak in this or that spot, and you are going to be able to pinpoint the weakness and end up with four working administrations within the AID agency? 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right.

Mr. BARRY. I would then envision a substantial cutback in the 8,500 personnel employed in the United States and since you have almost the corresponding number of foreign nationals working abroad, will this number increase or at least maintain its present size? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Most of those are engaged in clerical functions, bookkeeping, keeping accounts, records, secretaries, and things like that.

The question of what one does on the technical assistance side turns upon the question of how much you contract. Inevitably, I think, if a man is enthusiastic about hybrid corn, and he is an able fellow, and he gets in the government of a country that is interested, once that project is built in it is hard to get it loose. 

We have been trying to curtail a health program in one of the Latin American countries on the ground that it was good but it didn't amount to much, but I have gotten a half dozen letters from the minister of health down there saying what a terrible thing it is to curtail the program.

Mr. BARRY. I think your organization at the executive level is taking on a direction which I think is excellent from the standpoint of industrial management. 

My real concern is integrating 8,500 workers in the field as well as the 8,000 workers right in this country, as well as the problem of the delegation of functions to all those people. 

It seems to me there are too many to properly mobilize behind an effort unless you have an internal management that is unsurpassed. 

I would hate to have to do this in industry where you have an actual product to work with. In our business it is all words, the written word or spoken word. That is all we deal in. 

Would you consider going through your contract personnel now and selecting the ones that have an excellence so that you would be able to assign them as you put each new department into operation? 

Mr. LINGLE. We are certainly planning to address ourselves to that question as rapidly as possible. I have been spending my entire

time in the last month trying to get an understanding of the organizational concept and what our objectives should be in terms of making the organization efficient.

I have been sufficiently consumed at this point trying to get the concept clearly in my mind and understood and trying to make some assessment of the competence of the people that we have here in Washington and filling certain jobs that have not been filled, and trying to get our mission director recruitment program moving-keep it moving, I should say--because it has been moving. 

This question of how we can make the most efficient use of masses of people that we have inherited and what can be done, perhaps with fewer of them. We haven't been able to address ourselves to that question yet.

It will take time. We can't kid ourselves. This is something we can't fix next month or the month after that. We are aware of it. 

I would hope when we come back here next year we would be able to report concretely. 

Mr. BARRY. I would appreciate an interim report. I think we ought to get some kind of progress report of this because this goes to the heart of administration. 

Mr. LINGLE. That is correct.

Mr BARRY. Mr. FARBSTEIN. Will you please tell me how you intend to handle this alliance for progress reform business? Because I read different versions of it in the newspapers. It has been my understanding that reform will be a prerequisite. Then I read in order to get reforms, we will aid various countries to put reforms into effect.

Mr. HAMILTON. I will be delighted to. You can read all sorts of things in the press about the alliance for progress. 

First, let's get in mind, if we may, the total amount of money that has been committed under the alliance for progress by the Agency for International Development since November 4, 1961, which is when it was formed. 

At the outset I should say that the President has said, and Secretary Dillon has said, and of course they are correct, that the United States indicated it would make available $1 billion from March 13, 1961, to March 13, 1962.

That was done partly through a large sum of money from the social progress trust fund, a large sum of money from the Eximbank, a large sum of money on Public Law 480, and $100 million that was committed to Brazil from development loan funds. That makes up a large part of the billion dollars that was made available. 

The $100 million development loan money was a commitment made before Mr. Lingle and I had any responsibility. I don't mean to give the impression at all by that that we wouldn't have made that commitment, but I mean it was before our time. Of that $100 million of foreign aid funds that were committed in that regard, $65 million have been disbursed. 

That $100 million was committed to Brazil. [Security deletion.] 

Since November 4 of last year we have committed to Latin America all available funds, including this $35 million. But we have obligated only about $40 million of the funds that we have committed, because of the fact that our commitments, notably commitments to the Argentine, commitments to Chile, commitments to Colombia, are conditional commitments. 

[Security deletion.]

Mr. FARBSTEIN (continuing). To enter into or make the reforms that you think that country should to survive? 

Mr. HAMILTON. Right. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Once they have accepted that inducing money and commenced with the reforms, you then proceed further. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Installment by installment, taking into account their reform efforts.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. You do not make a payment of a very substantial sum unless this country meets with the preliminary requirements that you set down. 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I think that is a very excellent manner of proceeding, and I want to compliment you, because the impression I got was that in certain instances you would forward the money whether there were reforms or not. But as long as that is a prerequisite- 

Mr. HAMILTON. We have commitments in Latin America of $211 million. Of that amount only about $40 million has been obligated.

STATEMENT ON 621 PROCEDURE 

There follows a communication from Mr. Fowler Hamilton, Administrator, AID, to Mr. Clement J. Zablocki.

Hon. CLEMENT J. ZABLOCKI, 

House of Representatives, Washington, D.C.

DECEMBER 8, 1961. 

DEAR MR. ZABLOCKI: I have your letter of November 28 concerning the procedure the Agency for International Development has followed in implementing the mandate contained in section. 621 of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

For your general information I am enclosing a background statement we prepared for distribution in response to general inquiries from interested people which outlines the legal background and the procedures the Agency has followed. 

Your letter poses questions far more searching than those the general statement is designed to answer, and I am grateful for the opportunity to clarify the 

Agency's position.

I have felt a heavy obligation to abide by the mandate in section 621 of the Foreign Assistance Act and have done my utmost to do so. The congressional intent as you have stated it and as it is stated in the law and legislative history has, in my opinion been fulfilled. It is my earnest hope and my belief that AID is commencing with a revitalized staff adequate to the tasks before it. 

The group which was reviewed by special evaluation boards included approximately 850 people, who, in most instances, had prior performance records on the `basis of regular employee appraisal procedures which placed them in the lowest ranked categories of the civil service and Foreign Service. Their records were reviewed by boards comprised of one person not a regular Government employee, one employee of the Civil Service Commission, and one senior employee of ICA, DLF, or the Department of State. The composition of the boards accordingly was a cross section and not merely an ICA task group. In each case the boards were chaired by a non-ICA person. 

Of the personnel not transferred less than 15 percent were below grade GS-9 or a comparable Foreign Service level. This would constitute the clerical or subclerical personnel to which you refer. The balance were higher level personnel ranging up to our top grades. Most were technicians since most of the 

AID staff are technicians. However, the percentage breakdown between technical and administrative personnel generally parallels the overall staff breakdown indicating that no more technicians were affected than administrative or policy personnel. In this connection I should note that in the 621 procedure 

AID has not considered the records of mission directors, deputy mission directors, and many of our top level staff here in Washington because their appointments are such that they can legally be removed at any time without cause or notice. Many of such people have already left the Agency and separations and demotions will be effected as the reorganization proceeds and as necessary replacements can be found and appointed. 

As a matter of information over 20 percent of the mission directors and deputy directors of ICA have been selected for early separation or demotion and this figure will increase substantially as the result of actions planned over the next few months. When the present reorganization of AID/Washington is completed and the 63 top positions are filled, you will find that competence has been the only criterion for selection or retention. 

In the 60 days between the enactment of the Foreign Assistance Act and November 3, 1961, it was not possible to perform a meaningful review of ICA and DLF personnel and hear their appeals as well. Accordingly, a Review Board was established to review requests from nontransferred employees for employment in AID. Over 200 such requests have been received and it is expected that a final decision will be made on all cases within the next few weeks. 

The Review Board is comprised of men carefully selected for their impartiality, integrity, and background and were authorized to hear any employee or any Agency official they felt could resolve any doubts which might appear: relevant. The Board is chaired by a non-ICA person. Seven persons have. served on the Board, and only two ICA employees participated. Neither of these individuals has ever served in a policy position in Washington, nor have they sat together in the review of cases presented to the Review Board. None of the seven was associated in any manner with the initial screening process. 

I hope these comments are helpful to you in your consideration of the Agency's actions. If you wish to discuss this further in detail I will be happy to discuss

it with you personally or to designate a member of my staff to discuss it with a member of your staff. 

Sincerely yours,

FOWLER HAMILTON. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. On page 6, I think it would be helpful if you could clarify your answer to Mrs. Church, regarding mission directors and their contact 

Mr. HAMILTON. With the Ambassador? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Yes. On page 6, you state—

The chain of communication from Washington through the Ambassador to the AID mission is firmly established so that all U.S. economic and political representatives in foreign countries are now working together as a team, coordinated through the Ambassador.

In reply to Mrs. Church, you said that the Ambassador could not veto the mission director's decision. 

Mr. HAMILTON. That is right.

If there is a communication from Washington, it goes to the Ambassador in the name of the Secretary. It usually says "Rusk to so-and- So,"

If the sender is Mr. Gaud, or some other AID official, we say after that "From Hamilton to," and name our mission director. The cable then goes out from the Department of State to the Ambassador and he is obliged to make-to send it on through to the mission director.

If there is something he doesn't agree with, his statement of disagreement comes back to the Department of State and then comes either to one of my Assistant Administrators or me.

If, on the other hand, the director of the mission wants to communicate with me, he does so through the Ambassador in the sense that the Ambassador always knows what he is saying to me. That is the channel.

The Ambassador cannot block the channel. In other words, if he doesn't agree with the AID mission director, which happens sometimes with honest men having differences of view-the Ambassador will send a cable to me, saying "You just got a cable from the head of the mission. He recommends so and so. I don't believe that his recommendation takes adequate account of the following factors. I think something else ought to be recommended."

If that happens, I usually get the Assistant Administrator for the region and the Assistant Secretary of State for the region together and say "What do you advise?"

When it says "coordinated through the Ambassador," it means that people can't go outside the channel. They can't go around the Ambassador. But on the other hand, the Ambassador can't block the communication. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I am happy to have that clarification.

On page 10 in your prepared statement you refer to the authority contained in section 610 which permits transfer of program funds to meet administrative requirements. You stated that you are now using that authority, and will have to do so in the future. 

Apparently the $55 million will not be adequate for fiscal 1963. 

Would you supply for the record the amount of funds that were transferred under this authority in 1961 and the amount of funds that you anticipate you will transfer in 1962?

Mr. HAMILTON. Yes; we will have a memorandum covering that point.

Washington, D.C.

You both have statements. Which one of you wants to proceed first? 

Mr. MARTIN. Would you care to have me read it? It is short. 

Chairman MORGAN. You may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF HON. EDWIN M. MARTIN, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INTER-AMERICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. MARTIN. Throughout our history special relations have existed between the Governments and people of the United States and those of Latin America. Geographical proximity is only one reason for our special ties. We share a common history of revolt from colonial rule and a common heritage in the quest for dignity and freedom of man.

More than a century ago the Monroe Doctrine focused attention on the special concern of the United States with freedom and security in this hemisphere. Subsequently the good neighbor policy further strengthened our relations with Latin America. 

Cooperation between the United States and Latin America has grown steadily, marked by such events as the Rio Treaty of 1947 to assure the collective security of the hemisphere and by the establishment of the Organization of American States to promote a complex of political, economic, and cultural objectives. Modern technology and economic developments are bringing us closer together into a constantly more intimate neighborhood relationship. 

In times of world crisis Latin America has been our most reliable source of a number of raw materials and other products essential to defense efforts and civilian requirements, for example, petroleum, copper, tin, lead, zinc, drugs, vegetable oils, and animal fibers. 441

Despite the common ties and traditions held by the countries of this hemisphere our southern neighbors have not experienced the steady economic and social progress enjoyed by the United States. Mass poverty and discontent have brought an insistent demand for change and now present a challenge more urgent than the hemisphere has known before.

The Alliance for Progress is our response to this challenge. It signals another great advance in hemispheric cooperation and demonstrates anew our identity of purpose in the quest for dignity, freedom, and security. 

A little more than a year ago President Kennedy proposed thatthe people of the hemisphere join in a new alliance for progress a vast cooperative effort, unparalleled in magnitude and nobility of purpose, to satisfy the basic needs of the American people for home, work and land, health and schools *** Pursuant to the proposal by President Kennedy, the Inter-American Economic and Social Council met in August of last year in Punta del Este, Uruguay, for the purpose of developing policies, principles, and procedures for putting into effect the alliance for progress. 

From this Conference emerged the Charter of Punta del Este a statement of economic and social development policy in Latin America for the decade of the alliance for progress. After full and careful deliberation all member countries, except Cuba, subscribed to the charter.

The Charter of Punta del Este calls for change no less than revolutionary but in an orderly, constructive and democratic manner. In countries with much higher standards of living and more advanced levels of education reforms similar to those foreseen in the alliance for progress have come slowly and by stages. 

In Latin America what should have been done in decades must now be done in years. Time is running short. In carrying out programs under the alliance there will be ever present a strong sense of haste. 

Yet patience too must be observed. In a democratic system issues are thoroughly considered and all factions must be given opportunity to be heard. While progress may be uneven and occasionally be interrupted, and accelerating upward trend is the goal and the firm expectation. 

In addition to efforts of U.S. Government agencies to promote constructive change, the programs and procedures of the various international agencies-such as the Organization of American States and the Inter-American Development Bank-will influence the adoption by Latin American countries of self-help and reform measures. 

In numerous cases international agency opinion and prestige is invaluable in persuading a country to adopt constructive but controversial measures. These agencies have already intensified their efforts to promote the objectives of the alliance for progress. 

Included among these efforts of international agencies are the provision of technical assistance to countries in speeding the preparation of soundly conceived national plans, the establishment by the OAS of a panel of nine experts to review plans and make recommendations concerning both their modification and implementation, and the administration by the IDB of the social progress trust fund pursuant to the conditions indicated in the Act of Bogotá.

In order to facilitate the assessment of performance under the alliance, agreed procedures are now in effect to hold an annual meeting of the Inter-American Economic and Social Council at which the progress and the problems of the period will be considered before ministerial level representatives of all member countries. In this way the performance of each country will be examined both by all other member countries and by international agencies which are participating in the programs. 

In reviewing performance against a development plan the complexity of the country's task must be recognized. No economic development plan can clearly anticipate the future, and consequently all plans must be subject to adjustment in the light of unfolding events. 

Judgments must also take into account emerging political realities. 

While we propose that assistance be extended more readily to those countries who best help themselves, the goal for each country will be the achievement of a steady rate of self-sustaining growth, a rate of growth which requires no external aid other than that extended on conventional terms. 

The Alliance for Progress is designed to create conditions conducive to such growth under free institutions and constitutional processes. 

For the United States the Alliance for Progress represents a much more intimate political contact with the course of events in Latin America than heretofore. We must support and work with groups who cherish democratic values and constitutional government. We must help preserve them in the continuing contests with extremist factions and alien forces.

An immediate danger to constitutional government in Latin America lies in the fact that in few countries are there only two major political parties. Elections are frequently fought out among three, four, or even five parties or factions. For one party to gain a majority of the vote is more often the exception than the rule. 

In contests among several political parties it is possible for an extremist group to gain control of the government without representing the wishes of the majority. It is also possible for such a group, having once reached power and being fearful of free elections, to bring constitutional processes to a prolonged halt. 

The need is to develop more stable political parties which are based not upon personality cults but upon enduring principles of public service and conduct. Among the central political tasks of the Alliance for Progress is the unification of popular support behind groups who can represent the aspirations and the will of the majority, thereby avoiding the loss of free expression and free institutions through fortuitous circumstances.

A guarantee of complete success for the Alliance for Progress cannot be assumed. The alternative, however, to continued and even more resolute efforts is certain political catastrophe in Latin America, a weakening of our historical ties in the hemisphere, and an increased threat to our security. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. 

Mr.

Moscoso, you may proceed, and then we will question you both as a team.

STATEMENT OF HON. TEODORO MOSCOSO, U.S. COORDINATOR FOR THE ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

Mr. Moscoso. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, on 

November 14, 1961, I was appointed Assistant Administrator for Latin 

America of the Agency for International Development (AID). It was then, with Fowler Hamilton previously having been made Administrator of AID, that systematic effort was begun by the principal aidgiving agency of the U.S. Government to address the monumental task of overcoming the obstacles blocking attainment of the goals enunciated by the alliance for progress. 

The Act of Bogotá, signed during former President Eisenhower's administration, President John F. Kennedy's historic speech of March 

13, 1961, and the Charter of Punta del Este, signed last August, had set forth both the goals and purposes for which we were to strive. 

With these in mind, we in AID undertook to build an organization in Washington and attitudes and institutions abroad geared to fulfill the desires of people throughout the Americas for a peaceful, plentiful, free, and democratic hemisphere. 

My remarks here are in some ways a progress report on the 42 months I have been in office as U.S. Coordinator of the Alliance for 

Progress as well as an outline of the problems and actions which I believe lie immediately ahead. 

First, we must be clear on what it is we have undertaken and why. 

As for the latter, it is certain that while our goals for the hemisphere are essentially positive and grow from the traditional good feeling of the people of the United States toward their fellow men to the south, the United States is faced with intractable enemies already too influential in this hemisphere and already constituting a threat to the long-term national security of our country. 

The existence of well-organized Communist groups and an aggressive hemispheric campaign by Fidel Castro are clear and present dangers in a situation where many Latin Americans are searching for solutions to problems long endured but now deemed unbearable. 

It is because of this that the people of the Western Hemisphere cannot be indifferent to the success of the Alliance for Progress. It must succeed. The only questions are as to the best means by which we should proceed and the precise national expressions of the reforms for which we must strive in the quest for Latin American economic and social development and political stability. 

The problems we face in reaching these goals of the Alliance are monumental, both because of the nature of the problems and the high quality of our goals. We have embarked on a program calling on our part for large sums of money and large numbers of first-rate men.

On the part of the Latin Americans, we and they have talked of fundamental social and economic reforms, organizational and financial self-help measures, and long-term planning based on both careful projections and flexible assumptions which would encourage development of dynamic and democratic economies. 

But what are the realities with which we begin? We are attempting to change the direction and results of centuries of Latin American history in a very short time. In most Latin American countries, the

status quo we seek to modify is a polarization between the few who have much and the many who have little. 

These hierarchial societies have been static for many years and indeed it is only recently that they have been touched by the rumblings of change. Political instability is widespread, and even the best of governments is distracted from its developmental tasks by recurring threats to its life as a political unit and în a few cases to the actual lives of its leaders.

With a large rate of illiteracy among the population and a narrow base of educated persons, competent economists, engineers, and administrators to develop the necessary projects and plans are lacking. 

It is to these countries with this instability, this lack of trained human resources, and this history of static development and social immobility that we bring the message of change away from what has been known for hundreds of years to what becomes partially unknown once the process of change begins.

Even in the United States, ours is no easy task. Latin American bureaus of government agencies which hitherto were among the least in their respective departments, are now to be among the most, if not the most, important. Old employees are to be redirected and new employees to be hired with the economic know-how, political insight, organizational technique, and personal perceptivity to direct a smooth running operational agency embracing hundreds of programs and thousands of details.

Furthermore, and especially true for AID, the Agency must respond to countless queries from sources having a right, and in many cases even a duty, to make them.

And it must do this while determining answers to such problems as how it contributes most to the development of agriculture in Brazil and decides how it measures whether a tax reform law in Colombia is adequate, meanwhile dealing with other national and international lending agencies to insure a coordinated program. These are no mean feats.

It is for such reasons that it has been difficult to get the Alliance for Progress moving as rapidly as our office in AID would have liked. 

Furthermore, and not least important, we wish to insure that national development efforts we wish to foster and the means by which we attempt to do so are both realistic and in the long-term interest of the 

United States and Latin America.

We want to be sure that the national "planning" which is done is not such that Latin countries are laced into a straitjacket of dogmatic theory at the expense of a free economy and an open society, for we want democratic initiative and free enterprise functioning vigorously at all levels.

We want to insure that agrarian reform in the long run increases productivity instead of decreasing it. We wish to make certain that the self-help measures we require are both desirable and attainable, lest we press for measures which are not of fundamental importance or whose fruition for practical purposes is impossible. 

We wish to stimulate hope among the people but not at the expense of arousing expectations which cannot be satisfied, thereby increasing the grounds of dissatisfaction on which communism and Castroism can prey.

We must make haste quickly, but not too quickly. We must seek an evolution gradually, but not too gradually. The balancing of these requirements in an area in which 200 million people live in 19 cooperating countries, each of them to some extent different from the others in many respects, is a task whose difficulty you will understand.

I am happy to report good progress in formulating our organizational base in Washington and in the field for the implementation of our program. We have communicated a new attitude and a new set of procedures to the good people we have inherited from the past, we have recruited many fine new employees at all levels through a prodigious effort in which it seemed at times that most of the U.S. 

Government was taking a part, and we are well into a reorganization of the programs and personnel of our field missions. 

This activity continues, but our central organization has taken shape in an amazingly short time. Moreover, our relationships with the other aid-giving agencies grow increasingly tight and more cooperative, in part as a result of the interagency Alliance for Progress Committee, of which I am Chairman. 

We have fulfilled our commitment, extended to show the extent and seriousness of our purpose, to contribute $1 billion to Latin American development during the first 12 months of the Alliance. The largest dollar amount, $401,599,000, was made through the Latin American bureau of AID. Next highest was the $360,604,000 from the Export-Import Bank. Additional commitments were made totaling $129,682,000 through the social progress trust fund administered by the Inter-American Development Bank and $135,795,000 under the food-for-peace program from sales and grants of surplus_commodities. Other assistance, including Peace Corps activity in Latin 

America, totaled $1,896,000. 

It is particularly gratifying to me that most of these funds were committed as loans and not as grants. Some 87 percent is in development loans, while only 13 percent is in the form of grants. 

As for Latin American progress under the Alliance for Progress,. there is some cause for satisfaction-but satisfaction there is not. We cannot be satisfied when so little has happened in relation to what must happen and when continued dissatisfaction and impatience at the rate of change and growth is necessary on our part as a stimulant to the performance of the Latin American governments involved. This is not to say that meaningful progress has not been made. For example: (a) In Colombia, a progressive tax reform law was passed in 1960, and in 1961 an agrarian reform law was approved and a 10-year national development plan completed. (b) In Bolivia, the Government granted 71,000 land titles to smallscale farmers since August of 1960 under a stepped-up agrarian reform program. (c) In Brazil, the National Government took cognizance for the first time of its responsibility in the northeast region of the country and allocated $100 million as its first year contribution to a 5-year development plan for that region. (d) In Venezuela, the Government's 1960 land reform program has resettled 40,000 families, and its education program expanded its primary and secondary school enrollment to well over 50 percent since 1958.

(e) In Peru, the Government's stabilization program, begun in 1959, successfully reduced a soaring growth of inflation to a rate of 

4 percent last year.

Other examples could be cited, but the most accurate measure of self-help is no single governmental act or law but rather the total posture of a government in the light of the total assets available to it as against the economic and political problems in its path. 

Thus, to determine accurately whether a nation is engaged in selfhelp, we must judge the full range of its actions in the light of both its ability and its inability to attain the ends desired and of its will to make progress toward these ends.. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. Moscoso. If we are able to give our truest friends in the various countries this assistance in convincing their confreres of the necessity of change and of the intention of the United States to render assistance only on the basis of genuine self-help, we will strengthen democratic forces in these countries and give them tools they badly need. 

We should understand as well that few, if any, Latin governments would regard themselves as being opposed to self-help, and we must, to some extent, take their views into consideration. 

Some officials in these governments genuinely are convinced that one change would lead to another and thence to violent upheaval which would sweep away stable and anti-Communist governments. 

Others would like to address themselves to the process of reform but are almost fully occupied fighting for their political lives through a process of recurring crises. [Security deletion.] 

We must attempt to make them see the way in which change can be brought about gradually, without violent revolution, and we must aid them in fending off the short-range crises which prevent long-term development.

We have also to induce self-help with the instruments of training and education. Too many countries are presently bereft of the governmental administrators, economic analysts, and engineers who are necessary to undertake the practical process of determining basic needs, setting clear priorities, and taking effective measures against their problems.

The lack of trained and able human resources is a gaping need in the development requirements of all Latin American countries. The imposition of conditions and threats and the pronouncement of lectures to governments will not solve this problem. In this case, the selfhelp required must grow out of technical assistance, training, and education.

In the last analysis, it will be with these mixtures of patient understanding and impatient importuning, of slow circumvention and swift direct action, and of short-term measures and long-term programs that we hope the nations of Latin America may be moved to help themselves to a reasonable extent and thus enable them to use and use well the men, money, and material which we can make available. 

The tactics we will utilize will vary but our underlying purpose must be clear: our action must fit a strategy of economic and social development leading to political stability for the United States of America and her neighbors in this hemisphere.

Before leaving this brief discussion of central concepts which guide our approach, I want to stress one matter I mentioned earlier: the importance we attach to the development of vital private enterprise in Latin America. We have in mind both the protection and stimulation of U.S. and other foreign investment which contributes critically to the growth of these countries and the encouragement of an environment conducive to the development of homegrown private enterprise as the basis for a dynamic economy and for local initiative which does not wait on direction from the top of a governmental pyramid. 

You will hear much of this as our program proceeds. 

With all of the foregoing in mind, what do we ask of you this year to equip us for this tremendous task? 

The President has proposed an authorization of $3 billion for the alliance for progress for the next 3 years. Why is this necessary? 

In Latin America, where we are undertaking strenuous efforts to encourage long-range planning and long-term development plans, the ability of the United States to make forward commitments subject to future appropriations of the Congress is vital. 

When these countries obtain such a commitment, they will understand that the U.S. Congress, as well as the executive branch, is supporting the long-term development of our Latin American neighbors. 

This special authority is being requested so that we can clearly identify the source of authorization and appropriation for the alliance for progress. 

For fiscal year 1963 the President's request contains an authorization for appropriations of $600 million within the $3 billion authorization request. These funds will be utilized primarily for long-term development assistance on a loan basis. However, conditions remain where grant assistance, principally for technical assistance projects, continues to be necessary. We have therefore programed in the form of grant aid $90 million of the $600 million requested. Our policy is to continue to emphasize loans rather than grants. 

In addition, we are requesting for Haiti, Bolivia, and the Eastern Caribbean $15 million for supporting assistance. [Security deletion.] 

The amount requested for fiscal year 1963 assumes generally improved economic and political conditions in the recipients of such assistance, and therefore supporting assistance has been drastically reduced from previous years. 

It is also assumed that if the volatile situation in Latin America erupts, an increase of supporting assistance will be needed from the funds in the contingency appropriation. 

It may be questioned why, with a low rate of obligations in fiscal year 1962, additional funds are necessary. The low rate of obligations is the result of the careful review and screening of proposals prepared under the old and new criteria, new organization and new personnel. 

We have been proceeding prudently in committing our funds. 

Although the total obligations of grant and loan funds are relatively low, plans and programs now have been approved which utilize the major portion of funds available for obligation. 

Negotiations are underway for these projects and programs and we estimate that if these funds are not obligated by the end of the year—the funds are, for the most part, "no year" funds-the projects

will be implemented in the next fiscal year. This particular funding situation has been taken into account in the development of the fiscal year 1963 proposals. 

We believe that with these resources, with their effective employment by us in a many-faceted approach to a complex series of problems, with your cooperation in maintaining our posture that the U.S. 

Government is both seriously interested in the development of Latin America and seriously disposed to continue its aid only if self-help measures are present, and with luck, we can return next year with a year of solid progress in building the Alliance behind us and more importantly, a year closer to the general security and well-being of the people of the United States and Latin America.

Mr. Moscoso, I want to say first that I have a great deal of confidence in you and appreciate very much your presentation here. Mr. Moscoso. Yes, Mr. Congressman, I think that is a good question. The nine wise men, as you know, have just gotten themselves organized in January. They are starting to set down guidelines. 

These experts from Latin America-there is one from Europe and one from the United States-these nine wise men know Latin America very well. They feel like we do about the need for reforms. They know their economies.

They are aware of the political realities and they know how fast some of these countries are moving in performing these reforms. We will give great weight to their recommendations. They are not going to be the ones who will have the ultimate say on the use of our funds. 

We will have to do so, because the responsibility has been placed upon us by the Congress and the Executive. They will be able to make these reviews and make recommendations as to the speed in which these reforms have been made. So their annual review is going to be extremely valuable.

Mr. Congressman, I believe that they are going to be very tough about the countries that can perform and do not perform. 

Mr. BURLESON. [Security deletion.] 

Mr. Moscoso. No, this is a decision that we will have to take ourselves. The Congress will participate in this obviously because of the decisions that will have to be made every year to support the program.

There is another one on tax reforms, plus the one that the Inter-American Bank has prepared. We are going to have these reports for you gentlemen to see and to assess how much progress has been made. 

Mr. BURLESON. How would you help us answer this question? Are we going to give aid to those nations who failed to go all the way with us at the Punta del Este Conference? Mexico, Brazil, and Argentina, amounting to 65 percent of the population of Latin America, with the other three probably accounting for another 15 or 20 percent of the population-do we treat them in the same manner as those which fully supported the U.S. position? 

Dr. Judd referred to this matter of our coming into the picture and becoming concerned post-Castro. Whether before or after, our concern is against the spread of Castroism in Latin America. We are trying to get solidarity in the Western Hemisphere and if they don't do it at Punta del Este, what can we expect? Are they going along with us in the opposition to communism? I suppose that is on the end of all our efforts. If it is not, it certainly should be. 

Mr. Moscoso. Mr. Congressman, you will recall at Punta del Este two very important resolutions were approved unanimously, except of course for the Cubans who voted against them. One was the resolution which said that communism is incompatible with the American system. This is a very definite principle. 

The second one was that Cuba is Communist-dominated. Insofar as the method of getting Cuba out of the Organization of American States is concerned, there were all kinds of juridical arguments for

and against. Some of them were so fine that quite frankly it takes a much better man than any group of lawyers that I know of to understand some of these arguments, but it also requires knowledge of the Latin American juridical mind to know how they can think in those terms.

One of the reasons is this: When the Organization of American 

States was set up, no one thought of the possibility of someone having to be thrown out of the Organization, so no procedure was set for impeachment, if you want to call it, of a nation. In the principal resolution which was to say that communism is absolutely incompatible with the American system, and that Cuba was Communistdominated, they went along 100 percent.

Mr. ADAIR. Both parts of the question?

As you are aware, we have announced and are about to complete, I believe, an arrangement which I believe is consistent with the congressional intent as it was expressed to me at that meeting. I concurred fully in the Department of Agriculture actions which have taken place in the last 2 or 3 months on that particular question. 

Mr. ADAIR. Mr. Moscoso, at the bottom of page 9 on your statement, the fourth line up, "We have in mind both the protection and stimulation of United States and other foreign investment which contributes critically to the growth of these countries." 

You and I have talked about the Rio Grande do Sul incident.

What specific measures do you have in mind to implement that statement?

Mr. Moscoso. Mr. Congressman, one of the things that I believe we are going to have to do in our agency with the assistance of the private sector of the United States is to give technical assistance and support to local private industry in the Latin American countries themselves. 

There has been a disenchantment in many instances in Latin America with the way private industry has operated in those countries, and somehow or other they have equated that disenchantment with private industry in the United States.

I was a witness to that in Venezuela. We have information to the effect that whereas the workers in Venezuela had a preference for working for American firms, they did not like to work for Venezuelan firms. 

Why? For a number of reasons. The social awareness of the average businessman in the United States is lacking in many instances in

Latin America in business. The willingness to participate in the cost of government; their unwillingness of Latin American businessmen to go into those things which would do the most to develop their countries; their propensity to invest in things in which a big profit can be made, speculative real estate operations, and so forth. 

All of those things have weakened the posture of the Latin American private sector to such a point that I believe sincerely, Mr. Congressman, we are going to have to assist them just like we give technical assistance to a government that doesn't know how to run a budget or run a plan or program, doesn't know how to run a personnel system. 

Insofar as our business concerns-insofar as American investments are concerned, I know the Congressman's preoccupation with what happened at Rio Grande do Sul [security deletion]. 

We are in constant communication with these people. I sincerely believe, Mr. Congressman, that there isn't enough money in any of the government agencies, not only of the United States, but the free world and all the international institutions of credit, to do the developmental job that has to be done in Latin America or in the underdeveloped countries of the world. The private sector has to come into the picture if we don't create an investment climate. 

Mr. ADAIR. You said earlier today that you thought that aid should be withheld if these countries didn't undertake the proper programs. 

Would you think that aid should be withheld if they do not make proper payment for expropriated private properties?

Mr. Moscoso. Those are the kinds of things, Mr. Congressman, that would have to go through the courts to see what is proper compensation. As I understand it, you can deposit a certain amount in court for a property once it is expropriated, and I think everyone realizes that in the case of a public utility that may happen, and then it is a question for the courts to make a decision as to what the proper value of those properties are.

You will recall, Mr. Congressman, we had an incident like this in the case of Mexico quite a number of years ago. The case was finally resolved, payments have been made, and as I understand it, just a few days ago the final payments were made. 

I think that those are the kinds of things we have to be thinking about. 

Mr. ADAIR. Thank you.

Alliance for Progress?

Mr. Moscoso. A very important role, Mrs. Kelly, a major role, both here and in Latin America itself. We must try to distinguish between the two.

As I said before, the private sector of the United States is a very vigorous sector.

In the case of Latin America, the private sector is a weak sector. 

If we don't do enough for it and stimulate it enough, we will find ourselves with a group of socialist countries. We must be sure that this private sector is assisted in the same way that we try to assist the governments.

We try to help the governments have a good bureaucracy. We try to train their bureaucrats so they do a good job of budgeting, planning, personnel organization. We try to assure ourselves that they even know how to collect taxes. We also have to do a job with the private sector. We must teach them about productivity. 

You will recall that one of the great things about the Marshall plan was how we went into Europe and increased productivity through productivity centers.

Mrs. KELLY. You are talking about private enterprise? 

Mr. Moscoso. Yes.

Mr. Moscoso. We have the investment guarantee program.

Mr. Moscoso. Yes. I think we are going to have to undertake a major job of reinforcing private enterprise in Latin America. 

One of the ways I hope we can do so is organize touring teams of American businessmen who will go down to Latin America in an organized fashion and convince them that they have to take an entirely different stance toward their civic duties in each one of these countries, so that in turn the popular masses will start to feel differently toward private enterprise.

Mrs. Kelly, you will recall in 1929, 1930, 1931, 1932, we had a problem here in the United States with regard to private enterprise. All of a sudden it fell in disrepute, and a major job had to be done to build it up again in the eyes of our own people here. 

In Latin America it is much worse than we had here in 1929 or 1930.

Mrs. BOLTON. We had the good neighbor policy. What happened to it?

Mr. Moscoso. That's another- 

Mrs. KELLY. I didn't yield. I want you to finish your response. 

Mr. Moscoso. I didn't hear that. 

Mrs. KELLY. I wanted you to finish on that. 

Mr. Moscoso. I believe the job can be done, Mrs. Kelly. I believe an example can be of great use here. It can be done if the businessmen of the United States undertake a job of proselytizing, of convincing these people that they must save their own system, the system in which they say they believe, but they must show faith in that system by doing the kinds of things that are expected from the system, which is to take risks, take small profits, and yet create large volumes. 

Those are the kinds of things, Mrs. Kelly, I think will have to be brought to the minds of the private businessmen in Latin America if we are going to bolster them and help make that system survive there.

As far as the U.S. citizen is concerned, I think it will be much easier for them to have a fruitful experience in Latin America if first they try to establish joint ventures down there, if they try to bring in local national people into the ownership of the corporation. 

There is a very excellent example of a corporation operating now in Brazil and in Argentina, a very major corporation, which has sold a substantial part of its shares of stock to local nationals. 

Mrs. Kelly, I believe that their ability to get along there has been enhanced tremendously. They are probably more secure in their investment than if they had gotten investment guarantees from AID.

TAX REFORM IN LATIN AMERICA SINCE ACT OF BOGOTÁ INTRODUCTION 

In the Act of Bogotá (signed September 13, 1960, and approved by the Council of the Organization of American States on October 11, 1960), it was recognized that steps had already been taken by many of the American Republics to cope with the serious economic and social problems that confronted them. The act also recognized that the success of a comprehensive program of economic and social progress would require maximum self-help efforts and, in many cases, the improvement of existing institutions and practices, among other fields, in the field of taxation.

The act specifically included as recommended action for social improvement, and as considered appropriate in each country: 

1. In connection with rural living and land use (a) The examination of "tax systems and procedures and fiscal policies with a view of assuring equity of taxation and encouraging improved use of land, especially of privately owned land which is idle," and (b) The provision of "increased incentives (to the furtherance of the objectives of the act) in the land tax structure," and 2. In connection with the mobilization of domestic resources— 

The examination of "the equity and effectiveness of existing tax schedules, assessment practices, and collection procedures," "with a view to providing additional revenue for the purpose of this program." 

The Declaration to the Peoples of America, issued incident to the adoption of the Charter of Punta del Este, states, as one of the basic goals of the alliance for progress, work directed: "To reform tax laws, demanding more from those who have most, to punish tax evasion severely, and to redistribute the national income in order to benefit those who are most in need, while, at the same time, promoting savings and investment and reinvestment of capital." 

Section 201 of the Act for International Development of 1961 of the United 

States provides in connection with the establishment of the Development Loan 

Fund and with its use: 

****The President shall take into account * ** (5) The extent to which the recipient country is showing a responsiveness to the vital economic, political, and social concerns of its people, and demonstrating a clear determination to 

(In connection with the authorization of "Development grants and technical cooperation," a similar instruction is provided, in this case including the following additional clause: “*** and a willingness to pay a fair share of the costs of programs under 

*.") 

Section 618, in referring to economic assistance to Latin America, states specifically that such aid shall be furnished in accordance with the principles of the Act of Bogotá.

It is the purpose of this presentation to evaluate the progress of tax reform as defined above and as made in the Latin American countries since the date of the signing of the Act of Bogotá. 

Progress of tax reform—generally

Before examining the question of tax reform on a country-by-country basis, certain comments applicable to all countries as regards the question of tax reform in Latin America are necessary. 

As indicated in the Act of Bogotá itself, self-improvement steps, including some of a tax reform nature, were taken by several of the countries shortly prior to the adoption of the act. In particular, in several countries, significant tax reform legislation was enacted in 1958 or 1959. These enactments can be considered as directly allied with and as part of the same movement that gave rise to the Act of Bogotá itself. As such, they can be considered with the measures that have been taken by many countries, including these countries, since September 1960 for purposes of evaluating tax reform as a self-help measure in a context of planned, democratic, economic development. 

Second, it is recognized in the Act of Bogotá that, even as of September 1960, the need for tax reform was a need that varied from country to country. 

Third, it is recognized that tax reform is subsidiary to, and is only an aspect of, the broader question of improvement in fiscal policy generally. This area includes, for example, and most importantly in Latin America, questions relating to the control and administration of expenditures. It also includes, among others, questions relating to budgetary practices, and those relating to the control of inflation and to the use of fiscal policy in promoting private investment.

Fourth, certain constructive statements of the objectives of tax reform are set forth in the above documents. They can be restated as follows: 

1. Incentives are to be provided in the land tax structure to assure equity of taxation and encourage the improved use of land; 

2. Additional revenue is to be provided; 

3. Savings and the investment of capital is to be promoted; and 

4. "Equity of taxation” is to be assured. "Equity of taxation” is defined as: (a) the "demanding of more from those who have most"; (b) the examination of tax procedures; and (c) the punishment of tax evasion. 

It has been agreed between the member states that study needed to be given to the methods to be adopted that would best promote all of these goals. Thus 

Appended Resolution A-3 to the Charter of Punta del Este recommends participation by the member states in the program then being developed for the carrying on of this study. The resolution specifically contemplates the holding of two conferences, one on tax administration, in 1961, and the other, on tax policy, in 1962. 

The first of these conferences has been held. It was held in October 1961, at 

Buenos Aires, and was attended by leading officials and experts from the member countries as well as by observers from the sponsoring international organizations, speakers, participants, and others. The Assistant Secretary of the Treasury of the United States and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Mr. Caplin, were in attendance from the United States. 

The subjects covered at this conference were broad and were as follows: 

Methodology for Measurement and Study of Tax Burdens. 

Statistical Records and Their Use in Tax Administration. 

Data Processing. 

Management and Organization Techniques. 

Accounting, Auditing, and Knowledge of Business Practices. 

Taxpayer Relations and Other Compliance Problems. 

Problems in Administering Property Taxes. 

Sales and Excise Taxes. 

The conference on tax policy set for 1962 has not yet been held. 

A first goal of tax reform is, as indicated, the raising of greater domestic revenue, certainly in cases where present levels are inadequate. (The amount raised would, presumably, given proper administrative and governmental practices, be made available by the governments for capital formation and for other economic development purposes.)

The clearest measure of the effectiveness in any country of reform directed to this goal would be that country's record of collections under the reform. 

Table I below shows, for all countries and as of one fiscal year, on a comparative basis, the revenue-raising effort of each country. This is done by reference to the gross national product of the country and by the use of a percentage figure to describe the relationship of the domestic national revenues of that country to its gross national product. By going one step further, as is done in the country sections below, and by comparing the figures for each country separately for several years, the accomplishment of that country in revenue-raising reform can be evaluated. 

However, in evaluating reform for as short and as recent a period as the past year and a half-i.e., the task attempted in this presentation-the revenues received figures have not yet had a chance fairly to reflect any reform action that may have been taken. Projected estimates of revenue to be received must, therefore, be looked to and, unsatisfactory as they are, they become the only means of measuring accomplishment toward this goal. 

In table I the countries are arranged in order of per capita gross national product. This has been done since it is agreed upon among economists that a country's capacity for tax reform, whatever the need may be, is associated with per capita GNP, certainly where that figure is low. 

Table I also sets forth certain pertinent data of an informational nature bearing on the present rate of capital formation in each country. Where the rate is low it is to be noted that its improvement, as affected by taxes, is one of the stated goals of tax reform.

The goal of substantive tax reform that deals with the equitable distribution of the tax burden as between rich and poor is discussed herein primarily on a country-by-country basis. However, in the case of each country, and to the extent of available information, total revenue receipts can be broken down by each of the major taxes. The character of those taxes (as indirect and often falling on the poor, or as direct and borne by those best able to bear them) and the distribution of the tax yield as between them, can then be looked to in examining this goal. Trends from year to year (and even by groups of years where there are marked economic changes in such period) define the character of the changes, if any, put into effect by that country. 

Information as to all countries (applicable, however, only to 1 year, and to taxes in only the broadest of groupings) is set forth in table II. From this information certain generalizations can be made that are pertinent to a discussion of tax reform on an overall basis. 

First, with the exception of Colombia and Peru which are the two highest, it will be noted that the percentage derived from income taxes drops as one goes down the list of countries, and that it does so almost steadily, thereby paralleling the decreasing per capita gross national product pursuant to which the countries have been arranged. 

Second, it will be noted that the Central American countries are in a class by themselves as compared to the other countries as regards the emphasis placed on customs revenues of various types. However, except for Venezuela (and, possibly, also Peru, Paraguay, and Chile), the dependence on that source of revenue in all of the countries is high. 

Third, and except for Colombia, the revenue importance placed on indirect taxation (other than customs) is also generally conceded to be disproportionately high.

It appears from sources other than the above table that property and land-use taxation is, in most countries, not up to date, either in its structure, in its enforcement, in its relationship to the use of the land, or as to the assessment valuation methods or cadastral type of knowledge used in its determination. It is certainly not used as a major revenue-raising device. More important, until recently it has not been used as a social reform device.

A very rough summary of major actions taken by the countries in the tax area to date is set forth in table III. The changes noted in table III are the more important of the specific changes that have taken place in the particular countries. They, together with other and less important changes, are described at length of the country-by-country sections below. 

While there has been much action taken in the tax area, not all of this action can be considered to be of a tax reform nature. Indeed, many of the regressive sales and other use taxes and customs levies have often been increased in the last year and one-half, with a resulting increase in the burdens carried by sections of the population least able to do so. These changes may, it is true, increase revenues, thereby satisfying what has been stated above as being one of the basic reform criteria. But it is apparent that that is not enough. 

The real question is how the revenues are increased. At the least, as is the case in some countries, if increased, they can be increased in such a way as not to hurt the other objectives of tax reform.

Further, the accomplishment of tax reform must be measured, not only against the need, but also in terms of the country's ability best to meet that need. Thus, the making of one type of structural change might be actually detrimental if the need of the country was for a change of a different type. Similarly, the enactment of a poorly studied or of a hurriedly drafted law would not be reform, certainly of a permanent nature, where care might have produced a different result. The forces for economic and political unrest that even the slightest tax change can unleash are such that they should not be tampered with except for good, or even for the best of sufficient reasons. 

Tax administration

In Latin American the procedures and personnel practices in use in the tax and customs administration field are generally not as advanced as those in, for example, the United States.

In terms of impact on the revenues, and working from a pre-Act of Bogotá base, the revenue potential of reform in tax administration, i.e., in the workings of the Governments' tax collection procedures, is probably as important an ele-

ment in tax correction as the effect to be derived from changes in tax structure. 

In social terms, furthermore, since many of the inadequacies of the present tax administrative picture are in enforcement and since that means collection from the wealthier portions of the community, changes here also contribute to social reform.

The basic steps needed in the effecting of reform in tax administration as such are procedural, such as the institution of adequate training programs, the institution of up-to-date processing techniques, etc. On the other hand, the correction of problems raised by the generally existing and even obvious defects in personnel practices and in the meeting of personnel standards has political overtones that in most countries go beyond the tax field. 

The establishment of some of the necessary tools to accepted standards of auditing practices and to adequate enforcement will often require legislative change.

One of the most basic defects in both the administration and enforcement field is the underlying lack of confidence of the taxpayer in the stability of his Government and in the use to which it will put his money. This question is not subject to attack by tax reform, either structural or in administration. Its correction can only be achieved through a mounting of all of the forces of the 

Alliance for Progress.

The details of the problems and of the needs in any given country can only be examined country by country and then only, in this paper, in the most general terms.

By way of summary as to accomplishment, it can be stated that most of the Latin American countries are taking action with respect to their most obvious administrative inadequacies.

On the other hand, steps leading to enforcement against nontaxpaying groups are generally not receiving a comparable degree of attention. 

Lastly, assessment procedures and other practices bearing on the taxation of land and its use are receiving attention. Some countries are going ahead with the undertaking of the necessary surveys, cadastral and otherwise. Conclusion

In presenting certain of these overall reform objectives, it is recognized that many major internal problems and issues must be resolved in each country in the course of progress. 

Further, tax reform is being carried out by these countries in the context of other changes specifically referred to, for example, in the Act for International Development, namely, of a social, political, and economic variety, all of which changes are, in turn, part of and contributory to an accomplishment of the overall economic development of a particular country. 

A final aspect of tax reform is its continuing nature in the context of a, hopefully, rapidly changing economic development picture in the country concerned. 

Thus, at a different stage of development different objectives become appropriate and, as a result, different tax measures or emphases on tax measures may be required.

The ultimate criterion in the success of a tax reform program is the political forum of the electorate.

On the other hand, a continuing hemispheric interest in tax reform, both in its structural and in its administrative aspects, will result in the development of knowledge, of patterns of action in the different countries based thereon, and of forces for progress as between countries. In so doing, it will result in the area of controversy being materially reduced.

1. Introduction ARGENTINA 

With the population of 21,445,000, the per capita gross national product is $526. The literacy rate in Argentina is 86 percent, the highest in Latin America. 

Argentina had a developed economic structure during the 1930's and this structure is sufficiently intact to afford a base. Self-sustained economic growth is achievable.

2. Nature of the tax system

Domestic source revenue is 15.6 percent of gross national product. The bulk of the revenue in Argentina is national; 29.3 percent of 1961 revenue came from direct taxes; 32.7 percent sales and other indirect taxes, and 32.1 percent from customs levies. An income tax was first enacted in 1932. 

Tax bills were submitted to the legislature on January 12, 1960, designed to accomplish three primary objectives: (1) to permit more rigorous enforcement (thereby hopefully collecting up to 5 billion pesos per year); (2) to provide new stimuli for investment (such as better depreciation provisions, better net operating loss carryovers and granting exemption on interest and dividends from certain certified companies), and (3) to raise personal exemptions to reflect the inflation, with increases in other taxes designed to offset the loss in revenue, including income tax on corporations (with a 3-percent rise). 

The law in question was passed and was published in the Boletin Oficial of 

February 19, 1960.

Separate laws would include (a) A reduction of import surcharges in January 1960. The action, however, was expected to result in an increase of imports, raising 5 billion pesos in new revenue. (b) Law No. 15272 of February 15, 1960, permitting the reevaluation of assets to compensate for the effects of inflation. (c) Decree No. 2120, published March 5, 1960, dealing with the collection at source of the 8-percent sales taxes on exports. The action was devised to cut down on evasion. (This law was superseded by decree No. 3696 of 

April 8, published on April 16, 1960.)

Professors Surrey and Oldman of Harvard Law School, financed by the Ford Foundation, made a survey of the Argentine tax system and its administration in May and June 1960. Their report dealt largely with the problem of administration. The survey was prompted by governmental interest in the problem. 

To the extent that it dealt with systems, the survey clearly indicated that adequate study might suggest conclusions somewhat different from those that might be arrived at lacking such a study. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

In December 1960, the Government manifested an interest in entering into a tax convention with the United States to avoid double taxation. 

Law No. 15798, promulgated January 10, 1961, made a number of changes in the tax laws, the most important being an increase in the rate of the sales tax from 8 to 10 percent, effective March 1, 1960. Certain procedural provisions were also included. 

On June 14, Decree No. 4780 promulgated a unified tax system for the stamp tax laws.

In October 1961, the sales tax on exports of grain was eliminated. 

From June through October, five specific decrees dealing with special problems were issued, designed to stimulate private investment. Similarly, in May an investment guarantee agreement was ratified. 

A tax reform bill of wide coverage was passed in February 1962. It is designed primarily to plug loopholes and to make collections easier. It does not implement the Surrey report but uses its recommendations, if only in part. 

5. Tax administration

Dr. Manuel Rapoport, the "Interventor" (the official in charge of administrative improvement) visited the United States and Canada in April and May. He has since carried out an extensive reform of the tax administration organization. 

As a first step, the tax office was reorganized into a series of district and regional offices, with the central office being concerned primarily with policy, direction, and review. An inspection corps has been established. Courses are being established to explain the new system and train employees. 

An advisory council of representatives of industry, agriculture, commerce, and other fields meets once a week with the director of the general tax office to express the views of major taxpaying segments of the population. 1 A campaign to encourage voluntary compliance was started in June 1961 and still continues. 81496-62-pt. 3——7

In the area of collections, the first efforts were directed against the large tax arrearages. Another effort is aimed at eliminating taxes that cost more to administer than they bring in; as a first step, stamps on various types of official documents were eliminated in February 1962. 

The tax reform bill passed in February 1962 reduced the previously prescribed penalties to a realistic level and with a view to their being enforced as reduced. 

It also permits the closing of a business for 5 days for repeated violations of the sales tax law.

Starting March 1962 the names of persons convicted of tax fraud will be publicized. 

The next major move is expected to be the acquisition of new mechanical equipment, possibly automatic data processing, to speed up processing by replacing present euipment which is from 15 to 25 years old.
