As a result of the above interest of the Government, revenue collections in 1961 showed a marked improvement over 1960. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

Committees have been established to study- (a) Tax procedures. (b) Possible adjustments in the tax burdens. (c) Federal-State-municipal agreements to avoid double taxation. (In April 1960 a 1-year agreement was entered into between the Federal Capital and 14 provinces with respect to taxes on capital gains.) (d) The elimination of small taxes the collection of which is costly. 

BOLIVIA 1. Introduction 

Based on a population of 3,600,000, the per capita gross national product is $95. 

With Paraguay (and without reference to the Caribbean area) this is the lowest in Latin America.

Bolivia is the outstanding country in the hemisphere, in one respect, in that it has already had (in 1952) a fundamental social and political revolution. Furthermore, it has one of the first long-range development plans to be formulated and to be submitted to the so-called nine wise men. On the other hand, the country's infrastructure is inadequate. Without external assistance the country is unable to develop its resources. After a period of disastrous inflation, Bolivia undertook in 1957, with the assistance of the IMF and the United States, a stabilization program. While limited success has been achieved in the area of currency stabilization, economic development has stagnated and a large part of the country's industrial capacity is unutilized. 

2. Nature of tax system

Taxes are at 13.6 percent of gross national product. Of the total, customs levies account for over 50 percent, and sales, turnover, and excise taxes account for another 23 percent.

The country has been working on tax reform since 1952, but, with the exception of customs collections, has achieved only minimum results. Essentially the tax system has been the same since 1940. There are a multiplicity of often conflicting and unproductive taxes and, as in many countries, a confusing diversity in taxing authority. 

3. Tax reform prior to Bogotȧ 

In 1958, the rate of tax on gains arising from the sale of real estate was reduced from 24 to 8 percent, it being recognized that the previous rate was unrealistically high and that it gave rise to evasion practices. The fact that collections from this source have remained level despite the reduction supports the theory of the change. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

In February 1961, pursuant to a special ministerial resolution, a tax reform study was inaugurated under the sponsorship and with the advice of ECLA, TAO, and FAO. It was pointed toward the adoption of a tax code and to the development of new revenue sources that could be tapped without conflict with the purpose of the Alliance for Progress. 

In June 1961, a revised customs code was enacted pointed toward greater workability by the administrative forces. The principal change was the adoption of the so-called Brussels nomenclature

A first draft of the tax code referred to above was in hand on July 1, 1961. 

The mere fact of codification is recognized as beneficial. In addition, a number of useful changes are incorporated. The most significant relates to agricultural taxes as to which there is substituted for the existing production tax in the case of all products but cocoa, a so-called rural land tax. It is estimated to produce $4 million annually. A number of nuisance taxes are dropped. 

A second stage of development is planned in 1962. Thus, there is a question as to the treatment of urban realty. It is also recognized that there is a need for further statistics and study before changes can be made in the rate structures and levels of the income tax. 

On July 20, 1961, an agreement with respect to customs was signed with a British team providing for the furnishing of a chief (for 13 months) and of a five-member team (for 7 months) to study, recommend changes and implement them, with a view to doubling collections from that source. The project is 

United States and Bolivia financed.

By supreme decree, dated January 19, 1962, a national tax commission was established, the significance of tax reform thereby being reemphasized. 

Plans are in hand for reorganizing land title registration, presumably converting the same into a Torrens system. 

5. Tax administration

Starting in 1960, five U.S.-trained Bolivians have been in key administrative positions. Better enforcement and better collections have resulted in revenues in 1960 being 30 percent above their level in 1959, those in 1961 being 17 percent in excess of those in 1960. A budget for 1962, also recently approved, visualizes a further increase of 7.5 percent.

The Directorate General of Taxation has been revised and is in charge of tax reform.

Nondeclaration of taxes in La Paz alone runs as high as 30 percent; it may be higher elsewhere. 

The local AID mission has had in hand a Government management assistance project, including assistance in tax matters. Details of improvement in Government procedures include the commencement of auditing of major business firms, the institution of IBM operations, with a resulting disclosure of delinquencies, the creation of a research and advisory section, the drafting of an organic law with regard to the Finance Ministry, and the setting up of a port authority to deal with customs administration problems. (As regards customs, an AID-financed central building is being planned for La Paz as an essential step in the improvement of controls over imports.) 

Progress in training is being made, AID assisting through the furnishing of certain scholarships to Spanish-speaking courses and through inservice training. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

A significant area for improvement is in the area of real property taxation. 

As of the moment, the problem of delineating local governmental tax authority is beyond the scope of the existing reform group. 

1. Introduction

BRAZIL Based on a population of 67,385,000, the per capita gross national product would seem to be approximately $259. 

The striking feature of the economy of the country, certainly as it affects tax reform, is the continued inflation. A major factor contributing to the continuance of high budgetary deficits is the nature of governmental expenditures. On the other hand, its rate of growth of gross national product is high. 

Brazil has a markedly decentralized governmental structure, there being 21 states, 5 territories, a federal district and more than 3,000 municipalities. 

Taxing authority is likewise diffused. 

In terms of the Act of Bogotá, it is to be noted that "Operation Pan America," which was the prototype for the Act of Bogotá, originated in Brazil and under its sponsorship in 1958. 

2. Nature of tax system

National domestic revenues are only 8.6 percent of gross national product, (based on the best figures available). On the other hand, the total tax imposed on the Brazilian economy not only by the national, but also by the state and municipal authorities and by certain autonomous agencies, is approximately

double that amount. Data is not available to determine the precise extent of the nonnational tax revenues and, to the extent that it is available, it is confused by the existence of substantial intergovernmental transfers as between the national and state governments. 

Consumption taxes account for 43.3 percent of national revenues, income taxes for 31.6 percent and import duties and related fees for only 11.8 percent. The consumption taxes are imposed at rates ranging, effectively, and by tax, from 2 to 20 percent. Import duties average 15 percent and are applicable to approximately 60 percent of the physical importations into the country. 

The income tax structure is, typically for Latin America, schedular in the first instance with a graduated complementary tax being imposed on the total of all incomes, computed after taking account of the pertinent exemptions and deductions. Taking into consideration recent changes, the top bracket rate is presently 60 percent. In addition, Brazil has a compulsory loan feature, as regards both personal and business taxation, amounting to one-quarter of the personal taxes and to 15 percent of business income tax payable. 

The basic tax on business income is 18 percent for incomes up to 500,000 cruzeiros and 23 percent on amounts in excess thereof. There are additional taxes on such income, namely, 30 percent on undistributed profits under certain circumstances; 15 percent on additions to capital and surplus, 10 percent on revaluations and an excess profits tax ranging between 20 and 50 percent on profits determined to be in excess of applicable formulas. (The compulsory loan tax of 15 percent of the tax has been referred to above.) 

State taxes are made up to the extent of 56 percent, of sales taxes, the rates of which range from 4 to 8 percent. Municipal taxes total one-fifth as much as the state taxes. 

In view of the origination of Operation Pan America in Brazil, the 1958 tax enactments in Brazil are pertinent in considering its self-help measures on a tax reform variety.

The basic purpose of the 1958 tax program was to raise approximately 13 billion cruzeiros. This was one of three steps devised to implement the monetary stabilization program. The nature of the tax changes made, certainly in the income tax area, was expressly designed to further economic development. As regards the revenue total, the income tax was to raise 5 billion, the consumption taxes 6.8 billion, the stamp tax 1.7 billion and fees 0.5 billion.

As regards the income tax- (a) Revaluation of assets was to be allowed, thereby increasing public interest in private securities. (b) Investment in real estate was to be discouraged by higher taxes on profits on sales and by treating developers as corporations. (c) Accelerated depreciation was to be allowed and undistributed profits were to be permitted to be capitalized. (d) Government backing was to be given to certain equity securities, and (e) An industrial development fund was to be provided for. 

The law was enacted November 28, 1958 as Law 3470, to be effective with respect to income received after June 1959. As enacted, it was expected to yield 3.55 billion cruzeiros. In its passage through Congress the provision as regards the industrial development fund was dropped and administrative sections providing for prison terms for offenses and for net worth assessments were also left out of the bill. 

As regards excises, the new provisions omitted the earlier turnover feature. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá 

Law 3826 of November 23, 1960 and Law 3850 of December 18, 1960, included a 5-year extension, starting in January 1, 1961, of a 1956 tax (as raised by Law 

3470 of 1958) and the 3 percent additional tax on business profits.

Law 3898, sanctioned by the President on May 19, 1961, constitutes the major tax enactment of 1961. It dealt with the income tax, was expected to have little revenue consequence, and was designed primarily to adjust the tax structure to the fact of inflation. This was done by providing for the computation of deductions and of the brackets for determining the progressive rate schedule by reference to multiplicands of the minimum wage rather than by having them expressed in figure amounts. (The minimum wage is automatically adjusted as inflation progresses.) The law dealt only with the individual income tax.

In particular, the rate schedule for the complementary tax (1) was reduced in most of the lower brackets and (2) was increased for incomes of above 4,500,000 cruzeiros. The top bracket increase was to 60 percent. 

New withholding provisions and administrative provisions were added. 

In August a new bill was presented to Congress to encourage the reinvestment of profits. 

In September 1961, a second major step was undertaken in the field of tax reform. The Council of Ministers announced in favor of social reform and proposed to Congress the modification of income and consumption taxes for that purpose. The announcement was approved by Congress on September 30. 

The revenue was to be used primarily by way of paying 72 percent of planned investment in electric power facilities and 80 percent of planned investment in transportation and roads. 

The bill not not acted on during 1961. However, in the income tax field it would have sharply increased the income tax withholding rate on dividends on bearer shares and would have included certain features dealing with profit remittances. The consumption taxes would have been increased, particularly on luxury articles, the increase on alcoholic beverages, for example, to be 1,000 percent. Excise taxes would have been increased on vehicles and tires, a tax would have been imposed on property benefited by highway construction, the tax on electricity would have been converted from an ad valorem basis to a specified rate basis, and jail penalties would have been inserted in the law for fraud. The revenue potential of the bill, however, was estimated at only 

0.6 billion cruzeiros (the national deficit being 100 billion). 

A bill setting forth limitations on profit remittances was passed by the Chamber of Deputies on November 29. It is being seriously reconsidered at present. 

By decree enacted December 20, 1961, effective January 1, 1962, the first reductions in import duties for member countries of the Latin American Free Trade Association (LAFTA) were put into effect. Over a 12-year period the duties are to drop to zero. 

An agrarian reform law was passed by the State of São Paulo on December 30, 1960. It included a graduated land tax ranging from 2 percent of the first 

100 hectares to 6 percent on amounts in excess of 5,000 hectares. The rates can be reduced if more than 80 percent of the land is exploited and doubled if up to 70 percent of the property is nonproductive. 

A measure is expected dealing with the reassessment of property valuations. 

On February 15, 1962, the Council of Ministers was reported as having agreed to send a land reform bill to Congress, with large sources of tax revenue being set aside to finance it. The bill contains a constitutional amendment to permit the payment of property taxes in land. The rate of tax would be progressive up to 10 percent of the value of the land. 

5. Tax administration 

From an administrative point of view, it has been disclosed that evasion of income taxes is widespread. 

Part of the difficulty is attributable to administrative problems generally and part to the lack of effective penalties or sanctions for fraud or evasion. 

In the former regard, recent corrective efforts have been put into effect, including the rotation of Government personnel (to avoid the development of possible special relationships with taxpayers) and the conscious development of better taxpayer relationships. Already substantial increases in collections are traceable to these steps. 

President Quadros, while in office, undertook improvement measures in the customs field.

As regards penalties and sanctions, the legislation proposed in the autumn of 1961 included certain corrective provisions. It is possible that legislation may be taken up for consideration by the Congress now convening. Inflation has been a contributory cause to the nonpayment of taxes since, with the devaluation of the money, any postponement results both in a lesser real burden from the basic tax charge and to the lightening of the effect of a fixed value fine or penalty. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

The present problems of diverse tax sources and the Federal-State relationship generally are presently under study by the Vargas Foundation in cooperation with a local governmental group. Included in these studies is work pointed toward the possible standardization of municipal taxes.

CHILE 

1. Introduction 

Based on a population of 7,802,000 (for 1961) the per capita gross national product in Chile is $638, the second highest in Latin America. The economy of the country furthermore is advanced. On the other hand, gross annual additions to investment are only 9 percent of gross national product, a low figure, and domestic savings is only a little over one-half of that. 

The country has virtually adopted (it is in the last stages of World Bank review) a 10-year plan. The Cabinet is committed to self-help in many fields, including tax reform. The Government has had stabilizing measures in force and the March 1961 election results supported its policy in that regard. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic source revenue in Chile currently is 15.5 percent of gross national product (this figure representing an increase from 13 percent by reason of improvements in administration undertaken as part of a deliberate effort to finance the above referred to 10-year plan). 

In general, the tax structure is complex and incentives to private investment are inadequate. The revenues from city real estate are disappointing. 

Chile has had an income tax since 1924. 

The Government began tax reform in 1954- (1) With the appointment of a commission of experts to work with the Government and with a United Nations expert on codification and on administrative improvement. (2) In cooperation with the Administration Institute of the University of Chile to help the service on management and methods problems. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

In April 1960, by Decree 190, the administrative portion of a general tax code was enacted, effective January 1, 1961. Its enactment has resulted in material improvements in administration. The Government is interested in further coordinating improvement in administration. 

The earthquake in Chile was in May 1960. Late in October, a reconstruction bill was enacted in compromise form. The tax measures include temporary increases in income, property, sales, ammunition, and other taxes. 

Late in 1960, negotiations were had with the United States on a Double Income Tax Avoidance Convention. They have been suspended by reason of the present U.S. position on forgiven local taxes. 

Early in 1961, increases in salaries and other benefits were granted to Government workers and teachers, these benefits being financed with additional taxes on petroleum products and stamp duties. The large American copper companies' taxes were increased 8 percent effective, in large part, with respect to 1961 income. The President is authorized both to extend or to suspend this tax, if necessary, to finance future wage adjustments. 

Presently, Cabinet level and congressional task forces and committees are working in the tax area, the following subjects receiving consideration: tax reform, administrative reform and tariff reform. A bill is expected to be submitted to Congress this month. 

5. Tax administration 

Starting in June 1960, several AID commitments were entered into in the tax administration area for the purpose of helping to establish an enlarged tax administration unit in the service; 30 higher level employees have received training in the United States; 160 trainees have already been graduated from existing classes in Chile for the lower levels of employees. Local classes for higher levels are being instituted at the present time. 

Teachers are to return to Chile and the entire program is to be perpetuated with the expectation that students from other countries will attend the classes in Chile.

Developments in the administration area include the following: 

1. The probable institution of the first criminal suit for tax evasion. 

2. The question of possible assistance from AID with respect to the use in 

Chile of automatic data processing machinery. 

3. Aerial photographic mapping is being carried out by 4 companies (3 being American) with 30 American employees and 200 Chileans. The purpose of the mapping is not purely for revision of the basis for the proper land and

land-use tax but also as an aid in land reform, also regional development. The photographing is virtually completed and it is expected that the maps will be prepared by March and that the results will be available by October. 

4. A proposal is presently pending to reorganize the service along regional lines. 

5. The virtual completion, under United Nations guidance, of reform in the customs. 

6. A new organic statute for the Internal Tax Service, based on the U.S. model, is expected to be enacted in 1962. 

The AID effort in administration in Chile is one of its major efforts of this type in Latin America. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

There is still a need for more income tax revenue; also for a widened and higher rate.

It is expected that a sales tax with a higher rate and applicable at only a single stage will be substituted for the present multistage form. The producers will be effectively exempted. Changes by way of simplification are expected in the construction tax, the changes also being expected to stimulate construction. 

The policy of the Government is in favor of better investment incentives. 

A familiar and important recognized need is the existence of tax laws to help land reform. The mapping program referred to above is a major step in this direction. In the cities, property taxation is based on the value of the land and of the improvements, thereby effectively benefiting the speculator who holds the land in unimproved form for profit. 

1. Introduction COLOMBIA 

Based on a population of 15,191,000, the per capita gross national product is $292. The economy of the country is relatively advanced. Self-help programs got underway in 1958. Recently seven emergency programs were submitted to 

IDB and to AID, based on Punta del Este, none of them dealing with taxes. 

A congressional election has just been held and a presidential election will be held in May 1962. 

2. Nature of tax system

On a national basis, domestic source revenue is only 9.4 percent of gross national product. However, Colombia is one of the three countries in Latin America with substantial nonnational sources of revenue, these sources accounting for revenues approximately 60 percent as large as the national revenues. 

As regards national source revenues, direct taxes accounted for over 50 percent of the total, as high a percentage as there is in Latin America. 

The tax system is an advanced one relative to most other Latin American countries. The income tax, however, has the schedular aspects and the high exemptions typical of this tax in all of the Latin American countries. 

.

In 1959, a new customs tariff on imports was enacted replacing the one previously in effect that had been enacted in 1950. In general a 7.6 percent average tariff was replaced by one of 17 percent (computed after exemptions, or 23.5 percent before.)

Tax legislation was originally proposed by the government in 1959. It was finally enacted as law No. 81 in December 1960 (as to which see below). 

4. Tax report since Bogotá

At the end of August 1960, Professor Shere, an outstanding economist, arrived in Colombia under contract with the Pan American Union to make a study of tax reform.

Tax proposals that had been introduced in 1959, were signed by the President as law No. 81 on December 22, 1960. The law was effective "as from the 

1960 tax year." It was expected to produce a short-term reduction of between 50 and 100 million pesos a year. The codification of the law achieved was in itself a major accomplishment. 

The stated purpose of the legislation was to clarify existing laws and to provide for tax incentives as well as for a more equitable tax incidence. It purported to accomplish the last objective by reductions in the income tax rates on the lower income levels and by increases in those on the higher. In particu-

lar, the maximum income tax rate on individuals was raised from 48 to 51 percent and was made effective at 2 million pesos as against 5 million pesos previously. The maximum rate on corporations was raised from 31.75 to 36 percent and was made effective at 1 million as compared to 5 million pesos. (This last change was to discourage corporate splitting to avoid the graduated rates on corporations.) In other respects the provisions with regard to corporations were brought more into line with partnerships. 

As regards tax incentives, exemptions in certain instances were granted, through 1969, and a 10-year exemption was given to reserves, to the extent of 5 percent of corporate profits, where the amounts were used by way of substitution for imports. 

In order to redirect savings, a high rate of tax was imposed on speculative sales of real estate and a high presumptive rate of income was attributed to luxury properties.

Major municipalities were authorized to establish taxes on real estate (at 4 percent on undeveloped land and 2 percent on developed), the proceeds to be used for the improvement of municipal facilities. 

The Government was given the authority to fix taxes with respect to exports. 

On January 1, 1961, export taxes on major products were reduced from 15 to 9 percent largely to compensate for the drop in world prices of coffee. 

Decree No. 0437 of February 1961, taxed corporations 6 percent, the proceeds to be used in housing. 

Decree 1394, effective June 23, 1961, implements the authority granted in law No. 81 by granting exemption with respect to certain minor exports. Action was taken as to others in October.

Colombia's instrument of ratification of the Treaty of Montevideo, the treaty establishing the Latin American free trade area, was deposited on September 30, 1961. 

5. Tax administration

By a series of decrees in the spring and early summer of 1960, the various tax bureaus were materially reorganized with a view to better administration. 

An AID consultant was supplied to Colombia during the winter of 1961 for assistance as regards customs.

Since the Buenos Aires Conference on Tax Administration, which was held in October 1961, much has been done to implement the interest developed at that Conference and the suggestions derived from its discussions. Thus, permanent offices have been set up to study the questions of needed economic and tax legislation and steps have been taken to keep the public informed with regard thereto. 

Civil service has been broadened, training programs have been undertaken, and many procedures have been updated. It is expected that some electronic processing machines will be delivered at an early date. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects 

Professor Shere's report in 1960 made the following three recommendations: 

1. That a cadastral survey be undertaken to lay the basis for more national taxes. He recognized that the cost would be approximately $5 million and that it would take 3 years. 

2. That certain irrationalities in the system such as the necessity for valuing goodwill, etc., be eliminated. 

3. That the income tax rates on the middle and lower incomes be increased. 

The Government is pushing toward, and wishes to obtain approval for, the removal of export taxes with respect to its major products. 

To date, the taxation of the agricultural sector has been classed by the Government as for study and handling and as part of the land reform program and progress depends on actions taken in this field. 

1. Introduction COSTA RICA 

Based on a population of 1,224,000, the per capita gross national product is $343. Population growth is one of the world's highest. 

Traditionally Costa Rica is socially and economically democratic. It has a rapidly expanding middle class, a diffused money economy and diversification in economic activities and exports. 

The country has no overall development plan as yet but has inherited good sectoral planning.

During 1961, the country was looking forward to a presidential election. This has just taken place. The change of Government will take place in May. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenue is 18.7 percent of gross national product. Customs duties account for almost 60 percent of the total. Direct taxation supplies just over 

15 percent. Customs taxation is one of the main sources of revenue in Costa Rica.

The question of tax reform in Costa Rica, as in other Central American countries, is to be considered in the context of Central American economic integration.

Historically, Costa Rica has not tried to increase its revenues for the purpose of developing a public investment capability over and above current requirements. Costa Rica has traditionally followed a policy of borrowing for this purpose. 

Prior to the Act of Bogotá a so-called new industries law was enacted which included among its provisions certain tax concessions. 

One particular area of undertaxation in Costa Rica involves the taxation of real estate. On the other hand, a measure that was passed on Dcember 20, 1959 (Law No. 2500) which would have increased tax rates on realty to produce a 60 percent increase in revenues, was repealed on April 21, 1960, pursuant to strong protests.

In June 1960 a law was promulgated that persons paying back income or property taxes within the next 3 months would be forgiven all fines and penalties. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

Since the Act of Bogotá, a series of taxes have been enacted in order to increase revenues. On the other hand, they have been largely indirect and have often followed the practice of having the proceeds earmarked for specific expenditure projects. Certain of the enactments, in particular increases in utility rates, were required by the World Bank and other leading sources. 

Toward the end of 1961, an opposition-sponsored tax on real estate was enacted and has now become law, effective December 24, 1961. The tax is to be paid by those persons who do not pay an ad valorem property tax. The rates would be 

100 colones per hectare of rural land and 5 colones per square meter of urban land, 6.65 colones being equal to $1. One purpose of the law is to discourage large nonproductive holdings. 

By Law No. 2801 of September 3, 1961, import duties on essential goods were reduced, those on luxury goods being increased. 

In November 1961 a 2-percent tax was established on real estate operations, mortgages, and automobile licenses. 

5. Tax administration

The AID mission has been asked to help the Government in administrative matters and it has done so. This effort is being conscientiously reoriented to stress planning and policy decisions. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

During 1961, the Director General for Direct Taxation was preparing proposals to amend the income tax law and to replace the property tax law. These were originally to be submitted by November but, as of January 1962, they had not yet been sent to the legislature. 

The Central Bank is making a study of Government finances including taxation. 

1. Introduction DOMINICAN REPUBLIC 

Based on a population of 3,098,000, the per capita gross national product is $234. The literacy rate varies between 40 percent in the rural areas to 70 percent in the cities. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenues total 17.8 percent of gross national product. 

The tax system under Trujillo has been described as a hodgepodge. No reform was possible under his dictatorship.

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

The government of Joaquin Balaguer, which left office on January 1, 1962, introduced a number of changes in the national tax system. Excise and sales taxes and the tax withheld from Government workers' salaries were reduced, in order to lower the cost of living, and export taxes on coffee and cocoa were canceled. Export taxes on sugar and sugar products were replaced by a 50-percent net profits tax. 

As of January 1, 1962, a personal income tax was levied in the Dominican Republic for the first time. The new tax is schedular, taxing income from five different categories, and replaces a former head tax that had been based on monthly income. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

The Balaguer government formed a commission to study the Dominican Republic's tax structure, with the assistance of the United Nations' Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA). The Government's intention was to make the tax system "more just" and to promote economic development. In order to restore financial stability, however, some of the taxes which have been abolished or reduced may have to be reimposed, or new forms of taxation will have to be introduced. 

1. Introduction 

ECUADOR Based on a population of 4,455,000, the per capita gross national product for Ecuador is $185. Unemployment is a serious question. 

2. Nature of tax system

Al- Domestic revenues for 1960 were 17.6 percent of gross national product. though 15 provincial governments, more than 90 municipalities, and almost 800 autonomous agencies and funds have taxing authority, the revenue raised by these authorities is only approximately 10 percent of the national revenues. 

Not only are the taxing provisions of the national and other authorities both uncodified and often contradictory but the budgetary situation is uniquely complicated. Thus, there are three separate budgets, a capital, an operating, and a state enterprise one. In addition, there are so-called special accounts. 

Forty-one and two-tenths percent of the national revenues are derived from customs levies, 16.5 percent are derived from an income tax. 

Since September 1960, a number of indirect taxes have been increased so as to raise the collections from that source by approximately 10 percent. 

In September and October 1961, two of these earlier increases in indirect taxes were either invalidated or modified. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

By legislative decree published in the Registro Oficial No. 81 of December 8, 1960, the rate of tax levied on new joint stock companies was reduced. It had previously been imposed at an unrealistically high rate. The reduction was as much as one-quarter in the case of smaller companies. It was only one of 5 percent for the largest.

On April 14, 1961, a new tax of 2.25 percent was placed on the value of all imports. The imposition was expected to raise between $2 to $4 million. Other changes in customs duties are expected to raise additional revenues, particularly an increase in the tax based on the f.o.b. value of exports. 

Executive Decree D.E. 30, published on July 8, 1961, authorized the exclusion in certain cases of all or part of the fines and interest due on taxes owed prior to July 8, if the taxes were paid within 120 days thereafter. 

Ecuador's self-help actions of a tax reform nature date from the closing months of the year. 

1. The Congress passed an inheritance tax law, designed more for social justice than by reason of any resulting revenue. 

2. Legislation has been prepared modifying the basic law of customs and designed to regularize the administrative law and procedures relating thereto and the court procedures flowing therefrom. 

3. Laws have been prepared applicable to commercial transactions, contracts, etc., for inclusion in the new tax code to be enacted.

4. An income tax bill, originated by the previous administration, is now under serious consideration. The present administration has appointed a special committee, including the private experts who helped draft the original bill, to restudy it in the light of the current situation. 

The law is designed to ease the tax burden on the lower income groups, thereby increasing their purchasing power; also to increase it on those best able to bear it.

The expected revenue increase will not be substantial but the structural aspects of the change are believed to be contributory to the process of tax reform. 

5. Revision of the sales tax law is also under consideration, in particular, a proposal to limit the imposition of the tax to only one in a series of roles. 

5. Tax administration

A major task confronting the Government is the reform of tax administration and its implementing legislation. The local AID mission, starting in November 

1961, has been rendering technical assistance. The major drive is awaiting implementation of the so-called tax administration improvement project. 

Tobacco and cigarette taxes have been combined, thereby permitting increased collection efficiency as regards those imports. 

As regards evasion, under the income tax, and as regards all taxpayers, only between 50 and 70 percent of total income is reported. 

From the administration's point of view, its auditors lack sufficient authority. 

The legislative penalties are not realistic. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

Ecuador wishes the benefit of the best possible advice in its approach to the problems of overall substantive change. 

Whatever the answer given to the structural development of the law, and to its codification, the basic peculiar local difficulty is the extraordinary number of taxing authorities. This problem needs to be resolved. 

1. Introduction EL SALVADOR 

Based on a population of 2,711,000, the per capita gross national product is $180. This figure is in line with those of the other countries in the Central 

American economic integration group; Panama and Costa Rica have significantly higher figures. 

Based on construction in the 1930-40 period, El Salvador has the best network of roads in Central America. During the period 1950-57 its gross national product showed good growth and there was substantial capital formation. 

Historically, the Government of the country has been conservative and the society has shown contrasts between wealth and poverty. In October 1960, the Government was overthrown, that Government in turn being superseded in January 1961. Elections were held in December 1961, and constitutional Government was restored a month later. The social reform programs introduced in the interim by the ruling directorate were the primary issue. They were upheld. The election for President does not occur until April 29, 1962. 

The country has been active in the promotion of Central American economic integration. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenues constitute 15 percent of gross national product. Again typical of Central American countries, customs levies of different sorts, primarily import duties and an export tax on coffee, account for 60 percent of the total. (A weakness in this heavy dependency is, of course, that, when exports drop because of a drop in world prices or for other reasons, the effect on the revenues is immediate and significant.) 

None. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

Decree No. 154 of June 5, 1961, imposing a 0.06 colón-per-pound export tax on shrimps, is expected to raise $500,000. 

The interest of the directorate in self-help measures, which, in addition to agrarian and other reforms, included measures designed to stop the flight of capital and to repatriate current receipts, turned to tax reform during the summer. The Government at that time expressed a desire to have outside

advice and help (and has continued to do so since as regards further developments in its tax situation). The purpose of the reform was announced as being to enforce what the Government considered to be a social obligation of the rich to put their excessive profits at the disposal of the state. 

Decree No. 300 of September 19, 1961, is the self-help tax reform measure. 

It was made effective as of a date 8 days after enactment. The Government estimates that the measure would increase revenue (from the income tax) by 

32 percent.

The law amends the income tax (as first enacted in 1951). In general, exemptions were increased for children, thereby effectively reducing the income tax burden on large sectors of the population. The income tax rates in the higher brackets were increased. Thus, the bracket rate at $75,000 is now 76.5 percent. Although this increase in rates (to levels as high as any in Latin 

America and almost as high as in the United States) only affects possibly 90 returns in the higher brackets, these 90 returns produce 31 percent of the revenue obtained from the income tax. 

The usual schedular approach to income is used. The rates on unearned or mixed income were raised. 

The 5-percent tax on corporate income was converted to a graduated tax ranging from 5 to 15 percent.

A provision was inserted to tax the undistributed income of corporations, but this provision has since been modified (by Decree No. 442 of December 6, published December 9 and effective December 17, and by Decree No. 502 of December 

21, published December 23 and effective December 31). Further modifications have been promised. (The Government has Provisions are included dealing with administration. planned to apply to ECLA and to the IDB for help in this area.) 

Decree 443 of December 6, published December 12 and effective December 20, 1961 (the "Excise Tax Law on Sugar") reduced the existing excise tax on sugar slightly (to 3.50 colones per pound) but broadened the tax base, making the tax applicable to all sugar produced. The measure would raise $400,000 a year. 

In the customs area, tariffs as between participating Central American countries are being adjusted in line with the Central American Common Market. 

Work is proceeding on negotiating a common external tariff. 

5. Tax administration

Enforcement and administration constitute one of El Salvador's major problems. An organization and methods study at the Bureau of Direct Taxes is already in hand with the local AID mission. Work goes steadily forward on matters affecting customs. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

Since the enactment of Decree No. 300, there has been a specific sentiment in 

El Salvador for the equalization of income tax measures as between the Central 

American countries.

The present low tax on capital (primarily the real estate tax) is due for correction. The Government has asked for assistance in the development of a cadastral survey.

The present system of subjecting coffee to an export tax and exempting it from the progressive income tax is also due for correction. 

1. Introduction GUATEMALA 

Based on a population of 3,868,000, the per capita gross national product is $177 Up to 50 percent of the population is not incorporated in the money economy. 

There is a substantial urban middle class. 

Congressional elections were held in December 1961. 

Delays in legislation have held up some of the 4-year public investment program projects that were proposed in mid-1960 by the Economic Planning Commission. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenues total 13.3 percent of gross national product. 

Business income has been subject to taxation in Guatemala since 1938. 

Starting in 1946, the graduation of the income tax rates has progressed faster and has gone higher than in most of the other countries of Latin America. The top bracket rate is 43 percent.

During the period 1948-58, six general income tax laws were proposed but none was passed. 

None. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

A new stamp tax law became effective on May 16, 1961. 

Starting in February 1961, the problem of whether or not to inaugurate tax reform began to receive attention. 

In March 1961, a significant new income tax proposal was referred to the 

Joint Congressional Committee on the Treasury and Economic Affairs. That committee revised the proposal and issued it with a report in July, 1961. The proposal has had three readings in Congress, on August 22 and 23 and on September 21. It was not passed in 1961 but, if passed in 1962, it will be effective by 

1963. The proposal is expected to produce at least 1.7 million quetzals (1 quetzal equals 1 U.S. dollar).

Pnder the proposal, a 10-year exemption from the complementary tax would be given to new foreign capital. A deduction of up to 20 percent would be granted with respect to reinvested earnings. A 10-percent reduction in tax would be applicable in the case of agricultural income and of income of less than 12,000 quetzals. 

5. Tax administration

It is estimated that administrative reforms could produce added income. 

However, more consultants are needed. Training programs are also needed. 

The local AID mission expects within the next few weeks to substitute a resident tax administration adviser for its previous short-term consultants. The 

Government has also requested the help of an adviser in the customs administration field.

Improved administrative measures already introduced include the mechanization of the control and collection of the real estate tax. In this regard, properties are being reappraised, and revalued at an accelerated rate, especially those of large landowners. A new appraisal method is awaiting Presidential approval which will further speed up the process. A nationwide cadastral survey is presently planned, to take 10 years; $4 million of the cost would be sought from the IDB. 

Plans as to mechanization with respect to other taxes are in hand. 

Work has started looking to the establishment of an office to administer the new income tax.

Delinquent taxpayers are currently being taken to court, property is being attached, and fines are being imposed and collected. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

The political and economic situations are material determinants as to the tempo of tax reform in Guatemala. Guatemala, however, is a leading proponent of Central American economic integration.

There is a hope that land tax rates will be increased from 3 to 5 percent, with a possible increased revenue yield of 900,000 quetzals. The increase would be directed toward improving the economic use of the land. 

1. Introduction 

HAITI Based on a population of 32 to 4 million, the per capita gross national product is $76. The literacy rate is only 10 percent. Domestic revenues amount to about 10 percent of gross national product. Of total revenues only 8 percent are derived from income taxes. Indirect taxes provide 70 percent. The principal direct taxes are levied on business gross receipts, on income and on real estate. 

3. Tax reform prior to Bogotá

Prior to 1961, some additional indirect taxes had been imposed and rates had been raised on others. Reform, as such, was not undertaken. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

A new income tax law was enacted on September 7, 1961. The principal changes were an increase in the top bracket complementary tax from 5 to 10 percent, and application of a 20-percent surtax to the foreign-held net assets of

Haitian corporations. The law also contained some administrative improvements. Salary withholding was tightened and fines for evasion of withholding provisions increased. Prepayment of tax by business and professional taxpayers was inaugurated. Finally, the tax administration has been given broad powers to reassess taxable income in accordance with the taxpayer's visible standard of living.

On February 28, 1962, a tax for participation in the national effort was introduced to help finance the "self-help" program of public investment. It imposes a tax on imports and exports which had been entering Haiti free of custom duty under special legislation encouraging new industries and investments in Haiti. The rate is 20 percent on imports, 10 percent on exports. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

The U.S. AID mission in Haiti is not presently assisting the Government in reorganizing its tax administration. It hopes to be of help, however, and expects to assist the Government in the training of tax personnel. 

Customs administration personnel needs revision. 

1. Introduction HONDURAS 

Based on a population of 2,014,000, the per capita gross national product is $202, a figure typical of the countries which are the immediate neighbors of Honduras.

Honduras is one of the countries most interested in Central American economic integration. 

Current economic problems are (1) poor character of communications, transportation, and power, (2) unemployment, and (3) the investment climate. 

There will be an election in the country in October 1963. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic national revenue is only 9.1 percent of gross national product. 

The tax system is complex and many of the existing laws are obsolete. Fiftyfive and nine-tenths percent of the revenue comes from customs. 

A customs code was adopted in the period 1955-57. 

A 1959 industrial development law granted income tax benefits to income from certain industries, and exemption from import duties with respect to certain machinery, etc., imported in connection with those industries. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

Honduras is the only country in Latin America with a double taxation treaty with the United States.

Discussions were held with U.S. representatives in November 1960 with regard to possible changes. The schedules in the treaty were terminated, however, in 

January 1961 to permit Honduras to participate in setting a common external tariff for the Common Market. It has not yet ratified that agreement. 

The OAS is making a pilot study of land taxes. Presently, such taxes are administered by the central district and the municipalities. The ministry of finance and a congressional committee also are studying the taxation of idle land.

Requests were made to the OAS for a tax mission to deal with tax reform generally. The response was slow, although certain members of the mission commenced arriving during 1961. Study was begun in September 1961, and is expected to be completed early in 1962. 

A plan is now under consideration by a congressional committee to increase the income tax in the higher brackets and the inheritance tax rates. Thus, the 

Ministry of Economy and Finance, in January 1962, proposed legislation to Congress for a 20-percent increase in the tax on incomes in excess of $10,000. The top bracket rate would increase from 30 to 36 percent. The proposal would be expected to yield $500,000 in 1962 and $1 million in each of 1963 and 1964. 

The legislative recommendations also include a land tax, the insertion of differential rates into the indirect system and the gradual start, on an experimental basis, of a general tax on expenditures. In particular, the legislation in the income tax area would encourage, through exemption and lower rates, productive investment and discourage, through higher rates, nonproductive investment.

5. Tax administration 

In May 1961, under the aegis of the National Economic Council, a committee on fiscal administration was organized. The local AID mission is engaged in helping to improve tax and customs administration, with emphasis on the latter, and the OAS is particularly interested in the income tax administration area. 

Reference has been made to the study being conducted by the OAS with regard to the taxation of land, primarily in urban areas. 

Based on improvements in collection, it is expected that a 10-percent increase in revenues will become apparent in 1962 as compared to 1961. 

Action on proposals for administrative changes, and for implementing legislation is expected in 1962. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

It has been suggested that the making of tax changes should not be undertaken in haste. 

1. Introduction MEXICO 

Based on a population of 35,726,000, the per capita gross national product is $322. Mexico is developing at a fast rate. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic national revenues in Mexico in 1961 were only 9.1 percent of gross national product. However, Mexico, with Colombia and Brazil, is outstanding in having substantial regional and municipal tax collections. In Mexico, they total in all as much as 40 percent of the national revenues themselves. 

Direct taxes constitute 36.8 percent of the national revenues. 

A study was made in June 1960 entitled, "Mexican Tax Exemptions for Business. This study dealt both with the federal and state situations. It was noted that the oldest such exemption dated from 1941, that, as of the date of the article, current legislation was being passed and, lastly, that the more recent the law, the more liberal the incentive. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

A clarification of law, approved by Congress, was published on December 31, 1960 (effective January 1, 1961), that held as subject to a 3-percent gross receipts, tax royalties and fees for technical assistance paid by Mexican companies to companies residing abroad. 

On April 8, 1961, a tariff revision policy was announced under which (1) rates were increased on the existing tariff classifications but (2) new classifications were to be prescribed, with lower rates. This policy was implemented in July and August by announcement of certain of the new classifications. 

In August, an announcement was made of impending decrees to stimulate exports of manufactured goods, the stimulation to be based largely on the rebate of income tax attributable to any increase in manufacture that might be so exported. 

As published in the Diario Oficial of December 30, 1961, a number of fiscal and social laws were passed by the Congress in time to be effective starting in 1962. 

The increased income for 1962 over 1961 is estimated to be about $100 million, representing an 11.6-percent increase. A recent reform in the income tax is described below. In addition, the inheritance tax was abolished (the revenue loss will be of an amount equal to only 0.3 percent of national collections), the customs code was amended, the fiscal code was amended to provide for increased criminal penalties, and the social security law was extended to cover the armed forces. The purpose of the reforms had been announced in September as being to tighten administration, plug loopholes, and, as regards the income tax, to attempt to simplify a number of its provisions. 

As regards the income tax, a number of changes were made: 

1. For taxpayers with income on more than one schedule, and for amounts in excess of $14,400, a progressive surtax on total income, ranging between 3 and 15 percent, was provided for, with, however, a maximum 30-percent tax. 

2. Gains on sales of land and buildings are to be taxed, the rates ranging from 

5 to 20 percent, length of holding and smallness of gain being favored by the lower rates. 

3. Rental income in excess of $85 a month is to be included in income in lieu of the Stamp tax that had been previously imposed thereon. A 30-percent de-

duction of the rent is automatically to be allowed to take care of expenses and depreciation. 

4. A 2to 5-percent withholding tax is provided for with respect to interest on certain bonds that pay interest at rates in excess of 7 percent, the 5-percent tax being reached at interest rates of 11 percent and up. 

5. The distributable profits tax was retained (at 15 percent) but a 5-percent additional amount was imposed with respect to dividends payable on bearer shares. 

6. Incentives to new investment were given in the form of accelerated depreciation in certain areas; the provisions governing reserves for reinvestment were also liberalized. 

5. Tax administration 

No major developments. Improvements constantly being made. 

6. Outstanding problems and projects 

Mexico has no guarantee agreement with the United States. 

1. Introduction NICARAGUA 

Based on a population of 1,530,000, the per capita gross national product in 1961 was only $212. In addition, the investment or savings rate was low, being only 

5 percent.

Illiteracy is high. On the other hand, the road system is good. 

Development planning started in the early 1950's under World Bank auspices. 

The country has a presidential election next February. 

2. Nature of tax system

National domestic revenues are 11.3 percent of the GNP. They are almost 

60 percent based on various forms of customs levies. Only 9.1 percent is derived from income tax. (The income tax was introduced in 1955 incident to the World 

Bank's interest in Nicaragua in 1953.) Nonnational revenues are approximately 

10 percent of the national ones. 

No notable progress. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

In January 1961, seven new taxes were enacted that were either increases in existing indirect taxes or the imposition of certain new ones. The expected revenue was approximately $1 million (United States). Two additional proposed decrees were also advanced, one to increase the inheritance tax and the second to provide for a tax on the transfer and donation of real estate. Certain additional indirect taxes were also proposed. Of these, a proposed 17-percent increase in the gasoline tax has since been dropped. The consumer tax on cigarettes was raised a second time on December 20, 1961, by another 3 percent. 

During the summer, a proposed export tax was advanced. Significantly, this was substituted for, on January 15, 1962, by regulation, by the imposition of a 3-percent income withholding tax on cotton, coffee, and cattle. 

A significant self-help measure dealing with land reform, the agrarian reform law has been approved by the Conference Committee and is before Congress. 

It has a provision providing for a sliding scale land tax, the first in the history of the country. Its enactment, although expected last summer has been delayed. 

A new tax reform program involving changes in several taxes, was publicly announced in November and sent to Congress on December 20.

The announcement of the reforms stated that their purpose was to meet the requirements of the Alliance for Progress, to reduce indirect tax burdens on the poorer classes and to impose taxes on real estate, personal property, and exports of cotton, coffee, cattle, and lumber. The reforms were drafted by a governmental committee, (which had been appointed early in 1960) under the advice of an expert from the International Monetary Fund. Specifically: (1) Both real estate and personal property (in excess of certain minimum exemptions, and except with respect to property dedicated to agriculture) would be taxed at a 1-percent rate instead of at a rate of 0.65 percent, the exemption, however, being tripled. A 0.5-percent tax would be imposed on the assets of commercial, industrial, and mining companies. This measure has been passed by the Chamber.

(2) A 3-percent tax would be imposed (in lieu of a 0.5-percent tax) on the value of real estate sold and a tax of 5 percent and up would be imposed on real estate given or passing by death, in the latter event, in addition to the inheritance tax. (3) A new inheritance tax would be provided for. (4) The income tax would be amended in several respects: (a) by dropping the exemption from 20,000 córdobas to 12,000 and (b) by increasing the rates. For example, the 18-percent rate would be increased to 30 percent. (5) The stamp would be amended by way of substantial increases as to those areas where it is productive and by repeal where it is not. 

5. Tax administration

This question is critical in Nicaragua as in many other countries. Steps have been taken to improve collection but the collection is still poor. Customs collections, however, are good. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

Tax reform in Nicaragua must be considered in the context both of Central American Economic Integration and of the Treaty for the Equalization of Import Duties.

Prime tax needs of the country, certainly until the proposed reforms referred to above are enacted, are the need for a land tax, the need of additional tax from the commercial sector, and a marked cut in the regressive indirect tax field.

A study as to investment incentives is planned for early 1962. 

No real change, however, is expected until after the elections early in 1963. 

PANAMA 1. Introduction 

Based on a population of 1,084,000, the per capita gross national product for 

Panama is $411. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenues constitute 13.8 percent of gross national product: 44.2 percent of the revenues are derived from customs and 18.6 percent from income taxes; 12 percent of the total revenues are paid by the banana corporations. 

None. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá 

Law No. 112 as enacted December 29, 1960 (effective January 1, 1961), was designed to raise $2 million. Half of the increase is to be attributable to a simple percentage increase in the income tax rates. The urban realty tax, the stamp tax, and certain other taxes were increased and improvements were made in administrative procedures. 

Discussions have been had with the United States as regards the collection by withholding in the Canal Zone of income taxes on noncitizens of the United States.

Early in 1961 stamp taxes and customs tariffs were increased. 

In June 1961 a special committee was appointed by the President for purposes of studying revisions in the tax structure. Their recommendations were submitted to the President on September 22, the changes being designed to raise, supposedly, between $4 and $6 million additional revenue in 1962. (This full amount may not be repetitive in later years.) With changes made in the course of passage through Congress, the recommendations were implemented by law, passed December 30, 1961, to be effective January 1, 1961. 

Among the changes made in the income tax were— (1) The inclusion of dividends and interest in the individual income tax base. (2) Five percent withholding on dividends and interest; 15 percent on bearer shares. (3) A requirement for the filing of consolidated returns by corporations with over 50 percent affiliation. (4) Provisions for a pay-as-you-go system. 81496-62-pt. 3-8

A land control and ownership tax was imposed providing for a new tax on lands, graduated by size of ownership, where more than 50 hectares are in the same ownership. The bottom rate is 0.25 balboas per year per hectare. This law is designed to replace an unadministrable present law. Provisions were also included for realty reassessment. 

A surtax was imposed on all imported goods, and additional taxes were imposed on various forms of liquor and liquor consumption. 

Administratively, procedures were included for the enforcement of penalties dealing with fraud and, in other respects, designed to improve administration. 

A current tax question which is of national importance is the U.S. proposal for change in the U.S. law with regard to so-called tax-haven countries. is one of these countries. 

5. Tax administration Panama

Panama has laid the ground work for the improvement of tax administration with continuous efforts in the last 4 or 5 years to establish a modern Budget Bureau and a financial system that would include controls over expenditures. 

In addition, the internal revenue administration is now completely covered by civil service.

The U.N. conducted studies in administration in Panama during 1959 and 1960. 

Among the improvements initiated in the last 18 months were (1) The development of procedures manuals which have smoothed internal operations. (2) The initiation of a cadastral survey, expected to take 3 years. (3) The doubling of the size of the tax audit staff in February 1962 and the introduction of scientific sampling for the selection of cases for audit. (4) The assignment of definite quotas for collectors and the publication in 1961 for the first time of a list of tax delinquents. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

A criticism of the income tax system as it now stands is that the graduated rates remain low until the higher incomes are reached. At that point they jump to, for Latin America, the high rate of 42 percent. This situation is not untypical. Many tax experts believe that rates should increase more gradually, i.e., that they should move through all the income brackets. 

A special disadvantage of selective high income tax rates on only the higher incomes is that they affect relatively few taxpayers, often only the businesses which are doing the most to help its economy and are possibly the outstanding present examples of taxpayers which are already conscientiously paying their full tax burden. 

1. Introduction PARAGUAY 

Based on a population of 1,812,000 the per capita gross national product is $130. The country is economically depressed and there is a high degree of illiteracy. Elections for the Presidency are to be held in February 1963. 

As in the case of one or two of the Central American countries, self-help should probably only take slowly developing forms. 

2. Nature of tax system

The domestic revenue is 11.5 percent of gross national product. In addition there are some unbudgeted earmarked special taxes. Income from professional or personal services, as is not unusual in Latin America, is not subject to the income tax. The real estate tax is only 1 percent. The sales tax was abolished in 1957 except on cigarettes, alcohol, kerosene, and petroleum derivatives.

In terms of revenue yield, the 1958 export taxes were high, but exports dropped, with a loss in that source of revenue. 

Early in 1960 the Government increased certain tax rates in order to cover the 1960 budget. Decree No. 236 of January 11, 1960, raised the rate of income tax on net incomes in excess of 35,000 guaranies from 19 percent to 22 percent. 

The taxation of insurance companies was changed from a net income basis, as in the case of any corporation, to a gross income basis with the rate fixed at 3 percent. Decree No. 241 of January 25, 1960, increased the rate of certain sales taxes, notably on automobiles from 5 percent to 10 percent and imposed a new 3-percent tax on medicine and on all used car sales.

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

In March 1961 the basis for customs valuations was increased 20 percent. 

By decree 19347 of November 27, 1961, a four-man Technical Commission was established for controlling custom appraisers and warehousemen. 

5. Tax administration

Starting in September 1959, the local U.S. mission entered into an agreement for aid in customs administration and in the drafting of a new customs tariff. 

The latter task is expected to be completed in 1962, with primary emphasis being given to the adoption of the Brussels nomenclature. Codification of 200 laws is also being undertaken and is expected to be completed in 1963. 

Customs collections improved by about 25 percent in November 1961, as a result of a new determination on the part of the Government. The success of the effort promises increased interest in the methods used and increased accomplishments for the future. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

The Government has recently expressed a willingness to have a foreign mission for purposes of advice and study on tax reform. 

There is a possibility that customs revenues may be revised and that customs procedures will be further improved. 

1. Introduction PERU 

Based on a population of 11,161,000, Peru has a per capita gross national product of $180. This figure is one of the lower figures in the hemisphere. 

The problems posed by the condition of the poorer people of Peru are well known.

The country is financially stable. International capital is available; in that regard, however, the problem is the country's capacity to absorb it. 

Elections are scheduled for June 1962. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenue in 1961 was 17 percent of gross national product. Recent figures show that in excess of 42 percent of ordinary revenues were derived from the income tax. Previously, the great proportion came from indirect taxation.

There are a large number of special taxes. 

Land taxation and related forms of taxation of real estate and of its uses are minimal in the country. 

As compared to the above background, by a law effective January 1, 1959 (Las No. 31051 promulgated Dec. 31, 1958), a first major change was made in this pattern. This law- 

(a) repealed the excess profits tax; (b) increased the progressive rates of taxation on business profits to a top rate of 35 percent, as compared to 20 percent, and lowered the rates on the first two brackets; (c) increased the complementary tax on income from bearer shares and bonds by 30 percent and 80 percent, respectively; (d) instituted a 1½-percent interest charge per month taxes in arrears (but failed to enact a provision requiring certain information from banks); (e) established a 15-year statute of limitation; and (f) set up a commission to draft an amending bill. 

Late in 1959, by Law No. 13270, enacted November 30, 1959, an industrial promotion law was adopted which contained certain tax exemptions and benefits to encourage new investment. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

In October-November 1960, negotiations were held with the United States with regard to a double income tax avoidance convention. A draft, initialed at the time, is presently held up pending a determination by the U.S. Treasury of its position as regards the so-called "tax sparing" question generally. 

Early in 1961, increased taxes were adopted designed to balance the 1961 budget. They were expected to raise approximately $33 million. The increases included-

(a) new taxes on imported edible fats and oils, taxes on the undistributed profits of corporations and, in lieu of the real estate tax, a tax on the income of real estate companies: (b) an increase (20 percent of the previous rate) in the complementary tax on income from bearer shares; (c) an increase in the stamp tax rate (from 0.3 to 2.5 percent) estimated to yield $48 million; (d) an extension of certain 1958 customs surcharges; and (c) an increase in the provision for the advance payment of profits taxes. 

In October 1961, in an effort to aid the construction of low-cost housing, a decree was issued exempting from tax up to 50 percent of the profits of companies engaged in that business. 

In December 1961, the Congress enacted- (a) Law No. 13778, setting up a new development company. This com- pany was to be financed, to the extent of $2,200,000 per year by a 25-percent increase in the charge on certain imports and by adding an additional tax on the consumption of tobacco. (b) Law No. 13784 of December 23, 1961, providing for a tax on coastal oil companies not subject to the petroleum code, designed to raise the Government's income tax yield from 47 to 50 percent of profits. The total tax load on the principal company involved was thus raised to 68 percent. 

On December 28, 1961, the Chamber of Deputies accepted a Senate reduction in proposed taxes on fish meal and on the sugar industry, substituting a new profits tax for the originally proposed export tax. 

In January 1962, Congress passed a law imposing a tax on aviation gasoline of 2 soles per gallon, the revenue to be turned over to the Air Force. 

5. Tax administration 

In Peru, responsibility for various aspects of tax administration is divided between a private corporation created by a consortium of banks in 1927, the Tax Superintendency of the Ministry of Finance and Commerce, the Customs Superintendency, and the Callao Port Authority. 

Some progress in reform has been made. 

Basic studies were made by U.S. and Dutch tax advisers in 1960. Their recommendations have not yet been implemented. 

Early in 1960, the Tax Superintendency introduced self-assessment of income taxes. At the same time, the corporation required that virtually all taxes be paid at the corporation offices rather than to resident tax collectors. 

Automatic data processing has been introduced in the Tax Superintendency to check computations and issue bills for deficiencies. 

With respect to customs, automatic data-processing equipment is scheduled to be installed in April 1962 under a contract signed in November 1961. Revision of the customs code is nearly completed. Installation of a new system which reduces customs documents from 114 to 5 is expected shortly. 

The Government has requested assistance in training the people needed as a requisite to tax programing.

The expressed intention of the Government is to complete a reform of tax structures by 1966, and of tax administration by the end of 1964. The purpose is to produce a relationship between domestic source revenue and gross national product of 22 percent. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

In August 1961, the Finance Minister, in presenting the 1962 budget, stated that private enterprise would be encouraged with the object of increasing the general standard of living. 

1. Introduction 

URUGUAY Based on a population of 2,827,000, the per capita gross national product for 1960 was $450. The country is ready for economic growth. It is outstanding in Latin America for its long-continued stable democracy and its conditions of social justice. 

The country suffers from inflation and from lack of increases in agriculture. 

Annual investment is only 10 percent of the gross national product. 

Politically, the Colorado Party was in control of the country for decades and has only recently been supplanted by the Blanco Party. National elections are imminent.

2. Nature of tax system

In 1960, national domestic revenues were 11.6 percent of the gross national product, departmental revenues furnished an additional amount equal possibly to one-fifth of the national.

Of the national revenues, income tax made up only 7.3 percent. Sales and customs charges (including retention taxes on exports) together accounted for almost 60 percent.

The national real estate tax is approximately 6 percent. A substantial proportion of the departmental taxes come from that source. 

3. Tax reform since Bogotá

By Law No. 12804 promulgated November 30, 1960 (it had been originally introduced on February 15, 1960), a number of changes were made in the tax system, including, among others, an enactment for the first time of an income tax. In revenue terms, however, the law was not expected to add significantly to the level of collections. Most of the changes were made effective January 1, 1961. 

The income tax was made effective July 1, 1961, in most important respects. (The income tax as thus enacted was materially weakened in December 1961; personal allowances were then raised and additional deductions permitted. 

Rates of tax on personal income and on profits distributed to foreign corporations were reduced.)

In addition to the personal income tax, there was also a tax on the undistributed net income of business (of from between 8 and 15 percent), on the net income of certain financial institutions and on a calculated fictitious rate of income assumed to be derived from agricultural land held in large blocks. 

In addition to enacting the income tax, the law also repealed a number of special taxes and modified, simplified in some cases, and often raised the rates on a number of others. Thus, the sales tax (a 1941 tax) had the various rates of earlier laws unified and then the rate was raised to 7 percent for 1961 and 

8 percent for 1962.

A measure was introduced to prevent evasion through false intermediate sales. The rates on excises were also raised and the tobacco and liquor tax systems were increased but the initial exemption was doubled. 

The Government has cut the $5 retention tax on exports of wool in half. 

The Government is interested in this type of a reduction generally. 

In October 1961 a decree was enacted for the construction of schools, hospitals, and clinics. The decree provided for the raising of three-eighths of the costs, to the extent of 90 million pesos, as a contribution from wages. 

5. Tax administration

Improved collections in the period 1960-62 are expected to result in an increase in revenues of $26 million. 

Article 44 of Law 12803 of November 1960 authorized the making on a soundly conceived and properly oriented basis of a number of changes in the organization of the tax service. The article has since been implemented in many respects.

Training programs for Government employees have also been instituted. 

The customs law of December 7, 1961, specifically provides for the making of certain basic reorganization reforms in that area. 

1. Introduction VENEZUELA 

Based on unofficial data for 1961, the per capita gross national product would seem to be approximately $1,040. This is the highest figure in Latin America. 

The income, however, is unevenly distributed and the figure for the lower half of the population is only $150. 

2. Nature of tax system

Domestic revenues totaled in 1960 approximately 21.2 percent of gross national product. Only 11 percent are derived from customs. State and municipal revenues are small by comparison, being derived in large part from license fees.

The oil and mining companies, through both taxes and royalties, supply almost 70 percent of the total income of the Government. 

As regards the balance of the taxes received, i.e., those received from other taxpayers, the preponderant amount is derived from indirect taxes. The income tax is both schedular and complementary, as is usual in Latin America, the schedular rates varying from 22½ to 30 percent and the complementary

rates being graduated from 10 to 45 percent. The inheritance and gift taxes have graduated rates going up to 55 percent. 

Real estate taxes are low, are imposed by the municipalities, and are based only on the income-producing aspect of the real estate in fact. 

The junta of government took over early in 1958. In December it enacted a revised income tax law (decree No. 476, published December 19, 1958). The law was to be effective with respect to 1958 income. The law was expected to produce 500 million bolívares increase in revenue (3.3 bolívares equals 1 U.S. dollar).

In promulgating the law, the Government referred to the study made earlier in the year by the Shoup Commission and noted that the law purportedly implemented certain of the recommendations as regards the income tax. 

It was stated that other aspects of tax reform were being postponed. 

As regards the income tax, the most significant change made was to change the surtax rate (at the lowest level, from 1.5 to 2 percent and, throughout the levels, until at the highest it was changed from 26 to 45 percent). Incentives for investment were also included. 

The 1958 change also included repeal of a gross receipts tax. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

The first of two major 1961 changes (a promulgation of February 13, published on February 17 and effective February 18) provided for withholding on interest and royalties paid to nonresidents. It introduced a pay-as-you-go system for mining and petroleum companies. The lower bracket complementary rates on business enterprises were raised, the bottom bracket, fór example, being raised from 2 to 10 percent. Administrative provisions were also included. 

Revisions in the fiscal stamp tax law (to produce 16 million bolívares) and in the cigarette tax law (to produce 31 million bolívares) were published on 

February 15.

The second major change in the income tax law was promulgated on June 29 (under the name of the Law of Urgent Economic Measures). The law is applicable to income received after July 2. In addition to raising many rates, power was given to the President in the law with regard to rate increases (which he has exercised) and with regard to instituting withholding on dividends paid to nonresidents (which he has not implemented). Pay-as-you-go methods were extended to commercial and industrial enterprises. 

By decree 581 of June 30, the top inheritance and gift tax rates were raised from 30 to 55 percent and an increase was also enacted with regard to the gasoline taxes.

The expected revenue increase from the February and the June enactments is 

200 million bolivars.

Both the February and the June enactments contain tax incentive provisions (granting exemption for 10 years on interest on loans made for the purpose of inaugurating or expanding certain enterprises or on income from such enterprises).
