The recent agrarian reform law includes authorization for a tax on unused farmland. This tax, however, has not yet been implemented by decree. 

5. Tax administration

No significant change. General improvements constantly being made. 

6. Outstanding problems and prospects

The major recommendations of the Shoup report, referred to above, included: (1) Improvement in the administration of the inheritance and gift tax; (2) An increase in the tax on liquors by 50 percent or more; (3) An increase in the tax on gasoline; (4) Repeal of customs duties on many articles; and (5) Repeal of the gross receipts tax. 

Most of these changes have been accomplished.

1. Introduction

BRITISH GUIANA 

Based on a population of 566,000, the per capita gross national product (for 

1960) was $260. 

2. Nature of the tax system

In 1960, Government revenue constituted 19.5 percent of the gross national product.

In 1959, the income tax produced 34.39 percent of total revenues, and customs 

47.24 percent.

In general, the tax system is both soundly devised, being based on the British structure, and it has been honestly administered. 

3. Tax reform prior to Bogotá

None. 

4. Tax reform since Bogotá

Early this year the Government proposed the implementation of recommendations for tax reform presented by Nicholas Kaldor, a Cambridge economist. 

Kaldor had recommended a compulsory savings and capital gains tax, both designed to increase taxes on income and to “force (taxpayers) to disclose their true holdings and earnings."

The proposals, introduced on February 7, 1962, included: (1) A tax on capital gains at the income tax rates (but with a top rate of only 45 percent instead of 60 percent). (2) A "net property" tax of ½ to 12 percent on individuals, and ½ percent on corporations. (3) Increases in income and indirect taxes. (4) Compulsory purchase of Government bonds. The contribution was to be 5 percent of salary and 10 percent of other income. 

The scheme was bitterly opposed. The Government stated that the intention of the legislation was to "redistribute the wealth" as well as to finance an ambitious development program. 

Opposition groups were able to use the suggested tax changes as the catalytic agent for calling general strikes which degenerated into riots and arson. Following the disorders, the Government modified the proposed legislation which has not yet been presented to the Legislative Assembly.

SELF-HELP AND REFORM-THE AMERICAN REPUBLICS AND THE DEPENDENT TERRITORIES IN THE LATIN AMERICAN AREA PART I. INTRODUCTION 

The concept of self-help, including social and economic reform, is a cornerstone of the Alliance for Progress. The participation of the United States in this effort to bring about social progress and to develop the economies of the Latin American Republics and of the dependent territories in this area is predicated upon the assumption that these Republics and territories will help themselves by marshaling their resources and inaugurating or expediting reforms. 

This idea of self-help was first clearly set forth in the Act of Bogotá. This act embodied the aspirations and objectives of the American Republics as agreed to by the Committee of 21 of the Organization of American States at its meeting in Bogotá in September 1960 and subsequently approved by the Council of the Organization of American States (OAS) in October of that year. It recognized that the success of a cooperative program of economic and social progress would require "maximum self-help efforts on the part of the American Republics ***" It stated than an inter-American program for social development should include, as appropriate in each country, measures for : (a) Improvement of conditions of rural living and land use, with particular attention to land tenure, agricultural credit, tax systems, land reclamation and resettlement, increased productivity, and the construction of farm-to-market and access roads: (b) Improvements of housing and community facilities, with particular attention to the strengthening of legal and financial institutions public and private, to facilitate the construction and ownership of homes, especially in the lowincome field;

(c) Improvement of educational systems and training facilities, giving particular attention to eradication of illiteracy, training in the industrial arts and sciences, instruction in rural schools, broadening of the curriculum of the secondary schools, vocational agricultural instruction, and advanced professional education; (d) Improvement of public health, giving particular attention to the expansion of health services the development of health insurance systems the extension of hospital and medical services to areas of special need, the elimination or control of communicable diseases, with special emphasis on the eradication of malaria, the provision of water supply facilities, the training of public health officials and technicians, and the strengthening of programs of nutrition for low-income groups; (e) Mobilization of domestic resources, with particular attention to the creation of domestic savings and the improvement in fiscal and financial practices, the equity and effectiveness of existing tax schedules and assessment and collection procedures, and the allocation of tax revenues; (f) Adequate preparation of development plans and projects, utilizing as appropriate the technical assistance of inter-American and international agencies.

In the same month (September 1960) in which the Bogotá Conference took place the Congress of the United States enacted Public Law 86-735 providing for assistance in the development of Latin America. In this law the principles of self-help and mutual efforts were enunciated. On March 13, 1961, President 

Kennedy, at a historic White House reception, proposed an Alliance for Progress. 

He called for a "vast cooperative effort" and stressed that "only the most determined efforts of the American nations themselves can bring success to this effort. 

Unless these efforts are made by each nation, he said in effect, no amount of assistance from the outside will advance the welfare of the people. He stressed the interrelationship of political freedom, material progress, and social change and emphasized the necessity for social reforms, including land and tax reform. 

At the special meeting of the Inter-American Economic and Social Council at Punta del Este in August 1961, the representatives of the American Republics agreed upon a declaration to the peoples of America which stated that: "For their part, the countries of Latin America agree to devote a steadily increasing share of their own resources to economic and social development, and to make the reforms necessary to assure that all share fully in the fruits of the 

Alliance for Progress. "Further, as a contribution to the alliance for progress, each of the countries of Latin America will formulate comprehensive and well-conceived national programs for the development of their own economies." 

In this declaration the representatives of the American Republics reiterated many points included in the Act of Bogotá and added a few that had not been explicitly stated at the earlier meeting, including among others, the following which appear to have particular relevance to the objectives in which self-help may reasonably be expected to play an important role: 

1. To assure fair wages and satisfactory working conditions to all workers and to establish effective systems of labor-management relations; 

2. To maintain monetary and fiscal policies that will guarantee the greatest possible price stability and at the same time form an adequate basis for economic development; 

3. To stimulate private enterprise.

The Act for International Development of 1961 stated that assistance from the United States should be "responsive to the efforts of the recipient countries to mobilize their own resources and help themselves ***" The principle of self-help has thus been firmly established in declarations, addresses, hearings, and in legislation. The social and economic areas in which self-help is expected have also been fairly clearly delineated. The U.S. Government and the Governments of the other American Republics are agreed that serious and sustained self-help efforts are a precondition to any significant social and economic progress. 

The following country sections include a general statement on the country and individual statements on each of the following: National planning, agrarian reform, housing, health, education, public administration, financial stability, credit, investment, private enterprise, and labor. In view of the wide interest in taxation and its importance, a separate section has been prepared on that subject.

In the statements on the specific categories of self-help for each country some information is given on prevailing conditions as a background for the evaluation of measures taken. Although earlier efforts of each country are frequently referred to, emphasis is placed on actions or developments since the Bogotá Conference. In some cases there are no significant recent achievements to be recorded. In addition to definite achievements, some plans, policies, definite statements of intentions, and measures proposed are mentioned, although it is to be understood that such matters do not necessarily qualify as self-help measures in the fullest sense of that term. Such efforts must precede action, however, and signify in many cases the beginning of movements that are desired. 

Both the people of the United States and those of Latin America recognize that such plans and policies are truly of value only when they are translated into action.

PART II. THE AMERICAN REPUBLICS ARGENTINA 

1. General statement.—Argentina is often classified as an agricultural country because of its traditional production in beef and wheat, but industry now exceeds agriculture both in number of workers and in value of production. 

Literacy is about 86 percent. It has relatively high educational levels, a substantial middle class, many strong public and private institutions of national significance, a high protein as well as a high calory diet, and among the Latin American countries, the largest number of doctors per 1,000 inhabitants. Wages are low by U.S. standards but high in comparison with those of Latin America. 

The Government has done much in the past few years to restore economic stability. The initial steps for overall development planning are now being taken. At present Argentina appears to stand on the threshold of sustained economic growth.

The estimated population in 1962 is 21 million and it is increasing at a rate of approximately 2 percent a year. 

2. Planning.-The President of Argentina is convinced that the alliance for progress will realize its potential in Argentina only if his Government can provide a sound plan within which can be coordinated the actions taken in individual sectors of the economy. He has, therefore, accorded top priority to national planning. A national development council (NDC) was established by executive decree in August 1961. It is to serve as a "consultant agency of high technical level" with principal responsibility for coordinating and implementing studies and analyses necessary for the basic formulation of programs for national development. A budget equivalent to $362,000 was appropriated the NDC for the fiscal year beginning November 1961. 

3. Agrarian reform.-During the past three decades Argentine agriculture has stagnated, largely because the Government has concentrated on modernization and expansion of industry. Since 1958 Government policy has been more favorable to agriculture; but farmers, who must sell at world prices, still must pay two or three times world prices for their purchases from the protected domestic industry. Progress in agriculture is essential to continued rapid economic development as agricultural exports earn about 95 percent of the foreign exchange. Improvement in agricultural technology, farm management, and mechanization are the keys to increased production. 

Because of the development of frontier lands and Government policies, such as graduated provincial taxes penalizing absentee, corporate, and large landowners and regulation of tenancy conditions favoring tenants, over 75,000 net additional families have purchased farms since 1947. Yet only about 40 percent of Argentine farmland was owner-operated in 1961. Aside from a few small sales of Government land and continued implementation of the provision (now expired) of a 1958 law allowing tenants on large properties to purchase their land at advantageous terms, the Government has taken no action on land tenure since the Bogotá Conference. 

4. Housing.-There is a housing shortage of well over a million units and this deficit is currently increasing at the rate of 70,000 a year. A federal housing administration was established July 1961 by Presidential decree and it is responsible for administering the federal housing fund, formulating and implementing national housing policy, and coordinating the federal, provincial, and municipal housing efforts. It has drawn up a set of regulations called general, special, and technical rules and financial plans which was approved by the Ministry of Economic Affairs in October 1961. A decree issued in October

1961 authorized the Ministry of Public Works to arrange for construction of housing on public lands, and two contracts providing for 7,000 houses have been signed. 

5. Health. The nutritional status of the people is one of the highest in the world. Both Government and private agencies are interested in achieving an even more satisfactory nutritional status among the people and several years ago established committees to study and offer advice concerning the maintenance of an adequate diet and the proper methods of preparing foods. The 

Government is making an effort to raise medical standards and to insure a higher level of medical care. It exercises considerable control over preventive medical programs by enforcing protective measures for workers and implementing numerous regulations for the prevention of disease. The Ministry of 

Social Assistance and Public Health administers the national medical care and public health program. Throughout Argentina, indigent patients are afforded free medical care at Government hospitals and clinics. Strict controls govern the registering and licensing of physicians, dentists, veterinarians, pharmacists, and nurses. With assistance from the World Health Organization (WHO), the 

Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO), the Pan American Sanitary Bureau 

(PASB), and the Rockefeller Foundation, Argentina has managed to make progress in combating disease and improving sanitary conditions. 

6. Education.-Although Argentina is one of the most literate countries in 

Latin America, advanced education is seriously deficient, particularly in the fields of economics, science, industry, and agriculture. The Ministry of Agriculture has on its own begun a modernization program for agricultural schools and has received for the fiscal year beginning November 1961 the equivalent of $125,000 in addition to the regular budget for this purpose. Although a number of self-help measures have been instituted to modernize the curriculums and other aspects of public and private universities, these are recognized as being insufficient for the current scientific and industrial needs. Consequently, assistance has been requested, including a $10 million loan from the IDB to purchase laboratory and other special equipment. 

7. Public administration.-In August 1959, the Government established procedures to reduce the number of Government personnel. This step, along with other measures, resulted in a net reduction of at least 50,000 from 1958 to 1961. 

This program recognizes that further reductions are appropriate. The re- organization plan for the national railroad includes a reduction of employees from 210,000 to 140,000 and the transferral of railroad services to private business. To date there has been a reduction of about 30,000 railroad employees. 

A series of decrees were issued in 1962 designed to eliminate all state services and functions that can be performed by private industry. 

8. Financial stability.-In 1958 the Government of Argentina embarked on a program of financial reform with the counsel of the IMF and financial assistance from the United States. Frondizi has done much to correct the economic and financial errors. The Argentina "stabilization plan" limited monetary and credit expansion, stabilized the exchange rate in a free market, reduced budgetary deficits, removed trade and payments restrictions, eliminated price and rent controls, and attempted to control wages. The restrictive credit policy of the central bank has remained basically firm. Argentina is in a position, however, of having to steer a very careful course between an inflationary monetary policy and a tight credit policy which would choke the developing economy. 

9. Credit. The rapid expansion that is going on in many sectors of the econcmy is increasing the demand for cash and credit. Significant weaknesses are the credit shortage for agriculture and the absence of programs to finance housing. New legislation has been prepared for the establishment of a savings and loan system, for which a loan of $12.5 million has been requested from the 

United States to provide seed capital. 

Argentina is seeking a $10 million U.S. loan for seed capital to stimulate the establishment of an agricultural production credit system. This proposal would also provide for a survey and the services of technical advisers. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The steps taken to achieve financial stability have enhanced the climate for private capital and the move toward a free private enterprise system. The Government is also trying to stimulate private investment by according certain tax exemptions. In May 1961 the legislature ratified an investment guarantee agreement with the United States with respect to convertibility, and Argentina recently suggested an extension of the coverage to include expropriation and war risk. Investment guarantees

designed to stimulate the inflow of private capital are contemplated with Germany, Sweden, Austria, and the United Kingdom. 

Private enterprise is now active in the formerly wholly state-operated petroleum industry and has taken over former state railway repair shops and facilities, river-dredging operations, and cross-country buslines. 

In 1958 the oil resources of the country were opened to exploration, by foreign companies reversing the trend of the Peron era and making Argentina substantially self-sufficient in oil. Savings of $280 million annually in foreign exchange are estimated to have resulted from the new petroleum policy. 

11. Labor. The general framework of social legislation for labor enacted during the Peron era was preserved relatively intact after his ouster in 1955. 

Argentina, with a tradition of extensive government involvement in labormanagement affairs, has not had an atmosphere conducive to effective, collective bargaining. Some progress, however, has been made in this field. In 1960 the 

Government approved the Convention of the International Labor Organization (ILO) guaranteeing the right of free trade unionism, i.e., trade unionism without government interference or control. In March 1961 the General Confederation of Labor (CGT), the central organization which had been controlled by the Government, was put under trade union control. In 1961, for the first time in recent labor history, leaders of the CGT and Union Industrial (the national employers' organization) held a round-table conference arranged by the Minister of Labor to discuss labor problems. At the conclusion both sides announced that future meetings would be held to achieve harmonious relations between the employers and unions.

BOLIVIA 

1. General statement.-Bolivia at present faces one of the most difficult economic situations in all of Latin America. Income and educational levels are extremely low, and hunger and diseases are prevalent. The Indian element here is larger in proportion to the total population than in any other Latin American country with the possible exceptions of Peru and Guatemala. Since 

1952 Bolivia has attempted to push forward on a program of reform. including nationalization of the tin mines and agrarian reform. The social and economic condition of the people, however, has improved very little. Self-help measures will be effective only slowly and with persistent and active encouragement. 

Literacy is approximately 30 percent. 

The estimated population in 1962 is 3,600,000. The estimated annual increase in population is 1.4 percent. 

2. Planning. Bolivia has made a beginning at national planning. For some time it has had a national planning and coordinating commission. In July 

1961 a supreme economic council was created to coordinate sector development under the economic plan which was adopted at that time. This plan, which is essentially a 10-year projection of sector goals, was prepared with the assistance of ECLA technicians, and has now been submitted to the OAS panel of experts for review. A preliminary analysis of this plan indicates that it may be overly optimistic in several respects. Realistic planning in Bolivia is hampered by a number of factors, including a lack of reliable information and expert manpower. 

3. Agrarian reform.--Since colonial times there have been great disparities in land ownership in Bolivia. In 1950 three-quarters of the rural population had no rights to the land on which it lived and worked. Since 1953, however, Bolivia has carried out a drastic land reform program. The reform decree of August 

1953 set up six basic objectives: (1) redistribution of land, (2) development of 

Indian communes, (3) improved status of farmworkers, (4) increased agricultural productivity, (5) conservation of natural resources, and (6) promotion of internal migration. Latifundia, defined as extensive holdings of idle or poorly used land, were declared subject to expropriation. The implementation of this law, while tending to alter fundamentally the structure of society, has encountered difficulties, with many unlawful seizures of land and the awarding of land titles being greatly delayed. Between August 1953 and December 31, 1961, about 175,000 titles were issued to heads of families representing 35 to 40 percent of the total rural population. Of these titles 71,000 were issued between 

August 1960 and December 1961.

The redistribution of land at first caused a decline in output, but since 1957 the downward trend has been reversed and notable advances have recently been made in the production of sugar, rice, and corn where external technical and financial support have been provided. Bolivia's national development plan provides for greater assistance to the campesino along technological, economic, and

social lines and the executive branch recently sent to Congress a bill for the revision of the 1953 law, based upon the experience of the past 8 years. 

Bolivia has also been trying since 1954 to promote settlements in the eastern plains, where there is much unused land, in order to relieve population pressures on the Altiplano. So far this movement has not been very successful. Eight settlements have been made in the Santa Cruz area, four of them by people from Altiplano and four by Japanese and Mennonite immigrants. A settlement program was recently initiated in the northern Alto Beni region. 

4. Housing. The need for housing in Bolivia is acute and is increasing especially for the population (the majority) living in the relatively cold Altiplano. The present housing shortage is estimated at nearly 300,000 units. Ac- tually, although the population is increasing, construction activity has been declining. The Government established a housing institute in 1956, and it has begun to do some planning on a national scale, with help from IDB technicians. 

So far it has constructed approximately 1,000 units at an average cost of $1,600. 

5. Health.-Reliable statistics on health and sanitation in Bolivia are seriously lacking. Such data as are available, however, together with general observation, suggests that Bolivia health standards and facilities are below the average for Latin America. The number of inhabitants per doctor, for example, was 

3,900 in 1958, compared with 760 in Argentina and 1,900 in Chile. 

One of the goals of the national economic and social development plan is to supply water under suitable conditions to all cities of more than 2,000 inhabi tants. The plan also proposes to cover one-third of the current sewerage service shortage within 10 years. Bolivia's Ministry of Health is by law responsible for providing the people with the traditional public health facilities, such as environmental hygiene, prevention and control of communicable diseases, material and child welfare, and also general medical assistance. Because of lack of funds and trained personnel as well as other factors, the Ministry is unable to render the services necessary. A reorganization is planned making the central office a relatively small organization capable of carrying out staff functions for the Minister, setting up standards, making field studies, and preparing legislation affecting health matters. 

6. Education.-Literacy in Bolivia is estimated at 30 percent, compared with 

50 to 60 percent for Latin America as a whole. Approximately 6 percent of the population is enrolled in schools, compared to 13 percent for Latin America and nearly 25 percent for the United States. Progress is hampered generally by lack of buildings, and equipment, books, and other supplies and by a shortage of adequately trained teachers. 

The Bolivian Government has made a distinct effort since 1952 to improve educational opportunities. In 1952 a commission was appointed to study the problem. In 1956 a new educational code was promulgated. Between 1951 and 

1956 the percent of the national budget devoted to education rose from 16 to 28 percent. In the past decade the number of school buildings has more than doubled, increasing at a rate of about 250 per year. This school construction has been accomplished mainly by local communities. Also, the number of rural teachers has doubled in the past decade. The rural Indian in Bolivia, representing a large segment of the population, is generally anxious to have his children educated, and often initiates action to this end, which may later be supported by the Government. It must be noted, however, that the current economic condition of Bolivia is a severe limitation on what can be accomplished in the educational field. 

7. Public administration.-The general level of public administration in Bolivia is indicated by the fact that there is no civil service law, no merit system, and no tenure. Salaries are low. Efforts in 1961 to control contraband smuggling and to improve electric power rate administration are hopeful indications but are too recent to evaluate. In the customs field a 1961 law is expected to simplify administration and already some improvements have been made in the auditing of receipts and expenditures. Some improvements have also been made in general tax administration, but competent and adequate personnel are lacking and popular support is not strong. Mechanized procedures have been introduced for payments from the national treasury. Public administration on the whole is a field in which additional self-help measures would be most beneficial. 

8. Financial stability.—Bolivia has had severe inflation over the past decade. the cost-of-living index rising from 100 in 1953 to 3,600 in 1961. The value of the bolíviano declined from 90 to $1 in 1952, to 11,885 to $1 in 1961. This sitution resulted partly from domestic policies stemming from the political and

social revolution which began in 1952. It should be noted, however, that the monetary economy is confined largely, though not exclusively, to urban areas. 

Since 1956 the Bolivian Government has made efforts to achieve greater stability, and with IMF and AID help has succeeded to a point where relative stability has been achieved. 

9. Credit. There is a serious lack of credit throughout the Bolivian economy. 

Both the relevant body of legislation and basic institutions, such as savings banks, are in need of development. Bolivia has made some progress in this field through the national agricultural credit program, which was begun in 1956 and expanded in 1961. Bolivia has requested and received loans from the 

IDB to expand both agricultural and industrial credit. The latter includes $1,700,000 for expanded agricultural credit and $1,100,000 for expanded private industrial credit. The Bolivian Government is now studying the formation of a national industrial development bank. The national development plan provides for a reorganization of the entire banking system. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Although official policy favors the development of private enterprise and encourages both foreign and domestic investment, conditions existing in Bolivia are generally discouraging to private initiative and investment. Tax laws, labor laws, and policy, and credit facilities are not conducive to investment. An investment law of December 1960, which established tax incentives for foreign capital investments and some aspects of the national development plan, such as the reorganization of the banking system, give some hope for improvements in the field. In July 1961 the Central 

Bank of Bolivia increased its interest rate on savings deposits from 7 to 9 percent as a means of stimulating deposits. 

11. Labor. The policy of the Bolivian Government since 1952 has been to strongly support labor organization and benefits to labor. However, job tenure has been such as to reduce incentive to work and has saddled some businesses with an excessive number of employees. Work stoppages have been frequent. 

Improvements in the welfare of labor and in labor-management relations will depend primarily on the improvement in general conditions, rather than in specific labor legislation or reform. However, in 1961 the Bolivian Government took some steps to increase productivity in the state mining corporation including the initiation of a voluntary employee reduction program to eliminate surplus workers and the introduction of foreign management advisers. 

BRAZIL 

Its eco- 1. General statement.-Brazil occupies about 47 percent of the South American Continent and is one of the largest countries of the world. Its land area is almost equal to that of the United States. It has a population of approximately 

70 million, which is expected to increase to about 94 million by 1970. nomic development has been rapid but spotty, with agriculture not generally sharing in the progress. Per capita income in some parts of the country has remained at a very low level, especially in the northeast. Widespread poverty and illiteracy (estimated to be above 50 percent are to be found in both urban and rural areas. The country is beset by economic difficulties and uncertainties that are retarding its continued economic and social development. Inflation, which has recently brought price increases of up to 5 percent monthly, distorts economic development and breeds social unrest. 

The present administration has stated its desire to cooperate in programs of assistance, but until needed self-help measures are undertaken, accomplishments under the alliance for progress will be slow. 

2. Planning. Although Brazil has had long-range sector and regional plans the Government has not had any centralized long-range planning procedure for the country as a whole. Prime Minister Neves has recently taken steps to establish such a mechanism. He has reactivated the planning commission created under President Quadros in August 1961. He has also appointed an emergency committee to decide which projects are to receive priority consideration for help under the Alliance for Progress. The committee's general function is that of selecting those projects which Brazil will propose as an emergency or short-term program for immediate implementation while long-term plans are being developed. Once the emergency planning exercise is completed, the long-term planning group will work on reducing the budget deficit in fiscal year 1962 and draw up a preliminary outline of a 5-year development plan to submit to the next Congress.

3. Agrarian reform.-Both the Government and the public are beginning to realize the difficulties created for general economic growth and social peace by the lack of attention to agriculture. Political observers, therefore, expect favorable congressional action in early 1962 on pending bills for land reform, reorganization of the Ministry of Agriculture, and amendment of the Constitution to permit payment over a period of time for expropriated private lands. 

Of the measures adopted since the Act of Bogotá the most promising was a law passed by the State of São Paulo in December 1960 and made effective in April 1961. The law does not penalize large efficient landholdings, but imposes a progressive land tax to bring unused land into production or encourage its sale and redistribution. The burden of transaction and sales taxes was also lifted on small- and medium-sized farms. (Implementation of the law has been held up because the power to tax rural lands was removed from the States by the Federal Congress and transferred to the municipios-political subdivisions of the States.) The State of São Paulo has since submitted a bill to the legislature to earmark a percentage of certain taxes for the agrarian reform program and has applied to the IDB for a $38 million loan to help carry out the program. 

Other reforms, carried out at the Federal level, emphasize expansion of rural credit facilities. In 1961 the Bank of Brazil started a new system of extending credit to rural areas through means of mobile credit units visiting outlying areas lacking banks. The Government is also considering establishing a Federal rural bank. As a preliminary step for this, the Government has separated the rural and industrial credit from the general credit department of the Bank of Brazil. 

The Brazilian Association for Rural Credit and Assistance, has developed a 5year expansion program, which calls for opening 463 new regional and country extension offices. 

4. Housing.-Brazil has no central housing authority or national housing plan, although some projects for low-income groups have been carried out by the Popular Housing Federation and the Social Security Institute. A bill now in 

Congress proposes a reorganization of the Brazilian Housing Institute (IBH) in order to give it complete authority to plan and execute housing projects for lowincome groups. Housing construction and amelioration of slum conditions figure prominently in Brazilian requests for United States and other foreign assist- The Ministry of Labor and Social Welfare has also established a National Housing Commission to conduct surveys of needs and available resources for low-cost housing projects. ance. 

5. Health. The level of health among the majority of Brazilians approximates that of most Latin American countries. About 25 percent of the deaths are due to enteric diseases. In rural areas water is not potable unless boiled or otherwise treated. The infant mortality rate is about 100 per 1,000 live births. The average life expectancy is 45 years. Hospital facilities and welltrained medical personnel are insufficient in the urban areas and generally unavailable in the rural areas. Forty percent of the physicians live and practice medicine in two cities, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. The Government, with assistance from international agencies, has been gradually improving conditions. 

Brazil has in the past given much attention to community water and sanitation facilities, but the needs are still very great in this field. The special Public 

Health Service Foundation (SESP) has recently been charged with coordinating all organizations constructing and operating water and sanitation services and with supervising technical, administrative, and financial aspects of such projects. 

6. Education.—Ten percent of Federal revenues are, by constitutional provision, reserved for education. States in turn are required to allocate 20 percent of their revenues for the same purpose. The Federal Government took steps in 

1961 to implement a provision of the Constitution which requires that employers of more than 100 people provide elementary education for their employees and dependents. Needs are still far from being covered, however, and additional sources of revenue must be found. There are serious shortages of schools, teachers, and teaching materials. 

Certain States have also embarked on extensive school building programs, notably Rio Grande do Sul, Espirito Santo, Minas Gerais, Guanabara, and São Paulo. In December 1961 the Congress passed a special law (Norms and Bases 

Law) paving the way for revision of rigid curriculums and other reforms. The law also created a 24-man board of consultants to set overall goals and policies for the Ministry of Education and set up State boards of education to control and plan State educational activities. The intent of the law is the development of a school system providing 12 years of universal free education. The Ministry

of Education also has a program for building 7 pilot technical high schools, and establishing vocational training curricula in 300 academic secondary schools within a 5-year period. For 1962 the Ministry has a budget of 960 million cruzeiros for secondary education. At the university level, the Commissao 

Supervisora do Plano dos Institutos (COSUPI) continues its long-range plans to improve the scope and quality of higher education. 

7. Public administration.-Brazil is making efforts, with the cooperation of the United States, in several projects designed to achieve improvements in (1) financial management, including tax administration, (2) personnel administration, (3) organization and methods, and (4) city planning. Although there have been delays because of two changes in Government in the past year, some progress has been made. 

8. Financial stability.—Under the Quadros administration a financial stabilization program was undertaken in connection with which multiple-exchange rates were eliminated, new large balance-of-payments credits were extended, and Brazil's foreign debts were rescheduled; however, it was not fully implemented and did not succeed in curbing the rate of inflation. The dislocations caused by the resignation of President Quadros in August 1961 led to a considerable flight of capital as well as a substantial reduction in the rate of new foreign investment. The present administration has proposed establishing a central bank so that lending operations can be coordinated with Government monetary policies, and has charged the emergency planning committee with the task of trying to reduce the budgetary deficit for 1962, which is forecast to be about 250 billion cruzeiros, 115 billion more than in 1961. 

9. Credit. During the last decade Brazil has had a fairly good supply of credit for expansion in business and industry, but there has been a general lack of credit institutions in the rural sector. Although the supervised credit system of the Brazilian Association for Rural Credit and Assistance (ABCAR) helped more than 2,000 rural families in 1960 with credits totaling more than 100 million cruzeiros, the operation is far smaller than that needed. To remedy this situation, ABCAR has developed a 5-year expansion program, approved by the Government, which calls for opening 463 new extension offices. In 1961 the Bank of Brazil started a new system of extending credit to rural areas through means of mobile credit units.

The Government has already separated the rural and industrial credit from the general credit department of the Bank of Brazil. In the housing sector, the 

Federal savings banks are set up to provide mortgage funds for middle income housing, but the inflation has limited the volume of their operations. Congress has under consideration a law setting up financial apparatus through the Federal Real Estate Bank or the Federal Housing Association to make credit available for second mortgage financing of home purchases. Some mechanism is still needed to coordinate the Government's credit policies with its stabilization policies. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-At present the outlook for foreign investment and private enterprise in Brazil is not encouraging. Inflow of private capital amounted to over $200 million in 1959 and about $135 million in 1960. 

Indications are that this flow has been seriously affected since the end of 1961 by the political crisis in August, the profits remittance bill passed by the Chamber of Deputies in November 1961, and the expropriation of I.T. & T. properties in the 

State of Rio Grande do Sul in February 1962. 

11. Labor.-In spite of the rapid increase in industrialization during the past 

20 years, working conditions in Brazil remain relatively poor and wages have failed to keep pace with the rising cost of living. Labor management relations have been stabilized to some extent by strict Government control; but, while this method has reduced work stoppages, it has probably not provided the best incentive for productive effort.

The principal body of legislation affecting labor was enacted during the 15 years of Vargas' first presidency (1930-45). This legislation established a state-controlled syndical system which is the basis of Brazil's present form of labor organization. The 1943 labor code provided that strikes could be legally called only when authorized by the appropriate court. In March 1946 the 

Government enacted a law which stated that a strike or lockout could be authorized only in the event of the failure of the opposing party to obey a labor tribunal award. In the constitution of 1946 the right to strike was clearly stated, though made subject to regulation by law. The 1943 and 1946 laws remain in force. However, since no legislation has been enacted to implement the 1946 constitution, labor unions have not exercised much freedom in labor

management relations. Recently the labor movement has begun to gather strength among rural workers, particularly in the northeast part of Brazil. 

There have been no significant changes in labor legislation by the Federal Government since the Act of Bogotá. CHILE 1. General statement.-Chile is more advanced than most Latin American countries in the enactment and implementation of legislation designed to further economic development, and in the enactment of social legislation designed mainly for the benefit of urban and industrial workers. During the past 2 years the present administration has succeeded to a large degree in slowing down the presistent, and at times virulent, inflation that has plagued the country for 10 years. Although some tentative steps have been taken in the direction of tax and land reforms no substantial changes have as yet been made in these fields. Literacy in Chile is about 80 percent. The population in 1962 is estimated at approximately 7,800,000, with a growth rate of 2.6 percent per annum. 

2. Planning.-Chile has developed greater expertise in development planning than most countries in Latin America. A 10-year development plan for the period 1961-70 was completed in January 1961 by the Chilean Development Corporation (CORFO), which established in November 1961 a department to implement it. This plan has been submitted for review to both the IBRD and the nine-man panel of the OAS. The plan calls for investments of about $10 billion over 10 years, about 80 percent from Chile's own resources. Over 23 percent of this investment would go into housing, schools, hospitals, and water supplies and sewerage. It establishes definite targets for the 10-year period including: (a) an average annual growth rate of 5.45 percent of GNP representing an increase of 2.9 percent of per capita GNP; (b) an increase in consumption of 4.4 percent per annum; and (c) an average annual rate of increase in investment of 9.2 percent resulting in an increase of the investment rate from its historical level of less than 10 percent of GNP to 17.9 percent in the final year of the plan.

While these targets appear somewhat ambitious, the plan explores rather carefully the role and interdependency of the various economic sectors. The plan is in fact an overall analytical framework for Chile's economic development, rather than a fully elaborated ready-to-go action program complete with projects. 

3. Agarian reform.-Chile's agricultural sector has not received the attention it merits due to a national policy oriented toward promotion of industrial development. Lack of agricultural growth inhibits manufacturing development and keeps most of the rural population at a subsistence level. The low productivity of agriculture also contributes to Chile's continuing inflation and serious balance-of-payments difficulties. While underuse of as much as half of Chile's arable land is linked to the concentration of land ownership, it also reflects Government policies favoring industry. Agrarian reform to raise the depressed level of two-thirds of the rural population is now supported by most of the political parties and the church, and pressures are building up from both rural and urban labor. It is opposed, however, by the far right and some conservative elements.

Prior to the Bogotá Conference, Chile's efforts toward agrarian reform were not vigorous. Progress since the Conference has consisted largely of improved planning, contracting of new foreign loans for agriculture, and introduction of a constitutional amendment permitting deferred payment over 10 years (in cash) for expropriated land. The legislature, which convened in March, is expected to consider a land reform bill. 

4. Housing.-Chile is confronted with a serious housing shortage. The earthquake and tidal wave in May 1960 destroyed 58,000 housing units and seriously damaged another 117,000 units. The housing deficit is now estimated to be around 400,000 units. An additional 38,000 units annually will be required during the next few years to provide housing for the increasing population and to replace rundown units. CORVI has substantially increased construction of housing during the past few years. In the period 1953-58 only 14,434 houses were built, whereas during the next 3 years (1959-61) 69,389 were built. 

With U.S. grants for reconstruction, 3 low-cost housing developments built by 

CORVI have been completed with a total of 844 housing units; 2 housing projects with a total of 898 units are nearly completed; and 1,074 units in other projects are underway. The Fundacion de Vivienda y Asistencia Social has made a good 81496-62-pt. 3- -9

pilot effort in the construction of rural housing with funds made available by the United States. The savings and loan association system, established in 1961, has made more than $500,000 in loans for home construction. 

5. Health.-Chile's public health and sanitation programs are above the average for Latin America. A fairly broad public health service was established, particularly in urban areas, soon after the advent of the Popular Front (center radical) Government in 1938. U.S. assistance resulted in the creation in 1952 of a new Chilean National Health Service and the establishment of a school of public health, which today is a regional training center with half of the student body coming from other Latin American countries. The United States-Chilean 

Health "Servicio" built, equipped, and operated for varying periods of time, five demonstration health centers. Based on that experience, the National Health 

Service has established eight additional health centers throughout Chile. This institution today operates 175 hospitals, and 427 outpatient clinics, medical centers, and rural medical clinics. There are four medical schools in Chile each having a 7-year curriculum. The licensing of medical personnel is closely controlled. Medical facilities and personnel, however, are concentrated primarily in the central provinces, especially in the area of Santiago. 

6. Education. The rate of literacy in Chile is among the highest in Latin 

America. Primary education is deficient, however, with a great number of the rural and low-income urban school population barely finishing three grades and remaining semi-illiterate. Schooling is compulsory for children between the ages of 7 and 15, but some 170,000 school-age children each year go without schooling due to lack of sufficient schools. Technical and manual arts training is still in its infancy, and agricultural training is poorly developed. There is a realization of the need for improving opportunities for elementary education and for changing the character of professional training and preparing people with new skills. 

The Government increased expenditures for education from 9 percent of the budget or $67 million in 1959 to 14 percent or $129 million in 1961. The President of Chile in his message to the Chilean Congress in May 1961 and in a later message listed the following measures that had been adopted: (1) The Housing Corporation (CORVI) has undertaken construction of school units in all localities covered by its program; (2) New positions for teachers and principals have been added, making possible an increase in elementary school enrollment of more than 112,000 students; (3) To meet the needs arising from the 1960 earthquake, the Sociedad Constructora de Establecimiento Educacional undertook construction of 74 schools, thereby increasing the number of buildings to be constructed by that agency to 40 percent over the number built in 1959; (4) Three new high schools increased secondary enrollment by about 4,000 pupils ; (5) The Arica plan was initiated to carry out effective reform from the elementary level on, in an attempt to direct students along the lines of their natural or vocational aptitudes. To this end it is planned to establish schools specializing in such subjects as the humanities, science, industry, commerce, and agriculture.

In addition to these efforts aimed at improving education in Chile, the country's overall requirements need to be examined on a systematic basis. For example, the manpower needs for Chilean economic development need to be correlated with the 10-year plan. 

7. Public administration.-Chile has made some progress in improving admin. istration in the Ministry of Labor and under the United States-Chilean Cooperative Agricultural Servicio Agreement, which will be terminated in December 1962, there is a continuing inservice program for training the Chilean staff. The Ministry of Agriculture was reorganized in 1960, with a major emphasis on the decentralization of operations. As a result of U.S. assistance starting in June 1961, Chile has increased the allotted funds and personnel for the tax administration unit in the Internal Revenue Service and with U.S. assistance established a tax administration school in which 100 officials will have completed training by the summer of 1962. The Government is currently reorganizing the Internal Revenue Service in order to improve tax collections and to prevent evasion of taxes. 

8. Financial stability.-After two decades of increasingly severe inflation, the present administration was successful in slowing down considerably the rise in price level in 1960-61 while holding the foreign exchange rate constant. For example, price rises, which had amounted to over 30 percent in 1958-59, were

held to 6 percent in 1960 and 10 percent in 1961. However, in part because of the effects of the earthquake devastation of 1960, new inflationary pressures have been released which threaten both domestic price stability and Chile's foreign trade, with a resulting serious effect on Chile's balance-of-payments position. During the past several years the Chilean fiscal budget (including the 1962 budget) has shown a trend toward increasing public expenditures and increasing budget deficits. Unless the current projected deficit of at least $300 million can be reduced, through increased fiscal receipts and through reduction of unessential Government expenses, there could be renewed inflation this year with serious consequences. 

9. Credit. The Central Savings and Loan Fund, which was established in 

January 1961, will insure mortgage loans granted by private savings and loan associations and will refinance them. By the end of 1961, 15 private savings and loan associations had been formed and are now channeling private savings into housing for the low and lower medium income classes. The Banco del 

Estado has adopted needed loan regulations, procedures, and criteria for a supervised agricultural credit program. The Government is negotiating with the 

IDB for a loan of $10 million for the purpose of establishing a loan program for about 10,000 small farmers. The Chilean Development Corporation (CORFO) finances the establishment of new semipublic industries. The commercial banking system concentrates primarily on financing, foreign and domestic trade by granting short-term credit to the larger firms at very high interest rates (19 percent). There are as yet no adequate credit facilities for small- and mediumsize industries, or for farmers with small holdings. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.—A foreign investment decree law of 

April 1960 was issued for the purpose of stimulating foreign investment. This law, similar to an earlier one, extends benefits to new industries using a high percentage of Chilean raw materials and to those set up primarily to produce goods for export. It retains, however, the system whereby each investment must be processed through lengthy and arduous inspection before receiving special consideration. Because it does not substantially change the situation previously faced by foreign investors it may not stimulate a large immediate wave of new foreign private investment. Although the 10-year development program calls for a measure of centralized planning of investments in the private sector and detailed guidance of the economy by public regulations, it attempts to preserve the basic elements of free private enterprise. The Government is encouraging private sector investment, curtailing Government activities when possible. An investment guarantee agreement with the United States covering convertibility became effective February 15, 1961. 

11. Labor.-Chilean labor is relatively well organized. It has generally been strongly critical of the United States and has an influential Communist minority element. The Government has had established for some time a complex and generous social security system. However, the labor law, which was codified in 1931, is presently complicated, conflicting, and in some respects archaic. 

Chile's 10-year plan calls for extensive assistance through the Ministry of Labor in the areas of labor inspection and enforcement procedures, research and labor statistics, manpower, labor marketing, labor relations, employment services, and social administration. 

COLOMBIA 

1. General statement.-For more than a decade Colombia has been passing through serious difficulties due to social and economic friction and, to some extent, traditional issues of party rivalry. Civil violence has been a major problem. At the same time industrialization has been proceeding rapidly, although Colombia is still primarily an agricultural country, with coffee as its chief product. Colombia has made initial efforts in the past few years to improve public administration and planning and to terminate the strife that has prevailed. Heavy investments have been made in communication facilities thereby achieving a better balanced and more integrated development of the various regions. A 4-year public investment program has been prepared. An agrarian reform law was enacted in November 1961. Public revenues currently represent one-fifth of national income and in 1960 investment expenditures were reported to represent 40 percent of total Government spending. Assuming continued political stability, Colombia may be expected to undertake satisfactory self-help measures. It should be noted, however, that critical national elections are scheduled in 1962.

The estimated population for 1962 is about 15,600,000 and by 1970 it is expected to be nearly 20 million, an increase of 2.8 percent per annum. Illiteracy is estimated to be about 40 percent. 

2. Planning.-Colombia has a Department of Planning and Technical Serv ices which has recently completed a 10-year development plan, covering both public and private sectors of the economy. It calls for the expenditure of about $8 billion, the major portion of which is to be supplied by Colombia itself. The adopted target growth rate in GNP is 5.6 percent per annum or about 2.8 percent annually on a per capita basis. The plan incorporates Colombia's 4-year public investment program (1961-64), which projects capital expenditures of the National Government, the municipalities, and decentralized state enterprises. 

The 10-year plan is currently under review by the OAS committee of experts. (Colombia was the first country to submit its plan to this group for review.) 

3. Agrarian reform.—Lack of technical skills and shortages of credit, marketing facilities, and modern transportation retard agricultural expansion, but an uneconomic land ownership pattern is also one of the blocks to Colombian development. The 8,000 largest estates, less than 1 percent of total farms, occupy about 40 percent of the presently utilized agricultural area. Large amounts of the most fertile and accessible land, mainly in the valleys, is held by absentee owners and is left idle, while a majority of the peasants barely subsist on the hillsides. The first agrarian reform law was passed in 1922, but action was diverted from parcelization to colonization. A 1957 law promised to provide for the parcelization of underused land but became ineffective when land in unimproved pasture was considered to be cultivated. 

A new agrarian reform law was passed in November 1961. It provides the basis for a major parcelization of underused rich lands in accessible areas, with the objective of setting up family farm units. It also provides for the establishment of an Agrarian Reform Institute and would further encourage colonization. The institute's principal functions are to administer and award unused land, exercise control over land ownership and management, cooperate in preparation of tax surveys, promote, assist, or directly construct feeder and access roads, conduct reforestation operations, and assist in drainage and irrigation projects. The effectiveness of this program will depend on political and administrative decisions and on available financial resources. 

4. Housing. The principal agency in the low-cost housing field is the Territorial Credit Institute (ICT). In 1961, through its assistance, an estimated 

20,000 units were constructed. For 1962-65 the goal of ICT is to construct 

112,000 units. Other organizations participating with official support are the 

Military Housing Bank, the Popular Housing Bank, the Central Mortgage

Bank, and the Federation of Coffee Growers. Commercial banks and many industrial concerns are also implementing housing programs for their employees. 

The various plans together call for the addition of 30,000 housing units per annum by 1964. In consideration of an estimated backlog of current needs of 

250,000 dwelling units and rapid expansion of the urban population, plus the fact that approximately five-sixths of existing rural housing units are unacceptable from a sanitary point of view, the 30,000 target is still far short of the pressing requirements. 

5. Health. The most severe health and sanitation problems are found in rural areas, but city dwellers are also plagued by malnutrition and disease, a situation which is aggravated by the movement of population from rural to urban areas. According to available statistics, Colombia has the greatest number of cases of typhoid fever, smallpox, yellow fever, and hookworm in the Western Hemisphere. The infant mortality rate in 1959 was 96.0 per 1,000 live births as against about 26 in the United States. Life expectancy was only 46 years.

Colombia has now embarked on a major health program with the assistance of various international agencies and both the Rockefeller and Kellogg Foundations. The United States has been giving assistance in this field since 1942, but none of the cooperative programs has been on a sufficiently broad scale greatly to reduce the incidence of disease. Colombia's investment plan (196164) calls for the expenditure of $40 million for 7,000 new general hospital beds and 4,000 new TB hospital beds. About $70 million is to be spent on water and sewerage facilities. The Ministry of Health plans the establishment of a network of health services in all departments (provinces) of Colombia. 

The Municipal Development Institute, the principal Colombian institution for the expansion of water supply and sewerage services, invested in its first 3 years (1958-60) 113.4 million pesos (nearly $10 million) in water systems and 

20.7 million pesos (about $1.8 million) in sewerage projects.

6. Education.-Colombia's educational system has serious shortcomings but an impressive effort is being made to bring about improvement. In 1960 nearly 

30 percent of school-age children were not enrolled in any school. Colombia has relied very largely on private institutions above the elementary level. For example, only 25 percent of secondary school students attend public schools. 

The largest industrial education program is handled by the National Service of Apprenticeships (SENA) whose funds come from contributions of private companies and whose students are selected by the contributing companies. It is notable that in 1960 this program was supported by approximately 15,000 companies. Even though Colombia has 26 universities, each year some 8,500 graduates of secondary education are not able to receive advanced education. 

In general, there is a shortage of trained professors, and the curriculums are not fully in tune with the social and economic requirements of the country. 

The National Ministry of Education has a 4-year plan designed to raise the level of primary education. Its aim is to construct 22,000 classrooms, organize and equip 4 normal schools, prepare 9,000 new teachers through normal school training and to upgrade 11,000 present teachers and 3,000 administrators and supervisors, and to purchase and produce instructional materials and books. 

The objective is to provide at least 5 years of schooling for each child. The high illiteracy rate and the accelerated increase of the Colombian population in recent years has caused special emphasis to be given to primary education. 

More than three-fifths of all expenditures in the educational field are for primary education. 

7. Public administration.-The Government of Colombia established a Commission for Administrative Reform in February 1959 and a Civil Service Commission in April 1959. Presently these agencies are engaged in an administrative reorganization of the entire governmental structure and in the establishment of a Government career service. The National Administrative Reform Commission is actively engaged in the review of legislation initiated by the executive branch and specialized studies in the customs and postal areas. 

8. Financial stability.-Government policies in the monetary and external financial fields were particularly effective in maintaining stability between mid- 1957 and mid-1960. Inflation was reduced and balance of payments surpluses were achieved, permitting the repayment of large amounts of accumulated shortterm foreign debt. However, relaxation in monetary budget and import policies resulted in marked price increases in 1961 and a difficult balance of payments problem. The implementation of a development plan aimed at accelerated growth may reveal a basic balance of payments problem for several years to come unless strong new exports can be developed to supplement coffee. 

9. Credit. The Central Bank is pursuing a policy of encouraging industrial and agricultural credit. It has, for example, sparked industrial credit with 5year loans at 8 to 10 percent interest and it has authority to determine that a fixed percentage of total available credit be used for agricultural loans. The agricultural credit bank and the commercial banks must use a certain credit quota on a quarterly determination for agricultural purposes (fertilizer, equipment, seed and supplies). In addition, the Government is promoting the establishment of private financial corporations by according certain credit privileges and tax concessions. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Colombian Government investment outlays have been increasing appreciably in relation to current expenditures. In 

1958, investment expenditures represented 28 percent of total Government spending. In 1960, they were reported to account for about 40 percent of the total. At the same time the Government is promoting the establishment of private financial corporations by according certain credit privileges and tax concessions. United States direct private investment in Colombia of somewhat over $400 million and U.S. exports to Colombia of about $300 million per year rank about sixth or seventh in the scale of investment in and exports to the various Latin American countries. 

11. Labor.-Colombia's labor force comprises a little more than one-half of the country's relatively young population and includes a large number of women and children. Colombia's Labor Code, which was promulgated in December 1950, recognizes the right of both urban and rural labor to form trade unions, to bargain collectively, and to strike. A Social Security Act, passed in 

1946, provides health, maternity, old-age, and survivor benefits on a tripartite contributory basis, but many of the programs have yet to be fully implemented.

Workers in the larger industrial and commercial firms have been the chief beneficiaries of the program thus far. Hours and conditions of work are controlled for a limited number of workers, chiefly in the urban areas. 

COSTA RICA 

1. General statement. The population of Costa Rica, about 1,200,000 people concentrated in the central upland, is growing_at the rate of 4.3 percent per year probably the highest such growth rate in Latin America. Costa Rica has a fairly well developed middle class and the level of education is relatively high. 

Literacy is estimated at 88 percent. The estimated average annual growth of GNP is 3.4 percent, somewhat less than the rate of population growth. 

Nevertheless, the per capita GNP of $337 in 1959 was substantially higher than that of neighboring countries. Fuels are imported and extensive oil exploration has been disappointing, but hydroelectric power potential is high. Costa 

Rica already has more installed electric power capacity than any of the other Central American countries. Most of the industries are of small scale, confined to light consumer-type goods, including foodstuffs, footwear, and wearing apparel. Although the domestic market is limited, Costa Rica has been reluctant to participate in the Central American integration movement, and so far has not joined it. 

2. Planning. Some planning has been done in various sectors but without such plans having been integrated into an overall coordinated plan with targeted objectives. However, there is a National Production Council (NPS), an autonomous agency largely responsible for price stabilization, for development programs for basic consumption items, and for promoting the processing of products and the utilization of byproducts. This agency carries out its work in close collaboration with the Banco Nacional de Costa Rica, the Ministries of Agriculture and Industry, and three other banks. (All banks have been nationalized for several years.) The NPC's operations have been flexible and have adjusted to new conditions as they have developed. 

An year all-weather national highway and feeder road development program has been planned and the legislature approved the first phase for implementation on February 4, 1961. This is being financed by the Government of 

Costa Rica and by loans of $5.5 million from the IBRD and $5.5 million from IDA. 

A long-range program of urban and rural electrification has been planned through 1971. A hydroelectric plant is being built with a potential of 120,000 kilowatts and is being financed partly by Costa Rica and partly with an $8.8 million IBRD loan. 

3. Agrarian reform.-In November 1959 the department of land colonies and rural credits was established in the National Bank to finance land distribution and settlement. This program has been assisted by a loan from the IBRD. 

In October 1961 general agrarian reform policy was established in a law of lands and settlement, which provided for a program to be administered by the National Bank. (In late 1961 the DLF authorized a $5 million loan for agricultural development.) One objective of the new agrarian program is to give security of tenure to the large number of squatters and farm laborers. Tax measures are provided to encourage subdivision of land, thereby stimulating diversification of agriculture. Such land as is expropriated is to be paid for with Government bonds at prices not to exceed the value declared by the owner on his tax return. 

4. Housing.-In June 1961 the National Housing Agency, which was set up in 

1954 to promote construction and loans for middle-class housing, was given additional authority to initiate slum clearance. It reorganized its savings and loan operation, placing emphasis on a program to provide houses for lower income groups through a salary deduction plan. 

There is a recognized need in Costa Rica for new or replacement construction for 98,000 housing units. The Housing Agency (INVU) has had 6 years of experience in the construction field and has acquired large land reserve (about 4 million square meters) for future construction programs. The objective of the program is to construct 38,000 homes in 20 years, but it is questionable whether this goal can be achieved without additional financing. (Costa Rica received a housing loan of $3.5 million in late 1961 from IDB's Social Progress Trust Fund.) 

5. Health. The life expectancy in Costa Rica is 60 years, higher than that of other Central American countries. The number of people per physician is 2,800, equal to Nicaragua, but better than for most of the other Central American

countries. About 98 percent of the urban and 50 percent of the rural population have water service. However, only the San Jose area has potable water, and this is limited in quantity during the dry seasons. In the case of San Jose and its metropolitan area a study was made with financial assistance from ICA. This was the basis for a 1962 AID loan of $3.5 million and a $4.5 million Eximbank loan for a water supply system for the capital and its surrounding area. Preliminary to the loan, there was established in April 1961 a National Water and Sewerage System as a semiautonomous agency. The agency administers and supervises all aspects, technical and administrative and financial of these services, and sets the rates. This project is expected to solve the water supply problem in the metropolitan area until 1980. 

6. Education.-Literacy in Costa Rica is estimated at 88 percent, which compares with 50-60 percent for all Latin America and is considerably higher than that of neighboring countries. About 20 percent of the population is enrolled in primary, secondary, and vocational schools, which is higher than the Latin American average. In 1960 the Government devoted about 30 percent of its national budget to current education, operation expenses, school construction, and university expansion. In proportion to its budget Costa Rica makes a larger allocation for educational purposes than any other Latin American country. A school of medicine was recently opened; and the University of Costa Rica is leading a movement to establish higher education on a regional basis in Central America. An increased inheritance and death tax law was recently passed to provide additional funds for university development. 

Plans have been developed to augment elementary school facilities by improving and adding to existing school building and by constructing new schools over a 10-year period. External financing will probably be required to complete this program. 

7. Public administration.—The proliferation of autonomous agencies with separate budgets as well as inadequate budget practices of the regular Government offices call for a thorough overhaul of the present methods of budgeting and auditing. The Costa Rican Government and the U.S. AID mission are cooperating in a public administration project which will place stress on planning, programing, budgeting, taxation, and other policy areas of the Government. The 

Central Bank has been making a study of Government finances on taxation which will be the basis for future major policy decisions. Income and property tax reforms are expected to be introduced this year, broadening the base and increasing land taxes on properties adjacent to Government highways. 

8. Financial stability.-The cost-of-living index which was 113 in 1958 rose to 

114 by the end of 1960 and 115 by October 1961. However, gold and foreign exchange reserves which reached a peak of $24.6 million in early 1959 have shown serious deterioration, reaching a low of $3.7 million by the end of August 1961. 

By February 1962 reserves had risen to about $17 million. The decrease in reserves reflected lowered foreign exchange earnings resulting from a break in coffee, banana, and cocoa prices and an increase in imports. The rate of exchange which has remained the same for over 10 years-except for a downward revision of the export rate in September 1961 when a standby agreement was concluded with the International Monetary Fund. 

9. Credit. There appears to be a general shortage of credit available for the stimulation of agriculture and industry. The National Bank is the prime source of financial policy and there has been very little political interference in its decisions. The nationalized commercial banks suffer from lack of the stimulus of competition. With main interests being short-term coffee and other crop loans, they are weak in the industrial field. Under consideration is the establishment of a development bank to be financed in part by an international lending agency. Additional credit resources could be expected if Costa Rica were to participate in the Central American program for economic integration. Its membership in CAPEI would qualify it for loans for regional projects as well as offer the opportunity of expanded markets in the region. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The GNP grew at an annual rate of over 8 percent during the period 1950-56, but dropped to about 4 percent during the years 1957-61. This decrease reflects the break in coffee, banana, and cocoa prices, which had a serious multiplier effect throughout the economy. Since the population is growing at about 4.3 percent a year, there has been no net per capita gain in the GNP in the past few years. 

Costa Rica has taken several steps which should encourage potential investors. 

An Investment Guarantee Agreement with the United States was signed in 1955.

A law of industrial protection and development was passed in 1959. As indicated above, consideration is being given to the establishment of an industrial development bank, which is needed to provide medium- and long-term loans. 

11. Labor.-A social security system, established in 1943, guarantees the protection of workers against risks of illness, disability, maternity, old age, death, and other contingencies determined by law. Coverage has been increased considerably in the past 4 years. With few exceptions the existing labor organizations suffer from a chronic lack of effective leadership, financial stringency, indifference on the part of the membership, and a negative attitude on the part of management. 

A National Employment Service in the Ministry of Labor was established in May 1960 but has not become fully effective because of lack of funds and personnel. Also established recently is an apprenticeship program in the Ministry of Labor. It provides training in 19 different trades in various private industries and shops, vocational schools, the School for Industrial Training and in the Radio and Television Institute. The program receives support not only from the 

Public Works Department and the National Production Council, but also from some large private enterprises. The program appears to have promise of success. 

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC 

The Dominican Republic is predominantly an agricultural country with about 60 percent of the population engaged in farming. Much of the agricultural land was owned by the Trujillo family and close associates until the Government confiscated it in late 1961. There are wide inequalities in the distribution of income. Consumption by the masses is limited to bare necessities. The popu- lation is composed principally of a mixed race of Europeans and Africans (70 percent mulatto; 10 percent Negro; 20 percent white). The principal strains are comprised of the descendants of the early Spanish colonists and of the Negro slaves imported from Africa. For 31 years the country was under the dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo, who was assassinated in May 1961. The estimated population is 3 million and it is believed to be growing by about 3.7 percent annually. 

Literacy is reported to be approximately 43 percent. 

In September 1961 the Dominican Republic applied and was accepted for readmission into the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and the associated International Finance Corporation (IFC), organizations from which Trujillo had withdrawn in December 1960. At the request of the Government, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has sent a mission to advise and consult with it on external and internal monetary policy. A National Planning Board was formed in March 1962 for guiding the nation's economy and formulating projects which might qualify for assistance under the Alliance for Progress. It has requested advice from the OAS with respect to development planning, fiscal policy, fiscal administration and national income. 

The Inter-American Development Bank is providing consultants in agricultural credit, power and irrigation, housing and potable water systems to prepare the way for consideration of loans in these fields. The present Government has been in power effectively only since January 1962, and a series of political disturbances complicated by lack of adequate economic direction have prevented it from fully formulating concrete economic and social programs.
