While programs for social changes in the fields of agrarian reform, housing, and education are under active consideration and the Government has indicated willingness to proceed with reasonable reforms as soon as possible the capacity for self-help is somewhat limited by present conditions and the fact that general elections will be held in December 1962. ECUADOR 1. General statement.-Ecuador lies astride the equator on the Pacific side of South America, but much of it is in the chilly Andean highlands. It has unusual extremes of climate and great difficulties in transportation and communication. The population is about 4,500,000, literacy is estimated at about 

60 percent, and the rate of population growth at 3 percent per annum. About two-fifths of the population is Indian, with about the same proportion being Mestizo. Health, educational, and income levels are below the average for 

Latin America. In the past decade and particularly since the Bogotá Conference in 1960, Ecuador has shown a disposition to take greater initiative in development measures and programs. It has a national planning board, is studying agrarian reform, and has maintained a remarkable degree of financial stability.

2. Planning. Ecuador has had a National Planning Board since 1954 and some progress has been made in terms of surveys and preliminary plans. Since 

1961 it has been directly responsible to the President, has had additional funds, and has had authority to pass on ministerial budgets. A temporary 2-year plan of development, was announced in May 1961 and the Board is now developing a longer range 5-year plan. Programing for development is handicapped by a lack of reliable economic and social data, a lack of trained personnel to develop specific sector programs, and administrative difficulties. 

3. Agrarian reform. More than two-thirds of Ecuador's population depend on agriculture for a livelihood. Yet rapid development of farm output is extremely difficult because of the limited areas of fertile and presently accessible land and the prospect of weak markets for export crops such as bananas and cacao in which Ecuador has a competitive advantage. 

In the coastal area, land is available for those with the ambition and perseverance to clear and plant it. In the Sierra, population pressures on the limited land resource are heavy. In this area technological backwardness, poor worker health, and lack of capital as well as an uneconomic tenure pattern, greatly retard current production. Neither large estates nor small plots in the Sierra are managed efficiently: modern technology is not used; output is far below potential and considerable land is actually idle on the large estates. 

Distributing small plots to Indian families would help relieve the social pressures. Resources are not available, however, to pay more than token amounts as compensation for land redistributed because of the generally low productivity of Sierra land. Ecuador has tried token colonization schemes, but they have not generally been effective. Tacit recognition of squatters' rights along new roads in the coastal region has been a more efficient and cheaper means of opening new areas. Ex-President Velasco introduced an agrarian reform measure in Congress where it was stalemated in committee. A new agrarian reform law is now being studied and President Arosemena has promised to seek revision of laws affecting rural labor. 

4. Housing. Many of the country's health problems would be improved by widespread housing reforms. Except in the capital city of Quito and in a few residential areas of the industrial port city of Guayaquil, most of the population lives in earthen-floored crude houses or, in the tropical regions, in bamboo shacks on stilts. A division within the Ministry of Social Welfare has had the responsibility of housing but its staff and funds have been limited. 

A National Housing Institute was authorized in 1961 and the Government has obligated $5 million of its social security funds against another $5 million of DLF loan funds in support of a housing bank. The Housing Institute, with help from AID, plans to establish a program of self-help housing construction throughout Ecuador. The Housing Institute is now functioning. The Housing 

Bank and related savings and loan institutions are expected to begin operations sometime in 1962. The first self-help housing units will be built during 1962. 

However, for some time to come the population will probably grow more rapidly than new housing quarters. 

5. Health.-Significant progress has been made in Ecuador in the past decade in the control of disease, with major assistance from the United States and the U.N. The incidence of malaria and tuberculosis has been greatly reduced, and yaws and pinta have been nearly eradicated. Twenty major water and sewage systems has been constructed since 1950. In 1961 the total investment in health activities was $2,369,000. Of this amount, Ecuador provided 59 percent, the United States 26 percent, and international organizations 15 percent. 

Ecuadoran efforts have been handicapped by lack of a Ministry of Health to coordinate efforts in this field. 

6. Education.-The National Planning Board estimates that Ecuador needs 

2,000 additional primary schools and 4,800 additional teachers to provide for 200,000 children (25 percent of those of primary school age) who were not in school according to a 1960 count. Of the approximately 14,000 teachers now in primary schools, 4,000 have not graduated from either secondary or normal schools. Secondary and higher educational opportunities are also seriously lacking. Ecuador's educational system, however, has expanded significantly in the past decade with 90 percent more children enrolled and 64 percent more buildings available. Since the Bogotá Conference the portion of the national budget allocated to education has increased from about 10 percent to approximately 17 percent for 1962. Ecuador is planning to more than double its contribution to AID supported educational projects, increasing the amount from the equivalent of $507,000 in 1962 to the equivalent of $1,123,000 in 1963.

7. Public administration.-Ecuador is greatly in need of more and better trained administrators and technicians. It has no civil service system with merit and tenure provisions, and wages of nearly all Government employees are low.

Problems of organization and procedures also impede effective administration.

Some advances have been made in recent years. For example, the Ministry of the Treasury has created a Central Organization and Methods Office, the Controller is establishing an accounting system and procedures staff, and the universities have added courses in public administration. The Government and universities have requested help from the United States in improving training in public administration. 

8. Financial stability.—Although its cost of living indices are not fully reliable, it is significant that data available show no great change over the past 8 years. 

The Central Bank, the chief monetary instrumentality of the Government, has maintained a good record for financial stability. 

9. Credit. The banking system in Ecuador is relatively new and bank credit is in short supply for all elements of the economy. The existing system is oriented toward real estate development and building construction. A national development banking system was organized in 1947 and a National Housing Bank utilizing over $5 million in social security funds was organized in 1961. (See housing.) The 1961 legislation also provided for 12 savings and loan institutions. 

One of these has been organized with AID assistance, and opened in Quito, the capital city. The Housing Bank has secured capital but is not yet operating. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Investment as a percent of gross national product is estimated at 15 percent, a rate that is high in comparison with other underdeveloped countries in Latin America. Over the past decade it is estimated that 64 percent of investment expenditures were undertaken by the private sector. Lack of domestic commercial credit, however, has been an obstacle to business and industrial growth. Ecuador has an investment guarantee agreement with the United States. The increased influence of the industryminded National Planning Board and the complete assumption of the financing of the Industrial Development Center by Ecuador, which was previously shared by the United States, are indicators of self-help in this field. 

11. Labor.-The Ecuadoran Government has not yet developed a program favorable to the establishment of a strong and healthy labor movement. It is presently collaborating with AID in the establishment of two labor centers, one in each of the two major cities, Quito and Guayaquil. Labor organizations in Ecuador has suffered severe infiltration by Communists. 

EL SALVADOR 

1. General statement.-El Salvador is the smallest of the Central American 

Republics. It has a population estimated at 2,700,000 and this is expected to increase to about 3,200,000 by 1970. The population density is about 127 persons per square kilometer (compared with a Central American average of about 25 per square kilometer) makes it the most densely populated continental American country. Coffee and cotton are the country's principal export products, accounting in 1960 for 66 and 14 percent of exports, respectively. 

A small, wealthy, and sophisticated upper class has traditionally dominated the economic, social, and political life of the country, while the great mass of the people has lived at an extremely low economic level, with a marked lack of social organization and an unstable family life. Moderate changes introduced during the past decade of economic development did not significantly alter the structure of society or the locus of power. 

In January 1961 a civil-military directorate took control of the Government and pledged itself to a social reform program in line with the principles of the Act of Bogotá. The measures which were adopted during the past year add up to an impressive picture of self-help and reform, though these accomplishments have been achieved in the face of strong opposition. The legislation passed included laws having a direct impact on workers and farm laborers and others aimed at mobilizing domestic resources in support of the reform program. 

2. Planning. Although various attempts were made prior to 1961 to establish some planning mechanism, there were no significant accomplishments in this field. In December 1961 the Government requested that the United States provide assistance in establishing a planning commission. The Government

also approved a budget expenditure of 193,000 colónes in 1962 for the purpose of initiating action on the new planning commission. A group of four economists has been trained with ECLA in Mexico and will form the nucleus of the 

Commission's staff. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Because of the high population density and lack of unused arable land, a process of redistribution of the land alone would not necessarily help the majority of rural laborers and would probably lower productivity to a considerable degree. A reform of the land-tax system is more important since the current tax structure encourages the holding of unused land. A cadastral survey is now being made as a preliminary step to a revision of land taxes. Meantime the Government has undertaken other reforms to benefit the rural workers. Among the measures are the following: 

1. Decree 40 of February 27, 1961, established a mandatory weekly day of rest with pay for agricultural workers. This decree was later modified by Decree 350 of October 1961 which made temporary concessions to rural employers. 

These concessions were, however, minor and did not compromise the basic principles inherent in the former decree. The Ministry of Labor estimates compliance with the laws at 75 to 90 percent. 

2. Decree 190 of June 1961, the "law for the protection of farm laborers" regulated in detail working conditions for both permanent and migratory agricultural workers. This was followed by a Department of Labor resolution establishing a minimum diet for rural workers. 

This last measure triggered serious opposition from agricultural producers' associations, and the Government had to make certain temporary concessions to employers. However, the basic structure and intent of the legislation remained intact. Thus far implementation of the laws has been considered reasonably effective. 

4. Housing.-El Salvador has a housing shortage, especially in urban areas where the population is increasing rapidly and low-cost housing is scarce; however, the Government is taking steps to meet these needs. The Government has had a housing agency, the Instituto de la Vivienda Urbana (IVU) for the past 12 years, and during this time it has supervised construction of 6,000 houses and family units. In the course of the next 2 years, the Government hopes to construct an additional 4,000 units. The Government is presently studying legislation that would establish a system of mortgage loans, insurance, and home financing along FHA lines, and incorporate IVU in the new structure. 

Laws already adopted by the Government during the past year affecting housing include: (1) Decree 31 of February 1961 legalizing the sale of individual apartments in multifamily units, thus facilitating sale of this type of housing to individuals, and (2) Decree 30 of March 23, 1961, which ordered a one-third cut in rents which owners of urban slum housing may charge. 

The major problems faced at present by the Government in the field of housing are the lack of capital for low-cost housing programs and lack of basic legislation needed to permit the creation of new institutions which can mobilize domestic resources more effectively for a low- and medium-cost housing industry. 

5. Health. The principal health problems in El Salvador are lack of potable water supplies and a lack of minimum nutritional standards. The most significant measure taken since the Act of Bogotá to improve health conditions Iwas the decree of October 5 establishing the National Authority for Water Supply and Sewage Disposal (ANDA), an autonomous agency designed to carry out detailed projects in urban and rural communities. This decree consolidated authority for budgeting, financing, planning, engineering, and administration of municipal systems and provided local financing and authority for external borrowing. In 1961 the IDB approved $4.8 million in loans to ANDA for improvement of urban water supplies and sewer systems. The Government has also signed a health project agreement with the United States under the Alliance for Progress. The agreement provides for cooperation in the construction and staffing of 7 new health centers that will extend services to approximately another 150,000 persons by December 31, 1962. 

6. Education.-Literacy in El Salvador was estimated at 43 percent in 1950, and is thought to be at approximately the same level now. The secondary school system is also outmoded and needs revision of its curriculum to provide the necessary preparation for various fields of specialization in higher education, and there is need for a considerable expansion of facilities and teachers training in order to build literacy and skills. El Salvador devotes a larger proportion of its budget to the Ministry of Education than to any other ministry. Yet, although 25

percent of the national budget is devoted to all aspects of education, including Vocational training, it is insufficient to provide much expansion of capital equipment, such as new schools, demonstration supplies, or expansion of university facilities. In an effort to attract more teachers the Government increased teacher salaries in 1961 and 1962. It is also negotiating with the U.S. AID mission two projects aimed at increasing teacher training and school construction. 

7. Public administration.-Although El Salvador has no civil service merit system the level of public administration is fairly high. The administration suffers, however, from a lack of direction because of frequent changes in high-level executive positions. Since the revolution in 1948 El Salvador has taken several steps to insure greater efficiency, integrity, and stability in government. Among these were the establishment of a highly centralized judiciary headed by a Supreme Court of Justice, the creation of an independent Ministry of Justice, and the adoption of a constitutional requirement that public officials make a declaration of their assets before assuming office. 

In January of 1962 the Government adopted a new civil service law. Additional plans to improve public administration include establishment of a central personnel office in which personnel testing standards will be developed, creation of a placement office based on a merit system, reorganization of the budget office, and installation of modern techniques to encourage a more productive distribution of revenues. 

8. Financial stability.-During the decade from 1947 to 1957 El Salvador experienced a high rate of growth and a period of financial stability. In the following 3 years, due largely to falling world coffee prices, increasing demand for imports, and capital flight, net international reserves declined sharply and brought on a balance-of-payment crisis. Rapid credit expansion after 1959, particularly in the private sector, abetted continuing increases in levels of imports, and political unrest, commencing in mid-1960, contributed to a decline of public confidence in the stability of the currency. 

Since the first quarter of 1961 the Government has made strong and effective moves to remedy the situation. In April 1961, it introduced exchange restrictions on capital transactions, reorganized the Central Reserve Bank to remove control of monetary policy from private hands, and began limitation of credit to the private sector. The Government introduced further exchange regulations in June and made arrangements for the registration of foreign investments in order to assure investors of capital repatriation and profit remittances. In early July the 

Government regularized its temporary arrangements with the International Monetary Fund by entering into a regular standby agreement with the IMF, reinforced by arrangements with the U.S. Treasury and the Eximbank, for contingency reserves and supporting loans totaling $27 million. All these steps have had a significant and beneficial effect. 

9. Credit.-El Salvador has a well-developed commercial banking system; however, certain types of credit are not readily available. There is a lack of longterm credit in industry and in agriculture, and there is a need for better credit services in small industry and housing. 

In December 1961, the Government established a new supervised farm credit agency. It has helped the cooperative "Cajas de Credito" to expand their shortterm and medium-term credit facilities by obtaining external IDB credits. In legislation still under consideration, the Government has included proposals for the establishment of mortgage insurances and savings and loan systems. The 

Government's industrial development organization, INSAFOP, was reorganized in 1961 and, beginning in January 1962, will develop and promote joint venture industrial activities with foreign and local capital. The new operations will include industrial financing and industrial research promotion. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The atmosphere for private investment and enterprise is good in El Salvador. Manufacturing enterprises are owned and operated mainly by private Salvadoran capital. The role played by foreign capital, mainly from the United States, has been important in the development of several Salvadoran industries, especially through transfer of knowhow.

The Government has actively promoted the development of manufacturing industries in an effort to diversify the economy, provide employment for a rapidly growing population, and reduce the country's dependence on exchange earnings from coffee and cotton exports. The Processing Industries Development Law of 

1942 granted tax and duty exemptions to industries considered to be of special importance to the country. In 1955 the Production Development Institute (INSAFOP) was created to assist in the establishment of new industries and the

expansion and modernization of existing installations. The Government gave further impetus to foreign investment when, in January 1960, it signed an Investment Guarantee Agreement with the United States. 

El Salvador has actively pursued a policy of free trade with its neighbors, and in 1960 signed two treaties creating a common market with Honduras, Nicaragua, and Guatemala, a step with important implications for the economic development of the area.

The Government has decided to establish a new industry development program in 1962. The efforts of the Industrial Development Institute (IDI) will be directed at (a) the establishment of new industries in El Salvador, with emphasis on joint-venture programs; (b) a continued effort to develop incentives and encourage the participation of domestic capital in investment in private industry through the facilities of a newly established and Government-regulated "Security Exchange Market," and (c) continued efforts to assist existing industries in El Salvador, particularly in expansion and diversification of products. 

The planned goal of the IDI for the next 3 years is the establishment of 21 smalland medium-sized joint-venture industries. These industries would represent a potential capital investment of approximately $10.6 million and create job opportunities for many additional Salvadoran workers. 

11. Labor.-El Salvador has a labor force of about 1 million workers, but the lack of training of these workers constitutes a serious impediment to economic development. Generally, poor working conditions prevail throughout the country. The Ministry of Labor was established only in 1946 and still has insufficient technical and trained staff to provide effective labor administration services. 

These factors contribute to a generally low worker productivity and retard development of the country. 

The series of decrees issued in 1961, referred to above under agrarian reform, was designed to improve the conditions of work for rural workers. In the industrial and services sector, Decree 387 of November 7, 1961, provided for a new Department of Apprenticeship within the Ministry of Labor, and for the establishment of the National Advisory Council or Apprenticeship, made up of representatives of organized labor, industry, and certain Government agencies. 

Decree 160 of June 1, 1960, established a minimum wage of 3 colónes ($1.20) per day for employees of commercial establishments with assets in excess of 10,000 colónes. The decree also prohibits reduction in the number of employees or their salaries and the lengthening of the workday. It is the Government's intention to issue parallel decrees affecting the industrial and rural sectors. 

Decree 96 of April 24, 1961, liberalized previous regulations governing strikes and lockouts and prohibited the suspension of essential public services. Decree 

123 of April 15, 1961, protects salaries and wages through a series of provisions designed to insure prompt and direct payment to workers and employees, and through limitation on legal deductions and garnisheeing. 

El Salvador has done much in recent years to foster a free labor movement. 

GUATEMALA 

1. General statement.-Guatemala has been one of the leaders among the 

Central American states in social and economic reform. Significant advances were made after the revolution of 1944 but sound progress was impeded when Communists gained control in the early 1950's. Since the ouster of President 

Arbenz in 1954 some progress has been made. Recent improvements in public administration and planning provide hope for more satisfactory conditions in which to carry on a significant program. Guatemala's population is estimated at about 4 million. More than half of it is Indian, a group which remains largely separated from the national scene, still living according to its traditional folkways. Literacy is low, about 30 percent, but Guatemala hopes to solve this problem to a large extent by 1970 through a mass literacy program. Generally, Guatemala is responsive and prepared to cooperate with self-help measures. 

2. Planning. The National Economic Planning Council (NEPC) was established in November 1954. During the first years of its existence, NEPC's efforts were supplemented by an IBRD mission which assisted in the preparation of the 5-year economic development plan for the period 1955-60. Since that time, NEPC has prepared the 4-year public investment program for 1960-64 (see sec. 

10 for details). In August 1961 it took the initial steps for the preparation of a 10-year development program and approved its general objectives on October 7, 1961. For the last several months NEPC has been working on several studies and reviewing some 125 project proposals submitted by all branches of the

Government. In late January, it started work on a crash development program for the period January 1962 to mid-1964. 

Planning in Guatemala has not yet reached the stage of effective preparation or implementation, although some progress and tangible results have been noted. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Guatemala has a predominately agricultural economy with about three-quarters of the labor force engaged in agriculture. The principal crops are coffee (which usually earns 75 percent of the country's foreign exchange), bananas (which has been bringing in 10 percent of the foreign exchange, but whose production and export are expected to decline appreciably in the near future), and corn, the staple foodstuff of the nation. According to the 

1950 census, 158 farms, or less than 0.1 percent of the total, accounted for more than 40 percent of all farmland in Guatemala, while 266,000 farms, or 76 percent of all agricultural holdings, occupied only 9 percent of the land. Forty percent of all farms were being worked by tenant farmers, sharecroppers, and squatters. 

An agrarian reform law was enacted in 1952, providing for the expropriation of unused private land and the distribution in small sections of this and certain nationally owned land. A substantial amount of land was distributed under this law. After the revolution of 1954 a new program was started. By 1961, under this program, nearly 5,000 titles to units averaging 50 acres each had been issued to small farmers. In addition some 4,000 subsistence plots, averaging about 6 acres, were awarded to families for whom the operation of the farm was presumably not the sole source of income. Some 12,000 families were benefited by communal titles to Government-owned land where it was not feasible to divide the land into individually owned units.

Through the National Agricultural Bank the Government has extended credit amounting to several million dollars to farmers who were not eligible for commercial loans. The Government, with U.S. assistance, has maintained agricultural extension and vocational education projects. The public investment plan (1960-64) allots $11.3 million for agrarian reform. 

4. Housing. The need of urban housing in Guatemala in this decade is estimated at 75,000 new units and another 75,000 units to replace substandard housing. A self-help low-cost housing program, started in 1956, has resulted in the construction of nearly 2,500 homes. More are planned. The guaranteed mortgage law (FHA) of June 17, 1961, is expected to generate private long-term (20 years) mortgage loans not available until now. Besides U.S. grants and 

IDB loans of $5 million, the Government has contributed substantially to lowcost housing and the people for whom the units are being built have contributed with their labor.

The present scope of the housing program, however, will not be sufficient to fill the gap. Private investment in low-cost housing, which is needed to take up the major share, is not assured notwithstanding the above-mentioned FHA law chiefly because of the limited resources of the lending institutions. U.S. investors who could lend long-term mortgage money are still awaiting the ratification of the United States-Guatemala Investment Guarantee Agreement by the 

Guatemalan Congress. 

5. Health. The three principal diseases in Guatemala are malaria, intestinal disorders, and tuberculosis. Trachoma is also prevalent. The unfamiliarity of much of the population with elementary sanitary precautions and the lack of a sufficient number of trained physicians and health personnel are problems. The life expectancy is 37 years only, and the ratio of physicians to population is 1 to 6,453, but the latter figures do not tell the whole story because of the great concentration of doctors in Guatemala City and the other main urban centers. 

In cooperation with U.S. AID mission and international agencies, the Government has made a major effort in the public health field. The Health Cooperative 

Service (SCISP) is operating many public health projects. Since 1956, a program of public health training has made some progress. SCISP will be integrated in the Ministry of Health on July 1, 1962. The extensive malaria eradication program, started in 1955, has shown considerable results. Areas heretofore uninhabitable because of a high incidence of malaria are now planned for development and resettlement. Of the 189 townships in the malarious area, 108 were free of malaria by the end of September 1961. Work is continuing and malaria should cease to be a major problem in the next 2 or 3 years. 

A presidential order, signed on February 16, 1960, created the National Committee of Potable Water. With U.S. aid, a program to build 400 to 550 potable water systems in this decade is being implemented. By December 1961, 53 water systems had been built; they supply more than 90,000 persons; 23 additional

systems to service 72,000 people are under construction. This program should help to reduce intestinal diseases. Since 1956 hundreds of thousands of tuberculin tests and BCG vaccinations have been made. 

6. Education.-Of the 3 million Guatemalans who are of school age or older some 2.1 million are believed to be illiterate. However, Guatemala's education plans, and especially its 10-year mass education program, are expected to reduce the number of illiterate persons to a small percentage by 1970. From 1954 to 

1959, the Government's reinvigorated school construction program resulted in 90 new schools with 642 classrooms. The United States-Guatemala project agreement of February 1, 1960, calls for the construction of 2,250 classrooms in 445 schools with U.S. assistanc. The Guatemalan contribution in cash and kind is much larger than the substantial U.S. assistance. To this should be added the contributions in cash and kind of cooperating communities as well as those of private individuals and business firms. By mid-1961, under this program, 105 schools with 529 classrooms had been built, 73 schools with 351 classrooms were under construction, and several others were under contract. Apparently enough teachers and administrators have been or are being trained. The progress to date, the serious interest of the Government and people, and the recently enunciated high priority sector goal of mass education and elimination of illiteracy are indicative of a successful program in the field of education. Plans are now in process for constructing 3,000 to 3,500 additional classrooms by means of external borrowing and local resources after currently available cooperative funds are expended by the end of fiscal year 1962. 

7. Public administration.-With U.S. assistance, Guatemala has taken several steps to improve public administration. The Demonstration Secretarial Clerical 

Training School was started in September 1957. More than 3,000 Guatemalans have received the requisite 3-month training in its various courses. The school was integrated in the Public Administration Development Center in June 1959, when the latter was established. The center offers to Government employees several courses in public administration. More than 2,000 have already participated in its training program, and it will train about 1,000 a year. One-third of all Government employees should have received training by 1964. 

A number of reforms are contemplated and several decrees, dated August 1960 and July 1961, were issued toward their fuller implementation. A civil service merit law is under consideration by Congress and expected to pass this year. The Internal Revenue Agency is scheduled to be completely organized and its personnel trained in 1962 to administer the existing and new tax legislation now before Congress. 

8. Financial stability.—The maintenance of financial stability has not been a major problem in the past several years. The Government and the central bank have taken needed measures in ample time to avoid any possible crisis. In May 

1960, Guatemala entered a standby agreement with IMF for its full quota of $15 million. No drawings have been made, however, since the Guatemalan foreign exchange position tended to improve after June 1960. In 1961, for the first time in years, a detailed national budget was published and the fiscal year 1962 budget separates, for the first time, operating and investment expenditures. 

The Government has instituted tighter control on tax collections, which should result in increased ordinary revenue during fiscal year 1963. Domestic prices continued stable in 1961 and no significant change is anticipated in the near future. 

9. Credit. The main problems pertaining to credit are (1) the lack of facilities for medium- and long-term credit; (2) the conservative lending policies of the commercial banks and resulting extreme tightness of credit; and (3) the need for more effective administration of the Government loan agencies. The organization of a private medium- and long-term institution (capital $1.5 million) with Government financial assistance is underway. It is expected to become operative this year (1962). The Government credit institutions are being reorganized and modernized with the assistance of an IDB technical mission. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Since mid-1954 Guatemala has encouraged the investment of foreign capital in the country and direct participation of the Government in economic enterprises has not been extensive. There are no exchange controls and foreign capital may be freely invested and repatriated, and profits transferred without any limitation or official authorizations. 

The industrial development law of September 22, 1959, grants many privileges to new enterprises. These include exemption for 10 years from import duties and charges, a 5-year total exemption from the corporate profits tax and a further 5-year period during which one-half of the tax is paid, some protection

against foreign competition, and preferential treatment in Government procurement. Similar incentives are also offered to existing enterprises, but to a lesser extent. The Industrial Promotion and Productivity Center (IPPC) was created on October 12, 1960, to act as a catalyst to industrial growth by offering various services to the private sector. 

Guatemala has signed an investment guarantee agreement with the United States, which is now pending ratification by the Guatemalan Congress. 

11. Labor.-Guatemala's labor force is largely composed of farmworkers (about 75 percent of the total) and a small but growing number of artisans and tradesmen. Major developmental problems to be solved are unemployment, underemployment, and the creation of new job opportunities for the growing labor force.

Organized labor developed rapidly after the overthrow of the dictatorial government of President Jorge Ubico in 1944. The following 10 years saw hundreds of unions organized with the assistance of the succeeding administrations, but the labor movement was infiltrated and later dominated by Communists. 

After the ouster of President Arbenz in 1954, the Government suspended 533 labor organizations with a claimed membership of 100,000 and peasant organizations claiming 200,000 members in order to eliminate the political power of the Communists. There are now about 50 unions in 3 federations. In rural areas, with very few exceptions, agricultural labor is unorganized. 

A social security law was passed in 1946, and a labor code enacted in 1947. 

They offered many advantages to the workers. Since 1954, the Government has taken some measures helpful to individual workers, such as providing (1) training in better agricultural methods, (2) low-cost housing, and (3) general and Vocational courses. Some employers are opposed to rapid improvement of the workers' status, and many of the workers themselves are apathetic. labor is a problem on which action is yet to be taken. 

HAITI 

Child 1. General statement.-Haiti, a French-speaking Negro country, has a predominately agricultural subsistence economy. There is extreme poverty and the peasants till gradually eroding land with the most primitive tools. The per capita GNP is one of the lowest in Latin America. Agricultural productivity is low, health poor, and the diet is often close to the starvation level. Haiti made only limited progress in self-help in 1961, mainly in the beginnings of better budgetary formulation, overall fiscal restraint, national planning, and recognition of public debt obligation. It also showed increased interest in an effective program for literacy and rural education. Self-help measures will probably be. limited in the near future mainly project-by-project contributions. It is estimated that the population in 1962 is about 3,600,000, and it is believed to be growing at a rate of about 1.2 percent a year. Literacy is about 10 percent, the lowest in Latin America. 

2. Planning.—A National Economic Council exists, but has not been too effective. At the request of the Government a multilateral planning group representing OAS, IDB, and ECLA started working in November 1961 on a development plan for Haiti. Haiti's adoption of the plan being prepared and its subsequent fulfillment of the responsibilities specified by the plan should be of considerable assistance to the development of Haiti. 

3. Agrarian reform.-The most serious problem of the Haitian agrarian structure is the extremely heavy demographic pressure on limited land resources. 

The population density is 330 people per square mile, the highest in Latin America. Haiti also has the highest percent of rural population (90 percent). 

Although there is no exact information available on the distribution of property, the greater part of the land is in very small holdings. These small holdings: constitute a funadmental obstacle to the socioeconomic progress in agriculture. 

Most of the properties are worked by their owners, but there is a sharecropper system, as well as other forms of indirect farming. The land title system is chaotic, and no real progress can be made until there is a survey and the land titles are cleared. Large properties exist only among the sugarcane and sisal holdings, which are managed through a system of farm entrepreneurs. In Large-scale studies must be made in erosion control and land rehabilitation if in the future people are to be fed even at today's low nutritional level. 

1958 the Ministry of Agriculture, through its Department of Natural Resources and Rural Development, prepared an agrarian reform project, but to date no

legal measure has been adopted along these lines. In the meantime, the Government, through the Ministry of Agriculture, began to distribute certain publicly owned lands. It is reported that about 4,000 acres was distributed through 1961. 

Haiti is currently contributing about $1 million annually to a cooperative agricultural project. 

4. Housing.There is very little information available for an evaluation of the housing problem. Housing is generally inadequate, with widespread slums in urban areas and many thatched roofed earth houses in rural sections. Official efforts have tended to concentrate on the capital, Port-au-Prince, which has a population of more than 200,000. The rural population has received no attention. 

Although construction systems are defiicent, the deeply entrenched tradition of house building by the occupants themselves, aided by their friends, represents a significant contribution to rural housing. The Institute for Social Welfare and 

Research in 1961 prepared a plan designed to resolve, insofar as possible, the housing crisis as it affects low-income groups, especially public employees. 

However, only 100 housing units are currently planned. 

5. Health.-In Haiti, health and sanitation facilities, especially in the rural areas, are substandard. Haiti's infant mortality rate is 15 percent, and its life expectancy only 33 years. Malaria, tuberculosis, waterborne diseases, and intestinal parasites are common and limit the productivity of the worker. Malaria is one of the major health problems and is the principal disease of Haiti. Over 

65 percent of the area, containing 77 percent of the population, is considered malarious with an incidence of about 25 percent. Haiti, the United States, the 

Pan American Health Organization, and UNICEF are jointly supporting and operating the local malaria eradication agency (SNEM). 

6. Education.-Haiti's educational system is extremely deficient, both qualitatively and quantitatively. It is estimated that out of 800,000 children of school age (8-14) only 210,000 are in school. Nearly 90 percent of the children living in urban areas are in school only about 10 percent of those in the rural areas even start to school. In addition, only 10 percent of those in rural areas who begin school go beyond the second year, scarcely long enough to develop literacy skills. There is only one rural school providing schooling beyond the sixth grade.

In 1961 there were signs that the Government of Haiti might make a greater effort to increase literacy and improve rural education in general. Staffs from the 

Ministeries of Agriculture and Education were merged into a combined office of National Community Education (UNEC). The current budget, for the first time in many years, provides a 10-percent increase in funds allotted to rural education for the employment of 100 additional teachers. Instruction, which heretofore has been only in French, will be in Creole, the local language. 

Progress is being made in rural self-help school construction and cooperation of the Minister of Agriculture and rural education officials in current program planning has been helpful. Land, local materials, and unskilled labor is furnished by local communities eager for the opportunity to have schools. 

7. Public administration.-Training for public administration has been at a minimum level in Haiti. Ministers and other high administrative officials change frequently. Under the current IMF standby arrangement, Haiti has been taking some steps toward greater centralization of fiscal controls. In 1961 it enacted legislation establishing a Bureau of the Budget within the Ministry of Finance and is preparing a decree setting up the administrative organization and procedures of the Bureau. Four key officials who were trained in the United States have been appointed to the Bureau. There have been no steps taken toward the establishment of a civil service based on the merit system. 

8. Financial stability.-The cost of living has not increased as much as in many Latin American countries, the index based on 1953 fluctuating between 99 and 110 in the period 1954-61. U.S. grants amounting to $9.6 million in the 

3-year period fiscal year 1958-59 to 1960-61 played a vital role in balancing the international payments account and in reducing the budget deficits, and thus helped to maintain financial stability. 

Total lending capacity has been restricted to avoid depreciation of the currency which has been maintained at a fixed exchange rate since 1919 although its stability has been jeopardized by increased imports. Under the IMF standby arrangement, the Government in 1961 took some steps toward greater centralization of fiscal controls in the Ministry of Finance. A system was instituted for the rational control of monthly fiscal expenditures. Budgetary reform, however, is still needed. 81496-62-pt. 3- -10

Interest 9. Credit. Haiti generally lacks adequate credit facilities. A rural credit organization has been established through U.S. technical assistance efforts. 

Through this agency credit is provided for the production, storage, processing, and marketing of agricultural products, and for assistance to and establishment of cooperative groups of small peasant farmers. Credit is extended to cooperatives under terms which are in accordance with their ability to repay, ranging from short-term operating loans to maximum facility loans of 15 years. rates to cooperatives are low, averaging 4 percent per year. To improve credit facilities for small business, Haiti agreed in 1961 to transform its moribund Agricultural Development Bank (IACAI) into the Institute for Agricultural and Industrial Development (IDAI) which was created by a law of June 19, 1961. 

The existing four banks generally extend credit to well-established commercial and industrial establishments at an average annual interest rate of 10 percent. 

Many private moneylenders and merchants engage in credit activities, the interest rate beginning with a minimum of 12 percent per year. However, local banks and private lenders are faced with high risk factors, and total lending capacity has been restricted to avoid depreciation of the currency. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.—While the Government has passed laws intended to stimulate private investments, the general investment climate has not been especially favorable.

Haiti has signed an investment guarantee agreement with the United State covering inconvertibility and expropriation. 

11. Labor. The general level of wages is low, as is the level of productivity. 

Haitian labor unions are in general company unions and are not represented in any responsible international labor organization. There was a trend in 1961 toward collective bargaining, generally with American-owned companies. In 

October 1961 the Government passed a long-awaited labor code. It is mainly a codification, the first, of existing labor laws. It will probably be of limited value as long as Haiti's private wage-earning sector remains so small (now 17,000).

HONDURAS 1. General statement.-The economic development of Honduras has been slow and its resources and income are limited. About 80 percent of its population derives its livelihood from agriculture, which produces 40 percent of the GNP. 

Agricultural extension reaches only 4 percent of the farmers. More than half of the population is outside the money economy. Since 1954 the GNP has been rising at about 4 percent a year. The general health and sanitary conditions require improvement. 

The Government is anxious to make the necessary reforms and take within its capabilities, measures to improve economic and social conditions, but wellplanned, coordinated, and sustained efforts can come only gradually. Literacy is estimated at about 40 percent. The population is approximately 2,100,000, with an annual growth rate of 3.3 percent. 

2. Planning.-A national economic planning council was established in 1955. 

Under a bill recently drafted for the legislature, the council would become the national economic planning board and would be empowered to prepare a national economic development plan, including a scale of priorities. In July 

1961, the council drafted a 4-year public investment program for 1962-65. It calls for total expenditures of $376.5 million, to be financed as follows: domestic financing $249.5 million (66.3 percent), of which $228.5 million (91.5 percent) is to come from current revenue and $127 million (33.7 percent) from external sources. The plan will require further refinement. 

3. Agrarian reform.—Honduras needs agrarian reform primarily for economic reasons. The declining banana industry no longer provides export earnings adequate to finance development, and expansion and diversification of exports would renew lagging rates of growth. There is no lack of land but the absence of credit and assistance to smallholders has restricted cultivation of land by most of the farm population to small, uneconomic units operated at the subsistence level.

An agrarian reform institute was established in 1960 to deal with problems of land tenure and to resettle farmers on state-owned lands, which comprise 50 percent of rural land. Most such lands are, however, distant from population centers, and, to be brought into productive use, they require considerable support services, such as roads, marketing facilities and improved farm techniques. 

In November 1961, a law was adopted which prohibits subleasing of government-

owned lands, a practice that had led to exorbitant profits by middlemen at the expense of the campesinos. 

At present the principal rural problems are education, credit, and technology rather than resettlement or breaking up of existing tenure patterns. Diversification of output on large estates and provision of support aid to farmers both large and small need to be combined with land surveys and careful assessment of Honduras' land and forest resources so that meaningful agrarian development can be planned and implemented. 

4. Housing.-Between 1950 and 1961, the urban housing shortage rose from 

32,000 to nearly 41,000 units, while the rural shortage increased from 97,000 to more than 132,000 units. Taking into account the increasing population, about 

20,000 houses would have to be built annually to overcome this shortage. An autonomous housing institute was established in 1957 to expedite low-cost housing development. By 1961, it had built 255 units (a yearly average of 

50 houses) with a total investment of $650,000. Another institution devoted to housing development is the Banco de la Propiedad, a private savings and loan institution. It built 1,400 units between 1952 and 1960. Its housing investments to date, including loans for repairs, amount to about $6.5 million. 

The 4-year plan calls for the construction of 3,350 urban units at a cost of $8 million, of which $6.25 million is expected to be financed externally. The plan's target appears to be attainable, but it is obvious that the housing shortage in Honduras is far from solution, although the greater share of housing is expected to be built by the private sector. This will require several institutions similar to a savings and loan association now being organized, a mortgage insurance agency, and a credit system to enable private contractors to undertake mass production projects. 

Early in 1961 U.S. technical and financial assistance was requested by the housing institute. The IDB is considering a $2.75 million loan to the institute. 

5. Health. The principal diseases in Honduras are malaria, intestinal dis- -orders, including dysentery and typhoid, and tuberculosis. About 90 percent of the country's houses have no water or sewage facilities. Hospitals, health centers, potable water systems, and environmental sanitation are all needed. The 

Government has devoted a substantial portion of its income to health for many years, particularly in cooperation with the United States through the Health Cooperative Service (SCISP). This service has undertaken over 200 projects, including hospital construction, operation, and organization; water supply systems; sewerage; garbage disposal; health centers; and malaria eradication; as well as training. The Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare assumed enlarged responsibilities in 1958 and has been developing a national health plan with the assistance of the World Health Organization. During 1960, 15 health centers were built and 11 renovated, 4 infant maternity hygiene centers were erected in Tegucigalpa and 11 in rural areas, and 15 dental service stations were installed.

Two-thirds of Honduras' population live in malarious areas. Since 1957 the malaria eradication program has been making good progress. This phase is expected to be completed by 1963, when surveillance will predominate. Mass vaccinations against tuberculosis and typhoid have also produced satisfactory results. The 4-year plan includes $7.5 million for the construction of health facilities besides the $6.5 million for the Tegucigalpa water systems. 

In April 1961 the National Autonomous Water Supply and Sewerage Service 

(SANAA) was established. The Government has drafted an emergency plan for the construction of 38 water supply systems in rural communities at an estimated cost of $1,050,000. The service will also administer the water projects to be constructed for Tegucigalpa with IBRD loan funds. 

6. Education.-It is estimated that 60 percent of the Honduran population of 

10 years of age and over is illiterate. Although 40 percent of the school-age population is registered in elementary schools, less than 10 percent complete this phase of their education, and only an estimated 12 percent of the 14,000 students registered in secondary schools were expected to finish high school. In 1961, $7.5 million or about 17 percent of the total budgetary expenditures was devoted to education. In 1962, the Government plans to increase the amount budgeted for education by 7 percent over 1961, an increase of $500,000. The Government's goal is to provide 6 years of schooling for all school children by 1977, with 80 percent of this purpose attained by 1972. The program's goal is to reduce the illiteracy rate to about 50 percent.

In order to reach the 1972 target, it will be necessary to train an additional 4,550 elementary school teachers and add the same number of classrooms, although only 2,500 are now under consideration; to expand the existing normal schools so that a minimum of 500 teachers enter preservice training each year. 

Normal school enrollment is now 1,934. The 4-year plan projects an increase to a 3,076 enrollment by 1965. The Government, with U.S. assistance has also started a program of self-help school construction in rural areas. Under this program 43 classrooms have been completed and 41 are now under construction. 

7. Public administration.—With U.S. aid some improvement is being made in tax administration and enforcement, in the economic development projects, and in the reorganization, supply of equipment, and training of the law enforcement agency, the Civil Guard, which was established on January 1, 1962. 

8. Financial stability.—In January 1959, the Government, faced with a serious deterioration of the country's fiscal operations, undertook a stabilization program in cooperation with IMF and the latter entered into a $4.5 million standby agreement. Honduras initiated measures designed: (1) to tighten budgetary operations; (2) to restrict credit expansion, and (3) to support the gold and dollar position of the country. These measures were successful and the net holdings of foreign exchange increased. The standby agreement was renewed in 1960 and, at the request of the Government, raised to $7.5 million. In 1960 the Government did not increase its net indebtedness to the central bank and the latter's credit to the banking community declined. The standby agreement was renewed again in 1961 and will be extended in 1962. 

9. Credit. There is a lack of medium and long-term credit. The Government stabilization program since 1959 included the restraining of private credit expansion by maintaining high reserve requirements on time and sight deposits and by strictly limiting central bank rediscounting operations. Commercial bank rates have varied from 8 to 10 percent a year. The national development bank has as its principal purpose the development of the economic resources of Honduras. Its loans have gone mainly to the agricultural sector, but they have been limited in volume and have not met the demands of small farmers. As of 

December 1960, its outstanding loans were just under $6 million. This bank is now being reorganized with the help of IDB. The IDB recently announced a commitment to lend approximately $10 million to the development bank for relending as agricultural credits.

Active consideration is being given to the establishment of an industrial loan bank in the private sector. The Government is attempting to establish a savings and loan association, backed by the local equivalent of an FHA. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The Government is generally favorable to private enterprise. The 1959 industrial development law offers various incentives to new enterprises, such as taxation and customs duties waivers. 

The Government has signed an investment guarantee agreement with the United States, and several applications of U.S. investors have been processed. However, there are several steps which could be taken by Honduras to improve the investment climate. Among them are: (1) a more rapid and efficient implementation of the 1959 industrial development law; (2) ratification of the Central 

American integrated market agreements, and (3) clarification of laws affecting private enterprise and labor. 

11. Labor.-Reliable labor statistics are not available. However, the following statements are roughly descriptive of the prevailing situation: (1) selfemployed workers at the subsistence level and unpaid family workers represent two-thirds of the labor force; (2) only 2 percent of the workers are organized; (3) 80 percent of the force is employed in agriculture; (4) more than half of the population is outside the money economy; and (5) most of the workers are both illiterate and unskilled. 

A complex 875-article labor code, incorporating many favorable and forwardlooking clauses, was passed in 1959. It has been a mixed blessing to the workers, however, and opposed by employers, mainly because of the sharply increased costs of fringe and other benefits. The law of social insurance (social security), which provides mainly health benefits, became effective on July 14, 1959. It has not yet been implemented to any effective degree. With U.S. and international assistance, a limited vocational education program has produced some results in the last 2 years. The Government contributes appreciably to theprogram.

MEXICO 

1. General statement.-Since the 1910 revolution, the social and economic institutions of Mexico have developed rapidly and during the latter part of this period a degree of political stability unusual in Latin America has been maintained. Practically all this progress Mexico has accomplished through its own efforts. It has already done much in agrarian reform and plans more efficient agricultural development, but much of the rural population continues to live in impoverished circumstances at a low standard of living. Illiteracy, a major target of the Government for a number of years, has been reduced to approximately 40 percent of the population over 6 years of age and efforts are continuing in this field. Mexico has over the years offered good foreign private investment opportunities, but the present administration had embarked on a policy of "Mexicanization" under which foreign investment is considered less desirable if it is not in cooperation (preferably minority) with Mexican capital. 

The 1962 population is estimated at approximately 36 million with a growth of over 3 percent per annum. 

2. Planning.—In August 1961, a presidential decree recognized the need for programing and improved coordination in economic development and created the National Planning Board (NPB). NPB has already drafted a plan for the 

Yucatan Peninsula and is working on another for the states of Tabasco and Chiapas and adjacent areas in the states of Vera Cruz and Oaxaca, which are among the least developed regions of the country. The Government is also preparing a broad review of its investment needs for the next 3 years, which was expected to be ready in February 1962. The National Planning Board has not yet engaged in overall national planning, but regional and local planning efforts have been made with good results. 

The national development bank, whose purpose is to promote development by channeling domestic and foreign long-term capital, prepares forecasts for economic development of specific sectors, including the petroleum, railroad, and iron and steel industries. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Agrarian reform in Mexico dates back to the 1910 revolution. From 1915 to 1961 more than 124 million acres of land were distributed by the Government. However, in a majority of cases the plots were too small to be economical and often lacked water for cultivation. Up to 1950, only 22 percent of the land distributed to the public was tillable. 

The irrigation investments of the Government were among the largest public investments during the last 20 years, representing nearly one-eighth of the total Federal budgets during 1941–58. Irrigation investment was $56 million in 1959, $43 million in 1960, and in 1961 it was $72 million, including only those projects approved through September. Irrigation represented about 9 percent of the Federal budget in 1961. While agricultural production quadrupled in volume from 1940 to 1960, the annual per capita income of Mexico's farmers was still only $100 in 1960. Agricultural productivity reportedly doubled from 1935 to 1960 thanks to increased irrigation, greater mechanization, heavier use of fertilizers, and better techniques, but gains were mainly in large-scale operations and the small farmers were much less affected. 

In 1960, the Government initiated plans to open up new areas of unused land in currently inaccessible areas in the south through a colonization program which will include roads, housing, supervised credit, and other necessities. 

4. Housing. In 1960, according to the Bank of Mexico, about 84 percent of the 

Mexican families lived in one or two rooms each. Conservation estimates indicate a need for at least 1 million new low-cost housing units and a thorough reconditioning of another million units. According to the IDB report, "Social 

Progress Trust Funds, First Annual Report, 1961" the country should construct at least 200,000 low-cost units a year, of which about 140,000 will be needed in urban areas. This is greatly in excess of the present rate of construction. 

Mortgage banks, private banks specializing in housing, and some Government agencies, such as the Institute of Security and Social Services for Government Workers, the Mexican Social Security Institute, and the National Housing Institute have contributed to the construction of housing. The Mortgage Bank financed about 12,000 houses from 1933 to 1958. The National Housing Institute built 5,000 units in rural areas in 1960. The Social Security Institute completed 

2,500 units in the Mexico City area in 1959 and 1960. It has begun construction of 7,000 apartments in the Federal district. Expansion of the effort is underway, but the housing problem does not appear to be near a solution.

5. Health. The most prevalent diseases in Mexico are intestinal disorders. 

Tuberculosis and other respiratory ailments, venereal diseases, leprosy, and malnutrition also affect a substantial number of people. 

While health problems are still serious, Mexico has made a substantial effort in the last 15 years. The annual mortality from malaria was estimated at 

20,000 prior to 1956. The eradication campaign started in that year has practically eliminated malaria as a serious health problem. Mass BCG inoculations against tuberculosis were started in 1949 and the facilities for treatment improved. Still, thousands of new cases are reported every year. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 cases of leprosy, 10 percent of those affected being children. The Government has intensified its efforts in this field; treatment is mostly in clinics and mobile units. From 1947 through 1960, water systems serving 1,201 localities with 4 million people and 97 sewage systems for 1.2 million people were constructed. This resulted in a considerable drop in mortality from intestinal disorders. Thus, deaths attributed to gastronenteritis fell' from an average of 457 per 100,000 in 1938-42 to 206 per 100,000 in 1954-58. 

However, one-fifth of all cases of diseases are still attributed to deficient water. 

In 1961, work was actively in progress to provide water to 220 additional' towns and cities with more than 2 million inhabitants and 40 sewer systems with more than 1 million persons. A 20-year plan has been proposed to provide by 1980 water to all communities with more than 100 people, at a rising annual cost, beginning with $4.4 million actually spent in 1960 to a planned $24 million in 1965. 

6. Education.-The illiteracy rate of the population of 6 years and over is estimated at 40 percent. Attendance in elementary schools in relation to elementary school population (6 through 14 years of age) increased from 41 percent in 1950 to an estimated 66 percent in 1960. Enrollment in Government elementary schools rose from 2.2 million in 1958 to 3.2 million in 1961, an increase of 46 percent in 3 years. The enrollment in Federal Government secondary schools increased by 40 percent from 1958 to 1961 when it reached 119,000, while enrollment in public technical schools rose to some 19,700, an increase of 32 percent over 1958. The total enrollment in institutions of higher education exceeded 123,000 in 1958. Government expenditures on education have risen rapidly, increasing from $119 million, or 15.8 percent of the 1959 budget, to $207 million, or 20.9 percent of the 1962 budget. 

The Government plans to expand still further its expenditures on education in general and technical and vocational education in particular. An 11-year plan for education prepared by the National Commission in February 1959 is now being implemented. It has created over 4,000 new teaching jobs and 3,698 new classrooms, of which 2,646 are in rural schools. The Government is printing 

16 million textbooks to be distributed free in all primary schools. 

7. Public administration.-Government operations in many fields are becoming more efficient. The Institute of Public Administration, a nonprofit private institution was recently revitalized. Its purpose is to improve public administration in Federal, State, and municipal governments, and to bring about close coordination and planning between the Office of the Presidency and the various ministries. While it may receive limited U.S. and other foreign assistance, the institute is financed mainly by private businessmen and the Government. It is embarking on a threefold program: (1) inservice training in public administration; (2) research in the administrative field at all levels of government; and (3) dissemination of public administration information. 

The institute will provide inservice training courses in the second half of fiscal year 1962 and first half of fiscal year 1963 for about 200 employees of 2 ministries: Treasury, and Transportation, and Public Works. It plans to negotiate contracts with other ministries for inservice training of personnel in 1963 and subsequent years so that by 1967 some 2,000 key personnel will have received training. It plans also to undertake in the next 2 years four research surveys of selected Government agencies in order to institute needed reforms in such areas as organization, budget and fiscal procedures, personnel utilization. 

8. Financial stability.-Monetary and fiscal controls by the Bank of Mexico have resulted in control of inflationary pressures and reasonable stability of prices. The Federal budgets in 1960 and 1961 resulted in small deficits, which were financed through noninflationary loans. A substantial reform of the tax system in 1961, which included increased rates and better administration, is expected to lead to a small increase in receipts in 1962 and 1963 and larger increases in subsequent years.

The Government and the private capital market are unusually sensitive to fluctuations in the balance of payments. When reserves are threatened by reduced exports or investments, or for any other reason, the Government takes positive though indirect steps, such as credit restrictions, to reduce import requirements, especially in the public sector. Mexico has an excellent record of meeting its external obligations. 

9. Credit.-Mexico's banking and credit facilities are better developed and more adequate than those in most other Latin American countries. However, they do not cover adequately the needs of small farmers and those of small- and medium-size industries. The Government is considering a program of credit to small farmers and ranchers, mainly to enable them to introduce modern farming techniques. With U.S. assistance, a survey is to be made to ascertain the measures necessary to provide banking facilities, financial services and incentives, especially to small- and medium-size industries. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Mexico has a mixed economy, with the Government owning or controlling some 300 enterprises of varying size. 

Up to recent years, about two-thirds of total investments came from the private sector, the Government's share being mostly devoted to infrastructure needs and social services. The total investment pattern is gradually changing, however, with public investment becoming a larger proportion of the total and thus having a greater influence on the development of the country. The Government took some nationalization measures in the second half of 1960, which, while not on confiscatory terms, had an unfavorable effect on the private investment climate. Also pressures for Mexicanization of private foreign business enterprises were intensified, particularly with regard to new foreign investors. In general now, the Government insists on majority Mexican interest in joint ventures.

Within the limitations indicated above, foreign private investments are generally encouraged. Good opportunities continue to exist for foreign private capital in Mexico and many American companies are investing in that country. 

The Government has not participated in the U.S. investment guarantee program. 

Present U.S. investments in Mexico are estimated at about $1 billion. 

11. Labor.-Out of a population of 36 million, Mexico's labor force is estimated at 11,500,000 or 32 percent of the total. Nearly 60 percent of the force is employed in agriculture, forestry, and fishing. Much of the labor force, particularly in the rural areas, is illiterate and unskilled. One of the most serious manpower shortages in terms of skills and training is in the semimanagerial ranks of foreman, maintenance engineers, and technicians. Every year 350,000 new jobs are needed to take care of new entrants into the labor force. 

The potential trade union membership in Mexico is about 2.5 million of which an estimated 1.5 million is organized. The unions are fairly strong, receive help from the Government, and participate in political activities. Under the constitution and labor legislation, the worker is protected in various ways, enjoys fringe benefits, and is encouraged to organize. Social security is provided under a 1943 law which offers health and other benefits to about 4 million workers. 

NICARAGUA 

1. General statement.-Nicaragua is primarily an agricultural country with a variety of crops including coffee, cotton, corn, beans, sorghum, and sugarcane. In addition, there is considerable lumbering activity, principally for pine, mahogany, and cedar. Workable deposits of gold, silver, copper, iron, gypsum and other minerals exist; at present only the first three are being mined. The population of 1,500,000 is growing at a rate of 3.4 percent yearly, or only slightly more than the average estimated annual growth of GNP of 3.8 percent. Literacy is 35 percent, and the quality of schooling is deficient in several respects. As with the other Central American countries, poor transport and power capacity are major deterents to economic advance. However, there is a variety of manufacturing activity, mainly in the western areas. This includes sugar refining, lumber milling, food processing, textiles, and others. 

2. Planning. In 1953, the National Development Institute was established as a Government agency responsible for promoting, diversifying, and organizing national production and for preparing and financing regional agricultural and livestock development programs. It also provides technical and general advisory services to small- and medium-sized industry. From 1957 to 1959 the Development Institute carried out an investment program which had been prepared

with the assistance of the IBRD. In 1960, it prepared a new 10-year program to accelerate industrial activity and agricultural diversification. Domestic investment equivalent to $10.7 million in the 1961-62 period is to be supplemented to the extent of one-third by foreign financing. 

In December 1961 a Planning Office was established to expedite the country's economic and social development in a systematic and socially desirable manner. 

It is also to act as a coordinating and advisory agency to bring about the allocation of an increased share of the national budget to socioeconomic investments. U.S. AID is preparing a project to furnish technical advice and related services to the Planning Office. 

In December 1960, Nicaragua, along with Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, became a signatory of the General Treaty of Central American Integration. 

These four countries, who are also members of the new Central American Bank for Economic Integration, will presumably cooperate in the formulation of investment plans of a regional character. A planning organization in the Bank is established for this purpose. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Coffee and cotton constitute 60 percent of Nicaragua's 

1960 export earnings. Although its index of agricultural production per capita declined from 114 in 1956 (1953-55-100) to 89 in 1959, it has been estimated that it will increase to 108 in 1962. In November 1961, an agrarian reform bill was submitted to the National Congress. The main objective of the proposed legislation is to secure better land distribution, together with additional measures to increase agricultural production through adequate technical and economic cooperation. The bill provides for the organization of an Agrarian Institute, which would be directly responsible for the execution of the program. It also provides that a special tax on land be used to finance a part of the program for the reorganization of local agrarian councils and district improvement boards, for land settlement by private arrangements, and for settlement by immigrants. 

4. Housing.-Nicaragua's housing needs are acute. It is estimated that at the end of 1960 the overall housing deficit was 157,000 units-58,000 in the urban areas and 99,000 in the rural areas. In 1959 a Housing Institute (INVI) was set up to replace the Mortgage Bank of Nicaragua and to give exclusive attention to the problem of low-cost housing. It is authorized to seek financial assistance from the National Development Institute for expansion of the building materials industry and for the encouragement of the Organization of Cooperatives and Housing Associations. Persons acquiring houses through INVI are exempt from national, local, and municipal property taxes. From 1958 to 1961, inclusive, 145 homes were built under the self-help and mutual aid systems, 630 by the Mortgage Bank and INVI, and 105 through mortgage loan financinga total of 880 units. The program for 1962-66 calls for the construction of 2,850 at a total cost of $6.9 million equivalent. A national system of savings and loan associations is now under consideration to channel national savings into housing construction for low-income sectors. 

5. Health. The mortality rate in 1956 was 8.6 per 1,000 inhabitants and infant mortality rate was 64.2 per 1,000 live births. Only 12.6 percent of the urban population had water service and 4.6 percent had sewerage service in 1956. At present 51 percent of the urban population is estimated to be receiving water service. The construction of water mains and sewers was in the hands of the 

ICA Public Health Service until this function was taken over in 1956 by the National Department of Public Utilities. The Department has invested the equivalent of $500,000 in sanitation works during the past 6 years. The Department generally contributes 60 percent of the construction costs, and the remainder is borne by the community. 

6. Education.-It is estimated that approximately 35 percent of the people in 

Nicaragua are literate and educational facilities need improvement. Only 34 percent of the 350,000 children of elementary school age could be cared for in the 3,300 classrooms available in 1958. There is an urgent need for at least 

2,300 more schools, and by 1965 about 9,000 more classrooms and an equal number of trained teachers will be needed. In 1960 about 15 percent of the administrative expenditures of the national budget was allocated for education. 

Apart from the need for improvement of education in the primary and secondary schools, much needs to be done in the area of higher education and advanced training.

Efforts are currently underway to integrate the curriculums of the National Antonomous University with the programs of other Central American universities. 

The National University has recently added colleges of agriculture, dentistry, economics, education, and a school in journalism. In June 1961, the first private institution of higher education was established in Nicaragua with colleges of law, engineering, and business administration. 

7. Public administration.-There have been reasonably successful efforts to implement reforms recommended by an IBRD report of 1952. The reforms made include: (1) the establishment of a National Budget Office in the Ministry of Finance; (2) the reorganization of the power and light company as a separate autonomous agency; (3) the incorporation of the national customs as a branch of the Finance Ministry; (4) the establishment of a National Census and Statistics Agency in the Ministry of Economy; (5) reorganization of the National 

Economic Council; (6) the centralization of all major construction activities pertinent to national and public works efforts in a single agency; and (7) recommendations pertaining to the organization, structure, and functions of the 

National Development Institute. 

Its The Government set up a committee early in 1960 to study fiscal reforms. report made certain procedural recommendations that have been embodied in a tax reform bill now before the Congress. 

8. Financial stability.-Nicaragua's exchange rate has remained relatively stable over the past 10 years, with only a slight devaluation of the buying rate in 1958. The index of the cost of living which was 123 in 1955 (1953=100) declined somewhat in subsequent years and was 116 as of September 1961. The debt-servicing burden, in relation to foreign exchange earnings, has been kept within a safe margin.
