The fiscal position of the Nicaraguan Government was generally satisfactory during the period between 1950 and 1957. But the subsequent deterioration in the export sector as a result of falling coffee and cotton prices adversely affected Government revenues. Efforts to stimulate exports by the elimination of the coffee tax and subsidization of cotton production depleted revenues and increased expenditures, with resulting deficits in both 1959 and 1960. 

9. Credit. A central bank was established in January 1961. The National 

Commercial Bank is being revised to improve short-term and medium-term agricultural credit procedures. The participation of Nicaragua in the Central American Bank for Economic Integration should in due course broaden its opportunities for economic development projects of a regional character. Nicaragua re cently asked the IDB for technical assistance in organizing a savings department in the National Bank. It is also considering the establishment of a savings and loan system similar to that in Costa Rica. 

10. Investment and private capital.-Investment in cotton and cattle is increasing and industrial investment is expected to renew its recent growth in responseto the opportunities afforded by Central American Economic Integration. The 

National Development Institute has obtained assistance from U.S. AID in the organization and establishment of a technical and industrial center. It has also contracted for the services of International Consultants, Inc., for an investment survey. An Industrial Investment Incentive Office and a series of industrial parks are planned. A part of this program is the establishment of a mutual fund to attract local capital and encourage foreign investment. Nicaragua has an investment guarantee agreement with the United States and laws have been promulgated for the protection and stimulation of private investment. 

11. Labor.-Labor organization has not developed very far and has generally been under the control of the Government. There is no well-developed social security system.

PANAMA 

1. General statement.-Panama has made progress in the past year in economic planning, public administration, and in the adoption of reform measures. It has prepared a 5-year development plan (1962–66), whose implementation could have a substantial effect in the economic and social fields. However, realistic plans have not yet been made for financing the program. In other ways Panama has recently established a fairly good record in self-help measures. Education and training in technology and skills are needed, together with diversification of economic activities, especially to decrease dependence on canal activities, alleviate the chronic trade deficit and unfavorable balance of payments, and re-duce the high rate of unemployment. Agrarian reform has started and the

progress in road construction should improve the chances of higher agricultural production and farmer's income. 

Panama's population in 1962 is approximately 1,100,000. It is estimated to be growing at the rate of 2.8 percent per annum. Literacy is about 70 percent, a higher figure than for any other Central American country except Costa Rica. 

2. Planning. A National Planning Office was established under the Presidency in October 1960. It has done creditable work in four main fields: economic planning, Government administrative reorganization, the national budget, and personnel administration. It has prepared a 5-year development plan (196266), an ambitious program for social and economic development calling for total investments of about $209 million. Of this about $111 million is for projects in agrarian reform, housing, education, and public health; about $87 million is for economic development in agriculture, transportation, electrification, industrial development, tourism, and planning; and about $11 million is for public buildings and penal institutions. The plan provides for financing $100 million (47.8 percent) by grants, $52.8 million (25.3 percent) by loans, and $56.3 million (26.9 percent) by Government budgetary contributions in the form of investments.

A statistical analysis of the 1960 census will be undertaken during July- September 1962. The planning bureau is receiving assistance from the United 

States and international agencies, and is expected to continue to exert a strong influence for increased self-help on the part of the Government of Panama. 

3. Agrarian reform.—Panama's land is its only important natural resource, but farm output has actually declined in the past decade. Agrarian reform is needed to permit balanced economic growth within a framework of political stability. Expansion and diversification of agricultural output would relieve continuing balance-of-payments problems, lessen national dependence on the Canal Zone and tax-favored corporations and shipping lines, and it would encourage the economic and social integration of the rural population. 

Problems of land redistribution appear less pressing than improving the primitive technology of most farmers, providing roads, marketing, and distribution facilities, issuing land titles (80 percent of the farmers are squatters), conducting land and resource surveys, and providing credit to small holders. 

Projects along these lines are being undertaken largely through the sponsorship of the United States and international agencies. For its part, the Panamanian 

Government has proposed, as part of its $209 million 5-year development plan (1962-66) to spend $40 million on agriculture, chiefly to settle 18,000 families on 75,000 hectares of unused land. It has also presented to the National Assembly an Agrarian Code, which may be approved in 1962 session. Implementation, however, will necessarily be slow, particularly since it is dependent on a cadastral survey which, as planned, will require 5 years to be completed. 

4. Housing. The Government has publicly described Panama's housing needs as follows: "Two-thirds of the population is housed in overcrowded, unsanitary and unsafe conditions which cause high disease rates and inadequate development of individual and family values." According to a Pan-American Union report, over 9,000 units per annum over the next 30 years will be required to overcome the housing shortage. In addition, more than 1,700 units will need remodeling each year.

The Government's Institute for Housing and Civic Planning (IVU), has as its purpose the provision of low-cost housing. However, it does not as yet have the administrative organization to operate effectively. Continuing at the same level the program started in 1958, IVU built in 1960 1,434 housing units valued at $6.5 million. It is now undertaking several housing developments, the most important being the construction of 10,271 housing units in Panama City, Colon, Santiago, and David, of which 3,000 are to be financed by an IDB loan. With limited U.S. assistance, the Government expects to make possible the construction of 10,000 houses by 1967 through the aided self-help program and the establishment of financial institutions which will induce savings and financing for private home construction. It is also working on a draft of an FHA-mortgagetype insurance institution. Even with a substantial rise in private construction, Panama's housing needs will be far from satisfied in the foreseeable future. 

5. Health.-Despite the Government's rather extensive efforts in the health field and the fact that the population's general health is better than in most neighboring countries, health and sanitation problems in Panama are still great. 

The principal diseases are tuberculosis (incidence 173.4 per 100,000), malaria, intestinal disorders, influenza, and pnuemonia. Life expectancy is 52 years,

and infant mortality 60 per 1,000 live births. The basic problem is due to the inadequate facilities and personnel in the rural areas where more than half the population lives. Much has been done, however, in the last 10 years with U.S. and international agency assistance to improve the health of the population. 

Improvement of health and health facilities is one of the main objectives of Panama's 5-year plan. This effort involves the repair and expansion of existing hospital and clinic facilities, as well as the erection of new ones, at a cost of $15,675,000, and the improvement and expansion of the water systems and sewerage works at a cost of $17,391,000. With U.S. aid, the program has already made a good start. A special effort is being made in the central region with about two-fifths of the country's population where the health facilities are the least adequate. By 1967, at least 80 percent of the region's population should have available preventive and curative medical services and sanitation. 

Better administration, training of personnel, dissemination of sanitation information, and expansion of training facilities are also contemplated. 

6. Education.-Panama's Constitution requires the Government to provide the country's children with a primary education. Substantial progress has been achieved since Panama became independent in 1903, with the literacy rate having been increased from 30 percent in 1911 to about 70 percent at present. Since 

1951 enrollment in elementary schools has increased by 50 percent and at the high school and university levels it has more than doubled. About 30 percent of the population over 10 years of age has had 6 or more years of schooling, including 2 percent with complete or partial college training. However, about '67,000 children, particularly in the rural areas, or 30 percent of children between 7 and 15, do not attend school because of lack of facilities. 

The 5-year development plan allots $18,650,000 to education. Under this 'program, with substantial U.S. grants and foreign loans, the Government expects 'to build 3,800 new primary school rooms at a cost of $16,250,000 to accommodate an estimated primary school population of 200,000 by 1966. Additional high school classrooms will also be built. About 100 primary classrooms have been completed to date and several hundred are under construction. Projects are underway to improve the training of teachers and school administrators, as well as to improve and expand higher education facilities. Two pilot projects to combat adult illiteracy have been started with the assistance of a Venezuelan mission. 

The Government has contributed heavily to education. As an indication, onefourth of the total 1961 budgetary expenditures were for education. However, some reorientation, particularly at the high school and university levels, is needed in order to develop skills essential to the country's development. A beginning was made in 1959 and 1960 with the establishment of a school of agriculture in the University of Panama and a school of economics as a part of the College of Public and Business Administration. 

7. Public administration.—With U.S. assistance Panama's public administra- 'tion has been improved and some needed actions taken in the last 5 years. 

Among the measures taken are the creation of the National Planning Office and the enactment of a civil service law, which now covers about 2,000 of the total Government payroll of 26,000. A new salary scale equating similar positions and a law establishing new classifications of civil service positions are now before the assembly. A Department of Personnel is now functioning although its staff is only partially trained; it is planned to increase the number of inservice trainees from 500 to 2,000 a year by the end of fiscal year 1964. 

Some of the more important continuing needs are further organization and expansion of the civil service merit system, better capital budgeting, improvement of the tax administration, increase of the efficiency of the public safety and internal security forces, and improvement of inservice training. The Government is aware of these problems and interested in solving them. 

8. Financial stability.-One of the main weaknesses of Panama's economy is the continuing and expanding deficit in the overall balance of payments of the country. The continuing increase in imports which reached $109 million in 1960 and an estimated $116 million in 1961, coupled with a stable export situation, has caused a serious adverse balance of trade. The substantial receipts from tourists are not sufficient to balance the account. 

While ordinarily revenues of the Government increased at an annual rate of 5.4 percent in the last decade, current expenditures increased at the higher rate of 6.3 percent annually during the same period. The mounting current deficits and the borrowing for public investment projects have caused the public debt to increase from $34.6 million in 1951 to $102.8 million in September 1961. Of this, $66 million was external and $36.8 internal. The service and amortization of the debt takes up about 13 percent of the budget.

The cost of living has remained fairly stable. 

9. Credit.-Panama does not have a central bank with the range of power needed to provide effective control and guidance to monetary and credit operations of the financial system. There is no established security market. The limited loan capacity of the banking system is almost fully utilized. Most loans are for financing commercial operations, real estate, and housing, while relatively little credit is devoted to industrial, agricultural, and other productive activities. 

Recent banking developments include (1) the authorization of the Banco de Credito Popular, a savings bank, with a capital of $5 million contributed entirely by the Government, and (2) the authorization of the Agricultural Credit Bank in October 1960. Neither bank has started operations. Legislation was also enacted to reorganize the Savings Bank of the Republic. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Foreign private investment is welcomed by the Government. Article 225 of the constitution provides that "The economy shall be developed primarily through private enterprise." Panama has no restrictions on the remittance of earnings of the repatriation of capital. 

It also offers tax inducements to new industrial enterprises, including those established in the Colon Free Zone. The Government has signed an investment guaranty agreement with the United States, which was ratified on March 8, 1962. 

11. Labor. The main labor problems in Panama are the insufficient number of skilled and semiskilled workers, urban unemployment (about 10 percent of the total work force), both rural and urban underemployment, and the lack of mobility of the workers. Organized labor is not a particularly strong force. 

Union membership is estimated between 12,000 and 15,000, out of a total urban labor force of about 175,000.

The Labor Code of 1947 regulates working hours, child labor, employment of women, health and safety conditions, and establishes a limited form of workmen's compensation. The first minimum wage law in the country's history was enacted in December 1959 and became effective on January 1, 1960. It fixed the minimum wage at 40 cents an hour in Panama and Colon, 25 cents in the interior, and a minimum of $1.50 per 8-hour day for agricultural workers in all parts of the country. It should be noted, however, that much of the above is not fully implemented. The Government's Social Security Agency offers at present 74,000 insured workers coverage for sickness and maternity, old age and invalidity, death, social welfare services, and a limited loan service for housing. membership increased from 48,627 in 1955 to the present 74,000. By agreement with the U.S. Government, Panama secured many advantages for its nationals working in the Canal Zone the largest employer after the Government itselfand the elimination of the dual-wage scale. A comparatively modest vocational training program is being implemented by the Government with U.S. assistance. 

PARAGUAY 

Its 1. General statement.-The Paraguayan economy is one of the least developed in Latin America and its per capita income is among the lowest. It is primarily an agrarian country, and much of the farming and livestock activity involves subsistence operations. The population is a racial mixture of Spanish and Guarani Indians. There is only a small middle class and only a very small organized labor movement. Paraguay is making some creditable moves in the direction of self-help, but the country is handicapped by such factors as its isolation, inadequate capital formation, and lack of trained personnel. The estimated population in 1962 is 1,850,000 and it is believed to be increasing by about 2.6 percent annually. Literacy is reported to be approximately 65 percent, but this figure is probably high. 

2. Planning. The first step was taken recently to initiate a national development plan, with the establishment in March 1962 of a Secretariat for Social and Economic Planning. The Secretariat will be tied directly to the Office of the 

President and will be primarily concerned with long-range development. The immediate objective is a 5-year investment budget acceptable to foreign financing. Because of the lack of basic economic data and shortage of trained personnel, the development of an effective planning process is expected to take several years. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Vast areas of Paraguay have not been developed with the 

14 million acres under cultivation representing only about 1 percent of the land area. Paraguay's land is its chief natural resource. Increasing its productivity is the key to improving rural living standards and to developing the country's economy generally. The existing pattern of land tenure reduces efficiency

and is an obstacle to increased agricultural production. The size of most holdings is barely large enough to support subsistence. A large proportion of landholdings are occupied by squatters. During recent years, Government efforts to deal with conditions in the agrarian sector of the economy have been concentrated for the most part in the fields of transportation and land colonization. Plans for the development of a network of roads have been projected many years into the future, but lack of capital has limited actual implementation to the construction of two major access roads and improvements on the existing routes. 

Projects to colonize underdeveloped regions of the country have been periodically undertaken by the Institute of Agrarian Reform (IRA) established in 1951, and by its predecessor agencies. Many of the Government projects consisted of awarding former squatters the title to land which they were already working. Agricultural research and extension services have been carried on since World War II by the Servicio Tecnico Interamericano de Cooperacion Agri cola (STICA), a joint United States-Paraguayan venture operating under the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock. Recently a renewed effort has been made to deal with the problem of the insecure landholdings of the squatters. 

In August 1960, the Government promulgated a decree defining means whereby occupants of land owned by others can obtain legal title to their holdings. 

After a period of 20 years or more of occupancy, they may purchase up to 25 acres per family, at a price based on the average tax evaluation of land during the previous 15 years (usually substantially lower than its real value). Thus, it is now theoretically possible for a farmer to select a parcel of unused cultivable land with the hope that in time he may own it. Paraguay submitted a project to the IDB for study which would establish 2,500 families on 100,000 hectares (240,000 acres) of Government land in the upper Parana region. A loan to finance certain aspects of this project has been requested from the IDB. 

4. Housing. While there are no statistics on the magnitude of the current housing shortage it was estimated to have been 8,000 units in 1950 and population increases are estimated to have subsequently increased this shortage by some 500 units annually. The shortage in Asunción has been aggravated by an influx of unemployed from the depressed rural areas. The Government in 

February 1962 established a Paraguayan Housing Institute as a dependency of the Ministry of Labor to survey the nation's housing needs. The institute's plan for the first year consists of constructing 1,200 workers' houses and 5,000 rural houses at total cost of about $12.4 million. A draft executive decree calls for a 2-percent levy on certain imported construction material and other measures for partially financing the program. 

5. Health. Health conditions in Paraguay are substandard. The Ministry of Public Health has been responsible for the administration and operation of the malaria eradication program (SENEPA) which was started in October 1957 in cooperation with WHO and UNICEF as part of the worldwide malaria eradication program. 

Paraguay contributed over $1 million to this program from 

October 1957 through June 1961. However, due to administrative failures and faulty epidemiological surveys the initial spraying operations did not break the malaria cycle. The Ministry of Public Health prepared a 5-year plan starting in 1958 establishing four health regions in the country. The United States- 

Paraguayan cooperative health service (SCISP) undertook the administration and development of the third health region. The Government has agreed to integrate SCISP in the Ministry of Public Health, and the Minister has appointed a committee, two persons from the Ministry and two from the SCISP, to study and recommend an orderly process of transferring joint projects to the Ministry. 

6. Education.-Paraguay is severely lacking in educational resources and opportunities. There is a serious shortage of classrooms, trained teachers, textbooks, and other instructional materials. Of the 1960 school-age population, 73 percent were registered in schools. Even though the constitution makes elementary education compulsory between the ages of 7 and 14, there is an 87-percent dropout rate between the first and sixth grade. The Ministry of Education has a Department of School Planning and Construction which assists communities in a self-help school building program by providing architectural drawings in limited financial aid when funds are available. The Ministry allocates the equivalent of $65,000 per year to local school building construction. Although its resources are limited, the Government is prepared to contribute to a rural school construction program, and has stated that education enjoys "high priority" in the distribution of fiscal resources. Paraguay and the United

States jointly administer the Inter-American Cooperative Education Service (Servicio), an organization established to improve the teacher-training and educational programs. It is planned to transfer the activities of this organization. to the Ministry, but because the Ministry had not anticipated the immediate absorption of these activities and services, except for the Technical Vocational School, only the latter had been absorbed by January 1962. 

7. Public administration.—During 1961 several significant changes took place. which illustrate Paraguay's growing concern for planning and development in. public administration. Recent decrees and draft decrees in customs activity anticipate improvement in customs administration. Not only will administra-tive practices be improved, but increased revenues from better administration will contribute significantly to Government revenues. Paraguay's support of the new U.S. project for inservice training of Government employees illustratesits interest in upgrading personnel and operating practices in various ministries, and it is hoped this activity will lead to the establishment of the merit system. concept. The President has appointed a commission to draft a public service law. 

8. Financial stability. The monetary stabilization program which Paraguay entered into with the IMF in 1957 has slowed down the inflationary spiral. The 

Central Bank functions effectively and in recent years has pursued a generally sound monetary policy. The Bank has been instrumental in conjunction with 

IMF in making the stabilization program work. This is one of the outstanding examples of self-help on the part of Paraguay. Restrictions affecting both the public and private credit sectors have been reasonably well enforced. The multiple-exchange rate system was eliminated. In November 1961 Paraguay and the IMF signed a new standby agreement for $5 million, continuing the stabilization program for at least 1 more year. 

The economy, however, has remained static due to the lack of demand for Paraguayan exports and the lack of substantial capital inflow. 

9. Credit. There is a serious lack of credit throughout the economy of Paraguay. Recently, however, the Government organized the National Development 

Bank, which opened officially on November 20, 1961. Its organization is based in large measure upon the report prepared by a team from Stanford Research Institute, which went to Paraguay in 1960. The Government has assigned an 

IDB technician to the bank's staff in a key advisory role. The Government has: decreed a 5-percent import surcharge to provide the local capitalization. The 

IDB is providing a loan of $3 million to assist the bank. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.—The free market and stabilization pro-gram has helped to provide a climate favorable to free enterprise and private. investment. Encouragement to private industry was given by two laws of 1951 and 1953, which provided special concessions to new and economically desirable investments. Foreign investment is encouraged by duty exemptions. An investment guarantee agreement has been signed with the United States covering convertibility and expropriation. In August 1961, a draft law for the promotion and development of small industry was prepared. During 1961 the Government took specific steps to assist the depressed Quebracho industry by eliminating all import and export charges on goods related to the industry. During the same period the 12-percent tax on all exports was reduced to 7½ percent. 

11. Labor. Of the approximately 500,000 out of the total population of 

1,850,000 which are gainfully employed in Paraguay, only about 25,000 are organized. Organized labor is weak partly because of the lack of industrial development. Management and labor in Paraguay are not in the habit of settling disagreements by direct negotiation. These are instead settled by the Government. 

The Paraguayan Workers Confederation (CPT) is the only large labor organization, and it has not yet reached a point where it is able to play a very effective role. The social welfare program for urban workers is fairly extensive, but in 1960 benefits were reduced due to financial difficulties. 

PERU 

1. General statement.-Peru is potentially rich in human and material resources. However, it is marked by wide differences in the income levels of its various social groups. This country's population is half Indian, the latter being a depressed group living largely in the Andean highlands of central and southern Peru. Peru needs help to make substantial progress and is willing to receive it. 

Reform is urgently needed. As noted below, a central planning office has just been organized and a beginning at agrarian reform has been made.

1 Peru's population in 1962 is estimated at approximately 11,200,000, with a growth rate of 2.6 percent per annum. Literacy is estimated at 45 percent. 

2. Planning. By decrees of August and November 1961, the Government established a Central Office of Studies and Programs, under the aegis of the Ministry of Finance. It will coordinate the activities of planning offices already established or to be established in each of the ministries. A further decree of 

November 1961 concentrated all planning activities related to foreign aid requests in the central office. The Peruvian Government has requested the assistance of the World Bank and ECLA in preparing a 10-year national development plan and of AID in the preparation of specific projects and feasibility studies within the framework of such a plan. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Peru has a shortage of good land and productivity in the rural areas is generally low. Problems of agrarian reform center in the sierra region and involve not only redistribution of land but provision of social and economic services to several million Indians who are largely unintegrated in the national economy. Economic growth in other regions helps absorb some of the surplus sierra population, but migration of unskilled peasants from the rural sierra to the urban slums is a burden on the more advanced section of the economy. The Peruvian Government has sketched out plans for developing the eastern lowland regions beyond the Andes, and is now constructing penetration roads, has drafted an agrarian reform bill, and has underway various programs to upgrade the sierra economy.

The Government's proposed agrarian reform law is concerned with modification of existing land distribution patterns and systems of land tenure, with opening up new land, and with a program of rural education, technical and social assistance, and liberal credit to small farmers. In general it is designed to promote creation of small but viable farming units and to establish regulations protecting farm labor and tenants. The Institute of Agrarian Reform and 

Colonization would receive 3 percent of the national budget to finance its activities. Large estates could be subject to expropriation if operated on a notoriously inefficient basis or if special local circumstances caused unusual pressures for land. Graduated land taxes would be levied against idle land and land speculation. Land values declared for purposes of tax assessment would also be used as the basis for indemnification in event of expropriation. Provision is made for easy payments by the new settlers on distributed land. Exempt for the time being are cotton and sugar producing plantations in the coastal region, but provision is made to improve the position of farm labor on the plantations. 

This bill was presented to the Peruvian Congress in March 1961, but thus far it has not been enacted into law. 

4. Housing. The Peruvian Government has begun a low-cost housing program. It established a National Housing Institute in September 1960, to set up a housing program, including a self-help plan for which approximately $8 million was budgeted in 1961. In June 1961 the Institute estimated the housing shortage at 1,971,000 units, of which 1,146,000 needed improvements and 825,000 represented new units required. About two-thirds of this total was in rural areas. Present calculations call for an annual investment of about 600 million soles ($22.2 million). For the first 2 years the Government of Peru expects to finance about half of this program by means of external loans. A slum-clearance law was promulgated in February 1961 and two satellite cities on the outskirts of Lima have been established to help solve the housing problem. A $2 million bond issue finances this project. A law of April 1961 requires the Housing 

Institute to provide incentives to mutual credit associations, cooperatives, and other similar organizations by assisting in their organization and financing their development. Special tax relief has been given private enterprises engaged in low-cost housing construction. 

5. Health.-Standards of health and sanitation are low in Peru, particularly in rural areas, and especially among the Indians who constitute the bulk of the population in the highlands. The infant-mortality rate, for example, is estimated at approximately 90, compared with 58 in Argentina and 26 in the United States. The number of hospital beds, and trained personnel doctors per capita provides a similar contrast. Peru, however, has developed a national health plan, which has been underway since 1960. Under this program the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance has completed agreements to construct 12 new hospital-health centers in the next 2 years. The Executive branch has submitted to the Congress a bill to establish a National Sanitary Works Corporation to be responsible for the planning, construction, maintenance,

and operation of these facilities throughout Peru. Major water supply and sanitation projects are now being undertaken for Lima and Arequipa. 

The Ministry of Health has just published a "National Health Plan With International Assistance" covering special projects to be undertaken over a 3year period in the following five fields: (1) local health services, (2) malaria eradication, (3) control of tuberculosis, (4) sanitation in rural areas, and (5) the improvement and enlargement of the National Institutes of Health and Nutrition. 

6. Education.-School facilities are lacking for more than one-third of children of school age in Peru, although education between 7 and 16 years is theoretically free, compulsory, and state-controlled. While the literacy rate for the country as a whole is about 45 percent, it varies greatly as between the coastal area (68 percent) and the Sierra (27 percent). Nevertheless, 25 percent of the national budget is allotted to education. There is a general recognition of the need for radical improvements in the educational system but such changes are still mainly in the planning stage. In 1961 the Universidad Agraria del Peru established a College of Agricultural Engineering with financial assistance from the Special Fund of the United Nations. A technological school, designed to train professionals at the intermediate level, is being established in the University of Engineering with help from the same fund. 

7. Public administration.-Peru has had a Civil Service Commission since 

1950. However, salaries are low and relatively little progress has been made in the establishment of a merit system. The Government has recently decided to strengthen the existing Institute of Public Administration, which has already trained about 3,000 Government employees. 

8. Financial stability.-Peru has generally maintained relative stability in both prices and exchange rates. Following economic difficulties and a financial crisis in 1959, the Peruvian Government has succeeded to a remarkable degree in stabilizing the economy and restoring business confidence. Economic resources are relatively plentiful and general economic and banking policies have been conservative. Major changes in Peruvian society seem inevitable and the rapid development of economic resources to meet social requirements will be necessary to insure the continuance of financial stability. 

9. Credit. The banking and credit system in Peru is both structurally and administratively conservative. However, a bill to create a National Housing 

Bank (Banco Nacional de la Vivienda) was presented to Congress in 1961, with capital to be contributed by the state and by mutual credit associations. This institution may make an important contribution in the housing field. Pending passage of this bill, the National Housing Institute is serving as the interim credit agency. In November 1961 the capital of the Industrial Bank was raised to 1 billion soles (the sol is freely convertible at 27 per US$) and it was authorized to contribute up to 50 percent of the capital needed to establish essential productive enterprises. A private development bank, the Peru Investment Corp., is being formed to help meet the need for industrial financing. 

In addition, in 1961 a system of agricultural credit to small farmers was instituted. This system is to be handled through the Institute of Agrarian Reform and Colonization and the Agricultural Development Bank. Its beginning was facilitated by a U.S. Development Loan Fund agreement. The number of credit union cooperatives has now expanded beyond the 200 mark, with some very significant work being done in this field. Savings and loan associations have also made progress.

In February 1962 the maximum for commercial bank rates was lowered from 14 percent to 12 percent, with a ceiling for commissions and other charges set at 1 percent. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.—Conditions for private enterprise are generally favorable in Peru, except that the effective domestic demand for goods and services is relatively small because of low per capita income. Conditions mentioned above under financial stability and credit are indicative of the prevailing climate. The economic base for further development also is good. 

The annual growth rate is now about 6 percent; Peru enjoys a favorable balance of trade with both imports and exports on the increase; its dollar reserves have been substantially strengthened; flight capital is beginning to return; and deficit spending has been curtailed. The GNP rose from $1.6 billion in 1959 to $1.98 billion in 1960. In 1959 Peru enacted an Industrial Promotion Law, providing tax exemptions and other incentives for new foreign and domestic investment. 

In an 18-month period from 1959 to 1961, savings and time deposits increased from the equivalent of $107 million to $146 million.

U.S. enterprise has usually found Peru a favorable place for investment, the most spectacular recent development bearing out this fact being the investment of $230 million by a consortium of U.S. companies in a copper-mining project in southern Peru. 

11. Labor.-Peru has labor legislation providing for the organization of labor, conditions of work, fringe benefits, and tenure. The organization of labor has proceeded fairly rapidly in recent years. Labor is dominated by the militantly anti-Communist APRA. Communist influence, however, is strong in certain unions. 

No major self-help measures in this field have been reported.

URUGUAY 1. General statement.—Over the past half century Uruguay's record of selfhelp and reform has been outstanding. It has many of the social advantages that other Latin American countries have yet to achieve. Per capita income is relatively high and the distribution of income is probably more equitable than in any other Latin American country. Consequently, there are very few extremely rich or poor. The majority of the people are well-fed and healthy. 

There is a substantial middle class. Unlike other South American countries, Uruguay has no unsettled areas. In the 1940's Uruguay started to industrialize rapidly. In recent years, however, agriculture has remained static, inflation set in, and the rate of economic growth has been insufficient both to maintain the current living standards and to provide enough resources for increasing productive capacity. The Government now recognizes the need for a national economic plan and a new planning agency is just beginning to function. Literacy is estimated to be about 88 percent, one of the highest in Latin America. The population, which is largely of European stock, is estimated at 2,900,000 in 1962, and is believed to be growing by about 1.7 percent annually. 

2. Planning.-Uruguay established a planning agency (CIDE) in January 

1960. In practice the CIDE, which was created on a ministerial level, was not immediately operative. The Punta del Este Conference in August 1961 awakened 

Government leaders to Uruguay's needs in this area, and CIDE is now beginning to function. The agency is in the Ministry of Finance under the technical direction of an able and politically independent Uruguayan economist with a staff of about 15 economists and technicians. At the request of the Government, a joint mission of the IDB, the OAS, and ECLA is now assisting in drawing up a 10-year national development plan. A U.S.-proposed project would finance contract services for special economic studies to support planning. The equivalent of about $230,000 was appropriated by the Uruguayan Government in November 1961 to finance a population census under the direction of CIDE. The Bank of the Republic aided by a CIDE technician is compiling national income statistics. A study of the financial accounts of the entire public sector, never before done in Uruguay, is already underway. 

3. Agrarian reform.-For many years, Government policies tended to favor development of the urban sector and to discourage agricultural efficiency. Improved livestock feeding techniques, fertilizers, crop rotation, disease control, and animal sanitation are inadequately used. There is a shortage of agricultural credit and of rural extension services. Although no agricultural census has been taken, it seems likely that extremes in the size of land holdings prevent efficient cultivation. The Agrarian Reform Law of 1948 provides for the purchase and subdivision of land but has been used very little. 

The present administration has taken some steps to increase production and incentive in the agricultural export sector. Due to the monetary reform of 1959, ranchers and wool exporters now receive more favorable exchange treatment. 

Proceeds from export taxes have recently been earmarked for subsidizing increased use of fertilizers and animal sanitation methods. In mid-1960, an 

IBRD-FAO sponsored program to increase the productivity of grazing land was inaugurated. Public Law 480 local currency is also used to finance this program. 

The recently established national planning agency is to devote considerable attention to solving agrarian problems. There still remains, however, a need for greater expansion in credit and technical services to small holders, as well as producers for export, and for an examination of the present system of land tenure with a view toward improving productivity of land and labor. 

4. Housing.-In Uruguay, housing is not a critical problem as yet, but there has been little investment in low- and medium-cost housing in the postwar years and the current deficit is estimated to be about 60,000. A decree of November 81496-62--pt. 3-11

1961 set forth a national housing program. The Mortgage Bank of Uruguay and the National Economic Housing Institute were charged in January 1962 with the preparation of a national housing plan. The Mortgage Low-Cost Housing 

Institute will give technical assistance. Further assistance will be obtained from the autonomous entities, departmental governments, and the University of the Republic and cooperation is expected from public and private institutions. 

These activities will provide housing for low-income groups, who have in the past only had access to proper housing in exceptional circumstances. Montevideo has invested 2 million pesos ($180,000) in 216 dwelling units and other facilities and is constructing 120 additional units at a cost of about 2.7 milion pesos ($245,000). The Government recently requested a $3.7 million loan from the 

United States for low-cost housing in Montevideo and Mercedes. 

5. Health. Although Uruguay has achieved high standards in the field of health, physical facilities have deteriorated in recent years. Planning was started in December 1961 for a series of health centers. The National Council of Government expects to raise 45.1 million pesos ($4 million) by the proposed social development law, now pending in the legislature, for the construction and expansion of medical facilities. This represents about 38 percent of the estimated total expenditure required. The medical facilities to be undertaken include 22 polyclinics in Montevideo and 18 regional polyclinics in the interior. 

6. Education.-Uruguay has achieved relatively high standards in education. 

The physical plant of its educational system, however, has deteriorated and the country has more teachers than can be absorbed by existing classroom space. Planning was started in 1961 for the addition of a number of primary classrooms. The social development law now pending in the legislature calls for increased tax revenue to finance a contribution (45.1 million pesos equivalent to $4 million) to the school construction and expansion project which has been proposed to AID. This would represent 38 percent of the proposed expenditure. The number of classrooms to be constructed is 1,727, all in the rural areas where facilities are the poorest. The proposed legislation provides for local self-help by local organizations of all types down to the neighborhood level in carrying out the program. 

7. Public administration.-There is a plural executive system in which both majority and opposition parties are constitutionally represented in the nineman committee which is collectively the Chief Executive power. The built in political checks and balances of this system, while conducive to stability, inhibit dynamic leadership. There is a very small competitive career system. Uruguay has no present plans to improve public administration. 

8. Financial stability.-Under the exchange reform law of December 17, 1959, the multiple-exchange rate system was abolished, quota-origin controls on imports were eliminated, and the peso was devalued to bring it closer into line with its real value in international exchange. In November 1960, Uruguay signed an IMF stabilization agreement. In order to come under IMF agreed credit ceilings, the Government restricted credit in early 1961 in an effort to combat inflation. Prices rose less rapidly in 1961 than before and the exchange rate remained stable. Inflationary dangers persist, however, as a growing wage bill in both Government and private activity is forcing a large expansion of the money supply and legal control over bank credit is feeble. 

9. Credit.-Uruguay has a well-developed banking system. One of the purposes of the national housing program which was set forth in a decree of November 1961 is to stimulate the formation of savings and loan associations for the working classes and employees of the Government. The Mortgage Bank of 

Uruguay has applied to the IDB for a loan of $2 million per year for 5 years to be used to increase the capital of its housing finance department. There are no specialized credit institutions for agriculture. 

10. Investment and private enterprise. The resources law of November 1960 provides incentives to productive private investment through income tax exemptions for industrial profits reinvested in the acquisition or renovation of equipment. Between 75 and 90 percent of reinvested profits may be exempted, the exact amount depending upon the geographic location of the enterprise. It favors those in the interior. Also up to 75 percent of net farm income may be deducted if it is invested in soil improvements or the construction of housing for workers.

Many enterprises are owned by the Government and in some cases it exercises a monopoly. It owns the railroads and the major Uruguayan airline; has monopoly control of the telephone system, commercial fishing, electric power,

alcohol, and refined petroleum; manufactures cement; engages in commercial banking; issues insurance; distributes milk and dairy products; and operates the port of Montevideo as well as a meat packing plant. 

11. Labor.-Uruguay early adopted social legislation affecting labor. Every worker is legally entitled to a fair wage, a regulated working day, a weekly day of rest, and decent hygienic working conditions. The work of women and children is particularly subject to regulation and the law provides for the organization of trade unions and the right to strike. Social security and old-age survivor's benefits are assured to all workers. Although conciliation and arbitration courts are provided by law they have fallen into disuse. The various labor laws are in need of codification. 

In November and December 1960 Uruguay established its first labor court, organized a health insurance system for automobile transport workers, revised the health insurance system for the construction industry, provided for a complementary annual wage or New Year's bonus, and increased substantially the family allotment system benefits. A long-standing problem of noncompliance with international labor agreements (ILO conventions) was remedied in November 1960 by a decree which established procedures to insure compliance. 

VENEZUELA 

1. General statement.—Venezuela is the sixth largest country of South America, with an area of 352,000 square miles. It has vast natural resources, particularly petroleum and iron, as well as extensive and diversified sources of power which, if properly developed, will play a major role in the country's future development. Total population is approximately 7 million and by 1970 it is expected to exceed 10 million. It is estimated that about 50 percent of the population is literate. In spite of the abundant natural resources and a relatively high gross domestic per capita product, about US$1,000 in 1961, the country is beset by economic, social, and political strains inherent in a transition in one lifetime, from military dictatorship and an oligarchic social order to political and social democracy. The end of the Venezuelan oil boom, and greatly increased expenditures for politically necessary social welfare programs have put a serious strain on the economy. A severe economic recession and heavy flight of capital further complicated the situation. Unemployment has risen to about 13 percent of the labor force. 

In 1960 the Government adopted a 4-year plan subsequently designed to end the recession and to promote a coordinated and balanced economic development, including increased and diversified production, high employment levels, and a stable balance of payments. In order to carry out its programs for economic recovery and development, the Betancourt administration is counting heavily on external assistance to restore business confidence. 

2. Planning.-The Central Coordination and Planning Office assigned to the 

Office of the President announced in April 1960 a 4-year economic and social development plan establishing an order of priority for the country's most urgent needs. Under the original plan the Government directed 41 percent of its investments toward social development (sanitation, education, housing), 33 percent toward the basic economic sectors, and about 20 percent for infrastructural development. The plan is revised on an annual basis so that the Government may evaluate achievements and adjust goals for the following 4-year period. In 

March 1962 the President announced the latest revision to cover the period 1962-65, however, no great changes were made in the direction of Government investments. A U.N.-ECLA team of advisers has helped Venezuela in preparation of the plan. It is expected that Venezuela will present its revised plan to the OAS panel of experts for review. 

3. Agrarian reform.—A program of land reform was undertaken in Venezuela in March 1960, prior to the Bogotá Conference. Thus far; approximately 

1,600,000 hectares (nearly 4 million acres) have been distributed to around 44,000 families. The Government intends to settle perhaps another 75,000 families within the remaining 24 months of President Betancourt's 5-year term and to expand the technical and supervisory services to the rural population. Currently the financial outlay for the program is about 10 percent of the national budget, including appropriations for the various ministries and agencies involved. The Venezuelan program represents one of the most ambitious agrarian reforms currently underway in any of the Latin American countries.

4. Housing.—The housing shortage has been estimated at 800,000 units, with an additional annual demand of approximately 110,000 units, not counting replacements. In 1958 rural housing construction was turned over to the rural housing bureau in the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare. Government officials are now considering converting the Labor Bank (Banco Obrero), which handles the Government's participation in low-cost housing construction, into a National Housing Institute.

Under the 4-year plan, 668.4 million bolívares (US$200 million) have been programed for national housing projects for the period 1960–64. The Government program includes a system of small loans, provision of minimum public services, construction of emergency housing in the interior of the country, construction of "nucleus dwellings," and a rural housing program based on a formula of self-help. (The IDB has authorized a loan of US$12 million to the labor bank to be used by the rural housing division in this program). The 

Government has obtained a $10 million loan from the Agency for International Development to establish a system of savings and loan associations for housing and in November 1961 created an Urban Mortgage Bank to assist in the housing effort. 

5. Health.-Standards of sanitation and public health in Venezuela are comparable to or slightly higher than those in most other Latin American countries. For the first time in 1959, the primary cause of death was not due to an infectious disease. The infant mortality rate for the same year was the third lowest in South America. Present health problems stem mostly from a shortage of adequately trained medical personnel, insufficient potable water supplies and waste disposal systems, poor environmental and personal sanitation, crowded living conditions, and insufficient medical care facilities. According to estimates of the Pan-American Sanitary Bureau, 43 percent of the urban population is without water service and 67 percent is without sewerage service. 

Approximately 10 percent of the national budget is appropriated for national and local health services, rendered through sanitary units, health centers, rural medical stations, and hospitals.

In 1958 a national rural housing service was created within the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to provide for the construction of modern low-cost 2to 3-bedroom cement block houses. The 4-year plan also made provisions for improving water supplies and sanitation facilities. Among the proposed investments for 1960-64, the Government has allocated 7,033 million bolívares to the National Institute of Sanitation Works (INOS) to supply water service to an additional 1.6 million persons, 74.1 percent more people than were served in 

1960, and to supply sewerage service to an additional 1.4 million persons, an increase of 72.2 percent over 1960. The plan also calls for an investment of 48.7 million bolívares for water supplies for 640,000 rural inhabitants. The 4-year plan is directed toward the long-range goal of providing water supplies to 70 percent of the rural population by 1971. 

The 4-year plan also makes provisions for a soil drainage program designed to control certain endemic diseases. (An extensive malaria eradication program has reduced the number of cases of malaria and virtually eliminated it as a public health problem.) 

6. Education.-When the present government began its administration in 1958 nearly 500,000 school-age children (40 percent of the total) were not attending school, and most of those attending left school before entering the fourth grade. 

A rapid growth in the school-age population was aggravating the shortage in school facilities and teachers. Between 1958 and 1960 the Government took steps to improve the situation, and total school registration rose by almost 50 percent, making it possible to include nearly 400,000 children who were not attending school previously. At the same time 21 additional normal schools (teacher training institutions) were established, and between 1958 and 1960 the number of teachers rose from 20,900 to 33,600.

In the 4-year period (1961-64), in the field of rural education where the situation is most critical, Venezuela plans to train 2,800 new rural elementaryschool teachers, to establish 5 new normal schools, to have 28,000 additional elementary-school children enter the first grade each year, and to construct 700 new classrooms each year. In the fields of vocational and secondary education the 

Government is planning expenditures in the period 1961-64 of 55.5 million bolívares for 44 new secondary schools to accommodate 40,200 new pupils, and 53.5 million bolívares for 2,025 new teachers. (Total costs for the 4-year period will be approximately $32.5 million). The United States is helping to revamp

the curriculum of the secondary school system and to broaden its scope so that Venezuela can better meet its skilled labor needs. 

7. Public administration.-Administration of the Venezuelan tax system has been improved in recent years through introduction of various procedures for verifying tax declarations and by simplification of collection methods. These improvements increased income-tax collections from 526.2 bolívares in the 1959-60 fiscal year to 596 million bolívares in 1960–61. In May 1961 President Betancourt put before the Congress an austerity and recovery program envisaging a reduction in the salaries of Government employees, an increase in taxes, a cutback in administrative expenditures, and greater efficiency in Government agencies. This program met with strong opposition and was modified by the 

Congress to eliminate part of the salary cuts and tax increases. Under the alliance for progress the Government also started a project in November 1961 which aims at the following goals over the next 3 years: (a) training 100 to 

120 upper echelon Government officials abroad, mainly in the United States, (b) training approximately 120 middle-level public servants in Puerto Rico, and (c) training locally about 1,500 middle and lower echelon public servants. 

8. Financial stability—For the past 10 years Venezuela's gross national product has been one of the highest in Latin America and until recently, the boom provided by the development of petroleum insured the country against foreign exchange shortages and unmanageable budget deficits. The coincident end of the oil boom and the Perez Jimenez dictatorship in early 1958 and the ensuing political ferment and consequent economic recession brought on severe financial difficulties. The Government has utilized import licensing and exchange controls to restrict the outflow of foreign exchange. In keeping with its traditional practices, the Government has avoided currency inflation as a means of financing its deficit, relying instead primarily on short-term external credits. The Government plans to seek long-term loans to refund its present debts and to finance some of the investment expenditures which are now included in the budget. 

9. Credit. In the 3-year period 1959 through 1961, the Government of Venezuela made approximately $75 million in rural credit available to farmers in connection with its agrarian reform program. The Government reports that a high percentage of the repayments due on the $75 million is in default. The 

Farm Credit Agency has been authorized to seek a $10 million foreign loan for additional credits to farmers in the coming year. More attention will be given to provision of farm equipment credit and to organization of Government machinery to supervise credit activities. On December 15, 1961, the Congress passed a law authorizing the Agriculture and Livestock Bank to use $30 million to finance the importation of farm machinery, to promote production of certain crops, and to finance importation of improved livestock. An emergency economic law, approved in June 1961, authorized the creation of an insured savings and loan system. The Government set up preliminary institutions in June, and by Presidential decree in November established a National Savings and Loan System which will enable private resources to be channeled into housing investments. The U.S. Development Loan Fund, now merged into the Agency for International Development, approved a $10 million loan to assist this activity. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-During the present administration the climate for foreign investment in Venezuela has been mixed. Taxes on foreign petroleum companies are high. The Government has declared that it will respect existing foreign investment and concessions but has opposed granting any new concessions to foreign oil companies. It is considering, instead, the possibility of service contracts with the newly established Venezuelan state oil company. The Government has also undertaken increased regulation of marketing activities of the oil companies. Exploration by private companies has virtually ceased and new investments are not forthcoming. On the other hand, the 4-year plan, which the Government brought out in 1960, partly depends on investments in Venezuela from both domestic and foreign private enterprise. The emergency economic law, approved by Congress in June 1961, contained a provision authorizing the creation of an insured savings system to encourage private enterprise, and the Government is now considering signing an investment guarantee agreement with the United States. 

11. Labor.-Labor unions in Venezuela are presently a strong force in support of constitutional and democratic government. The largest group of trade unions in Venezuela is the Land Workers Federation with approximately 500,- 000 members. The federation is the prime mover behind the Government's

agrarian reform program and in many instances has taken the initiative in implementing the program. 

The labor situation in Venezuela is complicated by the high number of unemployed, approximately 350,000 or 13 percent of the labor force. At the same time, there is serious lack of skilled labor. Together with the program to restore economic development in Venezuela, the Government established a National Institute for Cooperative Education (INCE) in November 1960 to carry out a massive program of on-the-job and apprenticeship training in industry. 

The Institute completed a labor force census in February 1962 which will be used as a basis for further training programs. The Government also started a project under the Alliance for Progress designed to train union leaders and to develop standards and procedures for worker education to insure the continued growth of democratic trade unionism and the continuous supply of responsible labor leadership needed by the expanding urban and rural population. 

PART III. DEPENDENT OVERSEA TERRITORIES BRITISH GUIANA 

1. General statement.—The economy of British Guiana, a colony of the United 

Kingdom, is based primarily upon sugar, rice, and bauxite. The population is predominately East Indian and African, and 85 percent inhabit a narrow strip of low coastal land. Educational and health facilities are inadequate. Government institutions and laws, however, are relatively advanced as compared with those of many of the less-developed countries. At present it is in a stage of transition to independence, with some degree of political and social instability, as indicated by the riots in February 1962. Although British Guiana has had a high proportion of its development financed by the United Kingdom, it is at an early stage of economic development with insufficient resources to meet requirements. The Government is presently encouraging land reform, proposing tax reform, and supporting certain projects to develop the interior. The population is estimated to be 566,000 in 1962 and is growing by about 2.9 percent a year. Literacy is reported to be about 80 percent, but this figure is possibly somewhat high. 

2. Planning.—The present development plan (1960–64), amounting to $64 million, was drafted by British colonial servants in conjunction with the elected Government and is supported by the United Kingdom loans and grants amounting to $36 million. The present Government feels that the plan, which is lagging behind goals set, is grossly inadequate for the country's needs. A Ministry of 

Development and Planning was established when the new Government was formed in August 1961, but it is not yet fully operative. Personnel who have the necessary training and experience for planning are scarce. 

3. Agrarian reform.-The Government is encouraging land reform and has a pilot land resettlement scheme. The primary emphasis of the development program for 1960-64, which was prepared by British colonial officials, is on the expansion of the area devoted to rice cultivation. It is the intention of the program that the 185,000 acres under cultivation in 1960 would be increased to 200,000 acres by 1964. There has been set aside an amount equivalent to $18 million for drainage and irrigation, $1.9 million for land settlement in rice areas, and $1.5 million for credit to rice farmers. In the first 2 years of operation, the cost of developing the land was in excess of that planned and the number of acres being brought into production was less than planned. 

Earlier expansion of rice had been into the lands which were adjacent to existing holdings and which did not require extensive irrigation and drainage nor major Government assistance. New expansion is occurring primarily on land held and reclaimed by the Government at high cost for drainage, irrigation, resettlement, and loans to settlers. The Government is also stimulating the growing of coconuts. The plan calls for setting out new coconut plants in nurseries and later distributing them to farmers under a bonus system. Cattle raising is being supported by way of extension-type activities and subsidies to farmers. The operation of an experimental station in the intermediate savannahs at Ebini and of one in the far savannahs near Letham is also included in the program. 

4. Housing. There is not a serious housing shortage in British Guiana in relation to most other countries in the Latin America area, because the estates supply housing for workers, the development program for 1955-59 emphasized housing, and the East Indian rice farmers-the largest single bloc of the popula-

tion-build their own houses on the plots of land they are farming. It is estimated that at least 4,000 new houses a year are required to keep up with the annual increase in population of about 17,000. The estimated amount of capital allotted by the Government in 1961 for housing was equivalent to $316,- 000 of which about $183,000 was for the purchase and development of land, $89,000 for aided self-help housing and the balance largely for construction of flats for rent and houses for sale. The Government is providing the cost of salaries and international travel for trainees in the U.S.-sponsored project on community development training designed to assist groups and communities to realize their own needs and to encourage voluntary community action in undertaking activities, including self-help housing, to fill their needs. 

5. Health.-In British Guiana, medical facilities are so unduly modest and medical services so depressed as to cause operations to be conducted at well below minimum requirements for a developing region. Health education activities are inadequate and microfilaremia is one of the major health problems of the inhabited coast. An attempt has been made to relieve congestion at the 

Public Hospital in Georgetown by the construction of low-cost cottage hospitals in some of the outlying areas. The Government has increased its contribution to the joint United States-British Guiana project for Filariasis control from the equivalent of $12,400 to $98,300 a year for the 5-year period 1960-64. In addition, it is assuming responsibility for supporting and maintaining the staff presently employed in this work and making available the physical plant of the mosquito control services for the project. U.S. aid is cooperating with the medical department in a project titled "Operational Advisory Services, Public Health," which is designed to improve basic medical services essential to the health and well-being of the people. The Government spends annually an amount equivalent to $3 million for the maintenance of medical services and is to contribute an additional amount equivalent to $320,000 annually during the period 1960-64 to expand medical services. 

6. Education. More than 20 percent of the population of 565,000 are below the age of 21. The single largest group is that between the age of 1 and the schoolleaving age of 14; there are only 3,000 teachers or about one-third of the number that would be required if a full educational program were provided for both elementary and secondary school children. 

7. Public administration.—During the years preceding the election of August 

1961 the country was preparing for independence by gradual transfer to Ministers of Government of the functions formerly held by British Colonial officials. 

However, new ministries such as the Ministry of Finance, require consultant services as to organization procedures, and general operations. Of the senior staff of the civil service which totaled 800 persons, about 70 positions were vacant in August 1961, and it is reported that the number of vacancies has increased since that time. 

8. Financial stability. There are no central banking facilities in British 

Guiana, but the Government is actively considering the establishment of a central bank as well as the adoption of its own currency. It is currently consulting with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) concerning the structure, organization, and functions of a central bank and the resources required for its establishment and efficient operation. 

9. Credit. The Government established the British Guiana Credit Corpora tion in 1954 on the recommendation of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. It makes two types of loans-one is to finance the cooperative thrift and credit societies and the other is to individuals in the fields of agriculture and housing. Loans made directly to individual farmers have been small in total, since most borrowers do not have the required security. Loans granted by the cooperative credit societies have been largely the short-term rice production type and are not designed for development credit. Beginning in 1960 credit amounting to the equivalent of $1.2 million has been extended through the British Guiana Credit Corporation to cooperatives for capital imports of machinery for use in conjunction with rice development. 

The overall repayment situation is poor. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Four-fifths of all industrial capital is invested in the sugar industry. Industry is owned by private firms or individuals, mainly British or Canadian, except for some rice milling and small processing undertakings, which are owned by the Government. Since the election in August 1961, Dr. Jagan has emphasized his belief in public ownership of the means of production and in the development of new industries by Government.

11. Labor.—Extensive labor legislation in British Guiana, which is revised from time to time to give effect to current international conventions, regulates minimum wages, hours of work, and holidays with pay in various industries, the employment of women and children, and workmen's compensation. The policy of the British has been to foster the development of free trade unions, to create an atmosphere unfavorable to disputes, and to encourage labor and management to settle their difference by direct negotiation. There are 26 major unions in 

British Guiana, all of which belong to the British Trade Union Council, a free trade union movement. 

BRITISH HONDURAS 

1. General statement.-British Honduras is presently working under a new constitution, which went into effect in 1961. It grants the colony much internal autonomy. This territory is faced with many economic and social problems which stem from its small size, its small population (estimated now at about 92,000), a lack of mineral resources, and inefficient use of agricultural resources. 

In addition, there are other obstacles to development, including a shortage of skilled labor and trained personnel, a low level of public health, a housing shortage, and limited financial resources. The largest share by far of foreign assistance is received from the United Kingdom and is indispensable under present conditions. The United States has a modest program, mostly of technical assistance. Literacy is estimated at 70 percent. 

In addition to its basic problems, British Honduras is also periodically subject to destructive hurricanes. The one of 1955 caused substantial damages and that of October 31, 1961, was a major disaster. In 2 months, up to the end of 

1961, the British and Honduran Governments spent $2,782,857 on disaster relief, and in addition received relief supplies valued at $300,000 from the United States and other extensive humanitarian assistance. It is estimated roughly that the cost of rehabilitation may run as high as $40 million. The annual GNP is approximately $27 million. 

2. Planning.-Despite the official existence of a development plan since 1946, British Honduras does not have a planning agency and the plan mentioned above, weak as it was because of the lack of needed statistical and other data, has somewhat lagged in implementation. However, the Government has requested an economic survey team from the United Nations which is being sent. 

3. Agrarian reform.-The country's key economic activities are lumbering, citrus growing, and sugar production. They account for more than 80 percent of the country's exports and are the largest employers of labor. More than half of the 5.5 million acres of land is in forests. Land that is classed as agricultural amounts to a little over 2 million acres, much of it having limited potential. The land ownership pattern tends to decrease further the already limited and rather inefficient use of the potentially productive areas. Crown lands take up a substantial area and generally, are not suitably located for homesteads. 

They are being sold as needed, however. Many large underdeveloped areas are privately held for investment or speculation-one company owns a million acres. 

Some thought has been given to increasing the very low land taxes in the hope of encouraging development but even if this is done, it is not expected to have much immediate effect. 

Agriculture probably offers the greatest possibility for long-range economic growth, especially in view of the diminishing forests and the practical absence of discovered mineral resources. However, it now produces only about 15 percent of the national income. Efforts have been made to increase production of staple food products, particularly beans, corn, and rice. Some training in agricultural methods and the extension of some rural credit has occurred, but so far little progress has been made. In February 1962 the Legislative Assembly law providing for increased security for tenant farmers was enacted. They must now be given 1 year's written notice of intention to terminate their holding. 

4. Housing.-According to a rough estimate, there were about 20,000 houses prior to the hurricane of October 1961. Normal housing needs before the disaster were estimated at 430 new houses every year, each providing for five persons, simply to cover the population increase. In addition, 8,000 more were needed to relieve the prevailing serious overcrowding and 1,200 to replace dilapidated houses which then existed. The hurricane destroyed or damaged about 7,500 houses according to a preliminary estimate. The minimum cost of their replacement or repair has been estimated at $5 million. Prior to the 

1961 hurricane, the quantity of new construction was inadequate. The Govern-

ment had offered some help by making available a limited amount of housing credit on a selective basis. Some 200 families have organized 9 cooperatives, and others are doing the same, for the purpose of saving money and to undertake self-help measures, such as the making of concrete blocks. But this has not yet resulted in new housing construction. 

5. Health.-Tuberculosis, dysentery, enteritis, and intestinal parasites are common. Sewage disposal is a serious problem for Belize, the capital, where raw sewage is dumped into canals which run through the city. It moves gradually out to sea, much of it passing alongside the public market where the boats tie up to unload produce. Hospital and other public health facilities, which were grossly inadequate prior to the recent hurricane, were damaged by it. 

The level of sanitation among the people is extremely low. 

British Honduras is obtaining assistance from United Kingdom sources and from the U.N. in the health and medical sectors. With the exception of the progress made in the eradication of malaria, however, there has been apparently little progress in recent years. With the recent hurricane, obstacles to advancement in this field have been greatly increased and the potential for self-help correspondingly decreased. 

6. Education.-Between the ages of 6 and 14, education is compulsory for children who live near a school. There is limited schooling beyond the primary level and, except for a 2-year teacher training college, there are no educational institutions above the secondary level. The literacy rate, however, is 70 percent. Some improvement in secondary schooling in the rural areas has taken place in recent years, but it is still very inadequate. 

7. Public administration.-Very few Hondurans have had administrative experience. Service in British Honduras has generally been avoided by British colonial officers and those who came rarely stayed longer than the maximum of 2 years. In addition, practically all Government agencies are understaffed and underfinanced.

The Government and some of the country's leaders have recently shown a serious interest in improving the situation. The British commission which surveyed the hurricane damage in December 1961 has also recommended better quality administration staffing and more personnel. 

8. Financial stability.—The Honduran dollar is directly supported by the sterling bloc; the perennial budgetary deficit is made up by United Kingdom grants; and the recurring adverse balance of trade is believed to be greatly alleviated by grants-in-aid, development grants and loans, and other subsidies from the United Kingdom, as well as limited receipts from tourists, remittances, and sale of land to foreign speculators and investors. 

9. Credit. Two banks provide commercial banking facilities, but there are no sources for development credit or medium or long-term loans. 

The very limited agricultural credit programs of the Government were operated without critical appraisal of repayment capabilities, and were not successful. The number and importance of credit unions has increased in recent years and their assets now exceed $700,000. For several years there has been talk of creating a new agency which has been described sometimes as development bank or a development finance corporation to meet the needs for medium- and long-term capital loans. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The expressed attitude of the Government is favorable toward private enterprise and foreign private investment. 

Investment incentive legislation, which included tax holidays and waivers of customs duties, was enacted in 1960. Currency convertibility and transfer are not problems. While there might be opportunities for some small-scale, labor intensive, industries, the size of the population limits the local market and the lack of nonagricultural resources tends to discourage foreign investments. U.S. investments in British Honduras have been estimated at $6.3 million, $2 million of which are in oil exploration. To date no oil has been discovered.
