11. Labor. The total labor force is estimated at about 21,000. The major industries are all seasonal, with comparatively little opportunity for movement. 

Peak employment in timber extraction, sawmills and associated operations is around 5,000 to 6,000 men; seasonal agricultural work may use 4,000 men and women; chicle collection gives employment to about 1,000 men from July to 

January; there are an estimated 400 full-time and 200 part-time commercial fishermen, almost all self-employed. Many wage earners do some farming during layoffs. There is a considerable amount of unemployment and underemployment. Some workers seek employment, during certain seasons, in

Guatemala and Mexico. The labor force has a low productivity because of the lack of knowledge, skills, and management ability. There are 3,000 workers in three main labor unions.

BRITISH WEST INDIES-EASTERN CARIBBEAN 

1. General statement.—The eastern Caribbean consists of the British territories of Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windward Islands (St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Grenada, and Dominica) and Leeward Islands (Antigua, St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguillo, and Montserrat). Trinidad is by far the largest and most populous of these territories. The eastern Caribbean area is a producer and exporter of sugar, bananas, coffee, cocoa beans, citrus juices, and spices. In recent years oil production and refining have become dominant in the economy of Trinidad. In 

Barbados and Antigua tourism has become increasingly important, and efforts are being made to develop the tourist potential of the other islands. The population is primarily Negro, with a substantial number of East Indians in Trinidad. 

Under colonial administration, basic political, economic, and social institutions were established.

These territories with Jamaica had formed the West Indies Federation. With the withdrawal of Jamaica from the federation in September 1961, however, the future constitutional organization of the West Indies became uncertain. Trinidad and Tobago are now seeking independence which may be granted in late 1962 or in 1963. The prospects for becoming economically self-sustaining are favorable for Trinidad and Tobago but are less promising for the other islands. 

The estimated 1962 population in Trinidad and Tobago is 830,000, in Barbados 247,000, and in the Windward and Leeward Islands 454,000. The illiteracy rates are reported to be approximately 7 percent in Barbados, 26 percent in Trinidad, 42 percent in the Windward Islands, and 34 percent in the Leeward Islands. 

2. Planning.-Trinidad has a central planning unit. Statistics available for planning national development are adequate and reasonably reliable. The government initiated a 5-year program for national development in 1958 which covers such social improvements as housing, water supply, health and education, as well as expansion of the economic infrastructure, particularly of electric power, transportation, and communication facilities. This plan which terminates in 1962 has some of the characteristics of a list of public works projects to be accomplished by the government although it has been reasonably well related to government budget possibilities and to general government policies. The government is presently finishing their 1962-67 plan. The government party returned to power in the elections of December 1961 promised to establish a more formal planning board arrangement and recently consulted with a team of Indian planning advisers. It is probable that Trinidad will seek further planning assistance from non-U.S. free world sources. 

Barbados has an economic planning unit, financed from regular revenues, to advise on economic and social planning, coordination policies, and on preparation, implementation, and assessment of long-range programs. It has a 5-year development plan for 1960-65 which concentrates on tourism, industry, agriculture, and housing, with provision for some action in communications, education, and social services. The plan appears to be a good start toward a practical solution to Barbados' problem.

In general the development programs of the Windward and Leeward Islands are not carefully planned and integrated. 

3. Agrarian reform.-Much of the highly productive land in the eastern 

Caribbean is in sugar estates. In Barbados, Trinidad, St. Kitts, and Antigua the agricultural economy is based upon sugar, and the large estates are an economic necessity. In the other islands there is more agricultural diversification and small holdings are more common. 

In St. Lucia, a major cooperative effort with the United States is being made to improve conditions. Farm to market roads are being constructed; modern soil conservation practices and gravity flow irrigation are being introduced; livestock improvement programs emphasizing poultry and swine have been inaugurated; and cold storage, slaughterhouse, and feedmills are being erected. 

4. Housing.-The Trinidad and Tobago 5-year development program includes $15.8 million for housing and urban facilities. The government plans to meet the requirement for 107,000 new houses by 1965 by encouraging private investment in housing and by participating in aided self-help and rental-mortgage housing, and urban redevelopment. The first large-scale housing project (over 

2,000 houses) was started in April 1961. Trinidad has housing legislation pro-

viding tax concessions to encourage new home construction. Provision for housing units for sugarworkers is made from the proceeds of the sugar labor welfare fund.

Barbados' 5-year plan allocates $5.4 million to housing and urban facilities. 

The targets are to reduce overcrowding in homes, provide for slum clearance, and insure orderly and balanced development with services such as roads and water. 

5. Health. In the eastern Caribbean a variety of diseases such as helminthic infections, enteric fevers, and dysentery are prevalent and are directly related to the unsanitary living conditions on the islands. The number of medical personnel and hospital facilities is insufficient to provide adequate care for the population. Physicians and other medical personnel are concentrated in the capitals and principal towns of the islands, leaving few qualified personnel to serve the rural population. With rare exceptions, medical care facilities also are located mainly in urban areas and are overcrowded and understaffed. 

The Trinidad and Tobago 5-year development plan includes $7.5 million, of which $2.7 million were spent in the 3 years 1958-60, for the purposes of providing medical facilities for the cure of disease and for encouraging public cooperation in developing good health conditions. The goals are (1) to provide improved institutional facilities, (2) to expand specialist and general medical facilities and extend these to areas inadequately served, (3) to promote a healthy environment in which disease cannot develop, (4) to increase public awareness of basic health requirements, (5) to eliminate sources of communicable diseases, and (6) to expand facilities. 

6. Education.—Beginning in 1940, the local governments of the eastern Caribbean territories, using local funds and grants from the United Kingdom, took over a large share of the cost of education from the private and denominational schools by creating government schools, both primary and secondary, and by aiding the nongovernment schools. Each territory has autonomy in education and the governments allocate an average of 14 percent of their budgets for this purpose. The magnitude, quality, and emphasis in education vary, however, from territory to territory even though the history is the same. Primary education is free and relatively widespread. Adequate secondary schools are lacking in the Windward and Leeward Islands. Vocational and trade school opportunities are everywhere insufficient. In spite of recent efforts toward more vocational education, the vast majority of students in the eastern Caribbean enter the labor market with no skills or trade to earn a living and no preparation to participate in the modernization of their respective island societies. 

Trinidad has the most resources per capita and is in the middle of an educational development program which promises to improve significantly the educational and skill levels in the next 5 years. The development is on all levels and includes expanded primary and secondary schools and programs, teacher training for which a new college will be ready for operation in September 1962, technical and vocational education, and the development of the eastern branch of the 

University College of the West Indies. 

Barbados has developed its academic educational program to the level that it is recognized as the best in the British Caribbean. Its current efforts are to achieve the same standards in technical education. There is evidence that the government intends to use a larger portion of its available budget for practical training in future years. 

7. Public administration.-As the government of Trinidad and Tobago assumes increasing domestic responsibility and prepares for independence, it also increasingly faces the necessity of creating an organizational structure suitably constituted for an autonomous and independent government. There is a shortage of trained and experienced people competent to carry out management functions, particularly at the higher levels of government. 

A United States-West Indies cooperative program was initiated in 1960 to provide training in selected categories of public administration. From October 

17, 1960, through October 31, 1961, 30 participants from the West Indies and territorial governments were trained in the fields of general accounting, auditing, cost accounting, and government budgeting and accounting. A project agreement has been executed to continue this program through fiscal year 1964 but it is contingent upon funds being made available each year by the local governments. 

8. Financial stability.-Prices as a whole in the area have remained stable. 

Prices of food and clothing, which in the West Indies represent 64 percent of the

cost-of-living index, increased only by about 2.4 percent in 1960 in spite of the sharp increase of wages in the petroleum industry in Trinidad (30 percent). 

Basic to the present situation, and the adjustments in Trinidad which will follow independence, is the fact that practically all banking facilities are provided by branches of British and Canadian banks and that the territory is in the sterling monetary area. 

9. Credit.-Adequate credit facilities are lacking in the eastern Caribbean territories. Savings are not usually or systematically mobilized for production and particularly not for housing, and credit has been granted mainly for commercial and industrial purposes. An independent Trinidad will face the necessity of establishing a credit system to serve long-term industrial and agricultural needs. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The rapid growth of the Trinidad economy in recent years has been due largely to private investments, particularly in the petroleum industry. Foreign private investment in Trinidad has doubled since 1951, reaching $112 million in 1961. This investment has been accounted for mainly by new refineries and a fertilizer plant. The Government in Trinidad, like most of the other eastern Caribbean territories, has taken measures to encourage private investment with aid to pioneer industries through such measures as tax exemptions and duty-free arrangements. About one-half of the applicants for pioneer status are local. The general policy is to welcome foreign investment but with a certain selectivity as to whether the industry is a net earner or a net saver of desirable currency. An exploration license was granted in 1961 to three American oil companies-Pan American, Pure Oil, and Sun Oil-covering 2 million acres off the continental shelf of eastern Trinidad beyond the 3-mile zone. Dominican Oil, a subsidiary of Standard of California, also obtained a lease on 100,000 acres. 

In Barbados, the investment climate is good. Private investment which is about 25 percent of GNP, has been primarily from local sources. There has been a rapid growth in investments in hotels for the tourist industry in recent years and a fair amount of investment in manufacturing industries. Through its pioneer industries legislation, the Government offers tax relief up to 7 years and duty-free privileges on imports of equipment and capital. 

11. Labor.-Statistics on the current size of the labor force in the Eastern 

Caribbean Islands are not available.

In Trinidad and Tobago, where the Government is the largest employer, it is reported that about 20 percent of the labor force is employed in agriculture. 

In 1960, about 16,000 were employed in the petroleum industry. Most of the petroleum workers belong to the Oilfield Workers Trade Union, which in 1958 had a membership of about 12,000. It is the recognized union for negotiating wages, hours, and workers' conditions in the petroleum industry. Labor disputes in the petroleum industry have been settled by collective bargaining. The Oilfield 

Workers Trade Union and the National Trade Union Congress of Trinidad and Tobago (a federation of the major trade unions) are affiliated with International 

Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU).

In Barbados, the Barbados Workers' Union is the only recognized trade union of employees and embraces all types of workers, except Government employees. 

There are 50 divisions in the union which claimed a membership of over 17,000 at the end of 1959. The union is an affiliate of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU).

JAMAICA 

1. General statement.-Jamaica, the largest island in the British West Indies, is situated 90 miles south of Cuba and 500 miles from Miami. It has a population of 1,700,000 and one of the highest per capita gross national products in the 

Latin American area (approximately $417).

Jamaica is sympathetic with the alliance for progress and expects to become a formal member of the alliance when it achieves full independence on August 6, 1962. In all of the projects for which the Government has requested financial assistance, the Prime Minister has emphasized that Jamaica will match such loan funds with equal or greater amounts from Jamaica's own resources. 

2. Planning.-Jamaica has a highly competent and experienced planning organization. Overall economic plans for the country and coordination of separate ministry plans into a well-integrated development program are the responsibility of the Ministry of Development, which is headed by the Prime Minister. Within this ministry a Central Planning Unit functions as the principal center for review and coordination of Government development activities. The Central Planning

Unit is the organization responsible for liaison with foreign assistance groups and is charged with the coordination of development programs which require external financing.

During the course of the past year (1961) Jamaica made substantial revisions in its national plan for Jamaica, a 10-year development plan originally adopted in 1957. The withdrawal of Jamaica from the West Indies Federation, the failure of the economic system to distribute equitably the gains of increase production, the need to increase the allocation of resources devoted to social development, all contributed to the decision to revise the plan and, in effect, the Government has come up with a new 10-year plan for 1962–71. 

3. Agrarian reform.-For the 5 years from 1955 to 1960 the Government of 

Jamaica carried on a farm development program which was not very successful. 

The program consisted of aid to farmers mainly in the form of subsidies or grants. Under this scheme many estates were divided into small farm plots which subsequently proved to be uneconomic and productivity actually decreased as a result.

The Government's policy for assistance to agriculture has been thoroughly revised in its agricultural developmental program (ADP), which is included in the national plan for 1962-71. The new plan combines loan assistance with subsidies for farmers who operate small- and medium-sized farms and who can demonstrate effective use of fertilizers, construction of new farm buildings, and adoption of new programs to increase irrigation, improve livstock, and reclaim land. In order to encourage more efficient land use, the Government will expand extension education and instruction in modern scientific farming practices. 

The plan calls for an expenditure of $24 million over a 10-year period, $19 million of which will be in the form of loans to farmers. The Government of 

Jamaica plans to make $1.4 million available each year from 1962 through 1971 to fund this project and is seeking external assistance for the remaining $10 million. 

4. Housing.-One of the most sensitive areas and the one most visible as a source of discontent in Jamaica is the low standard of housing which now prevails for persons in the lower income groups. The Government has listed housing as the area of its greatest economic need. The Government has drawn up a 10-year housing development program and included it within its new 10year plan.

In the past 20 years, the Government of Jamaica has initiated 81 different housing projects. During the last 10 years the number of new residential units mostly rural has increased by approximately 2,500 units per year. During the next 10-year period, the Government plans to construct 5,000 low-cost housing units per year. It has based many aspects of the program on the observations and recommendations contained in an AID (ICA) housing team report which was completed in April 1961. As part of this program, construction was started in August 1961 on an impact housing project. The second step of the program will be a low-cost housing and redevelopment project which is to continue until the goals are achieved. Funding requirements for the entire 10-year program call for a total expenditure of approximately $150 million which is to be supplied in roughly equal amounts from governmental budgetary allocations, investments by commercial builders, investments from banks and private homeowners, external investments, and external public loans. 

5. Health. The health program in Jamaica suffers from a lack of effective planning. Although the national plan calls for broad expansion of all health services, the interrelationship of operating hospitals, laboratories, and health centers is not as effective as it should be. There is presently an acute shortage of doctors, nurses, and technicians. Dissatisfaction of employees has led to strikes of doctors and threatened strikes of nurses.

In a project-by-project analysis of self-help in the health sector, Jamaica has a better record. In a malaria eradication program, the number of test slides indicating the presence of malaria was reduced from 30 out of every 100 in 1953 to only 1 out of every 100,000 in 1961. The Government is continuing an active surveillance program for 3 more years until it is sure that the disease is eradicated. Jamaica has also incorporated an all-island water supply program within its 10-year national plan. The program is based upon an ICA consultant's report presented to the Jamaican Government in March 1961. The Government began implementing the recommendations contained in the report that same year. The Government's long-range plan calls for the establishment of an 

All Island Water Authority, already approved by the Cabinet, and the construction or improvement of 60 water supply systems by fiscal year 1967.

6. Education.-Jamaica is faced with a serious shortage of both classroom space and teachers. These shortages are aggravated by an expanding population (4.3 percent per year) and by an overly academic school curriculum. 

Within the framework of the country's national plan, the Government has drawn up a long-range program to solve these problems by 1972. 

In the national plan for 1957-67, the country projected an annual increase in classroom places of 16,000. The total increase over the 4-year period (1957-60) was only 21,000 or an annual increase of only 5,250. The main reason the Government was unable to reach its annual quota was a shortage of funds. Although the Government has increased the Ministry of Education's budget from 7 percent of total expenditures in 1955 to 15 percent in 1961, outlays are still insufficient to reach the goals outlined in the national plan. 

Over the 10-year period, the government of Jamaica is planning expenditures of approximately $50.5 million for capital needs, including primary and vocational facilities and teacher training schools. Recurrent expenditures for the 

10-year period will total approximately $236.5 million. The government will also seek foreign aid in the form of technical assistance and financing in the initial years of this plan in order to close the gap between resources available and those needed. 

7. Public administration.—Jamaica has a high standard of public administration. The present leaders in government have the benefit of having served more or less as counterparts to many competent British administrators. The record of honesty within the government is also good. This is in large measure due to a well-organized civil service system, the leaders of which are men of integrity. 

The central planning unit is one of the best in the Latin American area. 

The main weakness in the administration sector has been the home leave system under which every Jamaican civil servant earns 45 days of home leave a year and up to $3,000 for travel for himself and family every 3 to 6 years. Be sides being costly, the system results in a virtual shutdown of operations whenever a senior official departs for 6 months' leave (the average time). The Ministry of Finance is attempting to revise and improve this program, and in any case, the coming independence of Jamaica should end the problem. 

8. Financial stability.—Jamaica has a good record of financial stability. The government recently established a central bank giving it power to determine credit policies and to assist in the control of inflation. Jamaica is expected to take measures to prevent price increases from reaching proportions that might impair its reputation for stability and its high credit rating. 

9. Credit.-Jamaican banks have generally followed conservative policies. 

They have not as a rule served small- and medium-size industries and all their financing to date has been short term, at a high rate of interest, and with requirements of 100-percent collateral. In 1959 a branch of the First National City Bank of New York was opened in Jamaica. Its influence has been toward somewhat more liberal credit policies. 

The Jamaican government is now trying to extend credit to low-income families by reinforcing existing mortgage guarantees. The government is also planning to expand the operations of the small business loans fund (which is now limited to loans of $2,800 or less), to permit the fund to make medium-size loans, to bring it under the management of professional bankers, and to make sure that its operations are administered according to sound business principles. 

At the end of 1960 there were approximately 224 cooperative societies in Jamaica, of which 106 were thrift or credit groups. The government is planning within its agricultural development program to expand their operations within the agricultural credit field in order to encourage better farming methods especially on small- and medium-size farms. 

10. Investment and private enterprise.-The climate for investment in Jamaica is good. The government has so far relied almost exclusively on private enterprise to provide industrial capital. 

Jamaica's policy on industrialization remains as stated in the 1957 national plan and the government plans to increase its funding of the Jamaican Industrial Development Corp. during the next decade. Encouragement to industry in the form of tax and nontax incentives are expected to continue. Some of these incentives are included in the pioneer industries law, the industrial incentives law, the export industries (encouragement) law, the international business companies law, and a special law providing incentives to persons investing in factory construction. There is also a provision in the income tax law for a 20-percent initial or investment allowance for certain industries.

11. Labor. There is a widespread lack of skills among the working population and also among middle-level management, and industry is faced with high costs in production due to a lack of efficiency among workers and a resistance to mechanization. There is a close relationship existing between the political parties and the labor unions. 

Unemployment in Jamaica now stands at about 18 percent of the labor force and unskilled laborers are constantly shifting from rural to urban area. Migration to the United Kingdom presently provides some relief for the problem of unemployment. SURINAM 1. General statement.-In 1954 Surinam accomplished an orderly transition from dependent overseas territory to an autonomous state within the Netherlands Kingdom. It is strongly democratic in its interests, institutions, and approach. Furthermore, there is adequate political stability, despite its heterogeneous population, to permit an orderly economic and social development. It should also be noted that Surinam differs in population composition, language, religion, tradition, and outlook from other countries in the Latin American area and, until recently, had shown little interest in events and developments within those countries. Although Dutch influence is still predominant, the Surinamers appear anxious to enhance their national identity. 

Surinam welcomes U.S. and other foreign investments and encourages private enterprise. It has a sound 10-year development program, extended in 

May 1960 by an additional 5 years, mostly devoted to economic rather than social development. It is interested in supplementing it by action in the social fields with the help of U.S. development loans and technical assistance. 

Surinam has a population estimated at 326,000 in 1961 and a growth rate of 4 percent per annum. Approximately 80 percent of its people are literate. 

2. Planning.-Surinam initiated the implemention of its 10-year plan for national development in 1955. It called for expenditures of $68 million, onethird from Surinam resources and the remainder from the Netherlands whose contributions are equally divided between grants and loans. The plan concentrates on economically productive projects rather than social development. 

Initial implementation of the plan has been hampered by insufficient trained technical and administrative personnel, lack of adequate equipment and machinery, and bottlenecks in the planning and execution of projects. As a result, only $21 million was expended during the plan's first 5 years. However, the original weaknesses have been partially eliminated. About $11 million was spent in 1960, and the 1961 budget provided for expenditures of $12.8 million. 

3. Agrarian reform.—At present, agriculture contributes only 13 percent of

Surinam's GNP while occupying 60 percent of the population, three-fourths of which are settled on uneconomic family farms averaging less than 2 hectares each. Rice is the major domestic agricultural product and represents 80 percent of agricultural activity. There is a pressing need for the strengthening of extension services, diversification, and rural credit and marketing facilities. 

Some progress has been made in recent years. About 8,000 hectares of land have been reclaimed and 4,000 hectares of existing farmland have been prepared for cultivation. In the next 5 years another 14,000 hectares of land will be made tillable with dikes, canals, and sluices. Of this, 6,000 hectares is already in course of preparation. In addition, a number of paddy rice silos have been constructed, research and credit have been expanded, two experimental farms established, and an intensive inventory has been made of forestry resources. 

4. Housing. The serious inadequacy of low-income dwellings constitutes a major, and rapidly growing, internal political and social problem. The Government estimates that over 1,700 dwellings per year must be built to meet minimum national requirements. The Government-financed construction has only averaged some 140 new units per year over the past 10 years, although the rate of new starts has recently been increased. Besides the lack of sufficient financial resources, the housing problem is also affected by the low income of the urban population and the reluctance of many to assume homeownership responsibilities. 

The 10-year plan allocated $2,160,000 to low-cost housing, and from 1954 to 1961 the Dutch Government and insurance companies loaned $634,000 for housing construction. From 1952 to 1961, the Government of Surinam contributed a total of about $3,780,000 for housing with which it built 1,246 units and purchased 465 hectares of land for project development and resale to private developers at reasonable rates. From 1952 to 1960, the Government, with U.S.

assistance, built 285 units at a total cost of about $600,000 using aided self-help techniques. 

5. Health. The low level of public health is a widespread and fairly serious problem in Surinam, although the conditions are much better in its capital, Paramaribo. Urban water supplies are adequate in some instances, but the situation is unsatisfactory in rural areas and is an important element in the spread of disease. Sewage and waste disposal are national problems. Malnutrition is widespread. Parasitic infections, including bilharzia, hookworm, and other worm infestations are heavy, and malaria is endemic in most of the hinterland. There is a shortage of trained public health personnel. 

With U.S. aid since 1955, the Government has made efforts in the public health field and contributed substantial funds. Some public health personnel have been trained, the Ledydorp Public Health Center, with its comprehensive facilities for treatment and training, is operating satisfactorily and will serve as a model for other centers in the rural areas. With the assistance of international bodies, a malaria eradication campaign was started 4 years ago and is continuing. Some effort to curtail the spread of bilharzia through construction of privies and education in elementary sanitation measures has been made. Over the past 5 years the Surinam Water Co., an agency of the Government, spent $725,000 to modernize and expand the Paramaribo water system. The Government spent another $250,000 to establish community water systems in four regional centers. It also constructed 83 wells in 1959 at a cost of $18,000. The Government's 1963 budget includes $480,000 for the water program. 

6. Education.-Surinam's education is classical and provides good academic knowledge in the tradition of the Netherlands, but it does not completely fulfill technical needs. The current big problem is the construction of new classrooms and rehabilitation of some of the existing ones. The current rate of school construction is not sufficient to meet requirements. The Government estimates that elementary school enrollment, which totaled 53,000 on January 1, 1961, will reach 79,000 by January 1, 1966. Although the Government is willing and able to furnish land, site development, classroom furniture, supplies and materials, textbooks, and teachers, it has indicated its inability to finance the construction of schools, since this would mean diverting funds from the economic development program. 

7. Public administration.—Since Surinam became an autonomous state within the Netherlands Kingdom in 1954 there has been increased participation of Surinamers in the administration of internal affairs. Dutch technicians, however, continue to fill many positions at high cost to the Surinam Government, partly because of the shortage of adequately trained local personnel. This situation is slowly being remedied by education of young Surinamers. 

8. Financial stability.-Reasonable financial stability is maintained in Surinam. While the Government's ordinary budget has usually shown a surplus sufficient to cover the deficit of the investment budget, this was changed in 1960 when the surplus covered only 35 percent of the investment deficit ($2,735,500 and $7,918,000), the balance being secured from internal and foreign loans. 

With the increased rate of expenditures under the 10-year plan, the investment budget's deficit is expected to rise.

The Government has increased income taxes and customs dues. It has also made some effort to reduce administrative expenditures. The inflationary potential has been reduced and prices are generally stable. 

9. Credit. The three commercial banks and the Surinam Central Bank follow a generally conservative policy. Bank financing is adequate for low-risk, highreturn undertakings. Business construction and commerce, especially the import-export trade, are well financed. But the country's financial base is inadequate for many potentially productive undertakings. Low-cost housing cannot generate its own financing, and facilities for agricultural credit are not adequate. 

In fact, the Government feels that there is excessive liquidity available to the commercial banks which could become a potential inflationary threat. It has sought to mop up some of the liquidity by the sale of Government bonds and the relaxation of exchange controls to permit the banks to invest in foreign securities. 

The Government gives a high priority to facilitating agricultural credit. It has a plan to improve banking facilities and make more credit funds available to support agriculture, with the help of a U.S. investment loan. However, the proposed agricultural banking institution, whose capitalization is set at $3.9 million, is not expected to be established before 1963 at the earliest, and will not be fully operative before 1965 or 1966.

10. Investment and private enterprise.-Surinam is anxious for additional 

United States and other foreign investments. The expansion of industry is considered by the Government and business leaders to be essential in order to achieve economic diversification, to absorb the excessive labor supply, and to contribute to the productive capacity of the country. The Government encourages private enterprise and offers incentives to new foreign investments and the expansion of existing ones. Legislation has been enacted with provisions for tax holiday, accelerated depreciation, freedom from certain import duties, and other benefits. There is a ceiling of 30 percent on corporate income tax, no withholding taxes on dividends and interest, and no sales or turnover taxes. 

It established recently an industrial productivity center in the Ministry of Economic Affairs, whose advisory committee includes members of private industry. Its purpose is to offer extensive assistance to investors and also to develop the handicraft industry. 

A subsidary of Alcoa is the largest foreign investor in Surinam. It is now implementing a large expansion program, which is expected to be completed in 1965. 

11. Labor.-No figures are available on the size of the labor force. It is known, however, that skills are generally at a low level. There is an oversupply of unskilled labor and low-level white-collar workers, and a shortage of competent national administration people, and many key positions are occupied by persons on contract from other countries, primarily the Netherlands. Unemployment is a big problem, particularly in Paramaribo. About 2,000 are employed in relief work.

For all practical purposes, Surinam did not have any vocational training program prior to 1956 when, as a result of signing project agreements with the United States, some effort in that field was started with substantial U.S. assistance. A technical school, which is a secondary level pretrade school, was established in 1956 and provides training for about 550 students in such fields as metal trades, building trades, auto mechanics, architectural drawing, and mechanical drafting. The school is now doing an efficient job and all teaching and instruction is done by Surinam or Dutch instructors. The Surinam Government will assume all costs of the school after June 1962. Another U.S.-aided program for the training of about 100 young nationals as maintenance men and operators of heavy earth moving equipment for roadbuilding and jungle clearing, was started in 1957. It has resulted in training 91 operators and 24 mechanics. All have jobs in their specialty at this time. U.S. participation in this project came to an end in December 1961. 81496-62-pt. 3- -12

THURSDAY, MARCH 29, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

The committee meets this morning for a continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

The program this morning is Near East and south Asia. The witnesses are the Honorable William S. Gaud, Assistant Administrator, Bureau for Near East and South Asia; the Honorable Phillips Talbot, Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs.

We have with us the Honorable J. Kenneth Galbraith, our Ambassador to India. 

Mr. Secretary, you have a statement? 

Mr. TALBOT. Yes, sir. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Gaud, you have a statement? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes. 

Chairman MORGAN. You have no statement, Mr. Ambassador?

Ambassador GALBRAITH. I have no statement. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, you may proceed.

STATEMENT OF HON. PHILLIPS TALBOT, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR NEAR EASTERN AND SOUTH ASIAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. TALBOT. Mr. Chairman, I offer my statement to you and the committee for the record. Since it was prepared all of 48 hours ago, I would like to note a couple of changes in the area that has occurred since then. 

(The statement of Mr. Talbot is as follows:) 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is now nearly a year since I assumed the position of Assistant Secretary of State for Near East and South Asian Affairs and since I appeared before you in support of the fiscal year 1962 program. During this year I have visited most of the countries in the area and acquired greater familiarity with their problems and with the opportunities we can seize and the difficulties we encounter in seeking to implement our objectives in the Near East and south Asia.

A generalized statement that conditions are better or worse than a year ago would have little application to an area as diverse as the 18 countries in this area which as you know embraces the eastern part of the Arab world, Israel, and the rimland that stretches from Greece through India. 563

A few of the year's dramatic developments have posed policy dilemmas for the United States. Chief among these were India's resort to force of arms to end Portuguese rule over Goa, the Afghan-Pak border closing, the rekindled tension between India and Pakistan over Kashmir, Iraqi threats against the independence of Kuwait, Syria's break away from the United Arab Republic, abortive coups in Lebanon and Ceylon and the very recent exchange of violence between the Israelis and the Syrians in the Lake Tiberias region. 

Such events must, of course, be balanced against encouraging developments in the region during the past year. In Turkey there has been a return to constitutional government. In Pakistan a new constitution has been promulgated. Elections in India, Greece, and Syria have reaffirmed the democratic nature of the political structure of these countries. In Iran the Shah, fully supporting his capable Prime Minister Amini, has courageously launched a new land reform movement and taken commendable steps to correct abuses in government and bring about financial stability. 

Thus far-reaching, comprehensive economic and social development programs of India and Pakistan have made further rapid strides. Greece and Israel have maintained high rates of economic growth. The newly established Government of Syria has made determined efforts to achieve financial stability and progress. In Saudi Arabia the Government, with the assistance of private consultants, has given increased attention to broad economic development planning.

We wish to see the nations in the Near East and south Asia develop, economically and politically, with institutions so strong that they need not fear loss of independence from either Communist subversion of external attack. We wish to see them prosper and progress to such an extent that in time they, too, as members of the free community of nations can assist other countries less fortunate.

In this respect I am pleased to say that our European friends and Japan have joined us in assisting with the economic development of many countries in the Near East and south Asia. The consortia formula is proving an extremely valuable means for joint participation. 

I think that during the coming fiscal year these joint efforts, together with the invaluable help of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, will become increasingly important as a source of financing longterm requirements of countries in our area. 

As you know, the Sino-Soviet coalition has maintained unrelenting pressure in the area and continues to channel more than 60 percent of its foreign military and economic aid efforts to countries in the Near East and south Asia. 

Despite the unsettling events which I have mentioned, it has not been possible for the bloc to achieve noticeable new gains in the Near East and south Asia. 

The fact that the Sino-Soviet bloc has been held at bay may be attributed mainly to the resolute determination of the countries in the area to maintain their independence. However, I believe that much of this success is attributable to the aid programs which we and our allies have maintained. 

These programs have not only offered the recipient countries alternatives to the Sino-Soviet bloc as a source of much-needed assistance, but they have enabled us and our associates in the free world to work together with countries in the area to improve the lot of their citizens. 

I should like to return a moment to the question of intraregional disputes in the area. They are not only a source of continuing tension and a threat to the peace, but they also result in the dissipation of energies and resources badly needed for internal development. 

You readily understand the problem which this poses for us in the formulation of our aid programs. Accordingly, we are alert to every opportunity to help resolve these disputes. However, the countries involved are sovereign and there is a limit to what we can do to assist in the resolution of these conflicts. 

To attempt to deny aid as a leverage to bring about solutions of largely intractable conflicts, in our judgment, would be impractical. Such an action might prove counterproductive and further limit any useful role which we can play in these conflicts.

As you know, these intraregional disputes involve deep-rooted emotions of newly independent countries, each sensitive to any infringement of its dignity or freedom of action. In my opinion, these disputes require the balm of time. patience, and persuasion. 

I would like to refer in a little more detail to a number of issues which warrant further explanation:

ARAB-ISRAELI RELATIONS 

Fundamental aspects of the Arab-Israeli situation have not changed greatly. 

You will recall that since last summer an initiative, the first in a number of years, was undertaken under United Nations auspices to deal with the most difficult and tragic aspect of the Arab-Israeli question-the problem of refugees. 

The Palestine Conciliation Commission, a three-nation United Nations body composed of the United States, France, and Turkey, was charged by the 15th General Assembly to pursue its efforts for implementation of Paragraph 11 of U.N. Resolution 194 (Third General Assembly) under which the refugees could be offered the alternative of repatriation to their homes or compensation and resettlement elsewhere. 

Dr. Joseph E. Johnson, president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, was appointed by the Palestine Conciliation Commission to act as its special representative to discuss with the governments directly concerned means for making progress on the refugee issue. 

After a visit to the countries in the Near East, Dr. Johnson presented a report to the Commission during the 16th General Assembly. During this General Assembly the United States introduced a resolution which was passed directing the Palestine Conciliation Commission to continue the efforts initiated by Dr. Johnson.

Dr. Johnson has accepted reappointment as special representative and expects to depart within a few weeks for a second round of discussions with the governments directly concerned. 

We are most grateful to this distinguished and capable American, for his willingness to undertake such a difficult task. He has our fullest support and good wishes for success.

We have continued to give our full support to those other instrumentalities of the United Nations which play a vital role in the maintenance of peace in the Near East. Thus, we have endorsed continuance of UNTSO, UNEF, and UNRWA. 

We have encouraged the latter to continue its efforts to correct ration roll abuses and to insure that only those refugees legitimately entitled to relief assistance receive it.

By November of 1961 in Jordan the rate of removal of unqualified refugees and the substitution in their stead of qualified persons on the ration rolls had reached approximately 2,000 a month. Although some delays have developed recently, we believe the program will continue to move ahead with full support of the Jordanian Government. 

The fact that refugees are now voluntarily reporting deaths is encouraging evidence that UNRWA has succeeded in dispelling some of the formerly widespread suspicion that surrounded the rectification effort. 

The question of the Jordan waters is, of course, an important one, and I mention it because it is one more issue in the area which is a potential source of conflict between the Israelis and the Arabs. 

OTHER COUNTRY SITUATIONS IN THE NEAR EAST 

Through good use of U.S. Government aid, German reparations, and private contributions from abroad, Israel's economy continues to register impressive growth. Its industrial sector moves steadily forward to share an increasing proportion of the national product. With these technical and economic advances, U.S. assistance to Israel is now mostly in the form of food for peace programs and development loans.

Our The continued existence of Jordan as an independent political entity remains a major factor in the maintenance of peace and stability in the area. assistance to Jordan is mainly in the form of supporting assistance cash grants and is related largely to estimates of the budgetary assistance required by Jordan to maintain essential services. 

Recently a new government has come into power, and I have been favorably impressed by the energy and determination of the new Prime Minister who, under the leadership of King Hussein, seeks to improve internal administration and expand domestic sources of revenue. 

It is my understanding that the Government intends to strengthen the civil service, improve tax and customs administration, and fiscal management and complete the establishment of an effective highway maintenance organization. 

These improvements, if implemented, should result in a better utilization of the foreign assistance given Jordan.

I would like to mention also that because of the foreign aid which Jordan has received over the past few years, basic institutions to meet education and health needs have been established, a primary road system has been almost completed, and progress has been made in extending irrigated acreage. 

The Government recently published a 5-year economic development plan which suggests further possibilities for expanded production, particularly in agriculture, tourism, and the extractive industries. 

As I mentioned earlier, Syria severed its relations with the United Arab Republic and has become an independent nation. As a consequence of a 3-year drought, the new Syrian Government found itself at its inception facing severe economic problems.

Syria requested assistance from us as a result of which an agreement was made to sell Syria 100,000 tons of wheat and flour with payment to be made in local currency and to provide an additional 50,000 tons under title II. More recently, we have indicated our willingness to support a stabilization program which the International Monetary Fund has assisted the Syrians in developing. 

I think it is important to note that Syria is attempting to develop an economic policy which envisages a mixed private and public enterprise system. This attempt involves limited denationalization of a number of enterprises and adjustment of its fiscal policy to allow eventually the removal of foreign exchange controls. 

Elections have been held in Syria and a new Parliament is carrying out its combined legislative and constitutional reform functions. 

Following the loss of Syria, the United Arab Republic instituted a series of sequestrations in Egypt which resulted in the nationalization of many domestic and foreign firms. At the same time the Government of the United Arab Re public intensified its internal economic and social development programs including economic planning activities. 

Our assistance to the United Arab Republic has consisted principally of commodity sales under the food-for-peace program. This aid has helped the United 

Arab Republic with internal economic development and alleviated balance-ofpayments difficulties resulting from decreased exports caused by a reduction of 30 percent to 40 percent of its cotton crop. 

Although the U.S.S.R. has continued to furnish military and economic assistance to the United Arab Republic, the latter has maintained an independent foreign policy posture and its firm opposition to internal Communist subversion. 

GREECE, IRAN, TURKEY, AND CYPRUS 

U.S. relations with Greece continues to benefit from the large reservoir of 

Greek good will toward us, resulting particularly from the Truman doctrine which provided aid for Greece at a critical hour. Greece has given us virtually complete support for our policies in the United Nations and has faithfully endeavored to meet its obligations under NATO. The Greek Government under 

Prime Minister Caramanlis continues to demonstrate stability. 

Prime Minister Caramanlis emerged successfully in the last election of October 29, 1961. He obtained 51 percent of the popular vote and the pro-Communist 

EDA party was rebuffed, its percentage decreasing from 25 percent to 14 percent. However, the Communist opposition is still a potential threat to Greece. 

The non-Communist center group has increased its strength in the Parliament and is seeking to assume the role of the principal opposition, a position formerly held by the Communists. 

Faced with social and economic problems plus Communist pressure from within and without, the Greek Government realizes that it must concentrate its attention on economic development, while keeping up its defense to confront Soviet and bloc pressures on its frontiers. The cost of defense, while simultane ously demonstrating progress on the economic front, is a serious strain on the economy of Greece.

Economically Greece continues to make good progress. We believe that U.S. economic assistance to Greece in the future should be in the form of loans for development projects and programs rather than grant supporting assistance. 

The Greek Government has expressed concern over this change in the form of our aid. We believe, however, that the transition from grants to loans can be made without jeopardizing either the economic progress or the political stability which now exist. 

Iran continues to be a valued ally of the United States. Iranian-American cooperation and Iran's alliance with the CENTO nations have been two of the

4 foundations of Iran's foreign policy. Its relations with the Soviet Union still center about the abusive propaganda attacks broadcast by Radio Moscow and several smaller transmitters, and on alternating diplomatic threats and blandishments. Iran has demonstrated courage in facing these attacks. 

Internally, the present Iranian Cabinet has initiated the most significant land and fiscal reforms the country has experienced in years. Serious inflationary pressures and balance-of-payments problems have become manageable through the enforcement of import controls, lending limitations, and governmental budget restrictions. 

A pilot project area has been designated for the country's first land reform program, and the Government has very recently begun dividing some of the land there among the peasants. 

The Cabinet has taken initial steps which can lead to significant reforms in personnel, taxation, and budgetary policies. Despite attacks from extremists of both right and left, the Shah continues to support these reforms. The general outline of a third economic development plan to begin in September 1962 is now nearing completion. 

The new Turkish constitution, accepted by a public referendum in July 1961, is based on democratic principles and institutions. A coalition government with Ismet Inonu as Prime Minister was formed as a result of the national elections in October 1961. Its program, which was approved by the Grand National Assembly on December 2, 1961, emphasized the need for domestic political tranquility and economic development. 

The New Turkish Government has reiterated its strong attachment to NATO, CENTO, and the U.N., and has affirmed its determination to follow its pro- 

West foreign policy.

An abortive and ill-conceived attempt to overthrow the Government last February failed owing to the firmness of the Government and to the loyalty of the 

Turkish armed forces.

A very poor wheat crop has necessitated imports of about 1,500,000 tons of Public Law 480 wheat during fiscal year 1962, and unsettled political conditions have contributed to the continuation of a recession which started about the time of the coup d'etat of May 1960. 

Of special interest is a 5-year plan now being prepared by the Turkish State Planning Office which should be ready for Cabinet consideration this summer; it is expected that it will be put into execution in March 1963. 

The Republic of Cyprus is now over 1½ years old. During this period it has succeeded in preserving internal stability despite continuing and difficult problems deriving from disagreements between the island's Greek and Turkish communities. The latter revolve around differing constitutional interpretations regarding their respective roles in the Government. 

While electing to pursue neutralist policies in world affairs, the Cypriot Government has shown itself able and willing to draw ethical and moral distinctions between Communist and free world positions on key international issues, as President Makarios demonstrated in the pro-Western stand he took on Berlin during the Belgrade Conference of neutralist states in September 1961. 

We have provided Cyprus with Public Law 480 food grain assistance and are now in the initial stages of developing a program of technical assistance and development lending. Significant amounts of economic assistance are also being furnished, or are expected to be furnished, by the IBRD, West Germany, the 

United Kingdom, and the UN.

SOUTH ASIA 

The basic issue in south Asia, as I see it, is whether the free societies of the area, with the assistance of the West and Japan, can achieve the social and economic modernization that is their great ambition without succumbing to the claims of Communist powers that they know the best road to progress. 

That the Communist powers have high ambitions in south Asia is clearly evident. However, I firmly believe that we, in association with the more prosperous nations of the free world, have the capability and will to enable the south Asian nations to win their victory over poverty and disease. Needless to say, immense difficulties are ahead for all of us in this effort and I ask your patience and help in enabling us to discharge our responsibilities. 

Despite the Goa crisis, the difficulties between Pakistan and Afghanistan which led to a border closing and the breaking of diplomatic relations, and other unsettling events in south Asia, I believe that if we can look beyond these situations

we will find that progress has been made in the general direction of economic and social development. 

Furthermore, the movement in Pakistan toward a return to constitutional life is encouraging and the Indian election within the framework of representative democracy is reassuring. 

The temporary reopening of the Pakistan border with Afghanistan for the main purpose of permitting the movement to Afghanistan of United States aid material perhaps may presage a more permanent arrangement. 

My AID colleague, Mr. Gaud, in his statement to you and the individual country studies included in our fiscal year 1962 presentation to the Congress contain, of course, considerable data regarding the programs in south Asia. 

Nevertheless, I would like to say a few words about them because they are politically important in that it enables us and the south Asians to pursue together matters of common interest, that is, affairs pertaining to their welfare and the part we play in this matter. 

India's third 5-year plan contemplates an expenditure of $24.7 billion, an amount roughly equal to the total of the first two economic development plans, the last of which ended last year. Of this amount, India is depending on foreign aid for about $5.5 billion, and in May of 1961 a consortium of free world countries and institutions, meeting under the auspices of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, committed $2.2 billion toward this total. 

The United States offered to provide $1 billion of this amount, provided its offer was matched by the total of the contributions of the other member countries.

A new meeting of the consortium is scheduled for next May to consider these further contributions. Because of the long-term lending authority voted by the 

Congress, the United States has been able to play a leading and meaningful part in this operation.

In my view, the success of the third 5-year plan will buttress the supports for India's democratic system and enable it to withstand pressures on its frontiers with Communist China.

Pakistan is now in the second year of its second 5-year plan. This plan envisages total expenditures of about $4.8 billion. In January of this year a consortium, also meeting under the sponsorship of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, committed $945 million in aid toward Pakistan's foreign exchange requirements for the second and third years of its second plan. The U.S. commitment amounts to $500 million. 

The plan calls for considerable strengthening of the agricultural sector a major deficiency in the previous plan. This is another important instance where the long-term commitment authority has been a valuable asset. 

A matter to which I particularly invite your attention concerns the appeal to President Kennedy made by President Ayub last year for help in combating the baffling problem of waterlogging and salinity which is now removing from production each year more than 100,000 acres of farmland. In fact, so much land is being lost that progress in the agricultural sector under the second 5-year plan could be easily offset by this loss. 

In response, President Kennedy sent to Pakistan a team of experts, headed by his science adviser, which is now preparing recommendations on how to solve this most difficult problem.

I do not think that I need say much about the Indus waters project in this statement since I know the committee is familiar with this development. 

You will recall that this project was designed by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development in an effort to end the dispute between India and Pakistan over the use of the waters of the Indus Rivers system. 

I have been informed that two of the major contracts in the project-one for the construction of the Mangla Dam on the Jhelum River and one for the construction of the Trimmu-Sidhnai-have been awarded to American firms. 

With regard to Afghanistan, the prospects for a permanent settlement of the impasse with Pakistan appear good, and I am going on the assumption that it will continue to be possible to ship AID supplies through Pakistan. 

In the meantime we and the Afghans are surveying a possible complementary route through Iran, largely on the premise that the more access Afghanistan has to the free world the better.

Given continuous access to Afghanistan, I believe that it will be in our interest to furnish support for a number of important projects in Afghanistan and thus lessen the danger of forcing that country into total dependence on the Soviet Union.

I must say that the Soviets are deeply involved in Afghanistan's military and economic programs, but this fact should not blind us to the traditionally deep passion of Afghans for freedom nor stand in the way of our helping them to preserve it.

In conclusion I wish to state that although in our area the problems are many, difficult of solution and that the road ahead is long and hard, I am convinced that, with determination and your help, we can do the job. 

Mr. TALBOT. The reference to Syria has been placed out of date by a takeover by a military group which is establishing itself now. As far as we can judge, it is roughly the same military group that took over when Syria broke away from the UAR last September. 

The spokesman for the group has called in our Ambassador and told him there will be no change in the foreign policy of Syria and that the group now taking over is very anxious to maintain friendly relations with the United States.

The second comment I might make on late developments refers to the border situation between Pakistan and Afghanistan. As you know, sir, the border has been open for a temporary period of 2 months while U.S. aid shipments were passed from Pakistan into Afghanistan, even though no solution had been found to the differences between Afghanistan and Pakistan. That period comes to an end at nightfall on the 29th, in other words, today, and just about now in Afghan time. 

We have had a message saying that the Embassy understands it is the intention of the Afghan Government to close the border again tonight on the ground that they have not yet reached an agreement with Pakistan.

Our aid goods which were backlogged in Pakistan have been moved into Pakistan. We will, of course, be consulting with both governments on the next steps they hope to take. 

Speaking generally, Mr. Chairman, about this part of the world, it is well known, of course, this is a region whose countries are by and large stricken with poverty and struggling to get into a more modern pattern of life than they have enjoyed in recent centuries. 

Nationalism is a very strong force in the countries of this area, and this area also is the subject of considerable pressure by the Sino- Soviet bloc. Indeed, it seems to me, speaking quite personally, that on the assumption that some sort of detente is possible in Europe we can anticipate that the Sino-Soviet pressures on this [security deletion] area to the south will increase in the next several years and that the Sino-Soviet countries will continue the flattery of imitation, which they have already started, in developing aid programs and in trying to reach the countries of the Near East and south Asia through some of the same ways that we have been in touch with these countries for several years.

Our objectives, of course, are quite different from those of the Soviets in that we do believe firmly that the strengthening of these countries so that they can be viable will reduce their vulnerability to penetration.

We can live with countries having somewhat different points of view. We do not need to make satellites out of any of these countries. 

In this sense, we are in a good posture to cooperate with these countries and to try to help them gain strength. 

I might comment, Mr. Chairman, that in dealing with the sorts of peoples in countries in this Near Eastern-south Asian area, we find ourselves constantly involved in what I would call three levels of for-

eign policy, the first being the normal intercourse with the governments of the countries in an effort to strengthen our ties with them, and to reduce or ameliorate our differences with them; the second to work with them in their domestic affairs, particularly their domestic economic affairs, in an effort to help them fortify their own economic and social structures, so that they do become more resistant to the external pressures and they do face up to the problems of modernizing themselves.

The third is I think the problem of interregional disputes. We get involved in those as well. 

If I might, sir, speak a little more about these three: The first general category leads us into a group of problems that we will I think have to live with for some time in this part of the world. 

One simple way to put it is to refer to the distinctions if any between our relations with those countries that are allied to us and those countries that as a matter of policy remain nonallied. 

We have close and good relations with those countries that through the years have become allied with us. A considerable part of American security rests upon the maintenance of these relations. 

In our contacts with Greece, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, in particular, we are very anxious to maintain the close relationship and the common use of facilities which we have managed to achieve in recent years. 

At the same time it is perfectly obvious that even if these countries which are allied to us were absolutely invulnerable to any outside pressures, we could still be in a very bad way in the region as a whole if we ignored countries that are not alined, if we did not try to strengthen them. For our own national security we have a very strong interest in developing close relations with these nonaligned countries and in helping them strengthen themselves, recognizing, of course, that very often their views on particular issues will differ from ours.

In our national interest, therefore, we have to find satisfactory ways to maintain and strengthen our relations with allied countries and at the same time to develop and hold strong and friendly relations with nonalined countries. 

So far as the second level of foreign policy is concerned, the fortifying of these societies against the dangers that threaten them, against the tensions of modernization and all, this of course is one of the principal objectives of our aid program. 

Mr. Gaud, I am sure, will be talking about that in more detail, about these efforts that we have in the various countries of this region. 

It seems to me quite clear that even if we are able to put our general relations with each of these countries in fairly good order and if we are able to continue making progress in the strengthening of the domestic and internal situations here, we still stand in very great risk of having severe troubles in the area because of the intra-area disputes. 

Here is a field which I think our opponents in world affairs can exploit as vigorously as they can exploit anything in the area. disputes dissipate the energies of the country, sometimes they dissipate our efforts to help the countries. They preoccupy the attention and the emotions of the peoples of these countries very often to the exclusion of attention to those problems which I think are far larger and are more threatening in the long run. These

Many of these are old and intractable disputes, disputes between India and Pakistan on Kashmir, on Afghanistan over the Pushtunistan issue and the border disputes between the Arab countries and Israel, but also disputes among the Arab countries themselves, tensions between Iran and Iraq, so forth.

These intraregional disputes are dissipating and weakening the resources and purposes of the countries concerned. In terms of our own objectives it is important that we try to help ameliorate them. 

This is not easy. It is perfectly clear when two boys start fighting, the fellow that comes in to be the peacemaker is the one likely to be punched by both of them. 

We do stand very often in the position of being attacked and criticized by both parties when we are trying to ameliorate these difficulties. We also know these difficulties arise from deeply held emotional convictions, and they are not easily subject to our external influence. 

Nevertheless, the good offices that we are providing and the more subtle private ways in which we are trying to help some of these disputants come together make an important part of our overall effort. 

So when we discuss our relations with any particular country, Turkey, for example, or one of the Arab countries, or Ceylon, we are discussing relations at all of these three levels, the general, the assistance internally, and some effort to assist in the amelioration of interregional disputes, it is in these terms. 

In my report, Mr. Chairman, I have referred to some of the points wherein in the past year it has been possible to see certain progress, and other points where we have encountered very considerable difficulties. 

I think as we strive forward, looking at the area as a whole compared with, say, 5 years ago, or 8 years ago, it is possible for us as Americans to be encouraged by the gradual accretion of strength. As long as we don't expect miracles in these still quite fragile, still quite poverty-stricken countries, I think we can feel they are moving generally in the direction of modernization, of strengthening. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

Mr. Gaud, you may proceed, and then we will question the Ambassador and Mr. Talbot and yourself as a team. 

STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM S. GAUD, ASSISTANT ADMINISTRA- TOR, BUREAU FOR NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. GAUD. I have a statement I offer for the record. I would like to talk to the general substance of it Chairman MORGAN. Your statement will be incorporated in the record. (The statement of Mr. Gaud is as follows:) 

Mr. Hamilton has set forth the basic aid policies established by the President and by the Act for International Development. Secretary Talbot has emphasized the importance and diversity of our interests in the Near East and south Asia, and has discussed some of the political and military problems with which we are confronted in that area. 

The basic objective of our aid program in this part of the world is to apply the policies of the Act for International Development. Those policies call for sound long-range economic development efforts, effective planning of economic policies and programs, and maximum self-help.

The current year has seen a major shift from grant to loan financing in this region. A further increase in emphasis on loans and reduction of grant aid is proposed for fiscal year 1963.
