The congressional presentation volumes you have contain specific explanations of each of our country programs. I shall not attempt to review each of these programs in detail in this statement. I will summarize the progress achieved toward sound economic development in the major countries and the further accomplishments we believe can be made during the coming year. 

PROGRESS IN MAJOR COUNTRIES 

India is the most populous country by far in this region and our economic assistance program for India is the largest. India now has a comprehensive economic development program in full swing. It has become in many ways a model for other less-developed countries. It is now completing the first year of its third 5-year development program. Its development plan has been reviewed and endorsed by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and by a consortium of free world countries, including the United States, which are supporting the development program. The total scale of India's development effort has been stepped up sharply from second plan levels. Total outside assistance has risen to over $1 billion a year. India has taken an impressive range of self-help measures. During the past 5 years it has succeeded in raising per capita income by about 2 percent per year. Many problems still exist, but it is addressing these problems vigorously. India seems likely to maintain good progress if sufficient outside help can be made available. We plan to continue to provide a large volume of assistance in cooperation with other countries and international agencies.

Pakistan, too, is now committed to a comprehensive economic development program. Its first 5-year plan was approved only in its third year and was not effectively implemented until near its nominal completion. 

Little progress was achieved. The second 5-year plan is now in its second year. This plan is nearly double the size of the first plan and has been pursued with determination by the Government of Pakistan. 

Pakistan's plan has also been reviewed by the IBRD and by a consortium of aid-giving nations. In the most recent meeting of the consortium in January 

1962, the plan was found worthy of support. Foreign exchange assistance of some $945 million was committed by the consortium members to meet the plan requirements for outside help during its second and third years. We have agreed to provide $500 million of this total in addition to our food-for-peace program. 

In view of Pakistan's effective development program and of the greatly steppedup development lending committed in support of that program, we can now eliminate our supporting assistance grant program for Pakistan. 

We are hopeful that greatly improved development efforts will get underway during the coming year in two other key countries: Turkey and Iran. 

Turkey achieved rapid economic progress after World War II and in the early fifties, but during recent years inflation and [security deletion] other difficulties have limited its economic progress. The military caretaker government restored financial stability and began preparation of a new economic development program. The newly elected democratic government has continued the policies of the caretaker government and plans to complete the economic development program this year.

We expect to participate with other developed countries, perhaps under the aegis of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, in a cooperative effort to review Turkey's plan and need for aid. If the plan proves to be sound and the Government of Turkey is willing to undertake the necessary actions to carry it out, we will cooperate in providing the help needed. We expect to expand our development lending during fiscal year 1963. If Turkey's development program gets underway successfully and if adequate long-term development financing can be secured from the United States and other sources, it may be possible to phase out supporting grant assistance over the next few years.

Iran's social and economic development has not been all that we might hope. It has made some headway, but faster progress and wider distribution of benefits are needed.

The Amini government took office last summer. It is committed to extensive reforms and to a broadening of the economic development program. Important improvements in budget administration and foreign exchange utilization have been started. Other announced reforms include a campaign against corruption in government and land reform, beginning in northern Iran. 

Meanwhile, the Government is refining plans for its third economic development program which is to begin in September 1962. This program is expected to be more comprehensive than earlier plans. It will include provisions for stimulating, guiding, and adequately financing expanded private sector development activity as well as an expanded public sector program. 

We expect to join with other countries in considering the third development plan, perhaps under the auspices of the International Bank. The Bank has already conducted preliminary studies of the general outline of the plan. We plan to increase long-term lending for economic development in Iran. We intend to join other developed countries to support the third plan, once it has been reviewed and Iran has indicated its willingness to carry out the necessary measures to make it successful.

These four countries-India, Pakistan, Turkey, and Iran-will account for over 80 percent of the AID funds programed for NESA during fiscal year 1963. 

PLANNING FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN OTHER COUNTRIES IN THE NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA 

The effectiveness of economic planning and programs in other countries in the region varies widely. Improved economic progress is growing more important and awareness of this need on the part of the country governments is increasing. With the single exception of Yemen, some sort of economic development plan or program is in process or under active consideration in every single country. There is considerable variety in the form as well as in the sophistication and quality of the planning involved. 

Israel has not hitherto published a comprehensive long-term economic plan and forecast, although it is now preparing one. Nevertheless, it has achieved highquality economic planning. It has planned ahead over an appropriate period for all major projects and programs. Effective mechanisms exist for central evolution and coordination of economic policy. Integration and coordination of development projects and programs is achieved through the normal budget process. 

The actual rate of progress achieved has been extremely high, by far the best in the region and among the best anywhere. 

Greece, too, although it has a broad development program, has not produced as detailed or comprehensive a plan as some others. Yet it has achieved good general results by the pursuit of sound policies and major encouragement of and reliance upon private initiative. 

In many of the other countries planning remains considerably more rudimentary even though efforts are being made to produce comprehensive multiyear plan documents. Discretion is necessary in using these plans as a basis for aid programing. Careful review of project proposals is necessary even when they are included in formal plans. 

The steady increase in planning activities highlights the importance attached to economic progress by the Governments and people of the region. It emphasizes the need for us to assist these Governments in improving their planning as well as in carrying out sound economic projects and programs.

THE SINO-SOVIET BLOC ECONOMIC OFFENSIVE 

The concentration of Sino-Soviet economic assistance in the Near East-south Asia area shows that the bloc recognizes not only the political importance of the area, but also the desire of the people of the area to improve their economic status. 

Ever since it was launched in 1955, the Soviet bloc economic aid offensive has been heavily concentrated in the Near East and south Asia. The total committed in this region to date by the bloc is about $2.6 billion, representing about 60 percent of all Sino-Soviet foreign economic aid. This bloc assistance is concentrated in amounts and times to produce the maximum political effect. 

In India, the aid from Russia and the satellites has been considerable. However, it has been used to meet plan needs. It has, therefore, tended to reduce the level of aid which might otherwise have been required from the free world for India. Although Soviet aid has afforded a focus for effective propaganda, it has not been sufficient to create danger of Communist domination. 

In Nepal, Ceylon, and the UAR, bloc programs have been larger in relation to the size of the economies than in the case of India. In Ceylon and the UAR they have significantly affected trade patterns. But in none of these countries has the bloc achieved domination. Our own programs have continued to provide an alternative to exclusive reliance on the bloc. 

Finally, in Afghanistan and Yemen, aid from the bloc has been supplied on a massive scale in relation to the economies. As a result, there is a real danger that the bloc may be able to secure domination or control through substantial policy concessions. The availability of U.S. assistance has had the effect of reducing this danger.

PROPOSED PROGRAM FOR FISCAL YEAR 1963 

We propose to join with other developed countries to support effectively those serious economic development programs that are underway or will be launched during 1963. In fiscal year 1962, U.S. development lending-largely in support of such programs-is expected to be nearly twice what it was in 1961 in this region. An increase of approximately $200 million will be required in fiscal year 1963.

We also propose an increase of about $15 million in development grants for fiscal year 1963. The need for supporting assistance has declined as development programs have expanded and have become more effective. fiscal year 1963 program for the NESA region proposes that supporting assistance be reduced to $100 million, less than half the fiscal year 1962 level.

India and Pakistan have received assurances of U.S. assistance at specific levels, subject to contributions by other consortium members and appropriation of funds. The U.S. commitment to India for development lending for fiscal year 1963 is $450 million (provided this amount is matched by other countries) and for Pakistan it is $225 million. 

Iran and Turkey are both preparing long-term development plans which the United States expects to be able to support in concert with other developed countries and development financing institutions. In both these countries it is essential that the transition to major development financing be handled smoothly. We believe that the transition can be made successfully in Iran in fiscal year 1963. 

In Turkey we anticipate terminating supporting assistance at some time after fiscal year 1964. It may prove desirable to enter into formal lending commitments for these two countries during fiscal year 1963. In any case, we expect to act on a substantial volume of loans. 

In Greece and Israel we also plan to make development loans. Both countries are making good progress in their economic development. Both have demonstrated effective use of resources. Israel has the highest standard of achievement in the area. At present it has adequate foreign exchange reserves, but it faces a sharp reduction in reparations and restitution payments from Germany. 

To sustain its high rate of investment, Israel needs a continued large inflow of capital [security deletion]. 

Although we plan to end our supporting assistance grants to Greece after fiscal year 1962, we will continue to assist Greek development efforts. The amount of U.S. aid will depend partly upon the soundness of loan applications and partly upon the availability of funds from other free world sources. 

It is less easy to forecast development lending in the remaining countries in the region. It appears likely that loan applications will be received from the 

UAR, Syria, Cyprus, Afghanistan, and Jordan for projects which will promote economic development and contribute to the strength and stability of these countries, and that some such applications will be approved. 

Loans in the NESA region will be mainly for specific development projects. 

Program loans-those which are for the financing of needed imports in development programs will be made only where they are most effective means of supporting sound development. During fiscal year 1963 we expect to provide program loans to India, Pakistan, and Israel-and perhaps one or two others. 

DEVELOPMENT GRANTS 

Development grant programs totaling $78.1 million for the NESA region are proposed for fiscal year 1963. That is an increase of $14.6 million over 1962. 

The main purposes of our development grants are to assist the host governments in planning development programs, economic policies, and important sector programs; to establish educational institutions adequate to meet the needs for technical and managerial personnel; and to train and advise those responsible for important activities. A well planned and executed development grant program is an important precursor of and complement to the development loan program in most countries. 

The development grant programs are being ended in Greece, Israel, and Lebanon. These countries have developed extensive domestic technical skills and can now provide for outside technical services in their own budgets if the assistance is needed. Throughout the region it is our goal to eliminate all grant projects that will not make significant contributions to development of the countries involved. All projects are under continuous review to make certain that they meet legislative criteria. Many projects have been terminated and others are scheduled for termination as soon as practical. 

In six countries of the region development grants are increased. In two of these Cyprus and Syria-new programs are being started. These programs total $2.5 million for fiscal year 1963. The $1 million increase in development grants proposed for the United Arab Republic in 1963 will help to make United Arab Republic industrial planning more practical [security deletion]. The development grant program for fiscal year 1963 for Afghanistan is [security deletion], increased [security deletion] over the fiscal year 1962 level. Most of this increase occurs because the continuing activities included in supporting assistance in fiscal year 1962 will be shifted to the "development grant" category in fiscal year 1963. 

An increase in key education programs is also planned. The Afghan program will, of course, have to be reevaluated if normal transit through Pakistan cannot be resumed. In Pakistan and Turkey, the increases proposed for fiscal

year 1963 amount to $2 million and $600,000 respectively. These increases are to intensify planning and performance in key development sectors. Turkey requires help in its industrial planning and in export promotion, while in Pakistan stepped-up help in agriculture and public administration is especially important. 

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

In three countries fiscal year 1962 is expected to be the last year for grants under supporting assistance. The countries are Greece, Pakistan, and Iran. In 

Afghanistan, no supporting assistance is proposed for fiscal year 1963—former supporting assistance projects will be completed under development grants. 

In fiscal 1963 supporting assistance is proposed only for Turkey, Jordan, Yemen, and for the CENTO civil airway project. Requests total $100 million as compared with $206.9 million in fiscal year 1962 and $284.1 million in 1961. 

In Turkey supporting assistance was cut from $90 million in fiscal year 1961 to $58 million in 1962. The [security deletion] assistance recommended for fiscal year 1963 is needed to sustain the imports that Turkey must have during this critical year. Without this minimal amount, Turkey would be unable to sustain its economy and its military forces while completing preparation of its 5-year plan and arranging the necessary long-term development financing for the plan.

In Jordan, the national budget depends upon outside contribution. The proposed reduction in fiscal year 1963 assumed that more internal resources can be mobilized than has been the case in the past. Supporting assistance proposed for Yemen in fiscal year 1963 is the minimum required to proceed effectively with present projects. Support proposed for the CENTO airway project will enable it to continue on schedule. 

AID FOR PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

I want to make special mention of our activities in this region in support of private sector development. In most of these countries the development programs underway and planned are dependent upon expanded private activity. 

We are assisting the efforts of the governments concerned to encourage such private investment.

AID contributes directly to the financing of private investment by dollar loans and by loans in local currency under the Cooley amendment of Pubile Law 480. 

Important private sector development loans which have been approved this year include the $3 million premier automobile loan in India, the $9.8 million loan to the Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. to help it establish a plant to produce rayon tire cord fabric, and the $2.8 million loan to the Sui Gas Transmission Co. in Pakistan to assist it in expanding the production and distribution of 

Pakistan's natural gas.

Development banks and investment corporatives are important channels for lending to private development projects. Two recently approved loans are typical of this type of financing. The first is a $20 million loan to the Industrial 

Finance Corporation of India, which will relend the money to private companies in selected industrial categories to meet the foreign exchange requirements of their investment programs. This succeeds a $10 million loan to the same corporation which was announced in December of 1960 and has been completely committed. The second is a loan of $7.5 million to the Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation which will also be reloaned for the development needs of private companies in Pakistan. Three previous loans to this institution have been made totaling $21.7 million which have now been almost entirely committed. The IBRD has also made substantial loans to this institution. 

Probably the most important direct support for private enterprise provided under our program is the financing of necessary equipment, spare parts, and raw materials as nonproject aid, particularly program loans. To date this year development loans of this type have been approved totaling over $150 million for India, Pakistan, and Israel. The commodities financed under these loans mainly go to help private companies expand their capacity and increase production.

AID has recently assumed responsibility for administration of the Cooley loan program. We expect a large volume of activity under this program in this area. Already AID has entered into one such loan in India for a synthetic rubber plant and another in Pakistan to finance expansion of capacity for the manufacture of automobile tires.

Another program of AID which encourages private investment, particularly investment by American companies, is the investment guarantee program. The regular convertibility and expropriation guarantees continue available. Among those recently approved was one covering an investment by a private American company in the manufacture of refrigeration equipment in India. A number of additional applications are pending.

The new authority under the act for international development to provide broader guarantees against all risks short of the investor's misconduct will be instrumental in enabling some further private investments to proceed. Among the first four applications for such coverage is one from a Texas company planning to undertake the manufacture of well casings and the drilling of wells in Pakistan.

Finally, we can and do support directly the efforts of the country governments to attract and assist private investors. The Indian Investment Center has been established, with the assistance of AID-financed contract advisory services, to provide assistance to prospective investors in India and to Indian businessmen desiring to attract foreign investment. This center is now functioning actively. Also, we are now studying a new project to assist the Government of Pakistan in improving its services to private investors. 

AID FROM OTHER DEVELOPED FREE WORLD COUNTRIES 

Other developed countries of the free world and international financing institutions have greatly increased their aid in this region. Their initial commitments to India's new 5-year plan almost equal their total contributions to India's two earlier plans, and commitments made to date are only for the new plan's first 2 years.¹ Non-U.S. assistance to Pakistan has also risen with $445 million pledged for fiscal years 1962 and 1963. In addition, of course, 10-year commitments have been made to the Indus River Basin program. 

Various countries have offered aid outside consortia which further U.S. interests. German assistance of Afghanistan and Syria is particularly helpful. 

We are confident that the free world's other developed countries will play increasing roles in Near Eastern and south Asian development. As additional countries evolve sound development programs, larger contributions can be secured from non-U.S. sources. The use of consortia-which have been so conspicuously successful in the cases of India and Pakistan-is also likely to increase the amount of aid from other countries. The chances are good that the 

IBRD and the Development Assistance Committee of OECD will set up similar arrangements for other countries in the area. 

CONCLUSION 

The major countries of the Near East and south Asia are making determined efforts to improve their economic situation, and thereby increase their chances of remaining free and independent. It is of the utmost importance to the 

United States that they succeed in this. I most earnestly urge your support for the programs we are recommending, which will help them achieve that success.

Mr. GAUD. To get a quick idea of the volume and nature of our program in this region, you might look at the table on the bottom of the page. If you go back to page 1, the next item in the program is supporting assistance. There the drop is, I think you will agree, dramatic, from $284 million in 1961 to $207 roughly in the current fiscal year, to $100 million next year.

This sharp decline between 1962 and 1963 is due to two things. 

First, we are dropping out altogether from the category of supporting assistance, Iran, which got $44 million this year; Greece, which got $20 million this year; Pakistan, which got $25 million. We believe that these countries are now in a position to go it without supporting assistance and to get along on the basis of development loans and some technical assistance. 

Also, we are reducing the amount of supporting assistance for Tur key [security deletion] and Jordan [security deletion]. These two countries, Turkey and Jordan, account for the bulk ['security deletion] of the $100 million that we are asking for in this region. We don't believe that the economies of either of these countries is such that they can get along without supporting assistance.

The third category of aid, the development grants, also known as technical assistance, technical cooperation, point 4. These vary from year to year. For next year we are asking for roughly $78 million, which is about $14.5 million more than this year. As I say, this is a rather flexible category of aid. 

In this region, for example, next year, we are dropping out of technical assistance altogether three countries: Israel, Lebanon, and

Greece. We are doing this in the belief that they have reached a stage of being able to supply their own technical assistance, as it were, that they don't need any help from us in this regard. 

This has been communicated to the three countries, and I think everybody is perfectly happy about it. We have no problem. At the same time we have two new customers in the region. One is Cyprus, which has been in existence for a little over a year, and the other is Syria, which has been separated from the UAR a good deal less than a year. [Security deletion.] 

Afghanistan: There is a substantial increase in our development grant program for Afghanistan, but most of this results from a shift of projects from supporting assistance to development grants. There is some increase in Pakistan and one or two other countries. So much for figures.

What is our objective in this program? It is very easy to state; it is a little hard to realize. A good deal harder to realize than say. 

Our objective, to put it in a few words and perhaps to oversimplify it a little, is to achieve sound economic development in these countries with those countries making the maximum practical contribution to their own development. In other words, foster and further their economic development but insist that they do what they can in partnership with us.

You have to approach this problem obviously in different ways in different countries. At one end of the spectrum, let's take Israel. The best brains, many of the best brains inside of Israel and outside Israel have devoted a great deal of time and energy to figuring out how Israel can make the most of its resources. No one has to worry about self-help for Israel. We don't have to hold any carrots or hold any sticks out as far as Israel is concerned. 

There are other countries in the region which approximate Israel in this respect.

On the other end of the spectrum you have a number of countries, and I hate to take any one and single it out, although it would be easy to do. There are a number of countries in the region where you have a high rate of illiteracy, very insignificant resources, no knowledge of planning, very little knowledge of administration, perhaps a very unhealthy and dangerous land tenure system, no incentive for the farmer to produce more than he does, countries that can't do much in the way of planning, can't do much more than take the beginning steps of self-help..

Our program is worked out in these countries to take into consideration the capacities of the countries to help themselves. In some countries we can be tough, in other countries we can be less tough, we ask for less.

If a land reform program is instituted, is begun, this is a step forward. If steps are taken to increase the taxes, to increase tax collection, this is a step forward. We don't expect every country to achieve the same result, to get to the same pinnacle in the same length of time.

One thing on which we are concentrating particularly heavily in this region is the emphasis on planning, national planning, if you will, of a country's resources, and planning for the future as to what it proposes to do to increase its economic status.

We don't do this just because we like the idea of planning but because of what goes into the formulation and solution of effective planning. 

To prepare such a plan you have to study the resources, fix certain goals, decide what priorities are most important within that particular country. You have to mobilize internal resources. You have to set priorities all the way down the line. Take other similar measures. 

When you get through, if you have done a good job, you have a pretty good notion of what this country can do in the next 3 to 5 years a pretty good notion of what it is most important for it to do and whether it is utilizing its own resources to the best effect. 

On the basis of these claims, we are then prepared to consider how much aid we will give these countries. As I say, some countries can plan better than others. Some countries just don't know how to plan.

One of the first things we do for some of the countries, Nepal is an example, and others, is to encourage [security deletion] and advise them in the business of how you go about figuring out what you ought to do with your country.

India and Pakistan, as you all know from the past, have long-range plans. India is now in her third 5-year plan. Pakistan is in her second 5-year plan. Israel is in the front rank of planning. Greece is very well along in the business of planning and makes reasonably good use of her resources. 

Two other countries in the region, Turkey and Iran, are working on long-range plans, which we hope will come to fruition within the next few months to the extent where they can be examined by the World Bank or a Committee of the OECD or DAC, and form the basis of a consortium approach by free world countries, including ourselves.

Beyond that, and beyond those countries, every other country in this region, with the exception of Yemen, is engaged in some sort of a planning exercise at the present time. As I say, some of these are much more advanced than others.

This is a drive that we are making and that these countries are making toward figuring out what they ought to do, how they ought to do it, and how they can best utilize their resources. 

As is true in the case of India and Pakistan, our aid to these plans is and will be very largely in terms of individual projects. There are some program loans which are not related to specific projects. 

But in the main we deal still with projects, but projects which are given a priority by the country and which have some relation to where the country is trying to go.

This is still the main basis upon which we grant our aid. I have mentioned, and Mr. Talbot mentioned, the contribution made by other free world countries in this region. This is something we can be proud of and on which we are working all the time to increase. 

We are fortunate in NESA-as we call this region-we are fortunate that there are a number of countries here in which other Western nations and ourselves want to have a hand. The India consortium, for example, includes six nations there. The U.S. contribution to the 

Indian plan, the first 2 years of the current 5-year plan, is actually less than the contribution being made by other free world countries and the World Bank.

In the case of Pakistan, the total contribution for the commitment for the first 2 years is $945 million. Of that the United States is contributing $500 million. Other free nations and the World Bank are contributing $445 million. 

Germany has just recently made a 5-year, $50 million commitment to Afghanistan.

As an example of what is going on in the region and what we hope will go on continually: We have just signed a new loan to Syria to stabilize her currency. This is the main purpose of the loan. Our contribution to this is $9 million from AID and $5 million from the Eximbank, a total of $14 million from U.S. sources. The Germans are putting up $16 million. The Italians, $5 million. [Security deletion.]

Here is another example of cooperation on the part of free world nations and a definite indication of their intention and desire to take some of the load off our backs.

Cyprus, Greece, Turkey, Iran, Egypt, Jordan-there is scarcely a country in this region to which a country in Europe doesn't make a contribution.

Another of the problems we have been thinking about in the last half year, and which we will continue to work on in the future, is how to coordinate in the best possible way the contribution of ourselves and the other nations. The India and the Pakistan consortiums are good examples of how you can do this. You get all the countries interested under the aegis of the World Bank or OECD to review the plan, approve it, and then work out in coordination with one another what part of the plan they will support. We do it in India and Pakistan. We hope to do it within the next few months in Turkey and Iran.

Both the DAC and the IBRD are interested in other countries as well. We propose to push this just as hard as we can, to achieve more coordination, to achieve greater contribution from these other countries, and to take as far as we can the load off our back and make this thing a joint enterprise.

While I am on the subject of aid from other countries, I would like to say a word about the activities of the Sino-Soviet bloc in this region. Mr. Talbot said there were considerable. There is a very dramatic map-if you have this green book here, there is a very effective map on page 50 which shows the Sino-Soviet economic offensive throughout the world.

They started, as you know, imitating our economic aid program. 

They started in 1955. These figures are cumulative in terms of the amount of aid they have given to these countries since 1955. 

You will note with the exception of Indonesia and Cambodia and Latin America over here in the left-hand corner, substantially all of the economic aid that the Soviets have given has gone to this fringe of countries in what we call NESA. The reasons for that are obvious. To begin with, many are contiguous to either Russia or to China.

Also, consider how strategic this area is. You have the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, the Mediterranean, the Suez Canal, Near East oil, India, the largest country in the free world in terms of population and surely the bellwether of Asia on the continent. A lot of targets are here. You have the Khyber Pass, which explains of course a 81496-62-pt. 3- -14

This is large part of the interest that the Russians have in Afghanistan. 

This was the traditional route from the time of Alexander. the area manifestly in which the Russians have a great interest and in which they have been concentrating a great deal of aid. 

In a number of these countries their aid is greater than ours. It is true in Afghanistan, Yemen, Egypt, Iraq, Syria [security deletion]. 

We are not trying to compete with the amount of Russian aid in many of these countries, but we feel it is important in all of them to offer them an alternative to this Russian aid. We do not want to throw them into the hands of Russia and deprive them of any choice, because after all our objective here, the only purpose we have in this aid program in this region is to do what we can to increase the chances of these countries remaining free and independent. STATEMENT OF HON. J. KENNETH GALBRAITH, U.S. AMBASSADOR TO INDIA 

Ambassador GALBRAITH. I have no prepared statement, Mr. Chair- 

If the committee would so wish I might make a few observations about the country where I represent the United States and purely as a prelude to questions. 

I should suppose from the point of view of economic aid and from the point of view of economic development, one could properly describe India as one of the success stories of this part of the world. 

When I first became interested in India, if I may interject a personal note of 10 years ago, there were always two questions that one was asked about India: Will it go Communist? or, occasionally, when will it go Communist? And the other question was: How will it make out in the race with China?

Well, neither of these questions does one ever hear any more or very rarely. India has just now had its third election in which the Communist vote showed no appreciable increase, in which the great Central Party, the great Omnibus Party was returned with substantial majority in the Central House.

Of course, the comparison with China now is overwhelmingly favorable to India. The standard of living in China in these last years has been going down, people have been on tighter and tighter rations. 

One doesn't know what the political reaction of the people there is. 

But there is a measure of evidence to show the regime is not governing by the very enthusiastic consent of the people. 

By contrast, as I just pointed out, the Indian Governmer has just been returned in a free and democratic election by a majority.

This stability, and I think it can be so described, is based on a fairly solid economic achievement. agricultural production, and India is primarily an agricultural country-70 to 80 percent of the people make their living in agricuure-agricultural pre- In the last 10 years Very large duction has increased by about 45 percent,ich is a very sunt increase. Industrial production has ingeased by about 75 percent in 10 years.

Mrs. BOLTON. And the population?

Ambassador GALBRAITH. I will come to that in a minute, Mrs. Bolton, because that has also increased. 

The industrial production one can think of as falling into two parts, a sort of large-scale heavy furniture of the industrial revolution-steeĺ mills, heavy engineering, and so forth. This is the thing that we think of as the heart of industrial development. That has shown a steady and in some cases very substantial increase. 

But what has been much more remarkable in India in these last few years has been a renaissance of small-scale industry, employing anywhere from 10 to 500 people. This has been an explosive increase. 

Ten years ago, to give you one example, there was one bicycle manufacturer in India making complete bicycles. Now there are 10, an increase of 10 times.

Other examples are sewing machines and motion pictures. [Security deletion.] Motion pictures [security deletion] are produced very inexpensively for export around Asia. Pots and pans, footwear, the whole range of small-scale industry has had an enormous expansion. 

The consequence of all this has been that per capita income-Mrs. 

Bolton, I say per capita income because this takes into consideration the population increase has been going up 2 percent a year. I think we sometimes use these figures without having any good feeling about what they mean. Two percent a year means the individual can look at his situation every year and see that he is just a little better off than he was the year before.

That by and large is the comparison that most people make. The average Indian doesn't compare himself with an American, the Chinese, with the European, he compares the situation the year before, and if he sees that is improving he reflects on it with a certain amount of satisfaction.

I must attribute in very large part that Indian stability to this gradual small, year-by-year improvement. In real terms it means that the Indian villager has enough to eat. It means that he has a few more clothes each year. His wife has another sari. His daughter has a wedding dress. It means that he gets a bicycle if he is lucky. 

You wonder why I mention bicycles. As between a person traveling on foot and the person who is mounted on a bicycle, there is a greater improvement in mobility than there is between the person mounted on a bicycle and the person in a motorcar. 

I was in a village in the Punjab a few weeks ago where 10 years ago there was only one bicycle. Now 30 of the people in this village have bicycles. This represents an enormous increase in the mobility, and in the sense of the ability to visit friends and the ability to get beyond the confines of what one can do with two feet. 

I would also say, I think without any danger of serious exaggeration, that aid, including in a very substantial measure American aid, has made this possible. It has accomplished three things in this country in the last 10 years: In the first place, our Public Law 480 assistance, our food-grain assistance, has supplemented Indian agricultural production so that as you have increased the industrial population, increased the pressure on food supply, you haven't substantial price increases. It has enabled, in other words, the pinning down of food prices.

Since food and clothing make up about 75 percent of the budget of the average Indian, this means that if you have pinned that down, you have pretty well pinned down the cost of living. 

The aid has also provided, as they could have been provided in no other way, the dollars for essential industries, or the hard currency for essential imports, turbogenerators, diesel locomotives, steel, things which for the purposes of economic development could not be supplied from domestic sources. 

The third thing it has done has been to ease the pressure on the internal population. One gets investment as everyone here knows by saving, not spending by refraining from consumption. 

If you have an annual income of $75 or $100 a year, you don't have very much margin for saving. If you have to squeeze investment funds out of that much income, you are squeezing it pretty close to the bone.

Without question, one of the problems of China has been that they have been squeezing investment funds out of a population that had no real margin to spare. 

The external assistance that India has received has meant that you have substantially reduced the pressure on these extremely poor people for the investment funds which enable them at the next stage to have an increased income. 

It hasn't eliminated the pressure because by far the greater proportion of the funds for Indian development are coming from internal sources. It has provided the margin which, as I say, has helped to ease the pressure. 

I don't want in introducing this to give the impression for a moment that there are no problems. It is very hard to be Ambassador there and not be overwhelmed by it. There are still an enormous number of problems in India yet to be settled. 

One of them I have already mentioned, the fact that you have an average income of $75 to $100 per capita, and these figures don't mean much at this level, is an indication that you still have a situation of overwhelming poverty. People are still very, very poor. 

Congresswoman Bolton mentioned another problem. You still have a race between increasing production and increasing population. 

As a matter of fact, some of the things we have done in the last 10 years have helped the Indians, and have so far had their principal effect in increasing the population. 

One of our most successful technical assistance programs has been the elimination of malaria, which is the curse of this part of the world. In the last 10 years, malaria has been practically eliminated in India. The elimination of malaria means an increase in vitality, an increase in virility, and an increase in the birth rate. 

There is no question about it. Medical assistance, as it improves, brings the death rate down before the birth rate comes down. So there is in India this race in which you always have to go faster and faster in order to keep in the same place. 

In some of the industrial enterprises, particularly the large scale industrial enterprises, continuing improvement of management is important. [Security deletion.] 

Their exports in the end the most important thing for India to do is export enough goods so that the dependence on aid will decline and the dollars can be earned to purchase equipment, machinery, and all

the others things that are needed from overseas and will continue to be needed. Export performance is still not satisfactory. 

One can say of that that it is now engaging the energies and attention of the Indian Government, as it hasn't ever before. [Security deletion.]

I think there are perhaps some around this table who will say that India is still excessively independent in its foreign policy in some respects, that the help, assistance that India has had from the West has not been reciprocated by all of the cooperation on all of the issues that we might wish.

Let me say that an Ambassador becomes conscious of this particular point, too. On the other hand, there is no question that India is a non- 

Communist property-owning democracy, and I think it is also fair to say that independence, and a kind of assertive independence, is a factor in this state of development. 

We might remind ourselves in our early stage of development we also had a certain assertive independence as far as Europe was concerned, as far as the British were concerned, and it is perhaps not too unnatural that this would be the case with India. 

In conclusion, I would like to say there is one thing that has disturbed me and which I like to correct every time I come back. There is a feeling always in the aid discussions that there is never any gratitude, never any feeling of good will as the result of the efforts we put forward.

I have been in India now a year, and I have no doubt that the knowledge of what the United States is doing in India is extremely widespread and extends through a very, very large part of the Indian population, and that the response to that is in fact one of good will and fundamental gratitude. 

I could illustrate this by an example of something that happened 2 weeks ago. I took the President's wife, Mrs. Kennedy, when she was there, down one afternoon to pay a visit to the All India Institute of Medical Sciences. This is a large, enormous medical establishment in New Delhi, patterned somewhat along the line of the Rockefeller Institute, devoted to indigenous diseases, child welfare, child care, and encompassing a big medical teaching institution and a very large children's ward. Indeed, it was the children's ward that Mrs. Kennedy visited. We have put a lot of money into this, relatively speaking. We have plowed back into it a lot of the rupee funds growing out of the Public Law 480 program. It has had extensive technical assistance from us, some smaller assistance from New Zealand under the Colombo Plan.

I may say wherever Mrs. Kennedy went there was an adequate turnout of people, but when we came out there was an enormous crowd of people, some of whom ran for two or three blocks alongside the car, shouting "Thank you." She made the observation, a rather touching observation, that she wouldn't go back with the feeling that there wasn't a feeling of gratitude. 

People in New Delhi know what we have done for this institution, and they are grateful for it. They are grateful for the knowledge that this is a place where they can take their youngsters and get medical treatment.

I am not stressing this particularly because, as has been said many times, this is not the purpose of economic aid. We are not concerned primarily with a popularity contest in the world. I think this is true. 

I have always had the feeling that compassion in matters of cold strategy does play a certain role. I think that we can say with some confidence that there is a compassionate reaction to the efforts that we are making in India. 

Mr. Chairman, I started out by saying I didn't have a statement. 

I must say I did a very good job of producing one.

Ambassador GALBRAITH. I will, with the assistance of Mr. Gaud- (The following has been supplied for the record:)

PRESENT STATUS OF INDIA WHEAT LOAN-REPAYMENT Under the India Emergency Food Aid Act of 1951 (Public Law 48, the India wheat loan of 1951, loan No. ICA X 86-1, authorized providing up to $190 million in wheat assistance to India on credit terms in accordance with the provisions of section III (c) of the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948. The loan agreement originally provided for semiannual repayment over a 35-year period with interest at 2½ percent. The GOI drew over $189.6 million against the credit.

The first interest payment was for the period January 1 to June 30, 1952. 

Principal repayments started on June 30, 1957. As of June 30, 1958, the unpaid balance of the loan was over $186.2 million. Payments of $3,417,363.28 in principal and $28,321,270.05 in interest had been made by the Indian Government through that date. At that point the GOI requested a moratorium on wheat loan repayments because of the extremely heavy burden in servicing her external indebtedness. State and ICA, with the concurrence of NAC, agreed to defer payments of interest and principal due on the loan for 9½ years, payments to be resumed on December 31, 1967. As a result, deferred payments amounting to $24.5 million in interest and $41.9 million in principal will come due in the period subsequent to June 30, 1986, the original terminal date, which was thereby extended to December 31, 1995. No interest is being charged on the deferred payments of principal and interest. (It should be noted that an escape clause in the original agreement provided for consideration of such adjustments in the event of adverse economic conditions or for other reasons.) Further provision was made in the original loan agreement for repayment in strategic resources, at the option of the Eximbank, but this option has not been exercised. 

Under the Mundt amendment of the act, $5 million of interest payments made up to January 1, 1957, was made available for cultural and technical exchange, involving scholarships and the exchange of books, equipment, and other materials. This program is nearing completion. Over 99 percent of the $5 million has been expended or programed under the cognizance of the Department of State.

Mrs. KELLY. I wanted to know if Pakistan is going to be treated in the same way.

Ambassador GALBRAITH. I cannot answer that. I will get the 

Mrs. KELLY. Will you obtain the information for us? I thank you so much.

In- Under ICA Loan No. 1 of September 11, 1952, Pakistan was provided a $15 million wheat loan under terms similar to those of the 1951 loan to India. terest payments totaling $1,687,500 were made through March 15, 1958. In 

September 1958, State and ICA, with concurrence of NAC, agreed to defer further payments until March 15, 1967. Scheduled payments of interest and principal will run to 1988, with the deferred payments of interest and principal paid from 1988 to 1997 with no interest charged because of the deferral.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Broomfield.

Mr. BROOMFIELD.  

I would like to ask Ambassador Galbraith a couple of questions regarding the armed forces of India, the size of their army, and the quality of men and equipment. 

Ambassador GALBRAITH. I will have to get you the estimate of the actual size of the forces. It is somewhere around a half million. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. The quality of men and equipment? 

Ambassador GALBRAITH. The army is in the tradition of the British 

Army, still holds strongly to the British Army traditions. Training is extremely good. Morale is high. This is a very well run outfit, very proud armed force.

In recent years it has been badly starved for equipment. The most modern weapons, highly sophisticated, are not made in India. The foreign exchange shortage has been such that the imports for the army have been at a fairly low level. They have been under very rigid ceilings. The weapons are pretty out of date. They do extremely well with this equipment. 

But their most recent fighter plane-I am talking about the armed forces in general-their most recent fighter plane is an early model jet, subsonic, of course.

Their troops do not have automatic weapons. Many of the units carry rifles of post-World War I vintage. The armored divisions have tanks of World War II vintage, quite a few of which they got from us. 

On the other hand, the training and morale is maintained at a high level. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. One other question on the armed forces. On the deployment of their forces, are they heavier on the Pakistan border or China border?

Ambassador GALBRAITH. The two borders coincide. One border is an extension of the other. The same deployment is related to both borders. It is pretty hard to say which is which. 

Up on the Ladakh border the possibility of deploying any considerable number of troops is very, very limited. It takes 40 or more men to support 1 man up there. The answer to your question-there is no question about which border they fear the most. They are much more concerned about the China border. Whether you can deploy the troops between the two borders, I don't think you can. 

There have been examples that they have 75 percent of their troops along the Pakistan border. I think the figures are meaningless. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you, very much.

At the next stage you have a literate population which can learn machine skills, which will be more responsive to the improved agricultural techniques, which will be more productive.

One hundred years ago, if you had asked our ancestors what is the best way of developing the country, they would say to get a good school system. In a sense, this is what we are supporting in connection with this food feeding program.

EXAMPLES OF SPECIAL PROJECTS OF AID, NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA REGION DEVELOPING A MILK FARM IN CALCUTTA 

The purpose of this program has been to provide model facilities for production of sanitary milk products, to remove cattle from the streets of Calcutta, and to reduce prohibitive milk prices.

With the cooperation of the U.S. AID mission and four British Commonwealth countries, the Government of India has built the largest milk plant in Asia. On completion, its capacity will be almost 4.94 million pounds of milk daily, and the plant will also produce butter, ghee, and other milk products including "toned" milk, a mixture of dry skim milk and buffalo milk. 

An essential part of the plan has been development of a 6,000-acre farm for forage production, and modern, sanitary living facilities for individual milk dealers and their families. By providing these facilities for both cattle and the dairymen, the project will rid Calcutta of stray cattle and open-air cow parks. 

The milk scheme constitutes a vital part of India's national dairy development program. By providing machinery and technical assistance for the factory, AID is participating in an important demonstration of improved milk processing, and use of milk tankers as an economic means of transporting milk. 

The plant is scheduled to be in operation in May. 

SMALL BUSINESS LOANS IN TURKEY 

During 1961 the U.S. AID mission made a loan to the People's Bank of Turkey, using counterpart funds generated by U.S. commodity assistance. Small business loans began immediately. Within 6 months loans had been made to 202 small businessmen-each a member of the 140 credit guarantee cooperatives that were organized throughout Turkey starting in 1951. The cooperatives are independent organizations because their members are unable to tap credit sources individually. Total membership in the cooperatives is 55,000. The average loan is the equivalent of $180. 

Loans are made to small businesses. the program produces door and window frames with lumber that he buys from various parts of Turkey. He is expanding his shop through the purchasing of simple millworking machinery. 

One carpenter who is borrowing through 

Another borrower repairs agricultural machines and diesel fuel pumps. tinsmith who has borrowed from the fund produces small sheet steel stoves. 

He is now purchasing tools and a welding machine. A tailor is borrowing to expand his business. Through his loan he will purchase motorized sewing machines.

INTENSIVE AGRICULTURAL DISTRICT PROGRAM IN INDIA 

India's full food production potential can only be realized when all essential elements are combined into an integrated, simultaneous program. These essentials include improvement of seed and fertilizers, plant protection, and easy farm credit.

The Government of India has therefore begun a program with this goal in mind. The plan is to concentrate in promising areas where immediate gains can be made in farm production. Seven districts have been selected as target areas. Their total cultivated area is 5.8 million acres, of which 3 million are irrigated. With the help of AID and the Ford Foundation, the Government of 

India is supplying all essential tools and machinery, credit facilities, and technical assistance.

The program is being coordinated at the state level, by the district collectors of each area. Through the local governments and cooperatives, he will attempt to reach all farmers, and to help them formulate village and farm production plans that will progressively involve all farm families. 

Research and extension workers will demonstrate the practices that are being advised, and they will give estimates of increased profits possible through their adoption. 

TURKISH ARMED FORCES LITERACY TRAINING 

Literacy training centers have been set up in various towns of Turkey, each unit housing 422 servicemen. With nearly 100,000 illiterate men reaching military service age each year, literacy training is a vital program. 

Specialists in language teaching from Georgetown University are working in cooperation with the U.S. AID mission. They have compiled a list of about 

700 Turkish words, and insured that primers and practice writing materials were prepared.

Each illiterate recruit is assigned to a literacy training center for 4 months before beginning military training. He gets 22 hours of reading per week, writing, 8 hours of arithmetic, and 11 hours of civics and health. The value of this program transcends the advantages it brings to the military service since on release from the Armed Forces their new found skills aid them in advancing themselves in civilian life. 

Current facilities provide opportunities to give literacy to some 50,000 men each year.

WATER FOR JORDAN 

In 1960 the Government of Jordan created a central water authority to develop water resources of the country, and with U.S. AID assistance the authority began work in that year. Presently less than half of the Jordanian economically available water supply is being used. By employing its unusued water resources, Jordan can realize its full agricultural and industrial production capacity. 

Among the first tasks of the water authority was to rehabilitate Jordan's ancient water system-built in Roman times when this region supported a large population. In those days, every drop of available water was conserved through numerous reservoirs, cisterns, and irrigation systems that still dot the landscape throughout Jordan.

Again with U.S. AID, the water authority removed silt from a Roman reservoir whose capacity is 23 million gallons, and then repaired the reservoir for modern use. The reservoir now stores enough water to meet the needs of 

100,000 tribesmen and their flocks for 3 years. 

Old Roman wells were cleared and repaired, and new wells are being drilled throughout Jordan with modern drill rigs. 

KORANGI TOWNSHIP 

The Korangi Township is a resettlement project for Pakistani refugees, former occupants of slum areas in Karachi. The development provides housing for 70,000 refugees. It is scheduled for completion in 1965. On completion there will be 22,100 1-room houses, 17,500 2-room houses, 10,500 plots for selfbuilt houses, and 9,100 plots for middle- and high-income families who wish to build their own houses. 

The township has a primary school, three health centers, and seven markets. 

Many of its residents are employed in Karachi. 

A similar development is being built in north Karachi, for 30,000 residents. 

AID support for the project came from counterpart funds, and was the rupee equivalent to $8.9 million. 

ENVIRONMENTAL SANITATION IN IRAN 

Advice and assistance is being given to the Government of Iran in methods of providing safe water supplies, improving community sanitation, and sanitation in public buildings and housing, food processing and handling, sewage and waste disposal.

Assistance is being given by three U.S. technicians stationed in the provinces of Iran, and five technicians at the headquarters. Total financial support for the program with exception of salaries of the U.S. technicians, is being borne by the Government of Iran. 

THE RAPTI VALLEY IN NEPAL 

The Rapti Valley in southern Nepal was a malaria-ridden jungle wasteland until 1956. The valley, which is 20 to 30 miles wide, could only support a population of 5,000 extremely hardy tribesmen. 

Because of work done by the U.S. AID mission in cooperation with the Nepalese people, the Rapti Valley now supports a population of 50,000 prospering farmers. 

The Nepalese Government has resettled many landless peasants in the valley, and has turned it into a demonstration area for all of Nepal. In agricultural production, public health services, educational and transportation facilities the valley is more advanced than any other part of Nepal.

This program was made possible through a concentrated malaria eradication project undertaken in the valley by the AID mission, and because the mission was able to use heavy agricultural equipment to plow through an area formerly overgrown by elephant grass. This work made it possible for the land to be worked by Nepalese farmers, using their own equipment. 

U.S. agricultural experts established an experimental farm in the valley, demonstrated procedures to improve crop cultivation and land management, introduced new varieties of seed, and animal husbandry methods. 

The entire project was willingly accepted by the Nepalese, who learned what they could do to improve their livelihoods through village demonstration programs. A 2-year training program for 60 women who are now auxiliary health workers had particular value. The program was completed in 1960, and the women are now serving the villages of Nepal-immunizing mothers, and providing child care, nutritional assistance, and prenatal care. Preventive medicine is a definite part of the work.

Washington, D.C.

The committee meets this morning in executive session for a continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

Our witnesses this morning are the Honorable G. Mennen Williams, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, and the Honorable 

Edmond C. IIutchinson, Assistant Administrator, Bureau for Africa and Europe.

Mr. Secretary, you have a prepared statement. I understand you are going to summarize your statement. You may proceed first. Mr. 

Hutchinson will follow you after which we will question you as a team. 

STATEMENT OF HON. G. MENNEN WILLIAMS, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR AFRICAN AFFAIRS 

Mr. WILLIAMS. Very good. May we submit our statements as they are for the record?

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. 

(The statement of Mr. Williams is as follows:) 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a great pleasure to be back with you again to tell you something of the events that have taken place in Africa this past year and to discuss the program for international cooperation in Africa that we are proposing for this next fiscal year. 

A year ago, I reported to you on the dramatic changes that were occurring in Africa. The stress was on Africa as a continent in ferment-a continent newly awakened and turbulent, in which 18 new states had become independent during the preceding 18 months.

The political, economic, and cultural ferment is still there. The transition of Africa from a continent of dependencies to one of independent states is not complete. For most of the nations that are independent, their newfound freedom is a precious thing, to be jealously guarded and cherished. For the leaders of the new Africa, the independence they enjoy today is the product of a lifetime of dedicated work and planning. 

But there is a shift in emphasis in African thinking that is all the more important because of the remarkably short time in which it has occurred. I have seen evidences of it not once but many times in my travels in Africa and in working with African representatives here. Colonialism, independence, an African voice in world affairs-in more and more countries in Africa, these are no longer the questions of exclusive or even of first priority concern. Increasingly the major preoccupation is one of development. 613

This does not mean to say that there is any less a determination to carry on the difficult task of working out African solutions to the many political problems that they still face. It is rather that there is a heightened appreciation of the fact that nation building is an economic and social as well as a political task. 

As president Sylvanus Olympio of Togo said during his recent visit here, "We must now actually prove to our people that we can have a better life from now on." Human In a sense, it is the old struggle for human dignity in a new form. dignity suffers if a people is deprived of its freedom or a man of his rights as an individual. Human dignity also suffers from the onslaughts of hunger and disease, and it is against this tyranny that the new fight for freedom is now clearly and consciously being waged. 

When President Kennedy in his aid message this year spoke of strengthening the capacity "to master the inherent stress of rapid change," his words had special meaning for Africa, where the pace of change has been without parallel. 

The stress is great and may temporarily at times break through the bonds, only partially forged, of African society. But the experience of this past year gives me increasing confidence that, with the help of ourselves and other free nations, Africa can surmount these difficulties. 

We as a nation have a foreign aid program because we are trying to create the world described by President Kennedy in his second state of the Union address: "* * * A peaceful world community of free and independent states, free to choose their own future and their own system so long as it does not threaten the freedom of others. "Some may choose forms and ways that we would not choose for ourselves, but it is not for us that they are choosing. We can welcome diversity-the 

Communists cannot. For we offer a world of choice-they offer the world of coercion. And the way of the past shows clearly that freedom, not coercion, is the wave of the future."

The program we are proposing is necessary in the interest of our Nation and the cause of human dignity. It will help build self-reliant nations that not only can participate in a better life, but can make their own contribution to a free, open, and stable world community. 

THE NEW AID PROGRAM 

How, then, have we gone about devising a program that will strengthen Africa during these formative years, and that will give to Africa a constructive role in the world of the future?

In the presentation before you on our worldwide foreign aid program, five principles have been stressed: (a) The recognition that foreign aid can provide only one of the ingredients needed for development; the leadership and resources of the countries themselves must play the major role; (b) The need for the recipient governments to plan the use of their resources systematically and within increasingly long-range perspectives; (c) Our willingness to assure nations of significant financial assistance over an extended period of time, when performance and plans warrant and when assurances of our participation will help governments to take the difficult steps in undertaking a sound development program; (d) The need for the program to reach the people where they are; and (e) The recognition that foreign aid should increasingly become a cooperative effort of the free world. 

These principles are eminently well suited to Africa, and I would like to take a few minutes to show how each of them applies. In doing so, I will take the liberty of changing the order somewhat, to reflect the emphasis that we feel best fits the needs of Africa.

First, our help is designed to contribute to African leadership, to support Africa's own efforts and to make primary use of the human and material resources of Africa itself. We cannot and should not expect to transplant alien institutions to African soil. The nations of Africa are rightly insistent on building societies of their own, on developing their own personality. 

We need fear neither the lack of African initiative nor the nature of it. 

Imaginative self-help measures are being taken under enthusiastic African leadership. Barriers to trade and the free flow of resources among African countries are being reduced as a result of African meetings in Lagos, Yaounde, and Casablanca. New patterns of transport and communications are being created. New

kinds of agricultural cooperatives have been formed, organizations to encourage the development of small industries are being set up and financial institutions designed to mobilize savings are now being planned. 

Second, the program in Africa is designed to reach the people, in recognition of the need for social progress in the countries we help. By far the largest component of the program is in education, concentrated in particular at the secondary school and college level. To take just a few examples, we are planning to set up a secondary school in each of the three regions of Nigeria. We plan to provide American technical direction for an institute of education in Tanganyika. In Ethiopia we are giving broad support to the Haile Selassie I University. Without far more trained teachers, administrators and technicians, neither economic progress nor long-term political stability can be attained in Africa.

Training in agriculture is a necessary priority in a continent where the vast majority of the people live on the land. By helping set up country agent-type programs to teach Africans to be better farmers or raisers of livestock, we reach the people through their means of livelihood, while contributing toward the growth of the economy as a whole. 

Further, we must face squarely the fact that animal and plant disease and locust infestations are serious obstacles to economic development. Our assistance in the control of these age-old afflictions is therefore a logical element in our program.

In Congo (Brazzaville), for example, we plan on setting up some agricultural training centers, where Congolese farmers will learn the use of fertilizers, become acquainted with improved seed types and get a general grounding in modern farm practices. In the Malagasy Republic, where soil erosion is particularly serious, our proposed agricultural program will focus on soil conservation and the expansion of the agricultural extension service. In the cattle country of 

Upper Volta, our aid will help to improve range management. 

Health is also a way to reach the people and is first of all a matter of training-in sanitatiton, public health, and medical services of all kinds. It is important both on humanitarian grounds and as an essential means of maintaining human efficiency.

We are primarily engaged in an educational effort-a school for nurses in Upper Volta, for example, and a program of public health demonstration in Gabon-but we must also be prepared to provide limited capital support for potable water systems and certain kinds of basic equipment for public health use. 

Transport and communications are of particular importance to Africa because their improvement is both an economic and a political necessity. Economically, the most serious single obstacle in some areas to the transition from a subsistence to a cash economy is the lack of farm-to-market roads. 

Thus, in Niger we plan to provide road maintenance equipment and train operators, mechanics and supervisors. Elsewhere, African products are sometimes at a competitive disadvantage in the world market because of high transport costs. In the Somali Republic, it calls for the construction of a small deepwater port in the southern part of the country, where the agricultural potential is the greatest.

Politically, the lack of transport and communications is a major impediment to the development of a national consciousness to replace tribal loyalties. The isolation of large groups of Africans from a central government to which they have no tradition of allegiance remains a serious source of political instability in many areas of Africa. Here again, our effort is directed toward people in an especially meaningful way.

Only one of the major fields of aid activity in Africa might be considered as stressing general economic ends rather than social progress. Yet, it may have an effect on the lives of the people as profound as any other. I speak of electric power-particularly hydroelectric power-which is Africa's great hope for the development of a modern economy. 

Although some dramatic petroleum discoveries have been made, largely in the north, most of Africa so far as we know is poorly endowed with oil or coal. Its hydroelectric potential, on the other hand, is huge-over four times that of the United States. To African leaders, it is the key to developing a truly modern economy. A beginning at tapping this potential is being made where there are large-scale requirements for the use of power in the reduction of ores. An early byproduct will be more and cheaper electric power for homes, farms, and small industries.

Third, our program gives particular support for African action toward longrange planning and the establishment of sound economic priorities. To take a prominent example, we are providing assistance to the Liberian Central Planning Agency by financing a contract with a U.S. consulting firm. 

This does not mean to say that we are expecting in the near future to provide all assistance to Africa in support of comprehensive long-range plans. For many countries in Africa, a considerable period of time must pass before they can collect the data needed, train the economists, statisticians, and administrators required and think through their priorities. 

In some cases, the nature and extent of the domestic resources on which they must rely have never been adequately explored. The educational base may be too narrow as yet to provide adequate numbers of skilled technicians for programs embracing all kinds of economic activity. But even in these countries, the institutional foundations can be laid, and the assistance we furnish may be a key to important advances. The emphasis in these countries may be on project development, or on plans that concentrate on certain high priority sectors of the economy. This question of the varying stages of development found in Africa is one to which I would like to return. 

Fourth, we are actually moving ahead in Africa on advance commitments for loans, subject to appropriations, to African countries that have reached the stage where our encouragement to proceed on a comprehensive development program is warranted.

We have reviewed the development plans for three countries in Africa- Nigeria, Tanganyika, and Tunisia-and have found that they reflect both the high competence of the African leadership and the determination of these governments to make systematic efforts to improve the lot of their peoples. 

In all three plans, provision is made for stimulating and helping private enterprise. Priorities have been set up based not on the desire for showy prestige projects but on conscientious efforts to appraise economic needs. Responsible tax measures have been incorporated as integral parts of the plans. With these important assurances that our aid can be effective, we have made commitments to support the development plans of Nigeria and Tanganyika, and discussions with Tunisia toward the same end are well advanced. To

Fifth, the program for Africa is part of a cooperative effort by the free world as a whole. European aid expenditures in Africa are far greater than our own, and European technicians and teachers are numbered in the thousands. In fiscal year 1963, French aid to Africa, exclusive of Algeria, is expected to exceed $300 million, and United Kingdom aid will probably be more than $100 million. gether, these two countries will provide perhaps $450 million, and it is anticipated that their assistance will be matched by a similar amount from the Common Market, West Germany, and a number of other developed countries. When aid from international financial institutions and the United Nations is added, the total from other free world sources should again exceed $1 billion, as it will this year.

It is vital that this free world assistance be maintained and that the effort be thoroughly coordinated. We have accordingly had increasingly frequent and detailed bilateral consultations with the other major aid donors this past year, and we are arranging for still more intensive consultations in fiscal year 1963. 

In addition, procedures for continuous coordination have now been established through the Development Assistance Committee of the Organization for Eco nomic Cooperation and Development. 

It is occasionally suggested that, in view of the amount of aid going into Africa, U.S. assistance can be sharply limited or even withdrawn. These are several reasons why this would be tragically shortsighted. 

Despite the assistance provided from many sources, the volume still falls far short of meeting the tremendous needs of Africa. A few examples will serve to show how far Africa lags behind the rest of the world. 

While no reliable figures are available on the number of children of primary school age who are enrolled in school, recent estimates suggest that the average for the continent is perhaps 35 percent or less. Of those fortunate enough to get a primary education, only a small number-15 percent or more in a few countries, less than 5 percent in most-are able to enter secondary school. 

In agriculture, the Managing Director of the United Nations Special Fund has estimated that "productivity of Asian agriculture is approximately 10 percent of that of North American agriculture; African, 4 percent."

In terms of agricultural skills and the requirement for the kind of basic facilities for education and training long since available throughout Europe and North America, therefore, the gap is broad indeed. 

Perhaps even more serious is the fact that the gap between the standard of living in Africa and that in the developed West is not decreasing but is probably growing wider. Per capita income in many parts of Africa appears to be growing hardly at all, and in only a few instances do the estimates of growth exceed 3 percent. Almost certainly the average is somewhat less. In countries of the developed world increases of 3 percent have in recent years been almost the minimum, while in much of Europe the rate of growth is double that or more. The African is thus confronted with a world in which his relative position is declining rather than improving. 

There are also important political reasons for the United States to add its assistance to that of Europe. I cannot stress too strongly the significance to the Africans of avoiding economic dependence on the former colonial power. 

Moderate political leaders are open to severe attack from extremist elements within their countries unless they can demonstrate that they have developed new contacts in the world, as befits an independent nation, and that they are no longer solely dependent on the metropole for aid. By providing visible evidence of their change in status to one of sovereign equality, help from the United States makes it easier for the African nations to maintain the close ties with Europe that are in the interest of all of us. 

WHERE AID WILL GO 

The United States has security and political interests in Africa which justify assistance quite aside from the economic benefits that it will produce. Where there are special strategic interests or are military installations whose effectiveness must be maintained for the benefit of the free world, the nature of our assistance may necessarily be influenced by that fact. 

There may be a few cases where the need for providing assistance may be clear but the standard economic development criteria are not appropriate.
