While the amount of assistance devoted to these particular ends has been decreased it must be considered separately and is carried under the "supporting assistance" category.

The bulk of the aid to Africa is in the form of development assistance, most of which in fiscal year 1963 is expected to take the form of long-term loans repayable in dollars, but also including substantial grant aid. 

In determining how much should be spent and what kind of assistance should be provided, three rough groupings of countries have been distinguished. Mr. 

Hutchinson will discuss the economic aspects of the allocations proposed. I would like to touch briefly on certain of the political characteristics of these three groupings of countries. 

The first category, comprising those nations judged to have most of the requisites for a comprehensive development effort, must first of all be composed of countries which are reasonably well endowed with certain basic human or natural resources and which have both the ability and the desire to make good use of these resources. 

What I would like to stress here is that they must also, in our view, have governments dedicated to the maintenance of human freedom and motivated by a determination to improve the welfare of their peoples. Further, we feel that the prospects for their long-term political stability must be reasonably good. 

It is incumbent upon me to say quite frankly, however, that we must be prepared to take some risk. Africa is a continent in transition, and there are deep cultural, religious, tribal, and racial feelings-some long repressed-that are only now being released. It is impossible to be certain that the moderate and responsible governments of today will be succeeded tomorrow by governments equally capable. 

But if we wait for absolute certainty, we will deprive ourselves of a powerful instrument with which we can help shape a better Africa, for, given a stability reasonably well based, the assurances of long-term support that we can give will make that stability more durable and will give courage to responsible and foresighted leaders. 

If it is sometimes said that despair begets despair, it is no less true that hope begets hope. A commitment from us to provide help for sound economic activities over the years will not only strengthen the forces of freedom in the countries immediately concerned but it will give other nations something to strive for.

Nigeria and Tanganyika today and Tunisia tomorrow will hopefully be joined by others sometime in the future in the group of nations for which this kind of partnership can be planned. It will take time; few nations in Africa can be ready until after years of preparatory labor. But as they are ready, we of the free world must also be ready to join with them in what may become the most meaningful and fruitful relationship of the decade of development. 

In the second category of countries, which is possibly the largest group in Africa, neither the material resources nor the trained manpower may as yet be adequate to support a sustained, comprehensive development effort. By concentrating our efforts on certain high priority needs which are also receiving the attention of the Government concerned, we hope to make a significant contribu tion to their economic and social betterment. In some cases, obstacles to economic growth will be removed and the countries will hopefully reach a point where a major, long-range effort can be mounted to generate self-sustaining growth.

The economic resources that we will provide are badly needed. But hardly less important are the moral resources that the fact of free world participation brings.

A few moments ago I spoke of the enormous gap between the income of the average African and that of the average man in the more developed parts of the world. None of us should forget that even the most able and conscientious 

African leader, faced by this seemingly unbridgeable gulf, has moments of deep and bitter discouragement. Indeed, the more conscientious he is the more profoundly dedicated he is to improving the welfare of his people-the more often and keenly he is likely to feel the frustration of hopes disappointed. 

For the leaders who conclude that progress through the use of free institutions is hopelessly slow, there are always counsels of extremism near at hand, both homegrown and imported from Moscow and Peiping. 

Once well down the path of quick and easy solutions-the expropriation of foreign business, the expulsion of needed non-African technicians from the West, the adoption of discriminatory tax laws-the direction is hard to reverse. Almost inevitably there is a flight of capital. Foreign investment virtually ceases, and the economic situation worsens. In desperation new steps are taken to raise funds by any means available, while doubts about Communist offers to take over key sectors of the economy are swallowed. The sequence of events is only too clear.

No African country has as yet been lost to the Communist conspiracy. A very healthy and well-founded suspicion of any efforts, however disguised, to wrest away their new-found independence has so far prevented any African nation from taking the final, irrevocable step. But dangerous inroads have been made in more than one nation, and we cannot afford either the luxury of complacency or the ease of indifference. 

The third category of nations comprises those which appear, on the basis of what is now known, to be furthest from the point of being able to develop selfsustaining growth. Where trading or producing areas are small or resources extremely scanty, these factors must certainly be taken into account in determining what kind of a program we should have. In most cases, the absence of trained manpower and basic infrastructure will limit absorptive capacity. 

But I am constrained to say that, while our programs must take these factors into account and must sometimes be experimental in nature, we cannot afford to neglect those nations that need help the most. It would make a mockery of the decade of development to limit our assistance to the relatively favored nations, even though our expenditures there may have more immediate and more readily measurable results. The danger that the poorest countries of all will be left behind is a real one, with serious political implications for the future. 

To some extent, meeting this last and most difficult problem will be a test of the consistency of purpose and wisdom of the developed nations of the world ourselves included. It is a matter not of mobilizing our efforts to drive toward a goal in sight, but of patient efforts, modest in scope, over a period of time whose length we cannot yet estimate. 

There is one respect, however, in which the African nations themselves are moving toward a rational solution of the problem. They are working hard at developing increasingly close economic ties, including breaking down customs barriers, harmonizing development plans, planning transportation, communications, and even electric power networks on a regional rather than purely a national basis, making common use of educational institutions and research facilities, and arranging for the free movement of both capital and manpower.

Efforts of this kind represent the only hope for a real solution to the problem of limited producing and trading areas the only way in which resources can be used with maximum efficiency and the benefits of industrial and agricultural specialization can be significantly increased. 

It is not an easy road, but the African nations are devoting a great deal of time and attention to working out the multitude of problems involved. We must give them every reasonable support. 

President Kennedy has pointed out in his message to the Congress that we are still in the first months of a decade's sustained effort, and that it would be premature to make now any claims of dramatic results. We certainly would make no special claims with respect to Africa. But we can report to you that a firm foundation is being laid, and that there has already been a not inconsiderable measure of concrete accomplishment. On that foundation we can help build in Africa a community of free, stable, and self-reliant nations, capable of making their own contribution to the peace and freedom of the world. proposals before you are well designed to perform that task. (The statement of Mr. Hutchinson is as follows:) The Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am grateful for this opportunity to appear before you for the first time in support of the programs of economic assistance proposed for Africa and Europe in fiscal year 1963 and to discuss the reasoning underlying the recommendations. 

REORGANIZATION AND REORIENTATION 

The proposed AID program for fiscal year 1963 must be reviewed against the background of the situation which has existed and now exists in the AID and of the situation which exists and is projected in the countries within which programs are to be carried on. 

Insofar as the situation within AID is concerned, fiscal year 1962 to date has been a period of reexamination, reappraisal, reorientation, reorganization, and redirection of the aid program. 

This process has involved, insofar as the Africa-Europe region is concerned, first, review of country programs with changes in emphases and approach, and second, review of organization structures and operating procedures with consequent change in organization, methods, and personnel. In the about 32½ months during which I have been responsible for administration of the program for 

Africa and Europe: (1) A new organization structure, related to the consolidation into AID of the major elements of the assistance program has been devised and put into effect in Washington. The essential characteristic of the new organization is to fix in one place responsibility for the various aspects of a country program. (2) Certain key personnel have been recruited to staff the revised organization. (3) A review of all country programs has been conducted which has resulted in termination of some projects, initiation of others, and changes in program content. (4) New policies have been adopted relating to the approach to financing local costs of project activities and the financing of capital projects in the social development field on a loan basis. These problems will be discussed later in connection with the presentation of the 1963 program requirements. (5) A decision has been made to develop organization patterns for AID field missions which will vary in accordance with the type of program to be carried This will also be discussed in connection with presentation of the 1963 program requirements. on. (6) A number of new mission directors, deputy mission directors, and other key field personnel are being recruited and are expected to begin a period of training in the next few weeks. (7) Other key personnel and I have spent just under a month in the field to obtain a firsthand knowledge of programs in certain countries and to meet key AID and host-country personnel. 

This process, while well advanced, is not completed and must continue for some time and may produce some changes in the program now before you. It has inevitably brought with it some delays in program implementation. However, the decision to go through such a process even though it does result in a slowing down of program implementation has been a conscious one and seems to us to be clearly required for responsible administration.

STATUS OF DEVELOPMENT 

With respect to Europe, the situation is one in which economic growth and progress has made possible the attainment of virtually all the objectives to which use of economic assistance by AID is appropriate. 

Insofar as the situation in Africa is concerned, Africa is a mosaic with infinitely varied political traditions and structures and wide diversity in economic and social conditions. 

In terms of 1960 per capita GNP, for example, Somali Republic and Ethiopia at $42 and $44, respectively, contrast sharply with Ghana at $223 and Senegal at $177. Literacy ranges from 4-5 percent in Ethiopia and Sudan to 25 percent in Ghana. Infant mortality rates have been estimated in ranges from 80 per thousand in Nigeria to 150 per thousand in other areas of Africa, compared with 26 in the United States. 

Although a few countries earn significant foreign exchange from their exports, others are highly dependent on external aid to meet minimal import require ments. Population densities vary widely with concomitant variations in pressures on land use. Ruanda-Urundi is among the highest with 240 persons per square mile, contrasting with Mauritania with 2 persons per square mile. 

Mineral resources are abundant in such areas as the Congo, Ghana, and Liberia, while many African countries have virtually no known assets of this kind.

There are also wide divergencies in the effectiveness of governmental organization and leadership on which the development process is so dependent. Such countries as Tunisia, Nigeria, Ghana, and Senegal have a nucleus of well-trained, experienced leaders, while others have almost none. In Chad, despite independence, the Government is managed and operated almost entirely by French nationals.

Many countries are heavily dependent on the former metropoles for support of their operating and capital budgets while others obtain little or no support for their operating budgets and make substantial amounts available for their capital and developmental budget. 

Notwithstanding this diversity certain similarities are discernible and some generalities are possible. The most obvious of these is that practically all 

African countries are dominated by an overwhelming desire for independence. 

First there is the drive for political independence. Some 19 countries have attained such independence since April 1960. Several other territories are expected to obtain independence before the close of fiscal year 1963. The current is running strongly in that direction in still other areas. 

Coupled with this desire for political independence is an extremely strong insistence on economic independence. This manifests itself in part in the concentration on internal economic development and in the preoccupation with efforts to avoid exclusive dependence on any one country or bloc for trade and economic assistance. 

Part and parcel of this struggle for independence is the desire to develop cultures and social, political, and economic forms and philosophies of their own without domination by Eastern or Western influences and the impelling desire to gain the fruits of economic growth and development. 

In short, the fundamental long-range process upon which African countries are beginning is that of nation building. This is a process which is not without its complexities and problems, as is evidenced by our own history and that of other countries. 

In Africa the process is beset with special problems. There are a number of major impediments which are common to most of the countries of Africa. Tribal ties are still strong and the integration of various tribal units with varying customs, languages, and loyalties into cohesive governmental entities with common goals and purposes will not be easy. 

Present-day leaders are often inexperienced. Populations are not educated or trained. Domestic financial resources are limited. Natural resources have not been surveyed or exploited. Transportation, communication, and power facilities are inadequate. The African countries lack organizations and institutions to promote industry and trade and there is an overdependence on a few primary exports. 

All these problems must be addressed if economic and social development is to be fostered and if the process of nation building is to be successful. 

As this process goes forward considerable patience will be required. It must be remembered that most African governments do not presently have the same

al 

kinds of democracy that are traditional in the United States, although many have developed systems of checks and balances and have provided for a degree of popular participation. 

It also must be recognized that the African peoples are preoccupied with their own problems and are not as aware of or concerned about the conflict between the free world and the Communist bloc as we might wish. Nor do they have a full understanding of the nature of the issues involved. 

We cannot expect these nations to be well versed in the intricacies of world politics and international relationships or to side with the United States on each international issue with which this Nation is concerned. The erratic behavior of some African countries is likely to continue for some time. Short-term political developments or reverses should not becloud the basic objective of the United States to assure the true independence of the African countries. 

In spite of the complexity and staggering size of the problem and the certain frustrations which lie along the way, there are encouraging aspects of the situation. Considering that most African nations have gained their independence since 1960, the strides made toward developing workable government institutions, acceptable to the proud and nationalist-minded African people, have been striking. The generally responsible efforts toward the maintenance of economic stability, while planning for national development, have been heartening. While further changes in leadership and in political institutions are likely, both leaders and institutions are showing a greater durability than had been generally predicted. 

SELF-HELP EFFORTS 

The independent African governments, of course, bear the primary responsibility for achieving their long-term goals. They must provide the framework, the administration, the incentives, the security, and a very substantial part of the resources necessary for a broad attack on the numerous impediments to development. 

Although they have had only a limited opportunity to establish a performance record in these matters, forward motion is evident and there have been encouraging signs of interest in the principles of self-help and responsible governmental planning. Leaders are acquiring a greater recognition of the problems involved in development and are making serious attempts to address them. Increased emphasis is being given to improving the standards of education and the development of trained manpower. Fortunately, because of its importance, relative stability in governmental operations exists in most African countries. 

A number of African countries have commenced to develop long-range plans for economic development. In many instances these plans are only preliminary attempts to introduce more rational and systematic methods into the development process.

We are encouraging these countries to improve both their plans and their implementing machinery. While existing African plans vary widely in scope and quality, at least three countries, Nigeria, Tunisia, and Tanganyika, have developed comprehensive long-term plans that appear to provide a sound framework for both domestic efforts and foreign assistance. 

So far in fiscal year 1962 assurances of long-term support were extended to Nigeria and Tanganyika after careful analysis of their development potential, planning and prospects for effective operation. Assistance is committed at $225 million in support of Nigeria's 6-year plan and at $10 million for Tanganyika's 3-year plan. The Tunisian plan is currently in an advanced stage of review. 

Important steps are also being taken in the field of self-help measures. 

Nigeria, for example, is planning to take measures necessary to finance all of the recurrent expenses and 50 percent of the capital costs of its new development plan. Budget expenses are being cut through reduced salaries, allowances, and leave periods for senior government officials. Steps to reduce costs and increase productivity in the important but high cost construction industry are under active consideration. 

Widespread reforms have been made in educational practices which were unsuited to Nigeria's development needs, including the establishment of a landgrant university, comprehensive high schools, and a system of technical training beginning in the primary grades. 

Tunisia has demonstrated its imagination and administrative ability by vigorously attacking its chronic problem of unemployment and underemployment through a labor-intensive development program. Supported in part with grants

of surplus U.S. wheat used for wage and other payments, the program has put to work over 170,000 unemployed on hundreds of projects, such as land clearance, reforestation, terracing, and road construction. 

Tunisia and the AID are now cooperating on plans to integrate this program fully into Tunisia's new national development plan. As another measure, Tunisia hopes to finance half of its total investment through domestic savings. 

Liberia, determined to modernize its economy, has undertaken a number of self-help steps, including an economic survey, the country's first census, progress toward a central planning process, preparation of new banking legislation, and preliminary long-range programs in education and rural development. 

Examples of self-help in other countries include the reduction of government salaries in Dahomey, stepped-up taxes in Cameroon, Congo Republic, Gabon, Ghana, Guinea, Mali, Niger, and Togo; savings measures in Ghana, Ivory Coast, and Malagasy; and a sizable internal bond flotation in Niger. 

In this connection, as mentioned earlier, I returned just 2 weeks ago from a trip which took me to selected countries in west Africa, including Nigeria and Liberia, where it is proposed that the United States make available significant assistance. I spent some time also in Niger and Dahomey, two former territories of French West Africa where assistance will also be provided by the 

United States.

In addition, I arranged to meet with representatives of all U.S. AID missions in Africa to discuss the programs in the countries to which they are accredited. 

While the trip confirmed for me that the problems associated with African development are formidable, I returned more optimistic concerning the prospects for progress toward economic development in many countries. That African nations are looking to the United States and other developed nations for assistance was apparent. I was encouraged, however, by the evidence that most of these nations are determined to take the measures necessary for the effective mobilization and optimum use of their own resources. 

This, then, is the environment within which the program is being implemented in fiscal year 1962 and is being planned for implementation during fiscal year 1963.

NEW PROGRAM EMPHASIS 

The policy changes to which reference was made earlier have affected the nature of the programs carried on in fiscal year 1962 and of those proposed to be carried on during 1963. First to be mentioned is the policy of concentration of efforts and resources as was discussed last year in connection with presentation of the new Act for International Development.

Pursuant to this policy certain marginal activities were ended in 1962 and additional activities will be terminated in fiscal year 1963. In Ethiopia, for example, nine projects have been terminated this year and it is anticipated that arrangements will be made with the Ethiopian Government to phase out additional projects in fiscal year 1963. An additional example is the termination of a number of projects in Libya. 

The second policy and procedural change to be mentioned affects the composition of the programs being financed. In the past some commodity import programs have been financed on the grounds that there was a need to mobilize local resources for development activities by using local currencies obtained from the sale of the commodities imported with aid funds. Under this practice the nature, purpose, and justification of aid became confused and obscure. 

A decision has now been made to require a clear advance finding as to the nature of the country's need for assistance. If its needs are for assistance in importing commodities, assistance will be provided in the form of commodities. 

If the need is for the financing of particular projects or activities, including a part of the local costs of the project or activity, the assistance will be provided in the form of dollar financing (or local currencies if available). 

It is not planned to provide financing of commodities for this generalized purpose of generating local currencies. This change will provide for more direct identification of the real purpose of the assistance, and an improved control over the use of the funds. 

Another policy change deserving of mention relates to the form of financing to be provided. Previously capital projects were financed by the Development 

Loan Fund on a loan basis while at the same time ICA was financing some capital projects with grants. 

Under the policy now in effect it will be the general practice to finance substantial capital projects, including projects in the educational and health fields,

on a long-term loan basis. Exceptions to this policy will be made for projects already underway on a grant basis, and for relatively small projects primarily related to technical assistance activities. 

APPROACH TO ALLOCATION OF DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

The needs in Africa for outside developmental assistance are very great. 

Balancing this somewhat is the fact that at this stage of its development Africa's ability to assimilate effectively large amounts of assistance is limited. 

These factors, together with the wide variety of conditions and circumstances found in Africa, suggest that a major portion of U.S. assistance available for 

Africa must be concentrated in those countries and in those projects which offer the most promise for furthering long-term development. 

On the other hand, the needs and aspirations of the countries are such that we must be in a position to respond constructively to requests for assistance in connection with activities which offer hope for economic growth or which make a specific contribution to increased production. 

In determining the proposed allocation for development loans and grants within Africa for the fiscal year 1962 and fiscal year 1963 programs, the following factors were considered: (1) The need for external assistance; (2) The availability, current and prospective, of country resources, both human and material; (3) The organization and leadership of the government, to plan adequately for economic and social development and to insure that the self-help and other measures essential to successful program implementation are taken; (4) The magnitude and type of resources being made available from other free world donors, including international organizations; and (5) The ability of the United States to provide the type of technical assistance and the administrative supervision necessary to insure effective use of aid funds. 

On the basis of these considerations the nations of Africa fall into three categories for the purpose of determining the allocation of developmental assistance to be made available from the United States. 

Although it is not always a simple matter to determine into which category a country should be placed, the decision is influenced primarily by an assessment of the relative ability of a country to use resources effectively. 

When viewed in terms of these considerations the countries of Africa fall into three general categories or groups, the composition of which is determined primarily by the relative abilities of the countries to use effectively both local and external resources to further sustained economic and social development. 

The first category includes nations which possess most of the prerequisites for development. They are relatively well endowed with either human or natural resources, or both. These countries either have or soon will develop both the willingness and the ability to take the measures necessary to mobilize those resources. 

Public administration is relatively well advanced with a staff of well-trained local officials or a strong nucleus thereof. The long-term prospects for political stability in these countries appear to be better than average and the governments appear to be sincerely concerned with the welfare and freedom of the people.

Countries in this grouping would warrant consideration for assurances for help involving a substantial contribution of U.S. assistance over a period of years to be directed toward those needs which the United States could best meet. 

Assurances of development assistance for sound programs or activities over a period of years by the United States, subject to satisfactory performance by the aid recipient, will enable the leaders of these countries to plan the best use of their own resources and other foreign assistance with confidence for the future.

In countries of the first grouping, U.S. assistance may be the catalyst for obtaining additional assistance from Western sources, the United Nations, and other international institutions, and private groups and foundations. 

In countries falling into this category, AID will have full-fledged country missions and will use all or most of the tools available to it for assisting in the development process.

The second, and possibly the largest, category of countries includes nations possessing some prerequisites for development, although they might be seriously

lacking in others. Material resources may be limited; trained manpower may exist but in inadequate numbers, leadership may not be adequate; planning may be deficient; the country may be dependent to a large degree upon subsidized trade in a few commodities with former metropoles. 

Although some long-term development prospects may exist, U.S. assurances of substantial financial assistance over an extended period of time would be considered premature for countries in this category. In a number of these countries U.S. aid programs have been in existence in the past. 

In fiscal year 1962 and fiscal year 1963, we have attempted wherever possible to concentrate assistance to such countries in those sectors where the recipient country is itself making an effort and thus where additional U.S. financial and technical aid is most likely to make a significant contribution to economic growth and social advancement. Where inadequately trained manpower and a lack of basic economic facilities exist, U.S. assistance would be concentrated largely on the improvement of these essentials to growth. 

In this type of country, AID will have a smaller country mission the size and nature of which will be related to the type of activities to be carried out. 

There is a third group of countries and dependent territories whose prospects of becoming self-sustaining are remote. They may represent trading or producing areas insufficiently large or integrated enough to facilitate the development of self-sustaining economic growth. 

A number of these countries are receiving substantial budgetary and capital assistance from the former colonial powers and therefore may not require significant aid from other sources. 

The absence of trained manpower and extensive facilities such as roads, communications, and power may limit the absorptive capacity for external assistance. On the other hand, these countries want to be free to direct their own domestic affairs. 

The United States must support the aspirations of the leaders and peoples of these areas, providing an alternative to complete dependence on the former metropoles or in the Sino-Soviet bloc. 

It will be necessary to adopt a flexible approach in providing assistance to this third group of countries and territories. In general, of course, the amounts will be less than for countries in the other categories. We will wish to concentrate on those types of activities which assist these countries in developing the basic prerequisites or tools for economic growth now lacking. In many cases, programs must be experimental in nature, until more experience is gained. Because of their vast development needs, it should be possible to select projects or activities which require priority attention and which make a distinct contribution to social or economic growth. 

In other instances, it may be desirable to first conduct surveys to determine which activities best make such a contribution. Caution must be exercised, of course, as in the case of countries in other stages of development, to coordinate the various Western activities, to undertake activities for which the United States possesses special capabilities and to avoid implications of annual “aid levels."

The United States must also be careful to select activities which do not require increased budget-type support by other aid donors which they are unwilling to assume and to avoid creating a U.S. obligation to provide such support. 

For many of these countries it is difficult to recruit qualified U.S. technicians who have an adequate command of the foreign language required, and who are willing to accept the hardships involved-poor housing, inadequate medical facilities, et cetera.

It therefore will be necessary to select activities which to be successful do not require the provision of a heavy technician component or a large overhead of U.S. administrative personnel over an extended period of time. In a number of instances, activities in these areas may consist of specific and carefully chosen capital projects financed by development loans. 

Countries in the first group would be considered to have the greatest development potential and would be given highest priority and allocated greater U.S. resources over an extended period of time than those in the second and third groups. However, in some instances a country in a lower category might receive more U.S. assistance than a country in a higher category in a particular time period.

A loan or a grant for a large project, for example, might well result in a comparatively high aid level for a country in the year of approval, but this might

be offset by low levels in subsequent years because of the country's inability to absorb additional loans or grants effectively. 

It is not expected that AID missions will be established in each of the countries in this group. Where missions are not established personnel competent in 

AID matters will be placed on the Embassy staff. As occasion requires technical staff or contractors, they will be employed to carry out specific activities with a clear termination point.

AID PROGRAMS IN FISCAL YEAR 1962 AND FISCAL YEAR 1963 

The fiscal year 1963 AID program for Africa provides for an increase in economic assistance for Africa over the levels of fiscal year 1962 and fiscal year 1961. The increase is restricted to development-type assistance in both the grant and loan categories. Supporting assistance continues to decline. 

Development loans are expected to total from $200 to $270 million in fiscal year 1963.

This compares to $42 million approved to date in fiscal year 1962 and $53.3 million for fiscal year 1961. The total for fiscal year 1962 may reach about $150 million. 

As you know it is difficult to forecast the precise amount of loans which can be implemented in a particular time period until individual project applications are fully examined and negotiated. 

Development grant assistance of approximately $118 million is proposed for fiscal year 1963 compared to estimated fiscal year 1962 obligations of about $97 million and a fiscal year 1961 program of $69.7 million. This somewhat enlarged program reflects the African nations' improving capacities to use aid effectively, as well as the fact that the need for this form of assistance is greater in Africa than any other world region. 

The program will concentrate on the most urgent requirements of the less developed countries—improved public administration, expansion of the educational base, trained manpower, and agricultural diversification. Not only are advances in these areas crucial to political stability, but they are also necessary preconditions for a successful development effort. 

Since in many of these countries assistance programs were not initiated until fiscal year 1961, a greater flexibility is required here than in many other areas; and we must be prepared to expand them as additional requirements are accurately identified and implementation capacity is augmented. 

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

Supporting assistance in the relatively limited amount of $32.5 million is planned for fiscal year 1963. This sum is required for the few cases in Africa where specific U.S. strategic interests must be taken into account, or where there is a clearly identifiable need for aid but the criteria for development-type assistance cannot be met. The level of supporting assistance has decreased markedly from fiscal year 1962 and fiscal year 1961, when they amounted to $61 million and $82 million, respectively. 

CONTINGENCIES 

Uncertainties are prevalent in Africa-emergencies may turn out to be the rule rather than the exception. The course of future events in Africa is probably more difficult to predict than in other areas of the world. The urgency of the needs is clear. However, in spite of the advance planning that has taken place, it is extremely difficult to forecast the magnitude and timing of the assistance requirements. So much is dependent upon developing political situations in which the United States is not a direct participant. It is expected, therefore, that a number of significant requirements which cannot now be anticipated or measured or planned may rapidly materialize during fiscal year 1963 and will have to be met from contingency appropriations. 

PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

We have continued to promote private ownership and investment wherever possible through the AID programs in Africa. AID-sponsored industrial development centers are being established in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Nigeria, and Sudan, and are being considered for additional countries in the future. 81496-62-pt. 4- -2

Development banks to benefit small businesses and farmers have been supported with either loans or technical assistance in Ethiopia, Sudan, Tunisia, the Ivory Coast, Niger, Sierra Leone, Uganda, Somalia, Dahomey, and Liberia. 

Support to banks of this type is planned for additional countries in fiscal year 

Industrial development study tours in the United States designed to expose African economists and other professionals to development techniques as practiced in free societies have been conducted under the auspices of the AID's regional program for Africa, and more of these are planned for fiscal year 1963. 

The development loan program is also expected to play an increasingly important role in the continuing efforts to encourage increases in U.S. trade and U.S. private investment in the African countries. In many of the countries of Africa, markets for American materials and equipment have not been developed. It is hoped that the participation of U.S. private enterprise in Africa can be mobilized through the wider use of investment guarantee media and the investment survey program. 

OTHER U.S. ASSISTANCE 

Other tools for development which are available to the United States in its efforts to assist the African nations include the food-for-peace program and the 

Peace Corps.

As regards the food-for-peace program, fiscal year 1962 was marked by an expansion over previous years in the number of Public Law 480, titles I and II agreements concluded with African countries. While additional Public Law 480 agreements are anticipated during fiscal year 1963, there is a definite limitation on the use of this type of assistance in Africa where many countries are exporters of the food commodities which are surplus in the United States. 

Part of the local currency proceeds generated from the local sales of the U.S. surplus agricultural commodities provided under title I agreements will be used to defray local costs of development projects supported by the AID program. 

I have already described how grants of commodities under title II of the Public Law 480 for use in connection with work relief projects is an important element in Tunisia's development program. Morocco also is carrying out a large program of this nature. Serious unemployment situations in those countries are thereby being alleviated. 

Similar work relief programs were initiated in Dahomey and Ethiopia in fiscal year 1962 and are planned for additional countries in fiscal year 1963. 

Donations of foodstuffs through U.S. nonprofit voluntary agencies and intergovernmental organizations under title III of Public Law 480 are contributing to U.S. objectives in Africa. 

The Peace Corps is currently carrying out programs in four African countries and plans to initiate activity in 10 additional countries during fiscal year 1963. 

In several instances the programs support or complement specific projects being implemented by the Agency for International Development. 

OTHER OUTSIDE ASSISTANCE GREATLY EXCEEDS U.S. ASSISTANCE 

Aid from European and international sources is large and on the increase. 

The rate of annual economic aid obligations to all African countries from other free world sources has risen from about $900 million in 1959 to nearly $1.5 billion in fiscal year 1962. 

If aid to Algeria and other African countries not currently receiving U.S. assistance is excluded, other free world aid is estimated at over $1 billionfar more than expected U.S. aid. 

France remains the largest contributor, with annual obligations, mostly grants, of over $300 million to former French states. The Common Market 

Development Fund is currently obligating grant project aid at the rate of about $200 million per year to associated African states. United Kingdom grants and loans to African countries average over $150 million annually, while West German obligations have risen to nearly that annual rate, bringing Western European aid, including that of Belgium and Italy to about $900 million this fiscal year. 

Japan, Israel, and several other countries also extend some aid to Africa. 

Attempts will continue to be made to maximize such free-world aid and to achieve increasing coordination toward longrun development purposes. 

The role in Africa of international lending agencies-International Bank for 

Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), International Development Authority 

(IDA), and International Finance Corporation (IFC)-is becoming increasingly

important. Commitments from these organizations to Africa have averaged about $100 million per year during 1960 and 1961. Export-Import (Ex-Im) 

Bank developmental lending activity in Africa (excluding the United Arab Republic and the Union of South Africa) has increased from $7 million in 1959 to nearly $53 million in 1961. It is anticipated that the Bank will continue to expand its lending operations in Africa. 

The role of the United Nations in African development has also been increasing. This organization, of course, is heavily involved in the Congo operation. United Nations Technical Assistance and Special Fund grants cover a variety of specialized fields and have expanded considerably in recent years. 

In 1960 such grants amounted to approximately $23 million in Africa. Steps are taken to ensure that these programs do not overlap U.S. assistance programs. 

REGIONAL COOPERATION 

During the colonial era, each territory's external relationships were primarily with the metropole and only incidentally with neighboring countries. 

The lack of adequate transportation and a common language is still a barrier to African trade and economic integration. Markets are uneconomically small. 

However, the need for regional cooperation in both political and economic fields is being increasingly understood, and African leaders are devoting much time and effort to developing more effective intra-African relationships. 

The United States has sought to encourage African regional and multicountry economic plans and activities by assisting the various organizations in some of their projects. A major undertaking in fiscal year 1962 was participation in a project sponsored by the CCTA (an organization of nations south of the Sahara), for the eradication of rinderpest in Cameroon, Niger, Chad, and the northern region of Nigeria.

Assistance was also provided on a bilateral basis for projects involving the pooling of resources by adjacent states for coordinated development activities such as the curbing of locust infestations, or which further the regional use of existing educational and other facilities. 

In the latter case, for example, grants extended to 5 African universities have permitted these otherwise underutilized institutions to extend some 680 scholarships, approximately half of which will go to students from other African countries where adequate facilities do not exist. Thus, the program promotes both regional interchange and more effective use of existing facilities. 

IN CONCLUSION 

The attainment of self-sustaining development, for most countries in Africa, lies well beyond our present decade. African leaders are almost certain to face a shortfall in meeting the public aspirations of which I spoke earlier. 

However, we believe that a reasonable basis for political stability nevertheless can be developed by establishing the foundations for economic and social growth, while at the same time providing a sizable measure of achievement to create a sense of direction and accomplishment. 

The program proposals for fiscal year 1963 are designed to provide Africa with the essential measures of U.S. support it needs to progress toward these goals.

Mr. WILLIAMS. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a great pleasure to be with you again to testify in support of economic assistance. The U.S. aid assistance is based on two reasons, with which I am sure you are familiar: First of all, it is a genuine expression of the moral will of the United States to help other people who need assistance, and second, U.S. security is enhanced as we are able to increase stability throughout the world. We can increase stability through the program of assistance. 

As we look at Africa last year, we find four great forces are still in active being. First of all, there is a desire for freedom and independence. An expression of this last year was that Tanganyika and 

Sierra Leone came into existence. 

Recently, you have noted that Algeria has ended its seventh year of strife with an accord with the French that would seem promising for future cooperation.

Tanganyika came into independence with high hopes of a good interracial society. Some felt there was perhaps a slight dimming of these hopes when Nyerere went back to his people for support, but our people still think Nyerere has a chance for success. 

Uganda will be coming into independence this fall. The dates for 

Kenya and Zanzibar are being discussed in London at this stage. 

In the Rhodesias, Nyasaland now has black African self-government. Northern Rhodesia has a constitution under which elections are going to be held, and this looks as though it is going to be fairly successful and satisfactory to the people concerned. In Southern 

Rhodesia there seems to be more trouble in connection with their constitution and the elections that are coming up. Elsewhere the progress toward freedom and independence is somewhat slower. 

The second great motivating force in African life, I would say, is a desire for dignity and recognition as equal men and women and in equal nationhood. I think that the recognition of Tanganyika and 

Sierra Leone is a further step along to this direction. 

Of course, we in the United States have the problem of incidents with respect to African ambassadors. But I think that we are moving in the right direction and hopefully will be able to get the record straight in this regard.

A third very interesting force is pan-Africanism and regionalism. 

In its widest expression, pan-Africanism is perhaps rather ephemeral, but there are some hard operating associations being constructed. 

I think these are important because sometimes Americans wonder if there aren't too many small nations in Africa for them to be viable. 

I think this tendency toward association is a step in the direction of alleviating that problem. 

In this connnection, I would like to remark, first of all, on the economic conference in Addis. Here we have an organized secretariat which has studies underway, including one on transportation, and they are talking about a development bank. 

Second, I think it is interesting to look at what is going on in the Monrovia group. This includes both French- and English-speaking areas. They are starting a secretariat at Lagos. There seems to be an opportunity for fruitful cooperation. 

I would like to look with you for a moment at the Brazzaville group, which is perhaps best known for the OAMCE. Twelve countries of French expression are really working together. They have a fully active secretariat set up at Yaounde. They have a customs union in contemplation with an expert committee working on it. They are actually operating an airline, Air Afrique. They are moving toward monetary accords, and, as of the moment, they are contributing for the 11 or 12 countries only 3 different currencies which are highly interchangeable.

Inside the Brazzaville group there are such associations as the former French Equatorial Africa and Cameroon, which do actually have a customs union. The Brazzaville group has some political association. They tend to vote together in the United Nations and caucus together there.

Another group that we hear about is the Casablanca powers, which includes some of the Arab countries, and Guinea, Ghana, and Mali. 

[Security deletion.]

It is quite likely as Algeria assumes its free powers that there will be some sort of an association of Algeria, Tunisia, and Morocco. 

[Security deletion.] 

In the European Common Market there has been a tendency to try and use common approaches to some of the African problems, and there has been an African response. For example, in the field of education, when they set up a commercial college, instead of setting up one in a number of countries they have set up one in Gabon, which will serve most of the French-speaking countries in the area. In the same way they have set up in Brazzaville a secondary teachers' training college to serve several of them. 

In the English areas, Sierra Leone has decided not to set up certain training facilities but to use Nigeria's, and Nigeria is willing. 

In British East Africa, the School of Agriculture was put in Uganda to serve the entire area. Similarly, in Tanganyika a law school was set up. There seems to be a willingness in Africa generally to set up regional arrangements for economic improvement in particular. 

The fourth point that I would like to speak to comes directly to our interest in AID, and that is the tremendous desire for a better standard of living on the part of the Africans. 

I think Nyerere stated the situation very well when he said, and I quote:

Unless I can meet at least some of these aspirations my support will wane, and my head will roll just as surely as the tickbird follows the rhino.

In other words, one of the important political facts of life in Africa today is that each government is under great compulsion to raise the standard of living of its people. 

More and more this problem of nation building assumes importance for these people. I think these countries recognize they can't rely exclusively on foreign aid. For example, Nigeria's first multiyear plan was 80 percent local supported. Tunisia, as you know, has been a great country for self-help. It has used the food-for-peace program, for example, in order to alleviate its unemployment and to build. much needed public works. 

I think, however, that in the long run a continent where the average per capita income is $130 is going to need foreign assistance. 

As I am sure, Mr. Hutchinson will point out, we certainly look to private enterprise to play its part, and outside assistance from the Europeans will play a larger part than ours. 

But nonetheless, a need for aid persists. I think we have a number of standards to show the need here. First of all, perhaps only 35 percent of school-age children are in school. It is said that African agriculture is only 4 percent as productive as that in the United States. 

Infant mortality runs from 80 to 150 per thousand; in the United 

States it is only 26. With the people only 15 percent literate, the need, of course, can be shown to be tremendous. 

I think before taking a look at the character of our aid, I would like to say a word about the Communists. During the last two party congresses, they have indicated an interest in penetrating into Africa. If you look at the number of people they have there, they certainly are going about-lumping all of the Communist groups together, roughly, they have over 600 diplomats and something over 2,000 tech-

nicians. So the Communist presence is over 2,600. This figure is low rather than high. [Security deletion.] 

The Soviet opening of credit started very slowly with only about $3 million in 1959. In 1960, it went up to $206 million, 1961 only $234 million, and so far this year, $171 million, for a grand total of $614 million.

All of this hasn't been drawn down, but it does indicate the vigor with which the Soviets are attacking this problem. 

I think the United States, in its program, should endeavor to help African leadership, and we should endeavor to reach the people where they are. I think that this and other committees of the Congress have often indicated their feeling that our program should be practical so as really to help the people. 

I have had a rough summary made of the grants and special assistance given over the last couple of years. I find about a third of the sums we have given goes to education. About a fifth goes to agriculture, part of which is agriculture education. 

So that between the two, about half of our effort is in the field of education going directly to the people. About 8 percent goes to public administration, and 7 percent goes to roads. 

We have loan programs tied in with long-range planning and longrange commitments. I won't go into the details as I am sure that Mr. 

Hutchinson will.

With that, I will conclude my part of the testimony, saying that I think that Mr. Hutchinson has brought a great deal of drive and understanding to this problem of aid which are going to help us have an even better program in the future. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. 

Mr. Hutchinson.

STATEMENT OF HON. EDMOND C. HUTCHINSON, ASSISTANT ADMIN- ISTRATOR, BUREAU OF AFRICA AND EUROPE, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. HUTCHINSON. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I will summarize my statement also. 

I am grateful for the opportunity to appear before you for the first time in support of the program for Europe and Africa in fiscal year 1963. This program which we are proposing has to be evaluated in the light of the situation as it presently exists in the AID agency, and of course the situation that exists in the countries in which we are proposing to carry on the programs. 

As you know, fiscal year 1962 has been a period of considerable ferment in the entire AID program and particularly within the agency itself. It really has been a period of reorganization, reappraisal, reexamination, and redirection. This process, at least insofar as the 

Africa region is concerned, has had a number of effects, one being a substantive change in our emphasis and approach to a number of programs. Other effects have been on our organization and operating procedures.

I have been in the position which I now hold for about 312 months. 

During that period of time we have done a number of things. First, a new organization structure has been devised and put into effect.

The fundamental principle on which this structure is based is that authority for all the activities being carried out in a particular country are vested in one place within the organization. 

We have recruited certain key personnel to staff this revised organization, and are continuing to recruit for a few more of the key positions. 

We have conducted a review of all the country programs which have been carried on in the past, and those which are proposed for fiscal year 1963. This has resulted in the dropping of some programs, initiation of a few new ones, and a change in program content in a few others. the We have also adopted a few new policies, changes in approach as to the sort of program to be carried on, which I will mention in a few moments. 

We have made a decision to depart from a fixed organization pattern for the missions operating in the field and intend to relate the organization pattern more specifically and directly to the nature of the program being carried on in particular countries. I will also mention that somewhat later. 

We have recruited new mission directors and deputy mission directors for a number of posts, and they will undergo a period of training in a few weeks. 

Lastly, key members of my staff and I have spent a month in the field, coming back about 2 weeks ago. This gave us an opportunity to see some of the situations firsthand, to meet the key members of our own staff and of the host countries. 

This process is not complete and must continue. It has inevitably carried with it some slowing down in the program for fiscal year 1962. It seems to us, however, that this had to be, the decision was conscious, and it seemed to us that, even though this was the price we had to pay for this relook, responsible administration required it.

So far as the situation in Europe is concerned, we feel that basically the objectives which are appropriate for addressing with the AIĎ program have been accomplished. 

Insofar as Africa is concerned, as you know, the situation is characterized by a very great variety. Governor Williams has mentioned some of this. There are enormous variations in income, educational level, availability of resources, political background, all kinds of variations, which there is no point to dwell on in detail. 

It seems to us, however, that there are a few generalizations which are possible which affect the nature of the program which we intend to carry on. The first one, which Governor Williams has mentioned, is the desire for independence. The drive for political independence he has indicated with specific examples. This desire for independence also manifests itself, however, in the economic field. In particular, it manifests itself in the desire to be at least partially free from complete dependence on any particular bloc or any particular country for assistance. This has overtones of freedom and independence for the African countries and is very, very much to the forefront in their thinking. 

Another characteristic which is common is the overwhelming desire to gain the fruits of economic growth and development. This is

certainly common to all the countries. I suppose it would be fair to characterize the process which practically all the countries in Africa are going through as one of nation building, in all its aspects, politically, economically, and socially. 

We all know when we consider our own history and that of other countries, that this is a process which has its difficulties and frustrations. This is particularly the case in Africa. The great diversities even within the countries, the unrealistic nature of some of the boundaries, the strong tribal feelings within countries, limitations of resources, lack of national loyalties in certain cases, all make this process even more difficult in Africa than it is in most countries. 

So we would point out that as this process goes forward there are going to be many frustrations associated with it, that the Africans are going to try various experiments. They are going to experiment, I am sure, with forms of government that are not completely to our liking.

Their behavior in some ways is going to be erratic. They are not always going to be with us in the way we would like on questions of international policy. They are all preoccupied with their own domestic problems to a great extent. Those are much more important to them than many of the international issues. 

I am sure if we think back over our own history we can think of periods when this was true in our own country, perhaps not too far back in our history, as a matter of fact. 

In spite of all these difficulties, there are, it seems to us, many encouraging signs. Certainly I, and I think most observers, have been surprised, as a matter of fact, that the countries have been able to be as stable as they have, although most of them only became independent in 1960.

There has been a measure of governmental stability and of ability to address themselves to their problems in most countries that has been rather surprising. The way they have addressed themselves to the question of their development, with the recognition that there will have to be some priorities in the program, that they can't do everything at once, the desire to develop a rational plan, the development of certain self-help measures, all of these things are encouraging signs. 

This is one of the things that struck me on the trip that I mentioned just a moment ago. There is a clear recognition on the part of leaders in most of the countries which I visited that this is a long-term process, that they are going to have to address themselves to it in a businesslike way, that they are going to have to make sacrifices in order to accomplish it.

The way in which they are making some of the courageous political decisions that are necessary was most heartening to me. For example, in Nigeria the Prime Minister said to me:

In the development of our plan we were hard put to decide what our highest priorities should be. There was great pressure on us to put our resources into things such as hospitals and the ordinary type schools, to just increase primary education, general social overhead of this sort. 

He said:

As we thought of it, we decided we couldn't afford this kind of approach, that what we had to do was build up our own income and our ability to support this kind of program with our own resources. We put first priority on things

which are productive of increased income, agriculture, technical education, and industrial development. 

In a country which has just become newly independent and in which there are enormous demands for immediate social improvement, this strikes me as being an extremely courageous decision and a very encouraging sign. I could quote examples of this sort of thing throughout. But in the interest of saving time I will only mention a few.

For example, there have been reductions of government salaries in Dahomey, increased taxes in the Cameroon, Ghana, Mali, Niger, and Togo. Savings programs have been instituted in Ghana, the 

Ivory Coast and Malagasy, and a bond flotation is being undertaken in Niger.

All of these things then demonstrate the African countries are addressing themselves to their problems in a way that exceeds perhaps some of our expectations and does offer some real promise. 

Earlier, I referred to some policy changes we have made. I think we should mention those to show something of the nature of our stewardship over the past several months. The first of these relate to the policy of concentration which was discussed with you at some length when the Foreign Assistance Act was presented last year. 

In accordance with this policy, we have reviewed the program and eliminated a number of activities in fiscal year 1962 and are proposing to eliminate still others in fiscal year 1963. 

For example, we have terminated nine projects in Ethiopia in fiscal year 1962 and expect to terminate others in fiscal year 1963. 

We are likewise terminating a number of projects in Libya. We are also regrouping a number of projects under some common direction and administration, which will also have an effect of concentrating our resources. 

The next thing we have done affects the composition of the program we are carrying on. As most of you know, I think, in the past it was the practice, on occasion, to finance commodity imports for a country in order to raise local currencies to carry on other projects. 

Under this approach, the reason for the aid and its purpose and direction got a bit confused and lost. We decided to approach this problem differently and to require a clear decision in advance as to what the aid is needed for. If the need is for commodities, we intend to provide the country with the commodities directly. If the need is for the financing of a particular project or activity, we intend to finance that activity directly with dollars or with local currency, if we have local currencies, insofar as the local cost of the project is concerned.

In this way, we think we can get a clear delineation of the purpose of the aid and exercise better control over the use of the funds. We feel this will be a great step forward in simplifying our administration and in clarifying the purposes of our aid. 

Another thing we have done relates to the form of the financing as it is to be provided. We have changed the procedure which previously existed under which ICA financed some capital projects on a grant basis, while DLF was financing capital projects on a loan basis. We are putting all significant capital projects on a loan basis, including those which are in the social infrastructure field, such as hospitals,

schools, or anything of this sort that requires significant capital construction. We will make some exceptions for very small programs, primarily those associated with technical assistance activities. 

In the approach to the allocation of our resources we have taken a look at the situation which exists throughout Africa and have tried again to make some generalizations. I have mentioned the wide variety of circumstances which exist. We recognize that there must be some concentration of our resources, both personnel and financial, in the countries which are in a position to make the best use of them. 

We don't feel, however, that we can just write other countries off and we feel we have to be in a position to respond constructively for requests for particular activities that offer hope for growth or which in themselves make a specific and immediate contribution to increased production.

So, as we have looked over the countries, it seemed to us there are about three types which will affect the composition and form of our aid and our administration. 

The first group is rather obvious: those countries which have most of the prerequisites for development. They may have natural resources in greater degree than other countries. Certainly they will have human resources which are greater. Their people may be better educated, and their planning has developed to a greater stage. 

In these kinds of countries, we feel that we should concentrate most of our resources and should have a full-fledged organizational setup for the AID mission. We will have a director and deputy director and all the usual offices which go with an AID mission and will use all our tools there.

A second group of countries are those which, while they have many of the requisites for development, are not nearly as far along the road as the first group of countries for any number of reasons. 

In this type of country we would expect to have an AID mission but a smaller mission. We would expect to have usually a smaller program and perhaps not use all our tools. 

Then there is a group of countries in Africa whose prospects for self sustaining development seem to be rather remote, or they may also be in a situation where they are basically being supported by the metropole countries. In this type of country, we feel our program would be more limited. We would not establish in many of these countries an AID mission at all, but instead might have some people or a person on the staff of the embassy in these countries who are familiar with AID matters, who can respond and can let us know if there are particular things that seem to be worth doing. 

The logistics problem is such that we don't feel we can put a great number of technicians in, as a matter of fact. We would expect to approach many of the things we do there on the basis of the Government's entering into a contract for a specific thing which has a definite terminal point. When it is completed and the contract is finished, the people would leave. If something else comes along later to do, we would move in to do that. 

You may find from one year to another that a country which would appear to fall in one of the less promising groups has a higher obligation under the AID program than one falling in a higher category. 

This would be due to the fact that it just happened that at that par-

ticular time period a particular project which was considerable in size came along and distorted the annual figure for the country. 

We would like, as a matter of fact, to get away in these circumstances from a concept of annual aid levels and think of the program over time rather than being concerned with the amount that appears in obligations for a particular fiscal year. 

Let me speak for just a moment about the size of the program we are actually proposing for the fiscal year 1963 and what we have done in fiscal year 1962. In fiscal year 1963 the programs for developmental assistance are expected to increase in both the loan and the grant categories. We expect supporting assistance activity to decline pretty sharply. It is difficult to estimate the actual volume of development loans because of the necessity for getting carefully documented applications, completion of engineering and negotiation of loan agreements and this sort of thing. 

But we are estimating that in fiscal year 1963 the level will be from $200 to $270 million. This compares with some $53 million in fiscal year 1961, with present obligations and loans ready for commitment of $42 million at the present time in fiscal year 1962 and with an expectation that the volume in fiscal year 1962 may go as high as $150 million, somewhere in the range of $100 to $150 million. 

Development grants are contemplated for fiscal year 1963 at approximately $118 million. This compares with an anticipated level of about $97 million for fiscal year 1962 and an actual obligation in fiscal year 1961 of $69.7 million.

This program reflects the increasing ability of the countries to absorb a larger volume of assistance. It also reflects the increase particularly over fiscal year 1961 in the number of countries which are receiving assistance.

The grant program is going to be concentrated primarily in the fields of training of manpower and expansion of the educational base, agricultural activities of various kinds, and public administration as Governor Williams mentioned. 

We are also expecting to have a larger amount of assistance in the form of surveys of particular projects than has been the case in the past. This will be particularly true in countries in the third group which I talked about. We feel sure that their situation is such that there are things there that desperately need to be done to increase the production in these countries, but they just haven't been surveyed to bring them to a point where you would be able to make an economic and financial judgment on them. We expect to put resources into this field in a very large number of the African countries. 

With respect to supporting assistance, this category falls pretty sharply. We are proposing $32.5 million in fiscal year 1963 as compared to $61 million and $82 million in 1962 and 1961, respectively. 

This assistance is being provided in those countries which for strategic reasons, primarily, we are required to provide particular types of assistance. A large part of this, as a matter of fact, usually turns out to be in the form of commodity assistance. 

I would also point out that we have to anticipate the possibility of contingencies in Africa to a degree that is not contained in these figures. Probably more than any other area in the world we have all kinds of uncertainties here. So we are anticipating that it will

be necessary from time to time to call upon the contingency fund to meet requirements that cannot be anticipated at the present moment. 

I would like to mention also one or two other things that we are trying to do in connection with the Africa program. First, we are trying very much to get private enterprise involved in financing in Africa. 

We feel that there are enough natural resources in many of these countries to offer real possibilities of considerable private investment. 

As you know, this has already taken place to a considerable degree in a number of countries. We hope to use all our tools in this respect. 

We hope to use the development lending category. We hope to use the investment guarantee route. We hope to use the financing of investment surveys, for which authority was given to us last year. 

We don't expect, however, to confine ourselves to just trying to stimulate some American private investment. We feel that certainly this is most important. It is also important to try to do something to develop a strong, viable, healthy private sector within the particular countries concerned. 

I think this is important both in terms of the sort of society that it is in our interest to see developed there, and it is also important in the sense of this kind of a private sector being necessary if you are in fact going to get very much American investment going into these countries. So we are trying to establish development banks in quite a number of these countries, for example, in Ethiopia, Sudan, Tunisia, the Ivory Coast, Niger, Sierra Leone, Dahomey, and Liberia. We hope to do more in this field in fiscal year 1963. 

We are also working with a number of the, shall I call them, departments of commerce in the countries to get them to adopt programs that will try to stimulate investment locally. 

We have entered into a contract with a number of American firms to do some work in this field, including the Arthur D. Little Co. 

Other programs that are being carried on in Africa include the food-for-peace program and the activities of the Peace Corps. There has been an increase in fiscal year 1962 in the food-for-peace programs in most of the Public Law 480 titles. 

We are particularly proud of the use of the title II provision in countries like Tunisia, Morocco, and one or two others, to get them to establish programs for productively utilizing the large numbers of unemployed. The programs in Tunisia and Morocco seem to be working out very successfully, and in Tunisia we are working with the Government to get this project incorporated into its long-term development plan. 

The Peace Corps is currently carrying on programs in 4 countries and expects to increase this to 14 in fiscal year 1963. 

Of course, as you all know, the United States is far from being the only country which is providing assistance to Africa. As a matter of fact, the assistance from other countries far exceeds the amounts that we are providing. It is certainly our intent not only to keep these figures up to this level but to increase them if it is possible to do so. 

In this connection I would point out that free world sources have provided assistance which was first about $900 million in 1959 and which amounted to nearly a billion and a half in 1962. If we take out from these figures aid to Algeria and other countries not current-

ly receiving U.S. assistance, other free world aid is estimated at over a billion dollars. Again, this is far more than the aid we are providing. 

France is the largest contributor in this category, with their annual obligations, mostly in the form of grants, running about $300 million to the former French States. The Common Market Development Fund is currently obligating grant projects at the rate of about $200 million a year. The United Kingdom is providing about $150 million, and German obligations are beginning to approach this figure. 

Smaller amounts are being provided by Germany and Italy. The 

IBRD and other international institutions are also active in Africa. 

In this connection I think it would be of interest to note that IBRD just about a month ago established a new African department in the Bank, indicating an increased emphasis which they expect to put on the continent. IBRD's commitments have averaged about $100 million during 1960 and 1961. The Eximbank is also active there, although not nearly to the degree that IBRD has been. But even here their loans increased from $7 million in 1959 to $53 million in 1961, and we expect it will continue to expand its operations. The 

United Nations is also putting money in. 

Governor Williams indicated the interest of the Africans in regional development. We are also interested in this and are assisting the 

CCTA, an organization of countries south of the Sahara, which tries to undertake technical assistance programs covering more than one country. We have helped them with a program for the eradication of rinderpest. We have also provided assistance for projects involving the pooling of resources by states-for example, for regional approaches to the educational problem. We are working also on the question of a university for East Africa. We have provided scholarships on a regional basis for Africans to permit them to go outside their country for education, but staying within Africa in situations in which the types of facilities in their countries are available for their specialties. 

We are then trying in such ways as we can to support some interchange among the countries and some regional approach to problems as appears appropriate. 

I think we should all recognize that the attainment of self-sustaining economic development for most countries in Africa lies beyond the immediate future and probably beyond our present decade. 

The African leaders are certain to face shortfalls in their expectations and certainly in the meeting of the public's aspirations. We believe that we are providing a basis for reasonable political stability and for the foundations for economic growth with the program that we are providing. 

These are the bases on which the measures for U.S. support are designed and the purposes we have to accomplish in the program we are carrying out in fiscal year 1962 and fiscal year 1963.

Mrs. BOLTON. These brown books we can't do much with. I wanted very much to ask about this Upper Volta nursing school. That happens to be my job in the world. I believe you, Mr. Williams, spoke of it. On page 6 you speak of a school for nursing in Upper Volta.
