Mrs. BOLTON. I would like that if you don't mind. I won't take the time now. Will you please see that I get a very careful reply to that, because I want to know. (The information is as follows:)

The Ecole Jamot, a school for nurses in Upper Volta, is administered by the 

Organization for Coordination in the Control of Endemic Disease (OCCGE). 

The OCCGE was organized in June 1959 and serves as the coordinating and planning unit for several west African regional centers and institutions engaged in specialized research and experimentation in certain endemic diseases, formerly operated by France. The OCCGE is directed by an administrative council made up of the Ministers of Health of the member states (former French west African colonies) and a delegate from France. The OCCGE's annual budget is approximately $2 million, $1 million of which is contributed by the African States, the other by France.

The Ecole Jamot, located at Bobo-Diculesse, was established in 1939 although its present charter was issued in 1950. The school provides a 2-year training course for nurses and laboratory assistants. It uses the facilities and staff of the Centre Maraz which maintains separate laboratories for sleeping sickness, malaria, ophthalmology, oncbocercissis, yaws, and syphilis. Minimum admission requirements for the Ecole Jamot is a primary school certificate and an entrance examination is given. Thus far, about 1,400 persons have been trained in the school, including nurses now working for the OCCGE and engaged in the treatment of endemic diseases. 

The construction of additional dormitory facilities made possible by AID assistance in fiscal year 1962 will permit an increase in the school's enrollment from 42 to 62.

It would seem to us by concentrating at the secondary level, since we do have this great base of people coming through the primary school, that it is more desirable to concentrate at this level rather than

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Burleson. 

Mr. BURLESON.

Mr. Hutchinson, you will likely think the question strange, but simply put, what do you consider to be the purpose of our aid? 

Mr. HUTCHINSON. As I see it, our aid program everywhere and particularly in Africa has two fundamental purposes: I have a fairly strong-and this gets to be, I don't know whether it is a moral or religious, or whatever you want to call it-conviction; I believe that nations like people have to participate in the process of creation that is going on around them or else they lose their reason for being. This is fundamental and I won't push it any further than that. 

The second and perhaps more down-to-earth and pragmatic reason is that it seems to me that it is essential for the security of the United States that we have as much stability and growth in the world as we can possibly obtain. 

The Communist system was born out of chaos. It thrives on chaos. 

It seems to me that in Africa the situation is such that without some real assistance on our part in this process of nation building, which I mentioned, that we could have exactly the situation which would play completely into their hands. 

Mr. BURLESON. You have been in Africa and, of course, the Governor has been there. Do you find any real response to our efforts on the basis of philosophies? Do you think the leaders in Chad, Togo or Mali-or to pick out any of them in the area-have any burning conviction insofar as philosophies are concerned, whether it is socialism, communism, capitalism, or otherwise? Do you find any pronouncement of such philosophy?

Mr. HUTCHINSON. I do not find any pronouncement of the philosophies of the sort that you have mentioned. I do find a burning desire to be independent and not to be dominated, and to have a stable government and to provide their people with the fruits of economic growth and progress. It seems to me that all of those things are in our interest and deserving of our support. 

Mr. BURLESON. Do you see a responsibility on the part of people to equate and make this consonant with our efforts in Africa generally? At places and times we have taken a diverse course and serious issue with historic friends as opposed to Africa. 

Have you seen any responsibility and response on the part of African leaders to this very serious choice of policy? 

Mr. HUTCHINSON. I am not quite sure of the import of your question. I think you see responsibility in many of the African countries. 

Certainly you see it in places like Nigeria, which is the prime example.

alternative available to them, that there is a prospect for growth, development, and stability.

Mr. BURLESON. My question might indicate that I am opposed to people seeking and securing their independence and freedom. Of course not. Mr. HUTCHINSON. I would say this, sir, that you have to view the reaction of these people, as of all peoples, in the light of their history. 

All of us are very much prone to understand those things we have experienced, and are not quite so likely to understand things that are more abstract and that are far from us. They have not experienced 

Soviet colonialism. They have experienced other colonialism and the discrimination of white against black. They have experienced all sorts of things.

Republic, Gabon, Ghana, Mali, Niger, Togo: savings measures in

Ghana, Ivory Coast, and Malagasy. Those are countries in which something concrete and constructive actually has been done. What about the others? Are there specific examples of progress in stabilization of their governments, as well as their economic stability? 

Mr. HUTCHINSON. In the case of Niger-you said, "stabilization"-I was going to give you an example of increased savings through the flotation of a bond issue on which considerable pressure is being put on Government employees, Cabinet members, and others to make a subscription. In fact, there is almost a forced saving in this particular issue that I am talking about. If this is the sort of thing you mean, yes. I was regaled for almost an hour by the permanent 

Under Secretary for the plan in the eastern region of Nigeria about things that are being done at the local level to get some stability in Government by the provision of services themselves at the local level. 

One is a system under which the local people band together to build a school or health center and are responsible for the operation of that center for a period of 2 years. After this time, a review is made by the provincial government-by the regional government, I should saythe regional government, and if it conforms to certain standards, both in terms of construction and operation, then they will take over the operating cost. If not, then the local community must continue to operate it themselves. It seems to me that this kind of grassroots local participation in governmental affairs is the introduction of a very strong element of stability into the governmental structure.

We have got to recognize that other people

as well as ourselves may be permitted to be preoccupied with their self-interests. It is my hope that this approach, to the contrary vote of these countries in the United Nations, takes root in the minds of the American people.

House, totally unexpectedly, about late May or early June asking me if I would be interested in coming back to Washington. I responded by saying that I very much doubted it but I would at least be willing to talk. I came down and the possibilities were discussed. 

It was left completely open. I said it depended on who was going to be the head of the Agency, what my job was going to be, and a number of things would have to be clarified. Nothing further happened until sometime in November when I got another call and was asked if I would come down and speak to Fowler Hamilton, which I did. And a few days later I was offered the job which I now have. 

I can only assume that in those 20 years in Government which you mentioned I have built up some reputation, some experience, and that I was felt qualified on the basis of that experience for the job. 

This is the only assumption I can make. I don't know.

We certainly do not contemplate anything of this sort in countries falling into the other category which you mention. If you run down the list, you will find that countries like Liberia and Tunisia are the countries in which the great majority of our resources are to be concentrated. This is definitely the approach we intend to follow.

We have to know what the cost of the project is going to be. We have to address ourselves to the market potentials for the end product, or to the contribution that is going to be made by the project to production or development. 

We feel that they are sound loans. So far as the terms of repayment are concerned, we are generally making them on long enough terms that we feel that the prospects of repayment are good.

Mr. HUTCHINSON. Quite a number of them do offer special benefits in the form of relief from taxation. It isn't directed specifically and exclusively to American interests. American industry to participate in your program in Africa?

We have had some discussions with Kaiser on that score. 

We put $500,000 in a program in one country to work with this sort of thing, to see if we can't develop some interest in the smaller enterprise that could grow up around these large installations.

(The following memorandum has been supplied for inclusion in the record :)

BACKGROUND ON AMBASSADOR STEVENSON'S STATEMENT ON STUDENTS FROM CAMEROON TRAINED IN COMMUNIST CHINA 

In his U.N. speech on the admission of Communist China, Ambassador Stevenson referred to the capture in September and October 1960 of six young Cameroonians who were attempting illegally to enter the Republic of Cameroon from British Cameroons. These six young men were not students in the traditional sense. 

Papers found on their persons and information obtained during questioning established the fact that they were members of a group of nine Cameroon nationals who had just completed a 10-week course of intensive training in sabotage, guerrilla warfare, and political subversion in Communist China. 

The British Government, with the concurrence of the Government of Cameroon, issued a press release describing the capture of the six terrorists and also gave the details of the training which they had received in Communist China. Newspaper articles on the subject also appeared in the British and United States press. 

The information used by Governor Stevenson in his speech was taken from the British Government press release. 

Mr. JUDD. Do you know how many and which African countries have students being trained in Moscow or in Peiping? Is that information available?

Mr. WILLIAMS. Let me try to get as good a breakdown on that as we can.

Mr. JUDD. I think somewhere in our hearings we ought to have an estimate of the number of students from these countries, and which countries, that are being sent or enticed, or in whatever disguise, being trained in the Soviet Union or other Communist countries, which include Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and so forth. Have we got that in one of these books? I haven't had a chance to get through all of this material, I tell you frankly. 

Mr. WILLIAMS. This is just a part of the picture. If my memory serves me correctly there are about 3,000 African students who are in bloc-country schools. This compares to about the same number we have in the United States. But in England there are about 12,000, and there are probably that many in France. So that we are still drawing the major number. It is probably also true that the individual student, if he had the choice, would probably come to the United States if we had enough scholarships rather than go behind the Iron Curtain. The Communists do not insist on qualifications in their students, as you undoubtedly know. They take people and give them training, although not necessarily in a university, just so they can teach them the kind of thing you were talking about. 

Mr. JUDD. They are interested in their political orientation more than their academic qualifications.

Mr. WILLIAMS. Yes, sir. We will get together a memorandum for you.

Mr. JUDD. If you could, I don't see any objection to it, the name of the countries from which these approximately 3,000 students are being sent to the Communist countries. I am not asking this in a hostile sense at all.

Mr. WILLIAMS. Of course. I am sure some of it may be classified. 

We will give it to you and you will use it accordingly. (A classified memorandum was subsequently furnished in response to Mr. Judd's request.)

STATEMENT OF HON. W. AVERELL HARRIMAN, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR FAR EASTERN AFFAIRS 

(The prepared statement of Mr. Harriman is as follows:)

Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure to appear again before the Committee on Foreign Affairs in support of the undertaking by the United States to provide defensive and economic support in areas of the world where people seek to maintain their freedom and to improve their lot and their opportunity. 

Like myself, several members of this committee have been identified with this undertaking since the prospect of a reconstructed Europe was first pictured in the report to the Congress 16 years ago.

As you know, I was involved in the Marshall plan that was successful in helping Western Europe to rebuild its vitality from the devastation and dislocation left by the war. The Marshall plan stopped Stalin's ambitions to take over a war-torn Western Europe which he had thought would fall an easy prey to communism.

As a result of the initiative of the United States and the genius and hard work of the European people, the Marshall plan succeeded beyond anyone's hopes. 

It was a bipartisan program. As Senator Vandenberg used to say, it was unpartisan.

Today, we have in Europe strong and vigorous allies who are willing and able to join with us in assisting the developing countries. With the same energy and determination, the free nations of the world, working together, can now stop Khrushchev and Red China in their ambition to take over the underdeveloped nations of the world, just as we stopped Stalin. 663

In my present position as Assistant Secretary of State for Far Eastern Affairs, I welcome this opportunity to testify before this committee in support of the foreign aid program for the fiscal year 1963 for the Far Eastern area. My observations in support of the military aid and international development programs will be in general nature. Other representatives of the Department of 

State and the Agency for International Development will discuss the specific outlines of these programs. 

Geographically, my area of responsibility-the Far East-extends from Korea and Japan in northeast Asia through China and southeast Asia, westward to Burma and south through Indonesia to Australia and New Zealand. 

Altogether, the Asian Far East comprises approximately one-third of the entire population of the earth. The majority of these people are living under the control of communism and the remainder are directly under the shadow of the 

Chinese Communist threat.

The free nations of this area, lying along the periphery of Red China, share many characteristics other than this common danger arising from their proximity to Communist China. They are largely new nations. With the exception of 

Japan, Australia, and New Zealand they are economically only on the threshold of development.

Besides the economic poverty and low standard of living that accompanies this stage of development, these countries share other problems. Lack of developmental capital, lack of skilled labor, lack of administrative experience and persons trained to administer, lack of adequate public health systems, illiteracythese are but a few of the long catalog of problems that beset these countries. 

These, then, are the two key problems in the Asian Far East-the Communist threat of aggression and subversion against the free nations of the area, and the overriding poverty and lack of development of the manifold human and natural resources of these new nations. These are the twin and closely related problems which the foreign aid program seeks to meet. 

Stated most simply this program is the expression of this Nation's willingness to assist our friends and allies, the free nations of the Far East, to keep their freedom and independence and to achieve a standard of living which will make this freedom meaningful. 

As President Kennedy said in his special message on urgent national needs last year: *the adversaries of freedom plan to consolidate their territory-to exploit, to control, and finally to destroy the hopes of the world's newest nations; and they have ambitions to do it before the end of this decade. It is a contest of will and purpose as well as force and violence-a battle for minds and souls as well as lives and territory. And in that contest, we cannot stand aside. "We stand, as we have always stood from our earliest beginnings, for the independence and equality of nations. This Nation was born of revolution and raised in freedom. And we do not intend to leave an open road for despotism * ་ ་་ The military threat to the integrity of the free nations of the Far East is clear. 

Three million under arms in Communist China, 300,000 in North Korea and 350,000 in North Vietnam are all responsive to the Communist ideological and nationalistic objectives. 

An expression of the aggressive and subversive nature of this threat is to be found today in Vietnam, which I will discuss more fully later. 

The urgency of the economic and technical assistance is equally clear. The difficulties facing these countries in their task of development and satisfaction of the needs of their people are tremendous. They are compounded by the need to maintain large military defense forces in the face of the Communist military threat. But without tangible progress in achieving development and raising the standard of living, these countries cannot hope to achieve the stability needed to withstand the pressures and probing of communism. 

Vietnam again furnishes an illustration of the Communist fear of economic progress and the bettering of the life of the people. Land and economic reforms, malaria eradication, roadbuilding to give the farmers access to a market, schoolhouses, all of these have been and are today primary targets of Viet-Cong terrorism. 

The effort of the United States to assist these countries is based on a broad foundation of national interest. First, there is the simple fact that these countries are free and seek to remain so. Our aid is the direct expression of our own tradition and our natural sympathy and identity with new nations seeking to survive. We would not be the country we are if this were not so. But equally,

the struggle of each nation to maintain its freedom is an integral part of the struggle to keep freedom alive in the world. In the face of the Communist determination to extend its sway throughout the world, our encouragement, economic help and military assistance are clearly in our enlightened self-interest. 

The dimensions of the responsibility of the United States in the Far East are provided by the reaction of the Chinese Communists to the effectiveness of our role. The hostility and frustrations of the Red Chinese are focused on the 

United States because they realize that we are the principal obstacle to the fulfillment of their plans of conquest for Asia. Consequently, their overriding objective is to eliminate the presence of the United States in the Western Pacific.

I would like to reiterate today what I stated to the Congress in previous testimony in a broader context a decade ago: "I am firmly convinced that another world war can be prevented, providing, and only providing, we give the essential inspiration and leadership to the free world, and that we can act with wisdom and above all, consistency of purpose. As the threat of Communist imperialism has unfolded, our country has supported unprecedented policies and programs which have been successful in thwarting in many areas the Kremlin's aggressive designs." 

During the period when I made this statement I was primarily concerned, as U.S. representative in Europe under the Economic Cooperation Administration, with the pressing problems of Europe and later as Director of the Mutual Security Administration on a worldwide basis. 

The economic progress and stability that have been achieved in Western Europe are beyond what any of us could have projected 14 years ago. From a recipient of our assistance Western Europe has recovered to the point where it supports a substantial share of mutual defense costs, cooperates in economic and technical assistance to underdeveloped nations and has become, as an area, a vital trading partner of the United States buying more than $6 billion worth of our products annually. 

Today I am concerned with our relations in the Far East. I find that Japan has performed a miracle as striking as that which has occurred in Europe. 

We gave Japan assistance in the immediate postwar years primarily in the form of emergency relief supplies. Later, on the basis of its own efforts and relying on trade rather than aid, Japan mobilized its resources and achieved unprecedented economic success. 

Over the past decade, Japan has averaged more than a 9-percent increase in its annual rate of economic growth. It is now embarked on a plan, within the context of the democratic principles and the free enterprise system which has made its present achievements possible, of doubling the national income within the next 10 years.

Today Japan is the largest importer of American agricultural products in the world, and next to Canada, our largest single customer. As Japan's economy has grown, so has our trade with Japan. Our export sales to Japan have risen from $650 million in 1955 to $1.7 billion in 1961. And Japan buys more from the United States, more than she sells to us. During the last 5 years the United States sold to Japan some $1.7 billion more merchandise than we bought from Japan. This example proves again that our exports grow as other countries expand their industrial production. 

The disparity between the underdeveloped nations of the Far East and the solid base for economic reconstruction and progress which existed in Western Europe and Japan 10 years ago is great. One cannot draw a precise analogy between what has happened in Western Europe and Japan and what may happen with hard work, wisdom, and perseverance in southeast Asia. At the same time, the experience of Western Europe and Japan has taught us that while economic assistance at the appropriate time is essential, proper use of this aid requires the presence of other factors. These include a government policy of adequate education and technical training, of encouragement to investment and trade, rational planning by government and the private sector, a dedication to free enterprise and-most importantly-an ample supply of initiative and self-reliance. 

To assist Japan to continue her progress, she must have trade opportunities in the United States and the rest of the world. 

Happily, the Far East provides other evidence, besides the economic success of Japan, that this formula works. For example, the Republic of China has a high potential for self-sustaining growth and our program there is based on the desire to make the maximum use of this potential.

Malaya has defeated the Communist guerrillas, achieved a harmonious basis for racial coexistence, and moved into full sovereign status with dignity and prosperity.

Heartening progress has been achieved in the Philippines, where the new administration, dedicated to probity in government, has been able to remove controls on foreign exchange.

The failure of the Communist system in the most essential and fundamental of all production, that of food, contrasts dramatically with the success in the Far East of the free enterprise system in fostering agriculture. 

In the Soviet Union, Khrushchev had to hold a meeting recently of the Central Committee of the Communist Party to see what could be done about his failure to make the Communist system produce an adequate diet for the Russian people. 

In Communist China the commune system has collapsed and food production failed, not just because of bad weather, but again because of communism's failure to understand that agricultural production must be based on incentives to freemen.

In contrast, following on a land reform program which practically eliminated tenancy, the Japanese have increased agricultural production by almost 50 percent over the 1952-54 average. In particular contrast to the breakdown of the will to produce food on the mainland, the Republic of China has carried out a land reform program on Taiwan which is a model for all of Asia. The result again has been an impressive increase in food production. 

Our foreign aid program is designed to encourage, in particular, those factors and internal forces which most contribute to a self-sustaining growth and development. Among these factors are a sense of community purpose and regional interdependence-factors fostered in Europe under the Marshall plan which are now finding fulfillment in the European Common Market. 

Beginning with the individual countries of the area, I should now like to review briefly some of the major events in the Far East during the past year, with emphasis on those that are of particular significance to our foreign policy objectives and the most effective utilization of our foreign assistance. 

Three of the countries which account for the largest part of the aid program are artificially divided, with borders on Communist-controlled territories and Communist forces in position across the demarcation lines. The combined effect of a fracturing of economic ties and the poised security threat is to cause gross disbalance in military budget reguirements in relation to resources. As a consequence, material support from outside sources is essential. KOREA As long as there still exists in Korea a state of suspended war, it is evident that the United States has little alternative but to support Korea. Korea stands as a symbol of hope for freedom-loving peoples of Asia, and serves as evidence of the United Nations, supported by a determined America, in its posture against militant communism. 

The United States has supported the Korean Government in comprehensive measures to strengthen its military capabilities and stabilize its economy. 

In addition to the modern military weapons being furnished to the Republic of Korea, the United States provides sufficient funds for commodity imports, sales proceeds of which provide budgetary support to assist in the maintenance of the large military force required to counter the Communist threat from the north and strengthen the free world position in the Far East. 

The United States also provides economic aid in the form of development assistance to expand power, coal, and iron production; provide industrial as well as transport and communication development; and extends assistance in economic development planning. The aid program in Korea is keyed to reconstruction, control of any dangerous inflation and the expansion of Korea's economic base.

The Supreme Council (SCNR) now governing the country seems to understand the challenge it faces and appears determined to produce results. The Ministry of Reconstruction has been reconstituted as the Economic Planning Board and made a function of the Prime Minister's office. 

VIETNAM 

The Republic of Vietnam is under attack by Communist guerrillas who are directed, trained, supplied, and reinforced by North Vietnam-all in gross violation of the 1954 Geneva accords. Last year more than 4,000 free Vietnamese

died in the Vietnam war. This day, if the averages hold, there were more than a hundred casualties, and there will be nearly 500 violent incidents this week. 

The casualty figures testify eloquently to the determination of the Vietnamese people to resist Communist terror and protect the progress they have realized. 

Our aid has been directed in the past toward providing them with a stake in a free Vietnam. For this reason, nearly three-quarters of the roughly $2 billion we have provided Vietnam since 1954 has gone into economic aid. As the Communists stepped up the tempo of their attack, we have increased our military assistance to Vietnam.

But we are still determined that the average Vietnamese should have a better future to look forward to, something worth fighting to keep. For this reason we have recently undertaken to accelerate and expand our economic aid program and a coordinated, joint effort was announced in the United States-Government of Vietnam communique early in 1962. We are not alone, however, as 

Vietnam also received aid during 1961 from Japan, Malaya, France, Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Canada, and the Republic of China. 

I mentioned an increase in military assistance. This includes more American advisers and logistic and training support. It means the provision of U.S. airlift capacity to speed Vietnamese forces to areas under attack before the Communist guerrillas can fade back into the jungle. American combat troops have not been sent to Vietnam. The Vietnamese want to win their own war against the Communists but they need our material help and our advice. We are trying to give them the means to win. 

American assistance to Vietnam has been and will be expensive. We are in for a long struggle in Vietnam. We cannot expect quick, dramatic victories. 

But the price we are paying to help the Vietnamese defend themselves is a necessity.

I think all of us remember the tragedy of Dien Bien Phu, which marked the ending of a long and bitter war. For the Vietnamese it meant the partition of their nation and the yoke of communism on the backs of more than half their people. For the free world it was a danger signal. For Asian nations it meant that communism was on the march, that it might soon be at their door and that they, too, might soon find their people attacked, divided and conquered. 

We can ill afford to let the Communists prove the "inevitability" of their "revolution" in Asia by completing the conquest of Vietnam. The Vietnamese are fighting for the free world as well as themselves. 

The Vietnamese are a strong and active people. In the years since inde pendence, they have made important economic and social progress in spite of Communist threats and attacks. One index of this progress is education. In the fall of 1956, primary schools in South Vietnam had an enrollment of only 400,000; there are today more than 1,500,000 Vietnamese children in primary schools.

Since the Geneva armistice of 1954, agricultural production in South Vietnam has been generally restored to prewar levels. Some light industries have been started, particularly around Saigon, and power and coal production have been increased; the transportation network has been restored and, in some instances, improved. U.S. aid has played a major role in all these advances. 

During the period 1956-60, North Vietnam led South Vietnam in one overall category-industrial production—which increased 150 percent during the 5 years in the north and 100 percent in the south. (In both areas industrial production represents less than 15 percent of the total production.) 

South Vietnam led in fields which affect more closely the average man. The per capita gross national production was higher, for example, $110 in the south for 1960 and $70 for the north. Food crops increased 32 percent in the south, while it declined in the north. Production of rice increased 31 percent in the south to 5.4 million tons, as compared to 4.2 million tons for a larger population and representing an increase of 2 percent for the north during 1960. 

These gains are now threatened, however, by the growing insecurity from the depredations of the Viet Cong guerrillas, and by the measures required to suppress it, compounded by natural disaster. Insecurity caused a reduction of about 5 percent in the rice crop in 1951, resulting in the loss of about 50 percent of rice exports. Because of recent floods and continuing insecurity, Vietnam is now importing a large quantity of rice. 

LAOS 

The United States is continuing its efforts to conclude arrangements that would make Laos a neutral and independent state. Since the conflict in Laos

worsened in 1960, our Government has worked to settle the crises after the Communist-supplied forces scored major military victories and placed themselves in a position to seize the entire country. 

Our objectives were set forth by the President on March 23, 1961; namely, that the United States strongly supports the goal of a neutral and independent Laos, tied to no outside power, threatening no one, and free from any domination. He also declared in favor of constructive negotiations, among the nations concerned and among the leaders of Laos which would help Laos back to the pathway of independence and genuine neutrality. 

Shortly after a general de facto cease-fire had been accomplished in Laos, an international conference was convened at Geneva on May 16, 1961, for the settlement of the Lao question. Participating were representatives of the United 

States, the United Kingdom, the U.S.S.R., the Republic of Vietnam, North Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Burma, Thailand, France, Communist China, and the three members of the ICC in Laos (India, Canada, and Poland). 

After 7 months of negotiations, the conferees tentatively approved draft texts of a declaration on the neutrality of Laos, and of a protocol thereto. The draft declaration provides that the countries concerned would “recognize, respect and observe in every way the sovereignty, independence, neutrality, unity and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Laos." 

The draft protocol provides interalia for the withdrawal from Laos of all foreign troops and military personnel and for prohibition of the introduction of war material and military personnel, plus the prohibition against using the territory of Laos for interference in the internal affairs of its neighbors. 

I believe that these provisions when put into effect will serve U.S. security objectives. What is now barring further progress is the establishment in Laos of a coalition government of national unity based on policies of independence and neutrality. To this end, we are seeking to promote agreement among three 

Lao factions (those of the present rightist government headed by Prince Boun 

Oum and General Phoumi Ñosavan, Prince Souvanna Phouma, neutralists, and the pro-Communist Pathet Lao), for the formation of a government headed by 

Prince Souvanna Phouma, as the only Lao who appears acceptable as Premier to the two extreme Lao factions. 

The fate of a government of the sort envisaged would obviously depend upon the energy and effectiveness of its members in rallying the people's loyalty and to the external support given its economic, social and other programs. It would also depend in large part upon observance in good faith of the international agreements of the Geneva Conference.

It is envisaged that if and when a reasonably stable neutral coalition government is established, Laos will request assistance to promote a plan for economic development to which the United States would give sympathetic consideration. 

REPUBLIC OF CHINA 

The Government of the Republic of China (GRC) is one of the key links in the free world's chain of defenses in the western Pacific. U.S. policy is based on the full recognition of the Government of the Republic of China as the rightful government of China. 

In the face of the repeated declarations by the Communists of their intention to seize Taiwan, our assistance to the Government of the Republic of China is a vital deterrent to further aggression by the Chinese Communists and to the preservation of Taiwan as a symbol of freedom to all Chinese. 

Withdrawal of our aid would cause an economic and political crisis which would encourage a Communist takeover and endanger U.S. political and security positions in the western Pacific. 

Today Taiwan, of the underdeveloped areas, has one of the highest potentials for self-sustaining growth. Its most valuable assets are human resources, primarily the leaders in science, medicine, business, engineering, government, and education who came from the mainland. Education, health, and government institutions, communications and transport are among the best in the Far East.

Although agricultural technique is relatively at a high level, there is a tendency for the high rate of population growth, 3½ percent, to outrun food production. Progress in the already highly developed agricultural sector cannot be expanded as it can in industry, and if self-sustaining growth is to be achieved as rapidly as possible emphasis must be placed on accelerated industrialization in Taiwan.

The GRC armed forces represent the strongest anti-Communist military force in Asia, outside of Korea. Assistance to this force is a good investment, which contributes to the defense of the free world and to the security of the United States.

STRATEGICALLY PLACED ALLIES 

Two nations which are recipients of both economic and military support are strategically placed allies which contribute importantly to the "forward defense” of the free world in Asia. THAILAND Thailand is essential to the free world security position in southeast Asia. 

It is the headquarters of SEATO, and has consistently followed a policy of close alinement with the West. Thailand cooperates staunchly with the United States in various joint security efforts, and provides important support for free world positions in the United Nations and other international organizations. 

The Thai economy is basically agricultural and rests primarily on rice production. In the past few years, however, Thailand has made substantial progress both in the diversification of agriculture and in the growth of light industry. 

Thai fiscal policy is responsible, and has resulted in a convertible and stable currency, substantial foreign exchange reserves, and a consistently balanced budget. Thailand has an excellent credit rating with the World Bank, the 

Export-Import Bank, and other international financial institutions, and a World Bank team is working directly with the Thai Government in drawing up economic development plans. 

The Thai Government is convinced that security from Communist subversion can be obtained only through economic and social progress. This conviction has renewed urgency in view of recent developments in Laos and elsewhere in southeast Asia.

Militarily, Thailand's armed forces have contributed significantly to strengthening the defense of the area. The materiel and training provided by the 

United States has assisted the country to maintain order and resist the Communist subversive pressures at work in Laos and Vietnam. The defense of 

Thailand is of paramount importance to the United States. 

In summary, Thailand is an unusual example of an economically underdeveloped, fiscally responsible, cooperative country in need of external assistance. 

It is able and anxious to put such assistance to good use. 

PHILIPPINES 

The Republic of the Philippines is an integral part of the U.S. defense system in the Pacific. Because of its strategic location and the provision of its bases and other military installations to the United States, the defense of the Philippines must be considered within the context of the Pacific area. 

The Philippine people can be counted upon to defend their country and contribute to the defense of the free world. The Philippine armed forces have been progressively strengthened and brought into close association and cooperation with the United States and its Far Eastern allies. Continuing progress has been mnade in the training and modernization of its forces. 

The United States is continuing to help the Philippines attain a self-sustaining economy. The new administration has embarked on an attack upon the country's long-range problems, is pledged to reform and to an energetic program of accelerated economic and social development. It plans to concentrate on land reform, increased agricultural production, the decentralization of many governmental functions and the encouragement of private investment. 

The rate of population growth continues to be a formidable obstacle to improvement in the standard of living. However, in terms of health and education, the Philippines is ahead of many of its neighbors in the Far East. More than 70 percent of the population is literate. 

The Philippines has reason to be proud of its political and cultural development but it is also highly aware of its many economic and social problems. The new administration of President Macapagal is embarked on improvement in government administration and to a vigorous approach to economic problems. 

As an example of U.S. dedication to anticolonialism, the Philippines' importance to the United States transcends our normal interest in newly emerging countries. It is essential that the Philippines continue to reflect the advantages accruing from close association with the United States, both to its own citizens and to its Asian neighbors.

CAMBODIA, BURMA, AND INDONESIA 

Three other nations within my area of responsibility are dedicated to preserving their freedom and independence and achieving the social and material progress necessary to make this freedom meaningful. Cambodia, Burma, and 

Indonesia seek aid in this endeavor from all available sources. In addition to assistance from the United States these countries accept assistance from Communist nations. 

Sino-Soviet bloc credits and grants to Burma total $93.4 million, entirely economic aid; to Cambodia, $65 million, also all economic; and to Indonesia, $1.4 billion, of which one-half is military. 

Communist propaganda has bitterly attacked United States and free world economic and military aid as degrading, aggressive, and imperialist in design. 

The Communist objective is to create friction between the United States and recipients of its aid by purporting to provide aid on more favorable terms. In the case of its military aid, the objective of the bloc is mainly to create or exploit situation disadvantages to the free world. In the case of these three countries, their Communist tactics have been most apparent in Indonesia. 

Our aid to these countries, as in our assistance to all freedom-loving countries, is based on the belief that by helping those who seek to remain free we are helping our own security and our own efforts to preserve our freedom. 

As Secretary of State Rusk has said, "Whenever an underdeveloped country makes economic, social, and political progress it expands the frontier of freedom. 

Wherever we cooperate in breaking down the barriers of ignorance, poverty, disease and despair, we further not only the well-being of mankind but our own security." 

THE TREND IN U.S. ECONOMIC SUPPORT 

In recent years the Congress has urged that economic aid be phased out of grant aid into aid on a loan basis. This has not proved practicable in the case of Vietnam, Korea, and Laos, where the confrontation with Communist aggression is direct, requiring disproportionate military budgets for which internal fiscal and other resources are inadequate. It has proved possible, however, in the case of one of the former large recipients of grant aid-the Republic of China-to eliminate grants and substitute development loans. 

Projections of loans cannot, of course, be precise. Using the higher of a range of development loan figures, however, the proposals for 1963 envisage a substantial increase in the percentage of aid going to Far Eastern countries in the form of dollar loans, repayable in dollars.

INTERNATIONAL TRADE 

In order for the United States to achieve its objective of assisting the development of newly emergent countries of the Far East, we must support these countries in their participation in international trade. Only in this way can their standards of living be improved and their economies developed. 

Development grants and development loans are important in the promotion of international trade. Equally important is the availability of markets. These countries recognize the need to diversify their primary and agricultural production for export and to industrialize if they are to progress, raise their standards of living, and over the long run become self-sustaining. 

As the industrialization of these countries develops and their products are exported to pay for badly needed imports, the advanced countries must not hinder their efforts by erecting trade barriers. 

Experience shows that our commerce expands greatly as countries expand their own industrial production. In this connection it is a cause for satisfaction that the long-term cotton textile agreement reached at the international conference at Geneva provides for a growth factor in imports of textiles, traditionally one of the initial exports of countries commencing industrialization. 

The President's Trade Expansion Program should, through the most-favorednation principle, widen market opportunities for industries of the free Far East. If the needs of these countries for enlarged and diversified export are to be met, the underdeveloped countries must develop trade in other than the traditional products of rice, rubber, or tin. 

RECAPITULATION 

Last year the Congress was informed of the administration's intentions regarding the "decade of development," the intent of the United States regarding the

nature of future aid, and the belief that this is a "decade of decision" which will determine whether most of the peoples of underdeveloped countries will live in freedom or under Communist dictatorship. 

The developments of the last year underline this vital issue. The desire for modernization and industrialization is active and intense among the underdeveloped nations. In our world, shrunken by rapid communication, the irresistible yearning for a better way of life and the demand for progress is intensified. 

The Communists know this, and by their tactics in the Far East they are exploiting every possible means to subvert and subjugate the free countries of Asia. By providing long-term assistance for the lesser developed nations, the 

United States can over the coming decade, act decisively in helping people preserve their independence whose well-being and freedom is important to us. 

Fifteen years ago we took the initiative to block Stalin's plan to take over Western Europe. With the same determination, we can now help frustrate 

Khrushchev's and Mao's designs on freedom in the Far East. (The prepared statement of Mr. Janow is as follows:)

It is a great honor for me to appear before this committee, for the first time, in support of a program that I, as a private citizen, have come to consider one of the great endeavors of our time. I am aware that there is little, after 3 months in the Agency for International Development, that I can-or needtell members of this committee about the emergence of the present foreign aid program, its rationale, or its broad objectives. These things I must learn from you.

Perhaps I can tell you something of interest from my experiences of 18 years of almost continuous residence in Asia. As a new arrival in Washington this winter I found impressions of the Far East and also of our aid program there dominated by black headlines from Laos, Vietnam, and Indonesia. I have found here a tendency to see the Far East as an area of confusion and disorder containing little of hope or progress, a view that it is an area antipathetic to America where we will be embarrassed in our aid efforts by scandals and where politically and militarily we are doomed to failures. 

Dark predictions about the future have become an old story in the Far East. 

Japan in 1946, its cities 40 percent destroyed, its industries stopped, with no friends or trade, stripped of its empire and unable to feed a growing population, was seen as a hopeless case. Hong Kong in 1951 was expected to be gobbled up at any moment or at least-according to the "realists"-to stagnate because of its insecurity. Taiwan's days in 1950 were numbered almost from month to month by the prophets of doom. South Vietnam appeared, in 1955, to have no possible form of central government and little prospect of independent survival. Malaya, Burma, and the Philippines in the early 1950's were fighting what seemed a losing battle against Communist guerrillas who were reputed to have deep political roots in the countryside. More recently, some have been quick to conclude that Laos was "lost" to the Communists. 

I suggest that the record clearly refutes much of the pessimism and fears of the past. The record demonstrates solid accomplishment in the Far East. 

While it has not become an Atlantic community, free Asia in the 1960's is less alien, more compatible for Americans, more closely attuned to our ways, and with more prospects for our future than seemed feasible in the 1950's. 

To talk of our accomplishments in Asia it is natural to start with Japan. I served on General MacArthur's staff in the occupation headquarters. I recall clearly the conviction there in 1948 that Japan could survive only on an indefinite relief dole from the United States. One of my last assignments in the headquarters was to serve as chairman of a committee that was attempting to establish a single exchange rate. The Japanese argued that they could not afford to force all their industries, some damaged, some almost destroyed, to a single exchange rate until the level of Japanese exports had reached at least $50 million a month. As I recall, the head of a mission from Washington threw up his hands when he heard this export target and said, "That might not be reached in 10 years." It seemed a hopeless goal for the immediate future. That was in 

1948. Last year Japan's exports were about $400 million a month. Per capita income has risen from $200 in 1948 to $450 a year. The exchange rate we established in 1948, 360 to 1, is still the exchange rate and has been one of the most stable in the world. 

We furnished Japan about $1.6 billion in food and essential raw materials in these postwar years. Now the Japanese Government has agreed to repay a sub-

stantial part of this aid. Japan has become a major contributor of capital and technical skills to its Asian neighbors. Its reparations agreements with Burma, the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia total $1.2 billion. They are being paid off at about $70 million per year. In the first half of last year, Japan's foreign assistance including reparations totaled $231 million. It has moved from a recipient of American aid to a partner with us in aid to the Far East.

This, I submit, is an exciting success story-for us and for Asia; this is major progress achieved in Asia by Asians within a democratic framework and a private enterprise system. Our assistance did not produce this success. Japanese energy and organization and access to world markets did that, but our aid, our trading policies, our foreign policy and our military strength and its deployment in Asia have made it possible. 

I am convinced that at least some measure of the Japanese success can be repeated elsewhere, with the right mixture of foreign assistance, local energy and organization. Certainly in terms of natural resources per capita, Japan is no more blessed than Taiwan, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam or even southern Korea. It did have many advantages of organization, education, and experience in the late 1940's which its neighbors still lack. But just as Japan compressed the process of reaching this stage of development into 60 years between 1860 and 1920 some of its neighbors, especially if they are given enlightened domestic leadership and most-favored-nation treatment by all the free nations, may achieve a great deal in the decade of the 1960's. 

Lesser, but significant, success stories are being written today in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Thailand and Malaya. There are encouraging movements in the Philippines. And some key foundations for economic advances are being laid in Korea and elsewhere in the region. South Vietnam, given a period of peace, can become a bright spot on the economic map. 

This is the hopeful-but I don't believe it is wishful-framework of our aid request. I do not ignore the difficulties in a region of mostly new nations, former colonies, some truncated from former territory, whose handicaps of newness are compounded by the threat of Communist aggression or subversion. Nor do I predict that we can with aid or other U.S. actions assure uniform progress and universal freedom throughout the area. But I think it is demonstrab'e that our assistance has been an important instrument in achieving more than seemed possible in the 1940's and the 1950's. 

The Far East has been a major recipient of U.S. aid. The cumulative figures are large. But the annual U.S. investment is not out of balance with our total world programs and commitments abroad. 

We propose for fiscal year 1963 in the Far East a program composed of $349.1 million in supporting assistance grants, $75 million in development grants, and development loans expected to range between $200 million and $280 million. The total of somewhat over $600 million is slightly over one-tenth of 1 percent of the U.S. gross national product.
