This proposal involves an increase in supporting assistance above the level planned for fiscal year 1962, due largely to the restoration of demand for raw material imports in Korea and the proposed fulfillment of our 1959 commitment to help finance construction on the Rangoon-Mandalay Road in Burma. Grant

aid requirements are expected to remain large in part or all of fiscal year 1963 in Laos. Offsetting these factors, we are terminating supporting assistance grants to Thailand and expanding our loan program there, just as we have this year in Taiwan and the Philippines.

Development grants for technical assistance are proposed at slightly above the current year's level, the increase almost entirely due to the high priority progam in Vietnam.

Development lending in dollar-repayable loans represents a substantially larger part of our total aid program in the proposal for fiscal year 1963. We expect to increase the relative emphasis on loans in the future, as more Far Eastern countries take the steps to qualify. 

An important supplement to AID funds in the proposed program is the saleand-loan provision of surplus U.S. agricultural products under Public Law 480. 

We have anticipated a total $200.5 million in Public Law 480 sales agreements in the Far East, generating approximately $173.3 million in local currencies for subsequent loans and grant-for-aid purposes. This compared with $242.2 million in such sales agreements planned for the current fiscal year. 

I should point out to this committee that this program has been substantially prepared months ago before the new management of AID was in place. I have found in my review a faithful effort to emphasize assistance that promotes and responds to self-help-a recognition that the major efforts must be made by the Far Eastern countries themselves. 

The proposed new program will be characterized by these emphases, which, in fact, we are putting into effect as rapidly as possible in the current fiscal year: 

1. Renewed emphasis on the private sector.—Where it is possible, aid to private enterprise will be given priority. The development lending program, the investment guarantee authority, local currency lending under section 104 (e) of Public Law 480, and investment surveys will be used to channel capital into constructive private activity. 

2. Broader international participation in the aid effort.-Other developed nations are accepting a share of this responsibility, individually and through the World Bank, the Colombo plan and other international channels. Germany has recently made substantial credits available to Korea, Vietnam, Indonesia and Thailand. A growing list of nations are contributing technical services and capital to Vietnam's development. Japan's role in this field has been mentioned. 

We have had promising discussions with the Development Assistance Committee of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development in Paris for consortium operations in the Far East. 

3. Concentration on crucial activities.—In both technical assistance and capital projects there has been concentration on the most important leverage points. 

We have reduced the number of grant projects substantially. 

4. Rural activities.-Smaller endeavors are not being neglected. Feeder roads, community development, agricultural credit agencies, agricultural extension-type services, rural sanitation and water development have a substantial part in our programs. 

5. Systematic planning.—You will find study missions and investigative efforts on tax reforms, land reform, tariff measures, economic and engineering surveys throughout the area. We are trying to make certain that our efforts at planning do not mean encouragement of state or socialistic economies. In fact, we will discourage, where possible, plans which expand the public sector at the expense of private enterprise.

The We are changing almost entirely the top management of our field posts. new AID mission directors in the Far East, as well as our present staff, will operate within these guidelines.

I will not in this statement attempt to describe in detail our present and proposed programs in the Far East. I do wish, however, to make a country-bycountry survey of the scope and major features of these programs, particularly with reference to what has been accomplished in each country. 

Thailand is a good place to begin. Like Japan, Thailand had a prewar history of independence. And like Japan it has the potential to become an economic strongpoint for the free world. Its level of development is second only to Malaya in mainland southeast Asia. It has substantial natural resources and, by Asian standards, a relatively thin population of 26 million. Its per capita income has moved up steadily to close to $100 a year, reflecting an economic growth rate of 81496-62-pt. 4-5

4 to 5 percent annually. The Thai currency is practically convertible; its foreign reserves are steadily growing. 

The Thai leadership in recent years has shown a growing interest in making a national effort to exploit the country's economic potential and distribute these gains more equitably. Following a U.S. economic survey last summer, Prime 

Minister Sarit declared in a message to President Kennedy his determination to accelerate economic development. Significant self-help measures have been undertaken in tax increases, revenue administration, central budgeting, and the sale of Government bonds. Thailand also is working with the World Bank to focus its development plans in terms of priority and practicality. 

Further self-help measures are implicit in the shape of our proposed AID program for Thailand in fiscal year 1963: First, we are stopping supporting assistance grants at the end of the curent fiscal year. Long-term dollar loans will be offered, instead, for imports of goods and services essential to capital development projects. However, we will first make sure that AID does not compete with other potential sources of loans. Thailand's international credit worthiness is excellent, as evidenced by the credits extended by the World Bank, the Export-Import Bank, and recently by West Germany. I have every confidence that loans made to Thailand will be repaid in full and at interest rates approximating the cost of money to our Government. 

Second, Thailand will pay the local currency costs of loan-financed projects next year, except for two loans on which prior understandings exist, and will assume this responsibility on grant projects over the course of the next year. 

[Security deletion.] 

Thailand, a large exporter of agricultural products, does not require Public 

Law 480 assistance.

The technical assistance program funded by development grants will concentrate on increasing agricultural production, particularly in the impoverished upland areas of northeast Thailand; regional and community development to strengthen national unity, again with emphasis on the troubled areas near the Lao border; teacher training and other educational assistance; Government administration in such fields as statistics and budgeting; and public health. The development grant program we will continue in Thailand is intended to strengthen its institutions. This is in our interest to do, and Thailand has the capacity to absorb such technical assistance effectively. This is clearly a country which will develop and requires for some time foreign technical assistance. It needs external capital, which it will repay, and technical assistance which it will absorb and put to good use. 

Malaya, Thailand's neighbor to the south, is another bright spot today. 

Malaya won its decade-long war against Communist-led insurgents. I remember on several visits in the mid-1950's being met at airports by my clients in armored cars, riding in armored trains, avoiding any night driving, racing down highways at 70 miles an hour because of fear of Communist interception, and sleeping in guarded compounds. Personal security, political stability, and economic progress seemed a wishful dream for Malaya in the 1950's. Today it is stable, democratic, and relatively prosperous. The terrorists have been eliminated the communal issue between Malays and Chinese seems contained and subordinated to a national concept of Malaya. 

The Federation of Malaya now is discussing a larger federation with Singapore, North Borneo, Brunei, and Sarawak, surely one of the most promising political developments in the area. Malaya itself has not received U.S. economic aid, except for two small development loans several years ago. 

[Security deletion.] 

To the east, across the China Sea, is another stable and secure nation with great potential, the Philippines. In 1946-51 the Philippines was battling 

Hukbalahap Communists in numbers as great as the active and organized terrorist bands in Vietnam today. It was not safe to drive outside Manila at night, or from Manila to Clark Air Force Base, our major military base. There were still visible the terrible scars of the battle to liberate Manila; the psychological scars of the Japanese occupation were slow to fade. 

The great change came when Ramon Magsaysay, as defense secretary, crushed the Huk rebellion in 1951 and later, as President, integrated the former rebels into Philippine society. The political stability and promise of the Philippines of 1962 were not imagined by many a decade ago. 

Economic progress, however, has been sporadic in the Philippines. Recently the national income has barely kept pace with population growth, and unem-

ployment has been increasing. Despite abundant natural resources, a free economy, managerial and technical skills and special advantages, the Philippines has not approached its potential. Leadership sometimes has been lacking, waste and misuse of foreign exchange and natural resources have been excessive, and corruption has been endemic. 

Now a new administration is in power, pledged to reform and hard work on economic development. And so far, at least, it has shown proof that it means business. President Macapagal, almost immediately after his inauguration last 

December 31, eliminated exchange controls and import controls, lowered tariffs on essentials, increased customs on nonessentials, and introduced other desirable financial measures. It is developing a plan for economic progress, based upon these financial policies, in consultation with the World Bank and with us. The administration seems prepared to tackle its agricultural problems and to reverse a situation where a potentially rich agricultural country was a net importer of rice of 186,000 tons in 1961. 

The Philippines has excellent prospects for attracting foreign capital from several sources, especially if this renewed development drive is sustained. The 

World Bank, the Export-Import Bank, the commercial banks of the United States and Japan, and private investment are important sources of capital. The U.S. 

Government has responded to the new Philippine administration's need for stabilization funds with assurances of development loan assistance. 

We anticipate AID development loans of $30 to $50 million in fiscal year 1963 to the Philippines on projects. In addition, we propose to provide technical assistance in industry and mining, public administration, community and rural development including training of agricultural credit and cooperative supervisors, Mindanao Island area development, and in education, particularly in the very effective textbook publication and teacher-training program. 

[Security deletion.] 

No supporting assistance grants are proposed. This type of assistance terminated at the end of fiscal year 1961. 

Taiwan, the seat of the Government of the Republic of China, also is an economic success story that has not been told widely. Here we can see evidence of both the acute military burden common to several Far Eastern countries and the economic achievements which our aid has made possible. This, I assure you, was not the general assessment of Taiwan's prospects after the fall of the Mainland 12 years ago. Even 6 or 7 years ago anyone predicting that Taiwan could become a borrower of external capital without the necessity for gifts would certainly have been treated as an impractical visionary. 

Thoroughgoing land reform has made private landowners of 80 percent of the farmers, and their living standards have been broadly improved. The Joint 

Commission (American-Chinese) for Rural Reconstruction (JCRR) has achieved things not imagined 10 years ago. In the past 5 years there has been a 40-percent increase in gross national product (GNP), about a 20-percent increase in per capita GNP, a 20-percent rise in agricultural production, and an 80-percent gain in industrial output. Literacy is over 90 percent. Cholera, typhus, malaria, scarlet fever, and smallpox have been virtually eradicated. 

Taiwan was one of the first countries receiving U.S. aid to adopt a broad selfhelp program, President Chiang's "19 points." Taiwan also was, as a consequence of this and of its potential for growth, the first Far Eastern country selected for U.S. assistance in accelerated economic development. 

So long as Taiwan must carry one of the world's heaviest defense burdens, on a per capita basis, generous loan terms in dollars and an adequate surplus food program will be necessary. We have adjusted our aid program to Taiwan's needs and its growing economic vigor. 

No supporting assistance grants to Taiwan are being provided this year, and none is proposed for fiscal year 1963. This approach is based on the assumption of continued availability of substantial Public Law 480, title I, sales of surplus U.S. wheat, flour, cotton, tobacco, barley, and vegetable oil. A continued largescale development loan program and a small development grant program for technical assistance in agriculture, economic policy, and government management also are required. 

[Security deletion.] 

The progress now evident in Japan, Malaya, Thailand, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Hong Kong, I wish to note again, has been achieved in places which the pessimists (most called themselves realists) of the last decade called hopeless or sure victims of the Communist flood sweeping over Asia. There has been

no Marshall plan in Asia, no effective regional economic organization, payments union or common market, no Inter-Asian_Development Bank or Alliance for Progress. In the past, at least, the Far East has not been prepared for such regional associations. However, closer association is now developing in a variety of forms. 

The record of progress in the Far East of the past 15 years gives us greater confidence in our approaches to the problems of the more troubled nations of the region-Korea, Vietnam, and Laos-and for persevering in our programs among the neutrals-Burma, Cambodia, and Indonesia. 

The nature and history of our commitment to maintain the independence of the Republic of Korea are well known to this committee. Here economic progress has been slow, the aid program has been costly, the evidence of success still tentative if not largely lacking. The devastation of the Korean war has been repaired and the economic dislocation caused by the division of Korea partially remedied. The Republic has been defended. Our economic aidabout $2.4 billion from 1954 through 1961-has been vital in these achievements. 

But the economic statistics remain disheartening: More than 2 million unemployed or substantially underemployed in a population of 25 million; exports not much more than one-tenth of imports; national income rising just enough to match population growth. Political freedom there has suffered what we hope will be only a temporary setback. 

The military regime now in power has given good indications that it will be more competent than its predecessors in management of Korea's economic affairs, more effective in launching the long overdue drive for real economic progress. For the first time, a serious effort is being made to restore relations with Japan. If successful, this would bring some annual Japanese payments through a financial settlement, a sound trading relationship which would expand Korea's exports, substantial Japanese private investments, and possibly Japanese participation in economic assistance loans to Korea. The military junta has taken Draconian action against graft, bribery, and corruption in the past civilian regimes and in business against hoodlum terror, blackmail, smuggling, and theft of military supplies. It has expanded programs of public works, attacked the problem of the usurious loans which kept the farmers in near bondage, reduced tax evasion. It has drafted a 5-year plan for economic development and accepted the advisory services of American exports in devising new economic and fiscal policies. 

We pronose to continue our contribution, through supporting assistance, of a substantial portion of South Korea's essential import requirements. The local currency proceeds of this commodity assistance become an important contribution to the maintenance of the nation's defense forces and to economic development projects. The commodities to be supplied are limited largely to fertilizer. petroleum products, industrial raw materials and semifinished products, and spare parts for replacement. The development grant program of technical assistance has been concentrated on fewer, critical fields. A substantial increase in development loans is expected, primarily in the fields of electric power, mining, and transportation. Food for peace (Public Law 480) sales will be required on a large scale to provide food grains, fats, and oils and cotton. 

[Security deletion.] 

Vietnam's struggle for survival against Communist undercover aggression and rebellion needs no further description by me. But as critical as the situation today may appear, I suggest that the outlook also was even darker in the early davs of the southern republic 7 years ago. In 1955 it seemed extremely doubtful that any form of centralized stable government could be formed. The French had withdrawn and the Cao Dai, Hoa Hao, and Binh Xyuen sects and remnants of the Vietminh seemed capable of destroying all prospects for orderly government.

Economic progress since 1955 had been substantial until the Communist terrorists increased their attacks in 1960-61. 

A series of significant stens have been taken to meet this challenge. In the economic and social realm these include fiscal and exchange reforms, a general effort to raise domestic revenues, initiation or expansion of activities designed to demonstrate the advantages of a non-Communist system, especially among the rural population. There is no hope for an improvement of ties between the villagers and Saigon. 

Our aid programs are crucial to several aspects of the counterinsurgency effort. 

We are giving it the highest priority. Continued, large-scale supporting assist

ance grants and a substantial development grant program for both short-range and long-range activities are proposed. Public Law 480 deliveries will be an important contribution to our program. 

[Security deletion.] 

Our aid to Laos is often criticized as a huge expenditure in a tiny country, separate and distinct from the wider problem and danger in all southeast Asia. 

The fact is, of course, that our efforts in Laos are very much related to the security of Vietnam and of Thailand and may have a bearing on the ultimate status of Cambodia. There also is the misconception that our aid is confined solely to paying the Royal Lao Government troops and otherwise plugging the Government's budget deficits. This has been the paramount requirement for 

U.S. economic aid, but more than most people realize is being done with small, inexpensive projects that reach the people of the countryside. I think it will be worthwhile to describe these projects, not only to get a better picture of what we are doing and propose to do in Laos, but to appreciate the meaning of such terms as "community development” in our general presentation. 

[Security deletion.] 

The rural development program has supported about 2,500 village self-help projects since fiscal year 1959. The program has operated on the principle that the village itself will choose the project it wants-an access road or a school, a marketplace or a small dam. These projects are reviewed by the regional government. The AID representative participates in this review. 

The village involved must be found to be responsible. A school is not approved unless a teacher is available; no dispensary unless a medical technician is available. No further projects are approved until one is completed. 

Some 500 such small projects now are being carried out. This has brought the various Lao Government functionaries and people around to working together, for the first time. It has awakened an interest in both Vientiane and in the provincial capitals in the progress of small village development and it has developed a feeling of participation in and allegiance to the Lao Government. 

More than half the costs of the rural self-help projects have been borne by the local people and the balance by AID or AID-generated funds. 

In Luang Prabang, for example, three villages and 500 acres of land have been assured a year-around water supply by a dam which cost the United States the time of an engineer to help in the design and to make a dozen supervisory trips to Luang Prabang, plus $385 for cement. 

These small projects and similar efforts in the information field can have considerable influence in developing resistance to Communist propaganda and pressures. When a coalition government is formed, aid may be our most effective instrument in Laos. 

The three nonalined or neutral nations of southeast Asia-Indonesia, Burma, and Cambodia-seek to maintain their independence with a minimum of outside domination. They share in varying degree the problems of acute economic underdevelopment and some beginning aspirations for progress that are more actively expressed in the countries we have already described. And in varying degree they are targets for the Communist scheme of conquest in southeast Asia. Indonesia, with 95 million people, is the world's fifth most populous nation, with great natural resources and potential for trade. Cambodia, about the size of Missouri and with a population of 5 million, is the country "in the middle" of the Indochina peninsula. Burma, on the southern border of Communist China and the eastern flank of the Indian subcontinent, has just recently returned to military rule. 

We can recall when Indonesia, only a few years ago, was torn by rebellion and separatist movements and seemed on the verge of dissolution. Practically the entire Burmese cabinet was assassinated at a cabinet meeting in 1947. I vividly recall visiting Burma in 1957 when terrorist raids prevented the railroads from running at night and often by day. Earlier, white and red flag Communist insurgents and minority groups seemed certain to tear Burma to pieces. 

Cambodia has escaped internal or external Communist attack, but the outlook for this former Indochina state seemed hopeless when it was given independence in 1955.

Indonesia, of course, has been in a state of almost constant economic crisis. 

The current mobilization to gain control of West Irian, or Dutch West New Guinea, has intensified the military drain on the budget and entire economy. 

Inflationary pressures, a rise in the note issue, declining exports in 1961 and increasing complications in trade due in part to fluctuating world prices and a

severe drought in 1961 are some of the elements of Indonesia's economic distress. Foreign exchange reserves have declined more than 50 percent in 9 months. The price of rice quadrupled during a 6-month period. 

This economic setback and the New Guinea crisis have come just as the Indonesian Government appeared ready and determined to launch a serious drive to mobilize the nation's great economic potential. The Government committed itself to this objective in an 8-year plan adopted last year. President Kennedy sent a United States economic survey team to Indonesia last summer, with President Sukarno's agreement, to make recommendations for future United States aid policy. The team's report has just been submitted to the President and U.S. agencies concerned. 

[Security deletion.] 

Substantial U.S. technical assistance, development loans, and agricultural commodities clearly will be needed to help Indonesia resume economic development.

In Cambodia, our assistance has concentrated upon education and agriculture and assistance in the maintenance of the country's internal and external security. 

We furnish essential imports such as petroleum and industrial materials under supporting assistance; the local currency proceeds of the sale of these commodities are contributed to help finance the military budget and economic development projects. 

[Security deletion.] 

This, in outline, is the program we propose. I hope that I have heeded the advice of your committee's Study Mission and avoided when possible the "large orbital words of economic development, political stability, democratic institutions and national independence." I hope that trying to avoid these orbital flights hasn't grounded me. I wish to conclude with the observation that U.S. aid effort has been and will be a vital instrument of our foreign policy in the Far East. At least in my experience in the Far East our achievements in the 

1940's and 1950's have been both substantial and, seen from the spot and at the time, well beyond reasonable expectations. 

As a private citizen in the Far East, I was impressed by the objectives and wisdom of the foreign assistance program, so much so that what I was doing seemed unimportant. I am honored to have the opportunity now to serve you in the task of U.S. assistance to the Far East. 

Mr. HARRIMAN.  I want to express my gratification to be permitted to testify again before this distinguished committee. Some of you remember back in 1947 we started with Interim Aid and then the Marshall plan, NATO, and later on mutual security program in 1952. 

This committee, I believe, can be very proud of what it did during that period. The Marshall plan succeeded beyond anyone's fondest dreams. It was a bipartisan measure. Dear old Senator Vandenberg used to call it "an unpartisan measure," in other words, it was an American program. It succeeded, as I say, beyond anyone's fondest hopes. 

The European nations are now more vigorous than they have ever been in their history. Their economies are expanding. They are being of assistance in the worldwide problems that face us, not only in Europe but also assisting us in the needs of the underdeveloped nations.

I became convinced when I was Ambassador to the Soviet Union during the war that Stalin intended to take over Western Europe because of the dislocations of the war. He never contemplated the 

United States would have the initiative or the wisdom to develop the Marshall plan. Stalin was frustrated and now the Communists are held at bay and everywhere in Western Europe have been rolled back. 

Now we face a situation in the world which started with the point 4 program that President Truman proposed in his administration, to give assistance to the developing nations. Considerable prog-

ress has been made, of which you are familiar as you have followed it from year to year. We now come back to the committee with the hope that you will carry forward, and our strong recommendation is that you do carry forward, in the Far East, which is the area of my responsibility.

It is quite clear that Mr. Khrushchev now looks to the underdeveloped countries as the part of the world where communism will spread, where the advances can be made. He no longer looks to Europe. In fact, he has told me so specifically, that Europe and the United States would be the last to succumb to worldwide advance of communism. 

I think that due to the resiliencies of the countries themselves and the help of the United States, we can look forward to frustrating Khrushchev's ambitions as Stalin's were, providing we show the same determination and persistence.

Conditions are quite different, of course. These countries require aid to improve their standard of living, and to become industrialized and able to get a balanced economy in which the people can hope to take advantage of modern science and industrial development. The standard of living, of course, with the exception of Japan, is very low but it is rising.

I have just come back from a trip to a number of the countries in the Far East, and I am very much gratified by the progress that has been made in a number of countries. We read in the papers about the difficulties in southeast Asia, but very little is said of the growing strength of the area.

The most outstanding example, of course, is Japan. It has expanded its gross national product by about 9 percent during the past decade, which is greater than in the Soviet Union and belies Mr. 

Khrushchev's claims that it is only through communism that a country can have rapid industrial progress. 

Japan has done a good job in agriculture, land reform, and through new methods she has been able to expand her agriculture so that she is only, if I remember correctly, importing 15 percent of her food. 

One thing that is interesting about Japan is that it proves again what has previously been shown to be the case, as a country becomes industrialized our exports to that country grow. Rather an interesting figure is that our exports have risen from 1955, when they stood at $650 million; last year they went to $1,740 million. In other words, nearly a threefold increase in that period of 6 years. That shows again that as Japan expanded her gross national product, our trade grew.

She is our second largest single customer, and actually the largest importer of American agricultural goods. We hear a great deal about the imports from Japan, but we hear very little about our exports. 

Therefore I want to point out that for the last 5 years the United States has sold about $1,700 million more to Japan than we have bought from Japan. 

Other countries are moving ahead. It is very gratifying to find in the Philippines a new administration. They had won an election on an anticorruption campaign, and they are attempting to put new vigor and vitality into their government. They have a development program which we believe is worth backing. There has been a little

lull in the Philippine growth, although there has been progress ever since the war in reconstruction. 

Korea is a difficult country economically because of the need to continue a large military establishment of about 600,000, about which the military has testified. There is a new group who have taken over, of young army officers. Many have been trained in the United States. 

They have a desire to improve their country and have energy to stamp out corruption and smuggling and other immoral practices which had plagued Korea in the post-Korean war period. 

In Taiwan in China, progress has been made in agriculture and industry, although there again there is a need for maintaining a large military establishment and therefore the continuing need of assistance. 

One interesting thing in the area is that you see the disastrous effect of the Communist organization in mainland China on agricultural production, not only caused by weather, but the disaster of their commune system, and the loss in agricultural production. 

The reverse is true in the free world, and proves again that farmers owning their own land with an incentive system, free enterprise, can outproduce the Communist system. It is a fact that communism has failed in this most important of all production-agriculture. 

Mr. Khrushchev, as you have noticed, held a meeting of the Communist Party Central Committee several weeks ago in order to find out what was wrong with Soviet agriculture because they couldn't produce enough food to feed their people adequately, in spite of the enormous agricultural lands that exist in the Soviet Union. 

In an area-in Laos and Vietnam-the military situation is causing difficulties, and our military and economic assistance bears that in mind. It is difficult in Laos to know what next year will hold forth because there is under negotiation a settlement of Laos by peaceful means. There is the International Agreement which was almost agreed to in Geneva last year that required implementation by the formation of a government of national union, which has not yet taken office. When that will occur or whether or when, I can't prophesy. Therefore our figures on Laos are estimates of what may be required for a new government. It is very important that when a new government is established, it get aid from the West to strengthen the non-Communist group of the Lao Government and make possible economic progress. 

South Vietnam: You are informed about the military situation.

There has been progress in economic growth, and now considerable emphasis is being given to those things which will help most in strengthening antisubversion, assist the population to withstand the Communist subversion movement. It is a village program and has a number of different aspects.

Thailand has a new program of antisubversion and economic development which is important in making that country impervious to the same sort of thing that happened to Vietnam. 

Cambodia, Burma, and Indonesia seek aid in programs of economic assistance which will tend to, in our judgment, offset the influence from the Communist bloc and also make it possible for those countries to move ahead in a free society. 

I haven't touched on all the countries. Australia and New Zealand are strong forces in the Far East, and are assisting some of the countries, giving technical assistance, and aid through the Colombo plan.

I could go on in a good deal of detail. I do want to close by saying that we are in the middle of the stream. To turn back would be almost unthinkable. I do believe the program that is being submitted is one which will help progress, and I feel optimistic about the longrun future in the Far East. It will be slow because it will take a long time before these underdeveloped countries will be able to develop their agriculture and industry in order to break through to the kind of position that Japan has achieved. 

After they once break through, we should hope that they would have the same kind of development through trade rather than aid. 

There has been practically no aid to Japan in this last decade. Of course, we did help Japan with GARIOA, which they will repay in part.

I think we can look forward in the future to a reduction of assistance and very much increased trade with these countries which will add to our own prosperity, providing we stick to these programs long enough.

In the meantime, there will be an increasing number of development loans rather than forms of grant support in this year's program, which is an indication of a healthy advance. 

I think it is fair to say as far as the State Department, and as far as I am personally concerned, we have a great confidence in the direction of the AID organization, and I am particularly happy to be here with my colleague, Mr. Janow, with whom we will be working closely. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

Mr. Janow, you may proceed, sir, and we will direct our questions to you and the Secretary as a team after your statement. 

STATEMENT OF HON. SEYMOUR J. JANOW, ASSISTANT ADMINIS- TRATOR, BUREAU FOR FAR EAST, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. JANOW. Mr. Chairman, it is a great honor for me to appear before the committee for the first time in support of a program which I as a private citizen, consider one of the great endeavors of our time. 

I am very much aware that I, after 3 months in the Agency, cannot or need not tell this committee about the emergence of the present foreign aid program or its rationale. These things I must learn from you.

Perhaps I can tell you something of interest from my experiences in the Far East where I spent almost all of the last 18 years. As a new arrival in Washington this winter I found impressions of the Far East, also of our aid programs there, rather dominated by the bad news from Laos, Vietnam, and Indonesia. 

I have also found here some tendency to see the Far East as an area of confusion and disorder, containing little for hope or progress, a view that it is an area antagonistic to us where we are bound to be embarrassed in our aid efforts by scandals, and where politically and militarily we are doomed to failures. 

These dark predictions about the future are an old story to me in the Far East. Japan in 1946 had 40 percent of its big cities destroyed, its industries almost entirely stopped, no friends or trade, no merchant

shipping. It was stripped of its empire, seemed unable to feed its population, and was seen by many of those in the occupation as a hope- 

Îess case.

Hong Kong in 1951 was expected to be gobbled up at any moment; if it wasn't, because of the insecurity no one would invest there and the place would stagnate and be unable to manage the huge influx of refugees that it was getting. Taiwan's days in 1950 were numbered. 

Malaya, Burma, and the Philippines in the early 1950's were fighting what seemed to be a losing battle against the Communist guerrillas, who were reported to have deep political roots in the countryside. 

Recently we are hearing reports that seem somewhat familiar to me that Laos is lost to the Communists. I suggest that the record of the past refutes much of the pessimism of the past for Asia. 

We have a good record of solid accomplishment in the Far East. It has not become an Atlantic community. It doesn't have the forms of regional organization that are familiar in the Atlantic community. 

But free Asia in the 1960's is quite different and more attuned to our ways than ever seemed possible, at least to me in the 1950's. 

The Governor has talked of our accomplishments in Japan. I would like to add a personal note. I was in the headquarters of 

General MacArthur until 1948. My last assignment there in 1946 was the setting of an exchange rate for Japan. I clearly remember the discussions in the fixing of that exchange rate when I represented to Mr. Dodge and others the Japanese view that the rate should not be established until the level of exports had reached $50 million a month. 

Very important members of the Washington delegation threw up their hands and said that might not be achieved for 10 years.

Currently they are exporting at the rate of $350 million a month. 

The exchange rate we fixed by the way in 1948, 360 yen to $1, has turned out to be one of the most stable in the world. 

As the Governor mentioned, we have furnished Japan about $1.6 billion in food and essential raw materials during the course of the occupation. Now the Japanese have agreed to repay a substantial part of this aid.

Japan has completed reparations agreements with Burma, the 

Philippines, Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia, totaling $1.2 billion.

They are servicing these agreements at the rate of $70 million a year. 

For the first half of 1961, Japan's foreign assistance, including reparations, totaled $231 million. If that was kept up, that would be at the rate of nearly a half billion a year in foreign assistance of all forms. This is a great success story. 

I think it is very important to us in Asia because it has been achieved within a democratic framework and via a private enterprise system. Our assistance didn't do this. Japanese energy did it, of course. But our trading policy and foreign policy and our military strength in the area have made the growth of Japan possible. 

The important thing about Japan in this context is that it gives us reason to suppose that the experience there can be repeated elsewhere in Asia. Certainly in terms of natural resources per capita, it could not be argued that Japan is more blessed than Taiwan or Thailand or the Philippines or Vietnam or perhaps not much more blessed than southern Korea.

Japan had the advantages of organization, education, experience, and stability. But from what the Japanese achieved in the 60 years between 1860 and 1920 it is possible to imagine that some part of this great modernization, which the Japanese did for themselves, we can help the less advanced nations of Asia do in the decade of the 1960's.

As the Governor mentioned, there are significant success stories also in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Thailand, and Malaya. And there are encouraging developments in the Philippines. The important thing to remember is that South Vietnam, given a period of peace, might very well become a bright economic spot in Asia. This is hopeful, but 

I would argue that this is not a wishful basis for our aid request. 

I don't want to minimize the difficulties of most of the new nations; except for Thailand, all are former colonies, many of them truncated from their previous size. I do want to repeat that in fact the story in Asia is that much more has actually been achieved in the 1940's and 1950's than ever seemed possible at the time. 

The Far East has been a major recipient of U.S. aid and the figures are large. I don't think that the commitment that we have asked for Asia is out of proportion with the rest of the foreign aid program, and in fact may compare quite favorably. 

I have prepared a simple summary table on page 5 which indicates our aid for fiscal year 1963 and compares it to the two previous fiscal years. I don't think I need repeat that.

There is some growth in supporting assistance. But that arises in the course of the indications of a revival of economic activity in Korea, and because of our intention to fulfill a 1959 commitment to Burma. 

The development lending category for 1963 is larger than the previous year. The reason it is is because our development lending program was slow to get started in 1962, because we in the next year expect to be able to give some substantial loans to the Philippines, to Thailand, where there will no longer be any supporting assistance, to Korea, and possibly to Indonesia.

The development grant program is not very much larger. 

I would call to your attention the important part that Public Law 480 plays in our programs in Asia. I think it may very well play a larger part in Asia than in the other regions. 

I should point out to this committee that this program has been substantially prepared months ago before the new management of the Agency was in place, but I have found in my review that it faithfully reflects the intentions of the legislation, and I have come to respect much of the talent and energy that I found in the Agency. 

I won't repeat the categories that apply, but I would like to talk very briefly about each of the areas. I would like to begin in Thailand.

I would say, like Japan, Thailand had a prewar history of independence. It has the potential to achieve a very strong economy. 

Its per capita income is not high. It is about $100 a year. 

It has a growth rate of 4 to 5 percent annually. The important things about the Thai situation are that the Thai currency is convertible; its economy is relatively a free one; its foreign reserves are growing steadily.

Thailand's leadership is obviously making a strong effort at economic development. We have had a U.S. economic survey team there, and President Kennedy has personally expressed our determination to accelerate economic development in that country. 

In the category of self-help, I think the report from Thailand is encouraging. We are stopping supporting assistance at the end of the fiscal year 1962. Instead, they will have long-term loans. We are continuing a grant program, but this grant program is in our interest, and it is entirely devoted to technical assistance in the fields of education and agriculture. 

The Thai are a good risk. Any loans that we make to Thailand, in my opinion, have very high probability of being repaid; and more than that, the Thai can afford to pay a reasonable interest rate. 

The Thai have agreed that in the future they will not expect us to support their economy with local currency loans. They will look to us only for external capital requirements. There is no Public 

Law 480 program there. 

Malaya, Thailand's neighbor to the south, is another bright spot. 

Malaya won its decade-long fight against the Communist insurgents. 

I can remember in the mid-1950's visiting my clients there and being met with armored cars at the airport, being driven very fast along the road for fear of interception and sleeping in a compound that had guards patroling it. 

It seemed impossible that there would be personal security, economic development, and an end to the communal issue in Malaya in the 1950's.

Now, as you know, not only is Malaya prosperous with a per capita income of about $280 but, for example, it had some public bonds issued recently for Government activities, that were oversubscribed. 

If you have been there, you are aware of the wonderful condition of the roads, highways, the railway plan and the growth of their mines. 

Presently Malaya is trying to form a larger confederation. This, my opinion, is one of the most promising events in southeast Asia. 

If it is successful, it will include Singapore, North Borneo, Brunei and Sarawak. in Malaya is not an aid recipient for us and has not made application for loans. In the past it received two small DLF loans. [Security deletion.]

Across the China Sea is the Philippines. I think all of you members of the committee remember that in the period 1946 to 1951 there were about 30,000 Huks who were thought to be in more or less active opposition to the Government. 

When I was there during that period it was impossible to travel by night from Manila to Clark Air Force Base or to Baguio: and, again, you would not suppose in 1950 or 1951 that this threat could be completely eliminated so that it could be talked about only historically. 

I remember the great change that Magsaysay made when he was Defense Minister in 1951, and what a wonderful leader he was for the Filipinos, in fact, for all Asia when he was President of the Philippines.

Economic progress in the Philippines has not been steady. It has been sporadic, and obviously the economy has been plagued by favoritism and corruption.

I want to point out to you that President Macapagal immediately upon his inauguration in December, eliminated exchange controls and import controls, lowered tariffs on essentials, increased customs on nonessentials, and made the peso fully convertible. 

I talked with all members of the cabinet, except the President, less than 2 weeks ago on the question of stabilization. I was very encouraged to hear that if anything the peso is too strong. 

The administration does seem prepared to attack its agricultural problems, and to reverse the situation where a potentially rich agricultural country was a net importer of rice last year of 144,000 tons. 

The Philippines has good prospects for attracting foreign capital. 

The World Bank is very interested. They have a 4-year plan for the 

Philippines which may involve a very substantial extension of credit. 

We have reviewed the IBRD plan, as well as the President's plan. 

The Eximbank is concerned with it. The commercial banks of New 

York have recently doubled their revolving commercial credit line for the Philippines.

So far, we have programed some funds for development projects. 

In addition to this, we are continuing our assistance in the grant field, principally in the areas of technical assistance to education, agriculture, community development, minerals and other resources. 

Taiwan is an area where I hesitate to speak exhaustively because of the superior knowledge of Dr. Judd on all aspects of this area. But 

I will mention a few figures that I am sure are all familiar to you. 

In the past 5 years there has been a 40-percent increase in gross national product; 20-percent increase in per capita income; 20-percent rise in agricultural production; 80-percent gain in industrial output. 

There is almost universal literacy, and an elimination or a great reduction in the major diseases of cholera, malaria, typhus, scarlet fever and smallpox.

Taiwan was one of the first countries receiving U.S. aid to adopt a broad self-help program. This is President Chiang's "19 points.' 99 Taiwan is carrying one of the world's heaviest defense burdens on a per capita basis. In examining the AID program to Taiwan, one discovers how hard that program really is. It contains this year no supporting assistance. We will be giving them a substantial amount of 

Public Law 480 commodities. But for the rest, it will be on a loanfor-dollars basis. 

While the terms of these dollar repayable loans are soft, I submit that this is not another term for "gift." 

In my opinion, it is perfectly reasonable to assume that the Republic of China will be capable of servicing and repaying these loans.

The grant program there is very small. It is for technical assistance in a few areas, devoted very largely to improving the climate for private enterprise.

I would like to sum up by saying Japan, Malaya, Thailand, the Philippines and Hong Kong are all areas where progress has been made. These are areas that the "realist" of the last decade saw as hopeless victims of the Communist flood. 

There has been no Marshall plan in Asia. There has been no effective regional economic organization. There has been no payments union or Common Market, no inter-Asian bank or Alliance for Progress in Asia.

But on a bilateral basis I submit that the progress is good, and there are indications now that there will be an emerging regional cooperation.

The problem areas I haven't talked about yet: Korea, Vietnam and 

Laos, Cambodia and Indonesia. 

I will say in the Republic of Korea there are some disheartening elements. Unemployment or underemployment of 2 million in a population of 24 million. Exports only 10 percent of visible imports; and, of course, some retrogression in political freedom. 

There are two new big elements in Korea which I wish to emphasize to this committee.

One is the fact that the military administration for the first time really seems determined to eliminate the graft and corruption that has ridden that society, not only in business but also the hoodlums referred to in the press, in the customs and in the Government. I submit that this is a new element. 

The second big change in Korea is the fact that for the first time I think you would say that the Koreans are making a serious effort to settle their differences with Japan. 

Settling their affairs with Japan will, first of all, give them an annual financial payment, whatever the terms of that are, and secondly, it will give them back their natural trading partner. 

During the occupation I once tried to negotiate a trade agreement between Japan and Korea, and I remember how important seaweed, apples, and fish products were in that trade agreement. 

These are the things which the Koreans probably cannot export to any other place in the world but to Japan. Not only will it give them an export market, but it will give them a source of investment capital, which can utilize with some Japanese management, what is Korea's major resource-its abundant, skilled and cheap labor. 

Korea has a very active, intelligent, well-trained, articulate population. I say these two developments in Korea are promising and are new.

Where Vietnam is concerned, I don't think I can tell this committee very much that you don't know. I will say that we think some significant steps have been taken in the economy as a consequence of the Staley mission. Real measures have been instituted and matters are currently being discussed at very high levels between our Government and theirs.

There is reform in their exchange rate and in their fiscal policies. 

We do expect, as a matter of fact, that the AID dollars will yield more local revenue.

So far as counterinsurgency is concerned, we are devoting a large part of our program to immediate effects. 

Our AID program to Laos is often criticized as a huge expenditure in a tiny country. But I think that sometimes the nature of the AID program to Laos is misunderstood, as well. per- Of course, we are supporting the budget of that government and mitting it to pay for soldiers. But [security deletion] it is not generally recognized that nearly one-fourth of our AID grants to Laos are going to small projects that reach the people directly. 

I would like, if I may, to tell you a little bit about the rural development program in Laos which has been supporting community development works in 2,500 villages since 1959.

It operates on the principle that the village itself will chose what it wants, an access road or school, marketplace, or small dam. These projects are reviewed by the regional government, and the AID representative participates in this review.

The village must be responsible. A school is not built unless a teacher is available, and no dispensary unless a medical technician is available. 

No additional project is started until the one is finished. About 500 such small projects are being carried out. This has brought the various 

Lao Government functionaries and people around to working together for the first time. It has had a salutary effect in the provincial capitals of the country.

In Luang Prabang, for example, three villages and 500 acres have been assured a year-round water supply by a dam that cost the United States the time of an engineer to help in the design and make a dozen trips to Luang Prabang, plus about $385 for cement. 

These small projects and similar efforts in the information field can have a considerable influence in developing resistance to Communist propaganda and pressures. 

[Security deletion.] 

Mr. JANOW. In all of the three nonalined countries, Indonesia, Burma, and Cambodia, we find the problems of underdevelopment. 

Indonesia has, as you know, 95 million people and is the world's fifth most populous nation.

I would like to recall that Indonesia only a few years ago was torn by rebellion and separatist movements and seemed on the verge of disintegration. I can recall when the entire Burmese Cabinet was assassinated in 1947. I visited Burma as late as 1957 and could not go anywhere by rail at night and often not by day.

Cambodia has escaped internal and external Communist attack. 

But the outlook for Cambodia seemed hopeless in 1955. It does not now seem hopeless.

Indonesia, of course, has been in a state of almost continuous economic crisis, and its present problems with the Dutch have worsened this. 

We had a large Public Law 480 program last year to assist them because of their drought. The economic setback is indeed serious. 

They have lost, I am told, almost the whole of their foreign exchange reserves. 

The price of rice in the cities has quadrupled in the last 6 months. 

Their situation is indeed desperate. 

Our program is not devoted to this. It is based on grants to help build their institutions and on loans that may follow the recommendations of the President's task force that has just returned and made its report.

In Cambodia, we have concentrated our assistance on education, agriculture, and military budgetary support. I have outlined the program for you previously.

I hope I have heeded the advice of your committee's study mission and avoided the large orbital words of "economic developinent," "democratic institutions," "national independence" and stayed to the facts as I have seen them.

I wish to conclude with the observation that in my experience of the 1940's, 1950's, seen from the spot, more or less, the achievements seem even beyond reasonable expectations. 

I have been a private citizen until 3 months ago, except for brief periods in the Government way back. I will say that I was very impressed by the objectives and wisdom of the foreign assistance program, and that I felt that what I was doing was relatively unimportant. 

I am very honored to have the opportunity to serve you in this endeavor. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Janow.

Mr. HARRIMAN. There is a program of assistance that is going on for about 50,000 refugees, as I recall it. There is also a substantial military program which is required in keeping the military establishment at a high level of efficiency.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Janow, I see that the large bulk of our supporting assistance in your area of the world goes to two countries, South Vietnam and Korea. Approximately [security deletion] of the $481 million requested in the bill goes to these two countries. 

Mr. JANOW. That is true, sir. It is a reflection of their military situation, as you know.

I would like to suggest to this committee, however, that we have not taken the principle that the level of our assistance to Vietnam or Korea would be determined by their budget requirements. 

In both countries, as you will see in the brown book, we have tried to analyze their import requirements. The things that are sent to 

Korea and Vietnam under supporting assistance are essential to our programs: Raw materials for industry, equipment, things of that kind.

The levels are determined by resource requirements and not by budget requirements.

These supporting assistance activities are necessary here because of the state of that economy. They are just not able to manage their balance of payments and provide the finances for the importing of these essential commodities. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Janow, I see that the total figure requested for supporting assistance for your area is $349 million. 

Mr. JANOW. Yes, sir.

Mr. JANOW. Yes, sir. The reason for this you know better than I. 

It is a question of these economies that have, first, little development, and secondly, a large military establishment. That combination, plus the strain of trying to manage an economic development program are the reasons. That is quite true, sir. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Janow, traditionally this committee every year cuts the amounts requested by the Executive.

Because such a large amount of the total supporting assistance requested is for this area of the world, it will be dangerous to cut this figure of $481 million this year by very much. 

That is the reason I asked the Secretary the questions on Laos; 

I wanted to see whether for instance, the [security deletion] in supporting assistance requested for Laos, might offer an opportunity for some savings. I certainly feel that if we suspended some of these programs which we have been carrying on in Laos, we are going to be able to make some cuts. I would certainly vote for cuts that were earmarked so that they would not be hurting the program in any particular area.

You then feel strongly that the figure of $349 million in supporting assistance for that area of the world can be justified? 

Mr. JANOW. I do, sir. As I pointed out earlier, the increase in the figure in 1963 arises from our funding [security deletion] a commitment made to Burma in 1959. That is the Mandalay highway.

There is an additional increase [security deletion] in the Korea allocation which reflects the revival of that economy since the junta took over. The stagnation that characterized 1961 is over. 

If you were to ask me what percentage I could see now of the $349 million that might be able to be reduced, I would say very little unless something would happen to our commitments [security deletion].

Mr. ZABLOCKI. What was the purpose of the Bill Smith secret-I 

shouldn't use the word "secret"-the Bill Smith visit with the princes, Souvanna Phouma and Souphannovong?

Mr. HARRIMAN. Sullivan? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Yes. He was your assistant and he was visiting 

Thailand, and then went to Laos to meet with the princes. What was the purpose of his mission? What did it accomplish? 

Today's paper says that Lao princes with whom he met "demand that all U.S. aid be halted in Laos in order to bring about and tighten the pressure for the establishment of a coalition government."

In view of this report, and the report of March 27, stating that you have advocated, Mr. Secretary, that, in order to bring about a coalition government, the key cabinet posts of interior and defense should be turned over to Souvanna Phouma and Souphannovong, the two princes that we have had some trouble with- Mr. HARRIMAN. This is an incorrect story. It goes back 1 year. 

The President decided a year ago that we should attempt to find a peaceful solution for Laos. There was a civil war going on. As a result of the initiative of the United States and others a cease-fire was finally established early in May and a conference of 14 nations was started at that time. That conference was involved in the international aspects of a neutral and independent Laos, and a substantial agreement was reached, tentative, depending upon developments in Laos itself. I will mention some of the important provisions of that agreement.

As I said before, I felt the Soviet Union was desirous of reaching this agreement, and I believe would honor it for the time being, at least. 

The important provisions are that all foreign military personnel should be removed and no further interference in the internal affairs be permitted from the outside; Laos should not be used as a corridor or in any way to interfere with the internal affairs of the neighboring countries. This is quite important because of its effect on South Vietnam.

There is a provision in this tentative agreement to the effect that the cochairmen, from the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom, should undertake to see that the provisions of the agreement are carried out.

The Soviet Union indicated that they meant they were going to police their northern neighbors, the Communist group. During this period of negotiation at Geneva, there were discussions at Zurich and several points within Laos concerning the formation of a government of national union, which would be brought about through a coalition between the so-called three princes who represented the three elements: Prince Boun Oum, who represented the Royal Lao Government, the rightwing; Souvanna Phouma, neutralist, and Souphannovong, who is one of the leaders in Pathet Lao who is considered to be Communist.

Progress has been made from time to time. And in those discussions there was general agreement among all the other countries. 

Practically all of the free countries involved believed that the two wings should be kept small in size and that there should be a substantial center in order to insure the neutrality of the country. Those independents would come not only from Souvanna Phouma's followers, but also from Vientiane, and would be the main group. 

The question of who controls defense and interior, obviously involves the physical control of the country. It was tentatively agreed by all concerned, except for General Phoumi, who was the Minister of Defense of the Royal Lao Government, that these should be in the control of the neutrals, not controlled by either wing, and should not be divided between the two because if they were the battle would go on. So this has been a difference which has been under discussion ever since the Zurich meeting between the three princes in June.

We are one of the countries that have agreed that the control of these central and important ministries should be held by the neutral group, but that both sides should have some participation in some of the positions in those ministries. 

The agreement, which was tentatively arrived at, provided for the integration of the three forces into one much smaller army loyal to the new government. The others were to be demobilized and the soldiers returned to private occupation. 

There is a very large number of men under arms in that country and probably four or five times as many as are needed for a normal peaceful operation and to maintain peace in the country. 

General Phoumi has not been willing to cooperate. That is one of the reasons why the aid which the chairman mentioned has been stopped for the last few months. In January it appeared as if he had come to an agreement, but when he got home he repudiated what was thought to be an agreement reached in Geneva.
