WEDNESDAY, APRIL 4, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

 10:40 a.m., Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding.

The committee meets this morning in executive session for the continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

The witness this morning is the Honorable Harlan Cleveland, As sistant Secretary of State for International Organization Affairs. 

Mr. Cleveland, I see you have a statement. You may proceed in any way you wish, sir.

STATEMENT OF HON. HARLAN CLEVELAND, ASSISTANT SECRE- TARY OF STATE FOR INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS 

Mr. CLEVELAND. Mr. Chairman, we always come up here with a mimeographed script, which I don't propose to read out loud. I would like to submit it for the record. It has a rough summary- 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. (The prepared statement of Mr. Cleveland is as follows:) 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I appear before you in support of the request of $148.9 million for U.S. voluntary contributions to a number of multilateral organizations. The breakdown of this item is shown on page 

25 of the green volume entitled "Agency for International Development-Worldwide Summary" and detailed justifications follow. 

This item amounts to about 4 percent of the total appropriation requested for the Act for International Development.

As can be seen from page 25, this authorization request is to cover U.S. contributions to 11 international programs. Most of them are carried out within the framework of the United Nations; three are for regional organizations; and one is for an ad hoc international consortium. They cover activities ranging from medical research to military forces-from resource surveys to the care and feeding of refugees. Their scope, of course, reflects the range of pressing international problems.

As we said last year, each program supports one or both of two basic aims of U.S. foreign policy: First, the promotion of peace and security; second, the promotion of economic and social growth, which is one of the best ways to get peace and security.

Each program listed has, in our view, a high priority in support of these foreign policy objectives. Each has been pioneered or cosponsored by the United 

States, and stands as a symbol of U.S. leadership in international cooperation for security and development. 

Some of the international programs to which the United States contributes are analogous in character to activities which we also help finance bilaterally. I 81496-62-pt. 4—7 705

therefore should explain briefly why the programs represented in this part of the presentation are carried out through multilateral agencies and how they complement the rest of the aid program before you. But first I should like to say that we do not see bilateral and multilateral assistance as an either-or proposition. Both types are needed-and probably will be needed for the indefinite future for solid, practical reasons.

The choice between national and international institutions for maintaining peace and security or for channeling economic and technical assistance is not a theoretical but a pragmatic one. In any given case, one route may be more feasible or desirable than the other or a combination of both may offer the best alternative. 

Mr. Chairman, we have prepared background papers on each of the 11 programs for which a total of $148.9 million is being requested. These memorandums set forth the highlights of each program, provide illustrative examples of the activities of the international agencies in question, and pay particular attention to the relationships and methods of coordination between our own bilateral program and the international agencies. They are between four and seven pages long and will be submitted for the record if you would like to have them. 

If it is agreeable with the committee, I shall note the functional categories of the programs covered by this appropriation request and then proceed to an itemby-item discussion. 

For peace and security operations we propose a U.S. contribution of $1.3 million for the U.N. Emergency Force in the Middle East, looking to loans to be authorized elsewhere for continuing assistance to the U.N. military operations in the Congo and the Middle East after July 1, 1962. 

For economic aid and technical assistance we propose contributions totaling $115.1 million-$34.3 million for the U.N. in the Congo; $50 million for the expanded U.N. technical assistance program and the preinvestment work of the Special Fund; $0.6 million for the young program of the Commission for 

Technical Cooperation in Africa; $0.2 million for the work of the Asian Productivity Organization; and $30 million for our share of the international consortium which is helping to develop the waters of the Indus Basin. 

For assistance to children and mothers we propose to contribute $12 million to the U.N. Children's Fund.

For the care of refugees we propose to contribute $17.2 million to maintain the people still homeless in the aftermath of the Arab-Israel war. 

For the support of science we propose to contribute $3.3 million-$1.5 million for the NATO science program, $1,250,000 for the International Atomic Energy Agency, and $500,000 for the medical research program of the World Health Organization. 

As we go through these items, Mr. Chairman, you will note that many of them are the result of U.S. initiatives over the past several years. You will also note recurring evidence that U.S. contributions in the past have served as seed money to attract rising contributions from an increasing number of other nations-permitting a gradual but encouraging decline in U.S. shares of total budgets. And I trust you will agree with me as we go along that each of these programs does, in fact, support directly the basic aims of U.S. foreign policy. 

I do not, of course, appear before you as a spokesman for the international agencies I appear as the spokesman for U.S. national interest in them. It is my duty to be critical-to weigh carefully the shortcomings as well as the accomplishments of the international agencies. Let me mention several limitations which temper our assessment of the value of these international institutions at the present time. 

Looking backward for the moment, it seems to me that we have been going through a necessary period of initial organization and experimentation. This applies to the U.N. itself, its specialized agencies, the countries benefiting from these programs, and those which have contributed to them-all of which now know much more about this business than they did a dozen years ago. 

Certainly the need for further experimentation is by no means over. 

I hope that nothing I shall say will detract from the genuine sense of excitement and accomplishment that we feel about the pioneering work that has been done in the past years. After all, this has been a completely unprecedented and therefore uncharted field of endeavor; there is nothing in our history books to foreshadow the emergence of such a capacity for international action in the interests of mankind.

Nevertheless, it strikes me that with this much experience behind us, we are now in a position to take a hard look at the successes and failures of the past; to establish a clear sense of direction which could not have existed in the early years of our work; to clarify our objectives; and to devise ways to more effectively mobilize, organize, and apply our resources in the future. 

In this authorization and appropriation process, members of the committees in the House and Senate have raised questions about the nature of our "commitments" to these international organizations. 

I have sought on such occasions to indicate that any arrangement we make in our negotiations is an ad referendum one, always subject to our respective constitutional processes. This situation applies to such emergency programs as the 

Congo operation as well as to pledging conferences which may occur before we have concluded the appropriation process or to consortium groups such as the one existing in the Indus waters plan. 

In our presentation last year of this particular section of the AID appropriation, a series of questions was raised about the extent to which the U.S. Government commits itself to the support of these programs without prior congressional authorization. This is a problem inherent in our membership in international agencies and one which we have been discussing with Members of both Houses.

One way of helping to deal with it is to look ahead, as best we can on the basis of present knowledge. With your permission, I therefore should like to discuss the dimensions and directions that we have in mind for these programs over the next few years,

With respect to the United Nations Special Fund and technical assistance program, our representatives at the last pledging conference indicated a hope that the goal of $150 million for these two programs would be reached within the next few years. The U.S. Government would match 40 percent of contributions of other governments in order to achieve this target-a formula approved by the 

Congress last year.

Our present estimate is that we will require $50 million in 1963, but if the eventual goal is reached the U.S. Government would expect to contribute $60 million. 

This goal is an objective which can be reached in the next few years, especially in view of the U.N. decade of development which the United Nations launched at the last General Assembly, largely on U.S. initiative. 

With respect to the United Nations fund for the Congo, the overall dimension is less clear. For the time being we believe it to be in our interest to channel our economic assistance to the Congo through the United Nations. We would hope other governments would do likewise. 

As you know, our economic assistance has been provided with a stipulation that the amounts be used for U.S. purchases and subject to various other provisions of the AID legislation. The United Nations umbrella for assistance of this type should prevent unilateral action on the part of certain governments whose objectives may not be the rehabilitation of the Congo and its development as a sovereign and viable economy. 

In the case of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, I do not see at this time any sizable decrease in the amount of assistance we are making available to meet the minimum food, shelter, and other requirements of the refugees in the Middle East. 

We have sought through various other devices, as recommended by the Appropriations Committee several years ago, to reduce the cash outlay by utilizing surplus foods and local currencies available to the U.S. Government. We will continue to use such techniques and at the same time seek to reach agreements with certain governments in which these refugees are located in an effort to reduce the financial burden on the U.S. Government. 

I do not expect any major changes in the United Nations Children's Fund, a program which has successfully assisted governments to carry out long-range health and nutrition activities of benefit to the youth of many underdeveloped areas. This program has been financed through increasing contributions from other governments and private sources, and I believe the program can continue to expand without any increase in our contributions. 

Our request for the United Nations Emergency Force provides for a voluntary contribution for the period January 1 through June 30, 1962-a contribution which helps to reduce the assessments of member states least able to pay. 

As you know, the U.N. refinancing program now underway is designed to cover peace-keeping costs for 18 months beyond June of 1962. We therefore

expect that after that date our share of UNEF costs will drop to the 32.02 percent level of our regular assessments. 

In the case of the International Atomic Energy Agency operational program. we believe we have not yet reached the stage where we can integrate all of this voluntary contribution into the regular assessed budget of the Agency. As you may know, nations have established nuclear reactors for peaceful purposes in a number of countries and we believe it to be in our interest to provide technical assistance and training for the operation of these reactors until such time as governments themselves can provide the manpower and skills. 

The special programs of the World Health Organization, you will note, have been reduced considerably from last year's appropriation request. Apart from the voluntary contribution for medical research, no funds are being requested this year for voluntary contributions to WHO. For malaria eradication, adequate funds are on hand to finance the program's budget needs at its current level until the schedule for absorption into the regular budget is completed in 1964.

Our participation in the Indus Waters Agreement will continue over the next decade, this being the second appropriation request. Progress on this major undertaking has begun to accelerate; more refined engineering data has been assembled; contracts for the first important works have been awarded-to two groups of American firms; and the callups for our share of the financing have begun to increase. As more precise specifications and plans are developed, we will be directing our attention to a close examination of their financial implications.

There is one program for which we have no request for funds but which we expect will be firmed up in the course of the spring. This is the world food program-which is a 3-year experimental program now being planned with the United Nations and the Food and Agriculture Organization. It is designed to meet emergency food requirements resulting from chronic malnutrition, school lunch needs for children, and development activities which can be financed directly or otherwise through the provision of food. 

We will be back up here consulting with you when we know more about the details of the program as there may well be a need for some AID funds for this program during fiscal year 1963. 

These are the prospects as we currently see them as far as the levels of programs are concerned. Getting these programs going and expanding them to these levels has been the main task of the international agencies over the past 10 to 15 years. By and large they are now entering a new phase. 

In this second phase of the life of international organizations, there is a need for some administrative tidying up for a clarification of function-for an improvement in coordination both at the headquarters level and in the field. 

International agencies have their administrative and political problems and frustration. Life with them is no bed of roses. There is nothing surprising in this; it could hardly be otherwise given the inevitable growing pains of new organization taking on unprecedented tasks of enormous complexity. 

But the growth of these institutions, all of which in historical perspective are still in their infancy, is nevertheless a major success story. They have proved that they can survive; they have endured their early growing pains; and they have acquired what is, on balance, an extraordinary capacity to tackle jobs of huge dimension and great promise. 

To restore order to a nation far gone into chaos and civil war; to patrol a contested area for 5 years with but a single incident; to work toward the eradication of crippling diseases; to offer newly emerging nations support for their own organization of technical assistance; to plot a worldwide weather reporting system; to offer a fighting chance to tens of millions of children; to assemble scientists from all over the world in a search for new sources of energy-these are some of the many assignments of international agencies, most of which are less than 10 years old. Some of them already have written stories of striking success.

I would hope that in our very proper concern for prudent use of public funds, we bear in mind that while these are outright contributions they also are investments. Our contributions serve as seed money that attracts other contributions. And these investments promise enormous returns-not only in material wealth in the future but in orderly progress and stable peace. 

But now, having achieved a rather remarkable momentum by methods that sometimes have been rough and ready, we must now pay more attention to the

​management problems that come with greater maturity. We must see that the momentum is not only maintained but is maintained smoothly, efficiently, and economically.

This is a matter on which we shall be consulting with you and seeking your counsel in the months and years ahead. For the moment I shall only indicate the major areas of the management problems that will want attention during this second stage in the life of these international organizations. 

First, there are opportunities for streamlining and coordination-within the agencies, between the agencies, and between the programs operated by the agencies and the overall development programs of the countries in which they operate. We already have taken some first steps in this direction. 

Second, there is a need to start working out closer control systems over budgets, expenditures, and pipeline accumulations-both from the standpoint of magnitudes and timing.

Third, there is a need, in some instances, for more realistic formulas for financing continuing and expanding programs. This includes the question of arrearages. It includes the question of a further reduction of U.S. percentages for some programs financed by every-member canvass. And it includes the significant question of finding a substitute for the every-member canvass to finance some programs in a manner which reflects the enormous disparities in the capacities of the members to finance and guide some programs. 

During the past year we already have begun to pay a good deal of attention to these questions. We already have made some progress. We look forward to more, and we shall be consulting with you about our plans and prospects-not only when we come before you to ask for money, but throughout the course of the year.

Mr. CLEVELAND. The members of this committee have heard year after year executive branch witnesses describe the purpose and operations of international agencies. Most of it is rather familiar ground. 

I think that during the period since the Second World War we have grown out of several illusions in our Government, one of which is you have to choose between bilateral and multilateral forms of assistance, which is like choosing between your right arm and left arm, when it isn't really necessary to choose.

We use multilateral agencies where we think they make sense and bilateral aid where that makes sense. In practice, of course, the multilateral aid is a relatively small part of the total. 

So the statement before you covers this rather familiar ground, and covers in particular the items out of the whole panoply of international organizations' financial arrangements that happen to fall in the AID authorization and appropriation bills for historical reasons, and in a number of cases even for reasons of logic. 

For peace and security operations, which is the word of art for the peacekeeping assignments of the United Nations, notably that in the Congo and in the Middle East, we are proposing in this appropriation only an amount sufficient to bring us to our pledge on the period ending June 30, 1962.

From July 1, 1962, at least for the next fiscal year, the proposition, as you know, is to use for those forward peace and security operations expenses the proceeds of the financing proposal that was adopted by the General Assembly, involving the purchase of bonds or other forms of loans to the United Nations.

So provision for the Congo military operation does not appear in this authorization bill this year, although the Congo military and 

U.N. Emergency Forces have appeared in the past, right along for the last couple of years, and in the case of UNEF for the period going back to 1956.

The economic program, however, for the Congo is included in this bill. This is the nation-building side of the Congo operation, which will be with us in one form or another for some time to come as the Congo recovers from the trauma of sudden independence in 1960 and comes up to and begins to really organize itself as a nation. 

In addition, in the field of economic and technical assistance, there appears here the funds for our contribution to the expanded technical assistance program of the United Nations and the Special Fund for 

Investment Aid. That is the one run by Paul Hoffman.

Traditionally, our program for support of these activities is on the basis of 40 percent of the total on a matching basis. We put in $4 for $6 of other people's contributions. 

There are also small amounts: $600,000 for the young program of a 

Commission for Technical Cooperation in Africa, which is not an organization to which we belong, but a group of African nations now independent coming together for exchange of technical assistance and training programs.

And $200,000 for the work for the Asian Productivity Organization, which is the beginning of an attempt to apply in the Far East and Asian area some of the kinds of lessons that were learned through the very successful European productivity operation which was developed as you remember at the time of the Marshall plan. 

Also in the economic and technical aid category is an estimate of this year's share of the cost of the Indus Valley scheme. You will recall this is a scheme running for 10 years, representing a really extraordinary feat of diplomacy by the President of the World Bank, Mr. Eugene Black, to bring the Indians and Pakistanis together in settling the really extremely virulent and at some points violent dispute on the division of the waters of the Indus River Basin; $30 million is in here as the fiscal 1963 slice of a continuing program for 10 years. The program itself, as you know, is the subject of a special authorization act of 2 years ago.

Also in this program is the appropriation for the Children's Fund, $12 million, which is the same amount as it has been for the last 2 years. A further contribution is for that most intractable of all problems, the care and feeding and, to a limited extent, education of the Palestine refugees, still homeless in the aftermath of the still unliquidated Arab-Israeli war. 

Then three programs which are for the support of scientific activities: A million and a half dollars for the NATO science program; a million and a quarter for the so-called operational program of the International Atomic Energy Agency; and half a million dollars for the medical research program of the World Health Organization. 

Mr. Chairman, I am struck in my own responsibility for the administration of a lot of different U.S. relationships to a lot of different international organizations, how varied and complex this whole affair is.

I thought, therefore, that it might be interesting and useful for the committee this morning to take a look at a management tool which I have to have for my purposes on the executive side which might be useful also for you.

This is a spread sheet of all of the U.S. organizations that we belong to, and some that we don't belong to but to which we make contributions.

It includes the 11 items in the current appropriation. It also includes a lot of other money that is in other appropriations, notably the State Department, but also many others, the Post Office, for fisheries, and one thing and another.

I have never handled the presentation this way before. But I must say I get confused by the different number of international organizations we are members of, and maybe over the years you share a little of this confusion, too. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. May I interrupt at that moment? Will we have a copy of that spread sheet? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. We have about 10 carbons here, which I think would be enough for those in the room at the moment. Do you want to pass those around?

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. One of the problems is to find a piece of paper large enough to print them on. If I may just guide you through this maze for a moment, we think of international organizations really in four major categories.

The U.N. family of U.N. programs and specialized agencies, which is the first category here, the inter-American family, the regional organizations in other areas and a miscellany of other international organizations, most of them relatively small but two of them, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Intergovernmental

Committee on European Migration, which is the European refugee operation, being relatively large, and potentially also the International Control Commission in Laos which could be a substantial operating organization. That, of course, is not, again, an organization of which we are a member.

Mr. CLEVELAND. That is what hasn't been worked out. It is only 

14 nations. This includes 3 different years, 1961, 1962, and 1963, the first 2 years of which contributions have been financed by AID. 

The appropriations we are talking about here today are in the next to the last column under "1963." It is the column headed, "1963, AID contributions." If you work down that column you see that includes the organizations of which I was speaking a moment ago. 

But we thought it might be helpful, Mr. Chairman, to see this particular slice of the public business in the context of the other comparable slices of the public business. 

If I may say just a word about the overall problem of management here. We find ourselves, I think, at something of a watershed this year. We have had 15 or 16 years of building international organizations, an enterprise in which the executive branch and the Congress have been partners in a great many individual decisions to establish or assist in financing, or joining, and assuming obligations in organi-

zations of an international character, global and regional, functional and technical. 

I think that we have come to the point where it has become a major responsibility of the Government to manage this complex web of relationships and where the management problems involved are becoming almost staggeringly complex. 

We in the State Department and in AID-as you know, I really have two hats, because we administer the international organization contributions from both the State Department appropriation and the AID appropriation in the same office in our bureau-we are in a relationship to these organizations not unlike the relationship between the Appropriations Committee of the committees of the Congress and the executive branch.

That is to say, we are the legislature or at least a significant part of the legislature with respect to international organizations and have a very big voice in the budget process. So we have a problem of examining the financial state of the affairs of each of these organizations, of examining their programs, of trying to make sure they make sense, of examining the numbers, of keeping our percentage down, all in an atmosphere requiring a tremendous amount of political negotiation and international politicking. 

I am not myself convinced that we do enough of this, that we put enough administrative and technical energy into it. I am perhaps particularly conscious of that since 16 jobs were removed from my bureau this last year. We do have a very large management problem here.

We have another problem which is the increasing difficulty of coordinating all of these organizations so that they make sense in relation to each other and in relation to our bilateral efforts. 

You can have any number of meetings in Washington, New York, or Paris or Geneva and exchange lists of projects that are going to be implemented, and you still don't have very much coordination. The real coordination job in the field of economic and social development, which is the field in which two-thirds of these organizations operate, is at the country level. 

If you are the minister of finance of a small, underdeveloped country, you see coming at you from abroad a minimum of 15 or 16 different organizations and bilateral aid programs, country programs, and you may, especially if you are in Latin America, see as many as 30 of these coming at you.

I think it is fair to say that the Western World, the industrialized world, has not adequately coordinated its efforts, its transfer of resources and know-how into the underdeveloped areas, and that we are leaving to the underdeveloped countries themselves a task of coordination that is inherently beyond most of them at the present stage of development.

After all, the very definition of underdevelopment is the inability to coordinate things. This is perhaps the most advanced and sophisticated skill that is associated with economic and political development in a new society. 

The very proliferation of international organizations has created a problem in the receiving country, to which, in my judgment, inadequate attention has been given over the last decade or so.

It was relatively easy during the Marshall plan. We were dealing with governments that were well organized. In this case you are dealing with some governments, India, Pakistan, Brazil, and so on, which have a good deal of technical help and a good deal of administrative know-how.

But when you deal with Upper Volta or Togo, whose extraordinary and attractive President visited us here the other day, we have a problem of helping them to make sense out of all of the different opportunities that we are offering them. 

To this problem we are devoting a good deal of time and attention in our shop these days. I don't want to represent to you that that problem is solved. I don't think it is nearly solved. I think that the solving of it will be again as difficult as the building of these organizations has been. The solving of the problem of coordination has to be a matter of partnership between the Congress and the executive branch.

So, these are the reasons why I thought that contrary to the usual rules of this game, I would lay before you a spread sheet that goes way beyond anything that we are now asking you to do today or in this bill that is before you. Many of these numbers never come before this committee because they are under existing authorization. But you all have to face them on the floor and you all have to relate them to each other as I do and try to make sense out of them. 

So I thought before addressing ourselves to the specific programs involved-which we would be glad to address ourselves to at whatever length would suit you-that it might be useful to spread out the total picture and see what reaction this somewhat heretical form of presentation would produce.

I might mention this isn't even the total picture because it doesn't include the lending programs. It doesn't include the International 

Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the International Finance

Corporation, and the International Monetary Fund, the so-called Bretton Woods organizations, which are in a somewhat different category and to which our contributions are made in the form of an investment fund rather than annual appropriations in the manner of all these.

I might also mention that with respect to some of these the State Department, and specifically the International Organization Bureau of the State Department, has little or in a number of cases no jurisdiction.

There is a fisheries group here that is handled very specially by a fisheries adviser in the Under Secretary's Office and the Fish and Wildlife Service, of course, in the Interior.

The International Postal Union is handled directly in the Post Office appropriation and the appropriation never comes anywhere near the 

Department of State.

Similarly with the Postal Union of America and Spain, which is the Latin American edition of the Postal Union. Most of these are the 

State Department's responsibility in one form or another, however. 

I find it educational to look at the whole picture, and I hope, Mr. 

Chairman, that it also serves that purpose here.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, I notice in your discussion here on page 11 of your statement, and after seeing your chart here showing all these international organizations, that you list some suggestions that some sort of program should be worked out for limiting and simplifying this activity. I think maybe some of these organizations might be combined. Is your Department working now to coordinate some of these international organizations so that you can put this on a more workable basis? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. The Department, of course, has a responsibility to coordinate the U.S. representation to all of these organizations and the U.S. input of resources, of people and of funds into them. 

The coordination problem wasn't very significant 10 or 12 years ago when most of these organizations weren't very well developed and they hadn't really gotten underway very effectively and they didn't have any substantial amount of money to work with. 

But now they begin to collide with each other on specific things. 

The problem of oceanography. There are four different organizations that have a very important function and have an interest in oceanography which is very relevant to their own jurisdiction. 

UNESCO has a committee on oceanography which brings together oceanographers and coordinates the work in that field. The Food

and Agriculture Organization has a very important and very effective fisheries department, which is of course interested in research in the oceanography field. The International Atomic Energy Agency is involved in oceanographic science, particularly since some devices which are atomic in origin, isotopes, and so on, are used in figuring out where the schools of fish are, and so on. 

The World Meteorological Organization obviously also has a substantial interest in oceanographic science. 

Well, each one of them wants to do the whole job, of course, as organizations will. We are a most important member of each of those organizations, because we make the largest contribution to them. 

We in America are also a major scientific society and do a lot of work on this subject ourselves. So we have the problem of trying to figure out how best to have a single international oceanographic program in which the interests of these various organizations are appropriately represented, but in which we are not duplicating four or five times over the same piece of work. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, we would be interested to see if there was any military value in any of these particular types of organizations that you are talking about. Do they do anything to facilitate the operations of submarines? Are these worthwhile organizations? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. I am not sure that you can measure worthwhileness by the military need altogether. The Department of the Army and the Department of the Navy, the whole Defense Department setup the Air Force, too, on the meteorology side-are heavily involved in the problems of what to do internationally on oceanography. 

Obviously, what the major industrial societies do in this field is really the main thing that is being done. But there is a problem of coordination among the countries as to what is to be done. There is a problem of developing standard ways of referring to scientific phenomena that are agreed to internationally so that the scientists across borders can figure out what they are respectively talking about.

We see this very strongly in the field of communications. The telecommunications setup has developed a whole dictionary of communication symbols that are now a kind of international language in the communications field, and which will be carried over to the use of satellites when they get up into space there and working.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Chairman, I had a similar question in mind as to our contribution to the Congo. Of course, I may be $8 million plus or minus because I am reading off a carbon copy. I have added these items hurriedly, and it appears that the program for 1963 for the Congo will involve $261,702,113. 

I didn't expect that we were going to get that figure this morning, so I started to add up these items while listening to the testimony. 

I may be plus or minus $8 million, but $8 million is not supposed to be a large amount in Washington. It is in Milwaukee. 

Mr. Chairman, on page 3, we have an item of $17.2 million for the care of refugees. For many years past we were advised that this amount was going to be reduced and eventually discontinued,

1 and that the excuse of caring for these refugees would be borne by the Arab countries. We feel that, eventually, this expense should not constitute an obligation of the United States. We were told repeatedly that efforts have been made toward this end. 

How much less or how much larger is this amount than fiscal 1962 grant and what efforts are being exerted to see that this particular item will eventually disappear from our budget? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. A good deal of effort has been made. I am bound to say that I share the sense of frustration which your question reflects. This is the most difficult problem I think in this whole range of problems. Here are more than a million refugees in the 

Gaza strip, in Jordan, Syria, and Lebanon. They are the subject of a major political rivalry which covers a major unliquidated war, a war that is still in effect going on. 

It requires an agreement between Israel and the Arab States for them to be resettled. The Arabs want them all to go back to Israel, which they obviously can't all do. The Israelis want them resettled in the Arab States, which the Arabs don't want. This requires an international agreement between Israel and her neighbors, which has simply not materialized in the 13 years since that war started- Mr. ZABLOCKI. Would it help your efforts if we put a cutoff date, say that this is the last grant, or that we will carry this expense for 2 more years? If we amend the bill to put a cutoff date, will that help you?

Mr. CLEVELAND. I think the problem is to get the situation in that part of the world sufficiently quieted down so you can make some peace.

The judgment of everybody I have talked to about that part of the world is that the threat that 800-some-thousand refugees would not be fed next year would be enough to make the entire Middle 

Eastern area go up in smoke.

That is the problem. Everyone who has visited there comes to the same conclusion as to the difficulties. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. You say that this is a difficult problem and that many efforts are being expended. We have heard this year after year. We heard it from both administrations. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. I haven't told you that. If you can figure out the way to liquidate the problem- 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. That is easy. Stop the appropriation.

Mr. CLEVELAND. I think the result would be a major war which might or might not result in the subjugation of Israel by the Arabs or vice versa.

This is a highly emotional situation, and our judgment is that you can't work at it by deadline. You can only work at it by trying to nibble at the edges and quiet the area down sufficiently to develop an atmosphere in which the Arabs and Israelis can come to some kind of terms about their political relationship. This is the basis on which we are working.

Mr. JUDD. 

Mr. Secretary, I particularly applaud your emphasis in two places in your statement, that the time has come for tidying up and taking a

harder look at these programs. We had to start them on a crash basis. 

There were no precedents. We had to go from one crisis to the next. 

Last year the Executive asked for a division for development and research. Our committee added the word "evaluation" and urged them to start with evaluation. One of the first things they ought to evaluate is the sort of thing you mention, particularly on page 11; seeing what has succeeded and what has failed, and analyzing why this succeeded and why that failed. 

It is hard to go on year after year on a sort of ad hoc basis. As you say, the time has come when we ought to be in a position to get many of these programs on a firmer basis like those of our own Government's agencies here at home. 

Have you talked with that new evaluation division? Dr. Fei is in charge of it, I think.

Mr. CLEVELAND. They don't really have a top person yet on that subject.

Essentially, I don't think this is so much a matter for a research and development group in that office. The primary problem as I see it, Dr. Judd, is to get our whole executive establishment in the fieldthat is, the Americans in the field-seized of this problem of coordination.

Traditionally, the AID mission and the Ambassador concern themselves with our bilateral relationship with the country to which they are accredited, but they don't think of the World Health Organization input into their country even though we are 40 percent stockholders in what they do, or what is done with any special fund money or U.N. technical assistance money. They don't think of the food and agriculture program of the FAO as a part of the American input into the development program of the country to which they are accredited. 

Some of them historically have even thought of it as a kind of rival. 

We have to get our American program considered along with this international one. This international program is a part of ourselves with another glove on, in a sense.

So our problem is to get the AID people and embassies in the field concentrating on this problem of coordination at the place where coordination makes sense, which is at the country level in the development business.

Mr. JUDD. We have to admit that if we can't get our own people to work at it, it is pretty hopeless to get the international agencies to do so. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. That is correct. The traditional way of handling these things is to handle it through the American representative to the annual convention of the organization. By the time the American representative gets there, the budget is already frozen, the planning is already done. There isn't anything very much he can do about it. 

We have to catch this at a much earlier stage. We have to catch it at the stage of each project in each country and relate it to what we are doing bilaterally and to what other agencies are doing. 

Mr. JUDD. Here is $500,000 for the medical research program of the 

World Health Organization. Why should we have our regular appropriation to the World Health Organization, and then another of $500,000 for its medical research program? Why don't they integrate that research into their total budget of all the things WHO is doing?

Mr. CLEVELAND.

We didn't do a whole lot of what NIH would call medical research- Mr. JUDD. I know something about how they started this medical research as a special thing. But nothing ever stops. When can they move it in with the rest of the things in their general budget? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. This is precisely our intention. I think I can say that with some feeling and some honesty, Dr. Judd, because the two other special WHO programs, the malaria program and the community water supply program, are both in the last stages of being folded wholly in the budget. The process will be completed over the next 2, 3, or 4 years.

On malaria, we picked up 90 percent of the check. By the end of next year we would expect to be picking up our regular WHO share, which would be about 32 percent. So we got it going, and then caused everybody else to get in the act. 

Mr. JUDD. That would apply also to the NATO science program. 

It started as a sputnik-inspired thing, but it ought to get into NATO's regular budget.

Mr. CLEVELAND. The present arrangement in NATO is that by 1964 it will be a part of the regular budget and we will be paying 24-pointsomething percent.

It is a precarious business at best. The Belgians went through a long period of emphasizing preparation for economic improvement rather than political leadership, leaving them with an acute lack of administrators and political leaders. 

Mrs. CHURCH. And an appalling size of territory to be administered.

Mr. CLEVELAND. Yes. The hope is that all of the available political leadership can come together in a government, a federal structure of some kind, in which they are not so much fighting with each other as fighting against their common problem, which is the problem of modernization and development. 

As in other underdeveloped areas, this is an extraordinarily difficult problem of economy, of administration and politics. 

Mrs. CHURCH. And of force?

Mr. CLEVELAND. And of internal security force, in effect. 

The United Nations and we as a part of that operation have not, of course, been using force to enforce the unity of the Congo. 

Mrs. CHURCH. Would you repeat that, Mr. Secretary?

Mr. CLEVELAND. We have not been using force to enforce the unity of the Congo. 

Mr. HAYS. What was all the shooting about in Katanga? 

Is that some tea party they had there?

Mr. CLEVELAND. The Katanga Provincial government in one of its several efforts at secession tried to make the situation impossible for the maintenance of a U.N. force in Katanga. 

The policeman, in effect, had to defend his right to be on his beat. 

Mrs. CHURCH. What right had he to be there?

Mr. CLEVELAND. He had a right to be there because he was invited in by the National Government of the Congo, and indeed, by the Provincial government of Katanga. 

You remember the negotiation. Hammarskjold went personally in the fall of 1960 down to Katanga to negotiate with Tshombe. 

They were in there by permission and under Security Council resolutions with which, of course, we are associated- Mrs. CHURCH. Do I understand that Mr. Hammarskjold made the arrangement whereby it was agreed that if necessary force would be used to prevent secession? 

I had not realized that it went as far as that. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. That was not and never has been a part of the juridical basis for the United Nations being in there. That is not what the shooting was about.

The shooting was about whether they would be allowed to remain there at all, whether the U.N. forces would be allowed to remain there or whether they would be harassed out of there. 

Mr. CHURCH. It is not nearly as clear to me as it is to you. 

I am going to ask you the question that I have been frequently asked. 

You probably know the answer to it. When we permitted the French empire in Africa to break into so many little states, why did we take a different attitude in demanding union in the Congo? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. The union in the Congo was the product of the roundtable conference in Brussels to which the various political leaders of the Congo went, including Mr. Tshombe, in which it was agreed that the Congo would be given its independence as a unit rather than in chunks.

I think myself that that makes more sense for the long run of the 

Congo. But that isn't our jurisdiction. That is their problem.

If you split it up on the basis of chunks the size of south Katanga, you would have 14 different countries carved out of the Congo, which does not strike me as a particularly good idea. 

Mrs. CHURCH. It would increase your problems in the United Nations.

Mr. CLEVELAND. It would increase our problems in central Africa and increase the likelihood that one or two of those chunks could become a satellite- 

Chairman MORGAN. The gentlewoman's time has expired. 

Mrs. CHURCH. A last word, which a woman is entitled to. 

I cannot easily convince myself as to the rightness or adjust myself to the use of force as it has been used in the Congo by U.N. troops. 

This morning when the question was raised as regards our position on the bond issue, I think that it was Dr. Judd who made the point wisely that it is just because many people have an honest doubt about the right of the United Nations to use force as it has in the Congo, that you have the reaction of the refusal to take on the bond issue. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. We have gone over this ground, Mr. Chairman, in great detail, but in executive session, with a subcommittee in the 

Senate chaired by Senator Gore.

I would be very glad indeed if we had an opportunity, at some appropriate occasion with this committee, to go over the basis on which the United Nations was and is in the Congo, the story of how the shooting got started and the rest of it, with respect to which there

seems to be some difference in interpretation in the discussion this morning.

Chairman MORGAN. We will take that up with the chairman of the 

African Subcommittee and let you know.

Mr. HAYS. I have an interest in that with my Subcommittee on 

State Department Personnel. I would like to find out who made these decisions and why they were made and talk about some of the people who made them and their outlook, and then if Mr. Cleveland is not busy some day, he could explain how the Civil War was fought without force, since he seems to think they can do it in the Congo. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Farbstein. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN.  

Welcome, Mr. Cleveland, a fellow New Yorker. I am sorry that things have been made a little bit rough for you this morning. I hope I don't add to it.

Mr. CLEVELAND. I was hoping it would be interesting. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. I think you found it interesting. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. I always do with this committee.

Mr. FARBSTEIN. It has been said that the Middle East has become somewhat of a political problem rather than a problem of refugees, and that the Arab countries are using it as such. 

Will you please give me your opinion with relation thereto, and what you think should be done?

Mr. CLEVELAND. I think that it is indeed a political problem. We have, of course, been trying very hard to get the countries in the area to address themselves to this problem as a refugee problem. 

As you know, Mr. Farbstein, the Palestine Conciliation Commission, Turkey, France, and the United States, has asked Dr. Johnson of the Carnegie Endowment to go out there and see whether he can find some basis for discussion of real progress on the refugees. 

He is about to make his second trip to the area beginning later this month.

The atmosphere as a result of the shooting on the shores of the Sea of Galilee isn't exactly ideal at this moment, but we will be continuing this effort.

The view is held in some circles that the refugees are to some extent a political instrument. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. There is a better word than "problem," I might say, being used as a political instrument.

Mr. CLEVELAND. I think some of them undoubtedly would like to go to what they regard as home. A good many of them would perhaps just like to go and settle somewhere. 

The problem has remained there for years, in effect, as a part of the negotiating situation between the Arab States and Israel. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Are we doing anything to help those individuals who are in these refugee camps that want to get out, start a home of their own in some of the other countries? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. Yes, we are doing a good deal. The scale is pretty small on the funds that are available. There is a vocational training program which the U.N. Relief and Works Agency has started in on. 

About 1,500 refugee youth are now receiving specialized training, which enables them to get out. I think there is something of a pat-

tern of the youngsters, as they come to be of working age, wanting to get out and get jobs on their own. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Mr. Cleveland, can you please explain if it is possible to do so, why our delegate in the United Nations voted against the African resolution asking that Israel and the Arab States sit down for the purpose of talking peace when we know that the only success it has had in the area was when Mr. Ralph Bunche, as our representative, insisted that they sit down and which resulted in an armistice?

Mr. CLEVELAND. In order to get something started that would really lead to fruitful negotiations, both sides have to be in a mood to negotiate. Our feeling has been that to tackle this problem first on the refugee side through the Johnson mission was the most fruitful exercise. 

We announced rather early in the game that what we would like to see happen, is for the Johnson mission to give some new initiative to the Palestine Conciliation Commission. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. It has been in existence for 13 years, Mr. Cleveland, and nothing has happened. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. That is true of the PCC. The Johnson "mission" was an attempt on the General Assembly's instructions last year to revive the matter.

There were two other resolutions. There was a resolution sponsored by the Brazzaville States which said "Why don't you fellows get together and talk about it?" and a rather extreme resolution sponsored by the Arabs, and we said we would like to hew to the middle here and not go for any other resolution. 

The Brazzaville resolution was regarded by the Arabs as anti- Arab. The Arab resolution was quite naturally regarded by the 

Israelis and their friends as anti-Israel. 

We said "We don't want any part of these essentially political resolutions. We want to hew to the middle on trying to get an arrangement started."

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Wouldn't there be a psychological effect that might be had if this resolution were passed, voted upon by this country, so that the world at large would know that we favored that these countries that are at war have been asked to sit down for the purpose of discussing peace, in view of our past experience, rather than have us take a position that this country is opposed to the two opposing sides to sit down for the purpose of discussing a question of peace? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. În the parliamentary situation, as the Israeli dele gation recognized very well, this resolution served a very important and useful purpose of balancing off against the Arab resolution. The 

Israeli delegation didn't ever think it would go through. 

Indeed, as you know, in the final vote they voted for the resolution which we had cosponsored. So that I think that the way it came out served the purpose of peace in the area as well as any resolution, which is not very well, can serve.

What it mainly requires is for the people in the area to settle down sufficiently so that they can begin to talk seriously about the very serious problems of relationships 

Mr. PILCHER. Will the gentleman yield? 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Yes.

Mr. PILCHER. Mr. Secretary, do you think we are any nearer of ever getting agreement between Israel and the Arabs today than we were 10 or 12 years ago?

Mr. CLEVELAND. I do not know. 

Mr. PILCHER. Every Arab leader that we talked to would tell you right straight that they wouldn't even consider it, that the only way there would ever be peace in the Far East was with the destruction of Israel. They didn't make any bones about it. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. A lot of them don't. A lot of them say privately they realize that is nonsense, but it is what they have to say publicly, and it is what they say publicly. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. Don't you think that a public condemnation would have some effect, some beneficial effect? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. Public condemnation of the Arabs? 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. In the sense that they refuse to vote for the peace resolution, that they oppose the peace resolution and we went along with them in the opposition to the Africa peace resolution. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. We weren't opposing the substance of it. We were opposing the impression of it that the Arabs had, that it directed against them. The problem is getting the two parties to sit down together. You don't generally manage to accomplish that by hitting one of the parties over the head. You have to bring them both into the room to start with. This is our problem. 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. How did Bunche do it?

Mr. CLEVELAND. There was- 

Mr. FARBSTEIN. They were even in a worse situation than they are today. At that time they were at each other's throats, and he got them to sit down.

Here there ostensibly exists an armistice, and all we do is ask that they sit down for the purpose of talking peace and yet this Government's representative votes "no." It is beyond my comprehension.

Mr. CLEVELAND. As you know, during the period that they did sit down, those many years ago, it was in the interest of the Arab countries to sit down, because they were being licked militarily. They wanted to talk peace. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI (presiding). The gentleman's time has expired.

Mr. CLEVELAND. In the present situation, neither the Israelis nor 

Arabs feel a strong urge to make any concessions on any of the things that remain to be settled, which is most of the elements in the area. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The gentleman's time has expired. 

Mr. Broomfield. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. I would like to ask the Secretary regarding this problem between the Arabs and Israel: We are contributing $17 million apparently, at least programed, for fiscal year 1963. How long have we been putting this amount into the refugee problem? Has it been for 13 years, and what is the total amount? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. We have been putting in varying amounts all the way back to the beginning of this Palestine refugee problem, which was at the end of the 1940's. 

From the beginning of UNRWA, which was the beginning of January 1950, we have put in just over $250 million.

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Is there any other country that supports this refugee program there? Are we the only ones?

Mr. CLEVELAND. There are a number of countries. The three big ones are the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. I would like to yield the balance of my time to 

Mr. Seely-Brown.

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. Mr. Secretary, you have been a very helpful witness and I thank you for your testimony. And can you also indicate the countries that are in arrears in their payments, so we know how much of the bond issue which we are going to be asked to vote upon at a later date is going to provide for programs that you have listed here?

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. Regular assessments? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. Yes; in effect, the club dues.

Mr. CLEVELAND. That must be paid and to which we in a sense have agreed in ratifying the treaty that set up the organization to begin with in each case.

The AID column is the voluntary contributions which are not mandatory and which are a free-will action by the United States and other countries that put money in. 

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. If the bond issue is voted, will the money provided for in the bond issue enable other countries to pay up their share of any of the programs which you have listed here? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. The bond issue is relevant primarily to the Congo operation and the U.N. Emergency Force. 

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. Those are the only two? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. I say "primarily," because under the resolution. setting up the bond issue, the Secretary General can use the funds for any purpose for which any capital fund can be used, which, in effect, means any U.N. purpose. 

The two that are in trouble financially, the two that are creating the cash problem, are these two, and consequently our assumption is that substantially all the funds will be used either for forward expenses for those or bills due and payable in connection with those two programs. 

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. May I express, Mr. Chairman, the hope that when the U.N. bond issue comes up that the Secretary will be one of our witnesses on that particular topic, because of the importance

of what he has already said about the Congo, and because of the fact that the U.N. bond issue is to help pay for that operation. 

I think all of the committee, not just the members of the African Subcommittee, are tremendously interested in what he has to say. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. There is no doubt the chairman is going to have the Secretary before the full committee on that.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Murphy. 

Mr. MURPHY. 

Mr. Cleveland, I would like to ask you a question in reference to the Indus Basin project. How many countries are participating in the project? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. The United States, United Kingdom, Germany, 

Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and then of course Pakistan and India, in whose territory- Mr. MURPHY. Is the total project around a billion dollars? 

Mr. CLEVELAND. Total project? 

Mr. MURPHY. Estimate. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. The settlement plan on the estimate was just over a billion dollars.

Mr. MURPHY. Is the United States committed to 50 percent over a 10-year period?

Mr. CLEVELAND. The United States is committed to various pieces of money here: $177 million of foreign exchange grants, $70 million of foreign exchange loans, and $235 million of local currency loans and grants, which means the total runs to just over $500 million, and just about half- 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. $500 million, Mr. MURPHY. That is $500 million?

Mr. CLEVELAND. Yes. Some of that is loan money and will eventually come back, so it isn't- Mr. MURPHY. Is there any phase of this project under construction at the present time?

Mr. CLEVELAND. Yes, there is. Construction is just beginning. Two contracts have recently been let, primarily for the construction of the Mangla Dam, one of the major works, and several of the link canals. 

Mr. MURPHY. Where is the dam located, in Pakistan?

Mr. CLEVELAND. Yes. 

Do you have that map? We have a statement on the Indus water settlement problem with a map attached. It might be useful to have this in the record. It is a matter that has been of considerable interest to this committee. 

The Mangla Dam up on the border of Pakistan and India, is one of the largest installations, quite possibly as it finally works out the largest installation, that this plan will encompass. 

You know generally what the arrangement is, the attempt to Mr. MURPHY. The general purpose is to have a division of the waters of the Indus River whereby India and Pakistan will participate. 

Mr. CLEVELAND. There are six rivers altogether that are involved. 

The plan provides that the Indians shall have the use of the waters of

the eastern rivers and that the downstream irrigated areas in Pakistan, formerly supplied by these rivers, shall in the future be supplied with water brought from the three western rivers. The plan involves a rather elaborate engineering arrangement of diversions and link canals and is, of course, a rather expensive arrangement, over a period of 10 years.

Mr. MURPHY. Is it possible to receive a copy of this map?
