WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION SPECIAL PROGRAMS 

Largely at U.S. initiative, the World Health Organization in the last several years has undertaken to intensify its activities in the fields of malaria, community water supply, and medical research with a view to focusing worldwide attention on the importance of these areas in advancing the cause of public health, especially in less-developed countries. These programs were planned to complement the more extensive activities in these fields undertaken through U.S. bilateral and national programs. As a result there has been wide acceptance of the

Thus, in need for attacking these problems. Other countries have committed their resources on an increasing scale both in national programs and in support of WHO activities in these fields through contributions to assessed and voluntary budgets. 

The United States has encouraged the Organization to utilize more fully funds currently available for the special programs through these sources. the field of malaria eradication, adequate funds are on hand to finance the program's budget needs at their current level until the schedule for absorption into the regular budget is completed in 1964. In the event of unforeseen contingencies either through changes in the pattern of our bilateral programs or through other overriding considerations, further voluntary contributions to this program might be called for. Similarly, the community water supply program has adequate resources to meet currently planned activities, although there may be future requirements depending upon the evolution of the program. 

Purpose of the medical research program The United States has a deep interest in the progress and potentialities of the WHO intensified medical research program. It was initiated in 1958 on a proposal by the U.S. delegation to the 11th World Health Assembly; the study undertaken to set up the research program was financed by a U.S. grant; and this country has contributed to it since, both through technical and financial support. 

Under this program, WHO makes modest grants to investigators in many countries where these will have a stimulating effect on needed research; it provides services to research, such as support to international reference centers, the establishment of biological standards, the development of standardized nomenclature, etc.; and in 1961 began the training and exchange of research workers. 

These reference centers prepare, maintain, and exchange biological standards or collect, exchange, and study strains of pathogenic bacteria and viruses. There are also six regional laboratories which help coordinate research in polio throughout the world and disseminate information on its prevalence. The network of cooperating laboratories also includes institutions widely scattered throughout the world which maintain constant surveillance on the incidence of influenza. 

The mechanism for planning and carrying out these activities is identical with that for activities financed from the WHO regular budget. In the planning phase the Director General invites the advice of specially convened scientific groups and the WHO Advisory Committee on Medical Research. The Director 

General, through the relevant technical unit, then plans a series of projects to implement the program developed with the help of the Advisory Committee. vestigators in many parts of the world are then invited to undertake specific studies to implement these projects; this is done by contracts with investigators in and directors of national institutions. 

Significance of the program to the United States In- Continued development and expansion of WHO's research program is in the U.S. interest. It is an important complement to our own expanding international and domestic medical research efforts and gives valuable support to the disease control programs of the World Health Organization. 

Research on cardiovascular diseases and cancer is of particular interest to the United States. Through international research in these fields we can study the occurrences of these diseases in different racial and cultural settings, in populations with different diets and exposed to a variety of virus and other infections. 

In the United States the environment and habits of the population may be so homogeneous as to conceal the nature of a causal relationship because of the narrow range in which observations of a particular factor can be made. A worldwide laboratory for such research provides great advantages. WHO'S cancer research activity is directed mainly toward the epidemiology of cancer, its prevention and treatment, with emphasis on chemotherapy. In regards to both cancer and cardiovascular diseases, WHO is serving an additional function of great value in the development of standard classifications, definitions, and nomenclature as well as establishing international collections of tumor material. 

Examples of specially useful and succesful projects Many of WHO's research activities are of particular interest to member nations whose principal health problems result from tropical diseases. For example, it is proposed in 1962 to conduct research on leprosy, including standardization of lepromin and trials of antileprosy drugs; to study the cause the diarrheal diseases in tropical areas, including studies in the relationship between infec-

tion and nutrition; and to support research on bilharziasis and filariasis, as well as other worm diseases important to lesser developed countries. 

Relationship to other U.S. programs 

The National Institutes of Health as part of its program of medical research use the international facilities arranged throughout the world by WHO to find the answers to medical problems of pressing interest in the United States. During 1962 grants for this purpose have been either approved or are under review for projects totaling $913,000. 

Proposed contribution and relationship to prior-year financing A contribution of $500,000, the same amount provided in each of the last 3 years, is proposed for fiscal year 1963 to supplement activities of this valuable program undertaken under the regular budget. Although the United States is the chief contributor to the voluntary fund for medical research, we are in effect reducing our percentage contribution to the overall program each year since provision for medical research is being increased in the regular budget (to which we contribute approximately 32 percent) at an annual increment of $250,000. In 1963 provision for research activity under the regular budget has been made at a level of $1,250,000 to which other governments would contribute some $850,000. Until an optimum level of research activity can be absorbed into the regular budget, however, it is desirable that the United States sustain this important program by voluntary cash contributions as well as research grants of the National Institutes of Health. 

INTERNATIONAL ATOMIC ENERGY AGENCY 

Purpose of the program The IAEA was established for the purpose of encouraging research and practical application of atomic energy to peaceful uses; for fostering the exchange of scientific and technical information between the various countries of the world; for establishing and administering safeguards to insure that any nuclear materials or equipment which are provided by the IAEA or under its auspices are not diverted for use in such a way as to further any military purpose; and for encouraging and assisting in the exchange and training of scientists in the field of peaceful uses of atomic energy. 

One of the most important aspects of the Agency's operational program is its practice of sending technical experts in the field of atomic energy to various countries in the world. During the current year some 45 experts will be sent to about 25 different countries to help in the furtherance of the peaceful nuclear energy programs of those countries. The sending of these experts will be financed by the operational budget of the IAEA of which this proposed U.S. contribution will be a part.

Experience has indicated that the greatest current need in the field of atomic energy is for those scientists who can give advice on the use of radioisotopes in agriculture and medicine. Another important field is for experts in radiobiology. 

An understanding of radiobiology is relevant not only for agricultural and medical research, but also for devising methods of protection from radiated materials. 

It is estimated that during the current year the Agency will finance, from its own operational budget, some 400 to 450 fellowships, which will enable scientists from emerging countries to be trained in nuclear science in the schools and laboratories of the more advanced countries. 

Significance of the program to the United States The U.S. Government played a major role in the founding of the IAEA in 1957. 

Since that time, the U.S. Government has given strong support to the Agency both technically and financially. The support of the Agency has been based on the belief that the IAEA promotes closer ties of cooperation between the United States and the other nations of the world and on the further belief that the U.S. role of leadership in this organization enhances the prestige of American science and technology; moreover, it is believed that with the expansion of the peaceful uses of atomic energy the Agency will have an increasingly important role in establishing international rules and regulations in such fields as health and safety, third party liability, and waste disposal. Relationship to U.S. bilateral programs 

The U.S. Government has made bilateral grants to some 25 countries to assist them in the financing of nuclear research reactors. The IAEA has in the past

and will in the future provide the countries which have these reactors with related equipment, as well as with experts to assist in the management and utilization of these U.S.-designed reactors in programs of research. Since the U.S. research reactor program is being phased out in fiscal year 1962 it may be necessary to utilize savings under this title to provide modest quantities of equipment to assure the most effective use of these reactors. 

During the past several years, the IAEA has sent preliminary assistance missions to many of the underdeveloped countries in Asia and Latin America to help them determine the potential uses of nuclear energy in their countries. The reports of these preliminary missions are made available to experts in the U.S. 

Government and will be of value in helping U.S. authorities make a determination as to the advisability of giving bilateral assistance to these countries in the field of nuclear energy. 

Great care is taken at all times to insure that the U.S. bilateral programs and those of the IAEA are closely coordinated and that there is not opportunity for the two to overlap. 

Proposed U.S. contribution and relationship to prior-year financing 

A total availability of $1,250,000 is proposed for assistance to the International Atomic Energy Agency in fiscal year 1963. This sum would be utilized through two types of contributions: 

1. In cash-In each of the past 3 years the United States has offered to the IAEA operational budget $500,000 as a principal sum, and $250,000 on a matching basis after other members have paid $500,000. Our Government has offered this level of support with the thought that it would assist the Agency in launching programs which would prove beneficial to the member governments of the Agency-particularly, the governments of the underdeveloped countries. At the present time the programs financed by the Agency's operational budget include the provision of fellowships, experts and equipment to member countries as well as the letting of research contracts and the financing of some portion of the costs of the Agency's Laboratory in Vienna. The same contribution of $750,000 as was provided in fiscal year 1962 is requested for support to this operational program as a voluntary contribution in fiscal year 1963. 

2. In services.-In addition to the foregoing direct support to the IAEA operational program through voluntary contributions, it is proposed that a further $500,000 be contributed in services to strengthen the IAEA programs of providing fellowships, experts, and consultants for member states. This $500,000 would be utilized as follows: (a) Fellowship program ($350,000): As indicated in the foregoing, the IAEA has its own fellowship program which is financed from its operational budget. 

Through the years the Agency has, in addition, encouraged its more highly developed member states to present to the Agency a certain number of cost-free fellowships, these fellowships to be made available to students sponsored by the IAEA but with the training fully paid for by the offering member state. In past years the United States, the U.S.S.R., the United Kingdom, the German Federal 

Republic, France, and other advanced members of the IAEA have given such fellowships. It is particularly advantageous for the United States to give such fellowships since the Agency finds it very costly to send trainees to the United States under its regular fellowship program. The creation of a U.S.-oriented scientific community around the world has and will continue to receive impetus by the training of foreign nationals in the United States. 

The Agency has far more applications for study in the United States than it can finance from its operational budget. Using the average cost per fellowship of $7,000 per annum, the $350,000 requested for fiscal year 1963 would make it possible for the United States to offer the Agency some 50 fellowships for study in the United States during calendar year 1963. Such a program would not only support a major program of the IAEA but would also help to orient a group of 50 scientists from underdeveloped countries toward the United States. For (b) Experts and consultants ($150,000): While the Agency has its own program of sending experts and consultants to underdeveloped countries, it has never had sufficient funds in its operational budget to meet all demands. this reason, both because of the importance of the atoms for peace program and in an effort to strengthen the Agency, the U.S. Government as well as several others have from time to time offered the Agency cost-free experts to assist underdeveloped countries in the development of their nuclear energy programs. 

The countries who request these experts can express a preference for the nationality of the expert and because of the high demand for U.S. experts the

last U.S. offer has been completely used up. In contrast virtually no Soviet experts have been called upon. For this reason it is believed desirable for the 

U.S. Government to offer to make available to the Agency an additional group of such experts. 

From time to time throughout each year the IAEA calls together symposia and panels of experts to discuss subjects of interest to the Agency. The following meetings were held in 1961: 

Seminar on the Physics of Fast and Intermediate Reactors.

Regional Seminar on Educational Problems of Nuclear Energy. 

Symposium on the Detection and Use of Tritium in the Physical and 

Biological Sciences.

Symposium on the Effects of Ionizing Radiation on the Nervous System. 

Symposium on Whole Body Counting. 

Symposium on the Programing and Utilization of Research Reactors.

Symposium on Power Reactor Experiments. 

It is important that U.S. scientists participate in such seminars and symposia in 1963 as a reflection of our leadership position in the IAEA. 

Funds for the fellowship program and for experts and consultants have heretofore been provided from atoms for peace funds. Since U.S. contributions for these activities are made in response to requests from IAEA and are in effect contributions in services to the agency program, as well as the fact that a separate section of the bill has not been included for atoms for peace in fiscal year 1963, the request for funds to provide these services is included under this title.

Purpose of the program 

NATO SCIENCE PROGRAM 

In 1957, under the impetus of spectacular Soviet advances in the field of science, NATO embarked upon a program to strengthen the effectiveness of Western science. The basic decision in this field was taken by the NATO heads of government meeting in December 1957. The communique adopted by the heads of government stated: "We recognize that in most of our countries more should be done to increase the supply of trained men in many branches of science and technology. The full development of our science and technology is essential to the culture, to the economy, and to the political and military strength of the Atlantic Community. We seek to increase the effectiveness of national efforts through the pooling of scientific facilities and information and the sharing of tasks."

The Conference of NATO Parliamentarians, at its meeting in Paris in November 1960, adopted a clear statement of the objectives of the NATO science program, noting: "It is the scientific leadership of our Atlantic Community which has enabled it to achieve the world's highest standard of living. It is the same leadership which has enabled us to build the armaments needed to deter those who would destroy our way of life." "A continued flourishing of science and technology in our Community is needed to maintain our dynamic economic growth. It is needed equally if we are successfully to withstand the across-the-board Soviet challenge to our Community, a challenge which may persist for 25 or 50 years in the future."

To carry out its tasks, NATO has developed three main categories of activities: science fellowships; advanced study institutes; and research grants. Briefly, the amounts requested for these three main categories of projects are as follows: Fellowships.

Study institutes.. 

Research grants.

Significance of the program to the United States The Western World has great scientific resources, actual and potential, which must be utilized to the fullest if the West is to face up successfully to the challenges which confront it. The U.S. contribution in money and personnel to this program stimulates the productive activity and cooperative endeavor of the

entire Community. This is the chief significance of the program. For example, the NATO fellowship program gives advanced science students the best possible training wherever it can be had in the Atlantic Community. The study institutes and the research grants have the same purpose-to multiply our scientific research and achievements on a NATO-wide basis. In this way the use and application of scientific knowledge can be shared and intensified, especially in the less scientifically advanced members of the Community. 

Examples of especially useful and successful projects (1) Oceanography and meteorology have proved to be especially adaptable to multilateral research efforts. Consequently, NATO continues to emphasize research in these important fields, the results of which are of course available to both basic science and to defense research. (2) In addition to its valuable role in the conduct of scientific projects which especially lend themselves to multilateral cooperation, the NATO science program also performs a very important role as a stimulus to greater national efforts in science. Decisions by the Greek and Turkish Governments to set up national policy councils for science were stimulated by a NATO study; the present intensive examinations by NATO governments of the proposal for an International Institute of Science and Technology, which proposal was developed by a group of distinguished scientists under the chairmanship of Dr. James Killian of MIT, is another signal result of NATO initiative in this field. 

Relationship to bilateral U.S. programs of similar nature 

The NATO science program is distinctive in encouraging advanced training and scientific achievement on a NATO-wide basis. The main objective of U.S. participation is to encourage the fullest possible development of scientific talent and cooperation within the Atlantic Community. The administration of the 

U.S. segment of the NATO fellowship program is handled by the National 

Science Foundation, which insures against duplication and overlapping with other programs administered by the United States in this field. 

Proposed U.S. contribution and relationship to prior-year financing 

The total contribution proposed for fiscal year 1963 is $1,530,000. This compares with the total U.S. fiscal year 1962 contribution of $1,387,263. The slight increase will permit the United States to make a larger contribution to an expanded fellowship program and a higher level of support for advanced study institutes, and to pay its share of a research grant program of $1.5 million. 

Our contribution will enable the United States to sustain the momentum of this valuable program and to make possible a modest expansion to meet foreseeable needs and opportunities. The United States will thereby stimulate other members of NATO to increase their contributions, and also encourage them to assume a larger percentage share of the program as the United States reduces its own percentage contribution.

Special problems facing the program Two of the projects under this heading, for fellowships and summer institutes, were launched with an initial contribution of 50 percent by the United States. 

The research grant project developed later, and has from the beginning received a U.S. contribution of 24.2 percent, which is in line with the normal U.S. contribution to the NATO headquarters budget.

We have adopted the policy of a gradual reduction of the U.S. percentage share of the fellowship and institutes programs. The percentage declined from 50 percent to 45 percent in fiscal year 1961, to 40 percent in fiscal year 1962 and to 33% percent in fiscal year 1963. We plan to effect another decrease in fiscal year 1964 which will bring our share of these two programs down to 24.2 percent 

As to the future of the program, we look for a modest expansion which, together with a declining U.S. percentage contribution, would add up to a fairly stable level of U.S. appropriations toward the existing program. We do not, of course, wish to exclude the possibility that our scientific advisers will recommend to us significant new fields of NATO scientific cooperation, for which full justification, of course, would be given. 

Purpose of the program 

INDUS WATERS SETTLEMENT 

The Indus Basin settlement plan was devised by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) to settle a longstanding dispute be-

tween India and Pakistan over the use of the waters of the Indus River Basin. 

The dispute arose from the fact that the border demarcation between India and West Pakistan cut across six major rivers of the Indus River system, giving control of the upstream waters of those rivers to India. India wished to expand its uses of these waters; Pakistan was fearful that its historical supply of these waters might be cut off or seriously curtailed. Since 1952, the two governments had been negotiating under auspices of the IBRD for a resolution of this dispute. 

In 1960 agreement was finally reached on a Bank plan designed to ensure a water supply to both parties. 

Basically, the Bank's plan provides that India shall have the use of the waters of the three eastern rivers of the Indus Rivers system, and that the downstream irrigated areas formerly supplied with water from these three rivers shall in the future be supplied with water brought from the three western rivers through a series of diversions and link canals. The plan also provides for hydroelectric installations, storage areas, and drainage improvements to assist in controlling salinization of irrigated lands in Pakistan. Under it, too, India will be enabled to complete and operate her ambitious Rajasthan Desert irrigation scheme. The required system of works will provide by far the largest irrigation system in the world. 

Significance of the program to the United States The Indus waters dispute is one of two major controversies which have disturbed relations between India and Pakistan since the partition of India in 1947. This dispute and the Kashmir problem have posed a continuing threat to the political stability of this vital area in south Asia and have prevented the two countries from concentrating fully on programs of economic and social development. Settlement of this issue constitutes a major step toward closer relations between the two countries, which is a major policy objective of the United States. It was in support of these policy objectives that the United 

States decided to contribute substantially to the plan for solution of the Indus waters dispute formulated by the International Bank for Reconstruction and 

Development. 

Financial plan 

Since the cost of the necessary scheme of works, estimated at more than a billion dollars, could not be undertaken by India and Pakistan alone, the IBRD proposed that the United States and five other countries join with it in establishing a fund to assure the main part of the financial assistance needed for the construction recommended by the Bank. As finally agreed, the Indus Basin 

Development Fund, relating to works in Pakistan, included commitments of $895 million from Australia, Canada, Germany, India, New Zealand, Pakistan, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the IBRD. Works in India are to be financed by loans to the Government of India of $33 million by the United States and $23 million by the IBRD, and through the provision by India of about $144 million in rupees to cover local currency costs. (See table of contributions attached.)

The current U.S. commitment totals $515 million ($482 million to the Fund plus a $33 million loan to India) consisting of $177 million in dollar grants, two Development Loan Fund loans amounting to $103 million, and $235 million in local currency loans or grants. 

Congressional approval of U.S. participation in the Indus Basin development plan was contained in the Mutual Security Act of 1960-section 404 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended (see text attached). 

Status of project The Indus Waters Treaty, containing the terms of settlement of the Indus dispute, was signed by President Ayub and Prime Minister Nehru in Karachi on September 19, 1960. At the same time the Indus Basin Development Fund was signed by Pakistan, by the IBRD, and by the United States, Australia, Canada, Germany, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom, all of which contributed to the Fund. India's contribution to the Fund was made pursuant to an agreement contained in the Indus Waters Treaty. Ratifications of the Indus Waters 

Treaty were exchanged on January 12, 1961. 

As administrator of the Fund, the IBRD has proceeded to employ the necessary consultants. American firms have been hired by the West Pakistan Power and Development Authority as the general engineering consultant and as consultants for the dam on the Indus River and for link canals. Contracts were

​T awarded in January 1962 to American firms for construction of both the big Mangla Dam on the Jhelum River, and the first section of the top priority link canal, that of Trimmu-Sidhnai, totaling in value some $380 million. Construction is proceeding on rail spurs, bridges, and connecting roads required in the construction of the Mangla Dam. In addition, bids have been received and are under study for construction of the Sidhnai-Mailsi link canal and the Sidhnai Barrage. Tenders have been issued, or soon will be on several other aspects of the Indus works. 

Relationship to bilateral U.S. programs 

The system of works being carried out under the Indus Basin development program is integrally related to the national development efforts of both India and Pakistan and thus to the bilateral U.S. aid programs in both countries. 

Over time, the overall utilization of Indus Basin waters for irrigation and power-hence production-will be enhanced, thus furthering a major U.S. objective. Bilateral development loans to India assist in financing related projects in that country, as do U.S. contributions to the Indus Basin Development Fund the basic system of works in Pakistan. Special provision was made in the 

4-year food-for-peace agreement with Pakistan consumated in 1961 for directing a portion of the sales proceeds to meeting a part of the local currency requirements of the Indus program. 

Proposed U.S. contribution and relationship to prior-year financing 

Pursuant to requests from the Bank, the United States in fiscal year 1961 contributed $6.8 million toward its total dollar grant commitment of $177 million. The United States has also made a Development Loan Fund loan of $70 million to Pakistan, which accrues to the Indus Basin. Fund for administration with its other funds. 

IBRD calls on the United States for U.S. contributions to the Indus Basin 

Fund in fiscal year 1962 against our dollar aid commitment, will amount to $34.5 million; $94.5 million in Pakistani rupees, available from the sale of agricultural commodities under Public Law 480, will also be provided during fiscal year 1962 against our local currency commitment to the Fund. The rate of U.S. contributions, and that of other contributors to the Fund, is based upon the cost-sharing formula set forth in the agreement and the precise amount needed during specific 6-month callup periods as notified by the IBRD. The amount called for by the Bank in any given period is, of course, related to the rate of project progress. 

Present indications are that requirements for U.S. grant contributions to the 

Fund during fiscal year 1963 will be on the order of $30 million and the equivalent of $46.4 million in Pakistan rupees derived from the sale of agricultural commodities under the food-for-peace program. These preliminary estimates of requirements are, however, subject to adjustment depending upon the rapidity of work progress and the reexamination presently being made by the Bank of total estimated project costs in the light of more refined engineering data and other cost factors.

SECTION 404. INDUS BASIN DEVELOPMENT-THE MUTUAL SECURITY ACT OF 1954, AS AMENDED 

The Congress of the United States welcomes the progress made through the good offices of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development toward the development of the Indus Basin through a program of cooperation among south Asian and other nations of the free world in order to promote economic growth and political stability in south Asia, and affirms the willingness of the United States, pursuant to authorities contained in this and other Acts, to participate in this significant undertaking. In the event that funds appropriated pursuant to this Act are made available to be used by or under the supervision of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development in furtherance of the foregoing purposes, such funds may be used in accordance with requirements, standards, or procedures established by the Bank concerning completion of plans and cost estimates and determination of feasibility, rather than with requirements, standards, or procedures concerning such matters set forth in this or other Acts; and such funds may also be used without regard to the provisions of section 901 (b) of the Merchant Marine Act of 1936, as amended (46 U.S.C. 1241), whenever the President determines that such provisions cannot be fully satisfied without seriously impeding or preventing accomplishment of such purposes: Provided, That compensating allowances are made in the administration of other programs to the same or other areas to which the requirements of said section 901 (b) are applicable.

COMMISSION FOR TECHNICAL COOPERATION IN AFRICA SOUTH OF THE SAHARA 

Purpose of the program The Commission for Technical Cooperation in Africa South of the Sahara (CCTA) was established by the colonial powers in January 1950 for the purpose of encouraging and strengthening technical and scientific cooperation in that area. 

The CCTA is primarily a secretariat concerned with providing technical assistance, the sponsoring of symposia and meetings, and the initiation and coordination of multicountry projects. Neither CCTA nor its operating arm, the Foundation for Mutual Assistance in Africa South of the Sahara, have substantial funds of their own. They arrange for activities but expenses are borne by countries participating in the particular projects. Since the agreement governing CCTA's responsibilities and functions was signed in London in 1954 by the Governments of Belgium, Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, France, Portugal, Union of South Africa, and the United Kingdom, the organization's African membership has increased constantly. Ghana was the first of the newly independent states to join (1957) and was followed by Liberia in 1958, the Republic of Guinea in 1959, and Cameroon in 1960. At CCTA's 16th session at Lagos in February 1961, 15 additional African states joined CCTA. At the 17th CCTA session in early 

February 1962 the role of the metropoles was very much reduced and the organization has become completely African. 

CCTA attempts to work closely with such international organizations as the U.N. Economic Commission for Africa and the U.N. specialized agencies operating in Africa. It is advised on scientific and technical matters by the Scientific 

Council for Africa South of the Sahara which is comprised of private experts from various member countries. It administers the Inter-African Research 

Fund whose purpose is to promote joint research on scientific and technical matters of regional significance. From its headquarters in Lagos, CCTA supervises the work of over 25 specialized bureaus and committees in which member countries participate; e.g., the Inter-African Bureau for Animal Health, the Inter- 

African Bureau for Soils and Rural Economy, the Panel of Education Correspondents, and the Inter-African Labour Institute. 

Significance of the CCTA to the United States An objective of the United States in Africa has been to encourage the African states to attack common problems with their common resources and to make more effective use of their existing manpower and facilities. Since this is the primary purpose of the CCTA, great impetus can be given to the furtherance of this U.S. objective by supporting the plans and activities of that organization. 

Examples of especially useful and successful projects (1) Eradication of rinderpest: CCTA has developed a program, jointly with 

Nigeria, Cameroon, Chad, and Niger, for the vaccination of cattle against rinderpest. The project will extend over 3 years, beginning in fiscal year 1962, and will cost approximately $6.4 million. EEC is contributing about $2 million; the four countries are providing the equivalent of about $3.6 million. AID will contribute $800,000 for equipment and other costs. (2) Sea fisheries and oceanographic survey: The CCTA has developed a program, coordinated with simultaneous surveys of the U.S. Navy and the Fish and Wildlife Service of the U.S. Department of Interior, to survey the offshore waters of the Gulf of Guinea from Mauritania to Angola. The survey, which will extend over a 2-year period, will determine the fisheries potential in the area as a first step toward the development of indigenous fishing industries. The 

United States is contributing $700,000 toward the total cost of the project which will be about $1.2 million. (3) Development of vaccine against bovine pleuropneumonia: The CCTA has developed a 3-year research project, beginning in fiscal year 1962, to develop a vaccine against pleuropneumonia, the only major bovine disease that does not have a vaccine that will bring about any length of immunity within vaccinated cattle. The project, costing about $360,000, will be financed by CCTA member countries and the United States, and will use existing laboratories in Kenya and Senegal. The United States is providing $200,000 for this project. 

Relationship to bilateral U.S. programs of similar nature 

The CCTA seeks to stimulate economic progress by encouraging regional economic cooperation among the respective African states. This is also a primary objective of the United States in Africa which is being sought through such 81496-62-pt. 4- -10

projects as the regional insect control program, the regional education grants program, and a variety of multicountry vocational training and other activities. 

U.S. participation in CCTA projects therefore gives maximum support to this multilateral and self-help approach to the solution of many of Africa's problems. 

Proposed U.S. contribution and relationship to prior-year financing 

The total U.S. contribution to CCTA projects proposed for fiscal year 1963 is $600,000. This compares with a total U.S. contribution in fiscal year 1962 of $1.7 million. This decrease does not reflect a diminishing U.S. interest in the 

CCTA or its activities, rather, it results from the fact that during fiscal year 1962 the United States made large contributions to three major projects each of which are scheduled to extend over a 2or 3-year period. 

The funds requested in fiscal year 1963 will enable the United States to continue to support selected projects of the CCTA considered to be of prime importance for the economic development of the area. 

Although member countries are assessed a small amount each year to cover administrative expenses (approximately $2,800 each) of the organization, there is no established ratio for contributions to meet the cost of technical assistance activities or the implementation of "joint projects." Generally speaking, the recipient country bears the expense of the technical assistance it receives. The so-called joint projects are financed by contributions from the countries directly benefited, usually in the form of commodities, personnel, or services, and by external financial and other aid. 

Purpose of the program 

ASIAN PRODUCTIVITY ORGANIZATION 

The purpose of the Asian Productivity Organization (APO) is to help the free countries of Asia to raise their standards of living through increased productivity-primarily in industry-and thus to encourage sound industrial development.

In furtherance of its objective, the APO sponsors seminars and workshop meetings to bring technical and professional people together for training and exchange of ideas. These meetings cover such subjects as training for industrial managers and aid to small business. The APO will also sponsor multinational study teams-some to visit one or more member countries; others to visit more advanced countries outside the region to explore such subjects as the role of industrial estates in industrial development, standardization, and quality control. It also plans to facilitate the exchange of information through periodic publication of digests of technical information. 

The APO came into being in April 1961 with the signing of the APO convention by the following eight countries: Republic of China, India, Japan, Korea, Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines, and Thailand. Other countries in south and southeast Asia such as Malaya, Burma, Ceylon, and the territories of Hong Kong and Singapore may become members in the near future. 

During 1961 the APO recruited a secretariat staff from among the member countries. APO workshop conferences took place in New Delhi, India, and 

Lahore, Pakiston, and a special 3-month training program on machinery repair and maintenance, sponsored by the Yawata Steel Co., Ltd., of Japan, was held under APO auspices. The APO also sent experts to member countries to conduct surveys to determine how it could best assist in such fields as marketing and distribution, and production techniques. 

The APO is essentially an Asian organization and is open to membership by any government which is a member of ECAFE. The United States is not a member. Governments outside the Asian region may become associate members, subject to approval of two-thirds of the directors of the governing body. 

The APO charter provides for the establishment of formal or informal relationships with the United Nations, other international and national organizations (e.g., AID). APO activities supplement the programs of other international entities such as the U.N., ECAFE, Colombo plan, nonprofit organizations, AID, and the assistance activities of other nations. In time, by promoting multilateral cooperation among the Asian countries, the APO will help reduce the need for technical assistance from outside the area. 

It is proposed to contribute $200,000 in U.S. assistance to the APO for fiscal year 1963 to help finance the program activities described above and to supplement member country contributions. U.S. assistance will finance special training programs, including studies in the United States for multinational groups

in specialized fields of management and production, and will finance the participation of U.S. experts in multinational workshops and seminars held under 

APO auspices in various Asian countries. 

Significance of the program to the United States The The work of the newly established Asian Productivity Organization is directed toward the development of Asia's productive resources and the encouragement of technical and economic cooperation among the countries of the area. establishment of this multilateral organization, founded by Asian initiative and responsive to the needs of its member countries, represents a step toward the creation of regional economic ties among countries of Asia—a basic U.S. interest. 

Examples of especially useful and successful projects Illustrative of APO activities in 1961-its first year of operation-were two projects: 

1. The Workshop Conference on Aid to Small Business held in Lahore, Pakistan, from October 16 to 21.-This workshop was attended by delegates from eight Asian member countries and included officials from their national productivity institutions. The workshop stressed the need for providing assistance to small business, and for giving proper training to small business managers, many of whom lack broad educational backgrounds and experience. The conference delegates also considered the needs for standardization, quality control, improved product design, and technical information for small industry. The workshop conference summed up its work in a list of recommendations which, among others, urged that APO establish a special division responsible for work with small industries, and that priorities be given to those member countries in the early stages of industrial development. 

2. Management survey.—In recognition of the importance of management to increased productivity and the great need for management training and development, an expert group was selected to survey the needs of Asian management. 

The 3-man group visited 22 cities in the 8 member countries over a 2month period. Their report noted that technical training cannot suffice without corresponding training in management, and vice versa. It also contained more than 20 specific recommendations to the national productivity centers and to the APO on ways to improve management in the member countries. 

The Management Expert Survey Group concluded their report by noting the favorable impact that APO was making. The report stated: "Without exception the formation of APO has been welcomed by all member countries with open arms. The lack of political strings, the nonprofit motive, and the unique banding of Asians for purposes truly nonbelligerent and aimed at increasing productivity and raising living standards, are features which have had an immediate favorable impact in all quarters. The size of the country, the color of its people, and the wealth may vary from one member to another, but there still is a common denominator of problems, hopes and aspirations."

Relationship to bilateral U.S. programs of similar nature 

APO activities are complementary to U.S. bilateral assistance programs in 

Asia, particularly those portions of U.S. programs designed to assist industrial development in the free countries of Asia. The APO works directly with national productivity and industrial development centers located in its member countries; and is supplementary to and closely coordinated with U.S. bilateral work in this field. The United States maintains liaison with the APO Secretariat, presently located in Tokyo. 

Proposed U.S. contributions and relationship to prior-year financing 

The sum of $200,000 is proposed as the U.S. contribution to the Asian Productivity Organization for fiscal year 1963. The exact composition and extent of the APO's third-year program will depend on the progress made by this new Organization in calendar year 1962. Therefore, despite proposals that have been made for an increased program in fiscal year 1963, it is considered desirable at this time to plan for a U.S. contribution of $200,000, the same amount provided by the United States in fiscal year 1962.

In its first year of operation, it planned a series of multicountry activities, recruited the necessary personnel, and carried out its program on schedule. It has through its activities, developed strong interest on the part of its members.
