Washington, D.C.

10:44 a.m., Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding.

The committee meets this morning in executive session for a continuation of the foreign aid hearings for 1962. 

It is customary for the Secretary of State to be our leadoff witness when we open hearings on the foreign aid bill. Unfortunately he had to be at the Disarmament Conference in Geneva and we had Mr. 

Hamilton to open the hearings. We said then that when he returned from Geneva and had the time we would bring him back before the committee.

The Secretary has no prepared statement. He will give an oral statement and then he will answer questions. 

STATEMENT OF HON. DEAN RUSK, SECRETARY OF STATE 

Secretary RUSK. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee,

I appreciate this chance to be here to discuss foreign aid for the coming year. You have already had extensive testimony from my colleagues in the Department and in the aid program, so I thought that I would not submit a formal statement for the record or to take too much of your time with going over materials with which you are already familiar. 

I don't believe, Mr. Chairman, that it is necessary for me at this stage to set forth the basic policy case for foreign aid in all of its detail, because over the years this committee itself has taken a leading role in shaping our aid programs, and in articulating that policy both to the Congress and to the people in a very effective fashion. 

But the more deeply I get into what is going on in country after country in different parts of the world, the more convinced I am that the United States through its own experience, through its example, and through its enunciation of its own basic ideas, is responsible in a most direct and intimate way. 

The United States is itself directly responsible for two of the most powerful revolutionary forces that are at work in the world today. 

The first of those is the revolution of freedom, the stirrings throughout the world, both in the older colonial empires and other places for a freeing of political arrangements and political institutions. I think 793

this is a powerful force. I think it is not only working in the so-called free world, certainly not just among our allies but among the uncommitted countries and is making its influence felt behind the curtain. 

The second is the demand, the rapidly rising demand for economic and social progress. I do not believe this has come out of stimulation from the Communist bloc. I believe this has come about because of the example which this country has shown, the general notion that the miseries of practical life are not a part of an inevitable environment in which people have been placed by providence, but are matters which people can do something about, that the influence of the United States throughout the world in this regard has been very powerful. 

We do believe that this committee ought to be and will be interested in some of the underlying notions as to how we shape up an aid program which will be as effective as possible within the means of the limited resources which can be brought to bear upon it. 

Certainly a fundamental and indispensable requirement for the development of any nation is the determination of its own governing people to get on with the job. This is not just a policy. It is almost a truism, because it seems perfectly obvious to us that unless a nation is prepared itself to take the steps necessary to move on with its own development there is not much that can be done for it from the outside. 

In the case of the Alliance for Progress, for example, our commitments, our proposed investments there will run something less than 2 percent of the gross national products of the countries concerned as a group. The 2 percent is in relation to a 98 percent. What happens with the 98 percent will make the crucial difference, of course, whether development is possible. 

When we talk about self-help as a precondition of our aid, we are really talking about whether there is a situation in which our own investments can make any difference and whether in fact we can in good conscience go to the American taxpayers to ask them for the resources which we are asking them to put up in order to help out with these great jobs.

We have tried increasingly, both through official channels and through American business channels in association with our own foreign colleagues, to try to underline and emphasize the fact that these aid funds in the United States do not come out of some hidden reserve of unlimited dimensions, but come out of the taxpayer's pocket throughout the country.

Those taxpayers are people in all walks of life who make their own contribution to the program. Therefore we must insist that foreign countries who are applying for such aid make a case that such aid can be effectively used and that they themselves are doing the best job that they can do with their own resources. 

Our aid itself will be limited in quantity in regard to the affairs of any particular country, even a country like India where our aid is substantial. India has a gross national product of something like $36 billion and our contribution would be relatively small. But from the point of view of the American taxpayer they should be handled in the most effective way.

We are putting a great deal of emphasis on fostering long-range economic and social growth, trying to get away from the shotgun approach to particular projects, because, looking back over the last

15 years of aid effort, we are convinced that solid growth requires an approach on the basis of priorities, that we should try to work toward first things first, we should try to have some idea as to how the job we do this year is related to what is done next year, and that we not overlook the crucial bottlenecks which will prevent advance on a broad front, because to do so would lead us into futility and frustration.

The matter of developing long-range planning is difficult. In many countries the basic structural planning, the basic statistical base of planning is not present, and of course the presence of capable people who can conduct or direct effective planning is always a problem. 

We are giving considerable emphasis in these later programs, these newer programs on the education and training of the qualified leadership who will be needed for any substantial economic and social development program. 

I recall, if I may digress a moment, Mr. Chairman, that for a number of years I was associated with a private foundation that had been for the last 50 years working in the general field of what is now called technical assistance in many countries right around the world. That foundation was committed to the alleviation of the practical problems, to the welfare problems of mankind, particularly in the health field and in the field of increasing productivity-the practical problems of daily life.

But it soon became apparent as early as 1920 that almost none of these practical programs could go forward without a base of trained personnel. So it was no accident that this particular private foundation spent between 60 to 70 percent of its total resources over the years for the training of personnel, because that proved to be the crucial bottleneck in moving forward. 

We have been very much encouraged by the growing interest of the industrialized nations of the free world in taking a larger part in assisting developing countries. In 1960 our NATO allies and Japan provided $2.3 billion compared to our own approximately $3 billion. 

That particular sum on their part is somewhat larger as a percent of their gross national product than is ours. If you add private investment to it, their total investment was somewhat larger than ours, $4.2 billion, as opposed to about $3.8 billion on our side. I believe Mr. 

Coffin gave the committee detailed information on that. 

There is another point which shows considerable progress, and that is that the developing nations themselves do have an opportunity to help each other. We are more and more aware of steps which are being taken in this direction. For example, countries like Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, and Chile are receiving rapidly growing numbers of students from other American States for study in some of their best universities and scientific institutes and research organizations. 

This is the kind of thing which is going on in other parts of the world as developing nations find that there are ways in which they can lend a hand across their own borders. This is something that ought to be expanded just as rapidly as the situation will permit. 

We do also believe, and we are quite certain that this committee insists, that our administration of the aid program should be as efficient as possible. It is a matter which requires full-time attention, 24-hour attention. No matter how much progress we make we know there is room for improvement.

Again it is a question of getting the right people in the right spot. 

Our recruitment program has been going on intensively. We have been very pleased with the leadership that we have been able to recruit thus far in our key positions. We think there are many things that can be done there that will make the investment of our funds more significant. 

I would comment briefly, Mr. Chairman, on two matters that have already been discussed before the committee. The one is the recommendation that we separate out in a special title our program for the Alliance for Progress and give that a 4-year forward authorization commitment.

That is, quite frankly, a matter of judgment as to how we best relate what we do here to what will be required south of the Rio Grande. 

We are very much aware of the fact that the Alliance for Progress is going to create considerable tensions, complications and difficulties within the political systems of many of the Latin American countries. 

On the one side, we must be insistent that they meet certain criteria, that they are serious about their own commitments and they move ahead and do the best they can with their own resources. On the other side, we want those actions to be taken through democratic processes. In these democratic processes we will find much of the controversy which we have ourselves experienced since the times of Theodore Roosevelt in getting some of these things done in our own society. 

We do need for purposes of encouragement, for purposes of reliability, for purposes of negotiation with our Latin American friends, a considerable degree of assurance that this country is serious over a period of time; and on psychological grounds we believe it would be extremely helpful to us if the Congress would see fit to enact the Alliance title as proposed by the President. 

We recognize this is not a simple matter, that it has some elements in it which will undoubtedly give the Congress some cause for serious thought. But on balance we believe it would be important for us to be able to go to these Latin American countries with a maximum position of strength in order to elicit from them a persistent and strong effort which they will have to make, some of them under difficult conditions, if they are to get on with the Alliance for Progress in their own countries. 

I would like to conclude these brief opening remarks with a reference to the contingency fund. In many respects the free money, the contingency fund, is among the most valuable part of the AID appropriation itself. We do need on the one side a full understanding on the part of the Congress as to how funds under such a large program as the AID program will be used, but on the other side we need a considerable degree of flexibility in order to adjust to the unexpected situations.

During the past year, for example, it was a lifesaver to us to have a contingency fund with which we could move promptly as the situation developed in the Dominican Republic, and as the pace of pressures and infiltration stepped up in Vietnam-it was very important to us to have a chance to respond there. When a new Syrian Government came into existence it was possible for us to move promptly in giving them minimum assistance in getting off with a start on their balance of payments arrangements.

We do not look upon the contingency fund as an addition to those appropriations which the Congress has limited in one way or another, but a genuine effort to put ourselves in a position to respond promptly to fast-moving situations in different parts of the world. 

Mr. Chairman, I have spoken very briefly and very simply. I would welcome the chance to go into these matters or anything that would be on the minds of the members of the committee. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

Mr. Secretary, I am glad to hear you speak briefly about our program in Latin America because there are indications that the Alliance for Progress has got off to a poor start. The basic social reforms that are essential to progress in Latin America are meeting resistance. 

As you know, we had a recent episode in Chile that you are familiar with, that is evidence of the attitude there. The basic principle, that without these fundamental reforms our money will be wasted, is still sound.

Do you want to expand a little bit on some of the resistance we are meeting in Latin America in trying to get our program off to a better start?

Secretary RUSK. I think there are several types of resistance that have already manifested themselves. Some of them to be expected, some of them perhaps not so easy to understand. 

I think in the first place, when we talk about land reform, we are talking about changing the position of those who now control vast rural properties. When we are talking about tax reform, we are talking about collecting more taxes in most situations than has been collected for many years. When we are talking about administrative improvement, we are talking about moving in on various elements of corruption or inadequate work habits within administration, and an inquiring role in the actual conformation of governmental institutions. 

I was in a country not too long ago, Mr. Chairman, where government workers worked 4 hours a day. I discussed with one of the officials of that country how it was possible that we could spend our time up here working 6 and 7 full days a week to be of some assistance to that country and others when they were working 4 hours a day. 

In another country the habit of their own capitalists in sending off their capital outside the country for investment is one that we have to counteract if we are to make our investment in that country not only worthwhile but conscionable from the point of view of our own investment sources.

We know that this whole concept in the Alliance for Progress is delivering a shock to existing institutions in a considerable number of countries. Fortunately many of the businessmen, both American and local, are beginning to understand somewhat better what business prosperity in the long run calls for, what our own experience has been here, that the possibilities of rising standards of living: the prospects of expanding markets, are the great challenge for business rather than to exercise a restrictive position in a static or unyielding situation. 

These resistances are going to be real. In one country, for example, proposals which we had urged to be put forward have been blocked in the congress because the congress does not wish the present executive to have the political kudos of moving ahead on a particular aid program. They want to reserve that for the next administration, since

an election is coming up. That is being delayed; therefore our funds are marking time because the local congress does not see fit to enact the necessary legislation to move forward. We won't put in funds under those considerations.

I think this is a matter which will have to be nursed along country by country within the political and other possibilities of the time. The present Government of Korea, for example, is anxious to move against corruption. The report I have had is that the theft of American-supplied aid in the military field in Korea has been reduced to 4 percent of what it was before this present regime came in. But the present regime moved with great severity, if you like. They applied death penalties for theft and things of that sort. 

We would like to see these measures taken, but we would like to see them taken under the basic standards of justice if we possibly can. 

This is going to be one of our problems in Latin America. They have got to move. But if they move with democratic processes it will be complicated, it will be time-consuming. To a degree, we are talking about bringing the Queen Elizabeth into dock without tugs in some instances. I believe we should apply our own aid funds in pace with their reform efforts, in pace with their own performance, not wait until they have completed everything we had hoped they would do but to use them in relation to each other so that as we move ahead there will be real growth and real improvement in each of these countries. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, just one more brief question:

Does the fact that these reforms are coming slowly, reduce their capacity to use American dollars? 

Secretary RUSK. To a degree, Mr. Chairman. And also it reduces our willingness to put those funds up. We have funds in more than one situation which are being held back until they take additional steps. We do think that the pace of the Alliance for Progress, including our own effort, will be largely determined by their ability and willingness to get the things done which we consider are basic to an cffective development program. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. 

Mr. Chiperfield. 

Mr. Secretary, I sincerely believe you are doing the very best you can to do a good job. I think that is all that anyone can expect. 

I wish you well. In making that statement, of course, I reserve the right to disagree any time when I have a different viewpoint. 

The only question I have to ask you is this: I hear about a so-called new policy called a "no-win policy." Would you try to explain to this committee what that means?

Secretary RUSK. I would be happy to comment on that, Mr. Chiperfield. Perhaps our recorder would avoid the error that was made by a Louisiana newspaper a few days ago when this expression was used. It came out as "know-when policy." If we follow that policy specifically we might be better off sometimes. 

I think this expression has been used from different quarters without any attempt to elaborate the alternatives. Sometimes it seems to me that some of those who talk about a "no-win policy" want to participate in a hydrogen war. I think anyone who understands what that means in the modern world will not want to go down that trail

lightly, because this in fact means the incineration of the Northern Hemisphere. To become impatient, to let lags and frustration take over and let some of these critically dangerous questions go down the slippery slope to a hydrogen war, that would be, from a political point of view, from a view of diplomacy, the simplest policy and the most disastrous. 

The other approach is almost at the other extreme of the spectrum. 

Some who talk about a "no-win policy" think we ought to quit, get out of the United Nations, out of NATO, out of the Organization of American States, we ought to abandon foreign aid; a combination of steps which would mean that we would simply yield the field to the opposition.

I have not myself seen a careful articulation of the alternative policies which are urged by some who use this expression "no-win." 

I myself believe that the free world-I do not refer specifically just to the United States at this point, because there are many others in this with us that the free world is playing a policy which moves with the winning currents of history in this whole story of freedom, that we are doing it with a good deal of persistence. We are doing it at the cost of a good deal of sacrifice on the part of our peoples. 

I believe in fact this is a winning policy, this general approach; an approach which has been bipartisan in this country and has been broadly international insofar as the core of the free world alliance is concerned.

I think it is important that no country which has become independent since 1945 has moved behind the bloc. I think it is important that in situation after situation where in 1954 the Soviets or the Sino- Soviet bloc have moved in with economic and other types of assistance, they discover you do not seize control of a country through such blandishments. 

I am encouraged by the steady process. I am encouraged by the complications that people in the Communist bloc have run into in trying to make their own systems work. 

I believe that in the broadest sense, Mr. Chairman, the policies that have been worked out here in this country in the Congress, with the executive branch, on a bipartisan basis, and within the Alliance are the policies which are designed to take the best care of the interests of the American people. 

Mr. CHIPERFIELD. Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Zablocki. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI.  

I want to associate myself with the remarks of Mr. Chiperfield, regarding your sincerity and determination to do a good job. I comend you for your efforts.

Following Mr. Chiperfield's question regarding the so-called no-win policy, I think it would be enlightening to this committee, Mr. Secretary, if you could tell us about the task performed by Mr. Rostow in the Department. To what degree does he set policy, or to what extent do his recommendations influence our foreign policy? 

Secretary RUSK. Mr. Rostow and his group, the Policy Planning 

Council, take on a considerable number of tasks at my specific request. 

And their recommendations, their papers are circulated in the Department for consideration by what might be called the operational

policy officers. In other words, the Policy Planning staff itself issues no directives. It simply studies, examines, and makes recommendations to those of us who are carrying direct policy responsibility and are issuing instructions day by day. 

In any situation, of course, a group like that comes up with ideas from time to time which in one way or another are not actually adopted. That is not in any sense a diminution of their role because to some extent they are supposed to be the gadfly of the organization. 

My personal directive to them has been that they should question statements of fact, look at the range of policies, so that those who are carrying the harassed burden of day-by-day action will have the full benefit of the alertness and the thoughtfulness of a group of 12 or 15 top people who spend their entire time in a broader range approach to problems than the action officers in many situations. 

I have great confidence in that group and a great appreciation for their distinguished service.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. It is also true that the Department was in full operation and that Mr. Ball did a distinguished job as Acting Secretary during my absence. I would suppose during my absence the situation remained normal.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Chairman, I am sure all of us on the committee are very happy to have this clarified because, in your absence, Mr.

Secretary RUSK. To be entirely candid, Mr. Zablocki, what you say could happen in this sense: We have been trying to cut back, as you know, on what is called supporting assistance, in order to move into direct development work which is not just in effect on the basis of a dole as far as development is concerned. We are cutting down our programing for supporting assistance for quite a considerable number of countries.

We can't really be sure that we can make good on all of that program for the next year. So that it may be that it is necessary for us to use it in now unforeseen circumstances in those countries where we had hoped to move away from supporting assistance. 

There are other contingencies that are still somewhat unforeseen that would make us much more comfortable about a contingency fund which would make it possible for us to move rapidly. In the

case of the Dominican Republic, for example, we did need an ability to commit funds within a matter of hours. We may have other situations of that sort in which we need a fast access to funds which would give us a chance to move. 

We do not now have in mind that the sum we ask for in the contingency fund is specifically programed for particular countries, that, say, we are dropping off the supporting assistance list. If that was so, we would say so. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. This brief question on personnel. I was very interested in your report, Mr. Secretary, that the Rockefeller Foundation had you didn't identify it, but it was that foundation-had expended about 60 or 70 percent of its budget on the training of personnel.

Secretary RUSK. I would like to underline and emphasize the point of your question, because I think that we ourselves discovered-and I tend to look back in our own experience on these matters because we have demonstrated rapid economic development under free institutions, I think we have got a lot to learn from it-we have discovered in our own national experience that the role of the land-grant colleges, whose 100th anniversary we are now celebrating, was critical in our development. 

Had it not been possible to educate our county agents, our public health officers, our trained technicians for work, in whether agriculture, industry, or whatever, had we not had those institutions for this past century, particularly in the last 40 or 50 years, our gross national product would be far less than what it is at the present time.

I met it head on Saturday with a large group of veterans.

Mr. Hays. For his excellent cooperation in reorienting the Japanese Air Force as one of our arms of defense against the Communists. 

Mrs. BOLTON. That is what my veterans will want to know. 

Secretary RUSK. Let me furnish a statement for the record on that.

(The statement is as follows:) 

This award was presented to General Genda by the senior U.S. military officer present in Japan, who on the date of the presentation happened to be General Lemnitzer. General Lemnitzer was visiting Japan in the course of making an inspection of various military installations in the Far East. 

The award was made to General Genda for having distinguished himself by exceptionally meritorious conduct in the performance of outstanding services as the Chief of Staff, Japan Air Self-Defense Force, from July 18, 1959, to March 31, 1962. The leadership and dedicated efforts of this individual are reported to have contributed immeasurably to strengthening the relationships and furthering the interests of common defense to the benefit of Japan and the United States.

It is true that General Genda, while a rather low ranking officer did serve as one of the many planners for an attack which eventually took place at Pearl Harbor. He functioned as any other professional military officer would in a staff planning capacity. He was not in a position to make any decision concerning the use of the plans on which he worked. 

Upon conclusion of the peace treaty between the United States and Japan, at which time Japan as a nation again joined the free world, General Genda began service in the Japan Defense Agency. It is known that he served his country well. However, while so doing he also became a firm friend of the United States in Japan and the Far East. As was pointed out in the citation to his decoration, his inspiring leadership and dedicated efforts have contributed immeasurably to the strengthening of the relationships between our two countries, particularly during his tenure as Chief of Staff of the Japan Air Self-Defense Force. 

General Genda has retired from his military position in order to run for office in the hope of being elected to the Upper House of the Japanese Diet. His understanding of the U.S. positions and relationships, and his friendship for the United States, can only continue to serve the best interests of our Nation.

DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE DIRECTIVE Subject: Medal of Freedom. 

18 February 1953 NUMBER 1005. 2 

Reference: Executive Order #10336, Volume 17, #68 Federal Register, 5 April 1952 (Amendment of Executive Order #9586 of 6 July 1945, Estab lishing the Medal of Freedom).

I. PURPOSE 

The purpose of this directive is to furnish policy guidance to the military departments in implementing the provisions of the above named Executive Order. 

1. To whom awarded

II. POLICY 

a. The Medal of Freedom may be awarded to any person not hereinafter specifically excluded who, on or after 7 December 1941 has performed a meritorious act or service which has either: (1) Aided the United States in the prosecution of a war against an enemy or enemies, (2) Aided any nation engaged with the United States in the prosecution of a war against a common enemy or enemies, or (3) During any period of national emergency declared by the President or the Congress to exist, has furthered the interests of the security of the United States or of any nation allied or associated with the United States during such period, and for which act or service the award of any other United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate; or b. Under special circumstances, and without regard to the existence of a state of war or national emergency, the Medal of Freedom may also be awarded by, or at the direction of, the President to any person, not hereinafter specifically

excluded, for performance of a meritorious act or service in the interests of the security of the United States. c. The Medal of Freedom shall not be awarded to a citizen of the United States for any act or service performed within the continental limits of the United States or to a member of the armed forces of the United States. 

2. Standards a. Citizens and habitual residents of the United States. (1) The award of this decoration shall be based on the performance of an act, service or achievement in such a creditable manner as can be recognized as outstanding when compared with the performance by others of similar acts, service or achievement. The service performed must be over and above that required considering the speed of accomplishment, determination of the individual and its effect on the mission of the United States or any nation allied or associated with the United States in prosecuting a war or during any period of national emergency declared by the President or Congress to exist, its effect on furthering the interest of the security of the United States or of any nation allied or associated with the United States. (2) Awards will be made without reference to degree and the Medal of 

Freedom without Palm will be issued. b. Citizens and members of armed forces of foreign nations. (1) The award of this decoration shall be based on the performance of an act, service or achievement in such a creditable manner as can be recognized as outstanding when compared with the performance by others of similar acts, service or achievement. The service performed must be over and above that required considering the speed of accomplishment, determination of the individual and its effect on the mission of the United States or any nation allied or associated with the United States in prosecuting a war or during any period of national emergency declared by the President or Congress to exist, its effect on furthering the interest of the security of the United States or of any nation allied or associated with the United States. (2) The Medal of Freedom will be awarded in one of the following de grees which corresponds to the respective military decorations indicated: 

(a) Gold Palm (Legion of Merit, Chief Commander). 

(b) Silver Palm (Legion of Merit, Commander). (c) Bronze Palm (Legion of Merit, Officer and Legionnaire). (d) Without Palm (Bronze Star Medal). (3) No more than one Medal or Freedom shall be awarded to any one per son, but for a subsequent act or service justifying such an award a suitable device may be awarded to be worn with the medal. 

3. By Whom Awarded a. The Medal of Freedom may be awarded by the Secretary of State, the 

Secretary of Defense, the Secretary of the Army, the Secretary of the Navy, or the Secretary of the Air Force, or by such officers as they may respectively designate. b. The head of any department or agency of the United States not named above may recommend to the Secretary of Defense the award of the Medal of Freedom and appurtenances thereto for meritorious acts or services performed under the cognizance or direction of the head of such department or agency and the Secretary of Defense may make such awards. c. The medal may also be awarded by the President under the circumstances described in Paragraph II, 1(b) of this Directive. 

4. Description 

The medal of bronze is 14 inches in diameter. On the obverse are the head, shoulders, and headdress of Freedom (taken from the statue on the top of the United States Capitol dome). In the lower portion in an arc is the inscription "FREEDOM." On the reverse is the "Liberty Bell" without carriage, within a circle composed of the words "UNITED STATES OF AMERICA." The medal is suspended by a ring from a moired silk ribbon 1% inches in length and 1% inches in width, composed of red (16-inch), white (32-inch), red (1/8-inch), white (32-inch), red (%-inch), white (32-inch), red (-inch), white (32-inch), and red (16-inch).

5. Appurtenances a. Oak Leaf Cluster. (1) A bronze oak-leaf cluster will be issued in lieu of a decoration for each succeeding award to citizens of the United States and will be worn attached to the ribbon of the decoration. (2) Description-a bronze twig of four oak leaves with three acorns on the stem, 132 inches in length for a suspension ribbon and 546 inches in length for a service ribbon. b. Palm. (1) A gold, silver, or bronze Palm is worn on the suspension and service ribbons of the Medal of Freedom awarded to foreign personnel to denote the degree in which the decoration has been awarded except cases where the description has been awarded without Palm. (2) Description—a gold, silver, or bronze Palm 1% inches in length.

III. ACTION REQUIRED 

It is desired that each of the military departments forward to the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Manpower and Personnel), within one month following the date of this directive, copies of implementing regulations to place this policy in effect. 

JOHN A. HANNAH, Assistant Secretary of Defense (Manpower and Personnel).

As set forth in Reference (a): "Recommendations for awards of the Legion of Merit, in the degree of Chief Commander, to members of the armed forces of friendly foreign nations, will be submitted by the Secretary of Defense, after concurrence by the Secretary of State, to the President for his approval. DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE DIRECTIVE 12 January 1953 NUMBER 1348.5 Subject: U.S. Decorations for Members of the Armed Forces of Foreign Nations in Peacetime

I. PURPOSE 

The purpose of this directive is to furnish policy guidance to the military departments in regard to the award of U.S. decorations to members of the armed forces of foreign nations in peacetime. 

II. POLICY 

1. The award of U.S. decorations to members of the armed forces of foreign nations in peacetime is prohibited except to recognize : a. Service of marked international significance where the interests of the 

United States are involved. b. Service which has aided the United States in furthering its national policies. c. Service which has furthered the interest of the security of the United 

States or of any nation allied or associated with the United States during a period of national emergency declared by the President or the Congress. 

2. The Legion of Merit, in four degrees, or the Medal of Freedom, in four degrees, are considered the appropriate awards for the recognition of the services described above when these services meet the standards prescribed for such awards by the military departments. 

3. Procedures for processing recommendations for awards to foreign nationals will be in accordance with policies announced by the Secretaries of the Military Departments.

ANNA M. ROSENBERG, Assistant Secretary of Defense (Manpower and Personnel). 

Title: 110 Personnel. 

DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE DIRECTIVE 

Washington 25, D.C. 

31 July 1951

NUMBER 1348.1 Subtitle: 23 Awards and Decorations (MIL). 

Number: 1348.1. 

POLICY RELATING TO UNIT DECORATIONS IN JOINT COMMANDS 

I. The purpose of this directive is to provide a uniform procedure for processng recommendations for the award of unit decorations originating within a Joint command in order to assure that comments and recommendations are obtained from the appropriate joint commanders. 

II. The provisions of this directive apply to the Departments of the Army, Navy and Air Force. 

III. A. Recommendations for the award of a unit decoration to a unit of the armed forces of the United States or a cobelligerent nation serving in a joint command will be submitted through command channels to the commander or military department having authority to make the award. In cases where any such recommendation covers services, all or a portion of which were performed while the unit was operating under a joint commander, comments or recommendations concerning the meritorious services of that unit will be obtained from the joint commander concerned. 

B. Disapproval of a recommendation by an officer subordinate to the commander or military department having authority to award the decoration will

not alone constitute authority for the return of the recommendation to the initiator. 

IV. Each military department will transmit to this office a copy of instructions issued by it to put this policy into effect. 

ANNA M. ROSENBERG, Assistant Secretary of Defense (Manpower and Personnel).

Secretary RUSK. I think that Colombia, for example, has done better than some of the others, where our own estimate is that the Government cannot do all that we would hope it could do and remain in power, and that if it goes out of power the wrong people will come in to assume power.

We think there has to be some reasonable balance of forces there so that no one, no one of the extreme wings gets control of the basic security elements in the country, and that it should be worked out on a basis of some arrangement of the ministers and their deputy ministers and army commanders. 

It is too soon to predict how this is going to come out. I can say that the Soviets appear not to be pressing for an immediate conclusion. On our side we think that a little more time might be favorable to the government forces because the longer this cease-fire can stay reasonably well established the more difficult it would be for them to move on with any political support from anybody else. 

Mr. BARRY. IS Cuba paying off for any expropriated properties they have seized from us? There was a time when they were going to offer bonds, which we believed to be phony. Are they paying off at all?

Secretary RUSK. In general, I think the answer to that question is "No." I would like to check to see whether there is anything on it at all to add to the record in terms of specifics. So far, that whole subject has not been taken up actively- (The information is as follows:)

CUBAN PAYMENT FOR EXPROPRIATED PROPERTY 

Since June 3, 1959, when the Cuban agrarian reform law was decreed, the Cuban Government expropriated in excess of $1 billion worth of property of U.S. nationals. To the knowledge of the Department of State, nothing was ever paid to compensate any U.S. property owner. 

The Cuban agrarian reform law provided for payment in 20-year bonds to persons whose property was taken thereunder. The nationalization law of July 

6, 1960, also authorized the issuance of bonds to U.S. nationals in payment for expropriated properties. The amortization of these bonds was to be accomplished with foreign exchange earned from U.S. purchases of Cuban sugar in excess of 

3 million long Spanish tons at a price set by the Cuban Government. The Department has no evidence that any of these bonds were ever issued or even printed by the Cuban Government.

Mr. Pilcher.

Mr. PILCHER. No questions, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Barry. 

Mr. BARRY. 

Mr. Secretary, do you think it would be helpful to show other 

Latin American countries that we don't intend to be tramped upon and we do hold heads of government responsible for the American businessman's investment abroad by initiating a demand on Cuba? 

Do you think that would be a salutary thing in helping your Alliance for Progress?

Secretary RUSK. I think this is a matter that we certainly ought to up in each one of the other Latin American countries where the issue arises. take

I am going to think a little about whether we should make a move in this regarding Cuba. At the present time, we don't want to leave the impression that these questions are negotiable as long as that regime is in charge. We might open up discussions that we would not want at this moment.

Mr. BARRY. In other words, you feel negotiation with the Castro regime would be harmful. 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. They would come back with all sorts of counteroffers about trade and other questions. They, I think, would try to build on this a move toward coexistence. The President has said this regime is not negotiable. These other questions are negotiable.

Mr. BARRY. Do you think there is any way of making it clear to other governments that we expect some day to collect on the property that has been seized in Cuba?

Secretary RUSK. I think that is something that is pretty generally understood. But I think we might find a way to remind them of it if the occasion arises. 

Mr. BARRY. I note Indonesia is short of rice. Are we pressing our advantage with Sukarno now on the Dutch settlement? 

Secretary RUSK. The situation there is somewhat tense because the two governments are not yet agreed on an agenda for formal negotiations. But we are hoping very much that Ambassador Bunker as an informal third party in these discussions can work out a settlement.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Beckworth. 

Mr. BECKWORTH. Mr. Secretary, just this morning in the Washington Post there is an article that has a headline, "Wrong Students 

Travel, Brazilian Says." The first sentence of this article is this: "The wrong students come to the United States on exchange programs," and then it names a person.

Then there is a representative from Mexico who is quoted, and he says that, reading the article, "Agricultural classes in Latin America are very much neglected," he said, "and such students could benefit greatly from living and working on farms while attending high school here," referring to the United States. 

What comments would you have about that type of statement?

Secretary RUSK. Traditionally, the students from most of these countries have been, of course, from the upper classes. They have been geared toward the classical type of European university. In recent years there has been a movement toward students of the sort that we have trained in our land-grant colleges. These have been coming not only under government programs but under private organization auspices of various sorts.

We are also receiving agricultural workers and are sending back now a considerable number of agricultural Ph. D.'s into Latin America. The number of veterinarians and medical people, I think, is improving. 

I think it is still true that we have not yet fully enlisted the dedication of these students to economic and social development. In too many situations you would have the trained young person who does not understand that it is all right for an educated person to get his hands dirty in the fields. 

One of the first things our own people have to do in many of these countries is to demonstrate that the educated person has to go out and exert leadership in the practical jobs- Mr. BECKWORTH. The effect of this article is that people from the peasant classes don't get here in order to be given the opportunity to have an understanding of our county. 

Do you agree? Would it be a good thing for more of this type of students to come to this country? 

Secretary RUSK. I think this is steadily improving as more of the peasant classes get trained up to the point where they can make use of it. The Inter-American School in agriculture is sending young people to this country for further training. The agricultural colleges in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, are sending people up here. There is more of that happening. We have got to multiply it and move it on. 

Mr. BECKWORTH. Our Government is trying to do more of that; is this true?

Secretary RUSK. Yes. 

Mr. BECK WORTH. I have asked as I have seen students from other countries, this question, "What does your daddy do?" "He owns a group of mines," or some similar answer has been given me quite often.

That type of fellow could get here anyway. 

Mr. HAYS. And do.

Mr. BECKWORTH. Yes. The government doesn't have to pay for him. He could pay his own way here and for his own schooling. By the same token, I say it would be a good idea, perhaps, for more of our unwealthy classes to go to other countries from our country if the opportunity exists. They could not pay to go, in many instances, on their own. I fear we send too many of our own students to foreign countries who are in a position to go without Government help. 

Secretary RUSK. I think if you struck an average of the foreign students in this country, the average would be effected out of about 60,000 foreign students of which only about 5,000 are sponsored by any kind of official agency. The others that come on their own come from the upper classes. 

Mr. BECKWORTH. If you found anybody in the State Department that advocated a "no-win" policy, you would get rid of him just as fast as you could? 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct.

Mr. BECKWORTH. You believe that this is the policy of other high officials in our other governmental departments such as the Defense Department?

Secretary RUSK. I would want to know what is meant by this policy that they are talking about and

3 

Mr. BECKWORTH. I understand. If you found anybody that didn't want this country to win in all the efforts that we are making, yes, that you and the Secretary of Defense are making, you would get rid of them as far as you, the Secretary of State, are concerned? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. 

Mr. BECKWORTH. There are areas in the country, Mr. Secretary, where there is a great deal of sentiment directed against our staying in the United Nations. It is not confined to one section of this country. It is in a good many areas. It is so very important that the true facts, good and bad facts, about the United Nations be made available to all the American people. 

What effort is made by the State Department, for example, to make available some people that can explain our need to remain in the United Nations? What effort is made actually to get our people of stature from all departments of our Government into those areas to tell why we should continue to try to make the United Nations work? 

In other words, what effort is being made to give the people of our Nation the total truth about the United Nations? 

Secretary RUSK. We do think this is an important thing for people in the Department to do, to get out to meet with groups of citizens in other parts of the country to explain these situations. 

Quite frankly, our problem is funds and a built-in reluctance on the part of the Congress and many elements in the public, and also in the executive branch, against an excessive amount of public information domestically on the part of these executive departments. 

This has been with us for a long time. For example, in the last few months in the Department of State, we have invited in at their own expense editorial writers in one group, television, and radio editorial people in another group, broadcasters in another group. Those in turn have led to invitations for us to come to other parts of the country-Dallas, Denver, Chicago-to meet with several hundred people who would like the same kind of candid background briefing on some of these underlying elements of foreign policy. 

We would like to do that, not only because it is good for us to have a chance to explain the underlying bases of policy and some of the complications of policy, but it is also good, quite frankly, for other people in the country to discover there are human beings in the State Department. We get out to talk to them, and this does a great deal. 

I wish we could do more, but there is a limitation of funds. 

Mr. BECKWORTH. I have one suggestion in that connection. Assume that in Los Angeles, Calif., and I am not directing any charge against the people there, there is a lot of sentiment that the high officials of the State Department, yes and Defense Department, too, feel they cannot justify. It seems to me perhaps there is some person in the 

State Department or Defense Department that knows something about Los Angeles, a person who grew up there, a person of high stature, and a person about whom the Los Angeles people know and in whom they have confidence. Instead of sending somebody from Maine out to talk to those people in Los Angeles, send somebody they can identify immediately, probably through 100 years of his family having lived there, someone known to the Los Angeles people as a highly patriotic American and having the type of background of experience to speak with authority.

I hope some attention will be given to that kind of person to get over the true facts in the future, particularly if the efforts of the United Nations are as important to the welfare of America as we so often hear. 

Secretary RUSK. I think this is a very good suggestion, that we are trying to follow up on by letting local communities know what is happening to their own people in the Department and getting them back from time to time. 

We had a meeting in Los Angeles but we didn't get enough of those whom we wanted most to talk to to the meeting. 

There is another thing that we are trying to work on. That is to find ways in which we can better serve the Congress in getting them the information that they need when they are trying to explain these matters to their own constituents. 

I think Mr. Dutton has been trying to give some real attention to this, improving it some, but we have a lot to do. 

Mr. BECKWORTH. I concur that you do that. Each member of Congress faces this issue in his own manner and probably has to meet it in his own way. It does seem to me that not enough information from a high-level source is getting out to some of these places where there are real problems. 

Mr. Secretary, let me say this: A good many of us were here at one time when the draft was extended by one vote. It was said by many this vote saved the Army of the United States at a very crucial time. 

In the serious time that we face today, and you stress it every time you come before us, even mentioning a few minutes ago what a great calamity could happen in 5 minutes, we can't afford to be in a borderline situation, as I see it. We must stay off the brink at all times if possible. 

Secretary RUSK. I am sure that is right. One of the most important things that happened last fall was not just that the Congress passed the additional military appropriations the President asked for, but that they passed them so fast. It made a real impression. It made a big difference.

Because Peiping still insists that the sine qua non for any normal relationship is the abandonment of Formosa.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Monagan. 

Mr. MONAGAN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Secretary, with reference to the expropriations in Brazil, don't they in a sense constitute a failure to take self-help measures in this sense, that, as I understand it, most of them, as you have indicated, have inflationary problems and the companies would have to get rate increases in order to operate at a break-even level, and what expropriation means is that the country itself is going to take them over and then probably maintain their present rates and operate at a loss and be compelled to make up the loss from other financial sources within the country? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. I think, sir, the utility problem is an especially difficult one, because in an inflationary situation-I am not now thinking just of the inflation that is going on in Brazil at the present time even in a much more moderate inflation, the rate structure of utilities lags behind the increase in price levels. So that their situation is difficult. When foreigners are the ones that own the utilities, this creates additional tension. 

In this particular situation the State Department had pressed the utility for a long time to expand its services, because the actual extent of telephone service being offered was much less than the growing requirements demanded.

The utility, on the other hand, couldn't make the additional capital investments unless it had assurance of a rate increase that would pay for the investment and keep abreast of the inflation. 

The state government was unwilling to give that kind of rate increase. So it got to an impasse.

I think actually in terms of broad relationships, if the Brazilian Government were to buy on adequate compensation-I do mean adequate in terms of a fair value-certain of these utilities that have fallen behind the rate structure, and then on the understanding, as the companies have offered, to reinvest in other kinds of activities which have access to a free market where they can keep up with the inflation, that the relationship between private investment and government would be somewhat more relaxed. 

We have had the same problems in our own country. It wasn't lost on the Brazilians that on the week they arrived here a transit system was taken over by the State authorities in one of our own States here on something like the same kind of problem.

I think the utilities are a highly special problem of the foreign governments, and we ourselves ought to try to find an answer for that one without assuming that this represents the atmosphere for other kinds of private investment, because we have other private investments down there that are doing very well indeed. 

Mr. MONAGAN. The railroad that they took over in São Paulo, was one of the best in South America, I understand. Here once again there was an unwillingness to increase the rates to pay wage increases. 

Doesn't all this have an effect on the willingness of private U.S. and foreign capital, to go in on other industries than utilities? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes, indeed, sir. I think that the responsible

Brazilian authorities do understand that they need private investment, that they won't get private investment unless it is willing to come in voluntarily and they have to attract it. We can't drive foreign investment into another country. Incidentally, they have to attract some of their own capital into investment. So we are pressing them very hard on that and we are quite hopeful we have made some headway on it.

Mr. MONAGAN. Yet Mr. Goulart in New York emphasized the fact that they were going to take over a lot more companies. 

Secretary RUSK. I think these were utilities. These were on the basis of initiatives taken by the utilities themselves to make proposals to the Brazilian Government along these lines. 

Mr. MONAGAN. One other point I want to make. He is somewhat in line with what Mr. Beckworth has spoken about. One of the things that has come out in connection with the U.N. financial problem is a lack of liaison between the Congress and our people at the United Nations. I see from your nodding of your head that you seem to be aware of that situation. I just want to indicate the importance of doing something about that. 

Secretary RUSK. I think, Mr. Chairman, I would have to say that last November when this matter came to a head at the United Nations and the Congress was not in session, that we failed to establish adequate consultation in time to deal with that situation properly. We have learned a lesson on that. 

Mr. MONAGAN. Thank you.

Secretary, I am a member of the subcommittee of this committee called National Security and Scientific Developments 

Affecting Foreign Policy-unquote, I should say at that point. The committee has never met since I have been a member of it, and I have

made many protests to that effect to the chairman. I feel that once a year I would like to ask you this question, as long as I am a member of that subcommittee: How soon will China have atomic power that they can develop into military missiles? 

Secretary Rusk. I would be surprised, Mr. Barry, if they were to explode an atomic weapon within 1 year. I would not be surprised if they exploded one from 2 years onward. 

Mr. BARRY. Second, how long before they will have a delivery system?

Secretary RUSK. We believe they are working on missile delivery systems. We think it will take some time for them to work those out. 

I would think the time schedule might be somewhat the same. It depends a good deal on what assistance they have had from Moscow over the past several years.

Mr. BARRY. There would be a considerable shift in our foreign policy if they got this power, would there not? 

Secretary RUSK. It would create some change in the general situation but not necessarily in our policy. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Secretary, is any consideration being given to the shipment of wheat to Communist China? 

Secretary RUSK. I remember once someone got into trouble saying that consideration is given to something when in fact the problem is being studied. We are looking at this because there is the possibility we may get a request that we would have to answer one way or other. 

As the President indicated in his press conference, we don't see now a combination of circumstances which would make it logical for us to meet their food needs. They have not asked for it. They have not demonstrated in their policies in places like southeast Asia that they are prepared to use food for peace or peace for food. 

They are exporting some foodstuffs at the present time. So we at the moment don't think that is a very easy question to say yes to. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. My question should probably be addressed to Mr. 

Meany. Do you happen to know, however, the reasons behind Mr. 

Meany's recent statement regarding the shipment of our wheat surpluses to Red China? Where there is smoke, there is fire, they say.

Mr. Meany, by his statement, countributed prestige to the discussion of this issue. On what basis, do you surmise, he made such a suggestion? 

Secretary RUSK. I wouldn't want to speak for Mr. Meany. I didn't see the full statement. But you could make an argument that if the 

Chinese were to take some steps clearly demonstrating they were going to leave southeast Asia alone, if they would let international agencies come in and distribute, or our own people come in and distribute, that this would be worth considering. 

After all, you remember Mr. Hoover went into the Soviet Union after World War I to distribute food, and we still get the impact among Russian individuals of that effort made after World War I. 

I don't see that combination of circumstances coming about any time soon. I can assure you that if anything develops in that direction we will be down here talking thoroughly with this committee. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Secretary, would you care to comment on the report that Chinese rice delivered to East Germany was contaminated, and that some East Germans have died while 35 others are seriously ill, after eating it?

12 Secretary RUSK. We had a report this was Chinese butter that had caused an epidemic of dysentery of some sort. 

Mr. MCDOWELL. Don't you think we ought to encourage that? We might exchange wheat if they will sell butter. 

Secretary RUSK. On the point of how you deal with Peiping in this kind of problem-if they had a recurrence of cholera in Red China, and we were permitted to help with it-I think we ought to seriously consider doing what we can. It gets beyond their borders and it is something we have an interest in stopping at its source if possible. 

We have the same problem in Cuba. It is not in the interest of the 

United States to let the Panamaniam Health Bureau malaria campaign in Cuba die on the vine, because malaria is so easily carried across borders. 

Over the years we have relaxed our guard a bit on malaria because we have about gotten rid of it. We have an interest in the basic health situation in Cuba. 

On some of these points, I think the instructive political answer is not the final answer. At the moment, I don't see a basis for this food business going forward. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary. We are deeply grateful to you.
