TUESDAY, APRIL 10, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

10:55 a.m., Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding.

The committee meets this morning for a continuation of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. Our witness this morning is 

Mr. David Scull, member of the Policy Committee of Friends Committee on National Legislation. 

Mr. Scull, you have a prepared statement. You may proceed, sir. 

STATEMENT OF DAVID SCULL, MEMBER, POLICY COMMITTEE, FRIENDS COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL LEGISLATION 

Mr. SCULL. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen.

I am a member of the Religious Society of Friends. I am speaking for the Friends Committee on National Legislation, but we don't claim to speak for all Quakers. In fact, I don't think anyone could. 

We do find that many of us do arrive at very substantial agreement as we try to analyze national problems in light of our religious principles, and it is in that light that I am going to try to speak today. 

I am a businessman, president of the Turnpike Press, a printing firm in Annandale, Va., where I have lived for 21 years. Previously, I had several years of Government service, and in fact was with the point 4 program in its first 3 years before leaving to enter our family business.

In addition, I have been active in the cooperative and credit union movements for more than 25 years. For 10 years I have been a director of Nationwide Insurance, a cooperatively oriented group of companies of Columbus, Ohio. As chairman of the international committee of that board, I headed a five-man team which spent a month in India just last fall, studying the cooperative movement. In connection with this we came into close touch with many aspects of both publicly and privately financed programs of technical assistance. 

I can add that we were warmly welcomed by people of India, by Cabinet members and Mr. Nehru. We had a wonderful opportunity to see their movement and the extent to which India is trying to develop a cooperatively oriented economy. 825

At different times I have traveled in more than 25 foreign countries, and I think this perhaps lets me speak not as an expert but as an interested layman who has had good opportunities to look at this subject from several different points of view. 

AID EXTENDED FOR MILITARY REASONS MAY BOLSTER DICTATORSHIPS 

You probably know that as Quakers we have been supporting the economic and social aspects of foreign assistance rather than the military program. I am not going to belabor that point. I just would like to record our conviction that military assistance, and economic assistance determined primarily by military considerations, often bolster totalitarian dictatorships which may have as many unpleasant characteristics as any Marxist regime. 

Two Spanish-speaking Quakers, Nancy and Gerard Negelspach, have recently spent 15 months traveling in Spain. They quote a 

Spanish friend as follows: "*** The Spanish people do not understand why the United States concluded treaties with Franco which, although dealing in military matters are in fact helping to sustain the Franco dictatorship and, in consequence, do nothing to further the declining friendship that the oppressed Spanish people have for America. This does not mean that America should not care for its defenses against communism (which is but another form of dictatorship), but I do believe, however, that this dictatorship which exists today in Spain is potentially as dangerous for the 'free world' as communism itself." 

The Negelspachs go on to say: "*** During the recent 25th anniversary of the Franco regime celebrated in all parts of Spain but with a large military parade in Madrid, much of the equipment was from the United States. When the average Spaniard sees that, he is kept in line (and we can personally attest to one verifiable occasion when U.S. planes were used to 'dampen the spirits' of a particular town after a minor uprising) then he naturally concludes that the U.S. Government is in league with Franco against him."

ECONOMIC AID AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE VITAL 

We support the broad policy enacted by the Congress at the beginning of the Act for International Development of 1961, and give general support to U.S. bilateral economic aid and technical assistance programs. We heartily endorse adequate funds for U.N. technical assistance and aid for rehabilitation of refugees in the Middle East. We feel that these programs, along with the Peace Corps, represent some of the most constructive efforts that our Government is making in the world today. 

I shall not try to make any detailed analysis of the legislation before you, but there are some changes in emphasis which I will suggest, and I am sure there are many other improvements which ought to be made.

SUGGESTED CHANGES 

More funds through the United Nations U.S. aid funds should be channeled through the United Nations and other international organizations to the maximum extent possible. 

It is frequently politically and psychologically much easier for a country to accept multilateral than bilateral aid. International aid programs can also draw upon technically trained people of many lands and receive contributions from a variety of nations.

ale Increased confidence needed between Congress and the Executive The attitude of Congress, and the spirit in which Congress approaches the annual authorization-appropriation requests, are of the greatest importance, and I hope I will not offend if I speak frankly. 

A program such as this needs critical attention from Congress. As a taxpaying businessman I do not want my money wasted. But there is more than one way to waste money. 

One way is to try to operate too much by broad generalizations. 

One generalization that has worked its way into the foreign aid program is that loans are better than grants. Where a country can realistically meet the obligation, loans are better than grants. But countries and situations vary so much that their needs should be the determining factor and not our administrative and legislative generalizations.

Sometimes I also get the feeling of too much being expected too quickly by the Congress and by the public, with emphasis on getting funds committed and money spent before there is really time for the right decisions to be made. There needs to be a firm basis on which long-term plans can be laid, with congressional authorization supporting long-term planning for technical assistance as well as development aid. Such planning requires sound research which should be provided for.

Sometimes I get the idea that people in the Development Agency itself may not feel they can be completely frank about their problems for fear the information will be used, not to help solve the problems, but to try to disparage the whole program. 

A basis for confidence is one of the most important elements in all of this that we are doing-and I say "we" thinking of myself as an American citizen who is a part of it. Confidence is needed between the Congress and the Executive, between our technical staff abroad and their counterparts in the other countries. It takes time to develop such confidence, and it needs to be both personal and organizational. 

Example of Ford Foundation 

As one example of how long-term planning and firm support from the home base can operate, consider the wonderful work the Ford Foundation is doing in India, especially in increasing food production. Dr. Douglas Ensminger is doing a good job-a man formerly with our Department of Agriculture, and you may know him. He has been there 9 or 10 years and the key people of India know and trust him.

But this comes about not only because of his personal ability but equally because India knows the Ford Foundation is there to do a job, won't blow hot and cold, and won't end the program without plenty of notice. This does not mean the foundation does not take a very critical look at their own program. 

While we were in India we saw Dr. Carl Taylor, perhaps America's greatest rural sociologist, who had come to analyze certain aspects of their work. But Dr. Taylor was only looking for ways to strengthen the program; its basic objectives were fully accepted. 

Now I am realistic enough to know that foreign aid is a wonderful political issue lots of times, and I also know that there are abuses which

can develop whenever large amounts of money are spent all over the world. But I think we could more quickly and easily correct some of the problems of foreign assistance if you gentlemen and your staff assistants, and perhaps even more the members of some other committees, could put yourselves a little more into the shoes of the AID people, could convince them that if they are sick you are the doctors and not the undertakers, and could look at some of the fiscal and personnel restrictions built into the program and ask whether these are really helping the objectives you have stated and which the Agency is committed to carry out.

More emphasis on development of human resources If I were to make any one general criticism of the program, it would be that too much emphasis is placed on money and materials and not enough on people. We talk about the counterpart funds in foreign currencies. Sometimes we tend to disregard the most important counterpart of all, the local people. It is the people who need the technical training, the social outlook and the motivation to run the institutions which we help to set up, and put into operation technological advances.

For example, one of India's overriding problems at the present time is to achieve a substantial increase in food production. A great deal of agricultural experimentation has been done. The level of scientific knowledge is far beyond its adoption by the ordinary farmer. 

Fertilizers, cultivating implements, and production credit are needed. 

These take money. But the most acute shortage of all is in the human institutions which can help the farmer use what is already known. 

The Indian Council on Agricultural Research, with the Rockefeller Foundation cooperating, has now developed four very good strains of double-cross hybrid corn, or maize as they call it. These are now ready to go into production and distribution. In several hundred thousand villages of India there are cooperative societies dealing in seed and fertilizer which could handle this hybrid seed. But in between there is a tremendous gap; some capital is needed, but primarily the need is for trained management and the structure, whether cooperative or private, which can pick up where the agricultural scientists have left off. The production of millions of acres of corn land could be more than tripled if hybrid seed could be made available. You gentlemen know what hybrid corn has meant to American agriculture in the last generation.

More emphasis on social outlook When those in charge of the AID program do think about the human side, they tend to emphasize purely technical training. This is important, but it is often the easiest thing to get across. The social outlook, the ability to motivate oneself and others, the capacity for leadership within a democratic framework, or the well-rounded managerial outlook which is characteristic of the best examples of American cooperative and private-profit business-these are some of the most important things which America should be able to contribute from its vast experience to the newly developing countries of the world. 

Someone may say this broader approach is not our business, we should stick to purely technical training. Last February 6 a rebel movement was launched in Guatemala. It turned out that both the

rebel and the loyalist officers were trained in the U.S. Guerrilla War 

Training School at Fort Gulick in the Panama Canal Zone. No, we cannot avoid some responsibility for the context within which our technical training takes place. 

This is not just a matter of substituting training for other kinds of projects because effective training does not take place in a vacuum. 

If you are going to train a manager, he has to have something to manage. Therefore the United States should test virtually every project proposal by at least two criteria. First, will it meet a general economic need, and second, will it be installed or administered in such a way as to develop counterpart human resources as well. In many cases there should be a third criterion: will the activity strengthen the democratic fabric of the nation or the community. This is where cooperatives, credit unions, community self-help projects, and other democratically based organizations have a special value-they give people direct experience in economic democracy, in tackling problems which immediately affect them, in making decisions which they and their families will have to live with. I will not go into detail but if you have questions I can give other examples. 

More emphasis on education and community development It is not only individual projects which should be tested by these criteria, but the whole program for a country. In this sense we want to suggest that there may be an unfortunate tendency to downgrade the importance of education and community development in favor of projects involving concrete and machinery. 

In many countries a crash program on literacy should be undertaken. People cannot benefit from technical information, suggestions on health and sanitation, or proposals for increasing food production, for example, unless they can read. 

When Raymond Wilson of the FCNL staff visited Kenya last December, he was told by a leading official thatthere is an extreme shortage of secondary schools and of teachers to train teachers in Kenya. It is in these two areas that help is most needed from the United 

States so that we may have the necessary leadership for the development of education in this emerging country. 

Yet when these comments were passed on to Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, G. Mennen Williams, Raymond Wilson was told that such funds for Africa were very, very limited. 

Again I urge that you gentlemen of the Congress let the Administrator of the Agency for International Development know that you are looking beyond dollar expenditures and beyond dramatic physical symbols in evaluating his programs. 

More emphasis on following through on programs We also need more thinking through and following through on what we are doing. It makes little sense to help people to learn to read if we leave them with no reading materials in their language and at their level of interests. Yet this is what I have seen in Egyptian villages. 

It makes little sense to bring people to the United States for training and then to pay no further attention to them after they go back; yet in many countries we do not know who the alumni of our own programs are.

THE GOAL: DEVELOPMENT OF SELF-RELIANT, DEMOCRATICALLY ORIENTED PEOPLE 

Let me conclude with one example of the kind of activity which is capable of changing the face of the globe, both economically and socially. In Gujerat in western India, north of Bombay, is the Kaira 

District Cooperative Milk Producers Union. Its 54,000 members average 12 buffalo cows each. A modern, sanitary, efficient dairy plant supplies fluid milk to Bombay, and makes butter and milk powder products for sale all over India." 

If any of you have been approached for a UNICEF trick-or-treat contribution, there is a milk powder machine in that plant which was given to them by UNICEF on condition that they would give free milk to children up to the value of 150 percent of that machine. So our money has been multiplied by 50 percent. The children have the milk and the cooperative has a permanent piece of productive machinery which is a real asset there. 

The dairy plant has a manager who was trained at Michigan State, and most of his top staff have been to college in the United States. 

The income of the farmer member from his milk is eight times what it was when the co-op was organized about 15 years ago. The management is alert and progressive, and is reaching out in other fields to build for their members a lime juice processing plant and an animal feed mill.

Over a 7-year period they are aiming to double milk production per animal. Milk is collected in over 200 collecting stations. Members are encouraged to save 1 day's income a month. Some of the co-op's margin is going back into schools, libraries, improved water supply, and so on.

When the co-op began, it was just accepted that the untouchables and low-caste farmers waited at the collection points until their betters had been served. The co-op instituted the queuing system, and now if a Harijan (untouchable) gets there first, the Brahmin gets in line behind. Here is a combination of an active membership which supports a keen managerial team in performing a function which is both economically and socially useful. 

One of the best ways to improve our program of technical assistance is to look all over the world for opportunities to develop this kind of enterprise, and then to help the people involved with capital on a loan basis, with technical assistance-for example, this co-op is trying to find out how to make good cheese out of buffalo milk, which reacts differently than cow's milk-and with training assistance. 

We would not be able to claim the result as a monument to American aid. In fact, the more successful we are, the less we will have to exhibit, because the people of the countries with which we are cooperating will feel that these projects are really theirs. But this kind of people's institution, with economic, social, and human results intertwined, would be the best memorial we could leave. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Scull.

Mr. Scull, I want to congratulate you for a very fine statement. Mr. 

Scull, on page 3 of your statement, paragraph 3, where you speak of the doctors and the undertakers, I want to say as a physician and one

who has been fighting to keep people away from undertakers for 27 years, I wonder what personnel restrictions that you have mentioned are built into the present legislation. Can you name a few? 

Mr. SCULL. I am thinking of the problem of security clearance, for instance. I don't know how long it now takes to process a new appointment. I know the people who are in demand are not the people who will sit around indefinitely and wait for a job to turn up. 

This is something I am not speaking to as an expert, but this committee should be concerned as to whether the whole personnel procedure is one which enables the Administrator to tap the best people and get them on the job. I am thinking of the problem of reorganization. I know that when an Administrator, or even the President, feels defensive about a program it is very easy to say, "Well, now, gentlemen of Congress, give us a little time. The trouble has been we have been badly organized. We are going to reorganize the whole thing, and you wait a few months and we will have things licked.” 

But if you keep shuffling an organization around every year or so, staff members are frustrated and unable to function effectively. 

I am not trying to tell you your business, but I just feel that if there were an attitude of maximum mutual confidence between the Hill and the Administrator that you could really sit down and say, "What does it really take to make this most effective?" and there would be things that those closer to the program could suggest in more detail than I can that you could improve. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Scull. 

Mr. Chiperfield.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Fountain. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. I am delighted to hear one witness who represents a substantial number of people in America who says he doesn't speak for all of them. I continue to get mail and letters on sundry pieces of legislation, and the writer says: Speaking for 30,000 or 40,000, and even millions sometimes, I urge you to do so and so. I don't think anyone can speak for that many people. I know I can't in my congressional district. 

You made reference to military aid to Spain which is observed by people in Spain and which results in criticism of us. 

Do you oppose any aid to Spain?

Mr. SCULL. No. I think Spain is a seriously underdeveloped country whose people merit our assistance. But I think that sometimes we get ourselves into a very unfortunate frame of mind. We judge projects not by how they will really help the country but in military terms or other terms which don't really get to the heart of the problem of the country. 

As I said, we Friends, generally speaking, do not support the military aid program, yet I don't want to get into that as a major argument. I would just say that even in the countries which are felt to be militarily important there ought to be a way to evaluate the work by other than military criteria. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. What is your opinion as to whether or not we should give aid, military, economic, and otherwise to a Communist country? 

Mr. SCULL. I think that we need to be alert to differences which may develop between Russia, China, Yugoslavia, other satellites. I think

it is possible to have relative degrees of independence even within a Communist country which it may be to our interest to support. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Do you take the position that we should support only those forms of government identical or similar to ours? 

Mr. SCULL. I would take the position, sir, that if we really have faith in democracy and help the people of any country to such things as education, freedom of choice in occupation, in residence, even in consumption, freedom of dissemination of information, in the long run these things will make for democratically tending developments within the country. 

It may take a long time. If 20 or 40 or 60 years from now we hope a country now under dictatorship will become democratic, our best chance of effecting it, I think, is to help those people in the ways which will help lay the foundations for eventual democracy. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN.  

Chairman MORGAN. Mrs. Bolton. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I am sorry

I had to be late. We do have constituents. 

I am wondering about some of the experiments we have been part of in the way of hybrid corn-maize-the wheat. Do you know how successfully we have been able to use the wheats that we brought from 

India to experiment with? Do you have any knowledge of that?

Mr. SCULL. Not about wheat. We did get into a good deal of discussion with the Rockefeller people and the India research people on corn. We found some of the efforts made to carry over American hybrids to India were not successful, not because they weren't scientifically sound, but because the texture and appearance and the mealiness and so forth of the corn wasn't acceptable in the Indian market. 

They had to start out from strains of corn which were basic to India, although there certainly were supplementary strains brought in from elsewhere. They had to try to give the Indian farmer and the Indian farm wife the kind of thing that she was used to, in addition to making the ear bigger and better and the plant stronger and so on.

A laboratory experiment not related directly to the needs and desires of the people may be scientifically satisfying but doesn't- Mrs. BOLTON. That is one of the lessons we have to learn, isn't it, in every phase of life?

Mr. SCULL. Yes. 

Mrs. BOLTON. There are some interesting experiments going on down in Georgia. I am sorry Mr. Pilcher is not here. I think it is mostly with corn, but they started with wheat. They found it soon became quite different over here in the soils and climate and everything else, and I suppost that is what happens in India. 

I was so interested that there seems to be such an emphasis on milk. 

How does that fit in with the sacred cow?

Mr. SCULL. I hate to present myself as any kind of authority here. 

In accordance with our observations, it seems entirely acceptable to milk the cows but it does not seem to fit in with their religion and social approach to breed the cow eugenically, whereas they are perfectly willing to breed buffaloes on a scientific basis. There is a difference in the attitude.

There are dairy herds of cattle which have been in some of the veterinary colleges but they have not really been improved. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Then this milk plant-is that buffalo milk? 

Mr. SCULL. It is buffalo milk. They are using artificial insemination in connection with the veterinary college and developing records so they can show proven sires. There is an open attitude to doing this with buffaloes.

Mrs. BOLTON. That is very interesting. It is like the story we had told us several years ago of the "blue cow" that they had in one area and a very smart man showed the headman of the village that it wasn't a cow at all. It was a deer. 

Mr. SCULL. I think it is true in any area there will be a certain number of fallen cows in a given period of time. They have found in areas where there is an economic demand for better animals or for carcasses, the number of fallen cows will increase. These religious. things are subject to some extent to economic pressures.

Chairman MORGAN. Judge Saund. 

Mr. SAUND. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Scull, I wish to congratulate you on your forthright and very penetrating statement. 

I agree with you wholeheartedly on your emphasis when you say: 

It would be too much emphasis placed on money in the field and not enough on people. 

I believe the members of the committee know, and I have been saying it for 6 years, that we must attempt to reach the people with our foreign aid. I don't know very much about any other country, but 

I do know a little bit about India. In my estimation the benefits of our foreign aid do not meet the needs of the masses of India. 

I have made only two contributions to this committee in 6 years. 

Two of my amendments are not part of the AID Act. One of them is section 215. It is titled, "Loan to Small Farmers." I must say this about my colleagues on the committee. All my colleagues were unanimous in supporting my amendment.

What it says is that we should make use of our counterpart funds to make small loans to small farmer associations. 

We put a limit of not more than $25,000 worth of local currency for any one association. Unfortunately the administration, both under President Eisenhower and President Kennedy, have not taken any action under this section of the act. 

Do you think that small loans made by the U.S. Government to these cooperatives would make them more effective and would do real good to help them out?

Mr. SCULL. I do, if I may comment on that, Mr. Chairman. I think it is true, as far as our observation in India is concerned, that the administration has not been implementing this as we feel they should. 

There are all sorts of pressures I suppose to do the big dramatic things, the steel mills, and so on. Yet, as you well know, 70 to 80 percent of India's people live in the rural villages. This is where the real problem is.

There has been a privately financed program in a small district near New Delhi, which I think we can present as bipartisan. Nelson 

Rockefeller has given financial support, as have others, and the

Cooperative League has been helping to run the program. In this project, they have simplified the program of supervised credit which our own Farmer Credit Administration developed so successfully. 

That is, instead of lending money and hoping the farmer will do something with it, they work out a farm plan, through the cooperative organization, and develop a means whereby we can make sure the farmer spends the money for what the plan calls for. The loan is not based upon whether his farm will stand the mortgage or not, but upon whether his farm can produce enough to justify it. 

This program on a small scale, involving about 15 villages in the district outside New Delhi, has increased farm production by at least 15 percent in each of the last 5 years. It can be done. The soil is fertile. But the funds and the organization, the human institution, whether it is a cooperative or something else, is needed here to make this work. 

Mr. SAUND. Do I have any more time, Mr. Chairman?

Chairman MORGAN. One minute.

I certainly agree with the purpose of that.

Chairman MORGAN. Dr. Judd. 

Mr. JUDD. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Scull, your words are music to the ears of those who have worked a long time on this program. You put a sound emphasis all the way on the simpler things, the things that reach people. Always there is the temptation for us Americans to build monuments, big programs, which are all necessary but are unsuccessful if in building them we give the impression that we are what the Communists say we are, materialists worshiping material things, and that we don't see the intangibles properly.

I commend you for every sentence except one, and it is too bad to pick out just one sentence. I know that the emphasis of the Friends is on, as you well put it, "the economic and social aspects rather than the military program."

Some people think that the most important fact of our time and in our world is what they call the social and economic revolution that is going on, the revolution of rising expectations. I think that is true. I have tried to contribute a bit to that revolution down through the years, in personal effort as well as a Member of Congress. But some don't see that it also takes military strength to defend that revolution. The revolution of rising expectations isn't doing very well in Cuba today, it isn't going along very well in Tibet, very successfully in Hungary. 

We are up against the fact that it is the military strength we are building which makes possible the human revolution, in our time, and maybe in the next century.

You have placed very proper emphasis, indispensable emphasis, on the intangibles, the human values, the social and economic changes, and all the rest; but in the kind of world we face and the kind of enemy, the sine qua non is military strength to protect the opportunity for the social revolution to take place. 

When I came home in 1938 from being a missionary in China, many said "You mustn't get into politics. You mustn't be doing this or that. You must just serve the Chinese people."

I said "If we don't get our Government to do something different in Asia, there isn't going to be an opportunity for any of us to serve the Chinese people; we will be out." 

I felt that if it was right to do missionary work in China, it was right to try to change our Government's policies so there would be a chance to do missionary work in China. There is no missionary work going on there now. 

So I hope in your proper emphasis-I must interrupt myself to say that for one who is putting the emphasis where you are, there are 10 who are putting it on the other side, so you are still not out of balance. 

What we have to face is that we have to give both of them, military and economic aid, regardless of what we like or wish, or neither of them is going to succeed. The military won't succeed if people are alienated. The people can't improve their lives if they are under a 

Communist dictatorship.

Mr. SCULL. If I could comment briefly even though that wasn't quite a question. I would say realistically I know there is going to be a military aid program as part of this legislation. I would only say that when we talk about building a defensive shield against communism in order that we can negotiate, and develop behind that shield, the shield itself tends to become of primary importance. We lose sight of our ostensible reason for building up the shield. So I don't feel too badly about putting all the emphasis I can on that side.

If we are going to eliminate them because of this, at the expense of cultivating people who might give the appearance of being less than a chief of state, who are dedicated against us, then I feel that the goals that you advocate will have no chance to come forth or to be realized.

Mr. ADAIR. If you were to recommend to this committee, then, speaking for your organization, you would recommend that we would wipe out the military portion? We

STATEMENT OF BRIG. GEN. BONNER FELLERS, U.S. ARMY, RETIRED, NATIONAL CHAIRMAN, CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COMMITTEE 

General FELLERS. Mr. Chairman and members of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, I am grateful for the opportunity to make this my fourth appearance before you in opposition to the foreign aid program. 

On Thursday, March 29, I was startled by a dispatch special to the New York Times-by Mr. Richard E. Mooney. The dispatch pictured the recent flight of gold, which totals $279 million, so far, in 1962. But the final paragraph, sometimes called the upbeat, was to me incomprehensible. I shall quote in full:

As a practical matter, the United States has no immediate cause for concern about its gold supply. Despite the big drain of the last 4 years, and the lesser drain that has been going on longer, the supply is still some $16,600 million-40 percent of the known non-Communist world supply. 

Three years ago, in its brochure, "Foreign Aid and You-A First

Report," the Citizens Foreign Aid Committee warned: 

At the beginning of 1958 our gold reserve amounted to $22.9 billion. During 

1958 alone, $2.26 billion in gold has been taken from us by foreign countries. 

Should this loss of confidence in the dollar continue, the gold outflow could collapse our currency.

Today our committee brings this report up to date: 

At the beginning of 1958 our gold reserve amounted to $22.9 billion. 

It now stands at $16.6 billion-a loss of $6.3 billion in 4 years and 

3 months. This is an average annual loss of $1.48 billion or a daily loss of more than $4 million in gold. 

Of the $16.6 billion which remains in our reserve today, $11.5 billion must be retained by law to back up, but not to redeem, our money in circulation in the United States. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) can call on this reserve for $1.9 billion. Consequently, only $3.2 billion is available to meet possible demands of the foreign central banks which hold nearly $23 billion in short-term claims, redeemable in gold.

Thus, one is compelled to question that portion of the New York Times dispatch quoted above. When foreign central banks hold nearly $23 billion in short-term claims against our diminishing gold reserve of $16.6 billion, how can it be said thatsupplythe United States has no immediate cause for concern about its gold and thatthe supply (gold) is still some $16,600 million-40 percent of the known non- 

Communist world supply?

Should foreign central banks draw down our gold, at the same rate as during the past 4 years, the $3.2 billion would be exhausted in the spring of 1964. However, future foreign purchases of gold may not continue at a uniform rate. This gold situation could parallel the run on a commercial bank when depositors lose faith in the bank's solvency, withdraw their funds, and break the bank. If foreign confidence in the dollar continues to worsen, it is probable that there will be a run on our gold. And this would bring on a free world financial crisis.

ADVICE FROM FOREIGN ECONOMISTS 

Of course this run on gold need not happen if we put our economy in order. Our friends at the Vienna meeting of the Board of Governors, IMF, last autumn made it clear how we can restore confidence in the dollar. Here is the gist of their advice: 

A sound dollar rests on a solution to the chronic unfavorable balance of international transactions, which in turn rests on a balanced budget, strong domestic economy, and the ability successfully to compete in world markets. 

UNFAVORABLE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Over the past 10 years, more dollars have flown out of than into the United States; this outflow has now reached the staggering total of $19.6 billion. The administration is endeavoring partially to meet the balance-of-payments problem by resorting to stratagems. 

Stratagem No. 1.-Our Federal Reserve, acting as agent for the 

Treasury, is borrowing foreign currencies. When the dollar is weak, the theory is that these currencies will be used to buy foreign-held dollars; when the dollar is strong, dollars will be used to buy foreign currencies.

This stratagem fails in its purpose. Foreign central banks will hesitate to use the dollars they hold to buy their own local currency, because these same dollars can buy our gold. This procedure, thrifty 

France is now practicing. If the Federal Reserve buys foreign currencies, foreign dollar holdings increase. And more dollars in foreign central banks is the very thing which the administration is seeking to avoid. 

Stratagem No. 2.-Another stratagem is to persuade foreign governments which owe the United States to prepay their debts-as did West Germany in 1961. Debt prepayment alleviates an unfavorable balance of payments; but not being a recurring item it offers only temporary relief.

Stratagem No. 3.-Formation of an international gold pool is being discussed. This stratagem has neither been denied nor confirmed by the Treasury Department. It has, however, been reported in Barron's of March 19, in the Wall Street Journal of March 22, and in more than one issue of the New York Times.

Foreign central banks and the United States would stock the pool with most of the gold reserves of the non-Communist world. The largest share would be contributed by the United States. The Bank of England would manage the pool, endeavoring to prevent wide fluctuations in the price of gold and thus avoid heavy speculative demands to buy gold.

A New York authority on international finance, quoted in the Wall 

Street Journal, March 22, 1962, claimed:

The resulting outflow of gold from the United States may be delayed, but in the long run not stopped, by the new pool. 

One might venture the observation that, once U.S. gold is pooled with contributions from foreign central banks which have ample shortterm dollar claims on all of our gold, we are likely to lose control of our entire gold reserve.

Stratagem No. 4.-This stratagem requires an amendment to the 

Bretton Woods Act. It envisages a 10-nation bolster of the IMF by $6 billion. President Kennedy, in his Economic Report to the Congress, January 1962, outlines the plan: 

Agreement has been reached among 10 of the major industrial countries to lend to the Fund specified amounts of their currencies when necessary to cope with or forestall pressures which may impair the international monetary system. 

These standby facilities of $6 billion will be a major defense against international speculation and will powerfully reinforce the effectiveness of the Fund. 

They will provide resources to make our drawing rights in the Fund effective, should we need to use them.

In commenting on this proposed arrangement, the highly reputable Economic News, published by American Institute for Economic Research, Great Barrington, Mass., volume V, No. 3, for March 1962, wrote in part:

From the President's statement above; American citizens might conclude that the IMF actually had firm commitments like a businessman's standby line of credit at his bank, automatically available for use when needed. A standby credit agreement is described in Prentice-Hall's Encyclopedic Dictionary of Business Finance as credit available on call, which the borrower has a right to demand. But what is the actual situation?

In order to answer this question we turn to the official IMF document setting forth the precise terms and conditions of the agreement. These provide that a request by one country to borrow under the terms of the agreement shall be granted "* **only if it (the request) is accepted by participants." In other words, the potential lenders have not agreed to a standby credit to be available on call but have agreed only to consider making loans when requested to do so in the future. Presumably, willingness to consider such a request always would prevail between nations unless they were at war. 

To put all this in words that any businessman can understand, Uncle Sam, the debtor, claims that he has arranged a standby credit available on call from his banker. Actually, the banker has agreed to nothing of the sort but has merely agreed to listen to the debtor's request for a loan at some indefinite future time.

If a business corporation offering securities in Wall Street stated in its prospectus that it had arranged "standby facilities" for borrowing from its bankers when in fact the only arrangements were for the bankers to consider future loan requests, the officers and directors would be in danger of going to jail for fraud. Certainly the Securities and Exchange Commission, if it learned about the misrepresentation in time, would not permit the corporation to offer its securities for sale. ***Surely the participating nations that refused, at the meeting in Vienna, to grant actual standby credits will not be fooled by the Treasury press releases, Secretary Dillon's statements at his press conference, or the President's assertions in his Economic Report. 

We assume that President Kennedy knows little of these matters and that he has relied on his Secretary of the Treasury in preparing this segment of his report. For the latter, who is experienced in public and private finance, we can imagine no such excuse. *** Are not the American people entitled to a higher standard of conduct on the part of Government officials, to the same high standard that a Government agency demands of the citizens? 

Other efforts. Our Government is also attempting to correct its unfavorable balance of payments by- Increasing our exports enormously. (A top-level businessman is to be appointed export coordinator to oversee a national export drive. However, in view of unprecedentedly keen foreign competition, the coordinator's task will be difficult.) 

Inducing our allies to extend more aid and military assistance. (So far our pleas have not been very successful.) 

Restricting dependents of military personnel from oversea station.

Reducing free entry of items purchased by individuals abroad. (Savings on the last two measures will be negligible.) 

These proposed remedial measures have little chance of offsetting the enormous oversea expenditures now being made by the U.S. Government. So long as our Government continues to spend some $8 billion abroad annually, we shall face an unfavorable balance of payments, at least part of which we shall be obliged to pay in gold. 

OUR FEDERAL DEBT 

During the last 8 months the Federal debt limit has been raised $7 billion; it now stands at $300 billion. Before July of this year the administration will ask for an additional increase of $8 billion; if granted, in a single year, the debt limit will have been increased by $15 billion. Interest on the debt is $9.3 billion annually. It was not until the war year of 1942 that our total annual Federal receipts reached $9 billion.

OUR SPENDING PROGRAM 

In his March 8 press conference the President stated the cause of the dollar drain:

It is the combination of the $3 billion that we spend (annually) keeping our defense forces overseas, and combined with assistance we give in other ways, which provides for our dollar drain. 

While the President fully realizes that foreign economic aid and military assistance are responsible for our unfavorable balance of payments, he has said that foreign aid is as important as is our own defense. Rather than reducing foreign aid the President is increasing it. The shape of things to come in his spending program is reflected in his Economic Report, together with the annual report of the Council of Economic Advisers, which he transmitted to the Congress in 

January 1962.

Under the subhead of "Policies for 1962," and referring to proposals of the Commission on money and credit, President Kennedy said (p. 22): 

In its comprehensive new look at existing financial legislation, the Commission concludes that the following financial restrictions no longer serve the purposes originally intended and unnecessarily complicate or obstruct other Government policies: the ceiling on the public debt, the ceiling on permissible interest rates on U.S. Treasury bonds, and the required gold reserve against Federal Reserve notes and deposits. I am sure the Congress will wish to examine carefully the 

Commission's recommendations on these points. 

From the President's above-quoted statement, a debt limit and a gold reserve "unnecessarily complicate or obstruct other Government policies." This, it would appear, is a blueprint for unbridled spending with printing press money. 

FOREIGN ECONOMISTS' REACTION 

That foreign economists are disappointed in the handling of our economy is evidenced from the following:

The Right Honorable Sir David Ormsby Gore, British Ambas sador to the United States, was asked whether his Government contemplated a more extensive program of aid to less developed countries. He replied:

The first thing to say in answer to this question is that, of course, you can't do a great deal in the way of aid until you are earning a good surplus. You can't invest a deficit in foreign countries.¹

Franz Pick, American economist, several weeks ago went to London and Zurich, as he expressed itto get an idea of the present dollar climate over there. 

He reports the consensus abroad as follows: 

You Americans have committed every mistake that can be found in the history of monetary management. You have come rather near to the end of the currency rope, but you do not want to bow to the facts of life. You want to maintain the illusion of dollar prestige and cannot accept the debasement which you either favored or to which you gave in, without any resistance. You will, just as all other currencies did, devalue the dollar. Sure, you have to say that you will not do it. That is the famous sanctified lie that will not hold up, just as Sir Stafford Cripps' assurances were in vain in 1949. So why don't you plan 

1 Congressional Record, Feb. 2, 1962, p. A791.

for it in order to protect your country from an emergency which would really turn it upside down if forced upon you from abroad * * Therefore, dollar devaluation is inevitable. But I will refuse to give you any date for such an event, as I simply do not know when it will happen.' 

Constantine Brown in a column headlined, "A Swiss Looks at U.S. 

Spending," Washington Evening Star, March 27, 1962, quotes a director of one of the great banking institutions in Switzerland: 

You are still the richest country in the world, not only in raw materials but in inventive genius, know-how, and daring. But at the rate of your expenditures for domestic progress, defense, and particularly your indiscriminate desire to help the rest of the world-regardless of its desserts-you will not be able to continue to discharge this self-imposed obligation without serious consequences. 

The gold outflow should be a real warning. 

Your rate of taxation-direct, indirect, and invisible-has not yet reached the saturation point, but you are not far from it. Since it is obvious that all your political men are pledged to the continuation of this role of the world's good samaritan, I cannot see the end of these expenditures. 

The outflow of gold is continuing at a more alarming pace than the average 

American citizen and even your lawmakers realize *

Despite your present efforts, it will be difficult for you to regain your position in the world markets because of the high and increasing cost of production * In order to gather the necessary funds to continue your gigantic self-imposed task from cradle to grave the income tax collector will become more arbitrary and increasingly consider the taxpayer as a lemon which must be squeezed to the last drop. And in the long run, this will cause you serious trouble. 

OUR DEFENSES 

Huge foreign aid spending is partially responsible for cancellation of the development and production of the RS-70 and the nuclearpowered bomber. Elimination of these weapons is a major step toward disarmament at a time when we face the most fearsome military threat in our history. The Congress is to be commended for its support of the RS-70 program. 

Foreign aid spending has also made heavy inroads on the availability of funds for research and development in nuclear and space efforts. We have no adequate defense against intercontinental ballistic missiles and space vehicles. Nuclear propulsion and the military application of space vehicles await solution; the power which first solves these problems would have the means, if it so elects, to dominate the world.

Were the aid funds which we give to neutral and Communist countries made available for research and development, ascendancy in these unknown frontiers would come to us. And we must keep in mind that there is a vast difference between foreign aid handouts and sound domestic spending. Foreign aid puts dollars redeemable in gold in foreign hands. Domestic spending does not reduce our gold reserve. 

Our committee has reached the conviction that the greatest, and only lasting, service which our country can render freemen everywhere is to maintain a sound economy and provide overwhelming supremacy in aerospace striking power. Unfortunately, it appears that the present trend of our leadership is not directed primarily toward either of these objectives. 

2 From an address, "The Future of the U.S. Paper Dollar," before the Graduate School of Business Administration, New York University, Feb. 17, 1962.

The admonition of our Saviour-Matthew 16:26: 

For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? today could be paraphrased: 

For what are Americans profited, if we shall gain every material foreign aid objective, and lose our own God-given liberty? 

It cannot be denied that foreign aid undermines our economy. 

Without a sound economy, free men cannot survive. Without a sound 

American economy, the curtain goes down on liberty and spiritual values everywhere. 

RECOMMENDATION The Citizens Foreign Aid Committee respectfully urges the House 

Committee on Foreign Affairs drastically to reduce the foreign aid authorization for fiscal 1963.
