STATEMENT OF DR. ELGIN GROSECLOSE, ECONOMIC CONSULTANT, CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COMMITTEE Dr. GROSECLOSE. Mr. Chairman and members of the com mittee, my name is Elgin Groseclose. I am a member of the firm of Groseclose, Williams & Associates, financial analysts and consultants. I thank you for the privilege of again appearing before this committee in regard to the foreign aid program. I appear on behalf of the Citizens Foreign Aid Committee as I did also last year, but my first appearance before this committee to testify on the foreign aid program was in 1956 at the invitation of the late Lawrence Smith of Wisconsin, a distinguished member of your committee. The committee is therefore well aware of my general views on this subject. 

I have been concerned about the foreign aid program since 1951 when I had the opportunity to observe it at first hand in Iran while spending a year under a Fulbright advanced research fellowship to study the pastoral and village economy of that country. I was disturbed then by the hopes held out by the foreign aid program, by the theories and techniques by which it was operated, that is, by the prevailing confidence in the power of money to accomplish basic social and moral reforms necessary to build up the vitality and political strength of a country.

Uneasiness over the aid program was not unique with me; it was shared by many other observers, both Iranian and American, with whom I discussed the subject. I have visited the Middle East several times since 1951, and during the past winter I completed a trip around the world on business for my firm which took me into several countries receiving aid.

I might insert here in my prepared statement that I was also in India. While I was not received by Prime Minister Nehru or 

Krishna Menon, I did meet a number of Indian businessmen who were struggling with the problem of making a living under the political and economic conditions of that country.

I was also in India at a time when the President of Soviet Russia was being royally received by the Government of India. I was also in India at the time when this peaceful, peace-loving country was seizing the territory of Goa by force of arms. 

My subsequent observations and study of the program have only increased my uneasiness as to the potentially disastrous consequences of the program, both for the United States and for the recipient countries. 

My acquaintance with the problems of underdeveloped countries goes back over 40 years since my youth when I taught for 2 years in a mission school in Iran and did relief work in what is now the Soviet 

Caucasus. I am the author of "Introduction to Iran," a standard work on that country; a history of money recently republished as "Money and Man"; besides five mainly historical novels dealing with events in the Middle East. 

During World War II, I had the privilege of serving as Treasurer General of Iran by appointment of the Iranian Parliament, with major responsibilities for restoring the economy that was shattered by a manipulated inflation and by military occupation. 

SUMMARY OF VIEWS 

In our opposition to the foreign aid program we are not opposed to assisting other peoples. Neither are we opposed to such expenditures as tend to enhance the military and political position of this country. 

Our view toward the foreign aid program is that it does neither of these things. The foreign aid program is essentially an effort to solve the problems of the so-called underdeveloped countries with money and the techniques of engineering and economics. It is an effort to win friends and to create a political climate favorable to the United States by such means. 

We think that the dozen years' experience with this approach and the expenditure of over $85 billion have proved the futility of attempting to assist peoples by means of money and engineering and economic techniques to solve problems that really lie in other spheres-in the realm of political structures, cultural complexes, and the moral forces of religion. 

Moreover, regarding the foreign aid program as a philanthropy, we are opposed to it as being beyond the constitutional powers of the Congress.

FALSE HOPES RAISED BY FOREIGN AID 

I would invite your attention to some of the philosophical considerations behind the foreign aid program. A great deal has been spread upon the record regarding the inefficiency of the program, the corruption in its administration, and its failure to achieve results. 

Last year the new administration promised that a lot of heads would roll in the foreign aid administration because of these failures. 

I stated then that the attempt to make the personnel of the administration the whipping boy for these failures would only complicate the task of recruiting able people, since who wants to enter a service already tarred with the brush of corruption and incompetence?

I remember during President Truman's administration the President made a speech regarding the foreign aid program in India in which he promised a crash program that would substantially lift the standard of living within a decade. 

Well, a decade has passed. In this connection I remember talking with one State Department official in the Middle East who asked: What had the missionaries done in the hundred years they have been in the country? And added, "We intend to take over and get the job done." 

Such is the faith which people seem to have in the power of dollars to change conditions in the underdeveloped countries. 

FOREIGN AID AS SPURIOUS PHILANTHROPY 

The foreign aid program exhibits a basic dichotomy. Some people support foreign aid because they think it is our Christian or philanthropic duty to help the peoples of the underdeveloped countries. 

Others support foreign aid because they think it is in the national defense interest. A principal reason foreign aid obtains such heavy support in Congress is because it attracts two opposite classes of voters. 

Now let us examine this philosophy as it works in a specific situation. Let us take Iran, where we have spent over a billion dollars since the initiation of the foreign aid program. This figure does not include the $194 million lent by the World Bank-most of it U.S. dollars.

Since 1953, in addition to foreign aid, money has been poured into the Iranian economy from its oil wells at a rate undreamed of a decade ago-$300 million a year at present. The country has never known such an inpouring of wealth in its history. Yet on top of that we have given foreign aid to the extent of $150 million in the past 2 years. 

We are putting in airfields and barracks and financing an unending list of industrial undertakings through the plan organization. As a consequence the Iranian Government has been able to build up its army to around 200,000 men, but has this added to the national security of the United States?

The attitude I observed in Iran is that if trouble comes with Soviet Russia the United States will defend the country by bombers and missiles and take care of the country's security; the army in consequence is popularly regarded as a force to hold the tribes in subjection and the Government in power. 

I will not pass an opinion upon the merits or stability of the present government. I am a devoted friend of Iran and I have a great deal of confidence in the country and the people, but the plain fact is that good will toward the United States and American prestige become dependent not upon what we ourselves are doing or stand for, but upon how well the Government of the country is doing and its popularity with its people.

What is true in Iran is true generally. Our position and prestige become involved with that of the ruling group, and if it falls from disfavor the United States is carried down with it. Throughout the underdeveloped world we find ourselves committed to governments that may or may not be popular, and we are unable to control or direct the actions of these governments in ways that might make them more acceptable.

The result of all this is that what we stand for before the world as a nation and as a culture is lost sight of, and our ideals and purposes are identified with those of the governments that we are supporting. We find ourselves in the position of giving a blank check to politicians who exploit us. 

This is true in Iran, in Brazil, in Vietnam, and in other countries that could be named. Indeed the difficulties we are having in Latin 

America with our Alliance for Progress program are illustrative. We are caught like a finger in a basket trap.

FOREIGN AID AS POLITICS 

Some hold that foreign aid is or should be pure benevolence and humanitarianism. At times the State Department, fearful lest foreign aid be pared by the Congress, has rounded up claques of clergymen, priests, and rabbis to testify that we must vote these sums of moneys as a religious duty and as a national charity. 

A great deal is made of malaria control and the toothbrush program and the Peace Corps, but the fact is that a great share of the foreign aid appropriations has been to support military establishments or large-scale economic enterprises. 

I would like to insert into my prepared statement at this point, if I may, the statement that I am not a pacifist. I believe that a strong man, armed, keepeth his goods in peace. But I am opposed to the whole military aid program. By that I do not mean that I am opposed to military assistance in specific cases. I am opposed to the military aid program as set forth in the concepts and operations of the foreign aid program. 

I might just illustrate that by an analogy. A great deal has been made by foreign aiders of the fact that for most of the 19th century we were able to grow in peace under the shield of the British Navy, that we perhaps owe a duty to the world now to keep a shield over the world. I am not aware that the British Navy ever had a naval base on our shores or our territory, or that the British Government ever contributed to our military budget. 

I think we can maintain the peace of the world without necessarily contributing to the military budgets of numerous and sundry foreign countries. 

Of some $85 billion net foreign assistance during the postwar period through June 30, 1961, over $28 billion consisted of military supplies and services. In addition, an enormous though indeterminate amount of financial aid has been in the form of so-called defense support to assist in building up the military capabilities of the aided countries. 

In Iran over half of the $1,068 million in foreign aid since the war has been to build up the Shah's army of 200,000 men rather than to aid the underprivileged peasant or the trachoma-stricken villager. 

Next door in Iraq, of over $69 million of total aid, over $49 million has been for military purposes.

In poverty-stricken Ethiopia, $47 million out of $95 million total has been for arms and military purposes. Greece and Turkey, where from a total aid of $6 billion, $3.4 billion has been for military purposes, may be considered special cases; but in unspecified Near East

and south Asian countries, of $816 million in foreign aid, $520 million has been for military supplies and services. 

Meantime what is the expenditure for social welfare as defined by the Agency for International Development? In contrast to the vast number of economic and commercial projects for which money is being allocated, let us look at the figures for the number of social welfare projects of the type that was advocated by the distinguished Mr. Scull who was here before us, and the expenditure thereon in the last 3 fiscal years as provided by the Agency for International Development. 

Number of projects and dollar obligations for social welfare 1959 1960 1961 

Fiscal year 

Number of projects 663 Thousands of dollars 591 215 136 Note that despite the administration propaganda about the new emphasis on "social reform" as an object and condition of aid, the amounts being spent on projects in this field and the number of programs have been steadily reduced. 

Note also that the dollar figures are not, like aid figures generally, in billions or millions, but in mere thousands of dollars. 

OBJECTIVE CRITIQUES OF FOREIGN AID 

Foreign aid has become such an emotional complex for the American people that detached, objective reasoning in regard to foreign aid is almost impossible to obtain. Abroad, however, where the program can be viewed with more detachment or where people can see the aid in actual practice rather than as a theory, intelligent, discerning observers are increasingly critical of the whole program, both theory and practice.

I request permission to include as part of my testimony, for inclusion in the record, excerpts from comments by various foreign commentators, in Iran, in India, in Switzerland, in Honduras, and one comment from the distinguished writer, Lin Yutang, all of them critical of foreign aid. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection it will be so ordered. 

Do you want it at this point in the record? 

Dr. GROSECLOSE. At the conclusion. 

THE DELUSION OF COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY 

President Kennedy in his address to the diplomats on March 13, on the occasion of the anniversary of the Alliance for Progress, made this curious statement:

It-the Alliance for Progress-laid down a new principle in our relationships: The principle of collective resonsibility for the welfare of the people of the Americas.

Collective responsibility is the obverse of collective security-the delusive theory upon which American foreign policy has rested since

World War II. Anyone who dares to question this policy is apt to be tarred and feathered and run out of camp as an isolationist; nevertheless the situation requires that the concept be candidly examined. 

We have already seen the failure of this principle of collective responsibility in the reluctance of the principal powers of Latin America to take a responsible attitude toward Castroism. We see it in the reluctance of the Government of Brazil to put its own fiscal house in order. We see it in the lagging of the reform movement in Chile and elsewhere. We see it in the strains and tensions within NATO, in the refusal of France to integrate its military forces with those of its allies and its refusal to participate in the current negotiations in Geneva.

The fact is that collective responsibility is a delusion and contrary to the deepest meaning and teaching of the Christian revelation-itself a fulfillment of a revelation foreshadowed in the Old Testament, namely that responsibility can only be individual. In the Old Testament in the Book of Jeremiah we find this writing: "In those days they shall say no more, "The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge,' but everyone shall die for his own iniquity."-Jeremiah XXXI, 29-30.

If these generalizations are perhaps too difficult to grasp we have an example at home of the iniquitous consequences of this doctrine of collective responsibility. 

The other evening in the city of Washington a bus occupied by at least 30 passengers was entered by a group of hoodlums who beat up the driver until he was stunned and bloody. Not one of the passengers on this bus came to the driver's assistance; not one of them offered to identify the assailants or to assist in their apprehension. 

How do you account for such conduct on the part of American citizens enjoying the blessings of liberty? Here you find the wormy and pernicious fruit of the doctrine of collective responsibility. No doubt each individual in the bus was waiting for the group to act, but when the individual waits for the group to act the result is paralysis. The only occasion where you get collective action is under a state of fear and panic, and then the action is neither intelligent nor purposeful nor predictable.

This is why NATO is continually breaking apart except where fear of Soviet Russia drives its members to a state of quasi-cooperation. 

This is why our national security can never be trusted to a collective responsibility. 

And if you wish to seek further defaults and delays and failures to implement social progress in Latin America, continue to preach the doctrine of collective responsibility, which means that the only agency which assumes any responsibility is the U.S. Government through its foreign aid program and this aid is futile because it is not accompanied by the powers of sovereignty necessary to accomplish reform. 

THE DELUSION OF U.S. ECONOMIC SUPREMACY 

A final delusion under which the foreign aid program is carried, to which I must make reference in closing my testimony, is that the United States is the predominant economic power of the world with resources so much vaster than all the rest of the world that we can afford to pour out our wealth in unending and unlimited streams.

The idea a hangover no doubt from our boyhood geography booksthat the United States produces most of the world's economic goods is pleasant reading and creates delusions of grandeur. There can be no doubt that the willingness of the American people to bleed its economy for foreign aid derives in part from this delusion upon which it has been fed since infancy, that we are a Paul Bunyan among the nations of the world, the delusion that our economic power is unlimited, that we can outproduce, outfight and outspend any other country in the world.

The raw fact is that today this is only partially true. Let me cite just a few statistics. In 1910 the United States accounted for approximately a third of total world production of iron ore and at the end of World War II, largely because of the debilitation of Europe, our share of the total was two-thirds. Currently, however, the U.S. share is less than one-fourth.

The decline in our share of the world production and trade in steel is even more acute. 

From World War I to World War II, the United States accounted for some two-thirds of the world's petroleum output; since the end of 

World War II this share has been declining and currently is less than 

40 percent.

From 1900 to 1920 the United States produced between 55 and 65 percent of world copper output, but at the peak of World War II only 36 percent, and currently around a fourth. 

The trend in the case of gold is even more abrupt and disconcerting. 

In 1900 the United States produced 31 percent of world gold production; in 1961 it was less than 42 percent. The latter percentage does not consider Russian production, the amount of which is not known but is estimated to be from 5 to 10 times U.S. production. 

In the case of gold the decline in production has been both absolute and relative. U.S. gold production of 1,526,757 ounces in 1961 compares with 4,862,087 ounces in 1940 and 12,400,000 ounces in 1900. 

Russian production is estimated as being between 10 and 17 million ounces in 1961.

The decline in U.S. gold holdings, constituting the reserve behind the U.S. dollar, is cause for even greater anxiety, for the reason that since the war the dollar has become the money of account for about half the world's trade and foreigners have tripled their short-term claims on dollars through holdings of bank deposits and Treasury obligations convertible into gold. At the end of the war the United 

States was in possession of approximately $20.2 billion, or two-thirds of the visible gold stocks of the world. By September 1949, the 

U.S. gold stock had increased to $24.7 billion or over 70 percent of the world total. In the dozen years since, the U.S. gold stock has diminished by nearly a third and today stands at less than $16.8 billion and just 40 percent of the world's total. 

Meantime, as I have stated, foreigners have accumulated shortterm claims convertible into dollars in excess of $22 billion, compared with $6.8 billion at the end of the war, representing a continual potential threat to the monetary stability of this country. The cause of this outflow of gold and its consequent weakening of our monetary position is found directly in the foreign aid program. 81496-62-pt. 5- -3

Two years ago when we brought these facts to the consideration of your committee in our report "The Financial Consequences of Oversea Military Expenditures and the Foreign Assistance Programs" the State Department attempted to dispute our conclusions by a list of rather captious questions and we were requested to put in evidence a response to these questions. Our response was filed with your committee in March 1960.

Since then, I am happy to note, the State Department and the administration in power have done an about face in the subject and now concede that the principal cause of the weakening of the dollar is our foreign aid program and the costs of our oversea garrisons. 

However, instead of adopting the measures of fiscal soundness, the Executive power continues to request huge authorizations and appropriations far beyond the capacity of the recipients' economies to ab sorb and to throw the burden of balancing our payments deficit upon the exporter and to put the blame upon him for his failure to export more goods.

The administration appears, in fact, to be like Micawber, hopefully waiting for something to turn up, or like one of the occupants of the bus to which I referred, paralyzed and waiting for someone else to act. 

It is time that the administration assumed and accepted responsibility for its own fiscal excesses and reduced its requests for foreign aid authorizations. 

Thank you very much.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you. 

(Supplement to testimony of Dr. Groseclose is as follows:) FOREIGN VIEWS ON FOREIGN AID "PEOPLE DON'T DIE FOR A STANDARD OF LIVING" 

Atlas, for November 1961, reports a front-page editorial in the Zurich Die Weltwoche by Laurenz Stucki under the heading "People Don't Die for a Standard of Living." As to why masses of people all over the world display such enthusiasm on behalf of communism but almost never in behalf of freedom, the writer asks, "What can we pit against the religion of the anthill state which, like Islam, uses force-not to mention betrayal, violence and murder-to realize its vision?" and answers, "Some reply: 'Our standard of living.' But do men die on the barricades for that?" He goes on to comment that Americans "think that all the poor of the world need is more material goods. Thus in the eyes of the world Americans have become the apostles of the high living standard of the rich, who cling to their own wealth and are identified in many parts of the world with feudal exploiters." 

WARNING FROM IRAN 

"It is high time for American diplomats to realize once and for all that modern towns, luxurious buildings, fancy cars, or the increasing number of television sets neither indicate economic prosperity nor save a nation from disaster." (From an editorial in Teheran Ettela'at, Dec. 19, 1961.) 

COMMENT FROM INDIA 

An Indian scholar writes: "The dean of Allahabad University in India, Dr. 

Prof. A. N. Agarwala, in a letter to the editors of the New York Times of November 20, 1960, comments, 'The outflow of assistance from the United States seems to have built-in strains and stresses."" 

He goes on to say, "My own analysis is that the inflexible character of American assistance has a large hand in the situation. This assistance is represented by capital goods, technology, and managerial skills. All of these are tremendously important for growth. But they are inflexible in the sense that they are suited to American social and business environment and not to that of underdeveloped countries."

"These countries," he continues, “in many cases have ancient cultures which have withstood the tests of time and which have deep roots in our human thoughts and action. They are traditional and primitive, with heavy emphasis on smallness of scale and simplicity of method. Their world is different from the amazing modern and terrifically dynamic American society, growing unhindered by the weight of its history, manufacturing its own cultural patterns." 

FOREIGN AID IS PURE MARXISM Prakash C. Jain, writing in U.S. News & World Report for October 19, 1959, says: "America stands still hypnotized, hugging the Communist philosophy of life *** the basic doctrine of communism that man is a mere physical entity, a mutation in the evolutionary process of matter. * * * In other words, that man is a creature of his circumstances, and that his mind, personality, aspirations, values, and visions are mere concomitants of material changes. That the forms of laws, ethics, art, literature, philosophy, and religion are primarily determined by the system of production which obtains at a particular time and that, therefore, we live in a universe of objective and subjective necessities in which there is no freedom, and hence no place for faith. "That America, in clear violation of her own past tradition and the beliefs of her Founding Fathers, has today accepted this deadly philosophy in toto is clear from her persistent attribution of both democracy and totalitarianism to the material circumstances of a nation. "The Americans feel sure that communism grows on poverty, misery, disease, large-scale unemployment, lack of food, clothing, housing, and so on. And conversely, therefore, democracy grows on an ever-increasing agricultural, industrial, and mineral production, ever-increasing curves of operational efficiency, ever-expanding facilities in housing, schools, hospitals, restaurants, playgrounds, holiday homes; and an ever-growing consumption of motor cars, television sets, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, and other gadgets associated with modern living. "This is evident from the U.S. persistent belief that India, by the dint of her huge economic development program, has made herself the bastion of democracy in Asia, and that, should Prime Minister Nehru be able to raise India's standard of living to some degree, he will save democracy not only in India, but also in the rest of free Asia. *** "The materialistic interpretation of history and the resultant belief that communism thrives on poverty and penury, and democracy on surfeit and plenty, has sunk miles deep in the American psyche, and, once the American people see any nation advancing materially and technologically in whatever moral or ethical framework, they instinctively greet it with a full-mouthed hail and unconsciously associate it with peace and freedom. "My submission is that this belief, which has been lifted straight from Karl Marx's 'Manifesto' has obscured America's visions, has destroyed her powers to discriminate between facts and make-believe, has made American theoreticians and statesmen the sappers and miners of world communism, and has made America propaganda a complement to the Kremlin's campaign of lies." 

AN ASIAN VIEW OF FOREIGN AID 

And now the comment of one who can hardly be called a foreigner yet nevertheless writes with a profound understanding of Asiatic psychology, Dr. Lin 

Yutang. In his book "The Secret Name" he states, "Neither can the foreign aid program of the United States be considered a substitute for the basic war of ideas. Foreign aid is a timely political measure, but as an instrument for checking immediate Communist onslaughts, it is futile. "First, whereas the Communist threat is immediate, one cannot through foreign aid raise the standard of living of Asia in less than 30, 40 or 50 years. "Second, the rising standard of living is always a matter of relative degree, and at what point poverty itself provides, or ceases to provide, breeding ground for communism it is impossible to say. "Third, through foreign aid the standard of living is not necessarily raised-so much depends on the economic policy of the local administrations of the countries which receive such aid. "Fourth, lending and borrowing money is generally bad for friendship between nations as between individuals.

"Lastly, and most dangerous of all, foreign aid creates self-delusions, the illusion that you can buy friendship with dollars, the illusion that this is all we need to do and can think of doing in the cold war, and that there is no need of doing anything else. It is easier to give away dollars than to try to understand what the other man is thinking" ("The Secret Name", p. 236).

OPINION FROM HONDURAS 

Here are the comments of a dentist in Honduras in a letter to a constituent of 

Congressman Rivers of South Carolina : 

"You people as a whole are stupid and I'll give you two reasons why I say this: No. 1, you tax your citizens so heavily so as to have money for your socalled foreign aid when we both know much of it is wasted and that most loans are really gifts. My income runs between $25,000 and $50,000 per year. The maximum rate I pay is 10 percent and that is only on what I earn over $25,000. 

Why should we tax ourselves heavily when all we have to do is to have our Ambassador in Washington put up a poor-mouth story and you people fall over backward to hand us a gift? "No. 2, an even more important reason for saying you people are stupid is the attitude of your State Department with regard to your nationals and U.S. properties in our countries. "I am older than you and can remember when Mr. Coolidge was your President. 

During his time we made sure nothing happened to any of your citizens or U.S. properties in the event of troubles in our countries. We knew Mr. Coolidge would land marines and pin our ears back if trouble did occur. "Then Mr. Roosevelt and his good neighbor policy came along. What has happened to your standing in our countries since then? You and I both know it has deteriorated. Suppose several of your nationals are thrown in jail or get killed, what happens? Your State Department protests. Who is afraid of protests? It is bullets we are afraid of when the men behind them have the guts to back them up. We may not have loved you in Mr. Coolidge's day, but at least we respected you. Today we neither love nor respect you." (Congressional 

Record, June 30, 1960, p. 14151.)

An The U.S. balance of international payments problem is causing increasing concern among economists and hidden anxiety among Treasury officials. adverse balance or deficit has persisted for 10 years. This deficit has blasted the fondly held theory of a "chronic dollar shortage abroad" upon which were posited the Marshall plan and its successors the various global aid programs. 

At present, the balance of payments is a problem involving not only the credit of the United States abroad, but the stability of the dollar and the world monetary system for which the dollar is a principal reserve. 

THE NATURE OF THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Until 1922, the term "balance of payments" was known only to a few academicians, notably at Harvard University. They had begun to study the international flow of money and credit and sought to give an account of income and outgo for the country similar to a financial operations statement of a business.¹ 

Their chief difficulty was that of obtaining and collecting the required data. (Except in a totalitarian economy, receipts and payments of a country do not flow through a central treasurer or accounting office, as in a business.) Many items in the balance sheet, such as expenditures abroad by tourists and remittances by immigrants to their families, are not known precisely, and errors in estimates can cause considerable differences in the balance." 

In 1922, the Department of Commerce, with its vastly superior facilities for collecting information, assumed the responsibility of compiling and assessing the flow of payments. An early colleague of ours, Dr. Rufus S. Tucker, was appointed to head this important branch of fiscal economics. Since then, the Department has issued a yearly statement (also now quarterly), and this economic tool has now become part of the fiscal accounting of most countries. 

TERMS DEFINED 

A balance-of-payments statement shows all transactions with foreigners giving rise to credits or flow of funds. Originally, these transactions were classified either as exports or imports, but now generally as receipts and payments. 

Merchandise shipped and sold abroad is classified as a "visible export, and such items as transportation provided to foreign shippers or travelers, credits or receipts for insurance and banking services, are classified as "invisible exports." Other invisible exports are interest and dividends received on U.S. investments abroad, as well as funds invested here by foreigners (since they constitute a receipt of funds or give rise to a corresponding credit abroad). 

Payments, or imports, consist of like transactions in reverse direction, such as merchandise imports, payments to foreigners for shipping and insurance expense, tourist expenditures abroad, remittances to relatives and philanthropic and religious institutions. 

Any difference between exports (credits to United States) and imports (credits to foreigners) shows either as (a) a movement of gold, or (b) an increase or decrease in bank deposits and holdings of short-term dollar securities (chiefly 

Treasury notes).

Differences are settled by changes in credit balances here, rather than abroad, because of the more general acceptability of dollar credits rather than sterling credits or other European currencies (although sterling is becoming more competitive). The preference for dollar credits arises from (1) the great proportion of the free world's trade (about 17 percent) done with the United States, (2) the ease of converting dollars into gold in international transactions, and (3) the widespread use abroad of dollar credits as monetary reserves (nearly a half of the world's monetary reserves are dollars). 

The steady outward movement of U.S. gold during the past decade and the steady increase in dollar credits here raise storm signals over the balance of payments and give concern abroad over the stability of the dollar. The salient figures on the balance of payments for the years 1950-59 are shown in the table. 

1 In the July 1919, issue of Review of Economic Statistics, C. J. Bullock, John H. 

Williams, and Rufus S. Tucker, had published a study entitled, "The Balance of Trade of the United States.' "9 2 One early controversy occurred during the prohibition era and occasioned the resignation of a principal Commerce Department official over the estimated amount of dollars going abroad for smuggled liquor.

GOVERNMENT VERSUS PRIVATE TRANSACTIONS 

Until World War II, Government transactions were insignificant items among the total transactions comprising the balance of payments. Within the past decade Government payments have loomed larger and larger and today are the determinate element in the balance. In 1959, for instance, Government transactions accounted for approximately 12 percent of receipts from abroad and for 40 percent of payments abroad. Government payments in 1959 amounted to $9¼ billion, offset by receipts (or credits) of $2.78 billion. Government payments compare with total merchandise exports of $16 billion. 

It is obvious, therefore, that an appraisal of our international financial position, or of the tendencies in the international balance, cannot be obtained without an understanding of the nature of these Government transactions, their magnitude, and their responsiveness to changes in the economic climate. 

In view of the importance of Government transactions, it is paradoxical, if not disturbing, that so little attention is paid by analysts and official policy framers to the implications to the credit and gold position of the United States of these transactions.

We have seen most of the authoritative studies of the balance-of-payments problem. In none of them are Government transactions separated and studied as a category apart from private transactions. Where they have been given piecemeal attention, their importance has been discounted. The blame for the adverse balance and the gold outflow is laid upon the failure of the business community to export more, or it is assigned indiscriminately to a variety of influences. 

In the following analysis we have separated the two categories for analysis, and graphically in the attached table. 

RESULTS OF A DECADE 

The table shows that during the decade, the total adverse balance (or gain to foreigners) has approached $18 billion. This deficit has been settled to the extent of $5 billion by sales of gold abroad at $35 an ounce. The remainder has accumulated in the form of dollar deposits and holdings of Treasury obligations. 

BASIS OF CURRENT OPTIMISM 

Official equanimity toward the balance of payments is supported by evidence of slight improvement in the first 6 months of 1960. In the first quarter, for instance, merchandise exports totaled $6.3 billion compared with $5.4 billion for the corresponding 1959 quarter, and the improvement has continued to hold through the first half of the year. Imports were slightly less, due mainly to stronger competition here with foreign small car imports. Rising exports have been helped by a more aggressive trade diplomacy, which has achieved some liberalization of foreign exchange restrictions that in the past have excluded American goods-chiefly consumer items-from certain European countries. 

There has also occurred an exceptionally large demand for U.S. cotton, a rise in deliveries of jet airplanes to foreign airlines, and a partial recovery in exports of steel and copper after last year's temporary reduction in production. 

Despite these gains, the adverse balance is currently running at the rate of $3 billion for the year. This is somewhat better than the 1959 showing, but less than was anticipated earlier in the year. 

Rising U.S. prices make it more difficult for foreigners to buy U.S. products and easier for them to sell goods to the United States. This has happened with items ranging from oil and cotton to sewing machines. 

U.S. exporters will feel increasing competition for markets not only from industrialized countries, particularly Western Europe and Japan, but also from other sectors. India, for example, is now entering the competition for sales of unfinished steel, even to the United States. Existing portents also show a likelihood of imports increasing as a proportion of the gross national product. 

In the balance of trade in services, if it were not for U.S. tourists spending more than $2 billion per year abroad, the United States would show a sizable net realization of receipts rather than merely breaking even. Ironically, the 

Commerce Department has a budget of some $60,000 a year to promote U.S. tourism abroad and only this year is urging Congress for funds to encourage tourism to the United States. That such programs are at cross-purpose is obvious.

GOVERNMENT TRANSFERS ABROAD 

Government expenditures abroad are commonly believed to be only those of the foreign aid program, of between $3 and $4 billion annually. Proponents of foreign aid make much of the fact that this sum represents less than 1 percent of the gross national product. Here is a double error. First, the foreign aid program represents less than half the expenditures abroad to which the Government is presently committed by its foreign policy. Second, the burden these expenditures lay upon the economy arises not from the amount but from their collateral effects. Among these are the gold drain to which we have alluded. 

Another is the effect they have in building up foreign industry in competition with domestic industry through furnishing capital, equipment, and technical skills. 

Other payments to which the Government has become committed and which show increasing rigidity are oversea costs of maintaining garrisons and bases on foreign soil, military supplies furnished to allied powers, and interest payments on the mounting volume of Treasury securities held abroad. 

Despite the rising prosperity of our principal allies, and their ability to support armed forces needed for their defense, the cost of U.S. military forces and bases has steadily risen until 1959, when, for the first time, some reduction was effected. The point was brought out, in data which we prepared for hearings before the House Foreign Affairs Committee last year, that while we have been spending around 11 percent of the gross national product on the common defense, our European allies were spending less than 5 percent. 

A further burden, presently modest, but of increasing significance, is the interest cost on Treasury obligations held abroad. Since 1949, foreigners have added nearly $18 billion to their holdings of these assets. The interest burden has been rising and amounted to $281 million last year. 

It is significant, in relation to the U.S. gold position, that foreigners have preferred, on the whole, to keep their assets here liquid, in the form of bank deposits and short-term Treasury notes. Of total foreign assets and investments in the United States at the end of 1958, of around $35 billion, less than $5 billion consisted of direct investments, the balance being largely convertible Government notes and bonds or corporate securities traded in the exchanges. 

CLAIMS ON GOLD 

The U.S. gold stock is down from $24.4 billion in 1949 to $19 billion at the end of August. Some differences exist as to the extent of foreign claims upon 

U.S. gold. Those who prefer to discount the seriousness of the technical position use a figure for short-term liabilities to foreign official institutions, since the privilege of converting these liabilities into gold is extended only to foreign central banks and institutions. The amount of such liabilities was recently about $9 billion.

A prudent view would include all liabilities to foreigners that are readily convertible into cash and from cash into gold. The total of these, as of the end of 1958, was around $30 billion, as reported by the Department of Commerce, and has been increased since then. The more volatile of these assets include (in addition to deposits in U.S. banks and holdings of short-term Treasury bills) holdings of long-term Government bonds (since they are readily marketable), holdings abroad of U.S. currency, estimated at $900 million at the end of 

1958, and holdings of short-term bankers' acceptances and commercial paper. 

The sum of these is in excess of $23 billion. Finally, to be mentioned are banking liabilities to foreigners maturing in more than 1 year, reported by the Federal Reserve System to be in the neighborhood of $4 billion. Although not immediately convertible to cash, they represent a potential call upon U.S. gold. 

Opposing these various claims are short-term claims on foreigners, as reported by banks in the United States, totaling around $24 billion, leaving a net potential claim on gold in excess of $24 billion. 

THE NATURE OF THE THREAT 

The actual vulnerability of the U.S. fiscal position is not so much in the likelihood of a sudden "run on the dollar" as in the loss of control over our financial house. By the magnitude of foreign short-term claims on gold, the domestic banking and monetary structure, including the all-important interest rate, is no longer governed by domestic considerations, but is at the mercy of foreign

influences which are beyond our control. Thus, a political crisis abroad, having seemingly no relevance to U.S. affairs, may induce lack of confidence abroad, and a move to liquidate and gather in cash. Such a development is like pulling out one card in a house of cards. We have in memory the failure of the Austrian 

Credit Anstalt in 1931, which spread to the international scene the debacle that had been brewing in the credit excesses of the 1920's. 

THE CORRECTIVES TO THE BALANCE 

The various correctives to an adverse balance of payments are well known, and frequently used abroad. They include the use of tariffs, import quotas, exchange restrictions, and the like, to restrict the flow of capital and goods. The United 

States has shown commendable reluctance to employ these methods, preferring to keep the channels of international trade as free as possible. Regrettably, however, our foreign policy displays considerable flabbiness in its tolerance of such controls by our friends. Thus, of all the members of the International Monetary 

Fund, the United States is the only one fully to accept the responsibilities of international convertibility of its money. 

A classic corrective of an adverse balance is currency devaluation. An avalanche movement of dollars into gold could force such a course upon the United States. The consequences would be an international financial crisis, the beneficiaries of which are well known. An intermediate step, that appears inevitable under the present aspect of things, is a suspension of international convertibility of the dollar until the U.S. gold reserves are rebuilt. It is doubtful, however, whether the country would accept the austerity required for such a course. This leaves open the alternative of a gradual devaluation through an operation of an open market for gold.

General FELLERS. If I may, I will be happy to send a statement. (The information is as follows:)

FOREIGN AID, FISCAL YEAR 1963 GENERAL OBSERVATION 

In planning the foreign aid program, the practice is to seek immediate objectives which require annual dollar transfusions. The aid program envisagesduring the sixties-the achievement of a better life for everybody. This includes cultural improvement, better housing, increased income, and a higher standard of living. In some instances it includes sizable increases in military forces.

Thus, we are setting a standard, both economic and military, which the recipients cannot sustain. To continue the standard requires a continuous flow of dollars. Some foreign aiders predict at least a 50-year program. 

This concept of continuous aid must be stopped. Foreign aiders have already emptied the U.S. Treasury. 

After World War II, Germany had a greater recovery problem than any other European country. Every penny of our aid and every penny Germany was able to raise otherwise was channeled into productive enterprise. Better housing, increased wages, and all other measures to improve living standards, temporarily were sacrificed in a prodigious effort to produce. As a result, Germany quickly established a sound economy and the recovery which followed was phenomenal.

If other countries would show the same interest in self-help as was and is manifested by Germany, they already would have achieved economic independence. 

Our aid program deadens initiative, fails to instill a spirit of self-help, makes people dependent on handouts, and destroys the very goal it seeks to create. 

SPECIFIC OBSERVATIONS 

The industrial countries of Western Europe and Japan have economies more flourishing than our own. They need no aid and none should be extended. 

Such aid as is extended elsewhere should be only to those countries whose governments are Western-oriented, i.e., dedicated to free enterprise as opposed to socialistic and communistic systems. 

Underdeveloped countries need technical assistance and internal security. 

Neither of these needs is expensive. The following quotation on aid to the 

Philippines written by a Filipino newsman, A. L. Valencia, illustrates: "Modern Filipinos like to say: 'America's greatest export to our country was the Thomasites.' They were 600 young American men and women-teachers, engineers, constabulary officers, and public health workers-got their name from the U.S. Army transport Thomas which brought them to Manila. It is no exaggeration to say that these 600 young people laid the foundation of the modern Philippine Republic * ** 

"Schools were opened at first in shacks rudely built of bamboo and palm leaves. Many of the first teachers were American soldiers who had fallen in love with the Philippines and decided to take their discharge and stay on. Some of these men could do little more than teach the ABC's, but the English language began to spread. "Today the Philippines is the third biggest English-speaking nation in the world."

While the United States cooperated, actually the Philippine Government sought our aid and paid for it. Today the Philippines is a modern state. The kind of aid Americans extended to the Philippines is the kind of aid we should now extend to the underdeveloped countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

Since the specific amounts of military assistance being extended to various countries are not available to this committee, it is difficult, in turn, for us to be specific. The figures given below represent aid from July 1, 1945, through 

June 30, 1961.

THE ORIENT 

After more than $5 billion in aid, South Korea could be put on a much smaller allowance.

From our airbases in Okinawa, North Korea is within bombing range. An announcement that the Monroe Doctrine had been extended over South Korea would enable us safely to bring our Korean garrisons home and permit South 

Korean forces to be reduced.

While military assistance to the Republic of China must continue, it should be carefully screened and reduced. 

In South Vietnam we have already poured $2.1 billion. We now have this country on an annual dole. For the time being, aid must be continued. 

Following the principle that aid must be extended to countries directly threatened by Red aggression, an estimated $600 million annually probably should be allocated to the Orient.

SOUTH ASIA 

Here military assistance should gradually be discontinued. Possibly $50 million should be allocated as a tapering off figure. 

MIDDLE EAST 

Turkey has received $3.5 billion in total aid. 

Greece has received in total aid $3.2 billion. 

Greece and Turkey should reduce their military forces to the level which their own economy can support. Meanwhile, as a tapering off measure, $25 million each might be required.

AFRICA 

The countries in Africa require principally small arms for internal security. 

These weapons, for the most part, are already available. If this judgment is somewhat in error, certainly $25 million would be ample to meet essential requirements. 

EUROPE 

Europeans can and should finance their own defense measures.

LATIN AMERICA 

Aid to Latin America total $5.4 billion before the era of the Alliance for 

Progress. Military assistance, except small arms, would merely strengthen the temptation for aggression in some areas. Certainly $50 million would be ample. 

Summary of all military assistance.-Total estimate for military assistance: $775 million. 

ECONOMIC AID 

In addition to our annual aid programs there are seven lending agencies, which as of last year had a lending power estimated at $8 billion. 

Moreover, an enormous carryover from fiscal 1962 to fiscal 1963 may be anticipated. The unexpended funds from prior fiscal years which were available for fiscal 1962 totaled $5.849 billion. With a rather heavy change in AID personnel immediately prior to fiscal 1963 it is possible that an even larger carryover may occur in fiscal 1963. In view of extensive hiding of unexpended aid funds now being disclosed, this entire carryover should revert to the U.S. Treasury.

The Export-Import Bank should be used to make the allocations for economic loans. Loans repayable in dollars and for intermediate terms should be the rule. 

Long-term loans "with little or no interest" are disguised giveaways, a deception on the uninformed electorate, and should not be tolerated. No funds should be appropriated for such purposes. 

From the $1 billion foreign aid recommended by our committee, $225 million remains available for economic aid. 

This committee has not sufficient information to recommend which countries should receive loans or economic aid. We would not presume to recommend these allocations.

We do recommend technical assistance to countries which seek this aid and are willing to pay for at least part of it. It appears to us that $225 million is more than ample for this year's technical assistance. 

India, a socialist state, Africa and Latin America, all have enormous potential wealth. Wherever stable government is established, private capital will seek investments. 

AID PLEDGES 

Unusually heavy pledges have already been made principally to Latin America and India. Some of these pledges were made without the consent of the 

Congress. These are an unwarranted, unconstitutional usurpation of the legislative power of the Congress by the executive branch. They should be neither recognized nor honored. The above-mentioned lending facilities are so vast and flexible that this abandonment of unauthorized pledges should result in no hardship. It appears to the Citizens Foreign Aid Committee that justifiable requirements for the Alliance for Progress could readily be met by existing lending agencies.

DEAR CHAIRMAN MORGAN: At the hearings yesterday on the Foreign Assist ance Act of 1963, the acting chairman invited us, because of the lateness of the hour, to supplement our responses by a further statement which we might file with the committee for inclusion in the record. Taking advantage of this kind invitation, I now submit a statement in further response to questions raised by Congressman Robert R. Barry of New York.

JOBS CREATED BY FOREIGN AID 

Congressman Barry cited an administration argument for foreign aid to the effect that foreign aid expenditures had created an estimated 700,000 jobs in the United States in supplying goods and services purchased by foreign aid recipients.

No more spurious argument for foreign aid could be advanced than the claim that it creates jobs-unless it be for Washington bureaucrats. Here are two fallacies: (1) Relying upon administration estimates and guesses, the Congressman stated that 80 percent of our aid money which we dispense abroad finds its way back to this country. Now, it should be obvious that if 80 percent of aid moneys 

1 Secretary of the Treasury Dillon, in his report on the balance of payments, transmitted by the President to the Speaker of the House by letter of Mar. 28, 1962, stated that "Roughly two-thirds of the funds expended for all our foreign economic assistance programs in 1961 (including foreign currency sales of agricultural surpluses) were initially utilized for expenditure in the United States."

zi are spent for U.S. goods, then the balance, or 20 percent, are not spent for U.S. goods. What happens to the 20 percent? The increase in foreign dollar claims on gold and the outgo of gold indicate that this excess foreign aid goes to the fatty surplus of foreign economies. 

Total net oversea payments by the Government in 1961, exclusive of deliveries of military goods and services, amounted to $5,773 million, as shown by the following figures drawn from the U.S. Department of Commerce balance-ofpayments tabulation:

Assuming that two-thirds of these payments (or $3.85 billion) are used to purchase U.S. goods and services, the obverse conclusion is that one-third (or $1.9 billion) is used to accumulate as dollar balances or to purchase gold. 

This would account for nearly three-fourths of the balance of payments deficit for 1961 (totaling $2.4 billion absorbed by increase in foreign claims on U.S. dollars plus the outward movement of U.S. gold in 1961). (2) Now as to the claim that the $5.773 billion created 700,000 jobs, it is obvious that if the expenditure of these dollars created jobs, the same or equivalent jobs would be created if spent by the U.S. Government directly in the 

United States or-more to the point-if the tax burden had been reduced by $5.773 billion and U.S. citizens were allowed to use this sum to buy goods and services, including homes, or even to make investments. 

Actually, money sent abroad has reduced the number of jobs for the following reasons: (a) The main drive of foreign aid dollars abroad is to help industrialize the underdeveloped countries. In these countries, almost without exception, the moment a local industry is set up the government imposes a prohibitive tariff wall or an outright prohibition of the import of the article now being manufactured. This closes the market to U.S. exports and takes away jobs from 

American workmen who otherwise might be employed in manufacturing goods for export. We can document this with numerous instances from our own files of correspondence and dealings in our oversea professional practice. (b) The effect of giving foreigners the means to acquire goods in this market without the delivery of equivalent goods or services in return is inflationary in

effect since it takes goods and services out of the U.S. economy but leaves the same number of dollars within the economy, hence creating an upward pressure on prices.

This was conceded by Secretary Dillon in the report on the balance of payments referred to above. The Secretary stated that prices of American manufactured exports "rose 14 percent relative to those of other industrialized nations from 1953 to 1960." Meantime, "over the same period, our share of world exports of manufactures declined from 25.9 percent to 21.6 percent." These, let us note, are the years covered by the magnification of the foreign aid program into a gargantuan and apparently permanent burden on the economy. 

This would seem to contradict the Congressman's inference that the growth of our export trade over a 20-year period is to be attributed to demand generated by foreign aid. 

Respectfully submitted.

ELGIN GROSECLOSE. 

REPLY OF HON. ROBERT R. BARRY, TO STATEMENT BY MR. GROSECLOSE 

AID estimates that of its fiscal year 1962 funds for economic aid, 73 percent will be spent directly in the United States. If the military assistance programs are added, the total rises to almost 78 percent, and if the entire food-for-peace program, to about 85 percent. 

AID's target is to raise the share of its economic aid funds spent directly in the United States to 80 percent. Military assistance and food for peace would raise this figure further. 

It is true that on an actual disbursement basis the share of total AID expenditures during fiscal year 1962 made directly in the United States was not as high as 73 percent, but this is because these disbursements were to a considerable extent made from funds committed in earlier years before the balanceof-payments problem led to a change in foreign aid procurement policies. The quoted figures from the March 1962 and June 1961 issues of Survey of Current Business and in Secretary Dillon's recent report to the President on the balance of payments are on a disbursement basis, and thus reflect this earlier policy. 

Future expenditure of the funds now being sought by AID will reflect the current policy of emphasizing U.S. procurement except in unusual circumstances. 

Furthermore, of the 27 percent of fiscal year 1962 foreign economic assistance funds not expected to be spent directly in the United States, it is estimated that 85 percent (or 23 percent of total fiscal year 1962 funds) will be spent in the developing countries, and thus primarily in countries which are the beneficiaries of our assistance. These expenditures reduce their dollar gaps, which gaps in turn affect demands and needs for our assistance. And since they buy from us more than they sell to us, the dollars will likely soon return to the United States.

Of the 4 percent of fiscal year 1962 funds which it is estimated will be spent in the first instance within the other industrialized countries of the free world, only one-half is expected to be spent in countries having a surplus balance-ofpayments position vis-a-vis the United States. Thus, it is estimated that no more than about 2 percent of the total funds will be directly spent in countries where there is a substantial danger of an accumulation of dollar reserves. 

Mr. Groseclose quotes statistics from Survey of Current Business for June 

1961 and March 1962, without critical analysis of the items mentioned. These only purport to show "total net oversea payments by the Government," and of the total net payments shown for both years only about half appear to have any relation to the foreign aid program. The largest item is for "military transactions," presumably the expenditures of our Armed Forces abroad, not in foreign aid, but on their own direct account. 

It follows that both Mr. Groseclose's percentage and the base to which he applies it are inappropriate tools for analysis of the effect on the U.S. balance of payments of the foreign aid program now before the committee. His analysis is simply not relevant.

As to Mr. Groseclose's statements on the subject of jobs, AID has never maintained that the 700,000 people who are estimated to be at work in the United States supplying goods and services under the foreign aid program would be unemployed if that program did not exist. This is, however, the estimate of number of employees whose time is required to complete foreign aid goods and services. We do not know whether or not in the absence of the program these jobholders might still be at work since their employment would depend on an

expansion of demand in other sectors which might not be as easy to secure as Mr. Groseclose suggests. The essential justification for foreign aid, however, lies not in U.S. jobs for which it might be responsible, but rather in the vital 

U.S. foreign policy interests it serves. That it also assists the U.S. economy, nevertheless, remains indisputable. 

Mr. Groseclose's contention that U.S. exports to aid recipient countries decline as their productive capacities expand is simply contrary to the facts. It was estimated that in 1959 U.S. per capita exports to other developed countries were $22.80, compared with only $4.79 to the less developed countries. If per capita exports to the latter had been even half what they were to the former, total U.S. exports for that year would have been about $9 billion greater than they were.

The success of the Marshall plan shows most strikingly the effect which foreign aid can have in expanding U.S. export markets. In 1948, the first year of the plan, the volume of U.S. exports to Western Europe was about $4 billion, of which a large percentage was U.S. Government financed under the plan. 

Since that date the trend has been sharply upward, reaching almost $7 billion in 1961, of which only a very small fraction at most was U.S. financed. This represents an aggregate increase of about 75 percent, and a much greater increase as regards exports financed through regular channels. With the intense multilateral effort now being aimed at the reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers, it is reasonable to expect that U.S. exports to countries whose economies are developing and expanding will tend to rise in the future even more sharply than they have in the past. 

Finally, Mr. Groseclose's contention that foreign aid has been a substantial contributor to inflation in the United States, is equally without foundation. 

This aid represents only a small percentage of the total Federal budget, and a much smaller percentage of the total gross national product (for 1960, total net Government economic aid was 0.59 percent of our GNP), and thus it can hardly be said to exert a significant effect on U.S. prices. Accompanied by sound overall monetary and fiscal policies, the U.S. foreign aid program and price stability are perfectly compatible.

STATEMENT BY SHELDON Z. KAPLAN, FORMER STAFF CONSULTANT, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee; I appreciate the opportunity to present this statement in connection with the proposed Foreign Assistance Act of 1962.

I had the great privilege of serving as staff consultant to this committee, including the Subcommittee on Inter-American Affairs, from July 1, 1949, through July 31, 1957. Since that time I have been engaged in the practice of international law in Washington, with special emphasis on Latin American activities. 

My statement is confined solely to the Alliance for Progress, which is the main thrust of U.S. foreign policy toward Latin America. It is because I wholehearetdly believe in this program that I feel it my duty to point out certain weaknesses in its implementation which threaten to undermine its effectiveness. 

The Alliance for Progress is considered by Latin America as very probably the last chance the United States will have to help build a bastion of democracy in this hemisphere.

The Communists have made and are making far greater inroads in Latin America than the statistics would lead us to believe. Many of the brilliant young Latin American University students continue their education, not in the United States, but in Moscow. The Soviet Union is spending literally millions of dollars for this purpose. Unless the United States goes about the Alliance for 

Progress with a sense of urgency and a sense of doing battle-just as was the case with respect to our participation in World War I and World War II— Latin America will crack and fall easy prey to Communist blandishments and then domination.

I do not detect within the Executive arm of our Government among those agencies concerned with Latin American affairs any compelling sense of urgency whatsoever with respect to Latin America. Except for the President himself and for Mr. Teodoro Moscoso, Administrator of the Alliance, whose dynamic statements on United States-Latin American relations indicate clearly their great anxiety and great sense of urgency in this area, there exists in Government 81496-62-pt. 5-

circles an almost traditional continuation of a lack of comprehension of Latin American problems and of emotional rapport with the pulse of that area. 

To succeed, the Alliance for Progress must be wisely administered and executed by the most experienced individuals available, with imagination, warmth, skill, dexterity, and in such a way that it will be easily identifiable as responsive to their needs by the peoples of Latin America. To apply this program too technically or too bankerlike is to place it in a straitjacket that can only strangle it. 

Further, failure to coordinate all facets of Alliance for Progress activities carried on by the appropriate U.S. agencies, can likewise lead to strangulation and emasculation.

I include as part of my statement a memorandum which I transmitted to the Export-Import Bank, together with correspondence to that agency and to the Administrator of the Agency for International Development. This correspondence demonstrates how the left hand, in this case the Export-Import Bank, is undoing what the right hand, the Alliance for Progress, is trying to accomplish and is undermining the main underpinning of that program—the principle of self-help and the development of local talents, skills, and capabilities. The material follows: 

MARCH 26, 1962.

MEMORANDUM To: Export-Import Bank of Washington. 

From: Sheldon Z. Kaplan, counsel in United States to Consorcio Nacional Con structora Covalca, S. A. y Urruela, Sittenfeldt, Whitbeck, Ltda. 

Subject: Justification and support for approval by Government of Guatemala of direct guaranties instead of "performance bond" re highway construction project CA-8-49, Guatemala.

I. PROJECT CA-S-49 AND ITS IMPORTANCE 

This memorandum concerns a highway construction project in Guatemala, which together with two other such projects, is being financed by the U.S. 

Government (Export-Import Bank, hereinafter referred to as "Eximbank," and the Development Loan Fund, now a part of the Agency for International Development). The Export-Import Bank has the primary responsibility for the administration of this financing. The instant project, CA-8-49, involves a new highway in Guatemala, approximately 30 miles long, running from El Molino to Rio Paz, thus joining the Inter-American Highway at a point between Guatemala City and the El Salvador border, with the Coastal Highway at the Salvador border. This highway is important in that it will open up a new agricultural zone, will shorten the time and distance to El Salvador and supply an additional facility for Guatemalan-Salvadorean traffic and commerce. 

From the point of view of United States-Guatemalan relations specifically and the whole fabric of the Alliance for Progress generally, the project takes on added urgency. In view of the present emergency state in which the pro-United 

States Guatemalan Government finds itself and the urgent necessity for beginning work on this project immediately and putting the unemployed to work, this project is top priority. Indeed, it may be fairly stated that for all of Central 

America this constitutes a pilot project for the Alliance for Progress concept in that area because the project, although financed by the United States, involves a local construction company,' using its own funds to initiate the work ($400,000 deposited in a Guatemalan bank) and its own technicians, which is self-help in the best sense of the term. It is the first time that a local company will have worked on a project of such magnitude. 

Negotiations between the United States and Guatemala on this and the two other related highway projects have taken place over a protracted period of time. The projects have been the subject of widespread press comment in 

Guatemala. Because they vitally affect the economy and the unemployment problem of the country, the people of Guatemala have voiced their deep interest and solicitude. Upon the completion of the negotiations with the United States and the signing of the contracts with the construction firms awarded the contracts, including CONAC, the instant company, all attention and expectation in Guatemala, official and public, has been focused on the initiation of the work. 

Indeed, Guatemalan pride in the fact that a Guatemalan group will do the job has been raised to a high pitch.

II. CONAC'S READINESS TO PERFORM 

Illustrative of CONAC's capacity and willingness to perform all of its obligations in connection with the construction of this project are the following: (1) It has made the special deposit of $400,000 (referred to above) to initiate the work. (2) It has already expended some $100,000 in preparation for work on this project. (3) Of machinery and equipment owned and paid for by COVALCA (which will be used by CONAC), $1,200,000 worth was purchased in the United States and will be utilized on the project. This machinery, etc., will be shipped from 

Caracas, Venezuela, to Guatemala on a U.S.-flag vessel. (4) Further, certain materials (e.g., explosives) will be purchased from U.S. firms, as already arranged. 

III. APPROVAL BY GOVERNMENT OF GUATEMALA OF DIRECT GUARANTIES 

On February 26, 1962, CONAC signed an agreement with the Government of Guatemala covering highway project CA-8-49, described above, in the amount of $2,147,607.68. This agreement was signed following the approval of the award of the contract on this project to CONAC by the Government of Guatemala with the concurrence of the Export-Import Bank (hereinafter referred to as "Eximbank”).

This memorandum is filed pursuant to conversations which have taken place in Washington between representatives of CONAC (Sheldon Z. Kaplan, Dr. Juan 

Manuel Jimenez Pinto, and Gen. Ludovico Gaetani) and those of Eximbank (Frank Kimball, Tillman Neuner, and Daniel Rengers) on March 20 and 22, 1962. Those conversations were held with Eximbank at the instance of the 

Minister of Communications and Public Works of Guatemala, Col. Jose Luis Cruz- 

Salazar, pursuant to arrangements made by the Embassy of Guatemala in Washington.

The intercession of CONAC in this matter arises by virtue of a letter, dated March 13, 1962, from Colonel Cruz-Salazar to the Guatemalan Ambassador in 

Washington, Carlos Alejos. A translation of the text of this letter follows:

From this letter and from other communications to Eximbank from the Minister of Communications and Public Works, it will be seen that the Government of Guatemala has fully concurred in, and has accepted, the mechanism of direct guarantees from CONAC in lieu of a performance bond in connection with project CA-8-49. The Government of Guatemala is satisfied that these guarantees, coupled with relevant provisions of the project agreement, are ample to insure the satisfactory performance of the project and fully comply with the bidding provisions and the law of Guatemala. 

IV. THE BIDDING PROVISIONS 

It is conceded that the mechanism of direct guarantees, accepted by the Government of Guatemala, to be valid must be in accord with the bidding provisions. 

Those provisions are found in "Official Basis of Bidding," September 19, 1961, of the Government of Guatemala. 

1. Number 18 thereof requires a "fianza", (security or gurantee) of 100 percent of the value of the work to be performed, obtained from or issued by "an institution authorized to operate in Guatemala" on behalf of the contractor. 

2. CONAC, in its bidding offer, dated November 3, 1961, in No. 6(g), agreed to give a "fianza," covering 100 percent of its work in accordance with the requirements of No. 18 of the "Official Basis of Bidding." 

3. According to the law of Guatemala, which governs the contract between 

CONAC and the Government of Guatemala, "flanza" is also an instrument in which any institution recognized by Guatemalan law may give a mortgage or pledge to guarantee an amount of money to be paid if a contractor fails to perform its obligations. 

4. According to the Civil Code of Guatemala, the principle is stated that the laws governing a contract form part of such contract. "Fianza" (security, guarantees) is covered by the civil code, and a special law in full force and effect gives the Government of Guatemala the right to have as a "fianza" in construction contracts with the Government, direct guarantees from the contractor himself or another person. 

5. As noted above, the bidding provisions deal with "fianza." According to the law of Guatemala, a fianza in the present construction contract can be had by direct guarantees from CONAC or any other institution whose financial capacity is sufficient. 

6. It follows conclusively that the acceptance by the Government of Guatemala of the direct guarantees by CONAC as "fianza" is (a) not against the bidding provisions but is fully consistent therewith, and (b) is consistent with the project contract between CONAC and the Government of Guatemala, since the Government has the right to accept direct guarantees. Furthermore, it would be inequitable to fasten on the shoulders of CONAC via the project agreement any greater burden with respect to "fianza" than that contained in the bidding provisions. 

V. THE GUATEMALAN BONDING MARKET 

The mechanism of direct guarantees, approved by the Government of Guatemala, was utilized when it became clear that the regular bonding and insurance institutions in Guatemala were unable to give a performance bond, and the U.S. bonding market (as discussed below) was not interested in the bond. This applies to a direct bond as well as reinsurance. 

3 "Flanza," under Guatemalan law, is a secondary contract by which a person agrees to fulfill an obligation on behalf of another person. It is of 2 classes: simple and joint. 

Simple, when the "fiador" (person who has agreed to fulfill an obligation) has to perform it after the "fiado" (person on behalf of whom the obligation is incurred) has been unable to perform it. Joint, when the "fiador" must perform at once, without dealing with the "fiado." The kinds are as follows: "Fianza personal," when it is backed only by the personal credit of the fiador; "fianza hipotecaria," backed by mortgage; and "ñanza prendaria," back by pledge.

In Guatemala, there are 2 groups of companies engaged in the insurance business: (a) Guatemalan and (b) foreign. 

The Guatemalan group is subdivided into 2 classes: bonding companies and insurance companies. 

Bonding companies are (a) Credito Hipotecario Nacional: This company does not issue bonds, because it hasn't sufficient capacity. (b) Union Central de Pilotos Automovilistas: Limited to automobile driving licenses.

The group of insurance companies work mainly in the insurance field and only occasionally in bonding. They do not have the specialized personnel to handle bonds. This group consists of the following, all of whom were approached by

Lotonal was unsuccessful in securing reinsurance (it is now known, from American International Underwriters). Furthermore, the conditions which Lotonal wished to impose on CONAC consisted of control over the special cash deposit of $400,000 to initiate CONAC's work, which of course was unacceptable to both CONAC and the Government of Guatemala and is against the terms of the project agreement.
