The foreign insurance companies authorized to operate in Guatemala cover life and property damage, and in some cases automobile injuries, but no bonds (some 22 companies, operating through local representatives). 

VI. THE U.S. BONDING MARKET 

Efforts by CONAC in the United States have likewise proved fruitless. These have been carried on through COVALCA, S.A., one of the two Guatemalan companies forming the consortium CONAC. As a practical matter, most companies operate through two pools: (a) American International Underwriters 

Corp., and (b) American Foreign Insurance Association. 

American International Underwriters in a communication dated March 21, 1962, stated: "Underwriters feel that while the direct guarantee of Constructora Covalca, S.A., is acceptable to the Guatemalan Government because the land and machinery owned by Covalca are located in Guatemala, in the U.S. market those assets are not as readily convertible into cash so as to warrant the issuance of a performance bond. This casts no reflection on the financial strength of the entity-it merely shows that what one market will find satisfactory, the other will not be as flexible." 

Best's Insurance Guide, 1960, page 60B, states with respect to American 

Foreign Insurance Association : 

“*** AFIA provides American and oversea business interests with efficient insurance service and protection in foreign countries, except Canada, Hawaii, Alaska, and Central America." [Italics supplied.]

Nevertheless, negotiations have been conducted with AFIA, with no positive result.

Insurance Co. of North America was also approached, and in a communication dated March 23, 1962, declined the bond in these words: "This is to inform you that we respectfully decline to furnish a performance bond for Constructor Covalca S.A. "Our reasons for declining this bond in no way reflect upon the integrity of the contracting firm. We were unable to gather sufficient underwriting information that could be verified in such a short period of time. It is also our understanding that the Government of Guatemala wants a surety that is licensed in their country to furnish this bond.

I sincerely hope Constructor Covalca is able to obtain the bond they need in this case, and successfully complete the project." 

A number of other companies approached (such as Traveler's, Aetna, and Fidelity) stated that they worked through one of the two pools, described above. 

In effect, no bonding company in the United States will issue a direct performance bond involving construction in Guatemala, especially in view of the present political situation. No reinsurance is possible, since Guatemalan facilities are limited for local participation. 

The political situation, however, is not of CONAC's doing. It is precisely because there exists such situations in Latin America that there is need for an "Alianaza para el Progreso" (Alliance for Progress). 

VII. THE RISKS 

There follows material on the risks involved with respect to performance of the project contract, which discussion may be relevant to the question of adequacy of security to insure performance. 

From the point of view of a bonding company, for example, all its risks derive from clauses 6 and 8 of the contract. 

A. Clause 6—Translation 

Guarantees. As a preliminary requirement to approve the present contract by means of governmental decree and within a period of 15 calendar days counted from the date of the signing of the contract, the contractor should issue a bond satisfactory to the Ministry of Communications and Public Works, in a bonding institution fully authorized to operate in Guatemala and of sufficient financial capacity of solvency, in the amount of an equivalent of 100 percent of the total value of the contracted project a bond which will guarantee (i) 50 percent thereof (a) the complete fulfillment of the contracted work within the stipulated time period, and (b) the quality of the work in accordance with the technical specifications, design, and other requirements of the contract, and (ii) with the remaining 50 percent of the bond: the completion of all the undertaking and obligations by virtue of the contract which the contractor or his legal representative or his subcontractors assume to pay for manual labor, social security, technical and administrative personnel, and the purchase of machinery and equipment, tools, fuels, oils, and other required items. This bond of 100 percent of the contract price covers individually and collectively each and all of the obligations assumed by the contractor derived from this instrument and will remain in full force until the Government's final receipt and discharge of the performance of the contract (finiquito). The 50 percent of the bond which is referred to in (i) of this clause, may be claimed by the Government, in the manner outlined in clause 8, in accordance with the circumstances enumerated in parts (a) and (b) of point (i), above.

In respect to point (ii) of this clause, whenever it refers to labor, in that case, there will be a liquidated amount claimed by the Government from the bonding company, in such amount as the labor court will adjudge, except the provision in part (b) of point (i) of clause 8, in which case the liquidated amount that might be claimed from the bonding company will be the amount that the director general of the highway department presents, according to the information given to him by the resident delegate and the engineer; and with respect to materials where used in the work and with respect to equipment and other machinery there should be evidence before the Ministry of Communications and Public Works that they were acquired for the contracted work, and with respect to all cases provided in this paragraph, the obligation will be claimed from the bonding company since it can be claimed by judicial means from the contractor. (NOTE. The provisions of this clause dealing with equipment and machinery are inapplicable to CONAC as a practical matter, because CONAC will not need any more equipment additional to the $1,200,000 worth being shipped from Caracas, owned by Covalco of Guatemala. In other words, CONAC has all the machinery needed, all of which has been paid for.) 

The provision dealing with nonpayment of laborers and technicians and administration costs, as a practical matter, involve at most $20,000 for 1 month (salaries of laborers, etc., for 1 month).

This goes beyond the equivalent requirement in the bidding provisions respecting "fianza."

At this point, it is important to point out that the work will proceed month by month. Before the contractor can proceed each month, the previous month's work must be okayed by both a representative of the Guatemalan Government and the consulting engineering firm, and all payments for work, machinery, etc., must have been paid. When this is a fact, the contracting company is permitted to proceed to the next month's operations. 

In other words, Covalca has and owns and already has paid for the machinery which will be needed. The provisions dealing with nonpayment of laborers, technicians, and administrative costs as a practical matter involve at most $20,000 for 1 month, which covers the salaries of the laborers, etc., for 1 month. 

B. Clause 8—Résumé 

Because of the great length of this clause, there follows a résumé of its pertinent substantive provisions, rather than a translation. 

1. Cases in which the Government of Guatemala may unilaterally rescind the contract (a) Bankruptcy of contractor. (b) If contractor fails to pay at least 50 percent of laborers' wages for more than 30 days, except that the Government cannot invoke unilateral rescission here if the Government has failed in making two monthly payments to the contractor, unless such payments have been withheld pending the payment of the penalties by the contractor for delay in work, which are provided for in the third clause of the contract. (c) If the machinery, equipment, etc., of the contractor being used in the project have been attached pursuant to legal process, or if one of the monthly payments of the Government has been attached pursuant to such process, and the contractor for this reason is unable to fulfill his obligations. (d) Repeated and evident negligence of the contractor. (e) If the contractor commits a grave criminal act against the fiscal agency of the Government, or against the contracted works. (f) If the contractor fails to fulfill any obligation derived from this contract. (g) If the contractor refuses to proceed with the work with the necessary diligence. 

2. Proceedings re above cases

In all cases, the Government will issue a resolution stating the facts, which will be transmitted to the contractor and the bonding company. (a) Bankruptcy.-The Government will afford the contractor a period of 10 days within which to present his documents demonstrating that he is not bankrupt (15 days if documents have to be collected in a foreign country). (b) Failure to pay 50 percent laborers' wages.-Government will give a period of 10 days to contractor to prove that he has paid the salaries and social security of the workers. (c) Attachment of equipment.-Government will give a period of 10 days so contractor may show attachment has been released or that it was illegally placed. (d) Negligence.-Government will give 30 days to contractor to correct the negligent work. (e) Criminal act.-Government will give 10 days term to contractor to make the final payments to the Government, or to prove that the contracted work has not been damaged through the contractor's fault. (f) Failure to fulfill.—Government will give a period of 10 days to contractor to fulfill his obligations or to present documents to refute the charges. (g) Necessary diligence.—Government will give contractor 10 days period to reinitiate the work or take the necessary steps to proceed with the work with the proper diligence according to the terms of this contract. 

In the case of more than one violation with respect to any of the above categories, the specified period of time will not be increased or cumulative but restricted to such specified term. 

The next step in the procedure, assuming no satisfactory arrangement within the prescribed period of time, is as follows: (a) the Government will order suspension of the work; (b) the Government will choose a commission to liquidate the contract; (c) the Government will give a 5-day term to the bonding company to select a panel of three contractors who have performed similar work for the Government and the Minister of Communications and Public Works will choose one contractor from that panel to complete the work. -51

The next step: If none of the contractors of the panel of three is satisfactory to the Government, the Government will grant a 3-day term to the bonding company within which both the Government and the bonding company may agree on the manner in which the work is to be performed in any one of the following three ways: (a) by direct administration, or (b) by a contractor of a construction company acceptable to both parties, or (c) by new bidding. Further, they may agree to the manner in which the work will be financed. (NOTE. This last provision contained in the above sentence is inapplicable to this contract as a practical matter, since the financing institution in this project is the Export-Import Bank of the United States.) 

If no agreement results from the above, the Association of Engineers and Architects of Guatemala will decide on one of the three solutions, immediately above outlined. 

Next step in procedure: The new contractor shall fulfill the provisions contained herein in the contract. 

Next step: The new contractor will be required to secure a performance bond and the required accident insurance pursuant to and in accordance with the provisions of clauses 6 and 7 hereof, and complete the work at the same price of this present contract. (NOTE-This, of course, would decrease any risk incurred by the bonding company of CONAC. Further, no risk would actually be incurred since there would always be available the revolving fund to the credit of CONAC to take care of any breach. Indeed, this is a very vital purpose of Eximbank's requirement of a revolving fund.) 

The final provisions of clause 8 are in the case of the present contract inoperative in practice for the following reasons:

According to point VI in clause 8, the bonding company shall provide the funds required to complete the contracted works, but the Government will pay monthly to the bonding company for the work performed monthly by the new contractor. (NOTE.- In essence, the bonding company will simply be advancing funds each month as a revolving credit.)

The bonding company will pay the excess in costs of the work and the penalties for delay in work. The bonding company will have control over the expenses of the new contractor. 

The greatest risk involves the following provision: If the bonding company refuses to give the new contractor the necessary funds as agreed, the Government will ask by means of judicial process for the payment of the total bond referred in point (i) of the sixth clause (50 percent of the whole bond) and with these funds will perform the work. But it must be borne in mind that this is not a penalty clause, and when Eximbank pays for the work, the bonding company will get it. 

Next point: The Government will be responsible for the completion of the work with these funds and will follow the decision of the Association of Engineers and Architects of Guatemala. If the Government does the work by administrative means, it will use the material, equipment, and tools of Covalca. 

Next point: The bond is only a guarantee of completion of the work, therefore the Government will refund to the bonding company any excess after liquidation. 

VII. POSSIBLE OBJECTIONS 

Eximbank has posed several possible objections to approval of the direct guarantees approved by the Government of Guatemala instead of a performance bond. 

1. Objection 1: This runs contrary to the bidding provisions. Answer: This is inaccurate. See discussion above, under "Bidding Provisions." 

2. Objection 2: This will set a precedent with other local contractors. Answer: 

CONAC is in a unique position in that it has assets totaling the amount of the contract-slightly over $2 million, in land, machinery, mortgages, etc. Further, Guatemala is a special situation requiring special application, particularly where such special application conforms to the bidding provisions and the law of Guatemala. Certainly it is inequitable and onerous to impose a greater duty on CONAC than that it agreed to in the bidding provisions. 

This is, in effect, a test case for the Alliance for Progress concept-to determine whether the United States can adjust its technical process to local business customs and concepts. 

3. Objection 3: This may meet the subsequent criticism of the Congress. 

Answer: The U.S. Congress has maintained a special and continuing interest in

fi ​3 Guatemala, as a showcase for Latin America-referred to as the Guatemala experiment to demonstrate that a country once under Communist domination can progress further under free institutions and the democratic process. This is well understood by the Congress. For example, during the debate on the mutual security and related agencies appropriation bill, 1961, on June 17, 1960, Congressman Passman stated, in part, “* ** I feel that Guatemala is in a singular position and is deserving of special consideration." (Congressional Record, June 20, 1960, p. A5287).

Today Guatemala stands in even a more singular position, of a kind warranting the favorable consideration sought for a technical mechanism which is equivalent to the mechanism of a performance bond. 

CONAC was the lowest bidder on project CA-8-49. Its position has always been in conformity with the law and good business practice. It is composed entirely of private individuals who are of proven competence in the construction field, not entrepreneurs or speculators. 

This memorandum deals solely with project CA-8-49. 

4. Objection 4: The guaranties suggested are insufficient to insure satisfactory performance. Answer: The Government of Guatemala is satisfied that the guaranties are sufficient. It will have control over the assets of CONAC, immediately convertible upon breach. Further, CONAC actually will be taking the risks. It can be imagined what a loss would be suffered by CONAC to have $1,200,000 worth of machinery idle in Guatemala.

CONAC has deposited $400,000 in cash in a Guatemalan bank, enough to insure 3 months of work, instead of the required 2 months with such funds. 

The Government of Guatemala will retain 20 percent of the monthly payments to CONAC instead of the required 10 percent, as an extra guaranty. 

IX. CONCLUSION 

1. CONAC was the lowest bidder on CA-8-49. To deny CONAC the right to perform a construction job which was awarded to it after tedious and expensive preliminaries, would be inequitable. 

2. CONAC has taken all reasonable steps in Guatemala, Mexico, and the 

United States and elsewhere to secure a performance bond. 

3. It has not been able to do so despite its financial integrity and proven capacity. Insofar as U.S. bonding companies are concerned, the political situation in Guatemala is such that they have no interest in issuing a bond. It is precisely that political situation which requires prompt action, unfettered by narrow technical interpretations. 

4. The capacity of the few qualified Guatemalan companies is practically zero for this purpose. 

5. If CONAC is not permitted to initiate the work, the ensuing delay in finding a qualified contractor (taking 3 months at a minimum) will vitally affect the emergency state in Guatemala. Delay works against the mutual interests of 

United States and Guatemala. 

6. If a U.S. firm should be awarded this project, the reaction of the Guatemalan people would be against the best interests of the United States and the 

Government of Guatemala. 

7. In view of the difficulty to obtain a performance bond, to deny CONAC this job would be considered by Guatemalans as a device to ensure that local Guatemalan companies shall not participate in such projects and that the Alliance for Progress does not mean what it says and intends. 

8. The Government of Guatemala has accepted direct guaranties from CONAC as an equivalent of a performance bond. This is consonant with the bidding provisions and the laws of Guatemala. While the project contract signed by 

CONAC includes a provisions respecting a bond by a company authorized to issue bonds in Guatemala, the law of Guatemala grants a right to the Government of Guatemala to accept direct guaranties in construction contracts. effect, it has the right, under its law, to substitute such a mechanism for the applicable provision of the contract.

In A contrary opinion would be harsh and oppressive to CONAC, since it accepted the bidding provisions and those provisions deal only with "fianza" (security or guaranty) by an institution authorized to operate in Guatemala. CONAC is such an institution. 

9. The Alliance for Progress has at its root and substance the doctrine of selfhelp. The construction of the project by CONAC, utilizing local labor, skills,

and techniques and its own funds to initiate the work, will be a demonstration of the implementation of the doctrine in a vitally important area. 

10. The United States wants the projects completed after initiation; so does 

Guatemala. The negotiations have been protracted. All Guatemala is waiting. 

If there is any doubt as to interpretation of technical language, it should be resolved in favor of the interpretation and the wishes of the Guatemalan Government. 

11. In the final analysis, it is CONAC which is assuming the risks-with its equipment, its $400,000, and all its assets, which it is willing to tie up and place at the disposal of the Government of Guatemala in order to do the job and do it well. 

12. Some 1,000 workers and employees, all presently unemployed, will be involved in CONAC's project. Delay will prolong their unemployment. 

13. In view of the urgency of this situation, Eximbank should, in the best interests of the United States and Guatemala and in demonstrating that the U.S. Government can act quickly in an emergency, concur without delay in the approval by the Government of Guatemala of direct guarantees by CONAC in acceptance thereof as an equivalent to performance bond. 

14. It is stressed that the President of Guatemala, whose Government has taken the lead in the Central American area for defense against the Castro- Marxist-Leninist regime and pro the United States, has urgently requested the Minister of .Communications and Public Works of his country to bring this matter to a speedy solution. People are unemployed, and unemployment breeds discontent. 

15. The other company, forming part of the consortium CONAC, Urruela, Sittenfeldt Whitbeck, is made up of individuals who were educated and trained in the United States. They will be deprived of an opportunity to practice what they learned in the United States if a performance bond is insisted upon and they are not thereby permitted to work on project CA-8-49. 

16. This, therefore, is a test case for the Alliance for Progress. If a performance bond is insisted upon in this case, it may well be that the underlying concept of self-help of the Alliance will have been rendered meaningless, certainly with respect to competent local construction firms in small Latin American countries whose bonding facilities are limited. 

Dr. Juan Manuel Jimenez Pinto, of Guatemala City, counsel to CONAC in

Guatemala, joins with me in this memorandum. 

Respectfully submitted. 

SHELDON Z. KAPLAN, 

Counsel to CONAC in the United States. (Addendum: If Eximbank insists upon a performance bond, a 15-day extension is requested to enable COVALCA to attempt to secure a bond in Europe.)

LAW OFFICES OF MARTIN & BURT, 

Washington, D.C., April 2, 1962.

Re Highway Construction Project CA-8-49 Guatemala, jointly financed by Exim bank and Development Loan Fund. 

Hon. FOWLER HAMILTON, 

Administrator, Agency for International Development, Department of State, Washington, D.O. 

DEAR MR. HAMILTON: I have been informed by Mr. George Denney, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff looking into the above-captioned matter for Senator Morse, that the Eximbank will make no exception in this case and insists upon a 100-percent performance bond. The Bank states that it has always been that Agency's practice to require 100 percent performance bonds. Further, according to Mr. Denney, after checking with the AID Agency, the Department of State, and Eximbank, those agencies have stated that there is no political problem involved here. I assume that what is meant by "political" in this context is "foreign policy." Eximbank, therefore, will make no exception and remains opposed to either lowering the percentage of bond required or accepting the direct guarantees of CONAC in lieu of a performance bond, an arrangement which was approved by the Government of Guatemala as an equivalent of a performance bond. 

So that the record may be clear on this matter, I herewith state my disagreement with this policy of the United States, expressed through Eximbank, which requires a 100-percent bond of a local construction (or other industrial) company in a Latin American country, particularly a small country whose bonding and banking institutions are limited in their operations and capacity. In effect, such a policy flies in the face of the Alliance for Progress, administered by your Agency, and its underlying concept of self-help. To that extent, this situation is rightfully a matter of concern for your Agency, although it is of course recognized that the responsibility for the administration of the instant loan lies with Eximbank.

As a practical effect, the continuation of such requirement of a 100-percent performance bond by Eximbank will render it virtually impossible for Latin American companies to participate directly in U.S.-financed projects in that area. Putting it in another form, it will enable American companies, working quite properly through their own U.S. bonding connections and associations and with ample assets in the United States, to maintain an advantage over local qualified companies whose assets are in their own countries and who have little or no business relationship with American bonding organizations. Especially is this true with respect to local companies who for the first time may be working (if permitted) on U.S.-financed projects. The Eximbank policy may have had merit in other days, but in this new period of a decade of development through the Alliance for Progress it is archaic and undesirable. 

Let us see how this Eximbank policy works. There are three highway construction projects in Guatemala involved in the joint Eximbank-Development Loan Fund financing. For illustration purposes, let us call them project A, project B and project C. As originally approved by Eximbank, project B, a $4 million contract, was awarded to an American construction firm; project A, a $2 million contract, was also awarded to it, but to be subcontracted to a local Guatemalan company. That Guatemalan company was asked by the American company to get its own performance bond. This it has been unable to do. 

Therefore, the American company, having secured a bond covering both projects from an American bonding company with whom it has excellent relations, now has both projects A and B. This leaves project C, also a $2 million contract. 

This is project CA-8-49, awarded to my client, CONAC. CONAC has been unable to secure a 100-percent bond, as explained in the attached memorandum. Therefore, Eximbank dispatched a cable to the Government of Guatemala insisting upon a 100-percent performance bond from CONAC and stating that the contract on CA-8-49 (which we have designated "Project C," for illustrative purposes,

above) should be awarded to the next lowest bidder or open to new bidding. 

The latter is not feasible due to the time loss involved. In effect, then, the 

Government of Guatemala will be compelled to award this contract to the next lowest bidder (some $300,000 higher than CONAC's bid). But who is this next lowest bidder? None other than the local Guatemalan company which could not secure a bond on its subcontract from the American construction firm. Since it cannot secure a 100-percent performance bond, no award on project C can be made to it. The contract, therefore, goes to the next lowest bidder. Who is this next lowest bidder? None other than the American construction firm (whose bid is some $1,300,000 higher than CONAC's bid). The result is that 

Eximbank through its harsh policy of 100-percent performance bond-harsh to local companies, but easy for American companies will have made it possible for one American firm to get all three projects, instead of one. And at a much higher cost to the Guatemalan Government. 

There is involved here a fundamental foreign policy question as to whether or not Eximbank is to be permitted to continue its "banking as usual" or "bonds as usual" or "business as usual" policy in Latin America while the Alliance for Progress enunciates the doctrine of self-help. Is it in the best interests of the 

United States to permit the left hand to undo what the right hand is attempting? 

I believe this fundamental question goes to the very heart and core of the Alliance and that the AID Agency, carrying the top responsibility for the administration of this crucial policy, must effect a coordination in all branches of the executive arm of our Government, which will be consistent with the announced policy of 

President Kennedy to give priority to Latin America.

The objections of Eximbank to relaxation of its policy on the grounds of precedent have no validity. The success of the Alliance for Progress should take priority over a banking practice whose very philosophy has contributed to the deplorable state of Latin American relations which the Alliance seeks to correct and improve.

I urge that this matter of performance bond, insofar as it applies to Latin American qualified companies, be carefully reviewed by your Agency. It is unrealistic, inequitable, discriminatory, and works against the Alliance. It is a continuation of what the Alliance stands against-American business monopoly. 

If Eximbank's harsh policy is to be permitted to continue unchecked or revised, there must be devised some mechanism in your Agency that will assist qualified Latin American companies in meeting bond requirements for U.S.-financed projects. Perhaps a "performance bond program" in your Agency for qualified 

Latin Americans to be administered by the same section which deals with investment guarantees available to qualified American citizens. 

For your information, the National Filter Co., 147 West 22d Street, New York

City, has encountered similar difficulty from Eximbank, although in another context. I have asked offiicals of that company, which does a $5 million annual export business to Latin America, to write you directly on their difficulties which run counter to the Alliance for Progress. 

It is important to comprehend the reactions of Latin Americans to U.S. requirements or devices which they consider as against their own people and favoring Americans. This is not their concept of the “Alianza Para el Progress.' 

It is not President Kennedy's concept, as declared by him. Because it is not 

AID's concept, either, I have taken this matter up with you directly. 

In conclusion, I would like to indicate my own lawyer-client responsibility in this matter as well as my foreign policy interest. I do represent CONAC, the 

Guatemalan consortium of two Guatemalan companies, which was awarded the contract on project CA-8-49. CONAC has been unable to secure the requisite 

100-percent bond. The attached memorandum indicates the history of these fruitless efforts. CONAC was granted an extension until today by the President of Guatemala, to secure a bond. This CONAC has been unable to do. It will, therefore, lose its contract unless some joint venture arrangement is made with an American construction firm in return for its cosignature sufficient to obtain a U.S. bond. My relationship to CONAC on this matter is about to come to a close. But the policy of Eximbank lingers on. And this, I feel, is against the 

Alliance for Progress, a program in which I deeply believe. It is because I believe in it and you believe in it, that it must not be scuttled. 

Sincerely yours,

SHELDON Z. KAPLAN.

2 The illustration which I have given via the correspondence and material included in this statement on three highway projects in Guatemala involves only one small country in Central America, but the inability of the United States to act quickly and without redtape technical entanglements is not limited to that country alone. This inability is symptomatic of the lack of sense of urgency and emergency on the part of the executive agencies and departments of our Government dealing with Latin America. Bearing in mind that the Alliance for 

Progress is at least 10 years late, this inability may well wreck the whole program. At this late hour, it is sheer folly to attempt to superimpose on undeveloped social, economic, and political systems the sophisticated, mature, and experienced U.S. banking and financial mechanisms. If such mechanisms existed in Latin America, there would be little need for an Alliance for Progress. 

In conclusion, I recognize that my statement has not been directly responsive to the draft legislation before you. However, because of the leadership which this committee has traditionally taken in Latin American affairs, I have felt it my duty to express these views before you with the hope that through you, perhaps in the committee report, there will be infused into the executive branch a fuller and more realistic understanding of the meaning of the Alliance for Progress and its implications for the future of our hemisphere.

WEDNESDAY, APRIL 11, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

The committee meets this morning in open session on amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

Our first witnesses this morning are John O. Teeter, vice president of Pfizer International Corp., representing the Chamber of Commerce of the United States, and J. Warren Nystrom, manager, International Relations Department, Chamber of Commerce. 

Mr. Teeter, you have a prepared statement. You may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF JOHN O. TEETER, VICE PRESIDENT, PFIZER INTER- NATIONAL, INC., REPRESENTING THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES 

Mr. TEETER. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. My name is 

John O. Teeter. I am Vice President of Pfizer International, Inc., New York City.

I appear here today on behalf of the Chamber of Commerce of the United States to present its views on the subject of foreign aid. I am a member of the chamber's foreign policy committee, and a member of its foreign aid subcommittee. 

The national chamber supports the principle of foreign aid as an instrument of U.S. foreign policy dedicated to the purposes of— 

1. Security for the United States and the other nations of the free world through assistance to their military establishments. 

2. Development of the economic resources and living standards of the peoples of the free world through cooperation and selfhelp. 

3. Encouragement of responsible political freedom and stability. 

4. Fulfillment of the traditional humanitarian aspirations of our people.

On February 24, 1962, the chamber's board of directors reaffirmed this support of foreign aid in principle and spelled out in detail recommendations for improving the program. 899

We recognize that U.S. economic and military assistance to the less developed areas is still urgently required. The reasons for this are many growing population pressures on poorly developed resource bases, the so-called revolution of rising expectations taking place in these areas, the ferment created by highly nationalistic pressures for economic progress and political independence, and, of course, the continuing drive of the Communist bloc to exploit these conditions for its own purposes.

This support in principle does not mean that the chamber endorses every aspect of a particular program or every requested level of spending. We do not believe that more money will necessarily provide a more effective program. Basic improvements in the operation of our foreign aid activities are still needed. 

It is in this context that we present our recommendations on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. Although some of our remarks are directed more to the administration of the program than to legislation, we urge the Congress to take all appropriate steps to achieve the objectives outlined below. 

1. The organization, operation, and evaluation of the foreign aid program should be strengthened: Improved coordination among the various agencies engaged in economic assistance was provided for under the terms of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. Nevertheless, recent developments have shown that it is essential for the administrators to strive continually to eliminate waste of resources and duplication of effort.

It is particularly important in this regard that the Department of State exercise effective and consistent policy direction both in Washington and through the American Ambassador in each country abroad. 

Another key factor in the success of the program is the ability of the Agency for International Development to recruit and retain topflight personnel. Personnel policies and practices should emphasize practical competence and experience as well as language and diplomatic skills.

We applaud the steps taken by the Administrator of AID to weed out unnecessary and unsuitable employees, and we will continue to urge American industry to cooperate wholeheartedly with the Agency in its efforts to develop a competent management team. 

One of the fundamental goals of the foreign aid program is to eliminate the conditions which make such a program necessary. Because this is a long-range objective, long-range programs, tailored to meet the requirements of each recipient country, are essential for its success.

Accordingly, we support the authorization of funds for development loans, as well as for loans under the Alliance for Progress, for periods in excess of 1 year.

The need remains, however, for careful periodic scrutiny and reassessment of operations underway or in the formative stage. Congress should continue to oversee and control the size and direction of the foreign aid program through its investigations, hearings, and annual appropriations.

The present system of multiyear authorizations with annual appropriations seems to meet adequately the dual requirements of effective

long-range planning and continuous congressional control of loan operations.

There should be constant and increasing emphasis upon enlisting the cooperation of other industrialized countries in assisting the less developed areas. The national chamber strongly supports U.S. participation in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and in the work of its Development Assistance Committee, which offers promise in this direction. 

2. The administration's total request of $4,878,500,000 should be reduced by $1,088,100,000 to $3,790,400,000: In reaching this recommendation, chamber committees, the board of directors, and staff have reviewed the past performance of our foreign aid operations, and have examined carefully the limited data made available to the public on the program for the coming fiscal year. 

These are some of the major considerations which the chamber took into account in reaching this recommendation: 

The U.S. balance-of-payments problem is becoming increasingly serious as the cumulative deficit continues to mount. 

A number of the less developed countries have been either unwilling or unable to initiate the internal changes which must be effected if our economic and military aid is not to be wasted. 

In many other less developed countries, where there is an expressed desire to cooperate with the United States on the basis of the selfhelp criteria written into the Foreign Assistance Act last year, planning and study have not gone forward to the point where large amounts of U.S. assistance can be justified. 

The United States, through such programs as Public Law 480, and other industrialized countries and international lending organizations continue to make large sums available to the less developed areas in a variety of ways which supplement the U.S. foreign aid program. 

Finally, congressional investigators and other observers of foreign aid operations continue to uncover evidence indicating that there is considerable room for the elimination of waste of resources and effort in the program. 

For these general reasons, we believe that the administration's requests for fiscal year 1963 are unrealistically high and could safely be reduced.

The chamber makes the following specific recommendations concerning the major classifications of the program: 

Military assistance: The appropriation request for $1,500 million should be reduced by $150 million to $1,350 million. 

Because of the threat of Communist aggression, there is continued need for military assistance to such areas as southeast Asia, where the Communists are vigorously prosecuting so-called wars of liberation.

Since the end of World War II, however, over $15 billion-or about one-half of all U.S. military assistance-has gone to Western 

European countries. While the amount of this aid has steadily diminished, administration figures show that, for fiscal 1962, over onefifth of the total will go to Europe, and for the coming fiscal year $314 million, or about 18 percent of the total. 81496-62-pt. 5–

In addition to this direct assistance to NATO and the European military establishments, the United States continues to maintain substantial ground forces in Europe, supported by widely dispersed air and naval striking units which could be quickly deployed in the 

European theater if needed.

According to the budget for fiscal 1963, the emphasis of our military aid in the developed areas will be on newer weapons which are not yet fully within the production or financial capability of our allies. 

We are well aware that this type of assistance was urgently needed during the first decade after World War II. However, there no longer appears to be justification for aid on the scale proposed for the coming fiscal year.

Since 1954, estimated gold reserves and dollar holdings of the Common Market countries and the United Kingdom-the largest European recipients of our military assistance have increased by over $11 billion. During the same period, U.S. Treasury holdings of gold have declined by almost $5 billion, and our balance-of-payments position continues to be discouraging. 

We therefore urge that the administration intensify its efforts to persuade our principal NATO allies to assume a larger share of the cost of Western defense efforts, and to accelerate the reduction of our military assistance to these countries. 

We endorse the views expressed on this matter by Under Secretary of State George W. Ball, who told the West German Foreign Affairs 

Society in Bonn on April 2 thatwe are not wholly persuaded that Europe, growing continually stronger and more unified, has yet fully assumed that share of the burden that its growing strength warrants. 

Development loans: The appropriation request for $1,250 million should be reduced by $350 million to $900 million.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Teeter, will you continue?

Mr. TEETER. Returning to development loans, we support the shift in emphasis taking place in the aid program from grants to long-term development loans. Furthermore, we support the stiffening of the criteria under which loans are made to the less developed countries. 

If these loans are to be effective in the long-range development of the less developed countries, they must be granted only on the basis of sound planning and fully justified programs and projects. This will involve lengthy study and negotiation by the administrators of our aid program and representatives of the recipient countries. 

Evidence available at the present, however, indicates that this process has gone forward in only a limited number of countries. Consequently, we recommend a reduction in the proposed loan program until the United States can be reasonably assured that loan funds will be utilized with maximum effectiveness on the basis of sound planning. 

Development grants and supporting assistance: The appropriation request for a total of $816,500,000 should be reduced by $181,500,000 to a total of $635 million. Reductions in each category should be approximately $90 million. 

For the past several years, funds appropriated for these purposes (formerly designated defense support, technical and special assistance) have been reduced gradually as development loans and other programs have increased. 

During the present fiscal year, several countries have been removed from the list of those eligible to receive U.S. grant aid and supporting assistance.

Loans should replace grant assistance in more countries in the near future as the cumulative assistance of the United States and other developed countries and international organizations begins to take effect. 

We support the trend toward substitution of loans for grants, eliminating the latter wherever possible.

The Alliance for Progress: The appropriation request for $600 million should be reduced by $200 million to $400 million. 

This recommended reduction does not imply lack of support by the national chamber for the Alliance for Progress. On the contrary, we believe that the Alliance could prove to be an outstanding contribution to the development of regional cooperation among free nations.

Yet, there is little evidence that the amount of funds which the administration is requesting for fiscal 1963 could be effectively utilized under the terms set forth in the Charter of Punta del Este. According to data released in March by the Agency for International Development and the Inter-American Development Bank, only three countries in Latin America have completed long-range plans for economic and social development. Eight Latin American countries have not begun comprehensive planning. 

Data presented by AID indicate that economic assistance for the Alliance for fiscal year 1961 was $258 million, and the estimated total for the current year is expected to be $410 million. We recommend that appropriations for the coming year be held to $400 million. 

Contingency fund: The appropriation request for $400 million should be reduced by $200 million to $200 million. 

The chamber recognizes the need for such a fund, and is aware that in the past it has been useful in coping with crises brought on by natural disasters and unforeseen political events. It is our view that appropriations for this purpose constitute in essence a "blank check" over which there is no adequate fiscal control. $200 million should be an adequate amount for this purpose, especially in light of those provisions of the Foreign Assistance Act which permit considerable flexibility in shifting the allocation of foreign aid funds. 

Surveys of investment opportunities: The appropriation request for $5 million should be reduced by $1,500,000 to $3,500,000. 

Funds utilized for this purpose hold great potential for the promotion of both domestic and foreign investment in the less developed countries. We strongly support this program in principle. Since little or none of the amount appropriated for the current fiscal year has been expended, we recommend an appropriation of $3.5 million as adequate for fiscal 1963. 

Administrative expenses-State Department and AID: The appro priation request for $58,100,000 should be reduced by $5,100,000 to $53 million.

The recent integration of foreign aid activities should result in administrative savings. In light of this integration, the requested increase of over 15 percent appears unreasonable, and we urge that more strenuous efforts be made to reduce the costs of this part of the program. Our recommendation would allow an increase over the current fiscal year of about 5 percent, which should adequately cover administrative costs of expanded aid activities. 

Contributions to international organizations and investment guarantees: We have no recommendation for a reduction in these two categories. 

3. A concerted effort should be made to strengthen the role of private enterprise in the development of the less developed countries. 

Section 102 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 states in part: 

It is the policy of the United States to strengthen friendly foreign countries by encouraging the development of their free economic institutions and productive capabilities, and by minimizing or eliminating barriers to the flow of private investment capital. 

And section 601 of the same legislation begins: 

The Congress of the United States recognizes the vital role of free enterprise in achieving rising levels of production and standards of living essential to economic progress and development.

Confining ourselves to the development program in Latin America, we find a similar profession of faith in free enterprise on the part of the countries receiving our assistance. One paragraph of the "Declaration to the Peoples of America," issued at the conclusion of the conference of Punta del Este last August, reads: [The American Republics agree] to stimulate private enterprise in order to encourage the development of Latin American countries at a rate which will help them to provide jobs for the growing populations, to eliminate unemployment, and to take their place among the modern industrialized nations of the world. 

The role of private enterprise in the development process can hardly be overemphasized. Under the Alliance for Progress, for example, it is anticipated that at least 80 percent of the total resources devoted to development over the next decade will be indigenous, and of this the great bulk will have to come from the private sector. 

Nevertheless, the prospects for meeting this goal are not encouraging. It has been estimated that as much as $10 billion of private 

Latin American capital has fled the area for a safer environment during the past 10 years. Ironically, this is very close to the same amount which the United States has pledged to provide the Alliance in public funds over the next 10 years. It is obvious that if potential 

Latin American investors themselves have so little confidence in the future of their countries, the great sums of private foreign capital which are urgently needed will not be forthcoming. 

A central issue to be faced in this situation is the necessity to create a favorable investment climate. In the limited time available to use to discuss this complex problem, we shall touch on two broad areas: self-help efforts by the recipient countries and unilateral U.S. programs. Our discussion will be confined to the Latin American area, although the questions which we raise are, in most cases, applicable to our entire foreign assistance effort. 

Self-help efforts in the less developed areas: The Charter of Punta del Este establishing the Alliance for Progress sets forth a number of self-help measures which the Latin American countries have agreed to institute as their part of the hemispheric development program. Many of these have a bearing on the creation of a better environment for the operation of the free enterprise system. They include expanded educational programs, reforms of fiscal and agrarian policies, and regional economic integration. These measures, if carried out faithfully, effectively, and in a manner appropriate to each country, will do much to stimulate economic progress. 

One of the most important measures which received specific mention by the signers of the Alliance for Progress is monetary stabilization-the curbing of inflation. This has a direct bearing on the development process. Recent studies have shown that there is a high degree of inverse correlation between inflation and the rate of economic growth: the higher the rate of inflation, the lower the rate of real growth of gross national product. One study by a leading 

New York bank concluded:

On the basis of data for 12 Latin American countries for the years 1950-58 it would appear that, for countries with a rate of inflation above 5 or 6 percent a year, growth rates tend to fall substantially with further increases in the rate of inflation.

The administrators of our aid program should hold firmly to clearly defined criteria which will insure that each nation receiving our assistance will make every effort to help itself. 

Unilateral U.S. programs: U.S. programs designed to stimulate private enterprise in the less developed countries include: 

The investment guarantee program. 

Surveys of investment opportunities. 

Information programs of the State and Commerce Departments. 

The promotion of treaties of friendship, commerce, and navigation, which include clauses relating to the protection of U.S. interests abroad.

Assistance to private enterprise abroad through AID's Office of 

Development Financing and Private Enterprise. 

Assistance to U.S. foreign investors through the Department of 

Commerce's Office of International Investment.

There is need for improvement in many of these programs. For example:

Foreign aid legislation since 1954 has included provisions calling for accelerating the program of negotiating commercial treaties. Ten such treaties have been negotiated with Latin American countries. 

Five of these were ratified before 1860, but contain no reference to the protection of foreign investment. One was signed in 1927, and three more have been signed since 1945 but have not been ratified. 

We have only one treaty of friendship, commerce, and navigation in force in Latin America which adequately reflects postwar conditions. 

The investment guarantee program has proved a useful instrument for encouraging U.S. investment abroad. In recent months there has been a substantial increase in demand for guarantees, particularly to cover losses incurred due to expropriation or confiscation of assets by foreign governments. However, such coverage can be extended only after an agreement between the United States and the foreign government involved.

At the end of 1961 only 12 Latin American countries were listed as eligible for guaranteed U.S. investments, with ratification pending in 3 others. Significantly absent from this list were two of the most important countries in the area, Brazil and Mexico. In two other key countries-Argentina and Chile-risk of expropriation was not covered. Applications for guarantees in Latin America in process at the end of the year totaled over $800 million, but guarantees in force came to less than $50 million, mostly in the smaller countries. 

Thus, while these various U.S. programs hold out great potential for the encouragement of private enterprise in our development assistance efforts, the Congress should insist that they be more adequately implemented.

In summary, the national chamber recommends that foreign aid appropriations for fiscal year 1963 not exceed $3,790,400,000. We urge that the organization and operation of the aid program be strengthened, and that increasing effort be made to persuade both the industrialized and the recipient countries to do their part. We recommend that maximum consideration be given the need to expand the role of private interest in the aid campaign.

Finally, we support the foreign aid program as a vital instrument of U.S. foreign policy and recommend that it be continued within the limitations outlined in this statement.

TESTIMONY OF WALTER A. SLOWINSKI FOR THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES ON H.R. 10650 

I am Walter A Slowinski, of the law firm of Baker, McKenzie & Hightower, of Chicago, Ill., and Washington, D.C., appearing on behalf of the Chamber of 

Commerce of the United States. I am an adjunct professor of comparative tax law at the Georgetown Graduate Law School in Washington, D.C., and a lecturer in domestic and foreign tax law at the University of Virginia Law School in Charlottesville.

The chamber's board of directors and committee on taxation have met regularly during the current year on the changing tax proposals to be certain all points of view have been given an opportunity for full expression. The chamber's position on major sections of H.R. 10650 is as follows: 

SECTION 2. THE INVESTMENT INCENTIVE CREDIT PROPOSED SHOULD BE REPLACED BY MORE REALISTIC DEPRECIATION ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS 

The chamber recommends against the adoption of a novel and untried preferential tax credit subsidy for business. It is also unnecessarily complex and it will be difficult to administer such new concepts in our code as "section 38 property," "qualified investments," "carryover adjustments," and "unused credit years."

The opposition by the chamber to the tax credit is not influenced in any manner by the other proposals contained in H.R. 10650. If all other sections were stripped from this bill, the position of the chamber in opposition to the tax credit as a subsidy would remain.

The investment incentive credit has no place in an income tax law. Its rate and tenure are uncertain in the light of the last-minute downward changes which occurred during the last few days of March in the Ways and Means Committee. 

The credit gives preferential tax treatment to certain taxpayers in favored groups. It may actually be a windfall to a business which had already fortuitously planned to purchase new facilities later in 1962. On the other hand, it will work against small businesses or loss companies which have no current funds for expansion or no taxable income to be offset by the credit.

More importantly, the adoption of the credit at a revenue loss of at least $1.175 billion may prejudice or delay meaningful depreciation reform promised by the Secretary of the Treasury this spring. Even as little as a 10-percent improvement in depreciation rates will mean approximately $3 billion in additional depreciation deductions. It is questionable whether this added $1.5 billion loss in revenues can be supported by the economy in the light of the $1.175 billion loss on the investment credit.

As an alternative to the investment credit, the chamber strongly endorses a basic revision upward of depreciation rates and a simplified classification of depreciable facilities. An initial investment allowance may also be desirable. 

Many countries provide such initial allowance to measure reasonably the cost of first-year obsolescence. This type of initial allowance has already been adopted in our Internal Revenue Code on a small scale in the 20-percent firstyear depreciation allowance for small business in section 179 of the code, but it is limited to $10,000. The chamber recommends that Congress now remove the $10,000 limitation in section 179 to provide the stimulus and incentive the President is seeking. 

SECTION 3. DEDUCTIONS FOR LEGISLATIVE ACTIVITY SHOULD BE IMPROVED 

The chamber believes that section 3, as presently contained in H.R. 10650, is neither an adequate nor a proper solution to the problem of legislative activity deductions. In lieu of section 3 of H.R. 10650, it recommends the substitution of S. 467 introduced by Senator Hartke. A similar bill was reported favorably and unanimously by the Ways and Means Committee of the 86th Congress. 

The chamber proposes a general legislative rule which would state that- No expense which otherwise qualifies as a deduction relating to trade or business expenses (including, but not limited to, dues and other amounts paid to any organization) shall be disallowed as a deduction merely because paid or incurred to support or oppose or otherwise influence action by the Congress by any legislative body of a State, a possession of the United States, the District of Columbia, or any political subdivision of the foregoing, with respect to any legislative or constitutional proposal, or to support or oppose or otherwise influence action of the voters with respect to any legislative or constitutional proposal submitted or proposed to be submitted to the voters by initiative, referendum or similar proceeding. 

The general rule would not be construed as allowing the deduction of any amount paid or incurred (whether by way of contribution, gift, or otherwise) for participation or intervention in any political campaign on behalf of, or in opposition to, any candiate for public office. 

SECTION 4. ENTERTAINMENT EXPENSE PROBLEMS CAN BE HANDLED BY VIGOROUS ENFORCEMENT OF EXISTING LAWS 

The complications of section 4 will make it almost impossible for the average businessman to determine and substantiate his right to a deduction for legitimate business expenses.

There should be no objection by taxpayers to a requirement that business expenses be substantiated so long as such requirement is reasonable. However, most of the new rules in H.R. 10650 are too complicated for the average taxpayer and could create disrespect for an unreasonable tax law as well as an undermining of our self-assessment system of taxation. 

Vigorous enforcement of existing provisions will accomplish the objective and avoid penalizing all business taxpayers for the abuses of a relative few. 

On a related problem, the expense incurred with respect to a facility used for business entertainment purposes, such as a car, should be allowed to the extent that it is so used and can be substantiated as a proper business deduction. If the usage is less than 50 percent, for instance 20 percent, then such portion should be allowed. 

SECTION 8. MUTUAL SAVINGS BANKS, SAVINGS AND LOAN ASSOCIATIONS, AND COMMERCIAL BANKS SHOULD BE TAXED EQUITABLY 

The chamber supports measures which would provide that commercial banks, mutual savings banks, and savings and loan associations be subjected to the Federal corporate income tax in such fashion as to contribute to capital and reserve adequacy and to insure competitive equality to the extent that the Federal tax is a competitive factor.

SECTION 11. "GROSSING UP" SHOULD NOT BE ADOPTED 

The adoption of section 11 of H.R. 10650 involving the so-called grossing up rule would overturn principles of some 43 years' standing, upset long-established relations in our tax treaties, and penalize foreign trade particularly in the less developed areas. Here again the wisdom of changing long-established rules to gain a temporary economic objective should be carefully considered. 

SECTION 12. SECTION 911 INVOLVING EARNED INCOME FROM WITHOUT THE UNITED 

STATES SHOULD NOT BE CHANGED

Factual statements will be submitted to this committee by American chambers of commerce in foreign countries defending the present earned income exclusion of U.S. citizens working abroad. With your permission, we should like these incorporated into the record of the hearings since some of these groups did not receive word of these hearings in time to apply for scheduling on the witness list. 

SECTION 13. THE FOREIGN INCOME PROVISIONS OF SECTION 13 SHOULD BE ELIMINATED 

Although the chamber is as interested as the Congress in removing any possibilities for tax avoidance in foreign operations by U.S. companies or shareholders, it is clear the new provisions of section 13 are designed principally to discourage any further U.S. investment abroad even in less developed countries. 

To the extent the Treasury Department is interested in abolishing tax havens, it can do so through the new provisions of section 482 (b) in section 6 of the bill, coupled with the presently effective provisions of section 482 covering allocation of income between related organizations. 

The new section 13 will remove the possibilities for U.S. corporations competing in full and fair competition with foreign corporations on foreign soil. However, the President has specifically stated that he does not want to "penalize legitimate private investment abroad, which will strengthen our trade and currency in future years."

Regardless of the constitutionality or unconstitutionality of this proposed law-and the courts have challenged the constitutionality of taxing income which has not yet been received-such penal measures as contained in section 13 cannot but succeed in changing our Nation's attitude toward private investment in developed and less developed areas of the world. 

Foreign competitors will continue to employ multicorporate weapons in their war against U.S. private enterprise to drive U.S. corporations from the markets of the world in which we should have a fair share. Tying both hands behind the backs of U.S. corporations will not help the U.S. trade and currency in future years as the President suggests. U.S. private investment asks for neutrality, including the opportunity to compete with foreign corporations on foreign soil under the same rules of foreign trade and taxation. To set up artificial geographical rules as in H.R. 10650 is to restrict U.S. companies without limiting their foreign competitors who are in direct competition worldwide. 

As an example, if a Brazilian subsidiary of a U.S. corporation purchases property manufactured in Argentina by a related company and sells it to anyone for use, consumption, or disposition in Chile, the entire income is "foreign base company income" in the United States. This ignores the realities of the 

Latin American free trade area and yet permits foreign competitors to take over this international business. 

Another example involves technology in less developed areas. If a Brazilian subsidiary of a U.S. corporation uses an exclusive formula to make a product, even though it purchased that formula outright in an arm's-length transaction from a U.S. corporation at fair market value and U.S. tax was paid on the gain, any future income from the use of that formula in Brazil will be "subpart Fincome" in the United States because the formula was developed or created in the United States.

It is not enough to say that the U.S. tax can be postponed in some cases if the earnings are reinvested in less developed areas. The limitations on these provisions are totally unrealistic and are designed to make reinvestment even in less developed areas almost impossible. They are further designed to encourage less developed countries to pass laws limiting the percentage of ownership by U.S. interests contrary to the objectives of the Alliance for Progress.

SECTION 16. GAINS FROM SALES OR EXCHANGES OF STOCK IN FOREIGN CORPORATIONS SHOULD CONTINUE TO BE TREATED AS CAPITAL GAINS 

Section 16 of the bill would have a U.S. taxpayer go all the way back to 

February 28, 1913, and include proportionately as dividend income so much of the gain on a sale or exchange of foreign corporation stock as had been earned by that foreign company since February 28, 1913. 

Such a penalty provision is not necessary to achieve the objectives of this bill. It would be especially confiscatory in our Latin American areas where 

U.S. subsidiaries have reinvested these earnings in additional productive facilities in the less developed economies now a part of the Alliance for Progress. 

If such a provision is to be enacted by the Congress-and we recommend against it-it should be prospective only and apply to earnings after December 

31, 1962.

The effective date of the new liquidation provision according to H.R. 10650 is to be the effective date of this 1962 Revenue Act, thereby confiscating a part of these earnings and denying to U.S. businesses the opportunity of readjusting their operations and liquidating these foreign investments under the terms of the present law upon which reliance has been placed for more than 43 years. 

SECTION 17. COOPERATIVE TAX TREATMENT SHOULD BE REVISED 

The chamber has consistently held as a policy declaration that no form of lawful enterprise should be favored over any other form and each, whether corporate, cooperative, or individual should stand on its own merits with protection from unfair competition, but without benefit of tax exemptions or special exemption from legislative restraints, and without any other Government subsidies.

SECTION 19. WITHHOLDING 

The chamber is not unmindful of the loss of Government revenue involved in the recommendations presented to the committee in this statement. It is also mindful of the loss of revenue annually from unreported interest, dividends, and patronage dividends.

To see that each taxpayer pays his fair share of the burden is our objective. 

We therefore support the principle of withholding on interest, dividends, and patronage dividends at source.

In appraising these provisions of the bill, the committee will wish to evaluate such matters as the administrative complexities of a nonreceipts withholding tax system; the cost of administration to the Revenue Service, to taxpayers, and to paying agents; the problems of overwithholding of tax; the changes which must be made in the individual income tax return (form 1040), and whether now or in the near future the Service's automatic data processing installations, plus the use of taxpayer account numbers, can be a substitute for the withholding of tax. 

SECTION 21. EXISTING TAX TREATIES SHOULD NOT BE OVERRIDDEN 

American and foreign businessmen and Government officials were shocked and disturbed by the Ways and Means Committee's press release of February 23, 1962, which stated in part as follows: "The committee adopted a provision to the effect that in the event of conflict between a provision of the bill and a treaty, the treaty is overridden" (now sec. 21 of H.R. 10650). 

Europeans are seriously concerned with this type of unilateral abandonment and wonder whether this will be a precedent to be followed in trade agreements in future years. 

European competitors of American trading companies are now confident that the new U.S. tax bill will eliminate competition from U.S. companies regardless of the more favorable terms of any new trade agreements. To this extent, certain foreign income provisions of H.R. 10650 and the trade agreement provisions of H.R. 9900 run in direct contradiction to each other and destroy for 

U.S. businessmen the possibilities of full and fair competition with foreign corporations.

Chairman MORGAN. Our next witness is Mr. Richard C. Shipman, assistant director, Legislative Services Division, National Farmers Union. 

STATEMENT OF RICHARD C. SHIPMAN, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR, LEGISLATIVE SERVICES DIVISION, NATIONAL FARMERS UNION 

Mr. SHIPMAN. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, my name is Richard Shipman and I appear here as a representative of Mr. James G. Patton, president of the National Farmers Union, and the 250,000 farm families who are members of our organization. 

The National Farmers Union is and has been for many years deeply committed to the monumental tasks of helping to build a world of peace and plenty. We have been active supporters or participators in all foreign aid programs of the past two decades. We are here today to urge the committee to act favorably on the President's requests for the resources to carry forward a new "decade of development." 

However, we wish first to express our appreciation to this committee for the careful constructive role it has played throughout the years in the creation of U.S. foreign aid programs. All of them have been helpful, and some have been brilliant successes. One need only to look at the thriving economy of Europe to know the Marshall plan and other aid programs succeeded. 

Only a year ago you gave the "go" sign to a new program with requirements of social and economic reform as prerequisites to aid. 

As I listened to the testimony of AID Administrator Fowler Hamilton, before the committee, I got the distinct impression you intended to see that these reforms are carried out. 

National Farmers Union shares your concern that we promote the kind of practical down-to-earth programs which really reach down to the great majority of the people who suffer in poverty, hunger, disease, and ignorance for lack of opportunity and the know-how to do otherwise.

A large percentage of these people in the developing parts of the world make their meager living from more or less primitive agriculture. Their productivity by modern American standards is desperately low.

Although we have not solved all the problems of agriculture in the United States, we have solved the problem of production and we can help others do likewise. 

It is a well-known fact that the most important limiting factor to expanding agricultural production in the less developed countries is not only a lack of know-how of the farm people, but lack of both

$public and private institutions and programs to develop these capabilities. 

It is because of this fact that we have supported and participated in programs of technical assistance to agriculture and we urge the committee to approve new authorizations of $335 million for development grants, by means of which such significant programs can be expanded. 

We are extremely pleased that the administration is placing new emphasis upon these programs of technical assistance and cooperation which are a key part of the necessary social development to reach overall development goals. But we also believe they have residual values of friendship, good will, and faith in democracy which it is difficult to inspire in any other way. 

We in Farmers Union are not experts in all the areas in which the Agency for International Development operates, but there are some aspects of this program with which we have had long experience. 

We, as farmers, know what it means when we talk about land reform, land development, and credit requirements for family farms. 

Many of our families are only a generation removed from our own American frontier. We know what it takes and how hard it is to develop the social and economic institutions that go into making farm people secure and prosperous on family farms. 

We also know of the satisfaction of owning your own land. So we appreciate the "land hunger" of the peasants of many countries and the explosive revolutionary forces which exist when that hunger goes unsatisfied.

We compliment the administration for recognizing the important role of cooperatives. Through 60 years of Farmers Union experience in building and experimenting with cooperatives, we know how much education and organization it takes to establish them. 

We are, therefore, only too well aware that this is a long-range program, that it will take patience and perseverance. This is a program not only for the sixties but for the seventies and beyond. We can give these developing peoples the benefit of our experience and our knowhow, but we must not expect it to come about quickly or easily. 

The old ways die hard. Entrenched wealth and power and selfishness give way slowly and sometimes not at all peacefully. So it is a calculated risk with which we deal. 

There will undoubtedly be some failures, but also there will be gratifying successes. But what matters is that we have begun to shape the free democratic institutions which are tomorrow's alternatives to the hunger and despair which grips two-thirds of mankind today. 

But, Mr. Chairman, we raise this question: Should the United 

States carry these burdens alone? The Farmers Union urges that as much as possible we should encourage other nations to share the responsibility of helping the less developed and newly emerging nations into the 20th century.

At the most recent convention of National Farmers Union in March 1962, the delegates expressed themselves on this subject as follows: 

Long-term legislation should be enacted directing the use of the tremendous economic strength of the United States in cooperation with free nations, toward promoting the economic development of less fortunate nations of the world to the fullest possible extent through the United Nations, and the specialized agencies. and through private nonprofit foreign relief groups. Such programs of as-

sistance should be kept entirely separate from necessary military devices of foreign policy.

As one specific project along these lines, we urge the committee's attention to the creation of an international food reserve or food bank administered by the United Nations and Food and Agriculture Organization where surplus food could be loaned in terms of each country's ability to contribute, and made available both as food directly and as capital to other countries of the world according to their need. 

Mr. Chairman, may we say in closing, we support the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. First, because it is the only thing consistent with our principles of human dignity and worth, but also because we cannot as a nation hope to maintain an island of plenty in a sea of poverty. 

Unless we are instrumental in raising the levels of living of these tortured, hungry people of the world, then a system with more emphasis on food and less on freedom will do it for them. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Shipman.

Mr. Shipman, when was this resolution adopted? Was it adopted 

March of this year?

Mr. SHIPMAN. Yes; a few weeks ago. 

Chairman MORGAN. This meeting of your delegates to which you refer, were they delegates from all over the country? 

Mr. SHIPMAN. Yes. Our delegates come from every State that is chartered on the basis of the number of-it is completely democraticon the basis of the number of members in each State. So that it represents the opinion of the whole organization. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Shipman, I was interested in your comment on the creation of an international food reserve. 

Is this something that originated in your organization?

Mr. SHIPMAN. We have advocated this for a long time. Of course, as you know, in Rome this past year such an organization was set up but it needs the cooperation of the United States to really grow into something that will really amount to something. 

Chairman MORGAN. Did this come out of the FAO?

Mr. SHIPMAN. Yes; it came out of the meeting in Rome and it is to be administered by the FAO and the United Nations.
