STATEMENT OF MRS. WILLIAM H. WOOD, SECRETARY, LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF THE UNITED STATES 

Mrs. Wood. I am Mrs. William H. Wood of Bladensburg, Md., and I am secretary of the League of Women Voters of the United States.

We do have a short statement that we would like to present to your committee.

The League of Women Voters of the United States reaffirms our strong support for a new approach to foreign economic assistance. expressed last year to this committee. Our members have given much thought and study during the last 6 years to foreign policy in general and to foreign aid in particular. They were gratified when Congress passed the 1961 legislation which called for reorientation and reorganization of the foreign aid program.

We would also like to restate what we said to this committee last year: 

At this time when the revolution of rising expectations is in full swing throughout the world, we must strengthen our efforts to aid other countries in their struggle to aid themselves. This is no time to retreat, or even to hold the line. It is the time to go forward, to try new techniques, to use all our ingenuity to make these programs succeed. The We believe this statement is as applicable today as it was then. legislation, in our judgment, will implement the design of the decade of development in its present stage. 

Women in local leagues all over the country have agreed that the following ingredients are basic to an effective foreign aid program: 

A long-range program, so essential to efficient administration and planning. 

Unification and coordination of foreign aid administration, both in Washington and in the field. 

Longer term and more adequate financing, with special emphasis on development loans repayable in dollars. 

Encouragement of increased participation by and coordination with other developed countries in economic development programs. 

Emphasis on programs of maximum self-help, with the developing countries committing their resources to the fullest degree practicable, organizing comprehensive development plans to the best of their ability, making necessary fiscal reforms and emphasizing social progress, especially in education. 

In applying these league yardsticks to the 1962 legislation as well as to the 5-month-old Agency for International Development, it is our conviction that both the proposed legislation and the moves made in the administration of the program are in the right direction. We believe that the substantive changes called for and the amounts requested for economic aid under the 1962 act will serve to strengthen the new program. 

The major provision in the proposed 1962 act is, of course, the request for a 4-year authorization of a $3 billion Alliance for Progress fund. This the league recognizes as the logical development of the promise to administer foreign aid on a basis which is long range, coordinated, and adequately financed-with emphasis on maximum self-help and country-by-country planning. 

The pattern established through the Alliance may well serve as a guide toward what can be done with and for other parts of the world. 

Priorities for aid to Latin America, to promote growth and social progress, we believe are essential now. We urge this committee to approve the proposed long-term authorization for the Alliance. 

We want to thank this committee for the hard work and careful consideration that it gives to foreign aid legislation every year. We welcome an occasion to express the support of league membership for this country's long-term efforts in assisting the developing countries in their struggle for economic and social development.

THURSDAY, APRIL 12, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

10:43 a.m., Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding. 

The committee meets this morning in open session to consider amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

The first witness this morning is the Honorable Andrew J. Biemiller, director of department of legislation, American Federation of 

Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations. 

Mr. Biemiller, you have a prepared statement. You may proceed, sir. Again, Mr. Biemiller, I want to welcome you as a former Member of Congress to this committee. We always are honored and privileged to have you here, sir. 

STATEMENT OF HON. ANDREW J. BIEMILLER, DIRECTOR, DEPART- MENT OF LEGISLATION, AMERICAN FEDERATION OF LABOR AND CONGRESS OF INDUSTRIAL ORGANIZATIONS 

Mr. BIEMILLER.  

For the record my name is Andrew J. Biemiller. I am director of the department of legislation of the AFL-CIO. I am appearing here today to state the views of our organization on the proposed Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1962. 

The longstanding record of the American trade union movement in support of this Nation's foreign assistance efforts certainly needs no elaboration from me this morning. American labor has given enthusiastic support to the successive measures that have been taken since the inception of the Marshall plan to the present day to extend economic assistance to non-Communist nations in their efforts to develop and maintain viable societies in freedom. 

Our aid has long since shifted from Western Europe and Japan, now the fastest growing areas of the world, to the poverty-plagued developing countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The people of these countries look to us to give them a much-needed boost in the efforts they are making to bring about their own advancement. 

For us in the AFL-CIO, as for all concerned Americans, assistance to the economic and social development of the developing countries is a key element in the overall foreign policy of our country. It is not just a humanitarian effort, although we would be the last to deprecate 81496-62-pt. 5——8 933

our obligation to help those less fortunate than ourselves to eliminate hunger, disease, and illiteracy. 

Our foreign assistance activities also advance our fundamental national interest in establishing a sound international economic and social framework which is absolutely necessary if we are ever to have a stable and peaceful world. 

Let me not be mistaken. I do not say that our foreign aid program will guarantee that the recipient nations will remain democratic for all time, certainly not in our exact sense of the term, or even forever in the anti-Communist camp. I do say that our foreign aid efforts measurably improve the chances of the newly independent countries to develop the kind of institutions, both governmental and nongovernmental, which will permit freedom and democracy to take root. 

They may not be our institutions but they can be free institutions nonetheless. 

It was with the knowledge both of the great gains already made through foreign aid as well as the tremendous task that still lies ahead that the delegates to the recent AFL-CIO Convention declared their continuing support for an effective long-term foreign aid program. 

I should like to quote briefly from the convention resolution: 

Throughout the world real economic and social progress and a rising standard of living are the goals of most of the countries which have won their independence since World War II. The peoples of these countries look upon independence not just as the obtaining of national independence and sovereignty but as a means to greater material well-being for themselves and their children. 

It should bring, they feel, more and better food, housing, medical care, vocational training and education. 

The peoples in the newly developing countries are prepared to do much to help themselves but they also need assistance from the industrialized countries, especially the United States. They need from us long-term, large-scale economic and technical assistance. It must be long-term because economic development includes projects and programs which take years to complete. It must be largescale because economic assistance confined to small isolated projects cannot give the significant boost to the entire national economy without which real economic progress in the developing countries will continue to be blocked. Previous emphasis on scattered projects should now be shifted to promotion of sound national development programs. 

In these programs it is essential that due weight be given to the basic human element. Economic development requires the enthusiastic support of the people of the country, which will not be forthcoming unless the program is based on principles of social justice and promotes human well-being now and not just sometime in the distant future.

I request that the entire text of the resolution be included in the record of this hearing. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection it is so ordered. (The resolution above referred to is as follows:) 

POLICY RESOLUTION ON INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (Adopted December 1961 by the Fourth Constitutional Convention of the Amer ican Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations) Throughout the world, real economic and social progress and a rising standard of living are the goals of most of these countries which have won their independence since World War II. The peoples of these countries look upon inde pendence not just as the obtaining of national independence and sovereignty but as a means to greater material well-being for themselves and their children. It should bring, they feel, more and better food, housing, medical care, vocational training, and education.

The peoples in the newly developing countries are prepared to do much to help themselves but they also need assistance from the industrialized countries, especially the United States. They need from us long-term, large-scale economic and technical assistance. It must be long-term because economic development includes projects and programs which take years to complete. 

It must be large-scale because economic assistance confined to small isolated projects cannot give the significant boost to the entire national economy without which real economic progress in the developing countries will continue to be blocked. Previous emphasis on scattered projects should now be shifted to promotion of sound national development programs. 

In these programs it is essential that due weight be given to the basic human element. Economic development requires the enthusiastic support of the people of the country, which will not be forthcoming unless the program is based on principles of social justice and promotes human well-being now and not just some time in the distant future.

Private investment geared to the development needs of the newly industrialized countries has an important role to play. Most recent U.S. private investment has, however, been not in the capital-starved less developed countries, but in the established economies of Western Europe. Moreover, the small amount of 

American investment that has been placed in the less developed countries has been concentrated in petroleum and other extractive industries contributing very little to balanced economic growth in these countries. What is needed is removal of tax incentives for investment in industrialized areas and encouragement of the right kind of investment in the less developed countries. 

President Kennedy has called this decade of the 1960's "the crucial decade of development." To set in motion U.S. participation in the effort to speed economic growth in the less developed countries, the President requested the Congress for authority to borrow $8.8 billion from the Treasury over 5 years to finance lowinterest, long-term loans to the developing countries. For all phases of foreign aid in fiscal year 1962, he requested approximately $4.75 billion. 

Blind both to the critical needs of the developing countries and the fundamental interests of our own Nation as well, a reactionary coalition in the House of Representatives was able to block the President's request for long-term borrowing authority for development loans and to cut nearly $900 million from the amount the President requested for fiscal 1962. The inevitable result will be to seriously hamper U.S. programs to help the developing countries. Restrictions on our own efforts will also make it more difficult for us to secure the needed cooperation of our free world partners in the common undertaking to promote economic growth in developing areas: Now, therefore, be it 

Resolved: The shortsighted action in the last session of the Congress must be reversed in 1962 so that the United States will have a thoroughly efficient, adequately financed program for assisting the developing countries. To achieve this goal we call for the following specific measures: (1) The Congress should grant the President authority to borrow from the Treasury necessary funds for financing development loans. Year-to-year appropriation of funds needed for economic development is a wasteful, inefficient means of financing the program. Moreover, as shown by this year's experience, it permits a willful handful of benighted reactionaries to thwart the will of the Congress as expressed in the authorizing legislation it enacts. (2) Congress should authorize and make available adequate funds for foreign aid. The United States, as well as other industrialized nations, should be prepared to supply each year at least 1 percent of gross national product for assisting economic progress in the less developed countries. The deficiency between the amounts President Kennedy requested and the amounts actually appropriated this year should be made available as soon as possible in the next session of Congress. (3) It is essential that the foreign aid program emphasize the human aspects of economic and social development. Specifically, this calls for development of human resources as an essential contribution to long-term economic growth through assistance for housing, medical care, vocational training, education, and other programs promoting social progress. Economic development programs in the less developed countries should also promote tax reform, land reform, cooperative undertakings, and free trade unions and collective bargaining. 

(4) The new U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) must develop criteria for assistance to less developed countries that require a maximum

amount of self-help. Programs designed to improve the education, health, and housing of the people in the less developed countries, adequate tax programs aimed at a fair and equitable progressive tax system and land reform that encompasses the basic principle of permitting the tiller of the soil to reap the benefits of his labor are all essential aspects of any sound development program. 

The AID agency must be staffed at policy development levels by a diversified group of topflight and dedicated individuals coming out of the labor movement, as well as businessmen and university professors. The strengthening of the participation of trade unionists in implementing the program is rendered more than ever necessary because of the emphasis now placed on social progress and economic growth. It is essential that people with a social orientation be active administrators in the new Agency for International Development if the aims of the Alliance for Progress and allied programs are to be achieved. (5) With the recovery of Western Europe and Japan, efforts must be made to increase the role of these industrialized countries in the economic development of the world. One of the important functions of the newly formed OECD is to work toward this objective. Increased emphasis must be placed on multilateral programs which pool resources on an international basis for aiding economic development in the developing countries. The United States should work to strengthen the U.N. programs to promote economic development, including the programs of the various constituent agencies of the U.N. Lending agencies, such as the International Development Association, the World Bank, and Inter-American Development Bank must continue to assist the developing countries of the world improve their economies. (6) To encourage private investment in the less developed countries, special tax privileges encouraging U.S. private investment in industrial countries should be removed, but such incentives should be continued for U.S. companies locating in less developed countries, provided not more than a small proportion of their output is shipped back to the United States. 

Mr. BIEMILLER. The President has requested a total of $4.878 billion for both military and economic assistance of which $1.5 billion is for military and $3.378 billion for economic aid. The proposed authorization for military assistance is some $385 million less than last year's appropriation.

As in past years, I shall not presume to comment on the proposed amount for military assistance. We are glad to see that the two phases of the program are now separate. We ask only that whatever amounts are deemed to be necessary for military assistance should not be permitted to detract in any way from the funds required for the nonmilitary phases of the program. 

I should like to make one additional comment before turning to more specific aspects of the program. The total authorization for economic aid is $3.378 billion. However, since last year's legislation has already authorized the long-term development loan program, only $2.1 billion of the funds required would actually constitute new authorization. It is this requested authorization which we are supporting here today.

NEW EMPHASES IN FOREIGN AID 

Although the United States has been engaged in various kind of foreign aid activities for nearly two decades, in a very real sense, we are trying to launch a new and different kind of foreign aid effort today. To our mind, it is a more realistic program based on principles and procedures which are geared to the most urgent requirements of the poorer nations for economic and social progress. There are a number of new emphases in the program which we think greatly improve the likelihood of its eventual success. I should like to briefly mention four of these features:

1. LONG-RANGE NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

The new program of the Agency for International Development (AID) emphasizes the need for long-term measures to encourage economic and social development on a national basis. 

It is recognized that economic and social progress cannot be achieved overnight and that therefore what is needed is a relatively long-term commitment both by us and by the assisted nation to develop the necessary resources and institutions to stimulate advancement. 

Great stress has been placed on planning, not on a grandiose or theoretical basis by planning geared to the requirements and capabilities of the assisted countries. At the same time, planning is at best meaningless and at worst morale destroying without needed assurances of the tools needed to carry out the plans. That is why long-term financing is so essential to the success of the program. 

Each proposed project is now viewed not as a single isolated entity but in terms of its potential contribution to overall national progress. 

This means that projects will not be selected simply on their individual merits but on the way in which they fit into the development of the nation as a whole.

It also means that projects will be tailored to the particular characteristics and requirements of the country. Just because a particular type of activity has been successful in one country does not mean that it will succeed under what may be the entirely different circumstances of another country. 

2. SELF-HELP AND SOCIAL REFORM 

Under the new program, it has been made explicit that the United States is prepared to help other nations to achieve progress but their efforts are absolutely essential to get the job done. They must mobilize their resources both human and material, as the essential ingredients of the economic development process. 

While we can do much to assist their advancement, in the last analysis our help will fail unless the people of the developing countries are ready and willing to help themselves. One way of assuring that there will be the necessary mass support for progressive measures in these countries is if social reform goes hand in hand with economic development.

We have rightly emphasized the need for tax reform, land reform, housing, and support for trade unions and other democratic institutions as absolutely essential to the success of the economic goals of the Alliance for Progress. It is equally necessary for this same concern for social progress to be displayed in our assistance efforts in other parts of the world.

A good deal of our present difficulties in launching the Alliance for Progress program in Latin America might have been avoided if we had realized much earlier the importance of social reform in that region. This is a mistake we ought not to repeat in other areas. Therefore, it is essential that social reform and economic development go hand in hand in our assistance efforts all over the world.

3. ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

I have already mentioned this new large-scale effort to promote economic and social development in Latin America. At this time, I merely want to mention the fact that the Alliance represents a welcome evidence of our deep concern for the welfare of the people of the nations in our own hemisphere. 

While we cannot ignore the urgent needs of the people in other parts of the world, certainly we should be particularly sympathetic to the aspirations for a better life of our neighbors in Latin America. 

Therefore, we welcome the new emphasis in the Alliance for Progress on the need for large-scale assistance to this too long neglected area in our own part of the world. 

4. FREE WORLD COOPERATION 

The United States has rightly urged other free world industrially advanced nations to shoulder their fair share of assistance to developing countries. We think this insistence on cooperative free world effort is thoroughly justified. However, it is only fair to point out that in fact, the other free industrial nations of the world have evidenced a greater determination to join in this effort. 

Some of the assistance of other countries has taken the form of their own national foreign assistance programs. 

Some of it has been through such international channels as the United Nations, International Development Association, the European Common Market, and other multilateral agencies. 

Just the other day, it was announced that the Development Assistance Committee of the new Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development will spark increased assistance and more effective coordination on the part of member countries with the first step being selection of three or four less developed countries in various regions for coordinated assistance through the "consortium" method. 

Secretary of State Dean Rusk recently pointed out that during the last 5 years, our NATO allies and Japan have increased their foreign aid commitments from $1.3 billion to $2.3 billion annually. We hope that their efforts will continue to expand but we are glad to see the increase that has already taken place. It is evident that the United 

States is by no means alone in its concern for improving the welfare of the people in the developing countries. 

DEVELOPMENT LOANS 

The President has requested authorization of $14 billion for development loans for fiscal year 1963. In money terms, the development loans constitute the largest part of the economic assistance program. This is understandable because these are generally loans for sizable projects intended to give a significant lift to the productive capacity of the developing countries. They are our major tool for speeding economic growth in the less developed countries. 

Development loans in the new foreign assistance program will make a maximum contribution to economic progress in the developing countries if they are geared to both the capabilities and the requirements of those countries. The financial terms for repayment of

the loans should be those which the developing countries can realistically shoulder. Although the loans may be repayable in dollars they should be at very low interest rates and for long repayment periods. It would be self-defeating if we were to impose such a heavy financial burden on these countries as to hinder the very economic efforts our aid is intended to foster. 

Therefore, we would urge this committee to express its intent that development loans should be made on terms that would not be onerous to borrowing countries. While the precise financial terms need not be spelled out in the legislation, the principle that repayment terms should be geared to the capacity of the borrowing country should be established.

We are pleased with the emphasis that development loans should support long-range development programs. We think in this way the assistance we give will have the maximum impact on the economic development of the borrowing countries. We also wholeheartedly endorse the idea that where appropriate, development loans should be used for social investment, such as housing and education, as well as for economic investment. 

TECHNICAL COOPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT GRANTS 

The amount requested for development grants and technical cooperation is $335 million. This is a relatively small part of the total foreign assistance authorization but in many respects is the keystone of our entire foreign assistance edifice. 

The development grants will be used primarily to develop human resources although it is our understanding that they will be used also for capital projects in a few areas, such as the newly independent African countries, which simply could not undertake the financial responsibilities of development loans. 

In the main, the development grants will be used in technical assistance as well as in other fields emphasizing the development and improvement of human qualifications and human well-being. 

Development grants will be used in such important fields as education, agriculture and rural development, public administration, development planning, industrial development, transportation and communications, health and sanitation, housing, and labor programs. 

Each program proposed for a development grant will be viewed not as an entity but will be given a priority according to the contribution. it can make to overall economic and social progress in the country. 

As in the case of development loans, a national approach is being substituted for a project-by-project piecemeal approach. Each project to be approved will have to be related to the total development goals of the country. This coordinated approach makes sense to us and should mean that we will be getting the maximum value in terms of human betterment and human progress for our development grant dollars.

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

As you know, the proposed legislation contains a separate 4-year authorization of $3 billion for the Alliance for Progress program of which it is requested that $600 million should be made available during fiscal year 1963.

As I have already stated, the AFL-CIO places tremendous importance on the Alliance for Progress program and we intend to support it in every way we can. We particularly appreciate the recent appointment of a 10-man Labor Advisory Committee on Alliance for Progress activities. This committee will seek to provide the advice and cooperation of the American trade union movement in the drive toward social and economic progress of the people of Latin 

America. 

At its most recent meeting in February of this year, the executive council of the AFL-CIO adopted a statement of vigorous support for the Alliance for Progress. Let me quote briefly from that statement: 

The Alliance for Progress recognizes the magnitude and crucial importance of the task. Most vitally, it recognizes that social and economic progress are intertwined, that social advance is necessary to provide a sound base for sustainable economic advance. It also stresses the need, not only for international cooperation, but for dedicated national efforts for social and economic advance. 

I request that the entire statement of the executive council be included in the record of this hearing. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection it is so ordered. (The statement above referred to is as follows:) 

The American labor movement has continually pressed for accelerated social and economic development in Latin America. We believe that human dignity and concern for freedom in the hemisphere require great forward strides in the living standards of the masses of the Latin American people. This underlies our hopeful endorsement and support of the Alliance for Progress plans enunciated by President John F. Kennedy in March 1961 and drafted by the American 

Republics last August at the special meeting of the Social and Economic Council of the OAS, held in Punta del Este, Uruguay. 

The objectives of the Alliance for Progress were also endorsed at the recent meeting of American Foreign Ministers, also held in Punta del Este, where it was emphasized in a special resolution, that foreign aid, liberalization of trade in raw materials, social reforms, and self-help are essential to the security of the hemisphere.

The Alliance for Progress recognizes the magnitude and crucial importance of the task. Most vitally, it recognizes that social and economic progress are intertwined, that social advance is necessary to provide a sound base for sustainable economic advance. It also stresses the need, not only for international cooperation, but for dedicated national efforts for social and economic advance. 

The Alliance for Progress areas requiring particular attention are those of agrarian reform (to develop equitable systems of land tenure and use and elevate living standards for those who work the land), tax reform (to achieve more equitable distribution of income and to "demand more from those who have the most"), low-cost housing to meet needs of low-income families, health and sanitation programs to combat ill health, and educational advances to eliminate illiteracy and provide training needed for effective national development. 

At the initial stages of this movement for progress, emphasis is being put overwhelmingly on development of comprehensive longrun national plans. 

Although such planning is necessary, it must be accompanied by vigorous shortrun measures as well. The need for comprehensive planning should not be permitted to blunt needed immediate and short-run progress. 

To make the Alliance for Progress a meaningful current reality and to demonstrate that it yields results valuably different from erratic and inadequate development activities of the past, the AFL-CIO urges : (1) A series of immediate and short-run projects should be stimulated and financed to provide early and visible material benefits, while the longer run, broader plans are still in the planning phase. (2) Such initial steps should be selected, designed, and operated to demonstrate concretely that benefits of the Alliance programs are distributed to the needier parts of the population and not to those already in the upper income levels.

(3) Full and meaningful participation of free trade union movements and worker cooperatives should be sought and enlisted in each participating country both in the immediate programs and preparation of longer term plans. 

These are essential measures for getting the movement off to an effective start. 

Undue delay or excessive concern with the longer run plans, failure to demonstrate tangible and substantial results, or failure to draw heavily on worker organizations will permit creation of dangerous popular disenchantment and would thereby seriously hamper future progress. 

We particularly stress the need for efforts to encourage and strengthen free trade union movements and to provide them with an active role in development activities at both the international level and within each nation. This is necessary for social and economic development to proceed with democratic participation of broadly based private organizations rather than through control by limited groups of commercial interests, landholders, or other minor segments of the population. It is a necessary means of assuring that benefits of progress are distributed widely among persons at all economic levels. 

Free and strong organized labor movements and associated worker cooperative organizations representing large groups of workers are the most fundamental channel for gaining a direct, active, and constructive voice for the working population in the development process. Unless strong trade union movements are developed and drawn into active participation, labor understanding and cooperation may be lacking and worker expression may take negative forms through other channels. 

Meanwhile, we commend and cite as a constructive example the appointment last month by the U.S. Government of a 10-man Labor Advisory Committee on 

Alliance for Progress activities. This Committee will function to provide the advice and cooperation of this country's trade union movement in the drive for social and economic betterment of the Latin American peoples. 

Mr. BIEMILLER. We recognize that there have been problems_in launching the Alliance for Progress program on a sound basis. Indeed, the Executive Council statement I have cited points to some of the problems which are being met. It particularly stresses the need for early and visible short-run progress as well as essential longterm planning. It also stresses the importance of close association of democratic trade unions, cooperatives, and people's organizations in the program. 

Nevertheless, we recognize that it could not be expected that in a few short months a long-range comprehensive program for the economic and social development of Latin America could have shown much tangible achievement.

The key principles we are emphasizing in the Alliance for Progress program are self-help and social reform. Such changes do not come overnight. Seeds must be planted, incentives must be provided, every possible encouragement must be given to accomplish as quickly as possible the basic social and institutional changes without which social and economic progress will be blocked. 

But we must be realistic. Just as in our own country we have never transformed our basic institutions in a few short months, neither can we reasonably expect such revolutionary developments in Latin America to take place in such a brief time. Indeed, if they were to take place without proper understanding, they could not be sound. 

We cannot be satisfied with temporizing. Neither can we issue a blank check for economic development unless it is understood and agreed that social progress must go hand in hand with economic advancement. But we must realize that however impatient we and even more the people of Latin America may be for immediate tangible gains, real economic development and lasting social reform simply cannot be achieved in a very short time.

There must be visible gains as soon as possible. No unnecessary delay either on our part or by assisted countries should be tolerated. 

But we must realize that the goals we seek in the Alliance for Progress program are long-term and to their attainment we must pledge a long-term commitment.

The appointment of Teodoro Moscoso, who had an outstanding record of success in the Operation Bootstrap in Puerto Rico, to administer our Latin America assistance effort gives us confidence that this program will succeed. 

The AFL-CIO fully supports the President's request for a 4-year $3 billion authorization for the Alliance for Progress as well as the $600 million authorization he has requested for fiscal year 1963. 

AFRICA 

The turbulent situation in much of Africa is well known. Most of the African nations have just won their independence within the past couple of years while a few more are slated to become sovereign nations in the very near future. 

The American trade union movement, in cooperation with the international free trade union movement, has been bending every effort to help in the organization and development of free democratic trade unions in the newly independent African states. Since we long supported their struggles for political freedom, they have welcomed also our support for their efforts toward economic advancement. 

To date, only a trickle of this Nation's foreign assistance has gone into Africa. President Kennedy has proposed a moderate stepping up of the amount of this assistance in fiscal 1963 to the end that we can help the newly emerging African states to set themselves on the path toward economic and social development. Faced with extremely low incomes and, in many cases, a rapidly expanding population, the newly independent African countries clearly need both technical and economic assistance if they are even to begin to achieve economic growth.

Politically, Africa is obviously one of the most important regions of the world. Most of the African countries, intent on their own problems as fledgling states with primitive economies, seek to steer clear of alinement with either of the two great power blocs. 

This is understandable. Indeed, in taking this position, they are imitating the stance of our own Nation in its early days. By helping them to develop viable economies, we can also help them to maintain their political independence, particularly of the Soviet bloc, which is using every possible device to woo their support. 

In the present early stage of development of the African countries, clearly a flexible attitude must be maintained toward the amounts and kinds of aid we should extend to these countries. But there can be no doubt that our aid can be crucially important in their beginning efforts toward economic and social progress. For the United States, our assistance to the African nations may well be viewed as a timely investment in political stability and a boost to human aspirations in an important region of the world.

LABOR PROGRAMS IN FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

From the earliest Marshall plan days, trade unionists have long played an important role in the foreign assistance programs of the United States. Largely because of the influence of free trade unions at home and abroad, foreign assistance has always included programs geared particularly to the needs and hopes of workers and in which trade unionists were directly involved. 

This tradition has continued in the present foreign assistance pro gram. Section 601 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 specifically declares that it is "the policy of the United States *** to strengthen free labor unions."

Trade unions have played a particularly important role in both political and economic life in many of the developing countries. That role will be enhanced as industrialization in these countries progresses. 

It is therefore of the utmost importance not only to us in the AFL- CIO as democratic trade unionists but to our Nation as a whole that the unions of these countries develop along free and democratic lines to the maximum extent possible. 

The AID program has been assisting in these efforts with its trade union leadership training institutions at the University of Puerto Rico and the University of the Philippines, as well as other programs both abroad and at home.

AID now has trade unions or workers' education programs in Ceylon, India, Iran, Pakistan, Turkey, Indonesia, Ecuador, Chile, Peru, El Salvador, and Tunisia. 

We are pleased that Kenneth J. Kelley, for many years secretarytreasurer of the Massachusetts State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, has just been named Special Assistant to the Administrator of the Agency for International Development to coordinate its labor programs. 

An outstanding example of what can be done in the labor field through foreign assistance is the workers' education program in Turkey which has been in operation for about 7 years. This program was originally initiated in cooperation with the Turkish Ministry of Labor. But it has now progressed to the point that the Turkish workers themselves are carrying out the program. As a result, a cadre of labor leadership which was developed under the program is now carrying on a vigorous program for trade union workers' education in Turkey.

A program is now under consideration which would involve both cooperatives and trade unions in Latin America. George McGovern, Director of the food-for-peace program, has proposed for AID a program which would combine the use of food grains to produce protein foods with loans to Latin American cooperatives of urban workers and peasants which would provide a particularly economical use of AID funds to obtain housing, land reform, health, or education programs. 

The foreign assistance program fosters freedom and democracy not only in its programs affecting workers but also in other programs as well. For example, it gives particular support to the development of cooperatives as one way of achieving grassroots participation in the economic and social development efforts. Some of these cooperatives have been sponsored by trade unions while in other cases the cooperatives and the trade unions have worked closely together.

DOMESTIC IMPACT OF FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

There are some who maintain that we must drastically cut back or even eliminate foreign assistance in order to devote our efforts to urgent needs at home. The tremendous concern of the AFL-CIO for more rapid economic growth in the United States and restoration of full employment is known, I am sure, to the members of this committee. 19 In testimony before the appropriate committees of the Congress, we have urged support for effective measures to strengthen our own economy at home and to get the country moving again. We will continue to press for such measures in the future as we have in the past. 

We see no conflict, however, between our concern for faster economic growth at home and our support for an effective foreign assistance program. In fact, the two reinforce each other. We support the foreign assistance program not primarily because of its beneficial effects at home but because of the good it does in the newly independent developing countries of the world. But we do not ignore the fact that foreign assistance activities do benefit our domestic economy. 

The reason for this is that 73 cents of every dollar of foreign aid is spent directly for goods and services produced in the United States. 

We understand, incidentally, that this percentage is continuing to increase. This policy of encouraging the expenditure of AID dollars in the United States has had two important consequences. First, it reduces the pressure that foreign aid might otherwise place on our balance of payments. Second, the jobs of some 700.000 American workers are involved in the goods and services produced in the United States for foreign aid purposes. Thus, foreign aid reinforces rather than detracts from our domestic economic objectives. 

CONCLUSION 

In his foreign aid message of March 12, 1962, President Kennedy said: 

One of the brightest pages of the world's history has been the series of programs this Nation has devised, established and implemented following the Second World War to help free peoples achieve economic development and the control of their own destinies. These programs, which have been solidly based on bipartisan support, are the proud manifestations of our deep-seated love and pursuit of freedom for individuals and for nations. 

There are some who say we have failed in these programs, that they have accomplished nothing, that they have hurt America. But a comparison of the free world as it is today with the world as it might have been without our foreign aid efforts provides convincing proof of the value of foreign assistance. Instead of a Western Europe overrun by the Soviets, we have a Europe strong, democratic and prosperous allied with us in the struggle against the Soviet drive for world domination. Free democratic trade unions in Europe, fostered in large measure through the Marshall plan program, are an important bulwark to freedom and democracy in Western Europe. 

Now, we must do a similar job in the developing nations of the world. But in many ways our task will be harder and it will last

much longer. The difficulty and the long duration of the task we face is all the more reason for us to get on with the job as quickly and as effectively as possible. The funds the President has requested for foreign assistance will help make that possible. We therefore ask this committee to recommend to Congress the full authorization requested by the President for foreign assistance in fiscal year 1963.

Then we would add to that, which is not in the bill as it left the House, but we hope will be in the bill at least in the Senate, that we also would not extend the deferral of tax privileges to foreign subsidiaries of American companies if 10 percent or more of their product is shipped into developed countries, because then we are defeating the very thing that we are trying to do. 

In terms of taking jobs away, of shipments that might be coming from this country to the underdeveloped countries, we do not believe there is any immediate problem because of two factors: 

In the first place, we think as the standard of living increases in the underdeveloped countries there will be a demand for American goods as well as their own goods. 

Second, we have found that with the dollars that go abroad into underdeveloped countries there is also a flow of additional goods from America that are needed. That flow can be demonstrated statistically and we will be glad to furnish that, that shows the tremendous value that there is in increasing American trade with money that is invested in the underdeveloped countries. 

Mr. JOHNSON. In these underdeveloped countries, as the need and requirements grow, the American subsidiaries are going into those countries and are using only local labor. 

Mr. BIEMILLER. We don't think it is going to take jobs away from 

American workers, unless as I said they are permitted to bring their products onto the American market on tax deferrals. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I would like to ask Mr. Biemiller if the same principle that you have advocated for American subsidiaries abroad-the granting of tax deferrals should be applied to development loan funds that are used to assist industries abroad which may come into competition with our domestic industries?

Since the proportion of foreign aid funds spent in the United States in 1957 was about the same as that contemplated for 1963, it can be estimated that approximately 700,000 jobs will be attributable to foreign aid if the funds the President has requested are made available.

[From AFL-CIO American Federationist, April 1962] HUNGER KNOWS NO POLITICS 

(An editorial) The increasingly acute shortage of food and goods in some of the important countries behind the Iron Curtain has enormous international significance. Recently, President Kennedy took note of the deteriorating situation in Communist China by stating that: "If people's lives are involved, if there is a desire for food, the United States would consider it carefully." 

What can or should our country do when millions of people, under the Communist or any other dictatorship, are suffering from an acute shortage of basic foods and vitally necessary consumers' goods? Is there a way of helping the

people facing starvation, without strengthening the hands of their oppressors in the process? First of all, we must have the facts. What is the actual situation in Communist China? In Castro's Cuba? In the Soviet zone of Germany? 

In Khrushchev's Russia, which is the most prosperous and powerful country in the entire Communist world?

In Communist China, millions are menaced by starvation as a result of years of natural and manmade calamities such as the system of communes forced upon the people. Confronted with famine, the Peiping rulers have set up vigilance committees to make sure peasants should not eat too much. They have hailed this cynical policy as a "self-saving mass campaign for overcoming calamity." In despair, the Mao Tse-tung propaganda machine has frantically urged the people: "Up to the mountains, down to the waters, search for edible things, for fuel, for things of use." The shortage of food in the Chinese "paradise" has become so desperate that, in answer to the bitter cries for help, the Chinese in Hong Kong sent last year about 8 million parcels to their relatives on the mainland. 

In Communist Cuba, the people are facing a desperate shortage of all food staples and consumers' goods. To prevent the ravages of massive famine which might gravely endanger his regime, Castro is resorting to the most rigid rationing and to revising sharply downward the labor contracts won by the workers through years of struggle. 

In the Soviet zone of Germany, there is an increasingly acute shortage of all food staples and goods. In this walled-in Soviet satellite, life is becoming ever more drab, dismal, and difficult. 

Even in the U.S.S.R. the regime is now facing serious shortages, especially in agricultural products, as a result of the erroneous policies of the dictatorship. 

At the 22d Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, Khrushchev expressed his intense disappointment by the use of phrases such as the "routine and stagnation in Socialist production *** conservatism in technology * * * mistakes and miscalculations in estimating the volume of production." And on 

March 5, 1962, Khrushchev admitted to his central committee that, in 1961, agricultural production in U.S.S.R. "fell short of that envisaged in the 7-year plan; grain, 1 billion poods; meat, 3 million tons; and milk, 16 million tons." 

According to Khrushchev, these lags are most serious in Russia proper, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Byelorussia-the four largest of the constituent Republics. Despite this difficult situation, he went on to picture "Communism as a cup of abundance accessible to all * * * the abundance of material and spiritual wealth and a happy and secure life of all the working people." The Soviet dictator further stressed that: "The preaching of equality in the spirit of the first Christian communities with their low standard of living cannot be depicted as a table laid with empty plates and occupied by highly conscious and completely equal people. To invite people to such communism is tantamount to inviting people to eat soup with a fork. This would be a caricature of communism." 

But the reality of the situation behind the Iron Curtain is that millions of workers and peasant are not getting the food and goods they need and want because the Communist Party dictatorship continues to put into heavy industry, especially into military thermonuclear projects, the capital and technical resources that should be invested in developing agriculture and consumers' goods industries. 

Selling grain or goods to the dictators whose policies have brought misery and hunger will not help the people who are suffering. The menace of famine and the terrible shortage of goods will not stop these dictators from putting such imported supplies into reserve for their military forces geared to oppression at home and aggression abroad. The Chinese, Cuban, or Soviet dictatorships are known to have resold in the foreign market some of the very goods they imported for the ostensible purpose of alleviating the shortages and hunger confronting their own people. 

Trade with the oppressors is no way to aid the people who are the victims of oppression. On the contrary, such trade, as in the case of Communist China today, would actually help bail the Mao Tse-tung regime out of the difficulties in which it now finds itself as a result of its false economic and inhuman political policies. These transactions fortify the international Communist propagandists in their slanderous attacks against the free world as being interested only in profits and in taking advantage of the people's misery. 

The threat of famine in Communist China and the terrible plight of millions behind the Iron Curtain confront our country and the rest of the free world with a serious problem. This problem is humanitarian rather than commercial.

Hunger knows no politics. As humanitarians, we should naturally desire to relieve the victims of starvation, regardless of their politics. Being devoted to the promotion of human freedom we certainly would not want to engage in any commercial transactions which would serve mortal enemies of democracy, like the Communist dictatorships. 

There is, however, a practical humanitarian way of helping the starving people under the Communist yoke. It is the way the American Relief Administration (ARA) saved millions of lives in the Russian famine during the early twenties. Under the ARA plan, American relief teams, with food and medicines, went to the stricken areas and gave aid directly to the famine victims. Under this plan, there was no possible misunderstanding by the recipients of the aid as to who helped them. Moreover, this plan won the approval of Lenin, in whose name and by whose authority Litvinov negotiated its acceptance on August 21, 1921. It should, therefore, be welcomed by Mao Tse-tung, Khrushchev, Castro, Tito, and all the other Communist dictators who are now vying with each other in expressing undying devotion to everything Lenin ever said or did. de Under the ARA, directed by Herbert Hoover, our country did not sell grain to the Kremlin during the famine. Instead, it gave millions of dollars of food and medicines free directly to the suffering people, regardless of their politicswithout prior appropriation or dictation by the Soviet Government. No one could then accuse America of trying to profit commercially from the misery of the Soviet people. Our country then also made sure that the hungry would be fed and that our food supplies would not be diverted or exported. And the 

Soviet beneficiaries of our assistance knew clearly that the help came from America.

The achievements of the ARA were so brilliant that the world-renowned Russian literary figure, Maxim Gorki, warmly thanked its director, Herbert Hoover, in these stirring words: "In the whole history of practical humanitarianism, I know of no achievement that could compare in greatness and compassion with the help that you extended." By December 1921, the Ninth All-Russian Congress of Soviets expressed special gratitude to the ARA and "to other countries which have rendered help to the hungry in whatever form." The Soviet People's Commissars then declared: "The people of the Soviet Union will never forget the generous help of the American people." 

Our country has always shown great generosity and capacity in helping save people from starvation. The American people would rather give away free some of their rice, wheat, butter, textiles, and medicines to the needy people in Communist China, Cuba, and elsewhere behind the Iron Curtain than to sell these goods for gold mined by slave labor. 

The suffering is far too great and the human crisis is far too grave to be met with "business as usual" transactions and deals. The conquest of hunger must know no politics. The principles and experience of the ARA in saving Lenin's 

Russia from famine could well provide the guiding line for our country's efforts to help those now menaced by famine behind the Iron Curtain.-GEORGE MEANY.

STATEMENT OF FRANK MCGEHEE, CHAIRMAN, NATIONAL INDIGNATION CONVENTION 

Mr. McGEHEE. That is correct. That is perhaps an oversight on my part. I have never appeared before one of these committees before.

Mrs. BOLTON. And his organization. 

Mr. McGEHEE. May I stand?

Chairman MORGAN. Certainly. 

Mr. McGEHEE. As to my past record or my past identity, I am 33 years old. I am a 33-year resident of the State of Texas. I have served 42 years in the Armed Forces as a jet pilot and flew 100 missions in the Korean war. 

At the present time I am devoting my full time and energies to the direction of this convention on a national basis. 

I have a wife and five children and we are expecting another one. [Applause.]

Mr. McGEHEE. About the organization, I think the simplest way to state that is to take the elements of the name "The National Indignation Convention." As all you gentlemen know, a convention means a coming together. That is exactly what the American people are doing. They are coming together in their unity of purpose. That unity of purpose will ultimately result in the wholesale destruction of communism. 

As far as the "indignation" is concerned, this is, as you know, a righteous wrath based on a moral judgment. Therefore, when the 

American people hold a convention for the purpose of protesting a policy that they consider to be morally wrong, they are having an indignation convention. It is just as simple as that. If it goes on simultaneously or in rapid succession all over the Nation, then it is a national indignation convention. That is all that there is to it. 

Simple as it may seem, that is it. 

Chairman MORGAN. Do you want to sit down for your statement?

Mr. McGEHEE. I would like to stand, if I may, if the members do not mind.

Chairman MORGAN. We have no objection to a witness who literally wants to stand up for his convictions. 

Mr. GEHEE. Incidentally, Mr. Judd, I was at the commencement address that you delivered at the University of Dallas.

I forgot to add in my background that I was a graduate of the University of Dallas and was in their first graduating class. 

Mr. Chairman and ladies and gentlemen of this committee, American citizens in every congressional district of the United States have participated in the National Indignation Convention. I wish to thank you and the other members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee for affording me the opportunity to place in the public record the cause of their indignation.

The grassroots people of this Nation are dedicated to the preservation of their Christian heritage, their mode of family life, their political institutions and their economic system. The materialistic philosophy of communism expounds and implements, without regard to legal or moral values, policies which are destructive of everything they seek to preserve; therefore, the people of this Nation are categorically opposed to every policy which tends to sustain this despicable "ism." 

Yugoslavia is an admittedly Communist nation. The policy of the 

United States whereby Yugoslavia is supplied with military weapons and her soldiers trained in the use thereof tends to sustain communism: hence the righteous wrath of the grassroots American citizen is aroused and it will not be squashed until the elected representatives of the people eliminate forever this aid to their moral enemy.

Hypocrisy is a detestable vice. The folks of this great Nation are quick to detect this infirmity in people or in policy. The policy above stated is hypocritical. 

The U.S. Government declares to the enslaved peoples of Communist lands that it wishes them to be free in order that they may pursue their religious convictions, rear their children in an atmosphere of peace, develop their political institutions by unfettered debates, and mold their economic system out of the initiative of enterprising men. 

Yet by its official acts the U.S. Government provides the military steel whereby the Communist government of Yugoslavia is able to run its oppressive bayonet through the faltering hopes of a disillusioned people thereby flogging them forever with a satanic Scourge.

Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen of this committee, the folks in this country will not tolerate this detestable policy of their government. The people of the United States of America will not tolerate the giving of aid and comfort to their enemy regardless of the official reason and they are looking first to this committee to expedite legislation which will be efficacious to the accomplishment of their will. 

The propositions which state that you do not arm your enemy nor perpetuate the slavery of your fellowman are self-evident. There are no propositions more demanding upon the reason of man than those which are self-evident; therefore, the balance of my testimony will bring to the attention of the members of this committee the facts which demonstrate that the U.S. State Department was in error when in its official publications it justified the sale of 130 F-86D all-weather jet fighter interceptor aircraft to Yugoslavia in mid-January of 1961 by the declaration that they were "*** clearly obsolescent ***"

My personal qualifications to testify on this point stem from the various duties which I performed as a jet fighter pilot in the U.S. Air 

Force from the date of my regular commission in February 1951 until the date of my honorable discharge in May of 1954.

During this time I acted in the capacity of squadron engineering officer, combat squadron operations officer, and training command fighter-gunnery instructor with special training in the fighter delivery of atomic weapons. I flew 100 combat missions in the Korean war. My total jet fighter flying time exceeds 1,000 hours. 

The following is a résumé of the operational equipment in the F-86D: 

F-86D OPERATIONAL EQUIPMENT 

1. Machineguns: Number of, six; rate of fire, 1,300 rounds per minute. 

2. Air-to-ground rocket capabilities: Size of rocket, 5-inch (warhead equivalent to a 5-inch naval gun shell); number carried, six (normal configuration). 

3. Pylon racks: Number of, two; possible configuration: (a) 1,000-pound bomb each rack; (b) 185-gallon tank each rack (these tanks can be filled with napalm which is a form of jellied gasoline that explodes upon contact with the ground and spreads a clinging type of fire over a large area. Imagine dumping 185 gallons of gasoline at a speed in excess of 600 miles per hour. Remember there are two of these tanks). 

I have delivered this jellied gasoline on the Korean people in North Korea in the Korean war. It is not a pleasant sight at all. 

4. Special configuration: Atomic weapon designed especially for fighter aircraft. With this armament this aircraft is able to deliver a destructive power equivalent to that delivered by 500 conventional fighters in the Second World War.

5. Radar-controlled gunsight. 

6. All-weather fighter radar interceptor equipment. Designed to locate, track, and automatically fire the machineguns when the target is in range. 

7. All other necessary components that make this aircraft capable of speeds in excess of 600 miles per hour, at which speed it may locate and destroy a target even in weather that precludes the pilot from ever seeing that which he has destroyed. 

Under questioning of the members of this committee I would be pleased to amplify my comments concerning any of the F-86D operational systems which have been discussed. Frankly, it is my opinion that the facts speak for themselves. An aircraft with this destructive capability is not obsolete. 

Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen of this committee, the National 

Indignation Convention will leave no legally correct, no morally right means aside in its effort to get the elected representatives of the American people to take every step necessary to effect that- (a) No funds will be appropriated for the purpose of training military personnel from any Communist country or any country dominated by the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. (b) All Communists and other representatives of enemy countries now being trained in the United States as pilots, technicians, and other military personnel shall be returned to their own lands at the earliest possible moment. (c) The transfer to Communist and other enemy nations of all planes and other weapons of war, and materials that may be converted to weapons of war, shall be terminated at once. (d) Any such material in process of transfer shall be stopped in transit and returned to the United States, and any and all agreements relative thereto shall be canceled immediately. (e) Any persons in Government found guilty of violating the provisions just cited shall be removed from office. 

May God bless you and speed your deliberations. 

Thank you.

In the economic sphere, they are trying to carry out a kind of passive resistance by not producing. So we come in in that sphere and provide the grain.
