FRIDAY, APRIL 13, 1962  

Washington, D.C.

10:40 a.m., Hon. Barrett O'Hara presiding.

Mr. O'HARA. The committee will come to order. 

We are most fortunate to have with us today representatives of the American Association of University Women, the National Council of Churches of Christ in the United States of America, and the General Federation of Women's Clubs. 

Dr. Veon, will you proceed?

STATEMENT OF DR. DOROTHY VEON, PROFESSOR IN THE COLLEGE OF EDUCATION, UNIVERSITY OF PENNSYLVANIA, REPRESENT- ING THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITY WOMEN 

Dr. VEON. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I am Dr. Dorothy Veon, a resident of University Park, Pa., professor of education at Pennsylvania State University. I am here to represent the American Association of University Women in sup port of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

The association has a membership of approximately 150,000 college graduates organized into some 1,500 branches in the 50 States, Guam and the District of Columbia and has supported a policy of foreign assistance by the United States since the Marshall plan legislation was originally enacted.

At its most recent national convention in June 1961 the association adopted resolutions and an item in its legislative program reinforcing this longstanding position in favor ofexpanding and improving programs for sound technical assistance and economic and social development for underdeveloped countries. 

In keeping with the association's interest in this concept in American foreign policy, the association is here again to make clear its support of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. Last year in our statement for the record of this committee's hearings on foreign assistance, we welcomed the new approach to the problem of aid and the new direction these proposals made possible for the U.S. foreign assistance program.

As 3 months of the current fiscal year had passed before the appropriations bill for this program was signed by the President on September 30, it has not been possible, of course, to complete the redirection and reorganization of the program. 971

In the eyes of the association the caution with which these changes are being undertaken is understandable. We recognize, therefore, that the new trends, which we welcome, are now only in their earliest stages. We address these remarks in particular to the emphasis upon self-help, overall country development and long-term planning as well as to increased multilateral cooperation in aid efforts. 

It is equally understandable that in the 6 months since the signing of the appropriation for the AID program the recipient countries have not had sufficient time to familiarize themselves with the opportunities provided in the legislation. Six months is also not enough time for these countries to develop plans or make necessary internal adjustments to achieve self-sustaining growth. Since some of these agrarian, educational, and social reforms may take years to effect, the association feels that it is fortunate that the legislation enacted last year provides a 5-year period in which to get these changes underway.

For these reasons the American Association of University Women believes that appropriation of the full sums requested by the administration for the AID program for fiscal 1962-63 should be provided. 

Although we recognize that a substantial portion of the moneys appropriated for the current fiscal year have not yet been committed, we believe it would be most unfortunate if plans now gathering momentum were to be crippled by a shortage of funds in this second very important year.

Given the new philosophy of the Agency for International Development, its changed operational structure, and taking into consideration the time element to which we have just referred, the association realizes that AID will of necessity function with different emphasis and at a different pace in various parts of the world. The experiences of this country in assistance programs over the last 15 years in postwar Europe, in Greece and Turkey, in India, and recently in Africa, illustrate these variations in emphasis and pace. 

The association has watched with particular interest the developments in Africa by reason of the focused study among its branches for the last 2 years on these emerging nations. Because we in the association recognized the growing importance of Africa, in 1959 we presented as witness on the U.S. foreign aid program, Dr. Gwendolen 

Carter of Smith College who has spent over 2 years in Africa as a background for her writings on this continent. She is the author of many articles and books on Africa, the most recent of which is "Independence for Africa."

It was Dr. Carter's position 3 years ago thatthe leaders of these countries are determined markedly to improve the standard of living of their people.

Dr. Carter at that time expressed the opinion that what these countries need is not only immediate but long-range help-projects of the most basic sort.

These projects, as this committee well recognizes, required then as they do now careful planning, expert advice, materials from the outside, and long-term commitments from the United States and from the other countries of the western world who share this burden with us of working with these new sovereignties, notably in Africa.

1 We have been pleased in the past year to note the increasing emphasis upon education in the AID program. An emphasis which we feel is as important in the work in the Alliance for Progress countries as in the African countries. 

Recently conversations and negotiations related to the Alliance for Progress program indicate that in the coming decade we will be faced with the special problems arising out of the characteristics of the Latin American area. In our opinion, the greater use of the loan pattern and continuing emphasis upon self-help cannot fail to stimulate self-sustaining growth within these countries. 

The consolidation of our assistance efforts into the AID agency has been a most commendable move, but, as we have stated earlier, much of the success of these efforts will hinge upon recognition of the differences in the areas in which we are interested and upon the extent to which we are able to provide the tools for education; and to enlist expertise in the personnel we provide as consultants in government, economics, agriculture, health and education. 

It is our earnest hope that sufficient funds will be provided and sufficient effort made to attract the experts who will be able to assist in drawing up long-term economic and social development plans. 

We wish to thank this committee for again giving the American Association of University Women the opportunity to appear before it in behalf of this program which, on the one hand, can be regarded as a measure to combat the spread of communism, but which and even more importantly, will help to make the benefits of civilization increasingly available to greater numbers of the human race. 

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, may I discuss some of my experiences in Latin America?"

Mr. O'HARA. I was going to suggest that, Doctor. You have a broad background of experience in Latin America. 

Dr. VEON. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

During the year 1959 and 1960 while I was on sabbatical leave from the university, it was my pleasure and privilege to spend a good deal of time in Panama and Mexico. While I was in Panama I was disturbed and yet pleased about the educational progress that has been made in that particular country. I was disturbed, maybe I should say first because of a resentment that is prevalent among some of the teachers in Panama that we are not giving them sufficient assistance on their educational program, which is equivalent to that which we have in the Canal Zone. 

May I perhaps make a statement that I was in the Canal Zone at the time when Panama was pressing to have its flag also fly over the canal, and I think this resentment perhaps goes over into some other areas. 

Much of this, of course, is brought about by the fact that many of the persons who are on educational missions for the U.S. Government do live in Panama City, but they also send their children over into the Canal Zone because they feel the Canal Zone schools are better, which I would agree with them. 

This means that our schools in the Canal Zone over a longer period of time have had better teachers, because the teachers normally have come from the States, they have been prepared in well-qualified teacher education institutions. We have been able to send to the schools adequate visual instructions for them to work with, and we have given them assistance from the U.S. Office of Education.

I am very much pleased, however, to say that we do have some breakthroughs here, and one is evidenced by their technical institutes. 

We have four in Panama, four modern technical institutes. These include boys and girls, the equivalent of our secondary schools. Here they are offering predominantly vocational training. Much of this is the result of our ICA mission, educational mission, where we have been sending some of these teachers up into the United States, and particularly Columbia University and others on the east coast to help them get ready for this type of training. 

I am also pleased with the improvement which they are making in higher education in the city of Panama, especially with the university there. It is a very modern institution. It reminds me a great deal of facilities here in the District of Columbia, where so many people go to school after working hours. After 4 o'clock in the afternoon, the campus becomes a beehive of activity. 

Panama faces divergence of problems in education. Most of thisprimarily the problems that are predominant are in the Canal Zone, Balboa, and Panama City, but we also have the hinterland population which is most illiterate. 

I think there should be a redirection of our educational philosophy in trying to give a little bit more emphasis to the education of these people in the more remote areas. In vocational education we have been doing that in working with some of the Panamanian teachers. 

Probably in Panama as well as in some of the other countries, we need first of all awakening, I think, of responsibility for education. 

We provide education for the elite in all these countries-delightful education. We send them out of the country if necessary. But we fail, I think, many times, to provide adequate education for particularly the Indian population. We do not have sufficient schools. I think perhaps in Latin America that we might follow a pattern somewhat as we are doing with the Indians in the Southwest, since I have had quite a bit of experience in Arizona. 

Originally we would take the children from the reservations and bring them into the Phoenix school. This created a family problem because they did not want them taken out of the family environment.

The more recent movement, which I think is good there, is that we will provide schools in the Navaho Reservation. I think this might be one of the problems in Panama, Guatemala, in some of the other areas, to take more education into these backlands. 

In Guatemala, certainly we have more of a problem, I think, in mass education, than we do in Panama. I was very much pleased, however, to get into one of the small rural schools in Guatemala, and here was this young person who was 24 years of age trying to teach a class in science education, a very alert, a very excellent teacher in my opinion. His school was right on the edge of the marketplace. 

Here were these little boys and girls who came with their parents to market. Some of them did go in and take the schooling from him, others were more or less standing outside looking in, others had not even the vaguest interest. Right in the middle of this marketplace without even instruction materials he was doing a wonderful job. 

What could we do in the Alliance for Progress work in Guatemala, in Ecuador, in some of the other Central American countries? We

need certainly to work with them with regard to their philosophies of education in line with the aims of their country, in line with their natural resources, to the extent to which they could properly provide education. We need to work with them in a redirection of their emphasis on the programs. 

Probably a third one is that we need more long-range planning. 

Who should be educated? In my opinion everyone should have an opportunity, equal opportunity, for education. This means that we have educational problems when we are trying to educate the masses. 

The approach which frequently we have used in educational missions coming from the United States or from other countries, but more from the United States-we try to impose upon them our procedures, our methodology, our instruction materials, in a country in which they are just not ready to grasp them. 

The techniques which we would use, it seems to me, in mass education for the elementary schools, for the boys and girls who are the young population, would certainly need to be very different from elementary education for those who are in the older brackets. 

I think many of us from the United States, when we have visited in some of these schools, have resented the fact that elementary education has a vocational slant. I think we probably need to direct our educational endeavors toward the fact that many of these persons will not be going beyond the elementary level and they need a vocational atmosphere here. 

I would like to mention an experience I had in Brazil. I had the opportunity to go up into the Amazon Valley of Brazil, and to visit a girls school there. The Amazon Valley has many problems. One is to eradicate disease, and then they would place emphasis on education.

In the valley we have some modern schools, thanks to the British. 

But we also have, I think, a tremendous challenge there to educate the masses.

Let me mention one of the girls schools that I did visit. I was the guest of the principal that day, and the main thing that she was interested in was this more or less redirection of emphasis. She apparently had learned this from some pedagogical book from the United States. The first place she wanted me to see was the washrooms. Here in these washrooms she was attempting to point out sanitary problems in the school and hoping that this would carry over to the home.

She had started a domestic science department, where the whole emphasis was on sewing. We had 30 heads of one of our competitors sewing machines there, yet there was a neglect here, I think, in care and processing of foods.

In Brazil, there is a great deal we can do. I think that we can give technical assistance, but I think it is more important that probably we provide more consultants with regard to education. 

We need people who will not be sending down to these countries what I would call "carbon copies" of our American setup for our schools.

This is going to date me, I am sure, but after World War II it was my privilege to sit in on a conference on the educational problems of

the occupied countries. I was greatly disturbed at that time to think that in Japan and in Austria and Germany we were trying to superimpose our American pedagogy on those particular countries. 

I think this should not be the case in Brazil, Panama, Guatemala, or any of the other countries I have visited. 

I would be very glad to answer any questions that any of you would like to ask. 

Mr. O'HARA. Thank you, Doctor.

You are familiar of course with the proposal to give a 4-year authorization in the funds for the Alliance for Progress? Dr. VEON. I am, sir. 

Mr. O'HARA. Do you think that is a sound approach?

Dr. VEON. I think it is much better than what we have used in our previous commitments to these countries. For one reason, we can get better qualified individuals to go out on these educational missions. 

We have been criticized tremendously by having people say, "I am going on an educational mission more or less as an escape from my particular job." It has been difficult to recruit, I think, good professional educators who are willing to go only for 2 years, because they have to get leaves of absence from their schools. 

I think over a long period of time we can provide for these countries better personnel from the United States and also with this long-range planning of 4 or 10 years that they can look at their problems. 

Education is slow. You can't within a year look back and say that you have made good progress. You won't. It takes a long time to try to change behavior patterns in a country. 

Mr. O'HARA. Does your organization endorse the proposal of the 

4-year authorization for the Alliance for Progress? 

Dr. VEON. Yes, it does. 

Mr. O'HARA. Thank you. 

Mrs. Bolton. 

Mrs. BOLTON.

One woman had a very interesting experience. She had a splendid class of girls. They loved the work and they did well, so forth and so on. Dr. VEON. I wouldn't say it has wholly passed; no. Mrs. BOLTON. The girls don't go alone. I am wondering if we have adjusted more to that and accepted it more than we wanted to. 

Dr. VEON. I think we have more from Mexico than any of the others. We have had so many of our boys and girls going there for summer session. We were doing well before our Cuban difficulty, we had a large number going to summer school in Cuba and also the

As these younger persons come back, I think they help more than probably some of the older persons. On the other hand, we are developing more tourist trade into Latin America, and especially a quick 3-week trip around South America, so they are getting into Chile-

Dr. VEON. They see, of course, what they want to see.

Dr. VEON. I think sometimes we consider education as formal education. Education is a continuous process from the time you are born until the time you die. Many of the best educated people have never entered classrooms at the university. Maybe that is good. 

Mrs. BOLTON. To me, education is preparation for the living of life in the area where they have to live. So that I would be very sorry if we weren't fluid enough and elastic enough in what we take to these different countries to recognize the fact that the girl who comes out from the bush can't possibly accept the educational process that a girl who has lived in the city, even in central Africa. I hope that what is being done is on that basis. 

Dr. VEON. I would agree with you. I think this is one of our problems in trying to get more of this education out in the rural areas. 

I recall a good friend of mine who was down in the hinterland of Panama who said how difficult it was. STATEMENT OF DR. VERNON L. FERWERDA, CHAIRMAN, GOVERN- MENT DEPARTMENT, TRINITY COLLEGE, REPRESENTING THE NATIONAL COUNCIL OF THE CHURCHES OF CHRIST IN THE U.S.A. 

Dr. FERWERDA. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee.

My name is Vernon L. Ferwerda. I am testifying here in behalf of the National Council of the Churches of Christ in the U.S.A. by the authorization of its appropriate officers. I am currently chairman of the Government Department at Trinity College, and a member of the Department of International Affairs of the National Council of Churches.

While I am here as a designated representative of the Department of International Affairs of the National Council of Churches, I obviously cannot and do not presume to speak for each of the 40 million members of the 33 Protestant and Eastern Orthodox communions in the National Council. However, I am presenting policies and views adopted after careful study, discussion, and deliberation by the Council's policymaking bodies composed of official representatives of the communions.

The United Church Women, a general department of the National Council of Churches, has prepared a special statement which they are submitting to your committee for the record, which accords in general with the views in this presentation. 

GENERAL POSITION OF THE NATIONAL COUNCIL OF CHURCHES 

In keeping with numerous actions of the council's policymaking bodies, we hold it to be a Christian concern and a moral responsibility for the United States to take all appropriate action within its capacity and resources to promote economic betterment, social well-being, freedom, justice, and peace among the peoples of the world, including our

1 1 own and especially among the newly independent, emerging, and low-income nations. In support of these goals, the National Council of Churches has given its unceasing support to the improvement and expansion of technical assistance, loans and grants, educational and other exchanges, trade, private investment, and other measures to improve the conditions of life and aid in the development of free, responsible, and stable societies. 

In an important pronouncement entitled "Toward a Family of Nations Under God: Agenda of Action for Peace," the council's general board in 1960 summarized this concern in the following words: 

Improvement of standards of life of our fellow men is a privilege the United States shares, not a benefit it confers. Moral principle even more than concern for our own national welfare impels an abiding interest in our neighbors on a crowded planet. Their growth is part of our growth and their partnership for peace is essential to all security. 

COMPETENCE OF THE CHURCHES 

For over 150 years, the churches have engaged in administering oversea assistance and cooperative programs to improve conditions of life on all continents. These programs include education, literacy, medicine, public health, agriculture, industry, mass communication, and leadership training.

For many years the constituent communions and the National Council's Central Department of Church World Service have conducted large programs of assistance to peoples in distress around the world; for example, surplus food distribution, disaster relief, village and community assistance. 

We believe these experiences provide a practical basis on which to make some evaluation of Government assistance programs. Further, the position of the churches here presented rests primarily on moral and religious grounds. 

In the development of national policy and in the actual conduct of assistance programs, we are dealing with questions of life and death, the nature of man and his destiny, individual and corporate responsibility, and with questions of freedom, justice, brotherhood, and peace.

These are ultimately moral and religious questions. 

Mutual assistance and development programs go far beyond material considerations; they reflect moral and spiritual realities in international and human relations. 

FOREIGN AID POLICIES- -CRITIQUE 

It is our belief that American aid policies, generous and remarkable as they have been, continue to be motivated too much by fear and too little by that spirit enunciated so well by President Kennedy in his inaugural address:

To those people in the huts and villages of half the globe struggling to break the bonds of mass misery, we pledge our best efforts to help them help themselves, for whatever period is required-not because the Communists may be doing it, not because we seek their votes, but because it is right. 

The United States, since World War II, has sometimes been doing the right things for the wrong reasons, with too little perspective, and too often predictable disappointment. Instead of a clear, con- 81496-62-pt. 5- -11

sistent worldwide concern for meeting human needs and developing human potentialities, U.S. sentiments have moved largely from preoccupation to preoccupation. 

First it was Europe, then Asia, then Africa. And now, for various reasons, somewhat belatedly, the United States has rediscovered its neighbors to the south. There are strong reasons for full support of the program of aid for Latin America, and the proposal that it be put on a long-term basis. 

But must we here pretend that suddenly, in the language of the current bill, we have become convinced that "the historic, economic, political, and geographical relationships among the American peoples and republics are unique and of special significance"? Must we suddenly overwhelm our good neighbor to the south with vigorous protestations of "Amigo, you are the most"? Isn't he likely to have more respect for our integrity if we show him now less passion and more real partnership-not as a patronized friend, but as one of God's children in a worldwide Alliance for Progress?

So, while supporting new thrusts for aid to Latin America, as part of an improved and expanded program of mutual aid, I would also register a concern for our Government to develop a more consistent, more rational, more humane worldwide programing for mutual aid. 

ELEMENTS OF A STRATEGY OF DEVELOPMENT 

Our friends in the World Council of Churches recently issued through their Commission of the Churches on International Affairs meeting in Bangalore, an impressive statement dealing with the elements of a strategy of development. It begins as follows: 

The claims of justice, humanity, and indeed of order call for a more dynamic and coherent strategy of development, a worldwide concerted effort to help the economically less developed peoples of Asia, Africa, and Latin America achieve more decent material conditions of life. In our time God has given the nations the resources to remove from all mankind the burdens of massive poverty, ill health, and illiteracy. This gift poses corresponding obligations on the nations to cooperate in a really effective struggle for world development. While significant beginnings have been made, more vigorous, intelligent, and dedicated action is called for.

This concept of the need for a more dynamic and coherent strategy of development was set forth by churchmen from every continent, including church leaders from our own country. Expressing the hope that the whole world might "regard the rising expectations of the peoples, and the pressures generated by them, as a positive challenge, a creative opportunity," these eminent churchmen called for due regard for the tempo and scope of development efforts, and a sound overall balance in these efforts, as essential to an adequate strategy.

While accepting the need for some bilateral programs, we believe that a comprehensive strategy for development and the objectives our Nation seeks call for an increasing emphasis on multilateral programs through regional arrangements and especially through the United Nations and its specialized agencies. We support mutual aid programs, especially those which promise to develop mutual understanding along with immediate objectives of social and economic development for a more abundant life for more peoples of the earth.

We believe such to be in the highest interests of the United States and necessary for world development toward peace with justice and freedom. 

Mr. Chairman, if I may speak for a moment or two on the general theme of this presentation: We do of course support this most important section of the bill, that the Alliance for Progress be made a longer term program.

This, in fact, is the direction we have long as a National Council of Churches, proposed that our mutual assistance and mutual aid programs take. 

The main point to our remarks here, however, is that this continues to be an area in which we need to have a worldwide program, not just in terms of where the immediate danger seems to be and where communism seems to be the immediate problem, but going well beyond this, in perhaps rather idealistic terms, but in the moral and ethical terms which we find compel a worldwide program. 

We wish the term "Alliance for Progress" could somehow have been applied to a worldwide program. We are moving in that direction. 

We support the Alliance for Progress. We are glad that the present legislation also provides assistance, mutual aid for Asia and Africa. 

My particular background of experiences and interest has been emphasizing Africa. It was my very good fortune last summer to spend 

10 weeks in Africa as one of the leaders in the crossroads Africa program. We had, in our living with Africans in Dahomey and then in our study tour in Nigeria and Ghana, many opportunities to talk over just this kind of emphasis, why we were in mutual aid programs, what we were up to, anyway. 

I don't need to tell the members of this committee that Africans tend to be a little skeptical; they like to take these things out of cold war terms, and we tend to immediately respect their concern. 

If this is neutralism, at least it is one that we came to appreciate more and more, as they wanted not to be in any sense pawns in the cold war, but rather with our assistance, as we saw coming so well in Nigeria in particular, to lift the level of their educational development, economic and social development. 

This, Mr. Chairman, is the brief remark I wanted to add to this, that we certainly support the idea of an Alliance for Progress. We feel that clearly again in moral and ethical terms, and perhaps also in the political terms, that it is high time we got to an emphasis upon Latin America, but again as part of a comprehensive overall and continuing program of worldwide mutual aid. 

Thank you.

I appreciate your statement here, sir. That individual voluntary effort has an impact-redemptive, if I may use that word that I have seldom seen government programs have. Of necessity the latter are big, rigid, impersonal, and, to some extent, suspect"What is the reason the Government is doing this?"

Whereas if somebody comes only because he is interested in people, through a voluntary organization, like a church's missionary effort, CARE or MEDICO or World Neighbors or World Literacy, aid to refugees, or any of the whole range of programs, there is an impact all out of proportion to the amount of money spent and the number of people involved. 

You didn't stress that but I am stressing it for you. I know your present proper preoccupation with our Government programs doesn't mean that you are less concerned, or the churches are less concerned about the efforts of private organizations. 

If there ever was a time when missions in the right sense were merely justifiable, the time has now come when they are actually essential, imperative, to put soul and heart and meaning and content into a lot of the Government programs. 

You don't mind my making this statement?

Dr. FERWERDA. I would certainly agree with Dr. Judd on the continuing and in fact increasing importance of the private programs. 

Our Church World Service Division, of which you certainly know, is expanding its efforts in part in acquiring Hugh Farley from Government. 

The mission effort through our Division of Foreign Missions, which will soon be renamed World Mission-Dr. Judd probably knows some of the circumstances of this-is again reevaluating its position in the future mission effort. 

It will clearly be an effort in which people will continue to go abroad for the service they may render. But rather than with emphasis only upon soul saving, as important as this has been to religious people, we will have a Christian person who will come to render medical service and teaching, and so forth. 

I would like to add one word in this connection. Many times the 

Government programs do appear cold and impersonal. I would like to indicate an experience I had in a village in northern Nigeria which somehow personalized some of the best we have had in our Government programs.

In Riga Chikun we were shown, with some pride, a poultry flock that, as it turned out, was to be the best poultry we were to see all summer. They were chickens that we couldn't find in the markets when we went in the markets next to us, Dahomey. They were fine chickens because the village had had the fortune of having a poultry expert under the point 4 program.

These Nigerians learned if you feed properly and care for flocks, the results are remarkable, and the size of eggs, quality of meat, is good. Once this lesson was learned, the American was able to go on

to some place else or go back to his State university or extension service, wherever he had been, with a job well done and thereafter, one could say, almost in perpetuity with the results as given. 

As it was pointed out to me with great pride by the people of Riga Chikun, we as a people and Government should consider this with real pride. 

There is some real genius in some of the point 4 programs. I like to think again of that poultry expert in the "Ugly American" as one of the really good guys. As to what one witnessed in this village, I hope the Congressman will forgive me, we don't need to consider the Government programs as large and impersonal. If it can become one poultry expert in a village in north Nigeria, it becomes very real. 

Mr. JUDD. What you have said is what Mr. Saund and I have been emphasizing perhaps more than almost anybody else around here, because we both lived in relatively small and rural places in the Orient. 

We have tried to get our Government to put more and more emphasis on the things that reach people directly. 

We know that we have to build a big dam or fertilizer plant, and we are not opposed to that. We just want more emphasis on the things that reach people directly.

Referring to evangelism, I was in China 10 years as a Christian medical missionary. I never preached a sermon even if I could have. 

I felt that by meeting the needs of people in a way that they understood directly, I was demonstrating an estimate of the value of every human being which was, if you wish, the finest kind of witness to the things I believe about God and about man. 

So often in the olden days some went out and preached and that was it. I think the best short biography of our Lord is the one which describes Him as "A prophet mighty in deed and word." Normally we would put it "word and deed." I think the right order is "mighty in deed and word."

It is the deed that raises a question or makes an impression on the observer's mind. Why are you doing this? They wonder why. Then a few words explaining why you are doing it are much more convincing than any kind of exhortation that is not just in explanation of good deeds.

I apologize for this little lecture. I approve so much the work of the churches I might even get back into missionary work of that sort if I could. I could do just what seemed best.

(The prepared statement of Miss Butler is as follows:)

STATEMENT OF GENERAL FEDERATION OF WOMEN'S CLUBS 

The General Federation of Women's Clubs has continuously supported the foreign aid assistance to underdeveloped countries since the Marshall plan was adopted. In fact the general federation was among those first groups that supported the Marshall plan. 

The women of this country know when people are hungry, cold, sick, or need help to give their families a better way of life, they (the needy) will turn to those who help them.

The stakes are high today. A free society versus communism is the issue. 

The general federation sees the need for continued aid to those countries that have recently become independent and are trying to help themselves in stabilizing their own economy. Therefore we do support our Government in its effort to give aid to the underdeveloped countries and urge the Congress to provide adequate appropriations.

OF Miss BUTLER. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, our president wanted so much to be here herself, she made the basic statement for the General Federation. The General Federation is an organization of over 11 million women and they are in 50 different countries. So it is an international organization.

I am director of legislation, and have been able to make several trips abroad with our different presidents. I was in the Middle East with Mrs. Prout, a former president. Have been twice in South

America and have participated in forums with the women of those countries, discussing the common interests of clubwomen, and that, so far as the General Federation is concerned, is the programs that affect the family and the family life, including education, health, and general welfare in every sense of the word. 

The women in other countries are also extremely interested in what goes on around the world. 

The General Federation president points out that foreign aid is essential to the welfare of the people all over the world. It is essential for our own security. It is essential in planning for peace if there should ever be peace.

The General Federation has been supporting the foreign aid program since the Marshall plan, and had General Marshall come to their national convention only a few days after the Marshall plan was adopted, to speak to the women of the Federation. From that time the General Federation has supported the foreign aid program. 

Clubwomen believe in the necessary aid to the underdeveloped countries, because the women know that when people are hungry, sick, or cold, or need help to give their families a better way of life that they (the needy) will turn to those who help them. 

The stakes are high today. A free society versus communism is the issue. The General Federation sees the need for continued aid to those countries that have recently become independent and are trying to help themselves in stabilizing their own economy. 

The federation urges that the United States continue to help those who help themselves in stabilizing their own economy today. 

Therefore we do support the Government in its effort to give aid to the underdeveloped countries and to urge the Congress to provide adequate appropriations for that purpose.

Clubwomen believe the foreign aid program is essential to strengthen the influence of the Western World.

AN OUTSTANDING EXAMPLE OF SUCCESS 

During the past year, when the United Nations has been undergoing a series of dramatic trials, when its very existence has been threatened, the Citizens Committee for UNICEF finds much reassurance in the record of steady progress made by UNICEF during 1961. 

We also find, in its forward-looking program for 1962-63, evidence which justifies a substantial basis of hope--not only for the future welfare of the world's children, but also as a demonstration of the way in which the nations of the entire world can find grounds for cooperation in our mutual concern for the future of humanity.

When rival political powers can share support for programs designed to remove the worst hazards of disease and chronic malnutrition that afflict vast areas of the earth, perhaps it is not too much to hope that these same nations can also learn the necessary lessons of mutual understanding and self-discipline that could lead them to exercise restraint in the atomic arms race.

The Citizens Committee for UNICEF supports the executive branch recommendation for a contribution of $12 million by the United States to the Children's 

Fund for fiscal 1963.

GOVERNMENT CONTRIBUTIONS INCREASING 

In spite of the fact that this new fiscal year will mark the fourth consecutive year when the U.S. contribution has been held to the same amount, we note that contributions to UNICEF from other governments are steadily increasing-$1.5 million in 1961 by governments other than the United States, or 16 percent increase. This is evidence of the esteem which UNICEF enjoys everywhere. 

Twenty-seven countries increased their support substantially during the past year, with the largest absolute increases given by the Federal Republic of 

Germany, France, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Switzerland, and the U.S.S.R.

Perhaps even more significant than these impressive increases by the industrialized, comparatively wealthy countries of Europe is the fact that 25 countries that are themselves beneficiaries of UNICEF aid to help their own children pledged or contributed to UNICEF voluntarily during 1961 proportionately as much or more than they were assessed as their fair share for the regular U.N. budget.

Again this year we note with satisfaction the fact that newly independent countries of Africa including Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Madagascar, Mali, and Somali Republic contributed to UNICEF in 1962 among their first acts of self-government, thus demonstrating effectively their developing sense of social responsibility. 

UNICEF IN THE DECADE OF THE SIXTIES 

We have heard much discussion during this past year of the goals of the U.S. program for the "Decade of Development," as envisioned by the President, the Secretary of State, and the Director of AID. Increasingly stressed as a basic criterion for the multibillion dollar U.S. program of aid to developing countries is the necessity for self-help on the part of these nations. 

Those of us who have followed the work of UNICEF during its 15 years of successful operations have seen ample justification for this emphasis on selfhelp since that has been requisite to UNICEF assistance from the beginning. 

We are hopeful that our much larger bilateral programs can produce even more successful results through this commonsense approach. 

To cite just two areas where U.S. interest is especially high at this time, we observe that UNICEF's Executive Board approved allocations in 1962 of $4,- 160,000 for all types of long-range programs (health services, disease control, and nutrition) in 31 African countries, in addition to 3 regional programs. 

Likewise, for the Americas, $7,644,359 was approved for similar programs to go forward in 22 countries of this hemisphere. 

The benefits that will result for children and mothers from the work made possible by these funds should contribute in no small measure to the success of the ambitious Alliance for Progress programs for broad economic and social development.

Beginning last year, after a preliminary survey of the needs of children had been conducted by a number of governments, by the specialized agencies and the Bureau of Social Affairs of the U.N., the UNICEF Board decided to increase

舒​您 ​2 the range and flexibility of UNICEF aid by encouraging the countries undertaking programs of economic and social development to focus on the problems and the main needs of their children, and to plan effectively to meet these needs. 

This new emphasis recognizes the fact that opportunities for effective aid vary greatly from country to country. 

While the well established policies of UNICEF support in the fields of health and nutrition will, of course, continue to receive the major part of UNICEF assistance, new areas of concern are developing such as the greater help which will be needed in the rapidly growing urban areas where the health and social problems of children and youth are acute. 

Formerly essentially rural peoples are flocking to urban centers in great numbers too rapidly for existing facilities to absorb them. The impact of this sudden influx is creating serious slum conditions in urban centers where standards of living were not adequate even before this new growth. 

Thus the very eagerness and impatience of the newly developing peoples to raise their standards of living almost literally overnight can bring new and serious dislocations in patterns of family living, often with tragic results for the children. Already one modest pilot project is underway in the slums of 

Mexico City involving housing improvement, environmental sanitation, vocational guidance, and training for youth. 

In summary, UNICEF aid offers the nations of the world a unique opportunity to focus on investment on children and youth concomitantly with the broad programs of economic development going forward under the vast bilateral and multilateral programs of grants and loans. 

Direct measurable returns on this investment cannot be demonstrated from one year to the next in the way that statisticians can chart economic growth by indexes of industrial production, miles of roads built, or national income. Yet without such investment in children, the human resources of the future, permanent economic improvements have scant hope for success. The continued achievements of UNICEF, along the paths that it has already charted, offer one of our best hopes for the future.

Mrs. GRAY. The list of organizations which have authorized this statement you have before you. And we note with much interest the way the present administration is stressing that point in the big foreign aid program.

It is always good to have you here, Mrs. Gray. We are always interested. I think that it would be interesting for the record, as we have a good many new people in the House and so on, if you would tell us the type of work that UNICEF does. What do you do?

Mrs. GRAY. There are a number of different categories of programs, as you know. UNICEF continues the emergency program, which is only a small part of their budget now, but they are ready to go in in national disaster or any problem, as they did into Morocco a year ago, in Chile when the earthquake did so much damage. any

There is the emergency aid- Mrs. BOLTON. When you go into, say, Chile, the Red Cross is there, too, isn't it? 

Mrs. GRAY. Yes. 

Mrs. BOLTON. You work very much together?

Mrs. GRAY. That is my understanding. I have never seen it on the spot unfortunately. From what I hear from all the reports, there is a very close cooperation and no duplication of effort at all. 

In north Africa I remember UNICEF supplied blankets when the people were without homes, when there had to be some way of keeping them sheltered.

Mrs. BOLTON. When you supply the blankets they don't come back to you, do they?

Mrs. GRAY. No. After the emergency program, which as I say is a small part of it, there are the comprehensive long-range programs to not only aid temporarily but to develop the future programs within the country itself. There

There are programs of nutrition that include such things as, in India, for example, building the plant for the processing of milk. have also been plants in other countries built for developing skim milk that can be used for the countries' feeding programs.

There is the general program of the child welfare, maternal, and child welfare, which has been carried on by clinics for training of mothers in how to care for their babies, and in teaching them basic nutrition standards so that the children, even though they have food, will not be undernourished because they are not getting proper food. 

There is the training of the midwives in the health program; the training of native women who will have an opportunity to bring modern scientific methods to the small remote villages where this has never happened before. 

Another basic attack on the health programs have been the campaign against malaria in a number of countries. Mexico is now approaching the end of its 5-year program to eliminate malaria completely by destroying the anopheles mosquito which is the vector for malaria. Iran has a comprehensive malaria program, to mention another one.

The other major diseases that are being attacked are leprosy in Africa and in the countries where it still has epidemic proportions in some areas. This is done by UNICEF primarily by supplying the sulfone tablets. UNICEF, as you know, is a supply agency for drugs and services. The World Health Organization provides the doctors and nurses that are necessary. 

For the treatment of leprosy it has been found that among children when they are found to be exposed or to have beginning cases, the dosage of a tablet of the sulfone drug once a week, I believe it is, for about 3 years will completely cure them. 

This is one of the tremendous hopes of the future, that this horrible disease which we don't even know in this country to any extent now can be completely eradicated in time. 

Other diseases are trachoma and the yaws, which are being fairly well eliminated from southeast Asia, so that is not requiring quite as large a part of the UNICEF funds for the southeast Asian countries as it did in the past. 

Mrs. BOLTON. May I ask if you have had any studies made at all of the toleration of the African children for sulfone drugs? 

Mrs. GRAY. I don't know about that. I think that would be a good- Mrs. BOLTON. We had an experience when I was out there, and 

Dr. Hodgson from the Mayo Clinic who was with me was deeply impressed by the fact that the adults could tolerate so much more than they would dare give in this country. They have found that our people could not take the same dosages. 

Mrs. GRAY. I shall find that out and let you know if UNICEF has any information on that. 

Mrs. BOLTON. Thank you, very much. 

Mrs. GRAY. I am interested, too.

Mr. MURPHY. Mrs. Gray, first of all, must a country make a request of your organization for aid?

Mrs. GRAY. That is correct; with some idea or plan of how they would be able to carry it out and the plan of the amount of money or goods and services that they will be able to supply as their part of the project.

1000

Mr. MURPHY. Is the amount of money requested by these countries greater than the funds available? 

Mrs. GRAY. That is a difficult question to answer, Mr. Murphy, because I think that in most cases the request does not reach the formal stage of being an official request until exploratory talks have been conducted and they know that the money will be available to carry on the project. 

There is obviously a tremendous backlog of need. If the countries themselves have the funds or the facilities for matching the aid for the children, they could do a great deal more than they are doing. 

I don't think that we can say there are specifically x number of requests that are unmet, because UNICEF doesn't quite work that way. They wait until there is the chance of making the program a really effective one before the formal request goes in. 

There is certainly much need that is still unmet that UNICEF could supply, could the country itself do its part, at the present time. 

That is in many cases not quite possible. 

One of the developments in the last year-it took place in a discussion of the delegates at the June board meeting-was to reconsider their emphasis on the standard patterns of programs that they had been advocating in previous years, such as the campaigns for the eradication of yaws and and so forth that we have already mentioned, and have the burden of responsibility put more on the country itself to determine what, as it sees the problem, its chief needs of children are. They seem to differ in some areas of the world. 

For example, in Asia they seem to feel the most important need is in the health field. In Africa the people seem to feel that there is such a tremendous need that perhaps education of their workers, of the people to deal with the children, and to teach sanitation, to teach just the rudimentary necessities of healthful living is more important than trying to conduct the health campaigns themselves. And in 

Latin America, I understand that there is much concern about the plight of children who have no families, no parents available for them to live in homes with a normal child life. There are problems of institutional care of children. 

So the countries are being urged to concentrate, themselves, on what they feel is the greatest need, the fundamental need of the children first, rather than try because their next-door neighbor has a campaign for trachoma they must do that. It mustn't be an imitative process but a true evaluation of their greatest needs within their territory. 

Mr. MURPHY. Thank you.

VOLUNTARY PUBLIC CONTRIBUTIONS TO UNICEF 

Although UNICEF is financed basically by voluntary contributions from governments, the Executive Board of UNICEF has always encouraged the development of broad citizen interest and participation in all countries. Voluntary public contributions reflect a popular awareness of UNICEF's aims and activities, one being considered as desirable as the other. The rate of growth for public contributions has been faster than that for government contributions. 

Private contributions (including organized campaigns) amounted to $461,000 in 1954; that was the year after the General Assembly had decided to continue 

UNICEF indefinitely. There has been a steady increase each year, and in 1961 they amounted to $2,670,000. Forming only 3.1 percent of total income in 1954, the share of private contributions (including organized campaigns) in 1961 was 9.5 percent.

In 1961 fundraising campaigns benefiting UNICEF took place in 13 countries, yielding $2,554,029. Next to the proceeds from the trick-or-treat campaign in the United States ($1,595,278), receipts were largest from the shell-out campaign in Canada ($542,763) and from the milk campaign in Switzerland ($307,821). Other countries in which campaigns took place include Australia, Belgium, Denmark, Federal Republic of Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. 

UNICEF accounts show that contributions from individuals totaled $115,976 in 1961 and originated in 31 countries. Approximately 55 percent came from donors in countries other than the United States, mainly the United Kingdom. 

The above figures do not include income derived from the sale of UNICEF greetings cards. While 2.2 million cards were sold in 26 countries in 1953, the number has risen to an estimated 21 million cards sold in the last campaign in over 110 countries and territories. The proportion of cards sold outside the 

United States has risen from 35 percent in 1953 to approximately 56 percent in 1961. Pending the issuance of the financial report, it is estimated that net income in the last campaign will be in excess of $1,200,000. 

Popular support for UNICEF continues to grow in many countries. In 1962 and 1963 there will be some additional organized campaigns for funds from the public in countries other than the United States. In Australia and New 

Zealand, with the concurrence of the Governments, UNICEF and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) are jointly approaching the public for funds in connection with the freedom-from-hunger campaign. There will be income from public campaigns connected with freedom from hunger in some European countries. In the coming years increasing emphasis will be put by 

UNICEF on fundraising from public sources.

STATEMENT OF DR. N. R. DANIELIAN, PRESIDENT, INTERNA- TIONAL ECONOMIC POLICY ASSOCIATION 

Dr. DANIELIAN. Mr. Chairman, it is always a pleasure to appear before this committee. It is a great disadvantage to follow a beautiful and charming lady as Mrs. Gray. I hope you will be indulgent in listening- 

Mrs. BOLTON. May I say, off the record- (Discussion off the record.)

Dr. DANIELIAN. I have no prepared statement but I have read the bill and have tried to analyze it, and if you will be indulgent with me I will try to go over, first, some general concepts and then some comments in detail.

I would like to cover briefly the role of foreign aid in the creation of stable and progressive democratic-inclined societies, the role of private enterprise in achieving this end, and the balance-of-payments situation and the foreign aid program. 

In carrying out the objectives of the Government with regard to the creation of independent, self-reliant, democratic-inclined societies, I think it is very important to analyze the elements that would ultimately create such results.

There has been a current in American thinking, the idea that just a mere improvement by 2 percent per year in the standard of living of people who start at a very low level will insure the creation of democratic societies in the next 5 or 10 years. 

I must say at the beginning, if you will permit me, that our organization and I personally support the foreign aid program. We continue to support it. We are stating these views primarily in the hope that gradually the program will evolve into a more effective instrument of U.S. foreign policy. 

I think the experiences of the last few weeks have indicated that standards of living or improvements, annual improvements in such standards of living, do not necessarily guarantee the creation of a stable and democratic society. What has happened in Cuba, what has happened in Argentina underline the fact that a pure economic approach to the question of creation of stable and democratic societies may not be effective. There is an element here of political stability that we have to strive for, because without political stability we are never going to have enough time to allow these countries to reach a condition of self-reliant, democratic self-government. 

I would like to urge a thorough reexamination of some of these basic concepts that motivate the foreign aid program. It seems to me that one of the primary things we need to achieve is political stability, because otherwise, even with the use of instruments of democratic elections, it is possible that some of these countries may revert to a system of society that is antithetical both to our interests and to the evolution of democratic societies. 

Our organization supports the military assistance program because we believe that through this program both in the international sphere as well as in the area of internal security we make a contribution to the

3 preservation of the free world community, as well as stable governments where they are threatened by subversive elements within the country.

In this concept, I think private investment and private enterprise has a great role to play. I think the history of the evolution of democratic society in the West-in England, France, and the United States would indicate those people who have a vested interest to defend even against the encroachments of established authority are the ones who are going to fight for representative government. 

We are very happy, therefore, to note the emphasis that the present administration is giving to the development of private ownership of housing, private ownership of farms, channelizing the aid program through institutions of investment which have as their purpose the encouragement of private business-native owned or in partnership with American or Western European technologically and managerially qualified entities.

I think this should be encouraged, and the more of the aid funds that are channelized in such a way as to encourage the proliferation of privately owned institutions and property in those societies, the more allies we are going to have in defense of democratic institutions. 

You will note that the Communist theory is to eliminate the middle class, the bourgeoisie, which is, in their vocabulary, all propertyowning classes, and depress everyone into the proletariat. 

It seems to me that it should be a cardinal principle of our foreign policy to build up the middle class. And the way to build up the middle class is to give them the incentives and the opportunity to become entrepreneurs and farmers and homeowners in their own right. 

Our organization has developed several principles on the encouragement of private enterprise through the foreign aid program. With the permission of the chairman, I would like to make it available for the record so that it can be the basis of some further investigation along these lines.

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. (The information above referred to is as follows:) 

RECOMMENDED LINES OF DEMARCATION BETWEEN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS IN THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE FOREIGN AID PROGRAMS 

Projects or activities proposed to be financed under any U.S. grant, aid, or loan program, either in dollars or local currencies, will fall into one or the other of the following categories: (1) Public services: Roads, harbors, airports, sewage treatment and disposal, schools and similar non-revenue-producing, public-type facilities—these must necessarily be public activities. (2) Utility services: Railroads, airlines, buslines, navigation companies, water supply, dams, electric power, communications, and similar services which are income producing. Although these services are private enterprise activities in the United States, in countries where it is the traditional practice to conduct such activities on a governmental basis or where the nature of the particular project (such as size of investment) presents some insuperable obstacle to private enterprise undertaking, the project will of necessity fall in the public sector. The 

United States will respect local customs. It is not the purpose of the U.S. economic policy, however, to finance the transfer of such activities from the private to the public sector. 81496-62-pt. 5-13

(3) Manufacturing, farming, mining, smelting, drilling, and similar production of basic materials, and the processing of raw materials and food. In these fields, the following categories or choices are given in the order of prefer ence of the U.S. Government: 

A. Private financing, ownership and operation.

B. Combination public and private financing, and private ownership and operation. 

C. Public financing, but private operation and control. 

D. Public financing, public ownership, but private management, with provision for spinning of stock ownership to private investors, management, workers, customers, etc., over a period of time.

E. Public financing, public ownership, and public management. This is the end objective of Communist ideology, inconsistent with personal freedom of individuals in society, and should not be financed by U.S. taxpayer money, except for the most pressing reasons of military security or political alliances. Even in these cases, an effort should be made to obtain provisions for later transfer of control, management, and ownership to private hands through distribution of the ownership rights to citizens of the country. (4) Wholesale and retail distribution; commercial, professional, and technical services, including small businesses like the butcher, baker, shoemaker, plumber, electrician, grocer, private housing, etc.: These should be financed, owned, and operated primarily in the private sector, and where public funds are used, steps should be taken to insure ultimate private ownership and management. (5) Private financial institutions, such as investment companies, private banks, building and loan associations, farm credit banks for the purpose of facilitating saving and investment in the private sector of the economy, should be encouraged, with a view also of gradually reducing interest rates to foster private business activity.

Naturally, the most immediate problems in some of the underdeveloped countries have to do with the sustenance of life and the development of basic services without which economic growth is seriously impeded or made impossible. The cultivation of land for the provision of food is moreover of vital importance to buttress any industrial expansion. Consequently, the institution or expansion of agrarian reform measures by the Government of these newly developing countries is to be actively encouraged, with as much emphasis as may be prac ticable in the circumstances on the private ownership of land and its produce. 

Where conditions permit, the local government should be encouraged to make land available for acquisition and ownership by candidate farmers, such acquisition to be financed by long-term loans or comparable credit arrangements, preferably through private local agencies. But whatever the form or source of the financing, technical assistance to new farmers through local training must, wherever possible, be made available to increase their chances of success and independence.

There is need in such countries for lending or other farm credit agencies not only to finance the acquisition, or interim rental, of farmland but also to provide working capital to the farmer for the procurement of seed, animals, implements, and supplies (in relationship to his need for, and his ability to use, such items). 

Such agencies should preferably be private institutions, though perhaps governmentally assisted, to make credit available for new private enterprises. 

There is also need for industrial and commercial lending or credit agencies for longer term developmental financing, privately managed, to encourage new private enterprises to meet the growing needs and markets that will develop as a result of the basic economic program. Interest rates in relending publicly provided capital must be reasonable in order to encourage private enterprise. 

In order to insure efficiency and economy, to expedite the work, and to allow time for the training of native personnel in the conduct of the basic public and utility services being financed, it is recommended that qualified private organizations be utilized to build the project, directly or through subcontracts, and to operate it until local personnel have been trained in the management, operation, and maintenance of the project. Only in that manner, rather than by releasing funds unconditionally to the local government to build the project on its own, will there be assurance that the country will benefit fully from the expenditures made for the new facility.

In supporting the use of the institution of free private enterprise in the situations above indicated, the Government of the United States does not purport to accept or condone all of the practices of private employers in every part of

M. 1 the world. In fact, it is recognized that in certain instances the practices followed have been such as would offend the conscience of public opinion in the United States. Therefore, it must be stated here that although the U.S. Government does not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries, our concepts of enlightened private enterprise support the gradual improvement of wage standards and health and welfare measures, within the limits of productivity of the country's economy and its industry. 

These detailed guidelines are issued to implement the guideline policy statement previously issued by the Department of State to its representatives in connection with the encouragement of private enterprise in the foreign economic programs of the United States. 

Dr. DANIELIAN. The committee made very extensive improvements upon the bill last year. It is to be congratulated for taking such pains with the bill that was presented to it last year. 

I want to commend particularly the attention that the committee paid last year to the question of the balance of payments. As some of you will remember, we were among the first to raise the red flag about the importance and significance of the balance-of-payments problem. As time goes on, you will find that it is a controlling factor in not only the foreign aid policy but also in almost all aspects of our economic picture today.

The committee's improvements had to do primarily with the emphasis placed upon domestic procurement. This has been very salutary. I think this now has become national policy, proclaimed by the President.

There seems to be some question as to how effectively it is being applied, because it has been testified by spokesmen of the administration before other committees that the foreign aid program itself is still responsible for $1,400 million worth of outflow of purchasing power. This is equal to the so-called basic balance-of-payments deficit last year.

It is therefore important for this committee to find out whether there are ways and means of having somewhat better control over this situation, because as a result of this continued outflow some very important programs are being advocated by the Government, having to do not only with wages and prices but also having to do with the treatment of U.S. foreign investments abroad.

In other words, the Congress is in a position on the one hand of appropriating taxpayers' money which is being spent abroad causing balance-of-payments deficit, on the other hand it is anxiously trying to devise means of controlling the balance-of-payments deficits by imposing penalties upon private investors abroad. 

There is a little conflict of interest here, I think, in the appropriating authority in Congress. I think that to the extent that control can be obtained over this outflow of dollars, then some of these other measures which are being proposed may not be necessary. 

It is well known that international agencies have provisions in their charters that make it impossible to indicate procurement in any particular country. This must be kept in mind in any appropriations made to international agencies.

I think the amount of money involved as far as the United Nations is concerned is not very large. So I don't think this need be necessarily applied to that. But other institutions such as the International 

Monetary Fund, the International Development Association, World 

Bank, they all have charter provisions which say that the agency cannot direct the procurement under the loans to any specified country.

Last year this committee made a great improvement in the procurement sections of this bill, in section 604. But in conference, without adequate consideration by the committee, came a provision, section 205, which says in effect that 10 percent of the funds appropriated by title I may be turned over to the International Development Agency for use pursuant to the International Development Association Act and the articles of agreement of the association. 

So, whereas in section 604 the committee was trying to get control of this situation, because of the balance-of-payments situation, section 205 that was inserted-I don't know at whose suggestion in conference committee-appropriated 10 percent of the funds to an international agency over which the United States could have no control insofar as procurement policy is concerned. 

I would therefore suggest, and I am not against the use of the international agencies-I am only concerned about this balance-of-payments situation. I would therefore suggest that perhaps the committee would like to amend this section 205 to say that the money should be used pursuant to section 604 of the bill instead of the articles of the association. Since this is an additional contribution to the 

IDA, it does not involve any violation of the charter provision, because IDA can accept money under specified provisions. 

It would seem to me that in order to make the problem a little clearer, perhaps you would want to reemphasize the application of section 604 to title VI, the Alliance for Progress program. 

We support the Alliance for Progress program. I think it is one of the highlights of this administration's contribution to the foreign aid field. On the other hand, we want to make sure that it does not aggravate some of the financial and fiscal problems that we are faced with in this country. 

Our calculations indicate that this bill, plus other foreign aid programs underway, some proposed, some approved, including this bill, Public Law 480 extension, the military assistance program and the contributions that are promised, or suggested to international agencies, amounts to about $8,120 million. 

In addition to that, in this bill, there is a guarantee program of $1,300 million, a housing program of $60 million, and some other items which make another $1,500 million available for investment projects. 

This is a very considerable contribution by the United States and the U.S. taxpayers to this foreign aid effort. It is far beyond the 1 percent limit that we have been talking about with other nations. I think it is well to emphasize this in our international communications, not confine our comparisons to the existing foreign aid-to the aid bill itself-but consider the totality of our effort in this field. It comes pretty close to almost 2 percent of our gross national product. 

Therefore, I think we are in a stronger position to insist on participation by other nations in this effort. Perhaps the committee would consider a more specific directive to the President in the present bill, directing the negotiation through the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development, OECD, the conclusion of an agreement with the other nations for their participation on an agreed basis in this foreign aid program. Until there is growing interest in this matter in Congress it is not likely that we are going to get a very enthusiastic response from the other countries.

It seems to me that a recognition of the importance of this through a suggestion in this bill, encouraging the President to arrive at such an agreement and to report back on the results of the negotiations through OECD would be very helpful in impressing upon the other countries the importance that the Congress of the United States attaches to international participation in these programs. 

In the area of private investment in this field, it must be realized that most of the investable capital of the free world is in the hands of individuals, not in the hands of governments. 

In my travels I get the impression that many countries think that the U.S. taxpayer and institutionalized international lending agencies are limitless sources of capital. There is little understanding abroad that when we make these contributions we are really doing something for them which the U.S. Government does not do for its own people, not generally.

We are taxing our people in giving, at no interest, investment capital to them. They must be made to realize that the greatest amount of investment capital in the free world is in the hands of individuals, and to tap this, the individual investor must have some assurances of return and security of investment.

We have an investment guarantee program and the legislation authorizes the President to enter into investment guarantee programs covering expropriation, convertibility, and damage in case of war/or civil rebellion. 

Unfortunately many countries-and this is particularly true in South America and applies to the Alliance for Progress-many of these countries have refused to enter into an agreement on expropriation.

It seems to me that if you are promising them $20 billion in 10 years, of which at least $10 billion is supposed to come from private sources, then there must be a commitment by these governments on the security of that investment. Unless there is such commitment, the other $10 billion of the so-called Alliance for Progress is not going to be forthcoming. 

Our Government has a policy, announced publicly, that we cannot object, because of the sovereign power of the other countries, to expropriation; we insist only on adequate compensation. I am afraid that this theory, with the foreign aid program, is an invitation to many of these governments, with change of political atmosphere in the different countries, to expropriate and pay back through the foreign aid program the compensation to private investors. 

If we allow these two things to stand as they are, we may be encouraging the socialization of property in most of these countries. 

How do we get out of this bind? It seems to me that we may be reaching a period where some international conversations are called for concerning the role of private capital and private investment in this economic development program of the underdeveloped countries. 

But beyond that it seems to me that we should certainly insist as a condition of our foreign aid agreements with other nations that they make a commitment, either to approve a guarantee agreement with the United States, or as a part of the foreign aid agreement commit their nation for adequate compensation to any property owners that are divested through expropriation.

The next question that comes up is the method of measuring compensation. Again, here American and Western European and other investors are subject to the vagaries of local situations, local juridical systems and so on. And since this is an international program in which the United States, the United Nations, the OECD, are interested, it would not be inappropriate to raise the question of creating a machinery for the settlement of claims. 

Perhaps some arrangement should be initiated by the State Department with other nations to establish a court of arbitration in cases of property compensation in case of expropriation. 

These are suggestions I think that will take a little time to germinate. But I present them to the committee because in the long run. these programs are not going to operate very successfully, unless private investment is secure. Neither the foreign aid program nor the existing flow of private capital will be sufficient to raise standards of living of 2 billion people around the world fast enough to prevent the revolutionary movements. If we are going to mobilize the total resources of the free world, we have to do some of these things in order to insure the continued flow of capital into these underdeveloped countries. 

As a last word, I want to say that the present AID deserves sympathetic consideration. They have just come into the job. I think they should be given another year or two before they find their direction and tighten up the administrative machinery. 

For one, I am inclined to be less critical this year with regard to the administration because it is only fair to give the AID officials an opportunity to prove what they can do. 

There is one other provision of the bill that I think deserves attention. Last year the committee in its good judgment inserted a provision which prohibited the procurement of drug products, and I think this should apply to all products, from countries which violate the patent rights of the United States. The present bill eliminates this provision.

I think from a balance-of-payments point of view, as well as the equity of the situation, it would seem to me that a provision to require strict adherence to section 604, plus the respect for the patent rights of U.S. citizens, should be included in this bill. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.
