Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Seely-Brown.

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. I would like to ask one question. 

Would you care to comment on the statement that many other witnesses have made; namely, that as we increase the amount of our aid in South America a great deal of South American private capital is leaving the area, and being sent over to Swiss banks? In other words, we find ourselves in a bind right on that particular point. 

I wondered if you would care to comment on it, on what we could do to prevent that from happening, if it is happening? 

Dr. DANIELIAN. My observation is that it is happening. I was in 

Mexico in January, and as compared with the previous year when I visited the country, I was informed that the balance-of-payments situation of Mexico had deteriorated to the extent of about $180 million, and that much of it was accountable by the flight of capital, and they said, most of it Mexican capital.

Of course, these are not verifiable. They are statements of knowledgeable individuals. I have heard of figures as high as $3 billion a year flowing out of all of South America to Europe. 

I think this is the reaction to the political instability which the revolutionary forces have let loose upon the continent. I don't see that it can be corrected unless we reestablish stability. This is why I emphasize the importance of stability. Because I don't think we are going to be able to carry out this economic development program unless we do have political stability in those countries. 

Each country is a different political problem. It wouldn't serve any purpose to go into details as to the internal situation in each country. I think that perhaps this kind of an international convention concerning the protection of private investments which must lead, if taken seriously by the participating countries, to more serious and sympathetic approach to private investment, would possibly allay the fears of the whole citizenry as well as the foreign investors. 

I consider the execution of guarantee agreements either separately or under the foreign aid agreements with these countries, and the convention on the guarantee of adequate compensation, as two of the most important things our Government can do to encourage the economic development of these countries. Because I don't think there is enough capital that the taxpayers of different countries are willing or able to put up to do this development job. 

After all, taking the total figure of this bill, even if you take $5 billion, that is about $2.50 per capita for 2 billion underdeveloped people. 

How much economic development are you going to get out of it? And how long will you hold the dike on revolutionary movements with this type of aid program? Most of this goes into substructural investments, water purification. They need productive resources to pay the taxes that will support these services. 

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. Could I interrupt at this point, and ask the second question which I have asked many witnesses who have appeared here before you appeared, and that is, you have very properly in my opinion suggested that we should do all we can with the proper safeguards to encourage the investment of private capital in these underdeveloped countries. I am for that program. I am for that part of the program as it was written in the law last year. Do you feel that the recently passed tax bill in the House works in the same direction?

I am referring particularly to that section of the tax bill which is now over in the Senate that applies to the taxation on American firms that are either wholly owned or subsidiary firms in foreign countries. 

Dr. DANIELIAN. I have a very deep conviction with regard to that subject, Mr. Congressman. I think we are following an entirely wrong international economic policy in the concept which has been presented to various congressional committees that by certain devices we are going to keep industry here and we will have economic growth in the United States instead of in some other countries. 

I think that this is the same kind of mistake that we made, say, in the last 15 years, when at the beginning we thought we were going to have a monopoly of atomic weapons. We think that we are going to keep technology and management and so on an American monopoly by creating handicaps to American business going abroad.

My own thinking in this is that the future of American business and also the balance-of-payments problem is an increasing amount of investment in safe income-bearing investments, because return on capital is one of the three important ways in which we earn money abroad. 

One is exports. The other is sale of services, and the third one is income on investments. 

The place where we should permit income-bearing investment is in convertible, safe countries because there is where you can earn money and bring it back home.

Some of these other countries-under this bill, for instance, we are going to make no-interest loans by the hundreds of millions. It is very doubtful that these funds will be returned. 

To encourage U.S. private business to go into these areas you have to eliminate the risk element. You can eliminate it in one or two ways.

You can give them an opportunity to make such whopping profits in 2 or 3 years that they can get their money out in the short run when they can predict the political atmosphere. Or you have to give them investment guarantees so they can go in there with some security of recapturing their investment.

The future economic development of the world I foresee is going to be in the development of regional areas, like the Common Market in 

Europe, the Common Market in South America, Central America.

Possibly we should encourage common markets in Africa and southeast Asia because common markets are workable where there is a similarity and equality of standards of living and wage levels, and some interchangeability of not only management and capital but also mobility of labor.

With this kind of system then, I think we should encourage the investment of American private capital into these areas. I think that if we do this persistently enough, as England did for 150 years and Germany is doing now, we will have income on investment which will come in handy to pay for some of these other programs that we are appropriating by this bill and other bills before Congress. 

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. Thank you very much.

STATEMENT OF THOMAS J. BEDDOW ON BEHALF OF CHARLES 

PFIZER & CO., INC. 

Mr. BEDDOW. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I appreciate very much the opportunity to appear before you. I appear here on behalf of the Charles Pfizer Co., Inc., which is in the drug and pharmaceutical business.

I wish to oppose section 301 (a) of the draft bill of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962, which I understand is before you for consideration. Section 301 (a) of the draft bill provides for the repeal of section 606 (c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. 

Section 606 (c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, in substance, prohibits the use of foreign aid appropriations for the purchase of foreign drugs and pharmaceuticals pirated from American patentholders.

1 This provision was enacted by the 87th Congress in response to the conflict between the Constitution's policy to promote the progress of science and useful arts by giving inventors exclusive rights for a limited time to their inventions, on the one hand, and the increasingly widespread practice of U.S. Government procurement agencies deliberately to infringe U.S. patents particularly in the drug and pharmaceutical field-on the other. 

The practice of U.S. procurement agencies deliberately to infringe 

U.S. patents is of recent origin. 

In 1910 Congress passed a statute the forerunner of what is now 28 U.S.C. 1498-giving a patentholder the right to sue the United 

States in the Court of Claims for damages where the United States had infringed his patent. Such infringements by the United States were apparently unwitting violations in the usual case, and the sole purpose of the 1910 act, as indicated by its legislative history, was to give a patentholder a remedy where none had theretofore been available because of the inability of the patentholder to sue the Government without its consent. 

In line with this congressional purpose, until 2 or 3 years ago it was the policy of Government procurement agencies when buying a patented item to buy either from the patenholder or one of his licensees.

However, in the last few years, the Comptroller General of the United States has issued several opinions-see, for example, 38 Comp. Gen. 276-in which he, in effect, has construed 28 U.S.C. 

1498 as a statute which not only authorizes the United States to infringe patents but also compels the United States to deal with an infringing source for patented items where the infringing source is the cheapest source.

Operating under the cloak of these opinions, the Defense Medical Supply Center, formerly called the Military Medical Supply Agencywhich acquires drugs and pharmaceuticals for the Defense Establishment has been especially active in buying drugs and pharmaceuticals, covered by U.S. patents, from foreign copiers of the inventions covered by such patent rights. 

The Veterans' Administration has made similar purchases, and my understanding is that like acquisitions may have been made with foreign aid funds. For example, the two agencies just mentioned have bought large quantities of tetracycline tablets from Italian manufacturers. Charles Pfizer & Co., Inc., holds a U.S. patent on the product tetracycline and on processes for its manufacture. The Italian manufacturers have deliberately pirated and copied the Pfizer invention, and the purchases made by the Defense Medical Supply Center and Veterans' Administration from the Italian manufacturers violate the Pfizer patent.

This is the plight of the U.S. patentholder: The U.S. Government issues him a patent and says to him by so doing, "This is the guarantee of the U.S. Government that (at least in this country) your invention is protected from pirating."

A foreign manufacturer, in a land which will give no protection to the U.S. patentholder, pirates the protected invention. He did not have to invest in the complicated apparatus of modern research; he did not have to think any original thoughts; he did not have to sweat

He over the invention, or test it, or develop it, or market it. He did not have to nurse it to commercial maturity. In most instances, he need not pay U.S. social security or State and Federal income taxes. is free from the burden of various laws enacted to protect American labor. His costs are low, his investment small, and the booty of his piracy will be cached in a foreign land. He would like to tap the rich 

American market. And he can do so with the help of the same U.S. 

Government which granted the patent protection in the first place. 

Of course, the procurement agencies of our Government have sought to justify their infringing purchases of foreign drugs and pharmaceuticals on the ground that these purchases have saved money. But this claim is lacking in essential validity. 

In ascertaining whether money is saved, it is not enough to compare the contract prices for the infringing foreign-produced drugs with the lowest prices offered by domestic producers for domestic-produced drugs. The foreign-produced drugs cost more than the price quoted in the applicable contracts. There are a number of hidden costs incurred in the procurement of the foreign drugs. Among these are the following: (1) Transportation charges; (2) Expenses of sending inspection personnel abroad (such as 

Food and Drug Administration inspectors); (3) The extra administrative expenses of the Defense Medical Supply Center, FDA, and possibly other agencies of the Government as well, incident to foreign purchases; (4) The damages payable by the United States for patent infringement; (5) The loss of income tax revenues and import duties by the Federal Government; (6) The loss of tax revenues by State and local governments in the United States; (7) The loss of jobs by American workers; (8) The evasion of governmental policies established for the social protection of American workers (such as the Walsh-Healey Act); and (9) The damage done to American inventive incentive and American enterprise.

When these hidden costs are added to the contract prices for the foreign-produced material, any claim that money has been saved by the foreign purchases is indeed highly questionable. 

Not only have the foreign infringing purchases of drugs and pharmaceuticals by our Government been doubtful moneysavers, but it is clear that such purchases have contributed to our country's imbalance of international payments concerning which there is so much public and private concern these days. Just in the past 2 years, the 

Defense Medical Center and Veterans' Administration have spent over $3,400,000, directly in U.S. dollars, for just one foreign drug- 

Italian-produced tetracycline. 

Now I am obviously not going to contend before your committee that the retention of section 606 (c) in the Foreign Assistance Act will completely cure the situations I have dealt with in this statement. 

What is ultimately required to effect an across-the-board cure is legislation-such as H.R. 6811 introduced by Congressman Roudebushbroadly prohibiting the United States from intentionally violating

1 U.S. patent rights except where the national security otherwise requires.

Pending the enactment of such legislation, however, the 87th Congress took an important step in the right direction when it enacted section 606 (c) of the Foreign Assistance Act. That step forward should not now be lost by a repeal of the section. The section should be retained not alone because equity and justice and morality commend it but also because it is in the national interest. 

Thank you.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Beddow.

STATEMENT OF DUMOND PECK HILL, REPRESENTING AEROMARITIME, INC. 

Mr. HILL.  

May I say something off the record. (Discussion off the record.)

Mr. HILL. Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, my name is 

Dumond Peck Hill and I am a member of the law firm of Surrey, Karasik, Gould & Greene, located in the Woodward Building in Washington, D.C. I am appearing today on behalf of Aeromaritime, Inc., 1000 Vermont Avenue NW., Washington, D.C.

Mr. Chairman, I am here today to protest unwarranted and unfair governmental competition with private business. Aeromaritime and numerous other companies in related lines of business have suffered irreparable damage as a result of such competition and interference. 

In order to highlight the problem, I would like at this point to cite one concrete case. I would like to say at this point that this matter is still under consideration in the Department of Defense and has been for some several months. 

Aeromaritime is the exclusive sales agent for oversea sales to all foreign customers, with certain minor exceptions, of the Government Electronics Division of the Admiral Corp. of Chicago, Ill. 

Aeromaritime's English subsidiary spent approximately 1 year attempting to sell an electronic test equipment known as the AN/UPM- 98 to the British Admiralty. The Admiralty had decided to place this order with Aeromaritime but just before doing so it received an offer from the U.S. Navy. The U.S. Navy, in its offer to the 1021

Admiralty, took the irregular and unwarranted action of informing the British Government that the equipment was not available commercially and could only-I repeat "only"-be purchased through the 

U.S. Navy. 

In actual fact, the AN/UPM-98 has been sold by private companies, pursuant to valid export licenses, approved by the Department of Defense, to no less than six foreign governments. 

It has been put out on invitations for bid which means that any electronic manufacturing company can have access to the technical information. It has also been exhibited at the Paris Air Show. 

The Department of the Navy at first denied that such statement could have been made and then-after having been presented with written evidence of the event-defended its position on the grounds that security was involved. 

In actual fact, an identical piece of equipment is sold commercially to leading aircraft manufacturers may I say here the vice president of the Admiral Corp., informed me that the best electronic engineer could not tell the difference in these two pieces of equipment in less than 2 or 3 days-and a unit almost identical to many customers in the civil aviation field. 

The security argument is particularly ridiculous in view of the fact that the AN/UPM-98 is a test set and the items which it was designed to test are in the hands of dozens of air forces and navies throughout the world.

Aeromaritime, Inc., is engaged in a respectable and praiseworthy business; that is, acting as manufacturers' export agent for a fairly large number of well-known, well-qualified and indeed, world-famous medium-sized electronic manufacturing corporations. 

We are submitting herewith for the confidential information of the committee a list of those corporations which Aeromaritime represents. 

May I submit this for the files of the committee? 

Chairman MORGAN. You do not want it in the record?

Mr. HILL. No, sir. I prefer they remain confidential. 

Chairman MORGAN. It will be in the files of the committee. 

Mr. HILL. Aeromaritime acts as their sales agent to foreign customers, including governments, in the sale of industrial, military, communications, and scientific electronic equipment produced by them. 

Aeromaritime has sales subsidiaries in three foreign countries and four more are currently in the process of formation. In addition, highly qualified technical representatives act as sales agents in about 30 additional countries. These subsidiaries and agents, on behalf of 

Aeromaritime, conduct vigorous and aggressive sales campaigns for their American principals, an activity which is completely in accordance with American trade policy.

The Department of the Treasury is calling for increased export sales in order to decrease the dollar gap and to decrease the outflow of gold.

The Department of Commerce and the AID are advocating more aggressive campaigns for the sale of American products and they are advising smaller and medium sized firms, when they cannot afford the luxury of in-house representation in foreign countries, to utilize the services of such joint agents. In international trade such joint export agents are referred to as combination export managers.

[ICA Small Business Memo] INDIRECT METHODS OF SELLING IN FOREIGN MARKETS (ITEM 1); SIX POINTS TO BE CONSIDERED IN EXPORTING (ITEM 2) 

(Item 1)

Indirect selling in foreign fields is conducted by selling to or through American export firms, American export agents, American export associations, combination export managers, foreign companies' purchasing agents in the United States or foreign sales representatives. It has advantages which appeal particularly to the U.S. manufacturer who is not ready to undertake a considerable direct investment in selling abroad. As against this are the disadvantages associated with any less expensive method of doing business. 

1. Probable advantages (a) Economy: Indirect selling is generally less costly in out-of-pocket disbursements and should help to keep down overhead. You may avoid many details of expense and be able to deal with a limited number of customers, including some located in the United States, where they can be reached with less expense. (b) Simplicity: Indirect selling is less elaborate in every respect, and particularly in the matter of handling shipments. 

2. Possible disadvantages (a) Remoteness: The indirect seller may be out of direct touch with his ultimate foreign customers. (b) Lack of control: Once goods are sold to a buyer for foreign resale, the manufacturer's control over them ceases, unless he has stipulated conditions as to resale prices, servicing of the product, advertising, etc. This places a heavy premium on picking reliable firms to deal with. (c) Reduced gross profit: Since a considerable number of the functions of exporting are handled by the firm to which goods are sold (e.g., credits, preparing shipments, oversea transportation * * *), a portion of the manufacturer's potential gross profit naturally goes to him to help defray these costs of operation, but these costs might well be less than the manufacturer's expenses in doing his own exporting. Which way net profit is affected depends on how efficiently the manufacturer could operate in direct selling. 

3. Channels of indirect selling

Following are the principal channels open to the manufacturer who wishes to sell indirectly for export, with a brief description of the functions of each: (a) The export commission house should be mentioned because its functions occasionally form a part of the business of other operators. Originally the export commission merchant was a buying agent in the United States for foreign customers. As such he assumed all credit risks. Usually he facilitated shipments. An executor of purchasing commissions, rather than a creative seller, he was most useful to producers who did not need or could not afford to create a demand abroad.

In dealing with an export commission house, you may be only one of many sources of supply and you have no control over the placing of orders. A form of export commission house has recently arisen, which acts not only as purchasing agent for a foreign importer, but for some manufacturers as selling agent. 

Such houses may even seek to represent a number of competing manufacturers. 

They may or may not assume credit risks. (b) The manufacturer's export agent: An agent, a firm or individual located in the United States (though sometimes with foreign offices) selling on commission for the manufacturer. This agent is primarily a salesman, hence is most

useful in the export of specialty products. His usefulness as a creative seller may, however, be limited by his undertaking to represent too many lines for adequate attention to all of them. He may or may not finance orders and/or assume credit risks. Most agents can handle the entire activity for their employers, including the various functions outlined under "Combination export manager" below. (c) The export merchant is a merchant, buying and selling for his own account in the expectation of reselling abroad. He assumes all credit risks and carries on the operation of shipping. He can be useful to the manufacturer whose volume will not permit direct selling abroad, yet whose product has features that lend themselves to constructive selling. (d) Export associations: The Export Trade Act, usually known as the Webb- 

Pomerene law, authorizes the organization and operation of cooperative business associations to engage in export trade, and, with certain restrictions, grants such associations an exemption from the antitrust laws. The Webb law associations are required to limit their operations solely to export trade to foreign countries, and therefore they may not do business in import trade or in trade within the United States or any of its territories or possessions or between the 

United States and the latter.

The associations operating under this law have achieved many advantages in their efforts to build up a profitable export trade, among which are agreements upon price and terms of sale to foreign buyers, the centralizing of sales effort or the setting up of a joint sales organization, thus making possible economies in sales costs, the better handling and filling of large orders, cooperation in such matters as packing, storage and warehousing, freight rates, cargo space, insurance, standardization of goods and inspection before shipment, the handling of claims of buyers, the adjustment of matters relating to credit, currency exchange, foreign government regulations and restrictions, tariffs quotas, etc., and many other things. 

Inquiries as to the operation of the Export Trade Act, and requests for conferences looking toward the organization of new associations, should be addressed to the Division of Export Trade, U.S. Federal Trade Commission, Washington, D.C. (e) The combination export manager: The combination export manager is an independent export executive or organization serving as export manager or department for two or more firms with the principal's status being that of client, not of direct employer.

The combination export manager handles most or all of the entire export functions for the principal; i.e., the selection of foreign agents; direction of foreign advertisement and promotion; handling of billing, financing and shipping details; and performing all other functions of an export department for a fee or commission, according to the particular arrangement with each client. combination export manager frequently assumes credit risks, or may be furnished funds by the principal for the various major expenses in connection with each export shipment.

The The number of combination export managers has increased greatly of recent years because of the success with which men of high caliber have handled combined functions. Export management calls for skill and experience of a high order, and capable export managers do not come cheaply. By contributing to the salary and expenses of a competent man and his staff, each participating company can get a far better grade of service than would be possible at an expense commensurate with small export sales volume. 

Although most of the business transacted under the ICA program is through regular commercial channels, a portion is still carried out through governmental missions and agencies. A list of foreign government purchasing missions and other official agencies under foreign government supervision which are engaged in purchasing goods and services may be obtained from the U.S. Department of Commerce.

How to get in touch with prospective distributors, agents or salesmen for export selling: Lists of firms abroad engaged in the import business are obtainable from the Office of Trade Promotion, Bureau of Foreign Commerce, U.S. 

Department of Commerce, banks, chambers of commerce, and other business service groups also may have valuable helps for new exporters. It is the occasional practice to advertise for agents abroad in export trade journals, or in local trade journals and newspapers abroad. Responses to such advertising should be carefully checked by personal interview, wherever possible, and not by letter alone.

1 

FOREIGN FREIGHT FORWARDER 

The technical details connected with the handling of a shipment of goods for export have given rise to employment by many sellers of a type of organization known as the foreign freight forwarder who is prepared to render valuable assistance. A competent and reliable freight forwarder is equipped to look after numerous phases of the shipping problem for the exporter, including all functions connected with transferring, documenting, and dispatching. He is well informed on ocean freight rates applying from the ports through which the exporter's merchandise moves, and can advise authoritatively on all ocean shipping matters. His activities keep him in constant touch with the many conditions of entry in foreign countries. He is prepared, therefore, to execute efficiently all necessary foreign consular and other documents. 

Forwarders may handle a shipment simply through the port of export or, by means of their correspondents abroad, take care of the shipment to virtually any destination overseas. Unless the business of the exporting company justifies the maintenance of an export office at one or more ports in the United States, the services of a forwarder usually are employed to take care, at least, of all details connected with clearance. 

The forwarder is prepared to assist the shipper in proper packing, marking, invoicing, and other matters to meet the requirements of the buyer and those of foreign governments. He takes over inland transportation of the goods to the most favorable port of exit in the most economical way. He arranges for transfer of the shipment upon arrival at the port, attends to customs clearance, arranges for vessel space and insurance coverage, and takes care of the preparation of consular invoices and often banking and collection papers. Some forwarders perform many related activities, such as banking, financing, insurance, warehousing, customs brokerage, and general counsel in foreign trade matters. 

Firms interested in procuring the services of a foreign freight forwarder can obtain a complete list of those forwarders who have, in accordance with the 

Maritime Administration General Order No. 72, registered with the Administra tion and received a registration number, by writing the Maritime Administration, 14th Street between E Street and Constitution Avenue NW., Washington 

25, D.C.

The Federal Maritime Board of the U.S. Department of Commerce has issued a revised list of ocean freight forwarders registered pursuant to Federal Maritime Board General Order 72.

The list is compiled in alphabetical order by city, listing the registered ocean freight forwarders in each city, and telling whether it is the main or a branch office of the forwarder. The list may be obtained gratis from the secretary, Maritime Administration, Washington, D.C. (Item 2)

EXPORTING UNDER ICA FINANCING 

Whether done under ICA financing or otherwise, the exporter should take certain precautions to make sure that all the necessary conditions preliminary to processing an order are complied with. 

ICA's Office of Small Business has from time to time received complaints from firms which have been informed by buyers or agents abroad that certain transactions were being financed by the International Cooperation Administration only to discover-after the commodities were produced-that no ICA subauthorization or letter of credit was forthcoming. Many U.S. sellers do not realize that foreign buyers are sometimes overoptimistic about the chance of getting dollar allocations for the products they wish to import. For this reason every supplier should be certain that each of the six steps described below is taken before he proceeds to fill any order to be financed by ICA. 

Step 1

Supply the foreign buyer with full information on your product and its price to assist him in getting an import permit. 

Step 2

In executing a definite sale contract or accepting an order be sure that it is contingent upon (1) your getting an export license, if required; (2) your customer getting an import permit, if required; and (3) your receipt of an irrevocable, confirmed letter of credit issued by a U.S. bank.

Step 3 

Secure an export license, if necessary. 

Step 4

Await the import permit number (if required) from your customer indicating that he has obtained the permit. 

Step 5

Make no commitments for raw materials and do not start manufacturing until you actually receive the export license, import license number, and letter of credit.

Check all of them carefully and compare them with the contract. If everything is correct, you can then process the order in your plant. If not, immediately inform the buyer and request that the necessary changes be made in the letter of credit. 

Step 6

Read the ICA regulations. Prepare your order for shipment; then ship, and invoice your goods exactly as provided for in the letter of credit. Take the shipping documents required by your letter of credit to the U.S. bank issuing the letter of credit, accompanied by ICA form 280, filled out as instructed by ICA regulations, and obtain payment from the bank in dollars. 

Mr. HILL. May I read just a few sentences from that memo from the Small Business Office of the AID: 

The combination export manager: The combination export manager is an independent export executive or organization serving as export manager or department for two or more firms with the principal's status being that of client, not of direct employer.

The combination export manager handles most or all of the entire export functions for the principal, that is, the election of foreign agents; direction of foreign advertisements and promotion; handling of billing, financing, and shipping details; and performing all other functions of an export department for a fee or commission, according to the particular arrangement with each client. 

The combination export manager frequently assumes credit risks, or may be furnished funds by the principal for the various major expenses in connection with each export shipment.

By contributing to the salary and expenses of a competent man and his staff, each participating company can get a far better grade of service than would be possible at an expense commensurate with small export sales volume. 

This is the position of one of our Government agencies. This is exactly where Aeromaritime fits.

Mr. Chairman, Aeromaritime is not the only American small business firm engaged in this activity. American leadership in the field of electronics has fostered a number of such firms. I know personally of at least a number of these firms right here in Washington and elsewhere engaged in similar activities, but unfortunately their number is decreasing due to the frustrating policies of the Department of 

Defense. 

The policies adopted by the Department of Defense result in the competition by the Government with private enterprise and have the even more drastic results of direct and active interference with the conduct of these firms' business.

As the committee is well aware, having written the basic legislation, the Foreign Assistance Act provides, in section 507, for the sale of military equipment to foreign governments by the U.S. Government. 

The basic authority first appeared in the Mutual Defense Assistance 

Act of 1949, as section 408 (e) and has been continued in all the suc-

india cessor statutes in essentially the same form. Despite the passage of time, operations under this section are still governed by a directive issued by the Department of Defense in 1952; that is, Department of 

Defense Directive 2110.13 of June 16, 1952. 

That directive specifies that prior to any sale being made to a foreign government, the military service concerned must first determine whether the equipment or materials "are known to be of the types and kinds not normally procured through commercial channels in the 

United States."

As a practical matter, the Department of Defense does not observe its own directives. This committee, no later than last year, at page 

60 of H.R. 851 of the 87th Congress, recommended that the Department of Defense reexamine its existing directives and take certain steps to insure that private enterprise was protected. 

Despite the committee's recommendation, the directive has not, to the best of our knowledge, been revised and, in fact, the Department, contrary to its own directives and contrary to the executive branch's and the Congress' policies of reducing Government competition with private enterprise to a minimum, has increased its emphasis on government-to-government sales.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF DEFENSE, 

Washington, D.C., February 7, 1962.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, 

House of Representatives,

International Security Affairs. 

DEAR MR. MORGAN: This letter is in reply to your letter of January 23, 1962.

The existing directives relating to the sale of unclassified equipment have been reexamined. Some aspects of the directives require technical revisions, for example, to correct references to obsolete statutes and Executive orders; however, we believe that the policies stated therein are still sound. 

In examining the question whether our sales program improperly competes with commercial suppliers, it would appear desirable that there be a clear consensus as to the precise issue involved. As we view the problem, commercial suppliers may be divided into three classes: (1) manufacturers; (2) surplus dealers; and (3) manufacturers brokers. Alleged competition depends on

whether the item sold by the Department of Defense is from DOD stocks or from new procurement.

If an item is being procured from a manufacturer by DOD for a foreign country, DOD is obviously not competing with the manufacturer. In such a case, there would not appear to be any significant degree of competition with a surplus dealer since the item is hardly likely to be surplus. If an item is being sold from U.S. stocks and replaced by procurement from a manufacturer, the same conclusions would appear warranted. 

If the item requested by the foreign country is surplus to DOD supply requirements, three alternatives are possible: (1) DOD could sell the item directly to the foreign country; (2) DOD could sell the item to a surplus dealer, who, in turn, would sell it at a higher price to the foreign country; and (3) DOD could scrap the items in its stocks and require the foreign country to purchase its requirements from new procurement or from a surplus dealer (the item may already be owned by surplus dealers). Alternative number (1) above has the obvious advantages of (a) avoiding waste; (b) saving the taxpayers' money; (c) providing our allies the maximum amount of defense for their dollar, thus improving their defense posture and encouraging further purchases from the United States; and (d) avoiding leadtime problems involved in new procurement. So strong are these advantages that serious consideration of the other two alternatives does not appear to be merited. 

Many manufacturers of defense equipment employ inhouse sales managers and staffs to solicit orders for defense equipment from foreign countries. In almost all cases there is complete cooperation between such a sales organization and those responsible for government-to-government sales. Their efforts are complementary rather than competitive. 

Accordingly, the businessman most affected by government-to-government sales, is the manufacturers broker who must effect a sale to earn a commission. 

It would, of course, be to his advantage if no government-to-government sales were authorized. Or, where there is a general policy rule to limit or curtail government-to-government sales of items "commercially available" to have this term as broadly construed as possible. In one sense all items of defense equipment are "commercially available." Sales transactions involving them could probably be effected at some point by private contracts between manufacturers and foreign governments. Such a construction, however, reduces the term to meaninglessness. In practice, government-to-government sales are normally made of items which have a military nomenclature and a military stock number. 

There are hundreds of thousands of such items. 

It has been, and continues to be, the policy of Defense that it intrude as little as possible into the direct channel between U.S. commercial sources and foreign consumers. All purchase requests are screened and normally are denied if the item requested is readily available from commercial sources. 

There are, however, necessary exceptions to the above when government-togovernment sales may be required in the national interest. These sales may involve the following: (a) Special international agreements.-As one example, the United States is participating in the current NATO effort to establish a spare parts supply management system. The countries participating in this system have agreed that countries having stocks in long supply will make them available for sale or redistribution to the other NATO countries needing them. As another example, an agreement between the United States and the Federal Republic of Germany, signed at Washington, October 8, 1956 (TIAS 3660; 7 U.S.C. 2787), provides that the U.S. Government, on the basis of requests submitted by the German Government, will undertake to sell military equipment, materials, and services to the German Government "in cases where such items and services can be made available for that purpose." In connection with current balance-of-payments negotiations an agreement was executed November 24, 1961, with Germany, which provides for the United States to procure items which are not standard military items but which are directly related to, or essential for, the operational capability of the armed forces of Germany. (b) Transition from grant aid to self-sufficiency.-Grant-aid countries cannot abruptly change their channels of supply when grant aid is terminated, and it is often necessary for the United States to facilitate the progress of such countries toward self-sufficiency by offering military sales services. (c) Stretching allied defense budgets. When a country's requirements are not large enough for economical production, U.S. military sales at standard prices are made. These sales provide more defense for the free world defense

dollar. When the United States holds stocks which can be sold at a reduced price, the effect is often to lower the amount of grant aid required. (d) Prudent management of DOD stocks.-The sale of unneeded U.S. stocks results in savings to the U.S. taxpayer. Government-to-government transactions of this type are advantageous in that they permit allied requirements to be met quickly and at a minimum cost. (e) Terms and conditions of sales.-Defense will sell to foreign governments and international organizations when certain terms and conditions of sale and management services, such as the extension of long-term credit, the acceptance of local currencies, and the stockage of a full range of items, are not available from industry. (f) Surplus property sales.-Surplus personal property and foreign excess property of general commercial use may also be purchased directly by foreign governments from the U.S. Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps on the same terms as other purchasers. 

We believe that the overriding U.S. interest, including the large volume of business for manufacturers which is generated by U.S. military sales, dictates the policy which we are following. 

Sincerely yours, 

(Signed) GENERAL PALMER. 

LAW OFFICES OF SURREY, KARASIK, GOULD & GREENE, 

Washington, D.C., March 9, 1962.

Hon. HAYDN WILLIAMS, 

Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs, Washington, D.O. 

DEAR MR. SECRETARY: This is in reply to your letter, reference I-1639/62, of March 2, 1962, in response to our previous letters concerning a proposed procurement of electronic equipment by the French Government from the U.S. 

Air Force on a government-to-government basis. I regret that we have been unable to convince the Department of Defense of the merits and of the equity of our case.

We take note that you have enclosed with your letter a copy of a letter dated February 7, 1962, to the Honorable Thomas E. Morgan, chairman, Committee on Foreign Affairs, U.S. House of Representatives, outlining Department of Defense policies with respect to the sale of military equipment to foreign governments. Inasmuch as we disagree categorically with certain of the conclusions set forth in that letter, we deem it pertinent to make our comments for record purposes. Furthermore, since this letter has been brought to our attention, we also deem it appropriate that our comments should be placed before Chairman Morgan and, accordingly, we are forwarding a copy of this letter to him.

In the letter from the Department of Defense dated February 7, 1962, it is set forth that the Department of Defense views commercial suppliers in three classes; i.e., manufacturers, surplus dealers, and manufacturers' brokers. 

Omitted from the Department's letter is the salient fact that there is a fourth and distinct class, which is manufacturers' export agents. The export agent is distinct from the broker in that the agent acts and conducts sales campaigns for the manufacturer, whereas the broker does not. The agent category comprises the gorup which suffers the greatest damage as a result of Department of Defense policy. 

Most of the major integrated producers of military electronic and similar hardware maintain manufacturers' representatives in every major capital of the world. These representatives are usually on the direct payroll of the parent company, or at least on the payroll of a subsidiary of the American company. Consequently, it is of little significance to either the major integrated company or to its representative whether a particular contract is placed on a government-to-government or on a private basis. 

Furthermore, the vast majority of negotiated contracts goes to the integrated major companies, and, therefore, these companies can be sure that a substantial portion of any government-to-government sales made as a result of their sales effort will be provided by them on a negotiated basis. Most of the medium-sized and smaller companies cannot, however, afford the luxury of full-time oversea representation. The overhead charges and the results produced make the maintenance of such an office too expensive and too burdensome.

1030

Consequently, these medium-sized and small companies resort to the technique of utilizing an American export agent who will handle all of their representation problems overseas with foreign governments and clients. Inasmuch as the American export agent will usually represent seven or eight or more of the smaller and medium-sized companies, the support of foreign offices can be justified and can be met. These foreign representatives who are employed by the American export agent perform valuable services in maintaining constant liaison with the foreign governments concerned and in promoting U.S. sales. 

If Department of Defense policies preclude this form of representation, the medium-sized and smaller companies are faced with an inexorable choice of expending huge quantities of money for a worldwide sales organization or else losing all possibility of foreign sales. 

The argument will, of course, be made that the sales effort of the Department of Defense can be and will be, conducted by our attachés and defense personnel abroad. Such cannot, and will not, be the case. 

In the first place, these attachés and personnel have no real incentive to sell equipment, since there can be no monetary return. 

In the second place, their tours of duty are relatively short and their knowledge of the complexities of modern military electronics must perforce be exceedingly abbreviated.

Finally, and most unfortunately, some of our attachés and defense personnel appear to have more interest in insuring that the British, French and Belgians receive a share of the military market than in promoting U.S. sales. 

Typical of this attitude is the well-authenticated rumor that senior U.S. military officials in Paris have officially complained of the activities of American commercial firms, and have requested the Pentagon to keep them at home because they allegedly interfered in the relationships with our allies. 

The case against the use of service attachés is well documented in the second report from the Select Committee on Estimates of the British Parliament, printed on June 17, 1959. It is interesting to note how much more successful the 

British sale of electronics and aircraft is in comparison with the sale of other British munitions. Electronics and aircraft are sold privately by the British, whereas munitions are sold on a government-to-government basis. 

With respect to the discussion of surplus equipment contained in the letter of February 7, 1962, we think the record should indicate that we have never seriously contended that the sale of surplus items on a government-to-government basis should be curtailed. 

The letter of February 7, 1962, notes that the efforts of "inhouse" sales staffs are complementary to, rather than competitive with government-to-government sales. This may be true with respect to large integrated companies, but it does not apply to smaller and medium-sized companies. 

In the first place, only the very largest enterprises can maintain an "in house" staff.

In the second place, there have been repeated instances where a smaller manufacturer who does not have exclusive right to a particular piece of equipment has conducted an intensive sales effort through export agents and then has seen the business go on a government-to-government basis, and the material, if not placed with the large integrated companies on a negotiated basis, put out for competitive bid. In such cases, he frequently loses the bid. This means that his sales effort was a waste of time and money and, even more significantly, that he will not in the future endeavor to sell equipment. 

It is axiomatic that absent a sales effort, no sale will be made and our foreign competitors will inevitably secure the lion's share of such business as is within their capabilities. Furthermore, the export agent has lost his commission and has wasted his time and effort. 

We disagree categorically with the conclusion contained in the February 7 letter that all government-to-government sales are screened and that the sales request is denied if the item is already available from commercial sources. We will be glad to submit an itemized list of instances where this has not been the case, although these facts are readily ascertainable from the Department's own files.

The Department notes that several exceptions are made in its alleged policy. 

Among these is the category of sales pursuant to special international agreements. We cannot disagree with the position that where sales are made pursuant to such agreements, they should be on a government-to-government basis.

1031 ம் We do, however, believe such agreements to be improvident in that they involve our military departments in the procurement of common use items and of items having no relation to military requirements. Furthermore, this results in direct competition with purely commercial enterprises and involves significant expense for the Department of Defense and the American taxpayer. 

Another of the noted exceptions is that of "stretching allied defense budgets." 

We categorically reject the proposition that U.S. policy should be based on a possible saving for a foreign military establishment at the expense of American small business.

As noted previously, the Department of Defense's policy not only results in the possibility of smaller dollar income being earned by the United States but also drastically reduces the possibility of sales being effected by removing the incentive to conduct aggressive sales' campaigns. The policy is, therefore, totally inconsistent with the U.S. fiscal policy which is to reduce the dollar gap by increasing the flow of dollars into the United States as a result of increased export sales.

The competition with smaller business by the Department of Defense not only reduces exports but also tends to widen the dollar gap in that the relatively minor administrative charge levied by the Department of Defense on these sales could not possibly cover the true administrative costs of its services. The scope of these services is indicated by the hosts of personnel involved. 

We have no comments in respect of the other noted exceptions; namely, transition from grant aid, prudent management of DOD stocks, sales on credit, and surplus property sales. 

In conclusion, we disagree with the proposition that the Department of Defense is following the spirit of its own directives. We disagree with the enunciated policy in many respects, and we cannot believe that the Department of Defense would intentionally injure small business, including both manufacturers and sales organizations, in order to effect possible savings for foreign governments, at the expense of our own balance of payments position. 

Respectfully submitted.

DUMOND PECK HILL. 

Mr. HILL. Up until this point, I have dealt mainly in generalities. 

Now let's get down to more specifics: (1) Aeromaritime, on behalf of several medium-sized electronic manufacturing companies, sold a large quantity of an airborne system to the French Government and subsequently an even larger order of the same materiel to the Federal Republic of Germany and also to the aviation division of Fiat in Italy. At the time of these sales the 

French Government indicated that it would probably require an additional quantity of these equipments which Aeromaritime then made an offer to supply.

Subsequently, the French indicated that they might be able to purchase the equipment from another NATO government which had these available and which were surplus to its needs. Our information now is that the French decided not to buy these equipments from the other NATO country and they attempted to obtain this additional equipment directly from the U.S. Air Force. 

This proposed procurement was vigorously protested to the Department of Defense by us. The Department of Defense, however, explicitly stated that the Department of Defense would proceed with the procurement irrespective of the fact that the same equipments were previously purchased on a commercial basis from Aeromaritime. (2) There have been repeated instances where the U.S. military services have actually bid on foreign procurements in competition with commercial sources. One specific case is a procurement by the 

Chilean Government.

The above cases are but a sampling of the problems involved and, therefore, I would like with the permission of the committee, to sub-

mit for the record the case history on some items where the Department of Defense has either engaged in unfair competition or in actual interference with private enterprise. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. (The information above referred to is as follows:) 

CASE HISTORIES Case No. 1-Sale of meteorological instruments, 1959 

During 1959, Aeromaritime's local representative in a Western European country located a requirement for meteorological instrumentation. Lengthy correspondence ensued and after much research on the part of Aeromaritime, a system of equipments was put together which met the requirements of the government in question. Two bidders were then invited to bid on the system which included upper air radiosondes, suitable ground tracking equipments, and recorders as well as test equipment and accessories. 

The two bidders which tendered acceptable bids were the Bendix International Corp. and Aeromaritime, Inc. While Bendix was able to offer all of this equipment from its own subsidiary, the Bendix-Frieze Division, Aeromaritime assembled the equipments from a number of small manufacturers who were also able to offer identical equipments acceptable to the government in question. 

Aeromaritime was the low bidder and the government in question informed Aeromaritime's local representative that an award would be made to Aeromaritime. Through channels, the U.S. Military Assistance Group in the capital of the foreign country concerned obtained information to the effect that this requirement existed and after an award had already been indicated to Aeromaritime, the MAG placed an offer lower in price than Aeromaritime before the authorities of the foreign government in question. 

At this point, Aeromaritime protested the action of the Department of Defense. Aeromaritime was informed that the U.S. Government would not withdraw its offer and thus the foreign government consummated the transaction with the U.S. Government. The The specific equipments in question have been sold by Aeromaritime, Bendix, and others many times, to a large number of foreign governments around the world commercially, both before and after this transaction took place. equipments were and are commercially available from at least two sources. 

A vice president of Aeromaritime had discussed the entire problem with representatives of the Department of Defense prior to the actual time that the Department of Defense placed its offer before the foreign government. The po- sition of the Department of Defense was, however, that the mere fact that the equipment was commercially available was insufficient reason for the Department of Defense to withhold a bid to the foreign government. 

Case No. 2-Sale of control panels for radar set, 1961

Aeromaritime, for several years, has sold a certain control panel for a piece of airborne radar equipment which is manufactured by the Packard-Bell Electronics Corp. Thousands of these have been sold commercially and delivered to perhaps a dozen countries in Western Europe. In December of 1961 the air force of a government in Western Europe requested a routine quotation for 120 of these control panels from Aeromaritime and a responsive bid to the customer was immediately returned. 

Aeromaritime was subsequently advised that this order was placed on a government-to-government basis with the U.S. Government. This particular customer among many others had purchased the identical control panel under identical nomenclature from Aeromaritime on a commercial basis about 9 months before this event took place. 

Caso No. 3-Sale of spare parts for airborne radar equipment, 1961 

During 1960 and 1961, Aeromaritime furnished the government of a major Western European country several hundred airborne radar equipments. The government requested late in 1960 that Aeromaritime research and provide an extensive breakdown of spare parts for the maintenance of these equipments. 

The manufacturer involved and Aeromaritime spent very considerable sums of money preparing very extensive lists of the required spare parts and pricing them from over 200 sources.

All of this information was presented to the government in question which subsequently informed Aeromaritime that these requirements were obtained directly from the U.S. Government. 

Case No. 4-Sale of radar test sets, 1961 

The navy of a Western European government invited Aeromaritime to bid on 32 modification kits required to upgrade 32 radar test sets in the possession of the foreign Navy concerned. In June of 1961, Aeromaritime offered the specific modification kits required in the bid and in November of 1961 Aeromaritime was informed the modification kits had been obtained directly from the U.S. Navy. 

Case No. 5-Sale of radar test sets, 1960–62 

As the committee is undoubtedly aware, aircraft manufacturers located in Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Italy are manufacturing under licenses from the Lockheed Aircraft Corp., the F104-G Starfighter aircraft. The aircraft contains in it an airborne radar equipment which requires a particular radar test set for proper maintenance. Aeromaritime and its representatives promptly contacted the four governments in question. 

Knowing the need for the radar test set by one of these governments, Aeromaritime made an unsolicited offer to the air force of the government through its local representative. Originally, this proposal was well received and the foreign air force in question indicated that there was an excellent possibility that an order would be forthcoming. 

Subsequently the foreign air force advised an Aeromaritime representative that it could not utilize the offer because these equipments would be obtained through other channels and that Aeromaritime's offer would not be taken into consideration. All information on the progress of this matter was shut off from 

Aeromaritime by the foreign air force concerned and Aeromaritime's representative was advised later, informally, that local U.S. Government officials insisted on handling this business themselves. 

As it turned out, the U.S. Government was unable to supply the equipment in sufficient time to cover the initial requirements. Thus, the Lockheed Aircraft 

Corp. purchased an initial quantity of these equipments from Aeromaritime's manufacturing source. The balance of the requirements which have been in existence for over a year and a half are currently under negotiation for special procurement by the Department of Defense. 

The net result of this particular operation has been: (1) That Aeromaritime, which is the export representative of the manufacturer of the radar test set involved and which did most of the sales work, has gained absolutely no benefit from it. (2) That the Lockheed Aircraft Corp., who did very little work in the matter, has wound up making the profits on the sale of a part of the business. (3) That the foreign government concerned has waited for nearly a year and a half to fill the balance of its requirements. (4) That the U.S. Government still has not obtained the balance of the equipment for the foreign government. 

Mr. HILL. The Department of Defense still gives lipservice to its own directives but it is obvious in the letter from General Palmer to Dr. Morgan, which has previously been inserted in the record, that the exceptions to the policy are so many and so varied that the policy itself does not even exist. For example, the Pentagon asserts that it wishes to conserve our allies' defense dollar and will sell equipment when a sale will have that result. 

It seems somewhat strange that in view of the flow of gold problem and the export drive, that a U.S. Government agency would be interested in conserving the dollars of West Germany, France, or Italy. 

It should also be recognized that government-to-government sales as presently handled represent a hidden subsidy to the purchasing government. The Department of Defense sells at cost to itself with the addition of 5or 6-percent overhead charge for its services. 

You gentlemen, who are familiar with business practice, know that no business can be handled anywhere at a 6-percent overhead. The 81496-62-pt. 6- -2

point is particularly proven by the vast number of persons in the Department of Defense engaged in sales activities. It is obvious that the difference between the 6-percent overhead charge and the true cost, whatever it may be, represents a hidden subsidy to the purchasing government.

The Department of Defense has defended its position on the ground that any item which bears a military nomenclature is a military item and should be sold on a government-to-government basis. Suffice it to say that there are some hundreds of thousands of items which bear military nomenclature and military stock numbers. The list includes nylon stockings, canned milk, shoelaces, ladies' underdrawers, 155-mm. guns, oyster forks, guided missiles, destroyers, and pencils. 

The question may well be asked "Why does it matter whether a particular piece of equipment is sold by the Government or by a manufacturer's export agent?" The answer is that the manufacturer's export agent conducts a vigorous sales campaign; the Government does not. In the second place, the Government policy imposes a real hardship on smaller and medium-sized business. The integrated giants can afford the luxury of inhouse representation in every capital; the smaller and medium-sized companies cannot. 

The Government's policy removes the incentive to the smaller and medium-sized companies to push their products. There have been instances where a medium-sized company has conducted an aggressive campaign to establish requirements abroad only to have the Government sell the equipment and then put the equipment on an invitation for bid with the end result that some other company secured the business.

Obviously, there is no incentive to smaller companies to conduct a sales campaign. In the case of the larger companies which maintain inhouse representation, the items sold usually go on a negotiated basis and, therefore, the question of who effects the sale is immaterial to these larger companies. Again, small business and the mediumsized businesses are penalized. 

The argument will undoubtedly be made and has been made by the Pentagon that our military attachés and MAAG personnel will sell equipment for U.S. companies. This is patent nonsense, since (1) there is no incentive to forcefully push sales, (2) tours of duty are too short, and (3) such personnel are usually not electronics specialists. 

In this connection-I will not make a request that this be included in the record--a report by the Select Committee on Estimates of the British Parliament dealing with the question of government-togovernment sales, and the role of service personnel in pushing such sales. Suffice it to say that the committee is highly critical of the performance of military attachés in this area. 

In addition, the statistics contained in this report with respect to the relative success of the British in achieving government-to-government sales as compared with achieving commercial sales gives adequate and eloquent testimony to the superiority of the commercial sale technique of pushing exports.

Mr. Chairman, this is a subject which could be discussed at much greater length and in much greater detail. In the interest of brevity, however, I would now like to suggest a solution to the problem. As you know, last year an amendment was introduced by Mrs. Kelly dealing

1 with this topic.

The amendment provided for a new subsection (c) 

to be added to section 507 of the Foreign Assistance Act as follows: 

(c) No sale of equipment or materials which are available commercially in the United States shall be made under the provisions of this section: Provided, however, That the provisions of this subsection shall not apply to classified or excess equipment or materials or to sales of equipment and materials made to the government of any economically underdeveloped nation. 

We endorse this amendment. You will notice that this is not an amendment which would line anyone's pockets nor is it one which would legitimatize a grab of business. 

The proposed amendment is rather a carefully reasoned piece of legislation which gives due and just weight to foreign policy considerations while, at the same time, protecting U.S. business against unfair competition and against undue interference. 

In the first place, it exempts from its operations all classified material, thereby insuring that the security interests of the United States will be protected. Furthermore, the U.S. Government still maintains security control over any sensitive item by means of the export control technique which was enacted into law at the recommnendation of this committee. 

In the second place, the amendment in no way tampers with the situation where equipment is sold which is surplus to the actual needs of the various services. It would be foolhardy for private enterprise to contend that such equipment should not be sold for the mutual profit of the U.S. Government and the purchasing government. 

In the third place, it exempts sales to economically underdeveloped nations. We, as well as the rest of the industry, recognize that in some of the underdeveloped countries there is not the expertise to procure wisely and economically. Here, however, it is believed desirable to interject a word of caution with respect to the interpretation of the phrase "to the government of any economically underdeveloped nation." 

The use of the phrase "underdeveloped countries" is tied into the AID definition of what constitutes a developed country. Obviously, if this amendment were to be interpreted as giving the Department of Defense "carte blanche" to sell on a government-to-government basis to all underdeveloped countries in all circumstances, the purpose of the amendment would be defeated. 

For example, Argentina and Spain fall into the technical classification of "underdeveloped countries"; nevertheless, as we all know, Argentina and Spain have highly sophisticated economies and governmental apparatus. Consequently, we would earnestly hope that if the committee, in its wisdom, does adopt the amendment in its entirety, that the committee would express itself in its report as intending that the Department of Defense would encourage commercial sales in the case of countries with more highly developed economies even though such countries might technically qualify as underdeveloped.

With some such clear statement of congressional intent, we agree completely that this area may be handled on a government-to-government basis as circumstances may dictate. 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee, with the one qualification noted, we most earnestly recommend the enact-

ment of this piece of legislation. We believe that it would eliminate a most undue and most unwarranted competition with private enterprise.

Even more importantly, it will eliminate a gross form of interference with private enterprise and American salesmanship, which interference is in direct conflict with the statement of intent contained in section 601 of the act. We would have hoped that the Department of 

Defense could have set itself aright on this score but the events of last year conclusively prove that that unfortunately is not the case.
