(The following information has been submitted for inclusion in the record at this point:)

The executive branch strongly opposes the proposed amendment to section 507 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, presented in testimony before this committee on April 18, 1962.

The Department of Defense has been working with the Departments of State and Treasury in an attempt to offset the balance-of-payments deficits caused by our defense effort throughout the world. Spectacular progress has been made to offset the balance-of-payments deficiencies with the Federal Republic of Germany. At the outset of these negotiations the Federal Republic insisted that the 

Department of Defense depart from its ordinary policy of refusing to sell certain items which are normally purchased through commercial channels. They wish to avoid establishment of the large purchasing mission in the United States. In order to obtain an increased volume of purchases from the Federal Republic, the United States entered into the following agreement: "No. 240. 

"BONN/BAD GODESBERG, GERMANY, November 24, 1961. 

"EXCELLENCY: I refer to an exchange of letters between Minister Morris and 

State Secretary Van Scherpenberg dated April 14 and 18, 1961, respectively, in regard to general financial discussions in the military area taking place between representatives of our Governments. These conversations have been based essentially upon the principles of mutual cooperation and assistance as expressed in the Mutual Defense Assistance Agreement between the two Governments signed at Bonn on June 30, 1955, and the Agreement effected by an exchange of notes dated October 8, 1956, regarding purchase of certain military equipment, materials, and services, as amended. The following understandings have been reached: "1. The Government of the United States will perform for the Federal Republic procurement of items which have not heretofore been procured under the abovementioned Agreement on the understanding that the Government of the Federal Republic maintains a level of procurements acceptable to the Government of the United States. Such procurement services will include sale to, or purchase for, the Government of the Federal Republic of certain articles and services which are not standard military items but which are directly related to, or essential for, the operational capability of the armed forces of the Government of the Federal Republic.

"2. Orders for articles and services referred to in paragraph 1, above, which do not involve a source or sources of procurement specified by the Government of the Federal Republic will be subject to all of the terms and provisions of the aforementioned Agreement effected by an exchange of notes dated October 8, 1956 as amended. "3. With respect to orders for articles and services referred to in paragraph 1, above, which involve a source or sources of procurement specified by the Government of the Federal Republic, the Government of the United States shall act on behalf of the Government of the Federal Republic. In this connection, the processing, financing, the delivery of such orders shall, in all respects, be identical to the procedures established in the aforementioned Agreement effected by an exchange of notes dated October 8, 1956, as amended, with the following exceptions: "A. Contracts and purchases shall be made by the Government of the 

United States on behalf of the Government of the Federal Republic. "B. Payment shall be made by the Government of the United States from the account established by paragraph 3 of the aforementioned Agreement effected by an exchange of notes dated October 8, 1956, as amended, to suppliers on behalf of the Government of the Federal Republic. Title to such articles shall pass directly from the suppliers to the Government of the 

Federal Republic. 

"C. Articles and services not covered by specifications of the Government of the United States will be procured according to manufacturers' specifications and warranties unless the Government of the Federal Republic requests other specification, qualifications and warranties. If the specifications and warranties of the manufacturers are considered inadequate for procurement purposes, such specifications and warranties may be adequately supplemented by the Government of the United States after consultation with the Federal Republic. "4. In addition to the charges made in accordance with the aforesaid exchange of notes of October 8, 1956, the Government of the United States will charge a fee of 5 percent of purchase price of articles and services provided hereunder as reimbursement of general administrative expenses for normal contract administration including testing, inspection, and quality control. However, for a single procurement with a value exceeding $10,000,000, the Federal Republic of Germany may request from the United States a reduction in the percentage to be charged. 

Specific services, such as special inspection and testing services, requested by the Federal Republic, over and above those normally performed, will be charged and reimbursed at cost. "5. This exchange of notes will be implemented in such a way as to avoid competition or interference with the operation of the NATO Maintenance Services and Supply Agency and with NATO joint production programs. "I have the honor to propose that, if these understandings are acceptable to Your Excellency's Government, this note and Your Excellency's reply concurring therein shall constitute an Agreement between our two Governments supplementing the aforementioned Agreement effected by an exchange of notes dated October 8, 1956, as amended, which shall enter into force on the date of Your Excellency's reply. "Accept Excellency, the renewed assurance of my highest consideration. 

"BREWSTER H. MORRIS, 

"Charge d'affaires ad interim."

We are at present negotiating with the Federal Republic on other areas of cooperation which will result in additional purchases from U.S. sources. If the 

United States finds itself unable to fulfill its obligations under the above agreement, not only would it lose the orders which this agreement envisages, but it is safe to assume that the negotiations on all other projects would come to an abrupt halt and the structure of the United States-Federal Republic cooperation on balance of payments would collapse. Enactment of the subject amendment will insure that result. All other pending negotiations with more affluent countries would be similarly affected. 

Last year the House Foreign Affairs Committee recommended that the Department of Defense reexamine its existing directives covering military sales to "insure that the U.S. Government, while protecting its necessary security and economic interest, should not unduly interfere with or compete with private business." Also, that "we should do nothing to discourage sales of nonclassified military equipment by commercial suppliers." The committee remarked that

TER because of the complex questions involved, the subject is not easily susceptible to legislation. We have found it no less difficult to promulgate regulations on this subject which satisfy all interested parties. 

The intent of Congress in authorizing military assistance sales was stated in section 408 (c) of the first Mutual Defense Assistance Act (Public Law 329, 81st 

Cong.), which authorized the President "in the interest of achieving standardization of military equipment and in order to provide procurement assistance without cost to the United States" to sell military equipment from stocks or to procure equipment for sale. Although the wording has changed over the years, the two objectives of standardization and procurement assistance are still valid. 

During the past year we have reaffirmed the policy of not unduly interfering in commercial transactions between U.S. firms and foreign governments. As a matter of fact, the Department of Defense refers foreign purchasing officials to U.S. commercial firms on many items and renders every assistance in obtaining security clearances and in the issuance of export licenses. Each purchase request that is approved by the Defense Department to the military departments directs that "items which are normally or readily available from commercial sources will not be made available for sale." Each of the military departments use similar language in their implementing regulations. 

However, there are some circumstances in which, unless exceptions are made to this general policy, there would be adverse effects on both the U.S. Government and the foreign government. 

In addition to the agreement with the Federal Republic of Germany set out above, the Government sells to other purchasers in accordance with international agreements. The following are examples: 

1. NATO Maintenance Supply Services Agency 

The United States is participating in the current NATO effort to develop a spare parts management system. The countries participating in this system have agreed that countries having stocks in long supply will make them available for sale or redistribution to the other NATO countries requiring them. U.S. participation in this agreement was established in the U.S. proposal to NATO in November 1957 and confirmed by the U.S. delegation in the meetings of the NATO Ad 

Hoc Group in February 1958. Cash sales of $10 million have been made to NMSSA. 

2. NATO HAWK production organization

The United States has made arrangements with the NATO HAWK production consortium whereby certain equipment has been granted and other materiel furnished on a barter and exchange basis. The United States will receive complete HAWK battalions for its share. In addition, a dependable undertaking agreement was entered into whereby materiel is purchased from or procured for sale by the United States to this organization in order that production in Europe may be finalized. This latter agreement called for a total of $16 million in sales and for monthly progress payments to the United States. 

3. France

A trade agreement was consummated December 20, 1961, between the United States and France, in order to facilitate their respective purchases of military equipment and materials necessary to the common defense, and to reduce the effect of such purchases on the balance of payments. This agreement, subject to the availability of funds, calls for French purchases from the United States of up to $50 million in military materiel for payment in French francs. The United 

States will use these francs for purchase of military materiel in France and for troop support costs. This is the second of two similar agreements with France, the first was consummated in January 1958. Many types and kinds of materiel are involved in sales under these agreements including commercial purchases made by the French.

In certain countries to whom we have reduced grant aid, we are providing procurement services during the transition phase until the countries concerned can establish their own procurement organization in the United States. 

Again, we procure materiel for many countries where the volume of their business makes it uneconomical to establish a procurement organization in the United States. It would be unreasonable to force such countries to establish quality control and inspection services which they may readily purchase as a service from the U.S. military departments.

Another case is where a country wants to procure items and services under terms of sale, such as the extension of credit and the acceptance of local currencies, which cannot be had from private sources. In this situation, a government-to-government contract is the only practicable way for them to handle the purchase. 

Our review of military sales procedures performed over the past year convinces us that the Department of Defense policy and the exceptions made in this regard are sound and reasonable. Combining orders of other countries with those of the U.S. forces gives all a better price by virtue of the larger buy and makes for more orderly manufacturing procedure. The competitive bid process is well established in U.S. procurement procedures and is fair to all. 

We have had few complaints from U.S. manufacturers, large or small. The only significant complaints over the past several years have been made by brokers or agents who represent manufacturers. A detailed list of these complaints is as follows: Complaint

The fact of the matter, however, is that Admiral Corp., which has over 6,000 employees, is by no stretch of the imagination small business. curement Act. Parenthetically, I might note that it is not unlikely that Admiral

"Mr. Hill's letter further contends that the Department of Defense policy impedes U.S. exports and is deleterious to our balance of payments. I think it unnecessary to dwell at length on this charge. As you know from our testimony before your committee, our military assistance sales have resulted in an inflow of dollars to the United States greatly in excess of our military assistance expenditures abroad. "Finally, Mr. Hill alleges that government-to-government sales are made at the expense of the U.S. taxpayer. The contrary is true. For example, in the case of the AN/UPM-98, the Department of Defense is obtaining the item for its own use at a reduced cost because it has been able to consolidate procurement for its own use with procurement on behalf of foreign governments. "Sincerely yours, 

"Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, "Chairman, Committee on Foreign Affairs, 

"House of Representatives.” 

"W. B. PALMER, "Director of Military Assistance. 

Government-to-government sales are covered by the various military assistance agreements with recipient countries and many of the conditions contained therein apply to defense articles purchased thereunder. These conditions do not apply to sales made through commercial channels. 

It has been inferred that Department of Defense policy fosters doing business with small and medium size companies on a competitive bid basis whereas policy with respect to large companies fosters a policy of negotiated contracts. This inference is not well founded. Procurement policy of the Department of Defense encourages competitive bidding as opposed to negotiated contracts and applies to large and small firms alike. 

The point has been stressed that sales of military equipment by private companies at a higher price, and with an export agent's commission added, will bring more money to the United States than government-to-government sales. This is not necessarily so. Higher prices can drive the prospective customer to purchase from foreign suppliers. Moreover, defense ministries usually allot a certain amount of money for specific equipment. If the price is higher, the same amount of money is frequently spent for a fewer number of items, with a resulting lack in free world defense.

Clear from the testimony in support of the amendment under consideration is the fact that the words "available commercially" are intended to be broadly construed. The test apparently to be applied is whether the military equipment involved could be subject to sale by a private company to a foreign government. 

It follows that the amendment would, if passed, prevent the military departments from selling all types of defense articles (excepting classified and excess articles) to all but the economically underdeveloped nations. Section 507 of the act which authorizes sales by the military departments has proved in the past to provide a convenient method of supplying our free world allies with defense articles at no cost to the United States. We believe that a loss or material restriction of this authority will result in a serious blow to our military assistance program.

Mrs. Brown, you represent the National Council of Jewish Women, member of the National Public Affairs Committee. You have a prepared statement and you may proceed.

STATEMENT OF MRS. DONALD BROWN, REPRESENTING THE NA- TIONAL COUNCIL OF JEWISH WOMEN, MEMBER, NATIONAL PUBLIC AFFAIRS COMMITTEE 

Mrs. BROWN. I am Mrs. Donald Brown, member of the National 

Public Affairs Committee of the National Council of Jewish Women. 

I appreciate the opportunity of appearing before this committee in support of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

One of the major interests of the National Council of Jewish Women, an organization established in 1893, with a current membership of 123,000 in 325 communities, is to promote effective international relations.

In 1946 we adopted the following resolution which has been reaffirmed at every biennial convention since then: 

To urge the United States to expand programs of technical and economic assistance to the underdeveloped countries so that they may achieve the economic and social standards that are necessary to human dignity. 

Each year our organization follows the foreign assistance program of our Government from its inception in a congressional bill through its yearlong administration by the appropriate agency. In our yearly effort to reevaluate the foreign assistance program, we carefully study the President's message to Congress, proposed bills, joint House- Senate conference reports, and other source materials, so that our interest in foreign aid is neither transitory nor casual, but conscientious.

This study has led our members to believe that foreign assistance is such an important aspect of our foreign policy that they were prepared to expend their own financial and manpower resources in support of this effort. 

Since the fall of 1945, the National Council of Jewish Women spent close to $4 million on its oversea program of assistance to some 17 countries. The program has emphasized scholarships for graduate training of personnel in the field of social work, early childhood education, special education, educational administration, teacher education, graduate nursing, psychology, and rehabilitation services. 

Under this scholarship program we brought to the United States 177 men and women for study at universities so that they may acquire skills in these fields and use the knowledge for the benefit of their people when they return to their own communities. Among these were a number of community leaders who were brought here to observe our social institutions and citizen participation in community affairs. 

Our oversea program of assistance also includes support of the John Dewey School of Education at Hebrew University in Jerusalem and the establishment of a pedagogic library and an audiovisual center. 

Recently we undertook to construct a high school, at a cost of one-half million dollars, which is to serve as a practice teaching center for the John Dewey School. This is the way we feel we can make our small contribution to economic development with the limited resources available to us. 

I am citing our activities here merely to illustrate how strongly our members believe in the validity and importance of the foreign assistance program. 

We are, therefore, proud that our country has assumed a consistent responsibility for the welfare of other peoples and for meeting the challenge of needed economic development in other countries. From the Lend-Lease Act, to the point 4 doctrine, the Marshall plan, and the first Act for International Development passed by Congress in 1950, the United States has dedicated itself to the ideals of its own free tradition by encouraging rational politics, social justice, and economic stability in other nations. 

Certainly we are skilled in the techniques of economic development. 

We have the know-how, but we cannot just hand over our skills. It will take time for others to learn and to develop their own. Meanwhile, we and they must be patient as we face together the imperative of our century, the emergence of underdeveloped countries as nations able to help themselves and others in the modern world. 

We are aware that the 15 years in which our foreign aid programs have existed is a short period of time for any nation to help bring about the rehabilitation of war-devastated economies and the modernization and industrialization of emerging nations. 

These are vast tasks and though much has been accomplished it is not surprising that some mistakes would be made or progress seems slow. After all, though we are masters of the techniques of economic development and justly proud of our tremendous efficiency in agricultural productivity as well as our outstanding systems of sanitation and transportation, we have been nonetheless novices at giving aid. 

We are learning, through trial and error, how best to be helpful in a wav useful and acceptable to others. 81496-62--pt. 6- -3

So while there have been valid criticisms of our aid programs they do not invalidate the good we have accomplished. Though we may become impatient at our expenditures for what seems to us a slow rate of progress, we have to realize worldwide tasks are not performed with the relative ease with which we carry out more limited types of national programs. 

Within this context, we believe that the new principles introduced into the foreign aid program in 1961, which has been in effect but only a few months, will do a great deal to correct some of our past inefficiencies and will result in a more workable program. 

We would support continued emphasis on the use of domestic resources and self-help; long-term planning with goals and priorities and the development of permanent local institutions in the recipient countries; advance commitments for loans to encourage host governments in undertaking a development program; the need for social progress within the countries receiving U.S. aid; and a concentrated program within the Alliance for Progress. 

In addition the new Agency's structural reorganization should by its very nature insure a more workable aid program and help us to avoid some of the pitfalls of our earlier assistance activities. 

The Agency for International Development, as now organized on a geographic rather than on a functional basis, will be in a position to assess the overall needs of each country keeping in mind which projects will best further the overall development of the recipient country. 

It will also be in a position to provide better coordination with programs of other agencies or other countries, thus avoiding either conflict or duplication. 

In short, it is our belief that the present emphasis which is being put on the programing phase and on the organizational phase of the foreign assistance program will hopefully prevent improper stress on obvious but temporary needs unconnected with long-term development and promote the "system of growth" within a country; an overabundance of money or aid being poured into an economy unable, by its very weakness, to absorb it; a lack of use of domestic resources available, both in material power and human power thus undermining the importance of self-help, and many others. 

The United States has also worked for worldwide recognition of the needs of the less developed countries. Today the nations of Western 

Europe, together with Japan, Canada and others are joining us in assuming responsibility for assisting these countries. 

During 1959 and 1960, the total flow of resources, public and private, from these nations was larger than that from the United States. This is a tribute to U.S. leadership and a recognition of the value and urgency of aid to less developed nations. 

In conclusion we would like to urge this committee to consider favorably the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962.

STATEMENT OF HON. JAMES ROOSEVELT, MEMBER OF CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee.

I certainly appreciate and welcome the opportunity to appear before you in support of H.R. 10787 and the companion bill introduced by my able colleague, Mr. Halpern, from New York. I urge the language of these identical bills be included in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. This measure is to provide that the Government of the 

United States shall furnish no aid or assistance to any foreign nation or citizen thereof in carrying out any activity under which American citizens will be discriminated against. 

Some months ago a constituent of mine was made aware of and suffered from the Arab boycott. In fact, he presented to me such a well-documented case of discrimination I felt compelled to write to the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Commerce expressing grave concern over the submissive reaction of the United States to the continuation of the Arab League nations' discriminatory boycott against Americans of the Jewish faith, and protesting actions of certain governmental agencies which aid and abet the Arab boycott. 

In my letters to the Secretaries, I urged a complete reexamination and reformulation of American policies and practices related to the Arab League nations' boycott and full implementation of the congressional mandate to utilize foreign assistance funds in a manner which will most satisfactorily give practical effect to American principles of fairness and equality.

In the interests of brevity, I shall not read the complete text of my letters, nor that of the replies received from the Honorable Luther 1055

Hodges, Secretary of Commerce, and the Honorable Brooks Hays, then Assistant Secretary of State. Copies of each of these texts are attached to my mimeographed statement. 

Mr. Chairman, I offer these for the record. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. (The letters above referred to are as follows:) 

HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, 

Washington, D.C., September 8, 1961. 

Hon. DEAN RUSK, Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.

Hon. LUTHER H. HODGES, 

Secretary of Commerce, Washington, D.O. 

DEAR MR. SECRETARY: I am taking this occasion to express to you my profound concern and deep regret with reference to the policy and practice of the U.S. 

Government regarding the Arab League nations' boycott and the consequent invasion of American rights. 

I vehemently protest the actions of our Government which aid and abet the discriminatory actions of the Arab League nations in their perpetration of a boycott against U.S. business firms which are "Jewish owned" or "employs a percentage of Jewish personnel." I firmly believe that a boycott against an 

American business concern on the ground that it is owned or operated by persons of any particular race, religion, or ethnic origin, is contrary to American principles and traditions, and should definitely not be countenanced by governmental assistance.

Regardless of the general overall intent of the Arab League's boycott, it is in effect a boycott against Americans. As a consequence of the boycott, and our policy with respect to it, we are suffering a loss which no self-respecting nation can afford-the loss of integrity and prestige incurred by submissiveness to affronts.

Through a policy of accommodation, the U.S. Government has aided and abetted practices of discrimination against our citizens and has acquiesced in the invasion of American rights. The acts against our citizens to which I refer are: the blacklisting of American companies having Americans of the 

Jewish faith among their officers, owners, directors, or even personnel; the denying of visas to Americans of the Jewish faith and the subjecting of such persons to indignities and affronts while passing through Arab League countries; preventing American military and civilian personnel of the Jewish faith from serving at an Air Force base built in an Arab country with American funds and maintained by the United States; and the rejecting of U.S. diplomatic personnel and aides of the Jewish faith qualified to perform duties in the league countries.

It is true that in several instances the Government has issued statements with reference to the boycott. Thus, in 1956, when the boycott was extended to companies having Jewish ownership or participation, the New York office of the U.S. Department of Commerce announced: "The United States does not recognize the boycott." But the appalling truth is that the United States has taken no effective action. Mr. Secretary, what I found intolerable under a Re publican administration is even more detestable under the present administration. It is imperative that we do more than utter pious statements. 

Until recent years, the resistance of the U.S. Government to practices of a foreign government discriminating against a class of Americans had been forthright, consistent, and unequivocal. For example: When a foreign government protested the appointment of an Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of the United States, on the ground that he was married to a Jewish woman, Secretary of State Bayard, replying on behalf of our Government, declared: "It is not within the power of the President nor of the Congress, nor of any judicial tribunal in the United States, to take or even hear testimony, or in any mode to inquire into or decide upon the religious belief of any official, and the proposition to allow this to be done by any foreign government is necessarily and a fortiori inadmissible. "To suffer an infraction of this essential principle would lead to a disenfranchisement of our citizens because of their religious belief, and thus impair or destroy the most important end which our constitution of government was intended to secure."

Although this official resigned his commission, the U.S. Government declined to make another appointment. For several years thereafter the United States was represented in that country by a Chargé d'Affaires. 

Citizens of the United States have justifiably come to expect that their Government would take an honorable and implacable stand against invidious discrimination against American citizens and the infringement of American rights by foreign countries. But these expectations have not been borne out in recent years. Not only have Government agencies acquiesced passively to the boycott, they have served actively, in many instances, as its instruments. 

The Department of Defense has deferred to Saudi Arabia's exclusion of American Jews from the Air Force base maintained in Dhahran by the United States. 

The Department of Agriculture and the Commodity Credit Corporation have assented to contracts which prohibit vessels carrying surplus commodities to Arab countries from calling at Israel waterways or ports. The existing law requires that half of the deliveries sent abroad must go in American bottoms. The effect of the Department's assent is that we have permitted Arab governments, by constructing a blacklist, to render certain American vessels and owners ineligible for carrying these shipments.

The situation in the Department of Commerce is equally appalling. Through the medium of publicity releases, the Department advertises calls for bids in the United States by the Arab League nations presently engaging in discriminatory purchasing practices. Such cooperation is shocking and unpardonable. 

When Mr. Al S. Waxman of Waxman Publications, Inc., Los Angeles, Calif., wrote to the Secretary of Commerce protesting these publicity releases and presenting incontrovertible evidence of discriminatory practices in the calls for bids, his communication was sent to the State Department. Mr. Waxman received a reply from Mr. Nicholas G. Thacher, Deputy Director, Office of Near 

Eastern Affairs, which stated, among other things, that "the U.S. Government, as a matter of settled policy, neither recognizes nor condones discriminatory procedures of foreign business firms or governments * 

I cannot believe that the Department of State is unaware of the boycott activities of the Arab League nations. In light of this, I cannot understand why we continue to publicize these discriminatory calls for bids. This is not only recognizing discriminatory procedures, it is condoning them with support and assistance. 

This is intolerable, and I vigorously protest the continuation of such practices. 

On September 5, the House adopted an amendment to the foreign assistance appropriation bill which provides that "It is the sense of Congress that any attempt by foreign nations to create distinctions because of their race or religion among American citizens in the granting of personal or commercial access or any other rights otherwise available to U.S. citizens generally is repugnant to our principles; and in all negotiations between the United States and any foreign state arising as a result of funds appropriated under this title these principles shall be applied as the President may determine." 

Mr. Rooney stated that the objective of this amendment, which he introduced was to protect American citizens against distinctions because of their race or religion by foreign nations. Mr. Halpern, in a spirit of bipartisanship, declared that "nothing short of this amendment *** is satisfactory to carry out the sense of Congress as expressed heretofore in previous appropriations bills and it fulfills the principle espoused by the President linking social justice 

and morality to our foreign aid program It is a clear declaration of principle and a concomitant of American aid." 

Mr. Secretary, I respectfully urge a complete reexamination of U.S. policy and practice relative to our reactions to the Arab League nations' discriminatory boycott. I further urge that the United States totally abstain from any form of cooperation with the Arab League's boycott activities, fully implement the policy established by the Congress, and, in addition, seek to use the influence of our Government to eliminate such distressing practices. 

Very truly yours,

Hon. JAMES ROOSEVELT, House of Representatives. 

JAMES ROOSEVELT, 

Member of Congress.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE, 

Washington, September 19, 1961.

DEAR MR. ROOSEVELT: The Department has received your letter of Septem ber 8, 1961, to the Secretary with its comments on U.S. Government policy

with regard to the Arab boycott of Israel and discrimination by Arab States against American citizens of the Jewish faith. 

Let me assure you that the U.S. Government has never followed a policy of accommodation or acquiescence to the boycott or to other practices of the Arab States which we find repugnant. The often stated and continuing policy of this Government in these matters may be summarized as follows: We do not recognize or condone the Arab boycott, particularly as it affects American citizens and firms. Likewise, our Government does not condone measures which tend to discriminate against American citizens on grounds of race, religion, or creed. These positions have been repeatedly made clear to the foreign governments concerned and our embassies abroad are under standing instructions to reemphasize this fundamental policy at every appropriate opportunity. Our representations have from time to time achieved some abatement in implementation of these undesirable practices. 

Meanwhile, aware that the Arab boycott and discriminatory measures are an outgrowth of tensions arising from the Arab-Israel conflict, our Government, has persisted in efforts to achieve through the instrumentalities of the United Nations progress toward solution of this difficult question, one that continues to stir deep emotional responses on the part of the governments and peoples involved. 

While the Department maintains its active opposition to policies of boycott and discrimination, in some cases these are carried out in exercise of func tions normally recognized as coming within the purview of sovereign governments. Thus the United States has never agreed that Americans of the Jewish faith should not be included among personnel assigned to operate U.S. facilities at the Saudi Arabia airfield at Dhahran. Saudi Arabia has since the Arab-Israel conflict of 1949, generally refused to permit entry of American citizens of the Jewish faith on the assumption that such persons must be regarded as active supporters of Israel. In

No U.S. Government agency has sanctioned discriminatory ship charters for 

American-flag vessels carrying American surplus commodities to Arab coun tries under title II or title III of Public Law 480. In the case of title I Public 

Law 480 shipments, countries making these purchases take delivery at dockside and negotiate shipping arrangements directly with private carriers. these cases it is understood that ship charters negotiated by one Arab government have included a prohibition against sailing in Israeli waters for the single voyage involved. The Department has been successful, however, in persuading the country concerned to eliminate other, more restrictive clauses from charters of vessels carrying title I commodities. 

Your letter refers to the experience of Waxman Publications in responding to a request for bids by a Jordanian firm whose commercial proposal had been given dissemination by the Department of Commerce as part of the services it customarily renders for the assistance of American exporters. Upon learning of the apparent discriminatory intent of the foreign firm in this case, the Department immediately requested investigation by our representatives in Jordan. 

Whether or not the firm was operating according to boycott regulations or had made a unilateral decision not to deal with American businessmen of the Jewish faith will in due course be determined. 

You have referred also to the inclusion in the foreign assistance appropriations bill of section 108 regarding discrimination by foreign nations among American citizens because of race or religion. The Department supports fully the principles of this amendment and will continue to seek every appropriate opportunity to impress upon foreign states the opposition of our people and Government to any kind of religious or racial discrimination. At the same time we continue to believe that the specific purpose of abating discriminatory practices would be thwarted rather than advanced by linking it with foreign aid negotiations. We remain convinced that continued quiet representations through diplomatic channels, supplemented by efforts to abate through instrumentalities of the United Nations the underlying causes of the Arab-Israel dispute, remain the most promising courses for removal of these harmful practices. hope this letter may serve to clarify our Government's policies with regard to boycott procedures and discriminatory practices, matters which remain of deep and continuing concern to the Department of State. It is understood that the 

Department of Commerce is replying separately to you regarding matters raised in your letter which fall within its purview.

If the Department can be of further assistance in this matter, please do not hesitate to let me know. 

Sincerely yours,

Hon. JAMES ROOSEVELT, BROOKS HAYS, 

Assistant Secretary.

THE SECRETARY OF COMMERCE, 

Washington, D.C., September 27, 1961.

House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR MR. ROOSEVELT: I have carefully read your letter of September 8 con cerning U.S. policy and action toward the Arab League boycott of Israel, and, in addition, discrimination against American citizens based on race or religion. 

I am glad to learn that you have addressed a similar letter to the Secretary of State, for some of the practices to which you refer are of primary concern to that Department.

As you know, the U.S. Government does not recognize or condone the Arab boycott of Israel; however, it cannot ignore the fact of its existence. Like many other undesirable features of foreign governments' policies and practices, and those of private citizens in foreign countries with which we maintain diplomatic relations, we are obliged to face the facts and react in a manner best calculated to further the totality of American interests. It has been my Department's policy, therefore, to make information concerning the boycott available to any inquirer. Whether or not an American firm is to adjust its practices so as to conform to the rules of the boycott is a business decision to be made exclusively by the firm. The Department of Commerce does not give advice or counsel in such matters, although it will of course supply whatever factual information the firm may request in order to reach a decision. 

With regard to the Department's practice of publishing business opportunities in the Arab League countries, I do not believe that this constitutes recognition or condonation of the boycott. We are merely making such factual information as is available to us known to the American business community, leaving up to American firms what course of action they wish to pursue. This practice does not discriminate against American firms in any way. On the other hand, to refuse to publicize such opportunities would be a form of discrimination. Many 

American companies have chosen to comply with the boycott and trade with the Arab countries; to refuse to publish business opportunities of which these companies wish to take advantage would be to deny them a service of the Department of Commerce to which they are entitled. 

You have referred to discrimination on the part of the Arab League countries on the basis of race, religion, or ethnic origin. I should point out that the Arab governments have represented to us that the boycott does not involve such discrimination. They state that it is applied to Israel and to those firms and individuals in other countries, regardless of race or religion, who foster the interests of Israel. It is true that there have been instances in which certain 

Arab countries have attempted to apply such discrimination under cover of the boycott. In the case cited by Mr. Waxman, we have asked our Embassy to investigate and report to us. This investigation will determine whether the discrimination of which Mr. Waxman complains is attributable to the Jordanian boycott regulations or to the policy of the Jordanian firm. 

It is my view that this Government should continue to use every appropriate occasion to register its opposition to the Arab League boycott. However, while such representations may be successful in abating some of the more objectionable features of the boycott, as long as the present tension between the Arab states and Israel remains we are unlikely to induce the Arab governments to abolish the boycott altogether. 

Sincerely yours,

LUTHER H. HODGES, 

Secretary of Commerce.

Let us first examine the reply from the Department of State. Mr. 

Hays summarized what he termed "the often stated and continuing policy of this Government in these matters" as follows: 

We do not recognize or condone the Arab boycott particularly as it affects American citizens and firms. Likewise, our Government does not condone meas-

ures which tend to discriminate against American citizens on grounds of race, religion, or creed.

The letter goes on to state that— While the Department maintains its active opposition to policies of boycott and discrimination, in some cases these are carried out in exercise of functions normally recognized as coming within the purview of sovereign governments. 

Thus the United States has never agreed that Americans of the Jewish faith should not be included among personnel assigned to operate United States facilities at the Saudi Arabia airfield at Dhahran. Saudi Arabia has since the 

Arab-Israel conflict of 1948 generally refused to permit entry of American citizens of the Jewish faith on the assumption that such persons must be regarded as active supporters of Israel. men. 

It is my opinion that Saudi Arabia is entitled to keep Jews out of that nation if it so desires, if they seek to enter as tourists or business- But how can the United States accede to the assumption that an American citizen of the Jewish faith is "an active supporter of Israel" when such citizen wears the uniform of an American serviceman and is under orders of the U.S. Air Force? Yet we do accede in practice to this assumption by tacit consent to abide by Saudi Arabia's directive in this regard. 

In a further paragraph Mr. Hays states: 

No U.S. Government agency has sanctioned discriminatory ship charters for 

American-flag vessels carrying American surplus commodities to Arab countries * * * We are all well aware that our Government does not sanction discrimination. What we are interested in is what the Government has done and will do in the future to bring these practices to an end. 

It is to my mind intolerable for an agency of the U.S. Government to say we do not condone a discriminatory practice, we do not like it, but we will nevertheless submit to it. 

The Department of State's letter also mentions the inclusion in the Foreign Assistance Appropriations bill of section 108, which regards discrimination of American citizens by foreign nations. Here again the Department merely states that it supports the principles of the amendment. We are not seeking the Department's support by words; we are requesting a full implementation of the intent of the Congress in actual practice.

The reply from the Secretary of Commerce contains many of the same, almost identical phrases. What concerns me is a repeated reference to the Arab boycott of Israel; I quote the last paragraph of 

Secretary Hodges' letter:

It is my view that this Government should continue to use every appropriate occasion to register its opposition to the Arab League boycott. However, while such representations may be successful in abating some of the more objectionable features of the boycott, as long as the present tension between the Arab States and Israel remains we are unlikely to induce the Arab governments to abolish the boycott altogether.

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, none of us, nor any interested party, has brought this matter forward with the expectation that the U.S. Government will "induce the Arab governments to abolish the boycott altogether." The Arab boycott against Israel is an international matter between those two governments in which the United States should become involved possibly only as a neutral moderator during discussions and negotiations. Our only concern is for

Americans. Our protest is over the boycott against Americans of the 

Jewish religion. American businessmen object to their taxes being used by their own Government to further the commercial interests of foreign nations who seek business relationships with American firms but who practice a system of discrimination and boycott against Americans because of religious beliefs. 

The problem of discrimination has gained increasing importance. 

The entire world watches to see whether we intend to uphold our stated principle of nondiscrimination against any American citizen by reason of his race, color, or religion. We have failed to do so thus far. 

Now is the time to emphasize to the Arab world our opposition to the violation of one of the fundamental principles of the democratic way of life.

The Congress has previously stated its policy in foreign assistance appropriation bills, but it has become increasingly obvious that the language of such measures was insufficient. H.R. 10787 and Congressman Halpern's identical bill provide the language to clearly dispel any doubt as to the attitude of the United States. 

Congressman Halpern is going to testify before this committee. I am sure all of you know that his is the No. 1 example of what we are talking about. He tried to get into Saudi Arabia to inspect our own military base and has been refused a visa in order to enable him to do so. 

How long is this Congress going to say that one of its own Members cannot get to inspect an American base because another foreign government takes the position that he is of the Jewish faith and therefore is inadmissible to its territory? It seems to me this is shocking and something that if the American people understand it well would demand in the strongest language that something be done about it. 

I ask for your earnest consideration toward the inclusion of the language of H.K. 10787 in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Roosevelt. 

Mr. Roosevelt, I am sure you are familiar with the language that is in the 1961 act and I am sure you are familiar with the language that was in the previous act. 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. I am, Mr. Chairman. 

Chairman MORGAN. This is a very difficult amendment. Unless it is incorporated in the bill in both Houses of Congress there is inevitably a problem when the bill goes to conference. 

Mrs. KELLY. I am sorry that I was late, Mr. Chairman. Where is the language that is reccomended to be included in the bill? 

Chairman MORGAN. It is proposed as a separate bill. It is not in the statement. 

Mrs. KELLY. Thank you. 

Is this identical with the Halpern bill?

Mr. ROOSEVELT. Yes. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Roosevelt, H.R. 10787 would deny all aid? This is the penalty you recommend?

Mr. ROOSEVELT. Yes, Mr. Chairman, which we feel until we put it in there obviously the experience shows that the foreign governments will pay no attention to pious statements of intent. Once you put it in there, I think a reasonable action on the part of the executive branch will make it possible for everyone to receive aid and yet not do the

kind of thing that is being done to Congressman Halpern and the kind of thing that the Commerce Department carries on today. 

We are not asking for punitive action against these nations. But on American soil-when we say "soil," soil being occupied by Americans under agreement with these countries, and in the case of our own Government we need not further this discrimination. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Roosevelt. 

Dr. Judd. 

Dr. JUDD. 

As the chairman said, we have wrestled with this thing for years; how to do what all of us want, maintain our good relations and opportunities in those parts of the world, and at the same time eliminate such discriminations. 

I must say, talking about Saudi Arabia, that is not an American base. It has never been an American base. It is an airfield which under agreements we have rights to use. It never has been American territory. We have never had control over it in the same sense that we have over bases, for example, in Spain. 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. I think that is right. We do operate there. 

Mr. JUDD. The second thing is, do you think that if your language were put in, with this penalty clause, it would change the position of those governments on this matter? Do you think we are more likely to change their position by having that threat over them, or less likely to induce them to change their position? 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. Dr. Judd, I would have to say that the expressions of opinion in the past have not changed their opinion. So I would then have to reach the conclusion that we should try to seek some other method.

I would feel, knowing how much they value money in those areas, that perhaps if they became convinced we were going to be sincere about this thing, to carry it through, that it might effect a change. 

Mr. JUDD. Suppose it had the opposite effect and didn't change the discrimination in the least, and only denied our country opportunities and facilities which are of great importance to us in various places. 

With such a result there would be no benefits, and only harm. 

We are properly trying to get benefits without harm. But if in trying to get those benefits we don't get the benefit but do get harm, well, this is the hard nut we are trying to crack. 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. Dr. Judd, as I have examined it, and I have consulted with the Department of Defense, the only military base that would be affected by this is the base at Dhahran in Saudi Arabia. 

There is a serious question even in the minds of the Defense Department on the value of that base anymore. 

Mr. JUDD. It is not a base. 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. I beg your pardon. Airfield. Because it is not a base but just an airfield, I think the value to them far exceeds the value to us.

As to the activities of the Department of Commerce, where they actively assist the Arab countries in promoting their bids to American businessmen with this discriminatory clause advertised for them by the Department of Commerce, it seems to me that they would have nothing to pull away from us. We would lose nothing. But certainly they would lose something because they would lose the active help

of the Department of Commerce in spreading what information they want to spread.

Mr. JUDD. I am grateful for your lucid explanation. I must say that with the situation as unstable and the possibilities for deterioration as they are in that part of the world, we need to look twice at something which I am not sure will bring benefits and might increase the dangers.

This may be just one of those cases where sometimes time and persuasion and patience may do more to clear up an inequity or discrimination than a supposedly stronger method would. I don't know which is the better method. 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. Dr. Judd, I don't want to vouch for this because 

I haven't had time to thoroughly research it, but I believe in the time of Theodore Roosevelt he nominated an Ambassador to Russia whose nomination was turned down, which is their right. Upon asking why, they were told he had a Jewish wife. I understand the then President Theodore Roosevelt said that he would not nominate anybody until they withdrew this type of objection, that this was not admissible in this country, and the words were very eloquent. And 4 years went by and there were all kinds of pressures on our country by the interests that wanted to do business over there, and they renominated the same man and he took his wife with him. 

Mr. JUDD. It depends on the situation and the people. He was dealing with Russians and not present-day Arabs. 

Mr. ROOSEVELT. That is right. I think we better begin to deal with the Arabs the way we do with the Russians.

STATEMENT OF POLICY SEC. 2. Section 2 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended, which is a statement of policy, is further amended by adding at the end thereof the following: "(f) It is the sense of the Congress that inasmuch as- "(1) the United States favors freedom of navigation in international waterways and economic cooperation between nations; and "(2) the purposes of this act are negated and the peace of the world is endangered when nations which receive assistance under this act wage economic warfare against other nations assisted under this act, including such procedures as boycotts, blockades, and the restriction of the use of international waterways: assistance under this act and the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, as amended, shall be administered to give effect to these principles, and, in all negotiations between the United States and any foreign state arising as a result of funds appropriated under this Act or arising under the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, as amended, these principles shall be applied, as the President may determine, and he shall report on measures taken by the administration to insure their application."

Halpern, Member of Congress from the State of New York.

Mr. Halpern, you have appeared in front of the committee on behalf of similar resolutions last year. Do you have a prepared statement?

STATEMENT OF HON. SEYMOUR HALPERN, MEMBER OF CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF NEW YORK 

Mr. HALPERN. I do, Mr. Chairman. Unfortunately, I don't have individual copies for the members of the committee with me at the moment. My office is making some copies and is sending them down. 

I hope to have them before I complete my appearance today. In any event, I shall proceed with my own text and will make sure enough copies are available to you and the members of the committee. 

Mr. Chairman, I wish to express appreciation to the committee for the opportunity afforded me and my distinguished colleague, Mr. 

Roosevelt of California, to testify today. I would like also to commend this committee for its inspiring devotion to moral principles and willingness to consider all reasonable viewpoints in formulating mutual security legislation that will be in the best national interest and advance our foreign policy objectives. 

Let me state at the outset that I believe strongly in the principle of mutual security aid. There is no doubt that the Marshall plan saved 

Western Europe from communism. Nor can there be any question that Soviet infiltration has been effectively blocked in many other areas by timely programs enacted by Congress to support human dignity and raise living standards so that people could oppose totalitarianism and move toward democracy, crystallizing, animating, and solidifying a free world front.

It has been estimated that we have allocated over $100 billion in various forms of foreign aid since World War II. I feel that most of this has been well spent and projected the best American image around the globe while in the tradition of our major religious faiths-helping others to help themselves. 

This committee can take great pride in its wisdom and foresight in implementing our objectives in the most effective way. 

There have been, of course, various inequities in the program. 

This is inevitable, we realize, in so mammoth an undertaking. But time, experience, and, I should add, the wisdom of this committee, have resulted in considerable corrections of these flaws. But one glaring weak spot in particular remains one that has been a blot on the program and one which has been repeatedly deplored by this committee and by Congress. I refer to the granting of U.S. aid to certain nations which maintain national policies of discrimination against a large segment of American citizens and American businesses. 

Legislation recommended and reported out by this committee has on a number of occasions expressed the sense of Congress that the President should use Executive discretion in denying assistance to such nations that discriminate against American citizens and interests on an arbitrary and insulting basis of the religious faith of our fellow countrymen.

Congress has made known that this is an intolerable situation, by a number of expressions contained in various measures adopted by overwhelming votes through the years. Congress has looked to the 

State Department and the Chief Executive for implementing action.

But I regret to observe, Mr. Chairman, despite flagrant violations of the principle of these provisions, the sense of Congress has been ignored. That is why the legislation I urge you to accept is so important. 

Let it be clear that I fully support the continuation of assistance programs at the levels indicated subject to the wisdom and experienced judgment of this committee. But, as evidence from the legislation I am jointly sponsoring with Mr. Roosevelt, I am equally convinced that Congress must move without reservation to insure respect for its expressed position on the denial of assistance to those nations that openly maintain national policies of discriminating against Americans. 

The offenders, Mr. Chairman, as you know, are not our allies. They allege to be "neutrals" and most often vote against free world interests generally, and against America specifically-while repeatedly siding with the Soviet Union-at the United Nations. Among them are the so-called Arab League states, most of which not only bar Americans of Jewish faith from access to their territory but have entered into a coordinated boycott undertaking to punish American merchant ships and manufacturers solely because these firms, regardless of the personal religious convictions of their owners, dare to trade with Israel, a democratic state friendly to America and closely alined with the free world. This boycott even applies to doing business with American firms here, whose officers or employees are of the Jewish faith. 

Mr. Chairman, it has been alleged from time to time by State Department officials that we must appease admittedly discriminatory Arab tactics in order to serve diplomatic ends. I fail to see how much has been accomplished by such appeasement, a depressing departure from American dignity and tradition. We need only look at so many of the Arab States votes at the United Nations. We need only look at the Soviet guns, tanks, jets, and even submarines now forming the basic armed strength of the main Arab armies, especially those of Egypt and Syria, linking those countries logistically with the Soviet munitions factories and Soviet military instructors. 

I respectfully submit that the time has come when we must set forth standards of conduct by recipient nations toward U.S. citizens as a qualification for our economic assistance. And this should be spelled out unequivocally. Having a declaration of policy is evidently not enough. The executive branch has ignored the sense of 

Congress as we have solemnly expressed it. We owe it to self-respect of the American public, as well as the highest national interest, to now establish a firm position and incorporate mandatory language into the pending legislation before this committee. 

Accordingly, I would like to call attention to H.R. 10787 and H.R. 

10856, identical bills which Mr. Roosevelt and I have sponsored. This legislation clearly and unequivocally states that "The Government of the United States shall furnish no aid to any foreign nation or citizens thereof in carrying out any activity under which American citizens will be discriminated against." 

This proposal is consistent with the antibias principle established by this committee. It endorses the President's own expressed objective which he has made clear to Congress. He has said on various occasions that he wants foreign aid linked with the promotion of social justice and morality. I might add that the platforms of both our political parties make strong pledges to combat foreign discrimi-

nation against Americans, on a basis of religion, especially through travel barriers, boycotts, and blockades.

If these principles are to be realized and not just remain as highsounding ideals, then I urge the committee to adopt the mandatory provisions of our bill. 

Incidentally, I should point out that the President's concept was quite brilliantly and appropriately spelled out in the Charter of Punta del Este as an underlying principle of the new Alliance for Progress. Aid is to be interconnected with reform and the advancement of human rights. 

Mr. Chairman, let us be consistent. Why work so fervently for an 

Alliance for Progress in Latin America while financing elsewhere an alliance without progress by which we indirectly subsidize Arab governments that deny human rights to our own citizens? 

One could cite many examples of the discriminatory and offensive Arab tactics. Last July I narrated at some length before the committee my own disheartening personal experience in being denied a visa to visit Saudi Arabia because of my religion. Despite my repeated efforts and despite our own State Department's intervention, I have not been able to even set foot on our own American-financed projects in that country, which we in Congress authorized and the 

American public paid for. Isn't that ironic.

To bring the committee up to date on this issue, I have consistently pursued the matter with the Saudi Arabian Government and our own State Department, but to date I have gotten nowhere. But the issue far transcends my individual experience. 

This committee is well informed and no doubt aware that American merchant vessels have been subjected to discrimination while attempting to transit the Suez Canal just because these vessels exercised freedom of the seas and called at Israeli ports. The committee has heard on previous occasions the details of how U.S. citizens, businessmen, officials, soldiers, and yes, even Congressmen, are barred from Arab nations receiving aid financed through the taxes of all our citizens, regardless of faith. 

The time is much past due, Mr. Chairman, that offending Arab governments cease their discriminatory practices-practices known only too well by our State Department or face the immediate severance of U.S. assistance. As I said earlier, we have voiced the "sense of Congress" protesting this bias often enough. Obviously it has no effect whatever.

I feel that the only answer is the writing of mandatory language in the bill. That is the least we can do at this late date to remedy a situation that has persisted for too long. It is apparent the compromise of principle has marred our national countenance. The day is gone when we can sit quietly and permit nations soliciting our assistance to discriminate against our citizens with impunity. might add that either that day is gone or our national dignity, our heritage are going sadly undefended. When will we reassert our right to respect in the family of nations? 

The least we can do is to refuse to finance regimes that dip our flag in the dirt by intolerable demonstrations of bigotry against millions of our citizens.

Are nations to be permitted to take American aid for granted regardless of their conduct toward Americans?

Not only is the declaration of principle by Congress completely ignored, but the President's own announced principle linking aid with social justice and morality on the part of the beneficiary countries is apparently being disregarded. 

How can our Government continue providing public funds to those countries which not only discriminate within their own territory but are attempting to export, through economic coercion, their discriminatory policies to the United States? I might cite the case of a finding by New York State authorities against an oil company whose offices in this country refused to hire persons unacceptable to the Arab League.

Does not the committee agree that mutual security should be mutual? We cannot ask recipients of our aid to support our every stand at the United Nations. But we can and must ask that they accord our citizens the same rights we accord their citizens. 

Not too long ago, President Nasser of Egypt held up the U.S. freighter Valiant Faith in the Suez Canal for 28 days, denying its American crew shore leave, keeping our citizens virtually prisoners. 

Yet, the State Department took no effective action. Similar incidents of blacklisting and harassment of our shipping continue unabated. 

But now I read with dismay that the State Department intends to urge increased aid to Mr. Nasser's government. 

In the instance of the Dhahran Air Field, we sacrificed principle to no avail. We agreed with King Saud of Saudi Arabia by action of the executive department, to eliminate Jewish personnel from the crews of U.S. Air Force planes using the Dhahran Air Field. But 

King Saud eventually kicked us out anyway, despite this disgraceful sacrifice of principle. I can imagine what it did to the morale of our 

Air Force people in that area. 

The State Department has shamefully retreated from our position in the 1930's when U.S. diplomats fought tenaciously against Nazi discrimination affecting American citizens of Jewish faith. 

Mr. Sumner Welles, then Under Secretary of State, stated America's basic position as refusing to recognizethe right of other nations to apply *** to American citizens measures which would have the effect of arbitrarily dividing them into special classes and subjecting them to differential treatment. 

Ernest Woermann, an official of the Nazi Foreign Office in Berlin, received a lecture in this connection from our then Chargé d'Affaires, Mr. Prentiss Gilbert. Mr. Gilbert said on that occasion in January 

1939, to the Nazis, thatjust as within our country individuals of all origins having acquired citizenship were equally American citizens, they must all be regarded as American citizens abroad. Our passports were all worded in precisely the same manner and all carried the same weight. The German Government has endeavored to create distinctions between groups of American citizens. This action by the 

German Government struck at the very roots of our commonwealth. Such action was likewise intolerable to us and we would resist it and would continue to resist it.

So spoke a U.S. diplomat just a little more than two decades ago to the nation then the most powerful military force on earth. 

Mr. Chairman, where has our pride gone in so short a time and after so costly a war?

I emphasize that failure to make a mandatory stand in pending legislation will be interpreted as a retreat on the part of the Congress, an appeasement, that could only lead to more flagrant violations of decency and international law on the part of certain of the Arab States receiving our aid. We must be resolute on this issue or face erosion of our ideals and the heritage that is America. 

Lest the impression be given that Arab boycott and blockage restrictions affect only Americans of one religion, let me point out that the consequences of Arab sanctions have affected American seamen of all faiths, employers in many industries and their employees, and also their families; also stockholders and suppliers, as well as the very American home communities in which the businesses affected are located.

A stand taken through adoption of the measure Mr. Roosevelt and 

I advocate would implement a statement last April by our President who said:

I am determined that my administration, at all levels, shall exercise affirmative leadership to discharge both its constitutional obligation and its moral duty to achieve equal opportunity for all. 

Our historic national tradition has charted proud precedents. In 

1885, the United States refused to accept protests by Austria-Hungary on the appointment of our Ambassador to that kingdom because the designee's wife happened to be of Jewish faith. 

In 1911 the United States abrogated a trade treaty with Czarist Russia, in effect since 1832, because of Russian mistreatment of Jews. 

In 1924 we protested to Switzerland against exclusion of Americans of the Mormon faith. 

Our vigorous repeated protests to Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany are also part of that history. 

As far back as 1956, our President, then a Senator of the United States, described Egypt's Nasser as "the chief provocateur against the West." Last year at the United Nations General Assembly, Mr. 

Nasser voted with the Soviet Union on 53 occasions but only four times with America. Egypt's discrimination against our shipping and otherwise affecting our citizens continues unabated. But now we hear talk of increased assistance to Egypt. 

Mr. Chairman, enough time has gone by without the implementation of the various antibias and freedom of the seas clauses that have been part of our foreign assistance acts. The State Department doesn't hesitate to ask us to vote funds the Department terms imperative. But it gives little heed when we express the will of the 

American people as expressed in Congress, on the implementation of the antibias provisions of the aid program. 

I feel that the time has come that the only answer is the mandatory provision in H.R. 10787 and H.R. 10856 which I urge this committee to consider.

Democracy is not self-propelled like a rocket. We must keep building freedom to make it survive and spread. This is not done by hyprocrisy and appeasement. We cannot ask our people to die, if necessary, to fight a Berlin blockade while appeasing a Beirut blockade.

I wish to thank the committee for hearing me on this vital subject and to say that I am rewarded by a warm conviction that the

points Mr. Roosevelt and I have raised will be given full and fair consideration. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

STATEMENT OF DR. LEWIS E. LLOYD, ECONOMIC ADVISER FOR 

DOW CHEMICAL CO., MIDLAND, MICH. 

Dr. LLOYD. Mr. Chairman, I am Lewis E. Lloyd, of Midland, Mich.

I am an economist and head of business research for the Dow Chemical Co. I appear today not in my business capacity, but rather as a professional economist and a private citizen who is alarmed at the U.S. balance-of-payments situation and its implications with respect to foreign aid. Because I have given special attention to the study of monetary and fiscal problems, the Citizens Foreign Aid Committee has urged me to analyze these factors for this committee. It is to this aspect of foreign aid that I wish to direct my remarks. 

The advocates of massive foreign aid are greatly impressed by the endless wants of man. They feel a compulsion to fill as many of the wants around the world as possible. In their zeal to do "great good" they forget to examine all the consequences of their program. They fail to examine the fundamental economics involved, the natural laws that are controlling. It is only by directing our attention to these fundamentals that a sound evaluation of the foreign aid program can be made.

There will not be time today to discuss the inadequacy and the weakness of the program from the standpoint of the recipient; how that government-to-government gifts advances Socialist enterprise around the world, and not free enterprise which made this country great; how that education and a high level of business ethics is a prerequisite to developing a viable, industrial society; how that the development of skills, transportation, communications, marketing, banking, and many other complex factors require a delicate balance in a growing industrial society; how that a proper balance between consumption, savings and investment, coupled with the urge for constructive risk-taking, must exist before an economy can aspire to industrial status; how that the receiving of dole builds dependence, not self-reliance and independence. 81496-62-pt. 6- -5

Rather, let us direct our attention to some of the consequences for the United States and especially to the balance-of-payments problem and its implications. In October of 1960 the value of the dollar temporarily lost its standing in the world market when the price of gold on the London exchange went above the U.S. gold export point and a few days later reached $41 an ounce more than a 17-percent discount for the dollar. Since that time the balance-of-payments problem and the health of the dollar has been given much attention both by the press and by monetary and fiscal experts. In the past year periodic meetings of the heads of the important central banks of Europe and the United States indicate the importance which they attach to this problem. What is not generally recognized, however, is that this problem is deeply imbedded in the fundamentals of economic exchange. 

In order to fully evaluate the impact of foreign aid, it is necessary to examine the basic economics of exchange. În a division-of-labor society, some workers produce a given goods or service and exchange this with other workers for the products of their labor. When a society becomes complex and industrialized, barter is inadequate to bring about the exchanges of goods and services, and so money is used as a tool to expedite exchange. 

You will note the equation which shows this. 

It is important to note that the economic exchange process is not complete with the first step of exchanging goods for money, but only after the second step of exchanging the money for another economic good. If one individual or group of individuals exchanges goods and services for money and retains or hoards part of this money failing to exchange it for other goods and services, then an imbalance results. It means that others have production for which there is no market.

In this basic equation of economic exchange, we see the fundamentals of trade between nations. Normally, one nation will exchange goods and services for money and then with that money buy goods and services from other nations. If the export and import of goods and services does not balance, then money will flow into or out of the country and there are economic consequences with respect to the internal economies of the countries involved, both those that lose money and those that gain. 

The "balance of payments" is the term which is used to indicate the balance or lack of balance between the flow of goods and services between nations. The balance of payments will show the sum of: the net of our foreign trade; the net of exchange of services (shipping, insurance, et cetera); on tourism, the net on capital flow and the net on gifts and loans.

If the net on all of these show that foreigners have gained dollarsthat is, more dollars have left this country than came back-we are said to have a negative balance of payments. 

It is important to note that in the international marketplace there is no difference between dollars obtained from trade and dollars obtained from tourists and capital flow or from gifts. It is the total bal-

ance of payments that indicates our economic balance with the rest of the world. Since we have a negative balance of payments, more dollars are leaving this country than are returning. This is because we have priced ourselves out of world markets, on the average. Foreigners can take our dollars and buy goods elsewhere more cheaply. 

One of the largest items in our balance of payments is our merchandise account the exports and imports of goods. Commerce Department figures have shown in recent years $4 to $5 billion more exports than imports, and this is often interpreted as evidence that U.S. producers are competitive in world markets. Examination shows, however, that the Department of Commerce data on exports is meaningful only with a special interpretation of the word "exports." Included are products bought with U.S. tax dollars and shipped overseas. In other words, some of our foreign aid shows up in this category. Included in the so-called export figures are sizable quantities of agricultural products shipped under Public Law 480 and sold to nations for soft currency which is blocked and cannot be converted into dollars. 

Included also are sizable quantities of shipments to our military establishments overseas. Likewise included are subsidized agricultural exports, and even included are relief shipments of grain to famine areas. 

Chart 1 shows recent history of U.S. exports and imports as reported by the Department of Commerce and as corrected to remove the portion of exports which are purchased with American taxpayers' dollars and sent overseas. (Chart 1 is as follows:)

It is obvious that the portion we buy with our dollars and send overseas cannot be considered as commercial exports bought overseas. 

We follow the practice of tabulating imports on the basis of foreign f.o.b. values. The other important industrial nations of the world account their foreign trade on a c.i.f. basis (cost, including insurance and freight). Were we to count our imports on a c.i.f. basis, we would have to add from 10 to 25 percent on the value of our imports, depending on the country of origin. 

Chart shows the balance between our commercial exports and imports if we use only a modest 15 percent to increase our reported imports.
