1 It is not only valid, but essential, to do this because in most of our imports the freight and insurance is furnished by the foreign exporter and we have to pay, of course, dollars to cover this cost. 

Thus a careful examination of our foreign trade data shows that in truly commercial exports we have a deficit, not an excess. So when we seek an answer to the question, "Why do we have the continuing and growing balance-of-payments problem?" our attention comes to rest on the foreign aid program. This is the chief source of dollars. which leave our shores and do not return. 

When we examine the recent history of the U.S. balance of payments, we readily see the occasion for the alarm concerning the problem. Chart 3 shows the balance of payments for the postwar years.

Since 1949 there has been a persistent and growing negative balance, except for the year 1957 when the Suez crisis forced Europe to buy oil from the dollar area. In the early part of 1961, a divergence between the economies of Europe and the United States gave a temporary respite from the outflow of dollars. As recovery in the U.S. economy advanced, however, the negative balance became larger than ever, reaching a $5 billion annual rate in the fourth quarter of 1961. 

This sustained and growing negative balance of payments has resulted in loss of part of our gold reserve and increased foreign claims against our gold. Chart 4 shows this data for the postwar years.

We have a commitment to furnish gold at $35 an ounce to foreign central banks. Consequently, any foreigner can take his dollars to his central bank which can then convert them into gold.

Chart 5 shows the amount of gold we would have left if we paid off all the foreign claims outstanding, and also shows the amount of gold which is needed to meet the 25-percent reserve requirements of our banking law.

1965 It is obvious that since 1954 we have been unable to meet all our commitments if at any time the foreigners had decided to cash in all their claims. In the past year we could not even have met our foreign commitments if we had disregarded any gold reserve to support our own banking system.

When the exchange of goods and services between countries fail to balance, one country may be willing to hold claims against another country for a limited period of time. In the end, however, the money commodity, gold, is the only tangible way that the accounts could be balanced. Normally, foreigners with mounting dollars claims would present these for gold. So long as they trust the United States to be able and willing in the future to meet its obligations to supply gold upon request, they will be willing to hold the dollar claims in lieu

of gold. They have some special incentives not to ask for gold. Much of the dollar claims are held in Treasury notes and bills which pay interest. When the claims are converted to gold, there is a slight charge for safekeeping. Moreover, the industrial nations of Europe who hold the bulk of these dollar claims are well aware that were they to call for large amounts of gold, this would precipitate a liquidity crisis and force us to eliminate most or all of our foreign aid. Since many of our foreign aid dollars have found their way into the industrial economies of Europe and Japan, they are loath to make any move which would force us into cutting our foreign aid. 

Thus we see that through the continuing balance of payments deficit our international liquidity and the soundness of the dollar is now dependent upon the confidence of foreign nationals. Our own fiscal policies now must face the discipline of international finance. 

Returning now to the basic economies of exchange, we note that our negative balance of payments indicated the extent to which dollars have not returned to buy goods and services from American workers. 

In the past 4 years this outflow of dollars has averaged almost $32 billion per year. If these dollars had come back to this country to buy manufactured goods, it would have created at least 12 million more jobs than we had. 

Much has been made by the proponents of free trade of various "guesstimates" of the number of jobs created by our exports. These proponents fail to mention the jobs that are lost as a result of imports. 

What they do, in effect, is to talk only about the credit side of the ledger and completely ignore the debit entries. Actually, of course, it is the balance between the credits and debits which tells the only meaningful story. This is precisely what the balance of payments tells us. 

It is the overall balance between the jobs created by the dollars that enter our economy from overseas and the jobs lost due to dollars that go overseas. Since there has been a net loss of dollars, it is obvious that there has been a net loss of jobs. We can make a rough approximation of how many jobs are involved by dividing the $3 billion outflow of dollars of recent years by the average annual earnings of a factory worker. This number of jobs must then be increased by what the economists call a "multiplier factor" to take account of the service jobs which increased factory worker earnings would support. For example, the chamber of commerce reports that for every 100 factory jobs in a community, 174 other jobs will be added. 

U.S. PRODUCERS NONCOMPETITIVE 

The reason for the large and growing negative balance of payments is that U.S. labor and U.S. manufacturers have priced themselves out of the world market. When the foreigners get our dollars, they find that they can use these dollars to buy goods elsewhere in the world cheaper than from the United States. 

I might add this is precisely why, beginning from a period right after the war when practically all the foreign aid funds were spent back in this country, year by year the percentage spent here dropped until in the latter part of the 1950's it got down to only where roughly a third was spent in the United States, and why Government action was taken a couple of years ago to require more of the dollars be spent

here. Even these underdeveloped countries found they could buy the goods cheaper that they wanted in Germany and Japan than they could here.

There are three dominant factors which have contributed to the noncompetitive position of U.S. producers. 

During the war the plants of Europe and England and Japan were destroyed by bombs or by overworking and inadequate maintenance. 

As a consequence, when these industrial nations rebuilt their plants, for the most part with our foreign aid dollars, they built modern, new, automated plants. We went to great lengths to help them do this. We invited and paid the expenses of teams of foreign industrialists to come to this country and see our plants and learn our methods. With new plants and advanced methods, productivity in industrial Europe and Japan advanced by leaps and bounds. Unions in these foreign countries moderated their demands so that much of this increased productivity could find its way into selling price reductions in order that industry in each country could become more competitive in world inarkets. 

Another factor which is only now beginning to have its effect is the creation of the European Economic Community. As the so-called 

Common Market develops, there will exist in Europe a mass market sufficient to support mass production industries, sufficient to permit maximum efficiency through large production plants. In the past the 

United States had the only truly mass market in the world and hence had an enormous advantage, in a sense a monopoly of mass production. 

This is no longer true. 

First of all, Europe is building its own mass market, and secondly, through successful tariff reductions and particularly if H.R. 9900 is passed and implemented, we will have opened our mass market to any producer in the world so that we will have completely lost any special advantage through large-scale production. 

The most significant factor in the pricing of ourselves out of world markets is the inflation with which we chose to finance World War II. 

During that war and a little more during Korea and since, we have poured more than $90 billion of worthless, paper, fiat money into our banking system. Monetary inflation always brings with it certain consequences-maladjustments in the economy which show up in various ways. The first thing that happened during the war when this excess purchase media was created was that the velocity in the use of money dropped very low. There were no houses to be bought, no automobiles for civilians, no consumer hardgoods, not even good quality clothing available. Moreover, it was patriotic to save and to buy bonds. Consequently, consumers paid off their installment debt, paid on their mortgages, bought Government bonds, and increased the size of their checking accounts. 

In a word, consumers became more "liquid." After the war, as consumer goods became available, they began to use their savings and to buy on time, and thus gradually, little by little the inflationary money began to be used. 

Since more than one worthless dollar had been created for every good one and since $2 came to the marketplace to buy a dollar's worth of goods, and since the marketplace couldn't tell the good dollar from the worthless dollar, naturally the prices were bid up until a dollar's

worth of goods sold for $2. Thus we find that our dollar is now worth only 46 cents as compared to prewar. 

Now the price of labor went up along with the price of everything else; in fact, faster than the price of goods. Thus through the wellknown processes of monetary inflation, American labor and American manufacturers have established price levels above the average for world markets. This is the major maladjustment in our economy which has come out of our monetary inflation of the past two decades. 

We see the real consequences of this when we turn our attention again to the basic exchange equation. 

When foreigners exchange goods and services to us for our dollars, normally they would exchange those dollars for other goods and services from us. It just so happens, however, that one of the goods which we offer the world is gold. Through the process of inflation the prices of our other goods and services have essentially doubled, but the price of gold remains at $35 an ounce as it was fixed in 1934. 

Thus today gold is the cheapest commodity we offer the world. It is not surprising, therefore, that foreigners who get dollars prefer to keep part of those dollars to exchange for gold. 

Of course, as we have seen, they don't actually have to exchange them for gold as long as the world has confidence that we will honor our obligation to furnish gold upon demand. What they do is to keep part of these dollars and to use them to trade with other nations. 

The dollars which they keep and do not use to buy from us, reduces the total purchases from our economy and leads to reduction in rate of our industrial growth and causes unemployment here. 

Thus we see that for a variety of reasons, the most significant of which is the major inflation we have had, we are no longer competitive in world markets. For this reason the dollars are not coming back to buy our goods and services. Dollars are not returning to support jobs in this country. In the last quarter of 1961, and presumably in the first quarter of this year, our balance of payments has been showing a deficit at a $5 billion annual rate. The continuing and growing foreign claims against our gold cannot continue indefinitely. 

As we noted earlier, we are already bankrupt with respect to our foreign accounts. We could not meet our commitments even now, and day by day the situation grows worse. 

The continued acceptance of the dollar in world markets is only by the good grace of those to whom we are debtor. Sooner or later foreign confidence in the dollar will be shaken to the point where more and more of them will be tendered for gold. The time will come when we will have to default on these obligations. Then most surely the respect for the dollar will shrink rapidly. 

In the face of this, it is time that we reconsider the whole foreign aid program. It is clear that we can't afford the outpouring of these dollars at this level. The first step that we should take is to require that every dollar of foreign aid be spent in the United States for goods our goods and services. A similar requirement should be placed against the various loan agencies. By doing this, at least it would create jobs for our unemployed workers and for our factories which are operating well below capacity. 

It would stop the outflow of dollars from our foreign aid activities. 

This of itself would not solve our balance-of-payments problems, but

would reduce the level of dollar outflow and buy time during which more fundamental corrections could be worked out. 

The second step is to reevaluate the whole concept of trying to make people strong, of trying to make economies healthy, by putting them on a dole. If we still retain any belief in the free market system, then we should realize that private investment can better evaluate economic opportunities and risks than can Government bureaucracies. 

Under private investment we would not find situations such as this: 

Last year we gave Jordan $10 million worth of foreign aid; Jordan bought $10 million worth of gold from us. 

If we wish to advance the cause of freedom and the free market system that made this country great, we should be using our prestige and our leadership at the political level to induce other countries to establish a political climate which would welcome private business and private initiative to develop the resources of their country. We should be devoting our efforts to establishing commercial treaties against expropriation. We should be encouraging the kind of income distribution which will build purchasing power at the worker level in foreign countries, rather than luxury at the top. 

Recognizing that education and right attitude are the prerequisite to stable, growing, free societies, such aid as the emergent nations are offered might better be in the form of schooling, scholarships, trade school courses, and the like, rather than our designing a socialistic economic plan for them.

Since it is clear that we cannot afford and cannot continue the massive foreign aid which has been a major factor in our balance-ofpayments difficulty, we must devise a more realistic plan. It is clear to any careful student of economic history that the emergent nations cannot be brought to full industrial status in a few short years. To lead them to believe so is to doom them to disillusionment and to assure the loss of their respect and friendship. Our program must be redrafted to be in line with our abilities and theirs.

Mr. ADAIR.

Dr. LLOYD. The moment that we restrict the flow of gold we abrogate our commitments. We would have publicly acknowledged our bankruptcy with respect to our international commitments on exchange. The immediate reaction around the world would be for the dollar to lose its favored position, for the dollar to become a secondrate currency, and it would have tremendous impact on the standing of our country in the eyes of the people of the world. 

We would lose face very extensively. 

Mr. Adair. If we continue on our present economic course, do you see any possibility that we may have to give thought to such action; that is, restricting the flow of gold?

Dr. LLOYD. It is my judgment if we continue on our present course that we will most certainly come to the day when we will have to embargo the export of gold and probably devalue the dollar. 

Mr. ADAIR. What would be the effect domestically of such a step as that?

Dr. LLOYD. This will depend on some other factors. If we devalued the dollar-let me take first embargo of the export of gold. This would have little internal effect except as the trade between us and other nations would be affected. There would be certainly many actions taken by foreign nations to try to recoup by indirect ways the dollars, the gold that they should get for the dollars. 

So far as devaluing the dollar is concerned, if we merely devalued the dollar and took no other steps internally, this would increase the credit base, to expand credit in this country by whatever percentage we devalued the dollar. This would be an open invitation to lead to more monetary inflation, the very thing that is the major cause of the trouble we now have. 

If, however, the Congress, at the same time the dollar were devalued, were to increase the bank reserve requirements by the same percentage, this would prevent any increased credit base and would be no further invitation to inflation.

Dr. LLOYD. This is what I mean by the word "socialistic": There are two ways by which a society may allocate the resources and factors of production. One is by free market approach whereby the consumer, the individuals, by their buying of goods or refraining from buying of goods determine what production will take place and which product will succeed and which will fail. This is the free market allocation of resources. 

The alternative to this is a plan which is made at the top and enforced upon society-in the ultimate by police action-where some group, some group of planners decide what society should have and how the resources should be allocated. We are going to allocate so much to building a dam this year, a road this year, or airport, instead of letting the marketplace decide which is the most needed and valuable expenditure of these resources at that moment.

According to your theory we should wait until the climate is right before the private investor goes down there to build his plants. 

Dr. LLOYD. It is my conviction from a study of economic history we are doomed to failure in developing industrial economies in those nations if they are not ready for the kind of moral responsibility that makes it possible to guarantee contracts and give the kind of ethical base that we have in this country. 

I think few people stop to realize the kind of trust upon which our society is built. Why, businessmen every day pick up the telephone and call clear across this Nation and do business in a few minutes representing millions of dollars. Their word is taken right over the telephone for this. This kind of trust is not available in lots of these countries. You can't build this kind of an economy and this kind of society until you have done something to the moral and ethical position of those people.

Mr. SEELY-BROWN. I would like to ask two questions. 

First, on page 10 of your testimony, sir, you say if we wish to advance the cause of freedom and the free market system that made this country great, we should be using our prestige and our leadership at the political level to induce other countries to establish a political climate which would welcome private business and private enterprise to develop the resources of their country.

How would you exert that prestige and leadership at the political level? How would we do it? Or how would you suggest that we do it?

Dr. LLOYD. One of the ways we would do it would be in the commercial treaty area. We have made great concessions to foreigners to import into our markets here. Since 1934 we have reduced our tariffs by more than 75 percent on the average. 

We now are one of the really low tariff nations in the world. Our average tariffs of dutiable goods are now about 10 percent. We have no quotas except on agricultural commodities that are under the support program. 

Most of the other countries of the world have a great host of quantitative restrictions which influence imports into their countries. Many of them have specific restrictions against imports from the United States. Even some of the European nations still make a differentiation between U.S. goods and goods from elsewhere in the world. 

This is an area where we could use very much persuasion to make them honor their commitments, first of all, and urge them in the direction of developing free market economies.

We have always the possibility of offering to raise our tariffs, offering to put on a quota, or offering to do something of this sort, if somebody else does not give us reasonable treatment. 

As a matter of fact, our tariff law in many cases specifies that the Chief Executive is supposed to do this-if they don't give us equal treatment, he is supposed to cancel out the reductions we have made.

STATEMENT OF REV. JAMES L. VIZZARD, S.J., DIRECTOR, WASH- INGTON OFFICE OF THE NATIONAL CATHOLIC RURAL LIFE CONFERENCE Father VIZZARD. My name is Father James L. Vizzard, S.J. I am director of the Washington Office of the National Catholic Rural Life 

Conference at 1312 Massachusetts Avenue NW. On this occasion I am speaking not only for the Conference but also, by official authorization, for the Catholic Association for International Peace. 

As members of this committee know, this is not the first time I have appeared before congressional committees to testify on foreign aid programs and proposals. In fact, so often have I testified that I suspect that it was to me, among others, that reference was made by a witness last week when he remarked:

At times the State Department, fearful lest foreign aid be pared by the Congress, has rounded up claques of clergymen, priests and rabbis to testify * * * Frankly, I did not know whether to be insulted or amused by the gentleman's remark. All this time I had thought I was acting on another prompting and on another authority. The circumspection of the 

State Department must be recognized in being able, at least in this case, to get its way without ever letting its sinister hand be seen. I will be on my guard in the future.

In view of this gentleman's suspicions, which I fear are shared by some others, even Catholics, around the country, it might not be inappropriate to emphasize the right and the duty of a church spokesman to be heard on the issue of foreign aid.

It is unquestionably true that there are many motives for undertaking such programs of foreign aid as our country has conducted for the last decade and more. Most obvious are the reasons which flow from the military, economic and political necessities of the cold war. Unless we are to retreat step by step into ultimate defeat and disaster, we must strengthen the military capacity and the economic and political stability of the nations of the free world. On the basis of what it means to us, aid for these purposes should more rightly be called American aid than foreign aid.

But more fundamental than these reasons for aid programs are the moral reasons. As has been repeatedly emphasized, even if communism were to disappear tomorrow, our Nation, as steward of a God-given abundance, would be obliged to continue and to expand our programs of assistance to the needy nations and peoples. 

I hope it will not seem impertinent if I point out in passing that I think that politicians who are plagued by constituents who are opposed or at least indifferent to foreign aid would win the understanding and approval of those constituents much more readily if the argument were presented on the basis of moral rather than political or military necessity. In my many contacts throughout the country I have invariably found that approval of foreign aid is more readily won and opposition

more readily dissipated by the approach President Kennedy emphasized in his inaugural address: 

To those people in the huts and villages of half the globe struggling to break the bonds of mass misery, we pledge our best efforts to help them help themselves, for whatever period is required-not because the Communists may be doing it, not because we seek their votes, but because it is right. 

But, perhaps we have too often simply stated that such aid is right and failed to make it unmistakably clear why it is right. It is here, in spelling out the moral reasons why, that a clergyman can perform a service appropriate to his calling, his training and his responsibility. 

This committee has already heard representatives of other religious affiliations and traditions. I will indicate sources from which Catholics form their consciences on an issue such as foreign aid. 

From direct Scriptural teaching, Catholics, as all other Christians, are moved particularly by the description of the Last Judgment which we have from Christ's own lips. In that dramatic portrayal the Judge determines the salvation or damnation of each individual person on the basis of how that person responded in this life to the needs of the hungry, the thirsty, the naked and the homeless. "Amen I say unto you, "the Judge will affirm, "whatsoever you did to the least of these my brethren, you did it unto Me." No Christian can escape or argue away the urgent implications of these words.

Well-informed Catholics find in the church's traditional teaching a confirmation and application of this scriptural doctrine. Here let me quote from only two authoritative sources, one ancient and the other modern.

First, there is the voice of St. Thomas Aquinas, the most revered philosopher and theologian of the Catholic tradition. Perhaps the case for foreign aid has never been put in clearer or more inescapable form than, in effect, Aquinas did seven centuries ago: 

Man's laws cannot stand in the way of the natural law or the divine law. Now according to the natural law set down by God's providence, material things are meant for this purpose: that from them man's necessities might be provided for. 

Therefore, the division and actual appropriation of material things which results from human law must not prevent them from fulfilling their purpose of providing for man's necessities. And therefore, those things which some possess beyond reasonable needs are owed by natural law to the sustenance of the poor *** If a particular necessity is so evident and urgent and immediate that it must be met by whatever is at hand (when for instance, there is imminent danger to one's life and no other help is available), then one can lawfully satisfy that need from the goods of another either openly or secretly; and this is not theft or robbery.

The other authoritative voice guiding Catholics to right judgments on foreign aid is so new that this is the first time that I, or anyone else, I believe, could incorporate its teaching into a statement of this nature before a congressional committee. I refer, of course, to last year's encyclical of Pope John XXIII, "Mater et Magistra," or in its English title, "Christianity and Social Progress." Page after page of this remarkable document sounds like a statement on foreign aid prepared precisely with this committee and this occasion in mind. Much as I might be tempted to give here extensive quotations to demonstrate the timeliness and appropriateness of the encyclical for this occasion, for the sake of brevity let me quote only a few significant sentences: * * * nations enjoying an abundance of material goods should not remain indifferent to those nations whose citizens suffer from internal problems that result

TB in poverty, hunger, and an inability to enjoy even the more elementary human rights. (Par. 157.) 

We are all equally responsible for the undernourished peoples *** [Therefore] it is necessary to awaken men's consciences to a sense of the responsibility which weighs upon everyone, especially upon those who are more richly blessed with this world's goods. (Par. 158.) 

Justice and humanity demand, then, that the rich come to the aid of the poor. (Par. 161.) 

These two authorities, St. Thomas Aquinas and Pope John XXIII, are illustrative of the church's teaching. If they do not specify by name on which nations rests the responsibility for generous sharing of material abundance, no one can doubt but that the United States is one of them and unquestionably the principal one. 

Despite soft spots in our economy, despite persistent pockets of poverty in our rural and urban slums, despite balance-of-payments problems and gold outflows, our Nation enjoys a material prosperity that is the wonder and even the envy of most of the world. 

Our economy is so productive that major industries-steel and automobiles are examples can operate at 50, 60, 70 percent of capacity and still satisfy customers' demands. We can afford to have our supermarket shelves stacked high with over 5,000 separate items, many of which even we recognize to be in the luxury class. We find ourselves embarrassed by the superabundance that keeps pouring from our farm cornucopia; we have barns, bins, and warehouses bulging with $9 billion worth of unused food and fiber. To climax our affluence we spend each year many billions of dollars on liquor, tobacco, and cosmetics, not to mention the weight reducers and antacids we seem to need to counteract our overindulgence.

It takes, therefore, no subtlety but only honesty to recognize the moral urgency of our sharing our abundance. We are our brother's keeper. It was Cain who would have denied it. Unwelcome though it may be, it is not an unwarranted imposition to expect and demand that U.S. citizens pay the necessary price, even to the point of considerable sacrifice, to see that our affluence is used to moral purposes. 

I do not think that we have even begun to make serious sacrifices. 

If it should be said that it is necessary to choose one or the other, I would judge that we would be morally obliged to defer domestic expenditures which are not essential to our national well-being in order to be able to devote truly adequate sums to foreign aid. 

In the context of today's world and in view of our affluence, it is my opinion that the only limit on foreign aid funds which has any validity is the ability of the recipient countries to absorb and constructively to use such funds. 

I must here hasten to say that I see no obligation to impoverish ourselves to help the world's needy. A simple redistribution of presently available goods would only result in a temporary alleviation of their want and would reduce us to their level. În sharing our abundance we are not obliged to make paupers of ourselves. I would judge, however, that today we are doing far less than we could and should.

In Up to this point my remarks have been directed to what we of the United States can and must do. That, of course, is appropriate, for it is we who have these particular obligations and we are the ones who must fulfill them.

But we are not the only ones operating under a set of moral imperatives, nor can we, acting alone, achieve these ends. Other nations, particularly of Western Europe, have the resources and ability to join us in these efforts. It is most encouraging to see that they too are recognizing their opportunity and responsibility. 

In every way available to us we should urge their increased participation. 

The countries which so urgently need economic development also possess resources, some of them in great potential abundance. 

They are poor, at least in part, because their resources and institutions have not been mobilized and put to work in such a fashion as to promote progress. 

While our obligation is to share with them our abundance, their obligation is to so reform and reshape their economic and political societies as to make the most effective use of their own internal resources of both things and people as well as of the aid we bring to them.

This is particularly true of the resource-rich or at least resourceadequate regions of the world which have stagnated because the possessors of wealth and power have been much more interested in the preservation of their own status and prerogatives than in the essential changes and reforms which would release the creative energies and resources of their countries. 

The internal social reform which is now written into our foreign aid law as a precondition to receiving our aid should accelerate such changes. It undoubtedly will be difficult and it certainly is a delicate matter for us to encourage and demand land reform, honest and equitable tax collections, currencies made stable by sound fiscal policy, and the development of democratic institutions and practices. But unless these changes are made, economic and social development will be impossible. We must miss no opportunity to facilitate and accelerate such changes. Own Still we must not allow ourselves to get impatient, much less petulant, when the rate of social change seems to be moving too slowly. 

Perhaps we need to remind ourselves that even within our country such changes often come agonizingly slowly. Witness the civil rights struggle, for example, and the many years we have been striving for a rational and equitable tax reform. While we cannot tolerate social stagnation in the countries we are aiding, we need to realize that social reform takes longer to accomplish than the few months that this requirement has been in our foreign aid legislation. 

In addition to this insistence on internal reform, last year's foreign aid legislation clearly stated that it is the intent of Congress that the greatest feasible use be made of private and voluntary nonprofit agencies in our programs. Again, time has been short for working out basic policy and operational details for such cooperation. But I have to confess I would be happier if I saw more signs that guidelines were being developed. 

This seems to me to be particularly urgent in the case of the Alliance for Progress. We heartily endorse this newest proposal but we wonder how effective it can be without the fullest collaboration with the social reform efforts and projects of the voluntary agencies already operative and developing in Latin America.

1107

Finally, gentlemen, I would like to raise another question of broad policy, which, though widely and even heatedly debated in some circles, has not yet been adequately and dispassionately considered in relation to our foreign aid programs. 

It seems to me that in a relatively short time effective public policy will have to be adopted in the critically important area of population growth and economic development. Such a policy determination will be particularly urgent in regard to our foreign aid programs and the whole problem of emerging nations. 

I judge that not only the factual basis for such policy development but also the clarification of opinions and positions necessary before policy can be developed are at present wholly inadequate. I believe, for instance, that the facts, determinants, and consequences of population growth and its effect on economic development are too little known. 

Even such experts as we have often assemble facts, apply judgments, and arrive at conclusions on the basis of a relatively narrow and incomplete approach to a very complex situation. 

I don't think, moreover, that we have faced up clearly and courageously to the practical implications for public policy of the deep split between conscientious citizens over what means, if any, may be used in dealing with apparently harmful population growth. To be very explicit, Catholic citizens believe that artificial birth control methods are morally evil; other responsible citizens are convinced that such methods are not only morally licit but also, in some conditions, morally imperative. In a democracy how is public policy to be arrived at in the face of such conflicting—and strongly heldconvictions?

I suggest, therefore, that an important public service needs to be performed by bringing together for intensive discussions the best minds from all the sciences and disciplines with a legitimate interest in and a contribution to make to the field of population and development. Each field would be asked to present facts as they are known or appear from its viewpoint, and efforts would be made to settle on a body of commonly accepted facts. In addition, efforts would be made to enlarge as far and as clearly as possible the area of agreement and to define as sharply and narrowly as possible the area of irreconcilable disagreement.

I do not know whether such a study can appropriately be undertaken by this committee or by an agency of the executive branch, or whether it might more rightly be done under private sponsorship. 

But I suggest that if bitter conflict is to be avoided in the near future, a conflict which can be destructive to our foreign aid programs, a proper foundation must soon be laid for the development of public policy on this most delicate and vital issue. 

That is my statement, Mr. Chairman. I want to thank you for the opportunity to appear before you.
