(The following memorandum has been supplied for the record in response to a request by Mr. Farbstein. See p. 116.)

The appropriations of the military departments cover the military pay, approximately half the military permanent change of station, travel cost and medical care, dependent schooling and equipment costs for military personnel assigned to MAAGS, missions, Unified Commands and Washington agencies who support the military assistance program. It is estimated that in fiscal year 1963 the military assistance program will total $87 million : 

For military pay-.

For PCS travel (approximately one-half of the total cost). 

For medical care, dependent schooling, equipment, etc. 

Million $70 10 87 These are the only costs which are, strictly speaking, attributable to military assistance which are funded from military department appropriations. 

The other expenditure of military department funds which closely approximate the type of expenditures covered by military assistance are the expenditures for the operations in Vietnam (a classified insert on this subject was provided to the committee).

Expenditures for the maintenance of U.S. forces in Korea and Japan, Europe, etc., are not considered supplemental to military assistance expenditures. DOD cost accounting and varying deployments preclude attribution of specific price tags to the total of units deployed in any particular area. This accounting system is followed by DOD because the divisions in Korea, for example, fulfill the U.S. requirement for forces which would continue to exist even if the particular forces were not deployed in Korea. No attempt is made when the DOD fills its requirements for rifles to allocate in an accounting sense certain rifles to the defense of Korea and certain rifles for the defense of Europe. In addition, estimation of maintaining units in any given place is made more difficult because many units, such as air squadrons, are deployed on a rotating basis so that the equipment and personnel level in any given place varies appreciably during short periods.

In general, if one assumes that the U.S. units in various foreign countries would be maintained in the United States if they are not maintained in those countries, the differential cost is simply that of change of station cost minus or plus any difference in living cost. (The following information has been supplied by the Agency for International 

Development for inclusion in the record :)

The criteria for long-term commitments under section 202(b) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 have not inhibited the making of such agreements. AID has taken the position that the authority granted under section 202 of the act must be used only in cases when the plans and programs of the recipient country are well worked out in detail so that advance assurance provided for in section 202 is needed. The long-term plans and programs of development assistance must be prepared in extensive detail and must be clearly capable of orderly and effective execution.

For such reasons, the authority has been used sparingly in the 6 months since its enactment. Four long-term commitments have been entered into by the 

Government in relation to long-term development plans during the last year. 

The largest of these covering aid to India through fiscal year 1963 was entered into prior to enactment of the Foreign Assistance Act. The Congress was fully 1111

informed of that commitment. In view of the nature of the consortium agreement, the number of countries involved, and the extensive existing pattern of negotiations, it has been determined that it would not be advantageous to convert the commitment into a section 202 commitment. Long-term commitments have been made to Tanganyika and Pakistan. The Tanganyika commitment has been completed and was reported to the Congress. The Pakistan agreement is in the final stages of being formally approved by the respective governments. As soon as the agreement has been concluded, notice will be given to the Congress in accordance with the provisions of section 202 (c) of the act. Another long-term commitment has been made with Nigeria, based on extensive consultation with the Government of Nigeria and with other sources of assistance to Nigeria including the World Bank. This commitment was made prior to final completion and approval of the Nigerian plan. In each of these cases there had been a long period of plan preparation and emphasis prior to commitment. This planning process is proceeding in several other countries, and we expect a considerable increase in the use of the long-term commitment authority during the coming year.

It sometimes is necessary at an implementation stage of the development planning process to give a country some assurance of further assistance as a spur to successful completion of the planning process. This was the case in 

Nigeria where evidence of international support was needed by the Government to obtain parliamentary approval of the development plan. Similar needs have arisen in the Philippines, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile requiring a pledge of assistance subject to the availability of funds. In view of the early stage of the planning process in these cases, it was felt that this pledge should not be undertaken under the authority of section 202 (b) with its implied moral commitment of the Congress. As development plans are prepared and adopted in more and more countries and a larger share of aid is placed on a long-term program basis, it is expected that there will be a decreasing need for use of this informal commitment authority. AID will use the advance assurance given by section 202 of the act only when the plans and programs will support the need for such assurance. If there are still details to be worked out, a significant number of other contributors to be canvassed, unknown factors to be assessed, or major steps to be taken by the recipient country, the statutory long-term commitment authority will not ordinarily be used. 

Thus, the sparing use of section 202 is not inhibited by the statute; it merely reflects the desire of the executive branch to use the authority in those cases where it is needed the most. 

STATEMENT OF THE AMERICAN JEWISH COMMITTEE 

The American Jewish Committee, a national non-Zionist educational and human relations organization with 62 chapters or units and members in over 600 communities in the United States, was organized in 1906 and incorporated by special act of the Legislature of the State of New York in 1911. As stated in its charter, among the objects of the AJC is "to prevent the infraction of the civil and religious rights of Jews, in any part of the world; to render all lawful assistance and to take appropriate remedial action in the event of threatened or actual invasion or restriction of such rights, or of unfavorable discrimination with respect thereto; to secure for Jews equality of economic, social, and educational opportunity ***". 

In June of last year, Mr. James Marshall, AJC vice president, appeared on behalf of the American Jewish Committee before your committee during the hearings on the foreign aid bill (now Public Law 87-195). Mr. Marshall described the discriminatory practices of certain Arab League nations against American citizens of the Jewish faith and against American firms with Jewish ownership or Jewish executives and included as part of his testimony a detailed fact sheet in further support of his statement. As an indication of its concern with the facts as presented by Mr. Marshall, your committee included as part of the foreign aid bill (H.R. 8400) which it reported on July 31, 1961, the following strongly worded provision: "SEC. 102(e) It is the sense of the Congress that inasmuch as "(1) the United States favors freedom of navigation in international waterways and economic cooperation between countries; and "(2) the purposes of this Act are negated and the peace of the world is endangered when countries which receive assistance under this Act wage

economic warfare against other countries assisted under this Act, including such procedures as boycotts, blockades, and the restrictions of the use of international waterways; and "(3) any attempt by foreign countries to create distinctions because of their race or religion among American citizens in the granting of personal or commercial access or any other rights otherwise available to United States citizens generally is repugnant to our principles; assistance under this Act and the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, as amended, shall be administered to give effect to these principles, and, in all negotiations between the United States and any foreign state arising as a result of funds appropriated under this Act or arising under the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954, as amended, these principles shall be applied, as the President may determine, and he shall report on measures taken by the Administration to insure their application." 

Unfortunately this strong language was stricken in conference and section 102 of the present Act for International Development (Public Law 87-195) substituted therefor. The House conferees, at the time, noted in the conference report (H. Rept. 1088) the following: "The managers on the part of the House insisted on the inclusion in the statement of policy of a strong expression of U.S. support for the principle of freedom of navigation on international waterways and of the right of all private persons to travel and pursue their lawful activities without discrimination as to race or religion."

The deep feelings of the Congress with respect to this issue were further manifested with the adoption of the so-called Rooney-Halpern amendment to the Foreign Assistance and Related Agencies Appropriation Act, 1962 (Public 

Law 87-329) as follows: "SEC. 108. It is the sense of Congress that any attempt by foreign nations to create distinctions because of their race or religion among American citizens in the granting of personal or commercial access or any other rights otherwise available to United States citizens generally is repugnant to our principles; and in all negotiations between the United States and any foreign state arising as a result of funds appropriated under this title these principles shall be applied as the President may determine."

Concern was also manifested in the Senate. As part of its report (S. Rept. 

991) on the foreign assistance appropriations bill last year, the Senate Appropriations Committee stated: 

"RELIGIOUS AND RACE DISTINCTIONS 

"Section 108 of the House bill expresses the sense of the Congress that it is repugnant to the principles of the United States for foreign nations to create distinctions among American citizens because of their race or religion. This section was placed in the bill on the floor of the House of Representatives, and was also included in the appropriation act last year. "The committee urges the executive departments concerned to give force to the sense of the Congress as expressed in this section in the administration of the foreign assistance program, to the extent feasible, and by other appropriate means."

A strong caveat was inserted in the conference report (H. Rept. 1197) on the 

Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (Public Law 87-256). 

This legislation is a codification of all educational and cultural exchange programs authorized by law. The report reads: "The managers on the part of the House desire that in the administration of the various programs authorized by this bill no discrimination as to race, creed, or color will be practiced in the selection of individuals to perform functions under this bill or to benefit from the provisions of the programs authorized in the bill. Similarly they desire that countries that practice such discrimination shall not be the beneficiaries of any of the programs authorized in this bill." 

A similar expression is found in the conference report (H. Rept. 1239) on the 

Peace Corps Act (Public Law 87-293). Giving added force to this statement, Peace Corps Director_Sargent Shriver, in testimony on August 21, 1961, before the Subcommittee on Foreign Operations Appropriations of the House Appropriations Committee, said: "If a person is prevented from going to a particular country because he is a Catholic, Protestant, or a Jew, we do not go to that country, because our selection, recruitment, and training is on a nondiscriminatory basis. We offer our 81496-62-pt. 6-7

people on a nondiscriminatory basis, provided they have the skills that come in the request." 

Thus, it is quite apparent that this committee, and the 87th Congress as well, are deeply concerned with manifestations by nations receiving U.S. aid, of discrimination against American citizens and American businesses on account of creed or race. This concern is felt elsewhere in the national community. For example, on December 11 last, at its annual convention, the AFL-CIO, representing some 13.5 million workers, adopted a resolution 1 which said in part: "We insist that any attempt by Arab nations to create distinctions among American citizens because of their race or religion in the granting of personal or commercial access or any other rights otherwise available to United States citizens generally, is repugnant to our principles." 

Legislatures of the several States continue to adopt resolutions and memorials on the boycott. Seven States have so far done so; viz, California, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. The most recent is the Commonwealth of Massachusetts which on April 9, 1962, adopted the following resolution: "Whereas Arab nations including the United Arab Republic, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Libya, Sudan, Tunisia and Morocco, functioning as the Arab League, have been conducting a boycott of certain American citizens, business, and industry; and "Whereas the Arab League has blacklisted all American ships which have touched at Israeli ports of call; and "Whereas American firms doing business in Israel are cut off from trade with Arab countries; and "Whereas Arab League countries continue to make strenuous efforts to prevent most American companies controlled or managed, partially or wholly, by Americans of the Jewish faith from establishing commercial relationships with countries that are members of the Arab League; and "Whereas American servicemen and Armed Forces employees of Jewish faith are not permitted to serve at the Dhahran Airbase in Saudi Arabia; and "Whereas American citizens, because they are members of the Jewish faith, are generally not permitted to disembark in such Arab countries as Jordan and 

Saudi Arabia; and "Whereas approximately 500 American business firms during 1960 received warning through the United States mails from Arab boycott officers in Damascus and Kuwait that if Americans have commercial dealings with Israel, they must forgo doing business with Arab countries; and "Whereas individual Hollywood motion picture stars have also been blacklisted, and have been prevented from playing in some Arab League countries even under U.S. State Department auspices; and "Whereas American citizens of the Jewish faith are generally excluded from private employment in any capacity in any Arab owned or controlled company; and "Whereas, with the approval of the Department of Agriculture, Commodity Credit Corporation and the U.S. Navy, contracts for the shipment of U.S. surplus wheat to the United Arab Republic provide that the vessel may not have traded at Israeli ports; and "Whereas the Democratic Party platform of 1960 pledged the protection of the rights of American citizens to travel, to pursue lawful trade, and to engage in other lawful activities abroad without distinction as to race or religion, and has further pledged to oppose any international agreement or treaty which by its terms or practices differentiates among American citizens on grounds of race or religion; and "Whereas the Republican Party platform of 1960 pledged to seek an end to transit and trade restrictions, blockades, and blacklists, and further pledged to secure freedom of navigation on international waterways and the cessation of discrimination against Americans on the basis of religious beliefs: Therefore be it "Resolved, That the General Court of Massachusetts respectfully urges the Department of State to take a firm position against Arab interference in the conduct of the affairs of American citizens and businessmen, to abstain from any accommodation to Arab League boycott activities and policies, whether passive or overt, to resist any efforts by Arab nations to maintain or widen its boycott activities in the United States, and to exert all possible efforts and 

1 Resolution on Middle East, Resolution 152.

utilize its resources to the fulfillment of the spirit and purposes of these resolutions; and be it further "Resolved, That copies of these resolutions be forwarded by the secretary of the Commonwealth to the Secretary of State of the United States." 

Yet, this discrimination continues. A prime example is the case of the Hashemite kingdom of Jordan which, unlike most-but not all of its sister Arab States such as Egypt, Syria, and Morocco, persists in barring entry of American citizens of the Jewish faith. On the other hand the United States contributes almost half of the Jordanian national budget of $80 million; has helped the financing of sundry Jordanese health, education, and training projects to the extent of some $6.5 million; has provided military equipment assistance of about $60 million; has provided surplus foods to the extent of some $4 million and has helped the Jordanians develop its tourists attractions, such as Jeraz, an ancient Roman city where U.S. funds not only were used at the city site itself but were also employed to build a two-lane macadam road connecting Jeraz with Amman, Jordan's capital.

It has been well said that Jordan's hope for economic stability lies in expanding its tourist traffic. However, Jordan denies itself the opportunity of earning more tourist dollars by barring American visitors of the Jewish faith. This not only deprives Jordan of dollar earnings from such individual tourists but also it loses opportunities for dollar earnings from organized tours which are reluctant to include Jordan in their itineraries because this would be embarrassing to any Jewish participants. And the American taxpayer must make up these lost dollar earnings through our aid grants. By its stubborn adherence to this discrimination, Jordan is depriving itself of opportunities to become more economically viable. In this connection, it is interesting to note that the United 

Arab Republic (Egypt) and some other members of the Arab League do not bar American tourists of the Jewish faith. Moral considerations aside for the moment, the conclusion must be drawn that Jordan should be vigorously encouraged to drop its religious bars for its own good and for furtherance of the purposes for which the United States has been, and is, extending such great aid. 

Saudi Arabia has similar bars. While by no stretch of the imagination can that country be considered a tourist resort nor can it be argued that admittance of persons of the Jewish faith would appreciably increase its economic viability, as is the case with Jordan, nevertheless the discriminatory practices of the Saudi Arabs are so flagrant as to raise the question as to U.S. "loss of face" by our seeming condoning of them in an area of the world where firmness is respected. 

This committee is aware, we are certain, that as recently as early this year the Saudi Arabs have refused permission for a Member of the House of Representatives to visit installations financed by U.S. funds. And the State Department has been most negligent in pushing this issue. 

A similar incident was disclosed during hearings before your committee on March 14 when it was brought out that an aircraft containing a Foreign Affairs Subcommittee headed by Representative John Pilcher, of Georgia, was queried by the Lebanese last fall as to whether there were any Jewish members or staff aboard. If there had been, the plane presumably would not have been allowed to land.

It might be well at this juncture to point out that other governments, less powerful than ours, do not abide with this discriminatory treatment. Our testimony last year documented a number of such cases. A more recent one, to be added to these, is that of the firm stand of the Dutch Government. There follows a report on this incident from the Royal Netherlands Embassy, which is selfexplanatory: "On November 8, 1961, the Member of the Second Chamber of the Dutch

Parliament, Mr. Van der Goes van Waters (Labor Party) sent written questions to the Netherlands Minister of Foreign Affairs about the consequences of a regulation in Jordan for nonadmission of alien persons of Jewish origin, in view of the recently concluded Civil Aviation Agreement between the Netherlands and Jordan. "The Minister answered December 4 that this agreement contains no rules which may give grounds for exceptional treatment with regard to a certain category of people. "The Dutch Government rejects any discrimination based on religion or descent. It cannot lend cooperation in the application or implementation of foreign regulations, aimed at such discrimination." 

There can be little doubt that in Arab States which receive U.S. aid there is a growing realization that the boycott against U.S. individuals and firms is in-

jurious to their domestic economies, economies which we are endeavoring to strengthen. This question was raised as recently as last month by Pierre 

Gemayel, a member of the Lebanese Cabinet. 

We feel that, in practical terms, we cannot expect that the Congress will enact further language into the Act for International Development, or other legislation, giving yet further expression of its concern for the discrimination against American citizens and firms by foreign governments. Indeed, such further enactments have little meaning unless there can be some assurance that they will be given force by the administering agencies. We do believe, however, that it would be most helpful if this committee both in its report on the legislation before it and in followup action would give a strong expression of its continuing concern with respect to the Arab boycott as it affects U.S. citizens and firms, based not only on moral grounds and long American tradition but also based on the fact that the boycott hampers the aid program and the economic development which the Act for International Development is designed to further and, in addition, the fact that lack of U.S. resistance to the boycott is damaging to our image abroad and encouraging of further incursions against American democratic traditions and sovereignty as well as U.S. businesses and citizens. 

Also, there is no reason why the economic aid program cannot be utilized to ease the effects of the boycott. Departmental fears that such an effort would injure our aid program are, we are convinced, unfounded. For example, should 

Jordan follow the example of some of the more prosperous of its sister Arab States and lift its restrictions against the admittance of Americans of the Jewish faith it would increase its tourist earnings. Such an increase in tourist earnings would lessen its dependence upon U.S. Government aid and thus in turn lighten the burden on the American taxpayer. 

We hope that the committee will call upon departmental officials periodically to report on what progress they are making in easing the boycott. Such reports need not be public. But we feel they are necessary if the committee is to be informed that its will, as expressed both in this Congress and in previous Congresses, is being enforced. 

The moral issues involved are clear. The economic arguments also favor our view. Resolution of the boycott question has too long been delayed. It is our firm hope that during the term of this 87th Congress we will see it finally resolved.

STATEMENT OF MRS. FRED L. BULL, CHAIRMAN OF THE COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION OF THE NATIONAL CONGRESS OF PARENTS AND TEACHERS IN SUPPORT OF UNICEF 

(Presented by Mrs. Warren E. Cox, member of the Washington Committee on Legislation)

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am Roberta C. Cox, a member of the Washington Committee on Legislation of the National Congress of Parents and Teachers. I am submitting this statement for Mrs. Fred L. Bull, national chairman of legislation, to urge you to authorize the request from the Department of State for an appropriation of $12 million for the contribution of the U.S. Government to the United Nations Children's Fund. We appreciate the opportunity to speak to you regarding this important matter. 

The National Congress of Parents and Teachers is a national, nongovernmental, voluntary organization which was founded 67 years ago and has a record of constant dedication to its purpose: the promotion of the welfare of children and youth. This organization of more than 12 million memberships is made up of parents and teachers across the Nation. 

When UNICEF was brought into being in 1946, the National Congress of Parents and Teachers recognized its value and supported its program of emergency relief for the hungry children of postwar Europe. We have taken pride in the broadening perspective of UNICEF as it has grown from an emergency agency into a permanent worldwide effort to help people help themselves. The resources of the United Nations Children's Fund serves as a stimulus to local initiative around the world, fosters self-respect, and initiates awareness of available solutions for the health problems of children in the underdeveloped areas. The National Congress of Parents and Teachers is gratified to know that at present governments receiving aid from the United Nations Children's Fund are themselves putting in an average of nearly three times every dollar provided by the fund. 

While UNICEF began as an emergency program which we were proud to support and while it still gives emergency aid when necessary, the United Nations

Children's Fund approaches the overwhelming disasters that engulf childhood in When the underdeveloped and developing countries in a most practical way. 

UNICEF goes into a country, and it is on the request of the government of that country, there is, as you know, a requirement that the aided country provide matching funds for the expenses involved. This leads to the establishment of permanent, locally supported programs in these countries whether the particular undertaking be the setting up of a milk-processing plant or a clinic for basic maternal and child welfare, or whether it be an all-out attack on plague diseases like malaria, yaws, trachoma, and tuberculosis, or whether it be an attack on far-reaching problems of widespread malnutrition. We are all familiar with the way UNICEF stretches dollars to get phenomenal results through wholehearted cooperation with other United Nations agencies such as the World Health Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization, and the United Nations 

Bureau of Social Affairs. 

We in the National Congress of Parents and Teachers recognize the fact that, whether we like it or not, everything that affects children in India, or Greece, or Chile, or Egypt, or any other country, affects our own children. It is today an obvious truism that the welfare of children in what we think of as the remote parts of the earth has a profound effect on the future of our own children. 

Perhaps one reason the National Congress of Parents and Teachers has a very special feeling toward UNICEF has grown out of the fact that the Children's Fund has its world headquarters in our own country. Moreover, its Executive 

Director from the time of its inception has been, and still is, our own Maurice Pate, an American businessman who retired as a successful investment banker to devote himself wholly to the welfare of the world's children. We in the National 

Congress of Parents and Teachers agree with Mr. Pate that "* * * helping children is not a form of charity but an investment in the future." 

Despite the fact that UNICEF has already aided almost 57 million mothers and children in 107 countries and territories, there are still about 500 million children living in underdeveloped areas where disease runs rampant and death and crippling is a daily companion, where malnutrition is a specter, and where superstition and poverty and hunger compound the problems that make of childhood a nightmare.

We in the National Congress of Parents and Teachers care about this half a billion children, and we feel sure that you do too. Through the United Nations 

Children's Fund we have a share in meeting the real enemies of mankind and bit by bit destroying them before they destroy the hope of the world—our children. 

As you know, the United Nations Children's Fund is not financed by assessments on the member nations of the United Nations, but through voluntary contributions. In 1961 the United States was 1 of 100 governments to make a contribution.

Support of the United Nations Children's Fund is a priority item on the legislative program of the National Congress of Parents and Teachers. We urge that you recommend to the Committee on Appropriations that last year's contribution of $12 million be duplicated this year, and that this amount be appropriated in the current budget for foreign aid as the United States' contribution to the 

United Nations Children's Fund. 

STATEMENT OF THE WOMEN'S INTERNATIONAL LEAGUE FOR PEACE AND FREEDOM (By Dorothy Medders Robinson) 

I represent the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom, an organization which has functioned effectively for 47 years. It is composed of women of various races, nations, and philosophical backgrounds interested in working for peaceful change by nonviolent means. 

For a number of years economic aid has been one of the chief interests of the organization. Only as the basic needs of human beings are met everywhere can there be stability in our world. Without stability there is no peace. Ours is the richest nation in the world today and it is in our own self-interest to offer assistance to the newly developing nations. Members of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom do not, however, regard this as the primary reason for the passage of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. We would have this act passed primarily because we believe it is the right thing to do. 

It is both the obligation and privilege of our country to assist the developing nations to arrive at the place where they can raise enough food to eat. Food is a basic necessity for each individual. Without it he is concerned with nothing 81496-62-pt. 6-8

else, for hunger consumes him. Freedom is meaningless to a man with an empty stomach. Only as his hunger is satisfied and he begins to look forward with some assurance to his next meal can he think beyond his physical needs. 

It was my privilege to visit several cities in Germany for a few successive years following the war and I saw the effect that hunger had on the action and outlook of individuals and communities. Reaction to starvation and insufficient food is the same among people anywhere. When men are hungry they should be fed. 

Few problems in our domestic life today create more difficulty than our overflowing storehouses. In a world where most people never have enough to eat our granaries have become an increasing burden upon our economy as well as upon our conscience. Our organization believes that hungry human beings should be fed regardless of the politics of their government. When we read of starvation and famine in China or anywhere in the world we believe it is incumbent upon our Government to find ways and means to share our abundance. It is contrary to all humanitarian and religious teachings and beliefs to maintain enormous food surpluses when untold numbers are threatened by starvation.

As our Nation has attempted to provide economic assistance to the developing areas it has learned by doing. We regret that 5½ times more money has been put into military rather than economic aid but the proposed economic assistance act of 1962 shows what great progress has been made. The single administrative agency, the development fund; the area development plan; the many and varied facets of national life now being assisted indicates the many adjustments which have been made in the program and the sincere desire on the part of those responsible to make the aid as helpful as possible. The more the recipient nations themselves engage in the initial project planning the more successful the project. My organization appreciates the way in which programs from the start are now being entered into cooperatively by the host and assisting countries. It would be helpful to work out a set of criteria in the same way to govern each development expansion program. Only as more and more ways are devised to develop standards that are economically sound and suited to local conditions in each country, will the assisted nations come to the place where they can carry on themselves. As the next step in the long trek of world development the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom sincerely hopes that Congress will enact the Foreign Assistance Act for 1962. 

STATEMENT ON U.S. AID TO SPAIN SUBMITTED BY THE COMMITTEE FOR A DEMOCRATIC SPAIN, NEW YORK, N.Y. 

The Committee for a Democratic Spain wishes to present to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs our reasons for opposing continuation of financial aid through grants or loans to the Spanish Government. Events have proved that such aid in the past 9 years has indeed strengthened the financial position of the Franco regime, without however winning either its respect or gratitude, but has not in any way helped the Spanish people. Meanwhile the image of the United States as champion of democracy and improved living standards has been seriously tarnished, particularly in Latin America. 

A few recent figures will illustrate these general statements. A recent State 

Department publication, "Spain in the World," by Sax Bradford, director, Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, reports U.S. assistance since 1953 at more than $1 billion (other sources put the total at more than $1,700 million) and describes its energizing effect on Spain's industry. It also states, however, that the average annual income "is probably less than $350 * ** pitifully low in the light of modern living standards." Quotations can be cited from Spanish reports to amplify and correct this picture. For example, the Central Bank of 

Spain, in its yearend statement in January 1962, gave the following figures: "Per capita income is between $270 and $280 yearly, which places Spain at the head of the underdeveloped countries. This figure does not conceal the fact that in 6 provinces the income per person is above $300 yearly; but in more than 20 provinces it is between $100 and $150. In other words, there are Spaniards who must live a year on less than an American worker earns in a single week."

The statement concludes: "This inequality demands that Spanish economic development be undertaken not only with a view to profits and income-producing possibilities."

Not only is the average Spanish yearly income at a near-starvation level, but unemployment is increasing. As a consequence of both factors many thousands of Spanish workers are emigrating permanently. Recent figures show that some 90,000 Spanish workers have emigrated to West Germany, and many more thousands to Switzerland, France, Belgium, and Australia. Recently an agreement was reached between a committee of German business and financial men and representatives of the Spanish Falangist unions for the importation of additional workers into the Reich. Similar accords have been signed with 

France. Spain's Labor Minister has lately announced that for the next 20 years some 85,000 Spanish workers would have to leave Spain annually. 

Many more facts could be marshaled to show that the effect of American aid has been to enrich the Franco government and the industrial groups and individuals favored by the regime, while the condition of the workers and peasants of Spain has stood still, at close to the lowest level in Europe, or has actually deteriorated. As a result strikes and workers' demonstrations have multiplied and, since both are illegal, have been put down by the Franco government with increasing severity.

The Committee for a Democratic Spain asks most earnestly that financial assistance to the Franco regime be terminated since it accomplishes none of the social and economic objectives for which our foreign aid program was established. To subsidize dictators and their favored supporters is not a purpose for which the money of the American people can legitimately be spent. 

STATEMENT OF THE AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION 

The American Farm Bureau Federation is a free, independent, nongovernmental, voluntary organization of over 1,600,000 farm and ranch families in 49 States and Puerto Rico. Through an extensive policy development program at county, State and National levels, farmers and their elected representatives have discussed foreign policy and foreign assistance programs. Farm Bureau's 

1962 policies state: "We believe that trade is a better foundation for our foreign policy than aid." 

Our world leadership in the pursuit of lasting peace requires that the United States adhere to a sound foreign trade policy. This means a policy based on expanding free world trade. We have a strong conviction that trade is a key to the maintenance of peace and freedom in the non-Communist world. In this struggle, two principal elements emerge-free world strength and free world unity. Of course, we must be militarily strong if we are to contain the armed might of the Soviet Union. But of equal importance is free world economic strength. The ability and opportunity of nations to trade to buy, to sell, to earn-brings a vitality and vigor to a nation's economy that can be obtained in no other manner. This opportunity for trade also can be a tremendous attraction to uncommitted nations-offering them economic advantages that can far exceed anything the Communist empire can hold out through its political machinations of commerce.

At the same time, such trade can contribute substantially to free world unity. 

Indeed, throughout history it is clear that trade relations have been and are requisite to political alliances. In simple terms, customers and suppliers are usually friends. Expanding sources of supply should be the keystone in the free world's struggle for peace with freedom. 

Farm Bureau supports the major objectives of H.R. 9900, the Trade Expansion 

Act of 1962, and we have recommended certain amendments to strengthen the trade program and to make it more effective. 

BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

The balance-of-payments deficit has become a chronic and persistent problem which must be solved. Solution requires: (1) expanded U.S. exports; and (2) reduced foreign aid expenditures. 

Farm Bureau has recommended in the past-and indeed, there appears to be general agreement-that other nations, especially Western European nations, assume a greater share of the responsibility of the defense and development of the free world. Consortia have been formed, other nations are providing a greater amount of capital for underdeveloped countries, international institutions have been expanded and created-for example, the World Bank, International 

Monetary Fund, International Development Association, International Finance

Corporation, the Inter-American Development Bank-in the belief that this would stimulate multilateral efforts toward aid. 

Over $10 billion has been authorized by the United States toward the financing of such institutions. Despite this fact, our bilateral programs are not reduced, and the administration requests an increased level of expenditure for next year's program. Maintaining and expanding the rate of foreign aid expenditures will make the balance of payments deficit impossible of solution and inestimably more difficult even to control. 

We believe that the funds made available under the foreign assistance program should be based on good solid plans developed to meet the best interest of the United States. We have the feeling that the reverse is true now. For example, you make the money available for the various programs and then the executive branch of our Government makes plans to spend. In other words, "fit the money to the plans rather than fit the plans to the money." This is the only way we can continue to justify the vast expenditures for this program. 

FOREIGN AID FUNDS 

We believe the administration's request for foreign aid can and should be reduced. The total appropriation request for the foreign economic and military assistance program for fiscal year 1963 is $4.9 billion. The committee need authorize only $2.1 billion since $2,750 million of next year's program has already been authorized in last year's foreign assistance act. We believe it is unfortunate that the committee has relinquished control over a substantial part of the program. This is especially true in regard to the Development 

Loan Fund. We have recommended in the past against such advance authorizations. We regret the present situation and sincerely believe that the foreign aid program will suffer from the loss of this congressional control. 

We will confine our comments, of course, to those categories of the program still subject to this committee's recommendation as to authorization. 

Supporting assistance

Appropriated, fiscal year 1962. 

Requested, fiscal year 1963__ Million $425 481 This category contains the direct-grant economic aid provisions formerly included in the defense support section of the Mutual Security Act. It has been this category of the program which we have criticized most vigorously in the past and which has proved to be the least effective and the most wasteful. 

We believe that a conscientious effort is being made to limit the amount of funds requested for this program. However, progress has been slow. For example, in fiscal year 1961, $725 million was requested; $675 million was provided by Congress. In fiscal year 1962, $581 million was requested; $425 million was provided by Congress. This year's request is for $481 million, $100 million less than requested last year and $56 million more than was provided by Congress.

We recognize that it is important that countries on the perimeter of Communist nations remain militarily and economically strong. But assistance to these countries should be based on the Development Loan Fund and other existing avenues of aid.

We recommend that Congress reduce the authorization to $350 million, and that it be made clear in the committee report that this program is to be completely phased out in the next 2 years.

Development grants 

Appropriated, fiscal year 1962. 

Requested, fiscal year 1963_ Million $296.5 335.0

We should concentrate our efforts and limit our activities to those countries which demonstrate a desire for such assistance and which are willing to provide the economic climate and local cooperation requisite for the success of the program. 

We believe that this item should be reduced to the 1962 level.

We continue to have grave reservations relative to the benefits to be obtained from so-called multilateral programs for which the United States provides over 60 percent of the funds. Farm Bureau's 1962 policies state: "The United Nations is an intergovernmental organization designed to cope with international problems on a basis of open discussion and negotiation. "It is unfortunate that the effectiveness of this organization has been seriously impaired by the disruptive efforts of the U.S.S.R. and by the belief of a number of free world nations that neutrality is possible in the fight for freedom and self-determination. It has become obvious that effective implementation of 

U.S. foreign policy can be better obtained through organizations of nations committed to the fight for freedom, such as NATO and the Organization for Eco nomic Cooperation and Development. 

"U.S. financial support of the United Nations and its programs should be based on the demonstrated willingness of other member nations to contribute an equitable share of the cost." 

One of the real difficulties here is the fact that Congress has not been able to hear testimony from those charged with the responsibility of administering such programs. We believe that the committee should consider hearings in regard to the international programs such as the U.N. expanded technical assistance program and the special fund so that a better basis for evaluation of the effectiveness of the programs could be developed. Since the United States is taking over much of the responsibility for financing the United Nations, we believe this request could be further reduced from the $148.9 million requested. 

Contingency fund

Million Appropriated, fiscal year 1962Requested, fiscal year 1963– $275 400 Since only a little more than 40 percent of the program is subject to authorization control by Congress this year, it seems especially unfortunate that the decision was made to submit 20 percent of this in the form of an “unprogramed” contingency fund. With the tremendous amount of flexibility in the program, we can see no justification for such a large fund, and we recommend that it be reduced to $250 million. 

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

Farm Bureau policies state: "In our total effort we should give emphasis to the friendly nations of Latin America." 

We are in basic agreement with the objectives of the Alliance for Progress. 

The criteria established in the bill are, for the most part, reasonable, realistic, and sound. They should be adhered to. 

However, subsection 251 (d) would seem to give basis for serious misinterpretation of the purposes of the program. "Agrarian reform" and "redistribution of land" do not necessarily require massive expropriation of private property nor the disregard of private property rights. Indeed, the scarcity of land for the Latin American peasant is often caused by the inordinate amount of land held by the national governments. Effective "land reform" programs should be started by governments redistributing their own land. We have seen the example of "going operations" being taken over by a government in the name of land reform and for the purported purpose of redistribution to the campesino only to see such land remain indefinitely in the hands of the government. This has happened in Cuba. In many Latin American countries, effective land reform means simply a good "homestead act"; that is, permitting public land to be acquired by those willing to "work it." 

We regret that the effort is being made again to remove authorization control from a foreign aid program. We believe that the Alliance for Progress should be authorized and appropriated funds on an annual basis. We also oppose the establishment of a revolving fund in the manner prescribed in section 253. We believe strongly that the Alliance for Progress, like the Development Loan Fund, like the whole foreign aid concept, is dependent on public understanding and approval and on congressional review and control. 

We urge the committee to amend the bill to accomplish these recommendations.

STATEMENT OF ALFRED GLEN MAYS, ALEXANDRIA, VA. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, thank you for giving a country boy from Oklahoma the opportunity to give you my thoughts as a citizen on this subject of foreign aid. I am but one of the largest, most unorganized, and to a large degree, most uninformed groups in the United States-the U.S. taxpayers. It is an honor, indeed, to be here. 

Since this is the Foreign Affairs Committee, I will say to you what our be loved Will Rogers said, "There's the one thing no nation can ever accuse us of and that is secret diplomacy. Our foreign dealings are an open book, generally a checkbook."

In the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962, it has been recommended that some $5 billion of the taxpayers' money be appropriated for the fiscal year for the purpose of foreign aid in one way or another. We have given for this purpose, in various forms, already, some $87 billion of the taxpayers' money. 

This enormous sum of money has been given, for the most part, with absolutely no strings attached. I appeal to you to hold up aid to all countries until adequate assurances have been given or have been obtained that fair treatment will be given to all American capital seeking to bring our way of private enterprise and development to underdeveloped countries. Along this line, I say there is enough private capital and know-how in the United States to develop, in due time, every country if given this assurance and guarantee of safety for such investment. To this end, the Honorable Senator Russell Long has introduced an amendment to this bill. 

It is my firm belief that we have been subject to blackmail on an international level by many countries by the idea that if we don't come through, they'll go to Russia for help. If this blackmail were put to any citizen on an individual basis, you could not blame him for telling such blackmailer to go to Russia-or even to some other place and suffer the consequences that would come from receiving Soviet aid. However, with the taxpayer's own money, this blackmail has been paid and is continuing until it has reached the staggering total of $87 billion. As Lincoln said, in 1867, "If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher. As a nation of freemen we must live through all times or die by suicide."

It is noted in article III, section 3, of the Constitution of the United States that "Treason against the United States shall consist only in levying war against them, or in adhering to their enemy, giving them aid and comfort." 

From all the accumulated knowledge that I have been able to gather from whatever source, we have been doing just this, by giving airplanes to Tito of Yugoslavia, training pilots to fly them, and even furnishing the material which could possibly be used against us. The Honorable Senator John G. Tower, of Texas, clearly covered this in one of his speeches on October 16, 1961. which I feel all of you gentlemen have had a chance to read and study. There is plenty of documentary proof of this in a book by Slobodan M. Draskovich called "Tito- 

Moscow's Trojan Horse."

On giving aid to Poland, you have been warned by no less an authority than the former Ambassador, Arthur Bliss Lane, that all the aid given has been but for the one purpose of strengthening and rebuilding a government whose avowed purpose follows the Marxist line and whose sole purpose is identical with that of Tito and Khrushchev.

Now, all of this aid is provided by the American taxpayer. It is granted to 

Congress in article I. section 8. of the Constitution of the United States with respect to taxation, "To pay the debts and provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States." It appears to me, as a taxpayer, that unless we can show that we owe this foreign aid (1) as a debt. or (2) to provide for the common defense, or (3) to promote the general welfare of the United States, any amounts not in these categories would be unconstitutional.

Inasmuch as we are involved in a battle to the death between our philosophy and our way of living and that of a total materialistic godless regime, it seems to me that it is pure and simple logic that they go or we go. Somewhere along the line we have been conned and propagandized into this belief that the remedy for the Soviet threat is aid to underdeveloped countries. Let us not forget that this infection has also attacked economically highly developed countries like Czechoslovakia and France, for it is based on passions and myths just as much as on needs. 

Like Will Rogers, all I know is what I read in the newspapers. I read that we are building elaborate, expensive, complete electric powerplants in several countries with the idea of furnishing electricity for, among other things, electric lights. This is swell, except it appears that the electric lights are being used by the natives to read Soviet propaganda. Not only that, our teachers among the Peace Corps are teaching children and adults to read their A B C's, and what do they end up reading the glories of communism. 

America thinks that it has only to build schools, hospitals, railways in underdeveloped countries, hand out Spam and fruit juice, for their people to stand up automatically against Soviet imperialism. Meanwhile the U.S.S.R. works exclusively on minds. In its approach, a rise in the standard of living of peoples will be the result of their faith in communism and their hatred of the West. And the U.S.S.R. embodies this idea in an inexhaustible stream of books, pamphlets, leaflets, written in every language and adapted to every level of intelligence. The United States supplies foodstuffs, the Soviets supply billions for propaganda. 

Therefore, if this is going to be a battle for men's minds, I say, let's concentrate with all the resources, intelligence and with every possible medium at our vast command in this battle of psychopolitics. In S. 1689 in 1959 it was proposed "To create the Freedom Commission for the Development of the Science of Counteraction to the World Communist Conspiracy." It appears to me that if we have developed this in any form, it is divided among several agencies, and I suggest it be concentrated in one 24-hour-a-day Institute of Psychopolitics. 

In this regard I wish that you and millions of Americans would swear with me those immortal words of Thomas Jefferson on this subject: "For I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man."

I believe we have long since entered into the concept of warfare laid down by the British tank expert Gen. J. F. C. Fuller, also a pre-Hitler military psychologist in Germany named Ewald Banse, and the German general, Von Clausewitz, that whole nations can be destroyed and conquered without firing a shot. 

Modern totalitarianism has added something new. Morale disintegration is regarded as an absolute prelude to any successful fragmentation of natural unity and will.

Some of my ancestors were wild Cherokee Indians and I believe in total offense toward any hostile enemy which threatens our very existence as they did-if this is indeed a war for men's minds, fight it with an all-out effort and fight it as a battle for men's minds as Congressman Pillion has proposed in his House Joint Resolution 447.

I say to you, before paying one cent of tribute to any more Communist countries or giving away a single dollar of tax money, I believe we should look at just where this money is coming from. A very wise farmer-philosopher once said, the power of collecting and disbursing money at pleasure is the most dangerous power that can be entrusted to man, particularly under our system of collecting revenue by a tariff, which reaches every man in the country, no matter how poor he may be, and the poorer he is, the more he pays in proportion to his means. What is worse, due to hidden taxes it presses upon him without his knowledge of where it comes from, for there is not a man in the United States who can ever know how much he pays to the Government. So you see that while you are contributing to relieve, aid, or defend a clique of Communist overlords, you are drawing it from thousands who may be even worse off than they. 

Therefore, it is my sincere belief, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, that before trying to solve the economic ills of all the world, in whatever shape they may appear, whether under the guise of battling communism, or whatever, it would be very well to look to our own problems first. It appears to me that if we would really "sell" and "show" our way to all the countries of the world and that we have a system that works so well that it is "second to none" on earth, that system will be respected, admired, and eventually copied by other nations.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF HOME BUILDERS,

STATEMENT OF THE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF HOME BUILDERS ON THE PROPOSED FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1962 

This statement with a proposed amendment (attachment A) is respectfully submitted for the consideration of the committee with respect to the pending Foreign Assistance Act of 1962. (This is S. 2996 in the Senate. The bill has not yet been introduced with a designated number in the House of Representatives.) 

INTEREST OF AMERICAN HOMEBUILDERS 

During the past several years the National Association of Home Builders has taken a constantly increasing interest in measures to improve housing in the developing nations, particularly Latin America. The NAHB International Housing Committee was formalized to make a continuing study of housing needs and to make recommendations as to how homebuilders could contribute to the improvement of existing conditions. 

Since the pronouncement of the Alliance for Progress, the NAHB committee has concentrated its attention on the problems in Central and South America. 

Many members of NAHB volunteered their services to the International Cooperation Administration. Several accepted assignments on housing study tours to 

Latin American countries. The knowledge and experience gained on these missions provided the background for the intensive study which the committee has given to this tremendously important subject. 

The conclusions of the committee can be summarized as follows: (1) An effective housing program can alleviate a substantial amount of existing misery and human suffering in Latin America, although no immediate and overall solution can be anticipated because of the magnitude of the housing problem, particularly in the densely populated urban areas. (2) Measures to raise the living conditions of the lowest income families, with consideration for health and sanitation facilities, can be carried out only under government auspices. Thus, the aided self-help program, rural housing program, and loans to various governments for water distribution and sewage disposal systems are activities which appropriately fall to the public sector. (3) Measures to raise housing standards of middle and lower middle income families should be undertaken through the stimulation of private initiative and private investment. The plight of families comprising this segment of the population is often as serious as that of low income families. Although they may enjoy incomes relatively comparable to families in the United States who have become homeowners through the aid of the Federal Housing Administration, it is impossible for them to satisfy their needs because of the almost absolute dearth of long-term low-interest mortgage credit. (4) To solve the problem of those whose income is adequate to warrant homeownership without government subsidy it is essential that sources of mortgage credit be developed. Until such time as a reservoir of savings can be accumulated internally, long-term capital must be attracted from institutional investors in the United States.

The necessity of attracting mortgage credit from the American investment sources has been recognized by the Congress. The Act for International De velopment of 1961, section 224, Public Law 87-195, specifically authorizes guarantees to be extended to insure investment in self-liquidating housing projects in Latin American countries. (5) To develop a homebuilding industry in the emergency countries, it is desirable that each country enact legislation creating a mortgage insurance agency authorized to perform functions similar to, and with rules and regulations patterned after, the FHA in the United States. This would facilitate the development of a mortgage system conferring benefits similar to advantages enjoyed by U.S. citizens. (6) American homebuilders should be encouraged by the State Department, through the appropriate agencies, to participate with nationals in friendly countries in the development and expansion of a homebuilding industry wherever such participation is solicited. NAHB members who have been on missions sponsored by ICA and those who have gone on housing study tours report that nationals in all countries visited greatly desire participation by American homebuilders in joint ventures, sharing their know-how on mass production and financing techniques, as well as direct equity investment. 

To implement these conclusions the international housing committee proposed and the NAHB board of directors approved the following policy positions: (1) NAHB should support an amendment to the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954 (Public Law 480) to increase the maximum percentage of locked-in currencies available to American business interests from 

25 to 75 percent. (2) NAHB should urge the Agency for International Development to encourage foreign nations receiving economic assistance to establish mortgage insurance agencies patterned after FHA. (3) NAHB should urge the State Department to encourage American builders to participate with nationals of friendly countries to develop and expand the homebuilding industry through private enterprise. (4) NAHB should support legislation authorizing the President to issue full repayment guarantees to American institutional investment sources covering long-term mortgage credit for residential financing for middle and low-middle income families. 

AMENDMENT OF THE GUARANTEE PROGRAM (SEC. 221-224, TITLE III, ACT FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT) 

Amendment of the guarantee program to permit institutional investors to participate presents the only realistic and immediate means of channeling any substantial flow of private long-term mortgage credit into housing in Latin American countries. The alternatives are to continue the flow of public money or to settle for a token and limited volume. 

The chairman of the international housing committee, Paul L. Burkhard, appeared before the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, June 20, 1961, in support of an amendment designed to encourage the flow of private mortgage credit from institutional investors. Briefly, it was proposed that the protection available under the loan guarantee program be extended to include housing and that institutional investors be guaranteed full repayment of long-term mortgage credit for residential financing in underdeveloped countries. An amendment introduced by Senator Smathers, limited to projects in Latin America, containing the essential features of a workable guarantee program, was supported by Mr. 

Burkhard in his testimony.

The bill was amended on the Senate floor to include a limited version of this housing guarantee program. As enacted, all-risk guarantees provide protection for only 75 percent of the investment and the authorization was restricted to $10 million.

STATUS OF GUARANTEE PROGRAM 

It is reported that applications have been submitted to the AID for guarantees in excess of $50 million. No applications having been processed, and the rules and regulations under which the program is to be administered not having been promulgated, the number of applications which will qualify cannot be estimated. 

It is reasonable to assume that heavy attrition will occur. 

Since it was the intent of Congress that pilot projects be undertaken to demonstrate the soundness of the concept, homebuilders will make a formidable effort

to accomplish as much as possible under the 75-percent formula. It must be recognized, however, that homebuilders, who are among the greatest consumers of mortgage credit, cannot make permanent loans. Before undertaking any project it is customary to arrange a takeout for all mortgages which will be originated. 

Other than institutional sources, we believe there are no individual or corporate investment groups prepared to make long-term low-interest loans except in isolated and limited instances. The exceptions might include American corporations desiring to provide housing for their own employees, American corporations wishing to repatriate foreign investment where any guarantee would be better than none, foundations, or eleemosynary institutions. 

The fact remains that the only sources capable of supplying a sustained flow of credit in the volume required to effect a substantial impact on the peoples of the developing countries are institutional investors, including insurance companies, trust and pension funds. Since the investments of these institutions are prescribed by law, it is necessary that the legality of the instrument evidencing debt be established. 

PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO INVESTMENT GUARANTEES (SEC. 224) 

A proposed amendment to the housing provisions of title III of the Agency for International Development Act is attached to this statement (attachment A). 

It would simply add one additional specific provision applicable only to the investment guarantee program under section 224 for housing projects in Latin 

American countries.

The section already has a specific limitation upon the face amount of guarantees issued for houisng, $10 million which is proposed under the pending legislation to be raised to $60 million. Our proposed amendment would add to the end of section 224 (b) the following additional sentence: "Guarantees issued under this section shall cover the full amount of investment funds which are to be used for mortgage credit or residential financing."

This amendment does not necessarily increase the exposure under the program since section 221 which provides the general authority for investment guarantees specifically states that they may be issued only "upon such terms and conditions as the President may determine."

Therefore the equity in housing projects which will be invested by home buyers and homeowners may be set at 25 percent (thus limiting the guaranteed funds to 75 percent of value). Or, as determined by the officials vested with responsibility for approving investment guarantees, the required equity may be scaled downward, depending upon the specific transaction involved and the level of income of the prospective home-buying families. 

We believe that it is possible to develop a new application of the loan guarantee program to the field of mortgage credit under a full guarantee of funds, as proposed in the amendment described above. This would contemplate development of a procedure for the creation of a trust agreement under which a financial institution within a foreign country would originate, hold, and service mortgages for an American institutional investor, and issue trust certificates supported by underlying first mortgages subject to issuance of full repayment guarantees. Assurances have been given that a substantial volume of credit will be available on the adoption of this procedure. 

GUARANTEE PROGRAM--A SOUND RISK 

In weighing the risk or exposure, assumed under the proposed guarantee, attention should be directed to the tremendous success of the loan guarantee program since the inauguration of the Marshall plan. Information from the 

Agency administering guarantees states that only one claim has been filed and that the loss sustained was for a sum less than $10,000. There is currently outstanding $750 million in guarantees. 

The loan guarantee division exacts a premium for the guarantees affording protection covering the so-called political risks, convertibility, confiscation and expropriation, and war.

The total premium for the three-way risks is 12 percent annually of the amount for which insurance is written. It is assumed that for an all-risk guarantee the premium initially should be 2 percent annually. Should the risk be

2 guaranteed by the host government, a rate set at 1 percent of the declining balance may be deemed sufficient. 

There can be little doubt that the premium will prove to be more than adequate. Properly qualified as to credit standing the Latin American mortgagor is as good a risk as an American citizen. The FHA will confirm that no office in the 50 States can boast a better record than has been experienced in Puerto Rico. 

PRIVATE INVESTMENT FUNDS SHOULD BE USED 

A tremendous advantage in utilizing private investment funds is that these funds will flow through regular banking channels. The homebuilder will make application for a project, seek a permanent investor, arrange with a commercial bank within the host country for construction funds, and proceed with construction and sale of houses. The American institutional investor will have previously obtained a commitment for guarantees. Concurrently the trust indenture between the permanent mortgagee and the local bank will have been arranged. The procedure is to all practical purposes identical with the practice prevailing with respect to FHA-insured and VA-guaranteed mortgages. 

The mortgagor will not be concerned with the procedure, the guarantee, or that a U.S. investor is necessarily involved. He will know that the United States has made it possible for him to become a homeowner, although all his dealings will be with a local bank. Governments receiving direct loans from the U.S. 

Government may be reluctant in honoring their obligations when loans fall due but the Latin American mortgagor can be relied upon to discharge his obligations as assuredly as if he were a citizen of the United States. 

In housing, the guarantee program can be utilized to accomplish the objectives of the foreign aid program on a nonpolitical plane. Instead of bigger government-to-government loans, private investment sources can be relied upon to assume that part of the responsibility which properly belongs in the private sector. 

AID SUPERVISION AND CONTROL 

A question has been raised as to what extent the AID would be compelled to exercise supervision in connection with a loan program such as proposed. The 

Agency, will of course, make its own policy but it should be pointed out that private investment sources will make their own determination as to whom the loans will be made, in what amounts, and under what conditions. No institutional investor will commit funds on the sole basis of guarantee. 

Institutional investors will use the most prudent judgment possible in selecting sponsors and projects. While they must rely on the guarantee to comply with legal requirements, there will be little disposition to exercise their claims except as a last resort. Governments come and go, it is true, but in most instances life goes on as before and borrowers continue to pay their obligations. Barring a takeover such as occurred in Cuba, it is most unlikely that private residential property would be jeopardized. It should be noted that during the 3 years under the communistic regime in Guatemala the people continued life as usual. 

Private investment is preferable to a direct government approach since it is unnecessary to delay action on the investment or production flowing from the investment while the governments involved debate overall policy matters such as land reform, tax changes and other possible internal and desirable reforms. 

With a need that is urgent, and with time running out, measures to improve housing conditions cannot await the outcome of political debates or negotiations, important as these may be to achievement of long-range goals. Investment guarantees are an immediate answer when shaped so that they will stimulate and make possible the flow of private funds through private, as opposed to public, negotiations for the benefit of the private welfare of families in Latin America, with demonstrable results to be achieved in the near future. 

We should also make clear that we support the general concept of demonstration housing programs as envisioned in the Agency for International Development Act. It is important that as many of these demonstrations as possible be undertaken so that the Congress may better be be able to pass judgment on the program in all of its aspects. We feel that the amendments now pending to this program together with the proposed amendment submitted herewith will effectively further the objectives of the act with respect to housing.

SEED CAPITAL LOANS TO CREATE A SAVINGS CYCLE 

Legislation has been proposed and will continue to be implemented by administrative action to permit and stimulate the flow of seed capital loans from savings and loan associations or other comparable lending institutions in the United States to savings and loan associations or other comparable institutions in Latin American countries-either for the creation of such institutions or for their expansion. The proposal has as its long-range objective the creation of the savings cycle in which people are encouraged to save their funds in thrift institutions so that some of them may at a later date obtain mortgage loans for the purchase of land or the construction of homes or both. 

This savings-mortgage financing cycle has proved the foundation upon which the greater part of mortgage financing is accomplished in the United States. If ultimately successful in Latin America, it will undoubtedly prove of equal value in these countries. 

The NAHB International Housing Committee has in the past recommended that this association support permissive legislation whereby domestic savings and loan associations could make these foreign seed capital loans to thrift institutions in underdeveloped countries. For a number of reasons, however, the executive committee of this association hesitated to give its approval for this resolution and action by our board of directors on this matter has been deferred. 

Among the reasons prompting deferral of any action to approve legislation which would permit seed capital loans are the following: (1) Savings and loan associations are local institutions and it is agreed they should confine their lending activities to their own areas. (2) There is a growing and constant need for mortgage money within the United States, and should one area have an oversupply, excess funds in one area should, where legally permissible, be invested in areas having greater demands. (3) Members of our local associations and citizens of local communities object to the proposal that local savings be exported for use in foreign lands. (4) There are other types of institutional investors which customarily place only a portion of their funds in mortgages and which are not closely identified with local communities, so that it would be more appropriate for these sources to be relied upon first rather than the savings and loans. 

Our fear is that dependence on savings institutions might prove to be a bitter disappointment. However, as a long-range objective, measures to establish savings and loan association systems in the developing countries deserve support whether or not U.S. associations are permitted to participate. 

Unfortunately many of the countries in which it is proposed to establish associations have experienced constant and devastating inflation. The deterioration of the monetary unit has been so severe that there is a lack of confidence in thrift principles. Until stable governments restore fiscal responsibility and the experience of recent years is forgotten, the climate for savings will remain unfavorable.

The Development Loan Fund and the Inter-American Development Bank have committed loans in excess of $70 million for the establishment and promotion of savings and loan systems. It appears most likely that the institutions established under the policy now being pursued must have recourse to a constant flow of U.S. dollars to insure their growth. 

CONCLUSION 

Our Government can accomplish its objectives in its efforts to raise the housing and living standards of people in underdeveloped countries. 

There are two routes to this accomplishment. One is the continuation of the present policy of loans to governments, which is costly, which is unending, which, if ever repaid, will be done so reluctantly. 

The other is authorizing full repayment guarantees to private institutional investors channeling private investment funds through private banking institu tions in both countries. Encouraging private American homebuilders to participate with nationals of the host countries, and making it possible for private citizens to become homeowners without waiting for governmental preferment are most likely to occur first through this use of investment guarantees. 

We appreciate this opportunity to submit our views to the committee for consideration prior to action on the pending legislation. We urge the committee to give careful consideration to the proposed amendment to section 224 of the Agency for International Development Act and we respectfully urge its adoption.

ATTACHMENT A PROPOSED AMENDMENT (TO S. 2996 AS INTRODUCED MARCH 14, 1962) 

On page 3, following line 17, insert the following subsection: "(2) After the second sentence in subsection (b) add the following sentence: 'Guarantees issued under this section shall cover the full amount of investment funds used for mortgage credit or residential financing'." 

On page 3, at line 18, strike “(2)” and substitute “(3)".

EXPLANATION OF AMENDMENT 

This amendment will permit investment guarantees issued for housing projects in Latin American countries under the authority of section 224 to cover the full amount of investment funds which are used directly or indirectly for the financing of mortgage credit or residential construction to produce these housing projects. This, like the special limited amount of guarantees prescribed by section 224, sets a specific requirement which is different from the general limitations set forth under section 221 for investment guarantees. 

Under section 221 investment guarantees are limited to 75 percent of any investment. The amendment would increase this to 100 percent, but only for housing projects and funds to be used for mortgage finance for these projects. 

The general authority under section 221 gives the President and his designees authority to issue investment guarantees "upon such terms and conditions as the President may determine," which provides fully adequate protection for the Government.
